title: Endoplasmic Reticulum Stress Mediates Axon Initial Segment Shortening: Implications for Diabetic Brain Complications

text: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) plays many roles that are vital to cellular homeostasis including maintenance of intracellular calcium levels and the modification, folding, and targeting of proteins (Walter and Ron; Ghemrawi and Khair). The term “ER stress” refers to a state of mismatch between the ER protein load and its capacity to fold and excrete proteins. The accumulation of unfolded proteins induces ER stress and subsequent activation of the adaptive unfolded protein response (UPR) for restoration of ER’s function. The UPR is activated by three sensor proteins: protein kinase RNA-like ER kinase (PERK), inositol-requiring transmembrane kinase/endoribonuclease 1α, and activating transcription factor 6 (Ghemrawi and Khair). The ER stress and UPR have been shown to be involved in the pathogenesis of many neurodegenerative conditions. For example, ER stress and PERK activation occur in the brain of db/db mice with cognitive impairment (Li et al. Ye et al. Hu et al. Wu et al. Importantly, increased levels of methylglyoxal increase several key markers of UPR activation including PERK pathway (Palsamy et al. Barragán-Iglesias et al. Irshad et al. Xue et al. A structure termed the cisternal organelle formed by ER may play important roles for AIS plasticity during development (Schlüter et al.). Therefore, we reasoned that ER stress may mediate AIS shortening in diabetic conditions. To test this idea, we pharmacologically modulated ER stress in mouse cortical neuron culture and evaluated AIS geometry.
title: Endoplasmic Reticulum Stress Mediates Axon Initial Segment Shortening: Implications for Diabetic Brain Complications

text: Mouse cortical culture was prepared as described before Griggs et al. C57BL/6J mice (The Jackson Laboratory) were housed at Wright State University and used to collect neonate brains. Mice were housed at 22–24 °C temperature, 20–60% humidity, and 12-hour light/12-hour dark cycle, with food and water ad libitum. Postnatal day (P) 0 mouse pups (male and female) were euthanized by decapitation, cortices were removed, and cells were dissociated. All animal procedures were performed in compliance with the National Institutes of Health Office of Laboratory Animal Welfare Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals and the ARRIVE guidelines. The experimental protocol was approved by the Wright State University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (#1190). In some experiments, embryonic day (E)18 mouse dissociated cortices (SKU C57EDCX) were purchased from Transnetyx Tissue. Cells were plated in 35 mm dishes coated with poly-L-lysine for protein analyses or on coverslips coated with poly-L-lysine for immunofluorescence, and were maintained in standard growth media (Neurobasal Plus, 2 mM (final) GlutaMAX, 2% (final) B-27 Plus) in a humidified atmosphere at 37 °C with 5% CO 2.
title: Endoplasmic Reticulum Stress Mediates Axon Initial Segment Shortening: Implications for Diabetic Brain Complications

text: Because the ER may affect AIS length maturation (Schlüter et al.), experiments were started after 10 days in vitro (DIV) to evaluate the effects of drug treatment on fully formed AISs. Methylglyoxal (M0252; Sigma-Aldrich), sodium 4-phenylbutyrate (4PBA) (SML0309; Sigma-Aldrich), tunicamycin (T7765; Sigma-Aldrich), or GSK2606414 (HY-18072; MedChemExpress) were diluted in standard growth media (2x final concentration), sterilized by the syringe-filter, and pre-warmed to 37 °C. Then, 1 mL of experimental media and 1 mL of conditioned media were added to 35 mm dishes for a 1x final concentration.

text: Cell lysates for immunoblotting were prepared as we have done before Griggs et al. In brief, after rinsing culture dishes in ice-cold PBS, cells were collected in ice-cold lysis buffer, vortexed, incubated on ice for 10 min, centrifuged, then supernatant was collected. A BCA assay (23235, Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used to measure protein concentrations. Samples were heated at 95 °C for 5 min, 10 µg of each lysate were run on 4–12% gels, then transferred to nitrocellulose membrane. The membrane used for MG-H1 immunoblotting Griggs et al. was stripped with Restore™ Western Blot Stripping Buffer (21059, Thermo Fisher Scientific), then washed. After blocking for 1 h in 20 mM Tris, pH 8.0 and 0.05% (v/v) Tween 20 (TBST) containing 4% (w/v) milk, the membrane was incubated overnight at 4 °C in antibody to glucose regulated protein 78 (GRP78) (ADI-SPA-826, Enzo Life Sciences, RRID: AB_10617248), then washed 3 times in TBST. Horseradish peroxidase conjugated secondary antibody (Jackson ImmunoResearch Laboratories) was incubated at room temperature for 1 h, then the membrane was washed 3 times in TBST. Signals produced by a Pierce™ ECL Plus Western Blotting Substrate (32132, Thermo Fisher Scientific) were imaged using Azure 600 imaging system (Azure Biosystems). ImageLab software (Bio-Rad) was used for quantification of the band densities. The GRP78 band densities were normalized to the total protein staining by SYPRO Ruby (S4942, Sigma-Aldrich).
title: Endoplasmic Reticulum Stress Mediates Axon Initial Segment Shortening: Implications for Diabetic Brain Complications

text: Cortical cultures were immunostained as we have done before Griggs et al. In brief, after washing in warm PBS, cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde at room temperature for 20 min and washed 3 times in PBS. After blocking in PBSTGS (10% goat serum, 0.3% Triton X-100, PBS) at room temperature for 1 h, coverslips were incubated in primary antibody at 4 °C overnight and washed 3 times in PBSTGS. To label the AIS, AnkyrinG (N106/36, 75–146, Antibodies Incorporated, RRID: AB_10673030) or βIV spectrin (M.N. Rasband, Baylor College of Medicine, Texas, USA, RRID: AB_2315634) antibodies were used. To label neuronal soma and dendrites, antibody to microtubule associated protein 2 (MAP2) (CPCA-MAP2, EnCor Biotechnology, RRID: AB_2138173) was used. Then the coverslips were incubated with fluorescent secondary antibodies (Alexa Fluor 594, Alexa Fluor 488, or AMCA) (Jackson ImmunoResearch Laboratories) at room temperature for 1 h, washed in PBSTGS, 0.01 M PB, and 0.005 M PB. Hoechst 33258 (Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used to identify nuclei in some samples.
title: Endoplasmic Reticulum Stress Mediates Axon Initial Segment Shortening: Implications for Diabetic Brain Complications

text: To quantify AIS length, images were taken of neuron cultures with an Axio Observer Z1 microscope (Carl Zeiss), and ZEN Blue 3.0 was used to export images for use in ImageJ. A custom script was used to isolate each AIS and remove background immunofluorescence for easier processing in MATLAB. We amended MATLAB files written by Matthew Grubb (MATLAB Central File Exchange; https://www.mathworks.com/matlabcentral/fileexchange/28181-ais-quantification) to automate plotting of each AIS and measurement of the length that falls within 33% of the maximum intensity of the plotted segment. To quantify AIS start location, the soma boundary was determined by overlaying the MAP2 staining with a smooth curve along the edge of the neuron as previously done (Guo et al. Griggs et al. The distance between the soma boundary and the start position of the AIS was measured using ZEN Blue 3.0. AIS measurements for all experiments were completed under observer blinded conditions.

text: Phosphorylated PERK (P-PERK)/PERK ratio was measured in the same cultures where the AIS lengths were measured. After the imaging of AIS structures, the primary and secondary antibodies were stripped from the coverslips using a stripping buffer Micheva et al. composed of 0.02% sodium dodecyl sulfate and 0.2 M NaOH solution prepared with Milli-Q water. After soaking the slides in PBS overnight at 4 °C, previously mounted coverslips were gently removed and were washed 3 times for 15 min to remove all remaining mounting medium. Coverslips were then soaked in stripping buffer at room temperature for 30 min and were washed 3 times for 15 min in PBS. After verifying complete removal of immunostaining, coverslips were immunostained as described above. Antibodies targeting phosphorylated PERK (P-PERK) (Thr982) (PA5-102853, Thermo Fisher Scientific, RRID: AB_2815938) and PERK (bsm-51385M, Bioss Antibodies) were used to evaluate ER stress. 40x images were taken of the immunostained coverslips with an Axio Observer Z1 microscope, utilizing the same exposure time for each image. The intensity sums of the P-PERK (Alexa Fluor 488) and PERK (Alexa Fluor 594) fluorescence channels for each field of view were calculated with ZEN software. The intensity sum of P-PERK was divided by the intensity sum of PERK for each image (3 culture preparations, 26–36 images per culture preparation). For each preparation, each P-PERK/PERK ratio was divided by the mean of all the P-PERK/PERK ratios in the dataset. This transformation can reduce variation between preparations, while preserving the magnitude of change observed between groups.
title: Endoplasmic Reticulum Stress Mediates Axon Initial Segment Shortening: Implications for Diabetic Brain Complications

text: The viability of mature cortical cultures exposed to vehicle or tunicamycin was quantified based on immunofluorescence staining using a LIVE/DEAD™ Viability/Cytotoxicity Assay Kit (L3224, Thermo Fisher Scientific) following instruction provided by the manufacturer. After gently washing culture dishes 3 times in PBS, cells were incubated with LIVE/DEAD™ kit dyes at room temperature for 20 min. Three 0.6 mm 2 areas were analyzed for each coverslip, and three coverslips were analyzed from each group per n. The percentage of number of live cells divided by the total cell number was reported as the cell viability. This number was normalized to the mean cell viability of the vehicle control groups.

text: One-way ANOVA with post-hoc Dunnett’s multiple comparison test was used to analyze methylglyoxal dose responses of GRP78 levels, Live/Dead assay after tunicamycin exposure, and tunicamycin dose responses of AIS length. Two-way ANOVA with post-hoc Tukey test was used to compare AIS length and P-PERK/PERK ratio in vehicle, methylglyoxal, 4PBA, and methylglyoxal + 4PBA, and AIS length in vehicle, tunicamycin, GSK2606414, and tunicamycin + GSK2606414. Pearson r correlation was used to evaluate the relationship between AIS length and P-PERK/PERK ratio. Unpaired t-test was used to compare AIS length or location between vehicle and tunicamycin exposed groups. Statistical significance was defined by an α value of 0.05. Prism 10.5.0 (GraphPad) was used for all statistical analyses and generation of graphs.
title: Endoplasmic Reticulum Stress Mediates Axon Initial Segment Shortening: Implications for Diabetic Brain Complications

text: ER stress occurs in the brains of the T2DM model db/db mice (Sims-Robinson et al. Li et al. Ye et al. Hu et al. Wu et al. In addition, high glucose concentration and increase of methylglyoxal can induce ER stress and subsequent UPR (Palsamy et al. Barragán-Iglesias et al. Irshad et al. For example, 1 µM methylglyoxal increased the protein level of an ER stress marker GRP78 (also known as BiP) in cultured dorsal root ganglion neurons (Barragán-Iglesias et al. To further confirm these observations, we exposed mouse cortical cultures to methylglyoxal (0, 1, 10, 100 µM) for 24 h and analyzed the expression of GRP78. Western blot of cortical culture cell lysates showed that the GRP78 expression was increased by 1 µM (p = 0.0418), 10 µM (p = 0.0030), and 100 µM (p = 0.0021) methylglyoxal compared to media control (One-way ANOVA (F (3,8) = 11.56; p = 0.0028) with post-hoc Dunnett’s multiple comparison test, n = 3 culture preparations) (Similar to the AIS shortening in db/db mice Yermakov et al., methylglyoxal (100 µM for 24 h) induces AIS shortening in primary mouse cortical cultures Griggs et al. Therefore, these data demonstrate that ER stress is associated with AIS shortening in diabetic conditions.
title: Endoplasmic Reticulum Stress Mediates Axon Initial Segment Shortening: Implications for Diabetic Brain Complications
section_title: Methylglyoxal-Induced AIS Shortening is Associated with ER Stress

text: Next, we investigated the role of ER stress in methylglyoxal-evoked AIS shortening utilizing 4PBA, a well-documented inhibitor of ER stress. 4PBA acts as a chemical protein chaperone to reduce the protein load of the ER (Yam et al. Wang et al. Kong et al. Primary mouse cortical cultures were exposed to either media vehicle, methylglyoxal (100 µM), 4PBA (100 µM), or methylglyoxal and 4PBA for 24 h, then AIS morphology was examined by immunofluorescence (Fig. A, B). There was a statistically significant interaction between the effects of MG and 4PBA on AIS length (two-way ANOVA; F (1,12) = 5.080; p = 0.0437; post-hoc Tukey’s multiple comparison test; n = 4 culture preparations). The AISs of cultures exposed to methylglyoxal (26.80 ± 0.6127 μm, n = 4 culture preparations) were significantly shorter (p = 0.0390) than vehicle-treated controls (31.60 ± 1.182 μm, n = 4 culture preparations) after 24 h (Fig. C, D), as previously published Griggs et al. The AISs in methylglyoxal-treated cultures were also shorter than 4PBA and methylglyoxal co-treated cultures (31.54 ± 1.318 μm, n = 4 culture preparations; p = 0.0417). There were no differences in AIS length between vehicle controls and 4PBA treated cultures (31.42 ± 1.116 μm, n = 4 culture preparations; p = 0.9994) or 4PBA and methylglyoxal co-treated cultures (p > 0.9999). These data indicate that the 4PBA treatment prevents AIS shortening induced by methylglyoxal. Previous studies have demonstrated that methylglyoxal induces ER stress and activates the PERK pathway in UPR (Palsamy et al. Barragán-Iglesias et al. Xue et al. To test if AIS changes are associated with ER stress induction and PERK activation, the primary and secondary antibodies were stripped after the imaging of AIS structures, and these cultures were re-probed for activated (phosphorylated) and inactivated forms of PERK. Upon activation, PERK is autophosphorylated (Rozpędek-Kamińska et al.). The ratio of phosphorylated to unphosphorylated form of PERK (P-PERK/PERK ratio) is used as a marker of ER stress and UPR activation (Li et al. Ye et al. Wu et al. There was a statistically significant interaction between the effects of MG and 4PBA on P-PERK/PERK ratio (two-way ANOVA; F (1,8) = 17.03; p = 0.0033; post-hoc Tukey’s multiple comparison test; n = 3 culture preparations). Cortical cultures treated with methylglyoxal (100 µM for 24 h) showed 131% (± 3.737, n = 3 culture preparations; p = 0.0002) the P-PERK/PERK ratio when compared to the average P-PERK/PERK ratio of vehicle controls (100%±0.1879, n = 3 culture preparations). This result is consistent with an increase of GRP78 after methylglyoxal exposure, indicating methylglyoxal induced ER stress. As expected, 4PBA prevented the increase in P-PERK/PERK ratio caused by methylglyoxal (97%±2.927, n = 3 culture preparations; p = 0.8389). 4PBA and vehicle co-treated cultures had 88% (± 2.378, n = 3 culture preparations; p = 0.0461) of the vehicle P-PERK/PERK ratio. These results indicate that 4PBA effectively inhibits ER stress and AIS shortening induced by methylglyoxal in the mouse cortical culture. Finally, we observed an inverse correlation (Pearson r = −0.8552; 95% CI = −0.9586 to −0.5526; p = 0.0004) between AIS length and P-PERK/PERK ratio. These results suggest that ER stress is a key mechanism mediating AIS shortening in diabetic conditions.
title: Endoplasmic Reticulum Stress Mediates Axon Initial Segment Shortening: Implications for Diabetic Brain Complications
section_title: ER Stress Inhibition Prevents Methylglyoxal-Induced AIS Shortening

text: Next, we sought to examine the impact of ER stress induction, independent of methylglyoxal or diabetic conditions, on AIS morphology in vitro. We used an established ER stress inducer tunicamycin which causes accumulation of the unfolded glycoproteins in the ER by inhibiting the synthesis of glycoproteins (Oslowski and Urano). Although the apoptosis mediated by ER stress has been well studied, we are focused on the mechanisms underlying AIS shortening in the neurons without cell death (Yermakov et al. Griggs et al. We used a maximum tunicamycin dose of 1 µg/mL, because 24-hour exposure to 1 µg/mL of tunicamycin does not alter dendritic spine density or expression of synaptic proteins in primary neuron cultures (Shih and Hsueh). We confirmed that 0.25–1.0 µg/mL of tunicamycin did not significantly affect cellular viability compared with vehicle control (One-way ANOVA (F (2,6) = 0.06364; p = 0.9390; post-hoc Dunnett’s multiple comparison test; n = 3 culture preparations) (Thus, tunicamycin dose up to 1 µg/mL is appropriate to study the AIS changes in live cortical neurons in our culture model.
title: Endoplasmic Reticulum Stress Mediates Axon Initial Segment Shortening: Implications for Diabetic Brain Complications
section_title: Low Dose Tunicamycin Does Not Induce Cell Death in Mouse Cortical Cultures

text: To test if ER stress induces AIS shortening independent of methylglyoxal, we exposed mouse cortical culture at DIV10 to varying doses of tunicamycin (0, 0.125, 0.25, 0.5, or 1.0 µg/mL) separately for 24 h. AIS length after tunicamycin exposure demonstrates a dose-dependent shortening of the AIS length (One-way ANOVA; F (4,13) = 15.05; p < 0.0001; post-hoc Dunnett’s multiple comparison test; n = 3–4 culture preparations). Compared to the cultures exposed to 0 µg/mL of tunicamycin (29.76 ± 1.368 μm), AIS length was significantly shortened with tunicamycin concentrations of 0.125 µg/mL (25.66 ± 0.8100 μm; p = 0.0305), 0.25 µg/mL (23.95 ± 0.7020 μm; p = 0.0015), 0.5 µg/mL (21.90 ± 0.4268 μm; p = 0.0002), or 1.0 µg/mL (20.99 ± 0.7446 μm; p < 0.0001) (Fig. A-C). The 19.5% decrease in AIS length after 0.25 µg/mL tunicamycin exposure is similar to 16% AIS shortening in prefrontal cortex in db/db mice Yermakov et al. and 15.2% AIS shortening induced by 100 µM methylglyoxal in mouse cortical cultures. Therefore, we selected the tunicamycin dose of 0.25 µg/mL for subsequent experiments. Next, we investigated the time course of tunicamycin-induced AIS shortening. After 30 min of exposure, the AIS length was comparable between tunicamycin-treated (0.25 µg/mL) cultures (23.66 ± 0.3534 μm) and vehicle-treated (DMSO; 0.025%) cultures (24.85 ± 0.3395 μm, p = 0.0721, unpaired t-test). In contrast to the time course of methylglyoxal exposure Griggs et al., there was significant shortening of the AIS after 3 h of tunicamycin treatment (23.02 ± 0.1305 μm), compared to vehicle control (26.73 ± 0.1618 μm; p < 0.0001, unpaired t-test). Finally, since low doses of tunicamycin do not cause cell death in the mouse cortical culture, we assessed if tunicamycin-induced AIS shortening is reversible. After an initial 24 h of exposure, there was a significant shortening of AIS length in the cultures exposed to tunicamycin (0.25 µg/mL) (22.98 ± 1.145 μm) when compared to vehicle (DMSO; 0.025%) (26.95 ± 0.5334 μm) (p = 0.0199, unpaired t-test). Following the 24-hour initial exposure to tunicamycin or vehicle, all drug media were removed from the cultures and replaced with fresh growth media. After 24 h in drug free media, AIS length in the culture initially exposed to tunicamycin (28.30 ± 0.5169 μm) was similar to that in the culture initially exposed to vehicle (DMSO; 0.025%) (28.04 ± 0.2564 μm) (p = 0.6756, unpaired t-test). These data are consistent with the reversible AIS shortening induced by methylglyoxal Griggs et al.
title: Endoplasmic Reticulum Stress Mediates Axon Initial Segment Shortening: Implications for Diabetic Brain Complications
section_title: ER Stress Inducer Tunicamycin Causes Dose-dependent, Reversible AIS Shortening

text: The cumulative frequency distribution of AIS length showed a leftward shift after tunicamycin treatment. This suggests tunicamycin induces generalized AIS shortening across the populations of neurons. To determine the cell-type specific effects of tunicamycin on AIS structures, we immunostained for CaMKIIα to identify excitatory neurons (CaMKIIα positive) and putative inhibitory neurons (CaMKIIα negative). As seen with methylglyoxal Griggs et al., tunicamycin exposure did not alter the percentage of CaMKIIα positive neurons (80.4 ± 0.483%) when compared to vehicle control (78.2 ± 1.52%) (n = 3 culture preparations; unpaired t-test, p = 0.2525). We previously showed that methylglyoxal induces AIS shortening in both of these populations of neurons Griggs et al. Similarly, tunicamycin induced significant AIS shortening in excitatory neurons (21.68 ± 0.231 μm) when compared to vehicle control (DMSO; 0.025%) (26.34 ± 0.526 μm; p < 0.0001) (Fig. B, C). Additionally, AIS of putative inhibitory neurons exposed to tunicamycin (21.53 ± 0.366 μm) was significantly shorter than vehicle controls (26.48 ± 0.495 μm; p < 0.0001). These data suggest that ER stress is sufficient to shorten the AIS in both excitatory and putative inhibitory neurons.

section_title: ER Stress Inducer, Tunicamycin, Induces AIS Shortening in Both Excitatory and Putative Inhibitory Neurons

section_title: Tunicamycin Does Not Alter AIS Start Location

text: Three UPR pathways can be specifically targeted and have different downstream signaling effects (Ghemrawi and Khair). Therefore, uncovering the pathway responsible for AIS shortening could allow for development of more targeted therapeutics. Among three UPR branches, the PERK/eIF2α axis is most well studied as a potential therapeutic target to mitigate symptoms in neurodegenerative conditions such as Alzheimer’s disease (Halliday et al. Ohno; Rozpędek-Kamińska et al. Smedley et al. For example, inhibition of PERK activity by a PERK-specific inhibitor GSK2606414 in the hippocampal CA1 region enhances memories in middle-aged mice Sharma et al. Importantly, there was an inverse correlation between AIS length and P-PERK/PERK ratio. To test if the PERK pathway mediates AIS shortening, we exposed mouse cortical cultures to either vehicle (DMSO 0.025%), tunicamycin (0.25 µg/mL), GSK2606414 (0.06 µM), or tunicamycin and GSK2606414 for 24 h and examined the AIS morphology. There was a statistically significant interaction between the effects of tunicamycin and GSK2606414 on AIS length (two-way ANOVA; F (1,8) = 7.066; p = 0.0289; post-hoc Tukey’s multiple comparison test; n = 3 culture preparations). The AISs of cultures exposed to tunicamycin (23.37 ± 0.7546 μm) were significantly shorter than vehicle control (27.52 ± 0.5219 μm) (p = 0.0063). The AISs in tunicamycin-treated cultures were also shorter than tunicamycin and GSK2606414 co-treated cultures (26.29 ± 0.5682 μm) (p = 0.0409). No difference in AIS length was found between tunicamycin and GSK2606414 co-treated cultures and vehicle controls (p = 0.5300). These data suggest that the PERK pathway is the key mediator for ER stress-induced AIS shortening.

section_title: PERK Inhibition Prevents Tunicamycin-Induced AIS Shortening

text: The AIS regulates neuronal output as the site where action potentials are initiated. Recent studies indicate that subtle changes in AIS geometry (e.g. shortening of the AIS length) can significantly affect the neuronal excitability and firing properties Jamann et al. Given the importance of the AIS in regulating action potential initiation, it is not surprising that structural alterations in the AIS play important roles in various neurodegenerative conditions (Buffington and Rasband; Huang and Rasband; Garrido; Fréal and Hoogenraad). We have previously shown that the AIS is shortened in the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus in the T2DM model db/db mice when these mice show impairment of cognitive flexibility (Yermakov et al.). Since AIS shortening leads to decrease of neuronal excitability (Baalman et al. Evans et al. Jamann et al., it is conceivable that AIS shortening contributes to the pathophysiology of brain complications in T2DM. However, the cellular and molecular mechanisms of AIS disruption in disease conditions remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that ER stress induces shortening of AIS length. This conclusion is supported by three experimental results in mouse cortical culture. First, the diabetes factor methylglyoxal elevated ER stress markers GRP78 and P-PERK/PERK ratio. Second, ER stress inhibition with 4PBA prevented methylglyoxal-evoked AIS shortening. Finally, ER stress induction with tunicamycin caused dose-dependent AIS shortening, an effect that was prevented by the PERK inhibitor GSK2606414. Our findings will contribute to a better understanding of the pathophysiology of brain complications due to T2DM and potentially other neurodegenerative conditions that impact AIS geometry.

text: Methylglyoxal, a reactive α-dicarbonyl compound generated by glycolysis, has been implicated in neurodegenerative conditions such as diabetic brain complications and Alzheimer’s disease (Allaman et al. Yang et al. We have identified methylglyoxal as a potential mediator of AIS shortening in diabetic conditions Griggs et al. Here we show that methylglyoxal induces an increase in GRP78 protein levels in primary mouse cortical cultures, at the same dose (100 µM) required for AIS shortening (Fig. B-D) Griggs et al. Because GRP78 is upregulated in ER stress conditions, this suggests that methylglyoxal-induced AIS shortening occurs concomitantly with ER stress and UPR activation. This is further supported by our finding that methylglyoxal increases the ratio of activated PERK to inactivated PERK in our culture model (Fig. E, F). Upon activation, PERK is autophosphorylated and P-PERK then initiates downstream signaling to attenuate global protein synthesis and decrease ER protein load (Rozpędek-Kamińska et al.). Methylglyoxal increases the proportion of PERK that has been autophosphorylated, suggesting presence of ER stress and UPR in conditions of methylglyoxal-induced AIS shortening. Importantly, co-exposure to an established ER stress inhibitor 4PBA prevented the AIS shortening as well as increase of P-PERK/PERK ratio by methylglyoxal (This suggests that ER stress and UPR activation is required for the AIS shortening in diabetic conditions. 4PBA is widely used to inhibit ER stress because of its ability to function as a chemical chaperone. Similar to the action of the endogenous protein chaperone GRP78, 4PBA binds to aberrantly exposed hydrophobic regions in misfolded proteins to prevent aggregation within the ER Kolb et al. Similar to our results, in cultured retinal pigment epithelial cell line, inhibition of ER stress by 4PBA reduced the methylglyoxal-induced intracellular events and cell death Chan et al. Furthermore, in vivo administration of 4PBA attenuated cognitive deficits in T2DM rats by high-fat diet and a single small dose of streptozotocin Wang et al., and in a streptozotocin-induced diabetic mouse model Kong et al. ER stress occurs in the T2DM model db/db mice (Sims-Robinson et al. Li et al. Ye et al. Hu et al. Wu et al., in association with AIS shortening and impairment of cognitive flexibility (Yermakov et al.). Collectively, these findings support the idea that ER stress is a key cellular event that mediates AIS shortening, presumably contributing to development of cognitive impairment in T2DM.

section_title: ER Stress is Required for Methylglyoxal-Induced AIS Shortening

text: We found that the established ER stress inducer tunicamycin caused dose-dependent AIS shortening in mouse cortical cultures (Fig. A-C). ER stress and the UPR activation can trigger apoptosis (Ghemrawi and Khair). However, neuronal apoptosis was not driving AIS shortening, because low-dose tunicamycin (1.0 µg/mL or less) did not affect cellular viability in our neuronal cultures, and the tunicamycin-induced AIS shortening was recoverable (Fig. F, G). The time course of AIS shortening by tunicamycin differs from methylglyoxal induced AIS shortening. There is no change in AIS length after 30 min–3 h of methylglyoxal exposure Griggs et al. Conversely, tunicamycin induces AIS shortening more rapidly, with significant shortening after 3 h of exposure. The reason for this discrepancy is not understood. Our data suggest that tunicamycin causes generalized AIS shortening across the entire neuronal populations including excitatory and putative inhibitory neurons (Figs. C and). These features of tunicamycin-induced AIS shortening are similar to that induced by methylglyoxal Griggs et al. Furthermore, we did not see changes in AIS location, another AIS structural factor affecting neuronal excitability, in the mouse cortical cultures exposed to tunicamycin or methylglyoxal Griggs et al., or in the db/db mice Yermakov et al. These findings indicate that ER stress is sufficient to induce AIS structural changes similar to those in the diabetic conditions (Yermakov et al. Griggs et al. Importantly, AIS shortening caused by sub-lethal levels of methylglyoxal Griggs et al. or tunicamycin was reversible after washout of these drugs (Fig. F, G). Apoptotic cell death was not observed in db/db mouse brains when these mice show cognitive impairment and AIS shortening Yermakov et al. Therefore, the AIS shortening in diabetic brains could be reversible by treatment targeting ER stress, suggesting its potential for early intervention.

text: Among the three UPR branches, studies investigating the mechanisms for neurodegenerative conditions have focused on the PERK pathway (Halliday et al. Ohno; Rozpędek-Kamińska et al. Smedley et al. Previous studies showed that methylglyoxal activates PERK pathway in vitro (Palsamy et al. Barragán-Iglesias et al. Xue et al. Methylglyoxal-induced AIS shortening as well as PERK activation are prevented by the ER stress inhibitor 4PBA (Tunicamycin activates all three UPR pathways including PERK in vitro (Lu et al. Qureshi et al. Co-incubation of the mouse cortical culture with tunicamycin and the PERK-specific inhibitor GSK2606414 prevented AIS shortening, suggesting that the PERK pathway mediates the ER stress-induced AIS shortening. However, the molecular mechanisms through which activation of the PERK pathway leads to AIS shortening remain to be elucidated. P-PERK phosphorylates α subunit of eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2 (eIF2α) to decrease ER protein load by inhibiting protein synthesis (Halliday et al. Ohno; Rozpędek-Kamińska et al. Smedley et al. Phosphorylated eIF2α also upregulates activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4), which in turn promotes transcription of target genes in diverse cellular processes, including protein folding, amino acid metabolism, or autophagy. ER stress is known to trigger a variety of cellular responses without inducing cell death. For example, sub-lethal doses of tunicamycin induce ATF4-dependent autophagic degradation of stromal interaction molecule 2, a protein implicated in dendritic spine formation, and reduce dendrite arbor in primary rat neuronal cultures Zhou et al. Future studies are needed to determine the mechanisms of how sub-lethal ER stress leads to AIS shortening and how these structural changes affect neuronal circuit function. Additionally, it remains to be determined whether PERK inhibition can ameliorate methylglyoxal-evoked AIS shortening in vitro, as well as the AIS shortening observed in diabetic animal models in vivo. Previous studies show PERK activation in db/db mouse brains (Li et al. Ye et al. Hu et al. Wu et al. Indeed, treatment with GSK2656157, a specific inhibitor of the PERK pathway, improved learning and memory function in diabetic db/db mice Wu et al. These previous studies focused on neuroinflammation, synaptic alterations, neurodegeneration, and neuronal apoptosis as potential mechanisms for ER stress-induced cognitive dysfunction (Li et al. Ye et al. Hu et al. Wu et al. In addition to these pathological changes, our results highlight the importance of investigating AIS as the neuronal structure influenced by ER stress in diabetic conditions.

section_title: PERK Pathway in UPR Mediates ER Stress-Induced AIS Shortening

text: Although our data provided key insights into the mechanism of AIS shortening in diabetes, we must acknowledge the limitations of this study and unanswered questions to address in future investigations. For instance, acute ER stress induction in cortical cultures may not be generalizable to the chronic ER stress response seen in a more complicated in vivo diabetic brain condition. Similarly, there are supporting cells such as microglia that play critical roles in vivo (Baalman et al. Benusa and Lafrenaye) but are not represented in our culture model. A recent study indicated the roles of alterations in astrocytes in mediating AIS structural changes Benitez et al. Future research investigating the effects of ER stress and PERK inhibition using in vivo models, where endogenous glial cells are present, will be necessary to further confirm the impact of ER stress and PERK activation on AIS shortening. Finally, because the AIS has a critical role in neuronal homeostatic plasticity, functional deficits could be evaluated alongside AIS geometry changes in response to ER stress.

text: Our results indicate that ER stress, potentially through the PERK UPR pathway, is the key mechanism mediating AIS shortening in cultured mouse cortical neurons. In addition to T2DM, AIS shortening is associated with many neurodegenerative conditions including Alzheimer’s disease (Marin et al. Best et al. Ma et al. Benitez et al., aging (Atapour and Rosa; Ding et al., traumatic brain injury (Baalman et al. Vascak et al., neuropathic pain Shiers et al., attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder Usui et al., and autism-spectrum disorder Usui et al. These observations indicate that altered AIS geometry (e.g., AIS shortening) is a common mechanism of brain dysfunction in various neurodegenerative conditions. Importantly, ER stress has been shown to be involved in the pathogenesis of Alzheimer’s disease Ajoolabady et al., aging (Martínez et al.), traumatic brain injury Yang et al., neuropathic pain Kawanaka et al., and autism-spectrum disorder (Kawada and Mimori). These insights into the AIS alterations and ER stress will provide fundamental knowledge of the pathophysiology of cognitive impairment in T2DM and potentially in other neurodegenerative conditions, ultimately inspiring future therapeutic studies for patients living with these conditions.

text: Gastric cancer (GC) remains a serious global health issue, being one of the most prevalent cancers worldwide with a high mortality rate [ – ]. Early symptoms are often non-specific and easily overlook, leading to late diagnosis and poor prognosis. Despite advances in surgical and post-operative treatments, including radiotherapy and chemotherapy, the survival rate for GC patients remains low [ – ]. Hence, there is an urgent need to identify effective biomarkers and prognostic models that can aid in early diagnosis and guide personalized treatment strategies, ultimately improving patient outcomes [ – ]. The development of such tools is crucial for addressing the challenges posed by gastric cancer [ – ]. Programmed cell death encompasses various forms, such as pyroptosis, necroptosis, entosis, ferroptosis, and cuprotosis [ – ]. Among these, paraptosis is a unique type of non-apoptotic programmed cell death, distinguished by cytoplasmic vacuolization and swelling of mitochondria and endoplasmic reticulum. Unlike apoptosis, paraptosis lacks typical apoptotic features, including nuclear condensation and membrane disruption. Recent studies have suggested that paraptosis may play an important role in tumor progression, therapy resistance, and changes in the tumor microenvironment in gastric cancer. Paraptosis can regulate tumor cell stress responses, alter cell metabolism, and interact with immune cells, potentially influencing immune evasion and therapeutic responses of the tumor. Therefore, as an emerging form of programmed cell death, paraptosis may become a potential target for therapeutic intervention in gastric cancer [ – ]. Despite its recognized role in tumorigenesis and identified prognostic features in some cancers, the involvement of paraptosis in gastric cancer and its underlying mechanisms remain unexplored and warrant further investigation. Our study aimed to develop and validate a novel risk signature, termed the Paraptosis-Related Risk Signature (PRRS), for GC patients. We evaluated the prognostic value of PRRS and stratified patients based on their immunotherapeutic sensitivity. Our objective was to emphasize the significance of PRRS in assessing the immune microenvironment and survival prognosis of GC patients, while identifying potential therapeutic targets to guide personalized treatment strategies.

text: In our study, we investigated the expression profiles of paraptosis genes in normal and gastric cancer samples. Our findings indicate that a significant number of paraptosis genes show increased expression levels in gastric cancer tissues when compared to normal tissues.. Our research delved into the analysis of paraptosis gene expression and survival data from 375 GC samples, leading to the discovery of three distinctive subtypes of gastric cancer. Through consensus clustering analysis, we determined that the optimal number of subtypes was K = 3 (Fig. B-D), each displaying unique patterns of paraptosis gene expression. The heatmap representation showcased the consensus matrix at K = 3, highlighting the differences among the subtypes. Subsequent evaluation of the impact of these subtypes on patient survival revealed that C3 subtype displayed a significantly superior clinical outcome compared to C1 and C2. This Fig. G underscores the potential relevance of paraptosis gene expression in predicting survival outcomes for GC patients.

text: Somatic mutations were carefully studied across different groups of patients, leading to the creation of a detailed waterfall plot that highlighted the top 15 genes presenting the highest mutation frequencies (Fig. A-C). In group C1, notable genes with high mutation rates included TTN, TP53, LRP1B, MUC16, and ARID1A. In contrast, group C3 displayed TP53 as the fourth most common mutated gene, with a mutation frequency of 38.4%, which was significantly lower than the prevalence seen in group C2 at 61.3%. Moreover, SYNE1 and PIK3CA emerged as the genes with the fifth highest mutation frequency in group C2 and C3, respectively, standing at 30.6% and 32.3%. Upon analyzing the tumor microenvironment in both subtypes, we made a noteworthy discovery. The C2 group demonstrated significantly lower immune scores, matrix scores, and estimated scores in comparison to the other groups. In contrast, the C3 group, known for its superior survival rates, exhibited intermediate scores falling between the two groups. To delve deeper into the differences, we utilized the CIBERSORT method to visually represent immune cell infiltration variations between the two groups. The resulting box-and-line plot highlighted that CD8 + T cells, activated CD4 + memory T cells, T follicular helper cells, and resting NK cells penetrated the tumor more extensively in the C3 group. On the other hand, M2 macrophages and other immune cells showed an opposing trend. These insights shed light on the complex interplay between tumor microenvironments and immune cell infiltration, hinting at potential implications for patient outcomes. The immune checkpoint levels of different subgroups were evaluated in the study. The results, shown in Fig. F, indicated that the C3 group had notably higher expression levels of immune checkpoints compared to other groups. This suggests that patients in the C3 group may have a more positive response to immunotherapy.

text: This study utilized survival time, survival status, and gene expression data to identify four prognostic genes linked to paraptosis: SLCO2A1, VCAN, RAMP1, and MANEAL (Fig. A, B). The analysis was conducted through regression using the lasso-Cox method with a lambda value of 0.0714. The RiskScore model formula was determined as follows: RiskScore = 0.0548*SLCO2A1 + 0.0557*VCAN + 0.0204*RAMP1–0.0187*MANEAL. These findings shed light on potential targets for further research into paraptosis-related mechanisms. In our study, we delved into the relationship between survival rates and risk scores among patients, discovering a significant decrease in survival as the risk score heightened. Through our analysis, we pinpointed SLCO2A1, VCAN, and RAMP1 as risk factors, displaying an increase in expression with higher risk scores. On the contrary, MANEAL emerged as a protective factor, with its expression decreasing as the risk score rose. To further evaluate the prognostic value of the paraptosis-related risk signature (PRRS) for individuals with gastric cancer (GC), we conducted Kaplan-Meier analyses. In both the TCGA-STAD dataset and the GSE84433 validation set, we observed that patients in the low-risk group exhibited a more positive survival outlook. The statistical significance of these findings was evident, with p-values of 4.8 × 10 − 5 and 6.1 × 10 − 5 (Fig. D, E), respectively. These results underscore the effectiveness of our developed PRRS in predicting the prognosis of GC patients.

Additionally, we have devised a nomogram incorporating TNM classification, age, gender, and risk factors to accurately forecast survival outcomes, as presented in Fig. B. text: Gastric cancer is a major global health issue, prompting intensive research into identifying biological markers that can improve patient prognosis. Encouragingly, studies have unveiled various gene models linked to programmed cell death, including pyroptosis, necroptosis, entosis, ferroptosis, and cuprotosis. These models show promise in paving the way for potential therapeutic targets in the fight against gastric cancer. With further exploration and development, these findings may offer new avenues for treatment and improved outcomes for patients battling this malignancy. However, an often overlooked form of cell death is paraptosis, a non-apoptotic, programmed form of cell death that has emerged as a crucial factor in cancer biology. Among these pathways, pyroptosis is a highly inflammatory form of programmed cell death mediated by gasdermin proteins, which leads to cell membrane rupture and the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as IL-1β and IL-18. Pyroptosis has a dual role in gastric cancer—it can contribute to tumor suppression by promoting anti-tumor immunity, but excessive inflammation can also support tumor progression by creating an immunosuppressive microenvironment. Various studies have shown that modulating pyroptotic pathways, such as targeting the NLRP3 inflammasome or gasdermin D, can potentially enhance anti-tumor immunity and improve therapeutic responses in gastric cancer. Ferroptosis, another form of regulated cell death, is driven by iron-dependent lipid peroxidation and oxidative stress. Unlike apoptosis, ferroptosis is characterized by the accumulation of lipid peroxides due to glutathione depletion and GPX4 inactivation. In gastric cancer, ferroptosis has been implicated in both tumor suppression and therapy resistance. Inducing ferroptosis in GC cells has emerged as a promising therapeutic strategy, particularly in overcoming drug resistance. Recent studies suggest that targeting ferroptosis regulators such as SLC7A11 or ferroptosis-inducing compounds (e.g., erastin and RSL3) can sensitize GC cells to chemotherapy and immunotherapy. While pyroptosis and ferroptosis have been extensively studied, paraptosis has not received as much attention, particularly in gastric cancer. Paraptosis, a relatively new concept in cell death, has been overshadowed by better-known processes like apoptosis and autophagy in research studies. Distinguished by distinct vacuolization patterns originating from the endoplasmic reticulum and an absence of typical apoptotic features, paraptosis has not been extensively explored in scientific literature. Despite the limited research conducted in this field, the recognition of paraptosis as a unique method of cell death opens up promising opportunities for cancer therapy [ – ]. Its potential role in treating gastric cancer, along with the underlying mechanisms and pathways, represents a fascinating yet uncharted territory that warrants further investigation. Exploring paraptosis in the context of gastric cancer could provide a deeper understanding of how tumor cells adapt to stress and evade conventional therapeutic strategies. Given its potential to alter the immune response and enhance tumorigenic processes, paraptosis-related pathways could open novel therapeutic avenues for gastric cancer treatment. While other forms of cell death like ferroptosis and pyroptosis have garnered significant attention, paraptosis warrants further investigation as it may offer unique advantages in improving therapeutic outcomes for gastric cancer patients.

text: Exploring paraptosis in the context of gastric cancer could provide a deeper understanding of how tumor cells adapt to stress and evade conventional therapeutic strategies. Given its potential to alter the immune response and enhance tumorigenic processes, paraptosis-related pathways could open novel therapeutic avenues for gastric cancer treatment. While other forms of cell death like ferroptosis and pyroptosis have garnered significant attention, paraptosis warrants further investigation as it may offer unique advantages in improving therapeutic outcomes for gastric cancer patients. Our comprehensive analysis aimed to categorize gastric cancer patients into three distinct subgroups of paraptosis based on the expression patterns of 65 paraptosis-associated genes. The differential expression levels of these genes in cancer tissues compared to normal tissues were found to be significant, indicating potential implications for patient outcomes. Strikingly, our research unveiled that individuals belonging to different subtypes exhibited varying survival rates, immune cell infiltration outcomes, and overall prognosis (Figs. G and).To further investigate these findings, we utilized the limma method to pinpoint differentially expressed genes within the identified subgroups. Through the application of the cox-lasso method, we highlighted four key genes - SLCO2A1, VCAN, RAMP1, and MANEAL - as potential biomarkers for gastric cancer. These genes have been linked to cancer and inflammation processes, influencing immune responses in various ways.For instance, SLCO2A1 is recognized for its role in primary hypertrophic osteoarthropathy and inflammatory bowel disease [ – ], while increased VCAN expression is associated with advanced tumor stages and poorer long-term survival. Notably, RAMP1 signaling in immune cells plays a crucial role in inflammation-induced lymphangiogenesis and immune-mediated hepatitis pathogenesis. Our findings shed light on the intricate molecular mechanisms underlying gastric cancer subtypes and provide valuable insights for personalized treatment strategies. The combined results of the four genes indicate that individuals with low-risk PRRS have a better chance of survival, as demonstrated in Fig. D. This outcome was confirmed in the validation set, as depicted in Fig. E. These findings suggest that paraptosis may be used as a biomarker for diagnosing and predicting gastric cancer outcomes. Additionally, this study highlights the possibility of manipulating the tumor microenvironment as a potential therapeutic strategy. Overall, these results provide valuable insights into the prognosis and treatment of gastric cancer, pointing towards exciting new avenues for further research and potential clinical applications. The analysis of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in various subgroups revealed significant enrichment in processes such as extracellular messaging, cancer, and immune-related activities including extracellular matrix, cell adhesion, immune effector process, leukocyte migration, and infection pathways like human T-cell leukemia virus 1 and human immunodeficiency virus 1. The enrichment of these processes in the subgroups may explain the improved survival rates observed in GC patients belonging to subgroup C3. The findings suggest that the molecular pathways related to immune response and cancer progression play a crucial role in determining patient outcomes, highlighting the potential for targeted therapies in GC management.

The findings suggest that the molecular pathways related to immune response and cancer progression play a crucial role in determining patient outcomes, highlighting the potential for targeted therapies in GC management. The analysis conducted through our CIBERSORT boxplot showed that the C1 group displayed a significantly higher presence of various immune cells, including CD8 + T cells, activated CD4 + memory T cells, T follicular helper cells, and resting NK cells compared to the other groups. Furthermore, it was observed that M2 macrophages and CD8 + T cells within the C1 group were actively producing perforin, a toxic molecule that triggers apoptosis in target cells. These findings highlight the potential benefits of having a robust immune cell infiltration, especially with the presence of natural killer cells known for their effectiveness in cancer immunotherapy and memory CD4 + T cells that exhibit a rapid and strong memory response to immune challenges, thus contributing to protective immunity. Moreover, T follicular helper (Tfh) cells, found in abundance in the C1 group, play a pivotal role in supporting B cell immune responses. Additionally, the M2 macrophages present in the C1 group primarily contribute to anti-inflammatory and reparative processes, aiding in tissue repair and regeneration [ – ]. This may explain the better survival rates among gastric cancer patients in the C3 group, where increased immune cell infiltration was observed. Beyond immune cell infiltration, the immune checkpoint analysis revealed that the C3 group exhibited the highest levels of immune checkpoint expression, including key inhibitory receptors. The upregulation of immune checkpoints suggests that, despite the presence of active immune cells, T cell exhaustion may occur, leading to a suppressed anti-tumor response. However, this also presents a unique therapeutic opportunity, as tumors with high immune checkpoint expression are often more responsive to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), which restore T cell function and enhance anti-tumor immunity. Notably, clinical studies have shown that patients with tumors exhibiting high PD-L1 expression and increased CD8 + T cell infiltration tend to respond favorably to anti-PD-1/PD-L1 therapies. The findings in the C3 group suggest that these patients could potentially benefit the most from immune checkpoint blockade therapy, further reinforcing the clinical significance of identifying immune-inflamed gastric cancer subtypes. Upon delving into the relationship between PRRS and immune cell infiltration within the immune microenvironment, a multitude of significant insights surfaced. Initially, our analysis unveiled a direct correlation between the risk score and various immune cells, including naive B cells, resting CD4 + memory T cells, M2 macrophages, and resting mast cells. Conversely, the risk score exhibited an inverse relationship with activated CD4 + memory T cells, T follicular helper cells, resting NK cells, and M0 macrophages. These discoveries were further validated through meticulous examinations on the GSE84433 validation set, which corroborated our initial findings. The distinctive immune cell infiltration patterns identified mirrored those previously observed in the C3 group, shedding light on potential similarities and associations.

text: The mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) functions as an essential downstream effector of multiple oncogenes, including RAS and epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR),. The mTOR signaling pathway is frequently mutated and abnormally activated in lung cancer. Everolimus (Eve), a first-generation mTOR inhibitor, is approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for the treatment of several solid tumors, including breast cancer, advanced renal cancer and pulmonary neuroendocrine tumors. Currently, more than 30 clinical trials of Eve against lung cancer have been registered on ClinicalTrials. gov by the U.S. National Library of Medicine. However, the anti-lung cancer effect of the Eve monotherapy is modest. The median overall survival and the median progression-free survival are 6.7 and 1.3 months, respectively, in the Eve treatment group (NCT00374140). The adverse events of Eve, including anemia (22.5%), metabolism and nutrition disorders (10%), neutropenia (32.5%), dyspnea and pneumonitis (7.5%), frequently happen. High triglycerides or hypertriglyceridemia and hepatotoxicity or elevated liver enzymes in blood have also been observed in patients treated with Eve, highlighting the necessity of improving the efficiency and reducing the toxicity of Eve. Ginseng (Panax ginseng C. A. Mey.), one of the most famous tonic, is widely used as a cancer treatment option and has been recorded as a complementary and alternative medicine by the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (China). Ginseng improves physical stamina, stimulates immune function, and relieves various other health problems, such as respiratory and cardiovascular disorders. Ginsenosides are the main bioactive components of ginseng, many of which show immunomodulatory and anti-cancer activities,. Ginsenoside Rh2 (Rh2) presents anti-cancer effects in various solid tumors, including lung cancer, breast cancer, ovarian cancer, prostate cancer and hematological tumors,. Rh2 has been recorded to induce cell cycle arrest and apoptosis, inhibit cell migration and reverse drug resistance. Moreover, Rh2 acts on immune cells and regulates tumor microenvironment, thereby indirectly restraining tumor growth,. Paraptosis is a kind of programmed cell death characterized by cytoplasmic vacuolation, mitochondria and/or endoplasmic reticulum (ER) swelling, dependence on protein synthesis, caspase activation independence and lack of the typical hallmarks of apoptosis. Paraptosis frequently undergoes cellular stress responses, including ER stress and oxidative stress,. A large number of unfolded or misfolded proteins in the rapidly growing tumor cells causes ER stress suggesting that tumor cells may be more sensitive to agents that induce paraptosis than normal cells. This study has verified that the combination of Eve and Rh2 (labeled Eve-Rh2) shows remarkable anti-cancer effect in vitro and in vivo, which is mediated by the Eve-Rh2-induced paraptosis. The mechanical study suggests that Eve-Rh2 activates a unique function of c-MYC, through which Eve-Rh2 up-regulates the expression of tribbles homolog 3 (TRIB3), thereby mediating the accumulation of TRIB3/P62 + aggresomes and ultimately triggering paraptosis.

text: Our preliminary study showed that the combination of Eve (10 μmol/L) and Rh2 (10 μmol/L) remarkably triggered cell death in lung cancer cells. Afterwards, cancer cells were treated with the combination of Eve and Rh2 by using various treatment sequences, including pretreatment with Eve, pretreatment with Rh2, and concurrent treatment. The strongest anti-cancer effect in vitro was obtained in the group of co-treatment with Rh2 after the Eve pretreatment for 1 h, which was labeled as Eve-Rh2 and was chosen as the treatment manner in the following study. Herein, cell survival of the four human lung cancer cell lines (NCI-H1975, NCI-H1975/OSIR, HCC827, and A549) was tested under Rh2 (10 μmol/L), Eve (10 μmol/L), and Eve-Rh2 treatments for 24 h. Both Rh2 and Eve monotreatments induced a slight cytotoxicity in all tested cell lines (A), presumably because of the low concentration and short treatment time,. However, Eve-Rh2 triggered significant cell death within 24 h with cell inhibitory rates of 78.24 ± 8.74% in NCI-H1975, 66.56 ± 11.42% in NCI-H1975/OSIR, 54.80 ± 12.83% in HCC827 and 55.44 ± 4.73% in A549 (A). Meanwhile, the Eve-Rh2 treatment caused the formation of uneven-sized vacuoles in all tested cell lines (B). The anti-cancer effect of Eve-Rh2 was further evaluated in nude mice models by subcutaneously injecting NCI-H1975 or HCC827 cancer cells. Eve-Rh2 significantly suppressed tumor growth, and the anti-cancer effect of Eve-Rh2 treatment showed significant advantage over both Rh2 and Eve monotreatments (C–H). Eve monotreatment has been reported to cause hepatic steatosis in clinical case and hepatotoxicity in clinical trials,. In our study, about 30% livers in Eve treatment group exhibited pale spots in appearance, whereas the serum ALT and AST were not elevated after Eve treatment. Nevertheless, small vacuoles were observed in the hepatocytes around the nucleus as shown by H&E staining, and lipid droplets in livers were demonstrated by oil red O staining, which was used for fat droplet identification indicating that Eve causes hepatic fat accumulation. In contrary, all livers in the Eve-Rh2-treated mice were healthy and as normal as untreated mice as evidenced by the appearance, H&E staining and oil red O staining (K, L and), suggesting that Rh2 attenuates Eve-caused hepatic fat accumulation. In addition, Eve-Rh2 treatment did not cause any injury to kidney, the primary organ of excretion, as shown in histological sections (K and L), and the body weight of the mice in all groups had no difference after relative administration (I and J), further indicating the reliable safety of Eve-Rh2 treatment in vivo.

text: Thereafter, the type of cell death induced by Eve-Rh2 treatment was clarified. As shown in A and B, Eve-Rh2 induced caspases-independent cell death and did not trigger cell apoptosis. Bafilomycin A1 and chloroquine, which are autophagy inhibitors, did not reverse Eve-Rh2-induced cell death, even though the expression of LC3II was up-regulated by the Eve-Rh2 treatment. These data suggest that Eve-Rh2 caused neither apoptosis nor autophagic cell death. Then the IncuCyte S3 Live-Cell Analysis System was used to monitor the cell morphology regularly after Eve-Rh2 treatment (C). The formation of vacuoles was observed in cell cytosol after Eve-Rh2 treatment for 2 h. Increased cells vacuolized and ultimately died in a manner similar to balloon explosion. After Eve-Rh2 treatment for 6 h, the rough ER lesions were diffused, and the ER lumens were significantly expanded and vacuolated (D). Cytoplasmic vacuolation and ER swelling are regarded as the characteristics of paraptosis, which can be reversed by protein synthesis inhibitors. In our study, both CHX (the translational inhibitor) and A-D (the transcriptional inhibitor) reversed the Eve-Rh2-mediated cell death (E), as well as the cytoplasmic vacuolation (F and G). A similar phenomenon was also observed in A549 and HCC827 cells (H). Moreover, Eve-Rh2 reduced the expression level of Alix (I), serving as an inhibitory protein of paraptosis. Although Rh2 and Eve monotreatments were reported to induce caspase-independent cell death in cancer cells they did not induce cell death and cytoplasmic vacuolation alone in our tested cells (A and B), presumably because of the low concentration used here. In short, Eve-Rh2-induced paraptosis in lung cancer cells possess the following characteristics: independence of caspases activity, cytoplasmic vacuolation, antagonism by CHX or A-D, and down-regulation of Alix.

text: The Eve-Rh2-induced paraptosis could be attenuated by the co-treatment with CHX or A-D, whereas Eve-Rh2 suppressed the de novo protein synthesis instead of increasing it. Moreover, the cap-dependent translation was suppressed by Eve and Eve-Rh2 treatments owing to the inhibitory effect of Eve on the mTOR signaling pathway. Apparently, Eve-Rh2 induced paraptosis independent of the protein synthesis. Alix can interact with the endosomal sorting complex required for transport III (ESCRT-III), resulting in the regulation of protein sorting. Down-regulation of Alix may disturb the proteostasis and cause ER swelling by interfering with the function of the ESCRT-III,. Further study showed that Eve-Rh2 decreased the protein level of Alix without reducing its transcription level. The overexpression of Alix delayed but did not reverse Eve-Rh2-mediated paraptosis. The proteasome inhibitor, MG-132, reversed the Eve-Rh2-decreased Alix protein level but dramatically enhanced the cytotoxicity of Eve-Rh2 treatment. Eve-Rh2 with MG-132 pretreatment induced significant cell death within 6 h (A and B,), indicating that Alix played a marginal role in the Eve-Rh2-induced paraptosis. Besides, Eve-Rh2 increased the level of ubiquitin (C). Eve-Rh2 caused the accumulation of protein aggresomes similar with the positive control MG-132 (D), and the phenomenon could be reversed by co-treatment of CHX or A-D. These results suggest that Eve-Rh2 induced paraptosis by increasing the accumulation of protein aggresomes. It is well known that MG-132 induces aggresomes accumulation through proteasome inhibition. However, Eve-Rh2 displayed almost no inhibitory effect on the proteasomes (E), implying that Eve-Rh2 induced aggresomes accumulation through a different mechanism. The Gene Ontology analysis suggested that ER stress or unfolded protein response was the main biological process affected by Eve-Rh2 treatment (F), which was highly correlated with the protein aggregation,. The results of RNA-Seq and Western blot show that the regulatory factors related to ER stress, including BIP, CHOP, ATF4, IRE1 α and XBP1s, were up-regulated after Eve-Rh2 treatment (G and H).
