section_title: Epigenetic control of β-cell death pathways by Tet2

text: To determine if TET2 inhibition could modulate ER stress-induced responses and apoptosis in human islets, we cultured human islets from cadaveric donors (see for human islets donor information) with brefeldin A or thapsigargin, two chemical ER stress inducers, with or without Bobcat339, a selective cytosine-based TET1 and TET2 enzyme competitive inhibitor that reduces 5-hydroxymethylcytosine. We measured ER stress response gene expression by RT-qPCR and islet cell death by flow cytometry. The expression of 12 ER stress response genes that were evaluated was increased significantly when the islets were cultured with brefeldin A or thapsigargin (A and 6B). Importantly, Bobcat339 reduced induction of these genes when it was added to the cultures (A). We analyzed survival of human islet cells cultured with brefeldin A with or without pretreatment of Bobcat339 by flow cytometry (B). When the islets were cultured for 24 h with brefeldin A, the proportion of apoptotic and dead islet cells doubled (∗∗∗∗ p < 0.0001, for both, Tukey’s multiple comparisons test, ANOVA), but the proportion of apoptotic cells (∗∗ p < 0.01) and dead cells (39% reduction) was significantly reduced when the islets were cultured with Bobcat339 (C; ∗∗∗∗ p < 0.0001, 0.0024 respectively vs. DMSO). As a measure to confirm the β-cell specificity of the observed cell death phenotype, we measured the proportion of unmethylated INS DNA in the culture supernatants using a methylation-specific INS genomic DNA assay previously described. At the time of cell death, DNA released from β cells has unmethylated CpG sites, whereas these CpG sites are methylated in non-β cells. Unmethylated INS DNA/total (methylated and unmethylated) INS DNA proportions increased after 24 h of culture with brefeldin A vs. DMSO, but ratios were significantly reduced when Bobcat 339 was added to the cultures (D; ∗∗∗∗ p < 0.0001 by ANOVA). These findings indicate that pharmacologically inhibiting TET2 can reduce stress-responsive β-cell death. To assess the breadth of Tet2 inhibition effects on diabetes-relevant stressors, we tested the effects of the TET inhibitor on human islets cultured with cytokines inducing β-cell damage and death (IFNγ, IL-1β, IFNα, and TNFα). Both viable cells measured by flow and indolamine 2,3 dioxygenase (IDO), which is associated with the level of inflammation response, were reduced in a dose-dependent manner when Bobcat339 was added to the cultures (∗ p < 0.05 to ∗∗∗ p < 0.0001 by ANOVA) (E).

section_title: TET2 inhibition reduces inflammatory responses and prevents β-cell death in human islets

text: Using a multiomic approach we have identified the mechanisms whereby Tet2 modulates ER stress responses and β-cell death. Tet2 -deficient islets are protected from immune mechanisms of β-cell killing. In our previous studies, we found that the expression of cytokines and other immune response genes expression were modified in Tet2−/− islets, but the specific cell type(s) affected and the mechanism(s) through which Tet2 loss altered gene expression were unclear. Our new studies show that, while immune cells infiltrate the islets in both KO and WT recipients of WT bone marrow, the rate of infiltration is reduced in KO recipients starting 10 weeks post-transplant. Moreover, there were fewer T cells infiltrating the islets and they showed reduced cycling. o Tet2- deficient s islet endocrine cells show reduced responses to immune mediators and function compared to their WT counterparts. The expression of genes involved in Class I and II MHC antigen presentation, such as Type II IFNγ response genes, was decreased in all of the islet endocrine cell type. Most likely, this accounts for reduced activation of T cells and other immune cells. Our studies of chromatin accessibility revealed shared response programs for endocrine cells (α, β, δ), with IRF, STAT, and NF-κB TF motifs enriched in closing peaks of all three cell types. While all islet cells showed decreased expression of genes associated with inflammatory pathways, activation and recruitment of T cells, there were β-cell-specific regulatory and functional changes that suggest a mechanism for their increased survival. ER stress-responsive TF enrichment in closing peaks specifically in β cells suggests that β-cell protection in Tet2 KO mice may be mediated by their impaired ability to mount terminal ER stress responses. In support of these findings of reduced accessibility of ER stress-responsive TFs, blocking TET2 activity pharmacologically in human islets reduced expression of ER stress genes that were induced by brefeldin A or thapsigargin and, most significantly, reduced β-cell apoptosis and cell death. Although we did not directly measure death of α and δ islet cells, the increased proportion of unmethylated INS DNA would imply that the pharmacologic TET2 inhibitor Bobcat339 reduced β-cell death when brefeldin A was added to the cultures. This survival benefit arises from the suppression of inflammatory responses rather than from increased intrinsic β-cells growth or proliferation. We conclude that Tet2 plays an important role in the responses of β cells to inflammatory mediators by regulating the accessibility of genes that are linked to antigen presentation, ER stress and β-cell death. Inhibiting Tet2 may therefore improve β-cell survival during immune attack. TET2 has been shown to play a role in antigen presentation and inflammatory pathways through its effects on IFNγ and other cytokine signaling. TET2 promotes tumor antigen presentation leading to T cell activation and T cell-derived IFN-γ-induced signaling. Xu reported that Tet2 mediates interferon γ (IFNγ)-JAK-STAT signaling pathway to control chemokine and PD-L1 expression, lymphocyte infiltration, and cancer immunity. Reduced TET2 activity was associated with decreased production of IFNγ and tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes and the progression of human colon cancer. Deleting Tet2 in murine melanoma and colon tumor cells reduced chemokine expression and infiltrating cells in vivo, enabling tumors to evade anti-tumor immunity.
title: Tet2 modulates ER stress responses related to β-cell death and autoimmunity in diabetes

text: TET2 promotes tumor antigen presentation leading to T cell activation and T cell-derived IFN-γ-induced signaling. Xu reported that Tet2 mediates interferon γ (IFNγ)-JAK-STAT signaling pathway to control chemokine and PD-L1 expression, lymphocyte infiltration, and cancer immunity. Reduced TET2 activity was associated with decreased production of IFNγ and tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes and the progression of human colon cancer. Deleting Tet2 in murine melanoma and colon tumor cells reduced chemokine expression and infiltrating cells in vivo, enabling tumors to evade anti-tumor immunity. Our data show that in addition to altered antigen presentation pathways in islet cells, reduced expression of Lef1 and Stat5b, along with increased Dusp1 expression in CD8 + T cells, suggests that Tet2 deficiency in islets influences T cell differentiation and activation. As all immune cells originated from the same WT bone marrow donors, the observed differences likely reflect the impact of the KO islet microenvironment on T cell recruitment and activation. These findings, together with the effects on ER stress pathway genes in β cells suggest that both β cell-intrinsic and -extrinsic pathways that lead to their demise from autoimmunity were affected. Other investigations have shown that inhibiting or deleting Tet2 may confer a survival advantage for β cells in the setting of autoimmunity. Jakobsen et al. showed that TET2 mutant hematopoietic stem cells have a survival advantage compared to WT cells in the setting of inflammation and aging in patients with clonal hematopoiesis. Mutant cells had reduced responses to TNF signaling via NF-κB and showed distinct patterns of clonal expansion compared to WT cells. More recent data indicates that TET2 catalytic activity in post-transcriptional regulation may occur through RNA hydroxymethylation, and consistent with this survival advantage, TET2 mutations have been associated with myeloid malignancies including AML. However, in somatic cells, we have not observed similar transformation. We have tracked TET2 expression during differentiation of human embryonic stem cells into β cells and have found that the expression increases gradually with each stage of development from endoderm to endocrine progenitor to immature and mature cells during the 30-day differentiation period (unpublished data). Furthermore, Tet2 mutant mice have normal histology, functional mass, and glucose tolerance. In our experimental model, the Tet2 mutation was not in hematopoetic stem cells that may be more likely to transform because of their high rates of proliferation and development. Although overall gene expression trends were similar across the endocrine cell types, given the high synthetic activity of β cells, we hypothesize that preventing demethylation by Tet2 deficiency may affect stress-responsive CREs critical for β-cell survival. Indeed, a distinguishing feature of Tet2 -deficient β cells was enrichment of ER stress-responsive TF binding in CREs with reduced accessibility compared to WT, suggesting that preventing ER stress contributes to their protection in immune attack. Homeostatic (ATF4) and terminal (CHOP) ER stress-responsive TF binding motifs were specifically enriched in β cell reduced-accessibility CREs, suggesting that Tet2 −/− prevents β-specific activation or commissioning of ER stress/UPR-responsive CREs and regulatory programs.
title: Tet2 modulates ER stress responses related to β-cell death and autoimmunity in diabetes

text: Indeed, a distinguishing feature of Tet2 -deficient β cells was enrichment of ER stress-responsive TF binding in CREs with reduced accessibility compared to WT, suggesting that preventing ER stress contributes to their protection in immune attack. Homeostatic (ATF4) and terminal (CHOP) ER stress-responsive TF binding motifs were specifically enriched in β cell reduced-accessibility CREs, suggesting that Tet2 −/− prevents β-specific activation or commissioning of ER stress/UPR-responsive CREs and regulatory programs. ATF4 is among the PDX1-inducible stress factors in β cells that govern β-cell survival during stress, and transcriptional activation of the gene for C/EBP homologous protein (DDIT3/ CHOP) is among the first events associated with apoptosis. The β cell-specific effects on (and sensitivity to) ER stress responses may be a consequence of their greater synthetic activity vs. the other cell types, which can induce the unfolded protein response. Alternatively, the effect on accessibility of CREs enriched for ER stress response transcription factor binding may be the consequence of an immune repertoire that has cells specific for antigens primarily expressed on β cells, such as GAD and proinsulin. Thus, the changes in CREs related to ER stress response may be an indirect rather than direct consequence of Tet2 deficiency. In summary, our studies show that genetic ablation or pharmacologic inhibition of Tet2 (TET2) in islet cells can protect β cells from ER stress and killing. Tet2 -deficient islet cells show reduced expression of genes encoding components of the antigen presenting machinery and IFNγ signaling pathways. Most likely, as a consequence, T cells are not activated to proliferate. Deletion or inhibiting Tet2 can reduce ER stress and death of human islet cells. These findings suggest a pathway for engineering β = cells that can resist immunologic assault.

text: Our analysis was restricted to the islets and infiltrating cells at a single timepoint in each mouse, but our studies of immune infiltrates suggest that with time, the immune cell infiltration progresses. It is therefore possible that the infiltrating immune cells will also show features of activation with time. Similarly, our studies of human islets were not on a single cell basis, and therefore, it is possible that the reduced expression of apoptotic genes was not restricted to β cells as we had seen in the Tet2 KO mice. We did not determine the exact molecular mechanisms contributing to the epigenomic alterations we identified. In addition, we cannot readily determine how the reduced ER stress and IFNγ responses are linked. We cannot be certain which cells in the islet environment are the producers of IFNγ. Both islet endocrine and immune cells can do this, and therefore, it is possible that antigen presentation is the consequence of cytokines that are induced because of the ER stress in β cells rather than a result of cytokines and other inflammatory mediators produced by other cells. Since we used female mice, we cannot discriminate sex-based differences. Finally, while our studies in NOD mice indicated that Tet2, not Tet1 or Tet3, were induced during disease progression, Bobcat339 may inhibit the other two TET enzymes. Therefore, we cannot be certain that the effects we found are exclusively due to inhibiting TET2.

text: Female NOD mice for backcross or used as donors for bone marrow transplant were all obtained from The Jackson Laboratory. Tet2 −/− (Strain #:023359) male breeders under B6 background were originally purchased from The Jackson Laboratory and backcrossed with NOD females for over 14 generations for the study. text: BMT was done as previously described. Donor WT NOD mice 6–8 weeks of age were euthanized by CO 2. BM was flushed with ice-cold HBSS and the erythrocytes were removed by lysis. The recipient KO or WT mice (6–8 weeks of age) were irradiated with split dose (2 × 550 rads, 2–3 hrs apart, 1100 rads total) and donor BM (10 × 10 6 cells) transferred i.v. within 3 hrs of irradiation. 10-13wks or at the time of discovery of hyperglycemia after BMT, mouse islets were handpicked with a stereomicroscope after collagenase digestion of pancreases and single-cell suspensions were prepared by dissociation islets with cell detachment solution (Accutase, Stem Cell Technologies, Cat# 07920). Cells were then counted and checked for viability before submission for scRNAseq, scTCRseq and snATACseq.

text: Islets were harvested from mice at 10-13 weeks post BTM. The islets from 4-6 mice per genotype from each experimental condition were pooled and analyzed together. There were three pools of 4-6 mice used for snATACseq studies. Cells were lysed for between 3-5 minutes depending on the sample [SC2200283/84 were 3 min, SC2200373-76 were 5 min] according to the 10x Genomics demonstrated protocol CG000169 (Rev D). Nuclei were washed and suspended in PBS containing 0.04% BSA and immediately processed as follows. Nuclei quality was assessed via brightfield imaging and counted via Trypan Blue and a Countess II automated cell counter (ThermoFisher), and up to 12,000 nuclei were loaded onto one lane of a 10x Genomics Chromium chip H. Single nuclei capture, barcoding and library preparation were performed using the 10x Genomics Chromium X platform and according to the manufacturer’s protocol (# CG000209 Rev F). Libraries were checked for quality on Agilent 4200 Tapestation, quantified by KAPA qPCR, and pooled at 12.5% of an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 S4 100 cycle flow cell lane, targeting 6,000 barcoded nuclei with an average sequencing depth of 50,000 read pairs per nucleus. Illumina base call files for all libraries were demultiplexed and converted to FASTQ files using Illumina bcl2fastq 2.20.0.422. snATAC-seq reads (3 WT, 3 KO) were aligned to the mm10 genome build using the “cellranger-atac v2.1.0” count function. Aligned profiles were further processed and visualized using the “Signac v1.7.0” package in R. Doublets were identified by “Amulet v1” and removed from further consideration. snATAC-seq profiles were filtered based on the following criteria: number of fragments per peak < 2500 or > 25000, percent of reads in peaks < 30%, nucleosome signal > 1.5, TSS enrichment < 1, and blacklist ratio > 0.05. snATAC-seq profiles passing QC were clustered using the “RunUMAP” function with “lsi” as the reduction method and dimensions 2:10. The “FindNeighbors” function was then used with the same settings to identify the nearest cells for clustering, followed by the “FindClusters” function using algorithm 3 to identify and number the clusters. Clusters were initially assigned endocrine, immune, or other cell type identities based on the accessibility of nearby canonical marker genes (C; β: Ins2, α: Gcg, δ: Sst, Gamma: Ppy, Acinar: Clps, Ductal: Krt19, B-Cells: Cd79a, T-Cells: Cd3e, Monocytes: C1qc, cDC: H2-Ab1, Flt3,Ccr7,H2-Oa, Endothelial: Krd, Activated Stellate Rgs5:, Stellate: Col1a1, Plasma: Igkc) and these snATAC-seq-defined cell types were embedded into their respective scRNA-seq clusters (see below). To make comparisons between the peak sets of α- and β-cells, snATAC-seq β-cells were randomly down sampled to match the number of α- snATAC-seq cells (2,534) for each replicate. Down-sampling was also completed in triplicate to test for consistency (A).

text: Islets were harvested from mice at 10-13 weeks post BTM. The islets from 4-6 mice per genotype from each experimental condition were pooled and analyzed together. There were two pools of 4-6 mice used for the confirmatory scRNAseq studies. 5’ (2 WT, 2 KO) and 3’ (1 WT, 1 KO) scRNA-seq reads (10X Genomics) were aligned to the mm10 genome build using the “cellranger v7.0.1” count function. The data was cleaned by removing ambient RNA using “SoupX v1.6.2” with the contamination factor set to 20%. Doublets were identified and removed using “Scrublet v0.2.3”. scRNA-seq profiles with 250-4000 features and <25% mitochondrial percentage were retained for further analysis. The resulting counts matrix was processed using “Seurat v4.3.0.1”. Both 5’ and 3’ samples were combined into a single set for clustering. The data was normalized using “NormalizeData”, and the top 2000 variable features were identified using “FindVariableFeatures” with “vst” as the selection method. Principal components were identified using “RunPCA” with default settings, and UMAP was created using the “RunUMAP” function with reduction set to “pca” and the first 40 dimensions. The nearest neighbors for each cell were found using the “FindNeighbours” function with the same dimensions, and clusters (40) were identified using the “FindClusters” function with a resolution of 0.8. Cell types in each cluster (39 clusters) were identified using expression levels of the canonical marker genes (β: Ins2, α: Gcg, δ: Sst, Gamma: Ppy, Acinar: Clps, Ductal: Krt19, B-Cells: Cd79a, T-Cells: Cd3e, Monocytes: C1qc, cDC: H2-Ab1, Flt3,Ccr7,H2-Oa, Endothelial: Krd, Activated Stellate Rgs5:, Stellate: Col1a1, Plasma: Igkc) listed in A. Clusters showing expression of two or more marker genes were initially marked as unknown cell types.

text: The processed scRNA-seq (36,232 WT, 32,932 KO) and snATAC-seq cells (13,108 WT, 10,355 KO) were combined by embedding the snATAC-seq cells in Seurat. The gene activities of the most variable features identified in the scRNA-seq dataset, along with marker genes, were calculated for the snATAC-seq samples using the “GeneActivity” function. These activity values were normalized and scaled using the “NormalizeData” and “ScaleData” functions with their default settings, respectively. The two datasets were combined by first using “FindTransferAnchors” to identify anchors in the snATAC-seq data, which were then used in the “TransferData” function to complete the embedding. The originally identified snATAC-seq cell types were compared to the predicted cell types based on the scRNA-seq cells, and snATAC-seq cells with a prediction score of < 0.6 were removed. The resulting cells were batch corrected using the “RunHarmony” function. These cells were then clustered using the “RunUMAP” function with reduction set to 'harmony' and the first 40 dimensions. This was followed by the “FindNeighbours” function using the same settings. The clusters were identified using the “FindClusters” function with a resolution of 0.8.

text: For each cell type, genes expressed in <5% of cells were considered not expressed and removed from differential expression analysis. We identified differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between the NOD and Tet2 -/- genotypes for each cell type using the MAST test in Seurat’s FindMarkers function. Autosomal genes with adjusted p-value < 0.05 (FDR<5%) and average log 2 FC > 0.1 were considered differentially expressed. Up- or downregulated genes in α- (528 up, 1,047 down), β- (99 up, 493 down), and δ- (619 up, 456 down) cells were used as input gene sets to identify significantly enriched GO terms and pathways at FDR < 5% using DAVID.

text: snATAC-seq profiles for each cell type identified in snATAC/scRNA-seq co-embedded analyses were extracted and assembled into pseudo bulk using “Sinto v0.8.1”. For each cell type, multiple BAM files were created: one for each replicate, one for all WT/KO replicates combined, and one with all replicates in both conditions combined. These BAM files were then processed through a classical bulk ATAC-seq pipeline. The BAM files were sorted and indexed using samtools “sort” and “samtools index”. Duplicates were marked using picard “MarkDuplicates” with VALIDATION_STRINGENCY set to LENIENT. The files were filtered using “samtools view” with -F 0x004, -F 0x0008, -f 0x001, and -F 0x0400. Peaks were then called using MACS2 “callpeak” with -g 2.7e9. The autosomal peaks (α:112,902, β:107,962, δ: 113,540) identified by MACS2 in all cells and replicates were standardized to 300 bp widths by taking the ± 150 bp region around the summit. For each cell type, we used the merged all-replicate peak set to retrieve the read counts within each peak for all WT and KO replicates using “featureCounts v2.0.3” from subread 66 with the countReadPairs argument. All peaks were classified as proximal or distal based on whether 25% of the peak overlapped with a region ± 1000 bp of a transcription start site (TSS) from the “Gencode vM23” data. Proximal peaks were assigned the nearby gene as a potential target gene.

text: For each cell type, differentially accessible peaks (DAP) were identified by taking the counts matrix created above and using “edgeR”. TPMs were calculated using the “calculateTPM” function. Counts were then normalized using “betweenLaneNormalization”. The fold changes and FDRs for each peak were calculated using the “DGEList”, “estimateDisp”, “glmFit”, and “glmLRT” functions with coef = 2. Peaks with |log2FC| ≥ 0 and FDR < 0.05 were considered as DAP. Peaks with greater accessibility in KO - and WT were classified as opening (α: 167, β: 123, δ: 35) and closing peaks (α: 1,261, β: 757, δ: 401), respectively. Peaks that did not show a significant difference were classified as stable peaks.
title: Tet2 modulates ER stress responses related to β-cell death and autoimmunity in diabetes

text: The DAP for α-, β-, and δ-cells were tested for motif enrichment using “findMotifsGenome.pl” from HOMER with the mm10 genome and size 200. For each cell type, the background used was the set of peaks used to create the counts matrix. Motifs that were not expressed in at least 5% of the scRNA-seq cells for the same cell type were removed. Enrichment for each motif was calculated by taking the percentage of target sequences with the motif divided by the percentage of background sequences with the motif. Motifs with an enrichment of 2 and a Benjamini q value < 0.05 were considered enriched. Select interferon (Irf1, Irf8, Isre) and endoplasmic reticulum stress (Atf4, Chop, Nfat, Cebp, Nfe2l2) related enriched motifs in closing peaks were tested with “FIMO v5.4.1” to identify the exact peaks with a significant (p value < 10 -4) motif binding site.

text: All scRNA-seq T-cells (12,248) were re-clustered separately to identify subpopulations of cells. Once the cells were separated, they were processed similarly to all scRNA-seq cells. They were normalized, and the top 1000 features were identified. The data was scaled, and principal components were calculated. Initial UMAPs were created using the first 15 dimensions. These were then batch corrected using “harmony”, and the nearest neighbors were calculated. Clusters were identified with a resolution of 0.8. T cell subtypes were identified using canonical immune markers (Cd8+: Cd8a, Cd8b1; Cd4+: Cd4; Naïve Cd8+: Cd8a, Cd8b1, Ccd7, Lef1, Sell; Naïve Cd4+: Cd4, Ccd7, Lef1, Sell; Cycling Cd8+: Cd8a, Cd8b1, Mki67; Cycling Cd4+: Cd4, Mki67; Tregs: Foxp3; Mait: Il7r, Cxcr6, Ccr6, Cd3-: Cd3e-). Cycling T-cells and naive T-cells were re-clustered as well to identify the Cd8+ and Cd4+ cycling and naive cells. The final markers used for each cell type are in B.

text: scTCR-seq samples were processed using the “cellranger v7.0.1”, vdj function with “refdata-cellranger-vdj-GRCm38-alts-ensembl-7.0.0” as the reference. The “all_contig_annotations.csv” output file from each replicate was used for all further TCR-seq analysis. The barcodes from these results were matched to the barcodes in the scRNA-seq analysis to link the T-cell subtype identified before to the TCR sequenced here. For each cell type the number of cells with a specific TRBV were counted. Using these counts the diversity in TRBV and CDR3 regions for each replicate and cell type was calculated using Shannon's entropy with the “entropy” function from the “posterior v1.5.0>” package in R.

text: DNA was purified from culture supernatants using the Quick-cfDNA Serum & Plasma Kit (Zymo Research) and then bisulfite treated using the EZ DNA Methylation Kit (Zymo Research). text: Cellular senescence, a state of stable cell-cycle arrest triggered by various forms of stress, has emerged as a key contributor to aging and age-related diseases, making it an attractive therapeutic target. Senescent cells secrete a range of proinflammatory factors, collectively known as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), which can drive chronic tissue inflammation, functional decline, and the progression of age-related pathologies. In both humans and mice, the accumulation of senescent cells within atherosclerotic lesions has been implicated in vascular inflammation and dysfunction, and inhibition of the p53/p21 pathway has been shown to improve vascular function and attenuate atherosclerosis progression. Furthermore, in the context of obesity, the accumulation of senescent cells in visceral adipose tissue has been linked to increased inflammation and insulin resistance; notably, inhibition of the p53/p21 pathway in adipose tissue has been reported to attenuate metabolic dysfunction. Cellular senescence also plays a critical role in tumor suppression, yet paradoxically exhibits pro-tumorigenic properties under certain conditions; therefore, direct inhibition of senescence-regulating factors must be approached with caution. More recently, it has been suggested that the selective elimination of senescent cells (senolysis) not only ameliorates age-associated pathologies but also extends healthspan without increasing cancer risk. Consequently, there has been growing interest in developing senolytic agents that selectively target and eliminate senescent cells. To date, most senolytic agents have been developed on the basis of inhibition of antiapoptotic pathways activated in senescent cells. However, there is an increasing demand for more accessible and safer compounds. In this study, we screened food-derived materials for senolytic activity and identified Rhodiola rosea extract (Rosea), which contains oligomers of epigallocatechin (EGC) and epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG).
title: Natural senolytic activity of Rhodiola rosea extract alleviates age-associated phenotypes via paraptosis

text: To identify candidate senolytic compounds, we screened 481 edible plant-derived materials. First, we defined human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) with a passage number of 14 or higher as senescent cells. Compared to low-passage cells (passage number <5), these senescent HUVECs exhibited elevated markers of cellular senescence, including increased senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal) activity and higher mRNA expression levels of CDKN1A (which encodes p21) and CDKN2A (which encodes p16 INK4a), two canonical cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor genes that are widely used markers of cellular senescence (A and S1B). We conducted a primary screen of plant-derived extracts using senescent HUVECs as a cellular model. In total, 481 extracts were evaluated at a single concentration of 12.5 μg/mL. This concentration was selected as a practical primary screening dose to enable direct comparison across the entire library while maintaining the final DMSO concentration within a non-toxic and consistent range. Following treatment, cell viability in senescent HUVECs was quantitatively assessed (C). Based on the results of the primary screen, 29 extracts were prioritized for secondary evaluation using a predefined operational cutoff of ≤50% viability in senescent HUVECs relative to the DMSO-treated control. To assess senolytic selectivity, these 29 candidate extracts were subsequently tested in parallel in non-senescent and senescent HUVECs (A). Several candidates exhibited preferential senolytic activity in this secondary screen. Considering practical factors such as availability and feasibility for follow-up studies, including reproducible supply and quality control, we selected Rhodiola rosea extract (Rosea) for subsequent experiments. Consistent with this selection, Rosea preferentially reduced the viability of senescent cells compared with non-senescent controls (B and 1C). In senescent HUVECs, Rosea treatment did not significantly alter the expression levels of CDKN1A or CDKN2A compared with control-treated cells (D), suggesting that Rosea does not reverse the senescent phenotype under these conditions. To evaluate whether Rosea could eliminate senescent cells in vivo, we utilized a senescence-tracking model. We generated a Cdkn2a (p16 Ink4a) knock-in reporter mouse in which a 2A-lox-pA-Neo-lox-tTA-2A-luciferase (Luc) cassette was inserted into the endogenous Cdkn2a locus. Upon Cre-mediated recombination, the STOP/ Neo cassette is excised, yielding the Cre-excised allele (p16 tTA−Luc; Cdkn2a 2A-lox-tTA−2A−Luc), in which tTA and firefly luciferase are expressed under the control of the endogenous Cdkn2a (p16 Ink4a) promoter (E). Cellular senescence was induced ex vivo in ear-derived fibroblasts isolated from p16 tTA−Luc mice by X-ray irradiation, and the establishment of a senescent phenotype was confirmed by increased expression of senescence markers and enhanced p16-driven reporter activity (F and S1G). We then assessed the direct effects of Rosea on irradiated (senescent) versus non-irradiated (non-senescent) fibroblasts in vitro. Following irradiation, cells were treated with Rosea for 48 h, after which cell viability was quantified. Under these conditions, Rosea preferentially reduced the viability of senescent fibroblasts, consistent with senolytic activity (H). For the in vivo assay, to determine whether the senolytic activity observed in vitro could be recapitulated in vivo, senescent and non-senescent fibroblasts were embedded in Matrigel and transplanted subcutaneously into wild-type C57BL/6 mice (D).
title: Natural senolytic activity of Rhodiola rosea extract alleviates age-associated phenotypes via paraptosis
section_title: Rosea identified as a senolytic agent

text: Following irradiation, cells were treated with Rosea for 48 h, after which cell viability was quantified. Under these conditions, Rosea preferentially reduced the viability of senescent fibroblasts, consistent with senolytic activity (H). For the in vivo assay, to determine whether the senolytic activity observed in vitro could be recapitulated in vivo, senescent and non-senescent fibroblasts were embedded in Matrigel and transplanted subcutaneously into wild-type C57BL/6 mice (D). Robust luciferase signals were detected from the transplanted senescent cells. Importantly, in mice treated with Rosea, these luciferase signals were significantly reduced, suggesting in vivo elimination of the senescent cells (E). To further assess whether senescent cells induced in vivo could also be eliminated, we irradiated the skin of p16 tTA−Luc mice with 14 Gy of X-rays to induce cellular senescence (I), and administered Rosea 2 weeks later (F). Irradiation resulted in increased luciferase activity, although this increase was significantly suppressed in Rosea-treated mice, suggesting a reduction in the p16-positive senescent cell population (G). Together, these results suggests that Rosea exhibits senolytic activity both in vitro and in vivo.

text: To evaluate the effects of Rosea in a physiologically relevant model of senescent cell accumulation associated with lifestyle-related factors, we employed a diet-induced obesity model. A transgenic mouse model (p19 Arf -Luc) was generated using a phage artificial chromosome containing the mouse Ink4a/Arf (Cdkn2a) locus. In this construct, the ARF-specific exon 1β was replaced with a cassette encoding the diphtheria toxin receptor (human HB-EGF I117V/L148V) linked to firefly luciferase via a self-cleaving 2A peptide (DTR-2A-Luc). Mice were then fed a high-fat diet (HFD) for 8 weeks to induce obesity, followed by 4 weeks of Rosea administration via drinking water (A). Compared to control mice, Rosea-treated mice exhibited a significant reduction in luciferase signal, suggesting an attenuation of p19 Arf -associated reporter activity (B). We further validated these effects by using wild-type C57BL/6 mice subjected to HFD feeding (C). Rosea administration led to a decrease in SA-β-gal activity in gonadal white adipose tissue (gWAT) (D), a reduction in p53 protein expression (E), and suppressed expression of Cdkn1a, Ccl2, Il1β, and Cxcl1 mRNA (F). To evaluate the effect of Rosea on adipose tissue inflammation, we performed a quantitative analysis of crown-like structures (CLS) in gWAT. CLS were significantly reduced following Rosea treatment (A). Glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity tests demonstrated improved glucose metabolism in Rosea-treated mice compared to controls (G and 2H). Notably, no significant differences were observed in body weight, gWAT mass, water intake, or food consumption between the groups (B–S2E). These findings suggest that Rosea improves HFD-induced metabolic dysfunction and adipose tissue inflammation and is associated with reduced senescence-related readouts in adipose tissue.
title: Natural senolytic activity of Rhodiola rosea extract alleviates age-associated phenotypes via paraptosis
section_title: Metabolic benefits of Rosea in a HFD-induced obesity model

text: To investigate the effects of Rosea on age-associated senescence, we utilized middle-aged C57BL/6 mice in which senescent cells accumulate spontaneously with advancing age. Twelve-month-old mice received Rosea administered ad libitum in the drinking water for 12 weeks (A). Motor function was evaluated at the end of the treatment period using rotarod (B) and treadmill tests (C). Mice were sacrificed 2 weeks after completion of the motor assessments for tissue collection and subsequent analyses. Rosea-treated mice exhibited significantly improved motor performance compared to controls. Age-related pathological changes in skeletal muscle were also ameliorated. Loss of nuclear Lamin B1, a hallmark of cellular senescence, was ameliorated in the Rosea-treated group (D). Masson’s trichrome staining revealed a significant reduction in muscle fibrosis (A). Moreover, the expression of SASP factors such as Ccl2 and Mmp12, as well as the senescence marker Gpnmb was significantly downregulated in skeletal muscle following Rosea treatment (E). Similar improvements were observed in adipose tissue. SA-β-gal activity (F), as well as mRNA expression levels of Cdkn1a, Cdkn2a, Ccl2, and Gpnmb (G and B), and p53 protein levels (C), were all significantly reduced. There were no significant differences in body weight, food intake, or other metabolic parameters between groups (D–S3H). To assess the effects of Rosea in aged animals, 19-month-old mice were administered Rosea ad libitum in the drinking water for 16 weeks (H). Behavioral assessments were conducted at the end of the treatment period, and mice were sacrificed 4 weeks thereafter for downstream analyses. Compared to controls, Rosea-treated mice showed markedly reduced signs of aging, including decreased hair loss and/or graying (I). Dermal thickness, a parameter linked to skin collagen content and elasticity, was significantly increased in the Rosea group, suggesting an improvement in skin quality (J). In addition, Cdkn2a expression and Lamin B1 loss in the skin, were significantly reduced (K and 3L). To evaluate whether Rosea affected age-associated alterations in behavioral patterns, we performed a wheel running test. Aged mice were acclimated for 1 day, after which the number of wheel rotations was recorded hourly. It is known that aged mice exhibit disrupted circadian activity rhythms, characterized by increased activity during the light phase (normally the rest period) and reduced activity during the dark phase (active period). Although Rosea treatment did not increase the total number of rotations (I), it improved the distribution of activity between the light and dark phases (M). Furthermore, Rosea administration did not affect body weight, food intake, or water consumption in aged mice (J–S3L). These findings further support the notion that Rosea may be beneficial in ameliorating age-related physiological and behavioral decline.
title: Natural senolytic activity of Rhodiola rosea extract alleviates age-associated phenotypes via paraptosis
section_title: Effects of Rosea in middle-aged and aged mice

text: To identify the active constituents of Rosea, we evaluated its major components, as previously reported. These compounds were obtained as commercially available purified standards and were individually tested using the same HUVEC viability assay. Among the major components examined, only EGCG selectively reduced the viability of senescent cells (A). Previous studies have reported the presence of EGCG- and EGC-related oligomers in Rosea. We chemically synthesized two such oligomers, EGC-EGCG and EGCG-EGCG (B), and evaluated their effects on senescent cells. Both EGC-EGCG and EGCG-EGCG induced cell death in senescent HUVECs and senescent human preadipocytes at lower concentrations than the EGCG monomer (C, A, and S4B). EGC-EGCG induced senescent cell death in a time-dependent manner (C), and similar effects were observed in human preadipocytes rendered senescent by ionizing radiation (D–S4F). Senescent cells treated with EGC-EGCG exhibited a time-dependent increase in characteristic cytoplasmic vacuole formation, which was readily observed by light microscopy (D) and further confirmed by transmission electron microscopy (E). Similarly, treatment of senescent cells with Rosea also promoted time-dependent vacuolization (G). These morphological changes are distinct from classical apoptosis and are instead consistent with a form of non-apoptotic cell death known as paraptosis. To determine whether the observed cell death was distinct from apoptosis, we examined the effect of the pan-caspase inhibitor Z-VAD-FMK. Pre-treatment with Z-VAD-FMK did not suppress EGC-EGCG-induced cell death in senescent cells, indicating that the cell death mechanism is not attributable to canonical apoptosis (H). Paraptosis is thought to result from osmotic imbalance in intracellular organelles, primarily triggered by abnormal calcium dynamics between the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and mitochondria. Using ER-Tracker and Mito-Tracker, we observed pronounced vacuolization in both the ER and mitochondria of senescent cells treated with EGC-EGCG (F). It is well established that paraptosis is associated with rapid mitochondrial calcium accumulation. Previous studies have shown that senescent cells exhibit impaired coordination of calcium dynamics between the ER and mitochondria. To assess this, we measured mitochondrial calcium levels using Rhod-2 AM and found that senescent cells exhibited elevated baseline mitochondrial calcium compared to non-senescent cells (G). Stimulation with EGC-EGCG significantly increased these calcium levels (G and 4H). To evaluate whether the calcium dynamics altered by EGC-EGCG contribute to the senolytic activity of this compound, we utilized 2-aminoethoxydiphenyl borate (2-APB), an inhibitor of the inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptor (IP 3 R), a calcium channel in the ER, and ruthenium red, an inhibitor of the mitochondrial calcium uniporter (MCU). Pre-treatment of senescent cells with 10 μM 2-APB or 2.5 μM ruthenium red significantly suppressed EGC-EGCG-induced cell death (I). These findings suggest that EGC-EGCG induces senescent cell death via a paraptosis-like mechanism mediated by dysregulated calcium dynamics between the ER and mitochondria.
title: Natural senolytic activity of Rhodiola rosea extract alleviates age-associated phenotypes via paraptosis
section_title: Identification of EGC-EGCG and EGCG-EGCG as senolytic components in Rosea

text: The accumulation of senescent cells in tissues is accelerated by DNA damage caused by aging and metabolic stress. This accumulation of senescent cells contributes to the progression of age-related diseases such as diabetes and atherosclerosis. Thus, methods for eliminating senescent cells are being actively studied as both preventive and therapeutic approaches. However, some existing senolytic drugs have been reported to cause adverse effects, and there is a growing need to identify compounds with more favorable toxicity profiles. In this context, we identified Rosea, which contains EGC-EGCG and EGCG-EGCG, as a senolytic agent derived from an edible material with an already established safety profile. Rosea, a plant known for its adaptogenic properties, has attracted considerable attention for its potential anti-aging effects due to its potent antioxidant activity and stress-reducing capabilities. Its physiological activities have been attributed to a group of compounds such as salidroside and rosavins (including rosavin and rosarin). In the present study, however, these conventionally studied components did not exhibit senolytic activity; instead, the observed senolytic activity was limited to EGCG oligomers. The existence of EGCG oligomers in natural products has been reported in only a limited number of studies,, and it is possible that these oligomers are characteristic components of Rosea. In cancer research, the use of paraptosis inducers has attracted attention as a way to induce cell death in cancer cells that are resistant to apoptosis. EGC-EGCG, identified in this study, has a mechanism of action distinct from that of conventional senolytics that target anti-apoptotic pathways. Specifically, EGC-EGCG acts on the calcium dynamics between the ER and mitochondria, which become vulnerable during cellular senescence, and induces paraptosis-like cell death. To the best of our knowledge, there have been no previous reports of senolytic agents that induce paraptosis-like cell death, making this an important finding of the present study. Dysfunction of the ER and mitochondria in senescent cells is well known and is being considered as a target for senolysis. Our findings suggest that paraptosis-like senolysis may be a viable alternative to apoptosis-dependent mechanisms. This study presents a pioneering approach to extending healthspan through the use of naturally derived senolytics, based on both in vitro and in vivo data. The potential anti-aging effects of senolysis induced by Rosea and its EGCG oligomers suggest that further translational research on this compound could contribute to a method for achieving healthier and longer life.
title: Natural senolytic activity of Rhodiola rosea extract alleviates age-associated phenotypes via paraptosis

text: The p16-driven reporter activity in our p16tTA-Luc reporter mice does not provide a direct or absolute quantification of senescent cell numbers. We cannot distinguish whether Rosea primarily reduces senescent non-immune cells, modulates macrophage abundance or activation, or affects both cell populations. We were unable to evaluate the in vivo effects of EGCG oligomers alone and instead limited our analysis to the effects of Rosea as a whole. Further investigation is required to determine whether EGCG oligomers exert senolytic effects in vivo, and whether synergistic interactions with salidroside and rosavins may contribute to the observed efficacy. Because paraptosis lacks universally accepted, specific molecular biomarkers, we acknowledge as a limitation that the mode of cell death cannot be conclusively determined in this study. In addition, all in vivo experiments were performed exclusively in male mice, and thus potential sex-dependent differences in the effects of Rosea were not assessed.

text: Human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) and human visceral preadipocytes were purchased from Lonza and cultured according to the manufacturer’s protocol. These commercially obtained cells were authenticated by the supplier and were certified by the supplier as negative for mycoplasma contamination at the time of purchase. Mouse ear fibroblasts were isolated as described above. Mouse fibroblasts were maintained in DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS and 1% P/S. Senescent HUVECs were defined as cells that had undergone at least 14 passages, and those with fewer than 5 passages were used as young controls. For human preadipocytes and mouse ear fibroblasts, cells with less than 5 passages were categorized as young cells. Senescence was induced by exposing cells to 10 Gy of X-ray irradiation (IR), followed by incubation for 14 days before use.

text: All animal experiments were reviewed and approved by the Animal Experiment Committees of Niigata University (approval number: SA00601) and/or Juntendo University (approval number: 1656), and conducted in accordance with protocols authorized by the respective institutional presidents. Most C57BL/6 mice were obtained from SLC Japan. Aged C57BL/6 mice were provided by the Foundation for Biomedical Research and Innovation at Kobe through the National BioResource Project (NBRP) of the Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology (MEXT), Japan. Mice were maintained in a specific pathogen-free facility under controlled conditions (temperature: 20°C–26°C; humidity: 40–60%) with a 12-h light/dark cycle. For senescent cell-tracking studies, we used two transgenic reporter models: (1) the Cdkn2a 2A-lox-tTA−2A−Luc (p16 tTA−Luc) mouse, in which a tTA-luciferase cassette was knocked in immediately upstream of the endogenous p16 stop codon, and (2) the p19Arf-DTR-luciferase mouse, which expresses both the diphtheria toxin receptor (human HB-EGF I117V/L148V) and luciferase from the Cdkn2a locus, kindly provided by Dr. Sugimoto. Unless otherwise specified, mice were given ad libitum access to standard chow diets (CE-2, CLEA Japan; or CRF-1, Oriental Yeast Co., Ltd.) and filtered tap water. For experimental groups, Rhodiola rosea root extract (Rosea; ASK Intercity Co., Ltd.) was dissolved in drinking water at a final concentration of 0.05% (w/v), filtered through a 0.2-μm membrane to remove insoluble particulates, and administered ad libitum. Drinking water was replaced twice weekly. Control mice received untreated drinking water under identical housing conditions. For diet-induced obesity experiments, mice were fed a high-fat diet (HFD32; CLEA Japan) beginning at 4 weeks of age. Details of diet duration and experimental timelines are described in the respective figure legends. All experiments were conducted using male mice. Anesthesia was administered as needed using either a mixture of medetomidine, midazolam, and butorphanol, or isoflurane. All anesthesia procedures were carried out in accordance with institutional animal welfare guidelines, ensuring minimal discomfort to the animals.

text: Plant-derived materials were provided by the National Institutes of Biomedical Innovation, Health and Nutrition (NIBIOHN, Japan), which maintains a curated library of edible plant resources. The library comprises botanically authenticated plant species with documented historical dietary use and established safety profiles, enabling systematic evaluation of bioactive potential in a translational context. A total of 481 edible plant-derived materials were included in this study. Extracts were prepared from various plant parts, including leaves, stems, flowers, fruits, seeds, roots/rhizomes/tubers/bulbs, bark, branches, and in some cases whole plants. Plant materials were processed and extracted according to standardized protocols established by NIBIOHN to ensure batch consistency and reproducibility. Extracts were dissolved in DMSO at defined stock concentrations and stored under controlled conditions until use.

text: Ear skin was excised from 4-week-old p16 tTA−Luc mice and sterilized with 70% ethanol. The tissue was then minced and digested with a solution containing 2 mg/mL collagenase type II (Worthington, CLS2) and 1 mM CaCl 2 in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) for 20–30 min at 37°C. The resulting cell suspension was filtered through a 40 μm nylon mesh and centrifuged. Cells were resuspended in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM; Sigma, D6046) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) and 1% penicillin-streptomycin (P/S; Gibco, 15140122), then plated in culture dishes. Proliferating adherent cells were expanded and used as mouse ear-derived fibroblasts.

text: Cells were seeded in black 96-well plates and incubated overnight to allow adherence. Following treatment with the indicated compounds, cell viability was assessed using the CellTiter-Glo Luminescent Cell Viability Assay (Promega, G7571) in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. Luminescence intensity was measured using a VARIOSKAN LUX multimode reader (Thermo Scientific). The viability of the dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO)-treated control group was set at 100%, and the relative viability of each treatment group was calculated accordingly. text: We assessed the expression levels of ER stress marker proteins (A) in the neural retina and RPE-choroid of 2- and 12-month-old mice. In the retina, the expression levels of ER stress markers—including nuclear form of activating transcription factor 6 (ATF6n), spliced X-box binding protein-1 (XBP1s), ATF4 and GRP94—remained unchanged between the two age groups, while phosphorylated eukaryotic initiation factor 2α (p-eIF2α) and C/EBP homologous protein (CHOP) showed a significant increase or increasing trend (, B and C). In contrast, in the RPE-choroid complex of 12-month-old mice, all of the aforementioned proteins were significantly upregulated (, D and E). Therefore, in the aging eye, ER stress may be induced especially in the RPE-choroid, before it affects the neural retina.

text: To explore the impact of ER stress on POS phagocytosis by RPE cells, we used an established in vitro RPE phagocytosis system using fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC)- or pHrodo-labeled POS (A). FITC-POS inherently emits fluorescence, allowing tracking of its uptake into cells. The intracellular localization of FITC-POS was confirmed by cell membrane staining (B), and phagocytosed FITC-POS was colocalized with LC3B puncta, indicating association with the autophagic pathway (A). In addition, POS were labeled with pHrodo, a pH-sensitive fluorescent dye whose fluorescence intensity increases in acidic environments (pHrodo-POS). After treatment of RPE cells with pHrodo-POS, the fluorescence of pHrodo was merged with lysosomal-associated membrane protein 1 (LAMP1) positive puncta, reflecting POS degradation in lysosome (C). To evaluate RPE phagocytic activity, intracellular fluorescence intensities of FITC-POS and pHrodo-POS were quantified. The intracellular fluorescence intensity of FITC-POS peaked at 6 h after POS treatment, whereas pHrodo-POS fluorescence increased in a time-dependent manner (, B and D). Detected fluorescence signals were significantly higher in fluorescent-labeled POS-treated RPE cells than in POS-untreated cells (Blank) which was regarded as background in phagocytosis assay (, C and E). Following fluorescence-based phagocytosis assay, to investigate whether high ER stress conditions affect phagocytic activity in RPE cells, we evaluated the effect of pharmacological ER stress induction using tunicamycin (Tm), known as ER stress-inducible compound by inhibiting N-linked glycosylation (D). Tm treatment at 10 μg/ml for 6 h significantly attenuated the fluorescence intensity of FITC and pHrodo in ARPE-19, suggesting a downregulation of both intake and degradation of POS (E). In human primary RPE cell (hRPE), treatment with Tm at 10 μg/ml for 6 h significantly attenuated phagocytic activity (F). Treatment with thapsigargin (Tg), another ER stress inducer that inhibits sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca 2+ -ATPase, similarly reduced the phagocytic activity of ARPE-19 at 100 nM for 6 h (G). Excessive ER stress can lead to cytotoxicity and cell death. To confirm whether the observed phagocytic impairments were due to cell death by Tm or Tg, we evaluated the cell death rate after ER stress induction. Under the same protocols, no significant cell death or decline in cell viability was observed (H). To further evaluate the effect of long-term induction of ER stress on POS phagocytosis, we co-treated cells with Tm and pHrodo-POS for 6 h following a 2-days pretreatment with Tm at 0.01 to 1 μg/ml (total 54 h). Short-term treatments did not attenuate phagocytosis, but Tm treatment at 0.1 or 1 μg/ml for 54 h significantly reduced the phagocytic activity in both ARPE - 19 and hRPE (, I – K). To compare the degree of ER stress, we examined the protein expression of GRP78, a well-established ER stress marker that is upregulated upon ER stress induction, under both (6 h and 54 h) Tm treatment conditions. GRP78 expression was significantly increased in ARPE - 19 cells treated with Tm at 10 μg/ml for 6 h and at 0.1 or 1 μg/ml for 54 h (, A and B), consistent with the observed downregulation of phagocytic activity (, E and J). These data suggest that severe ER stress reduces the phagocytic activity of RPE cells and that the degree of ER stress is more important than the duration of its induction.
title: Age-dependent induction of ER stress in retinal pigment epithelium impairs phagocytosis via ADAM17-dependent MERTK shedding

text: To assess the effect of ER stress on lysosomal and mitochondrial activity in RPE cells, we performed lysosomal staining and measured mitochondrial OCR. LysoTracker fluorescence intensity was not altered by brief (3 h) ER stress induction with Tm (, A and B), but decreased significantly after 6 h treatment with 10 μg/ml of Tm, suggesting lysosomal dysfunction (, C and D). Low concentrations of Tm, such as 0.1 or 1 μg/ml, also reduced LysoTracker fluorescence intensity of lysotracker after 54 h treatment (, E and F). Regarding mitochondrial function, OCR was already reduced 3 h after Tm treatment at 10 μg/ml (, H and I). These data suggest that ER stress impairs both lysosomal and mitochondrial activity in RPE cells, with mitochondrial impairment occurring particularly early in the process.

text: Sodium 4-phenylbutyrate (4-PBA) is a chemical chaperone that is reported to suppress ER stress-related phenotypes. To investigate the effectiveness of pharmacological mitigation of ER stress, we assessed the effect of 4-PBA on ER stress-induced phagocytic impairment (A). Treatment with 4-PBA attenuated Tm-induced downregulation of pHrodo and lysoTracker fluorescence intensity in a dose-dependent manner (, B and C). In response to intracellular stress, ER stress is tightly controlled by chaperone proteins such as GRP78 and GRP94 to prevent excess protein accumulation, and their expression is regulated by ATF6- and XBP1-mediated UPR (A). To evaluate the effect of chaperone induction on ER stress-induced phagocytic dysfunction, we transfected ARPE-19 cells with ATF6n- or XBP1s-expression plasmids. We confirmed the upregulation of ATF6n protein, XBP1s mRNA and their target genes including GRP78 and GRP94 (, D – F). Importantly, overexpression of ATF6n and XBP1s attenuated tunicamycin-induced phagocytic impairment (, H and I). Interestingly, a single treatment with XBP1s plasmid somehow promoted phagocytosis in ARPE-19 cells. These data suggest that the pharmacologically reducing ER stress and activation of the ER stress-suppressive system could help attenuate ER stress-induced phagocytic impairment in RPE cells.
title: Age-dependent induction of ER stress in retinal pigment epithelium impairs phagocytosis via ADAM17-dependent MERTK shedding
section_title: Effectiveness of ER stress inhibition on phagocytic dysfunction

text: To explore the underlying mechanisms of Tm-induced phagocytic impairment, we assessed changes in the expression of phagocytosis-related proteins such as MERTK and FAK, which are initially activated during phagocytosis in RPE (A). After Tm treatment at 10 μg/ml for 6 h, ER stress marker proteins, including p-eIF2α, ATF4, and GRP78, were significantly increased. In contrast, p-MERTK and p-FAK were downregulated (, B and C). Interestingly, the expression MERTK at approximately 170 kDa, representing the full-length protein, showed a significant decrease in ARPE-19 (, B and C). In ARPE-19 cells under long-term ER stress induction, the same pattern of protein expression changes was observed (, C and D). Gene expression of GRP78 and MERTK mRNA was significantly increased after Tm treatment, which was the opposite of the MERTK protein expression (D). Since MERTK contains multiple N-linked glycosylation sites, it was possible that inhibition of N-linked glycosylation by Tm affect maturation of MERTK. In lysates from Tm-treated hRPE cells (10 μg/ml, 6 h), the abundance of glycosylated MERTK (= Full length-MERTK) around at 170 kDa was markedly reduced, whereas the level of un-glycosylated MERTK around at 110 kDa remained unchanged. As a result, the ratio of glycosylated MERTK to un-glycosylated MERTK was significantly decreased (, E and F). To examine whether the reduction in full length-MERTK was due to its release into the extracellular compartment, we next examined the presence of MERTK in the culture medium. By ELISA analysis of the culture supernatant, the level of the extracellular domain of MERTK was increased after Tm treatment for 6 h in both types of RPE cells (G). In the culture medium of Tm-treated hRPE cells, increased levels of full length-MERTK (170 kDa) and soluble MERTK (120 kDa), consistent with the molecular weights reported previously, were detected using antibodies against the extracellular domain (, H and I). Additionally, a MERTK fragment around 65 kDa, representing un-glycosylated soluble MERTK, was also detected weakly which is consistent with the molecular weight estimated from the amino acid sequence. These data suggest that Tm-induced ER stress leads to shedding and release of MERTK to attenuate phagocytic signaling (see Discussion).
title: Age-dependent induction of ER stress in retinal pigment epithelium impairs phagocytosis via ADAM17-dependent MERTK shedding
section_title: ER stress induction attenuated phagocytosis-related signaling

text: To investigate the mechanism of Tm-induced MERTK shedding, we focused on the function of ADAM17, protease known to cleave the extracellular domain of MERTK in macrophages. After Tm treatment, the mature form of ADAM17 (matADAM17), which is responsible for ectodomain shedding, significantly increased in a time-dependent manner (A) Treatment with Tm at 1 μg/ml for 54 h also induced ADAM17 maturation (B). ADAM17 maturation is driven by the proprotein convertase Furin, which is localized in the trans-Golgi network. In ARPE-19 cells treated with Tm for 1 or 3 h, ADAM17 was significantly and highly expressed in regions marked by Golgin-97, a known trans-Golgi marker (C). To determine whether tunicamycin-induced ADAM17 maturation is mediated by Furin, we examined the effect of decanoyl-Arg-Val-Lys-Arg-chloromethylketone (CMK), a Furin inhibitor. Treatment with CMK (100 μM) suppressed Tm-induced ADAM17 maturation. Furin's protease activity is dependent on Ca 2+ concentration. Additionally, high ER stress conditions induce the upregulation of intracellular Ca 2+ through Ca 2+ release from the ER via membrane-localizing Ca 2+ channels such as inositol-1,4,5-trisphosphate receptors (IP3R). Tm-induced ADAM17 maturation was suppressed by the Ca 2+ chelator, 1,2-bis(o-aminophenoxy) ethane-N,N,N',N'-tetraacetic acid, tetraacetoxymethyl ester (BAPTA-AM, 100 μM) and the IP3R inhibitor, 2-aminoethoxydiphenyl borate (2-APB, 100 μM) (, E and F). We hypothesized that ER stress-induced ADAM17 maturation contributes to MERTK shedding (G), and we generated ADAM17 knockdown ARPE-19 cells using ADAM17 siRNA (H). After Tm treatment, the expression level of the extracellular domain of MERTK was significantly decreased in siCont; however, ADAM17 siRNA attenuated this Tm-induced downregulation. These data suggest that ER stress triggers MERTK shedding via ADAM17 maturation, which is dependent on Ca 2+ release from IP3R. MERTK is a key molecule involved in recognizing POS and initiating their uptake. To investigate whether ER stress affects POS uptake, we evaluated POS phagocytosis in ARPE-19 cells using a FITC-labeled POS assay with chloroquine (J). Given that FITC fluorescence decreases under acidic conditions, the fluorescence intensity of internalized FITC-POS gradually declined, reflecting POS degradation within lysosomes (, A and B). Based on this characterization of FITC-POS, chloroquine was used to inhibit lysosomal acidification, thereby increasing lysosomal pH and allowing visualization of the internalized POS. Under chloroquine co-treatment conditions, while Tm treatment decreased internalized POS, ADAM17 siRNA treatment suppressed this downregulation (K). These data suggest that Tm-induced ER stress promotes Ca 2+- dependent Furin activation and ADAM17 maturation via Ca 2+ release from the ER, resulting in MERTK shedding and impaired phagocytosis.
title: Age-dependent induction of ER stress in retinal pigment epithelium impairs phagocytosis via ADAM17-dependent MERTK shedding
section_title: Tm induced MERTK shedding via Ca 2+ -dependent ADAM17 maturation

text: To determine whether ADAM17 activation is induced in RPE-choroid tissue in aging mice, the expression levels of ADAM17 were assessed by Western blot analysis. In RPE-choroid tissue from 12-month-old mice, both the precursor form of ADAM17 (preADAM17) and matADAM17 were significantly increased (, A and B).
title: Age-dependent induction of ER stress in retinal pigment epithelium impairs phagocytosis via ADAM17-dependent MERTK shedding
section_title: Expression of ADAM17 in aged murine RPE-choroid

text: We showed that ER stress marker proteins are upregulated in middle-aged murine RPE-choroid tissue. In RPE cells, elevated ER stress conditions promoted MERTK shedding through ADAM17 maturation, leading to impaired POS uptake and induced organelle dysfunction. Our findings suggest a fundamental molecular mechanism underlying age-related phagocytic impairment in RPE cells. With aging, the capacity for protein quality control declines, inducing ER stress. Several studies using aged rodents demonstrated that the upregulation of ER stress-related proteins occurs in several tissues and cells such as adipose tissue, kidney, neurons, osteocytes, and the retina. Age-related alterations in ER stress proteins are suggested to be tissue dependent due to differences in the tissue environment. The RPE is continuously exposed to metabolic stress through daily phagocytosis of shed POS, whose degradation products are reused in the retinoid cycle. Retinoid cycle–derived all-trans-retinal (atRAL) is cytotoxic and induces ER stress in RPE cells and A2E, a major bis-retinoid fluorophore in RPE, has also been reported to impair RPE phagocytic function. In this study, we analyzed ER stress marker expression in middle-aged mice to capture early aging-related changes. As a result, ER stress marker proteins were significantly upregulated in the RPE-choroid earlier than in the neural retina in middle-aged eyes. The triggers for age-related ER stress induction in the RPE-choroid remain unclear, but this expression pattern was consistent with our previous findings, where mitochondrial dynamics and lipid droplet-associated proteins changed in the RPE-choroid, but not the retina. These results suggest that the RPE may be particularly sensitive to various stresses, including ER stress. ER stress is characterized by the acculturation of proteins in the lumen of the ER. To investigate the impact of ER stress on phagocytosis by RPE cells, we mainly treated the cells with Tm in vitro experiments. Both short-term treatment with 10 μg/ml Tm and long-term treatment with lower concentrations significantly reduced the phagocytic activity of ARPE - 19 and primary hRPE cells. A previous study using macrophages demonstrated that a 6-h treatment with 10 μg/ml Tm reduced phagocytic activity. These data suggest that when the demand to respond to unfolded proteins in the ER exceeds the cellular capacity, ER stress may trigger phagocytic dysfunction. Additionally, based on RPE's tendency to accumulate ER stress, it is hypothesized that ER stress may contribute to age-related phagocytic dysfunction. A detailed investigation is needed to reveal the relationship between ER stress upregulation and complex regulation of phagocytosis by RPE in vivo, however, our findings might suggest the possibility of resolving the underlying mechanism of phagocytic impairment not only in RPE but also in other phagocytic cells. During POS phagocytosis in the RPE, discard POS are internalized into cell and degraded within lysosomes, a process that requires proper lysosomal acidification maintained by vacuolar-type H + -ATPase (V-ATPase). In this study, ER stress induction caused lysosomal and mitochondrial dysfunction, with an early reduction in mitochondrial oxygen consumption following Tm treatment. Excessive Ca 2+ transfer from the ER to mitochondria disrupts mitochondrial membrane potential and impairs ATP production. Considering ATP is required for V-ATPase activity in the lysosome, ER stress-induced acute mitochondrial impairment could contribute to lysosomal dysfunction in RPE.
title: Age-dependent induction of ER stress in retinal pigment epithelium impairs phagocytosis via ADAM17-dependent MERTK shedding

text: In this study, ER stress induction caused lysosomal and mitochondrial dysfunction, with an early reduction in mitochondrial oxygen consumption following Tm treatment. Excessive Ca 2+ transfer from the ER to mitochondria disrupts mitochondrial membrane potential and impairs ATP production. Considering ATP is required for V-ATPase activity in the lysosome, ER stress-induced acute mitochondrial impairment could contribute to lysosomal dysfunction in RPE. Moreover, excessive ER stress disrupted lysosomal homeostasis by reducing the number of lysosomes in human trophoblasts. Our data indicated that ER stress might suppress direct and/or indirect lysosomal function, leading to impairment of POS phagocytosis. Organelle functions are tightly interconnected, and our previous studies demonstrated age-dependent alterations in mitochondrial dynamics and lipid homeostasis in murine RPE-choroid. Together with the present findings, these results suggest that organelle dysfunction may contribute to impaired POS phagocytosis in the RPE. Further studies are needed to clarify how age-related organelle dysfunction influences AMD pathogenesis. ER stress has been increasingly recognized as a therapeutic target for various diseases. Chemical chaperones, such as 4-PBA and tauroursodexycholic acid, are known to enhance the cell's activity to handle ER stress and have the potential to suppress the progression of ER stress-related disorders. In our study, treatment with 4-PBA attenuated Tm-induced phagocytic impairment and lysosomal dysfunction. These data may indicate that controlling ER stress with chemical drugs could be an effective approach. Originally, protein unfolding reactions are typically processed intracellularly, with chaperone proteins such as GRP78 and GRP94 involved in protein folding. To demonstrate the effectiveness of chaperone protein induction in conferring stress tolerance to ER stress-induced phagocytic dysfunction, we used ATF6n- and XBP1s-expression plasmids to induce chaperone proteins, confirming that they can improve phagocytosis. Collectively, the inhibition of ER stress by directly targeting unfolded proteins using chemical chaperones and activating the ER stress-suppressive system might be a novel strategy to improve age-related dysfunction of POS phagocytosis. MERTK is an essential factor in POS phagocytosis. MERTK plays a key role in the engulfment of discarded POS and functions directly in the RPE phagocytic process as a signaling molecule that triggers POS internalization in RPE. Indeed, RPE isolated from Mertk −/− mice have compromised phagocytic activity. In our study, under ER stress conditions, MERTK was cleaved, and the expression level of the extracellular domain of MERTK was significantly decreased. Additionally, Law et al. reported that soluble MERTK inhibits POS phagocytosis by acting as a decoy receptor. Considering that full-length MERTK on the plasma membrane could initiate POS uptake into the cell, the integrity of MERTK is essential to maintain the phagocytic activity of RPE. Our results indicated that ER stress could impair the protein integrity of MERTK, leading to phagocytic dysfunction. In addition, we confirmed the presence of full length-MERTK in medium sample and their expression level also increased by Tm treatment. Although it remains unclear whether full-length MERTK is released via extracellular vesicles, such as exosomes or plasma membrane-derived microvesicles, it would be interesting to investigate the detailed mechanisms by which full-length MERTK is secreted into the extracellular compartment.
title: Age-dependent induction of ER stress in retinal pigment epithelium impairs phagocytosis via ADAM17-dependent MERTK shedding

text: Our results indicated that ER stress could impair the protein integrity of MERTK, leading to phagocytic dysfunction. In addition, we confirmed the presence of full length-MERTK in medium sample and their expression level also increased by Tm treatment. Although it remains unclear whether full-length MERTK is released via extracellular vesicles, such as exosomes or plasma membrane-derived microvesicles, it would be interesting to investigate the detailed mechanisms by which full-length MERTK is secreted into the extracellular compartment. Because cells under high ER stress contain unfolded proteins that must be properly folded or degraded, ER stress-mediated MERTK shedding may serve as a protective mechanism to reduce cellular burden by limiting phagocytosis. In addition, we confirmed ER stress induction reduced the phosphorylation of FAK. In integrin αv–mediated phagocytosis, the activation of FAK is required to initiate POS internalization and to induce MERTK phosphorylation. Moreover, in endothelial cells, ER stress induction by Tm and Tg has been reported to downregulate FAK phosphorylation via tyrosine phosphatases and calcium signaling. These findings suggest that ER stress may broadly impair the overall POS internalization process. In terms of the mechanism of MERTK shedding, we identified ADAM17 as a key regulator in this phenomenon. A previous report by Thorp et al. showed that MERTK shedding requires ADAM17 in macrophages. Rzymski et al. reported that ER stress induces ATF4 expression, leading to ADAM17 transcription and shedding of the tumor necrosis factor receptor 1 in HeLa cells. In our in vitro study using RPE cells, Tm-induced ER stress promoted ADAM17 maturation. Furthermore, our data suggested that ER stress induction promoted 1) excessive Ca 2+ release from the ER via IP3R and 2) Ca 2+ -dependent ADAM17 maturation by Furin protease in the trans-Golgi (, C – F). These data indicated that ER stress triggered Ca 2+ overload, followed by MERTK shedding mediated by matADAM17, which contributed to phagocytic dysfunction. In the trans-Golgi network, the secretory pathway Ca 2+ /Mn 2+ -ATPase (SPCA) plays a crucial role in Ca 2+ uptake and influences the protease activity of Furin. Although the detailed mechanism by which ER stress induces furin activation remains unclear, it may be interesting to focus on the involvement of SPCA in this sequential mechanism. In addition, the proposed mechanism in this study was mainly based on findings from in vitro experiments using Tm, an inhibitor of N-linked glycosylation, as an ER stress inducer. Since N-linked glycosylation originally involved protein modification such as proper protein folding and stability, it will be necessary to further elucidate the relationship between ER stress and age-related phagocytic dysfunction using multiple experimental approaches, including strategies distinct from inhibition of N-linked glycosylation. In contrast to ER stress-induced cultured RPE cells, both preADAM17 and matADAM17 were elevated in the RPE-choroid tissue of middle-aged mice, although the maturation ratio remained unchanged. ER stress activates ADAM17 transcription via ATF4 in HeLa cells. In this study, severe ER stress induction by pharmaceutical treatment was required to induce phagocytic impairment in our in vitro experimental system, so we focused on the proteomic changes of ADAM17 under these conditions.
title: Age-dependent induction of ER stress in retinal pigment epithelium impairs phagocytosis via ADAM17-dependent MERTK shedding

text: In contrast to ER stress-induced cultured RPE cells, both preADAM17 and matADAM17 were elevated in the RPE-choroid tissue of middle-aged mice, although the maturation ratio remained unchanged. ER stress activates ADAM17 transcription via ATF4 in HeLa cells. In this study, severe ER stress induction by pharmaceutical treatment was required to induce phagocytic impairment in our in vitro experimental system, so we focused on the proteomic changes of ADAM17 under these conditions. The difference in the degree of ER stress between aged RPE-choroid tissue and pharmacologically induced ER-stressed RPE cells may account for the observed differences in ADAM17 expression. Considering that the matADAM17 possesses cleavage activity, the age-related upregulation of ADAM17 may contribute to the shedding of ectodomains from various substrates, including MERTK. It would be interesting to investigate whether increased ADAM17 expression in RPE is associated with age-related phagocytic dysfunction and could be a potential risk factor for the onset of AMD. In summary, our findings indicate that ER stress induction in RPE reduces phagocytic activity through multiple integrated mechanisms, including lysosomal dysfunction and MERTK shedding mediated by Ca 2+ -dependent ADAM17 maturation. Furthermore, this phenomenon may play a role in the pathogenesis of age-related disorders such as AMD.
