text: The pro-inflammatory cytokines play a critical role in OA progression. In order to determine whether IL-1β exerts its effect on chondrocytes, we observed the viability of the chondrocytes at different points (12, 24, and 48 h) after treatment with different concentrations of IL-1β (0, 5, 10, and 20 ng/ml). Results of the CCK-8 assay showed that the cell viability was significantly decreased after 24 and 48 h of treatment with 10 ng/ml and 20 ng/ml IL-1β (A). Therefore, we further investigated IL-1β-induced cell death in more detail. It has previously been shown that IL-1β induces apoptosis during OA progression. We assessed the level of apoptosis in chondrocytes after IL-1β induction. The results revealed that IL-1β treatment led to a dose-dependent increase in Annexin V/PI double-positive chondrocytes, indicating a link between IL-1β-induced cell death and the activation of apoptotic pathways. Furthermore, our studies demonstrated that the caspase inhibitor Z-VAD decreased IL-1β-induced chondrocyte death. However, this protection was limited, with a death rescue rate of merely approximately 30 % (B–C). These results imply the existence of additional mechanisms promoting cell death following IL-1β exposure. Notably, while assessing cell viability, we observed a significant formation of massive vacuoles instead of morphological changes typically associated with apoptosis (D and Additional file 1:). Transmission electron microscopy revealed the ultrastructural changes, including swollen ER and mitochondria, disrupted ER organization, and single-membrane vacuoles encircling intact nuclei in IL-1β-treated chondrocytes (E). The autophagy inhibitor 3-MA, the apoptosis inhibitor Z-VAD, the pyroptosis inhibitor MCC950, and the ferroptosis inhibitor Ferrostatin-1 were used to investigate whether IL-1β-induced vacuoles were associated with autophagy, apoptosis, pyroptosis, or ferroptosis. However, none of these inhibitors prevented the formation of IL-1β-induced vacuoles (F–G and Additional file 1:).We transfected IL-1β-treated chondrocytes with either a fluorescent mitochondrial marker (GFP-Mito) or an ER marker (DsRed-ER) to investigate the origin of vacuoles. Rather than GFP-Mito fluorescence, vacuoles colocalized precisely with DsRed-ER fluorescence (H–I). These findings suggest that the vacuoles induced by IL-1β originate from the ER.
title: SHP2-mediated ROS activation induces chondrocyte paraptosis in osteoarthritis and is attenuated by low-intensity pulsed ultrasound
section_title: IL-1β induces cytoplasmic vacuolization in chondrocyte

text: Given that cytoplasmic vacuolization is closely associated with paraptosis-like cell death, we presumed that IL-1β may induce the paraptosis in chondrocytes. Previous reports have shown that unfolded protein accumulation and ER stress are associated with paraptosis, including extensive vacuoles originating from the ER. Therefore, we next explored the effects of IL-1β intervention on the ER of chondrocytes. The experimental data indicated that IL-1β treatment triggered p-PERK activation and increased ATF4 and CHOP protein expression, thereby confirming IL-1β-induced ER stress in these cells (A and Additional file 1:). Paraptosis, a non-apoptotic cell death, requires protein synthesis. To further determine whether IL-1β induces paraptosis, we pretreated chondrocytes with CHX, an inhibitor that blocks protein synthesis, and found that CHX pretreatment significantly reduced IL-1β-induced vacuoles and ER dilatation (B–C). In line with this, pretreatment with CHX decreased IL-1β-induced upregulation of p-PERK, ATF4, and CHOP (D and Additional file 1:), indicating that IL-1β-induced ER stress was alleviated. Alix inhibits paraptosis without affecting apoptosis. A dose-dependent reduction in Alix protein levels was observed when IL-1β was administered (E and Additional file 1:). Moreover, exogenous overexpression of Alix in chondrocytes attenuated IL-1β-induced ER stress, cytoplasmic vacuolization, and cell death (F–I). Altogether, these results indicate that IL-1β induces paraptosis in chondrocytes, characterized by ER stress-mediated ER dilation, protein synthesis dependency, and Alix-dependent negative regulation, which collectively define its unique features.
title: SHP2-mediated ROS activation induces chondrocyte paraptosis in osteoarthritis and is attenuated by low-intensity pulsed ultrasound
section_title: IL-1β induces ER stress and consequent paraptosis in chondrocytes

text: Another characteristic of paraptosis is the activation of the MAPK pathway. Under pathological conditions, activation of the MAPK pathway can promote de novo protein synthesis, with a consequent increase in misfolded proteins and activation of ER stress, ultimately inducing the occurrence of paraptosis. The phosphorylated forms of MAPK were used to assess MAPK activation. IL-1β treatment resulted in a time-dependent increase in phosphorylation of MEK1/2 and ERK1/2 MAPK (A–B), indicating that IL-1β-induced MAPK activation promoted nascent protein synthesis. We then explored whether IL-1β-induced ER stress and paraptosis were mediated through MEK/ERK activation by using U0126, a MEK1/2 inhibitor. IL-1β-induced vacuolization and ER dilation in chondrocytes were significantly diminished by U0126 treatment (C–D). IL-1β-treated chondrocytes in the presence of U0126 showed less phosphorylation of MEK1/2 and ERK1/2, as well as less upregulation of p-PERK and CHOP (E–F). Additionally, U0126 mitigated the reduction in cell viability caused by IL-1β (G). In summary, these findings suggest that MAPK participated in the IL-1β-induced paraptosis in chondrocytes.
title: SHP2-mediated ROS activation induces chondrocyte paraptosis in osteoarthritis and is attenuated by low-intensity pulsed ultrasound
section_title: MAPK signalling pathway participate in IL-1β-induced paraptosis

text: To identify the key genes involved in IL-1β-induced paraptosis, we analyzed four datasets related to OA from the GEO database and the GeneCards database. We performed an intersection analysis between these datasets and the set of genes related to the MAPK pathway and ER stress in the GeneCards database, both of which are closely associated with paraptosis. This analysis identified 27 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) that were significantly upregulated in OA (p < 0.05) (A). Among these, we focused on PTPN11, which encodes the SHP2 tyrosine phosphatase, because it previously has been shown to be associated with OA progression and paraptosis. Complementing these findings, analysis of a publicly accessible single-cell RNA sequencing dataset revealed widespread PTPN1 1 mRNA expression across chondrocyte subtypes in articular cartilage tissue samples from patients with OA (Additional file 1:). We next treated human and rat chondrocytes with IL-1β and observed a significant upregulation of PTPN1 1 mRNA levels by qPCR (Additional file 1:). To delve deeper into the link between SHP2 and OA progression, we created a post-traumatic OA model through DMM surgery. Results from immunohistochemistry indicate that DMM surgery rats' cartilage contains significantly more SHP2-positive chondrocytes (B). Next, we used IL-1β to establish an inflammatory cell mode and assessed SHP2 expression levels in vitro. When the duration and concentration of IL-1β intervention increased, the expression of collagen type II 1 chain (COL2A1) and Aggrecan decreased, while the expression of matrix metallopeptidase 13 (MMP13), cyclooxygenase-2 (COX2), and inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) exhibited the opposite trend. Moreover, p-SHP2 and SHP2 expression also increased, especially at 24 h. Notably, p-SHP2 expression increased with IL-1β concentrations of 10 ng/mL, indicating that 10 ng/mL IL-1β for 24 h is sufficient to induce an inflammatory state in chondrocytes (Additional file 1:). To further validate the relationship between SHP2 and inflammatory chondrocytes, we regulated SHP2 expression at the gene level. First, western blots and qPCR were used to confirm the efficiency of SHP2 knockdown and overexpression (Additional file 1:). The results revealed that SHP2 knockdown downregulated the expression levels of catabolic markers MMP13, inflammation-related markers iNOS and COX2, and upregulated the expression levels of anabolic-related factors COL2A1 and Aggrecan in inflammatory chondrocytes (Additional file 1:). Conversely, SHP2 overexpression produced effects opposite to those observed with knockdown (Additional file 1:). Furthermore, the immunofluorescence assay revealed a similar trend, SHP2 knockdown reversed the increase of MMP13 fluorescence intensity and the decrease of COL2A1 fluorescence intensity induced by IL-1β (C–F), while overexpression had the opposite effect (Additional file 1:). Collectively, the findings suggested that SHP2 promotes an OA-like phenotype in chondrocytes and is positively correlated with OA progression. Research has shown that SHP2 is critically involved in paraptosis through its activation of MAPK pathways. Considering our findings that SHP2 is closely associated with OA progression, we hypothesized that SHP2 is involved in IL-1β-induced paraptosis in chondrocytes. To investigate this, we again regulated SHP2 at the gene expression level. The findings demonstrated that knocking down SHP2 significantly reduced IL-1β-induced vacuolization in chondrocytes (G).
title: SHP2-mediated ROS activation induces chondrocyte paraptosis in osteoarthritis and is attenuated by low-intensity pulsed ultrasound
section_title: SHP2 contributed IL-1β-induced OA-like chondrocytes phenotype and paraptosis

text: Research has shown that SHP2 is critically involved in paraptosis through its activation of MAPK pathways. Considering our findings that SHP2 is closely associated with OA progression, we hypothesized that SHP2 is involved in IL-1β-induced paraptosis in chondrocytes. To investigate this, we again regulated SHP2 at the gene expression level. The findings demonstrated that knocking down SHP2 significantly reduced IL-1β-induced vacuolization in chondrocytes (G). SHP2 knockdown also inhibited the IL-1β-induced elevation of p-ERK1/2, p-PERK, CHOP, and prevented the reduction in Alix levels (H and Additional file 1:). Furthermore, we found that SHP2 overexpression exacerbated IL-1β-induced loss of chondrocyte viability (Additional file 1:). The elevated ER stress levels observed with SHP2 overexpression were reversed by using the protein synthesis inhibitor CHX (I and Additional file 1:). To confirm the necessity of MAPK pathway activation for IL-1β-induced paraptosis, we utilized U0126. The results showed that U0126 effectively inhibited MAPK pathway activation and reduced ER stress levels (J and Additional file 1:). Collectively, the results of our study indicate that SHP2 is a critical target for IL-1β-induced paraptosis in chondrocytes.
title: SHP2-mediated ROS activation induces chondrocyte paraptosis in osteoarthritis and is attenuated by low-intensity pulsed ultrasound
section_title: SHP2 contributed IL-1β-induced OA-like chondrocytes phenotype and paraptosis

text: ROS production has been reported to mediate paraptosis. We speculated that ROS might contribute to IL-1β-induced chondrocyte paraptosis, given its close relationship to ER stress and MAPK activation. A DCFH-DA fluorescent probe was employed to assess ROS production. The results showed that IL-1β treatment increased ROS levels in chondrocytes, and with the addition of ROS scavenger NAC, ROS generation was suppressed (A–B and Additional file 1:). Furthermore, NAC treatment significantly reversed the IL-1β-induced up-regulation of p-ERK1/2, p-PERK, and ATF4 in chondrocytes (C and Additional file 1:), suggesting that ROS may act upstream of both ER stress and MAPK signaling cascades. IL-1β-induced changes in paraptosis-related features in chondrocytes, such as vacuolization, ER dilatation, and reduced Alix expression, were also reversed by NAC treatment (C–E). Moreover, ROS scavenging decreased inflammation and restored ECM homeostasis in chondrocytes (Additional file 1:). Taken together, these findings indicated that ROS generation contributed to IL-1β-induced paraptosis in chondrocytes. Mounting evidence demonstrates that SHP2 indirectly affects the redox state of cells by modulating various signaling pathways, including PI3K-Akt and MAPK, which affect ROS production. Therefore, we examined the effect of SHP2 on ROS levels in chondrocytes. We overexpressed SHP2 while simultaneously applying NAC treatment. The results indicated that NAC effectively eliminated excessive ROS produced in chondrocytes under IL-1β treatment combined with SHP2 overexpression (F–G), and also prevented ER stress levels and MAPK activation in paraptosis-related pathways (H and Additional file 1:). Together, these results indicated that SHP2 further promoted ROS generation and facilitated IL-1β-mediated chondrocyte paraptosis.
title: SHP2-mediated ROS activation induces chondrocyte paraptosis in osteoarthritis and is attenuated by low-intensity pulsed ultrasound
section_title: IL-1β-induced ROS generation contributes to paraptosis in inflammatory chondrocytes

text: We established a rat OA model to investigate the relationship between SHP2 and OA development. Intra-articular injection of AAV-KD- SHP2 was used to knock down the expression of SHP2 in the knee joint of rats, with AAV-Vector serving as a control. The rats were subjected to either Sham or DMM surgery three weeks after the AAV injection (A). The body weights of the groups were not significantly different (B). As compared to a control group, AAV injection significantly decreased SHP2 expression in cartilage (C–D). Micro-CT analysis revealed that, compared to sham group, the DMM group exhibited significant cartilage surface damage. In contrast, KD- SHP2 alleviated this damage (E). In the DMM group, H&E and Safranin O/Fast Green staining revealed cartilage degeneration, marked by proteoglycan loss and elevated OARSI scores. Notably, the KD- SHP2 group showed milder cartilage degeneration and lower OARSI scores after DMM compared to the Vector group (F–G). Furthermore, we investigated whether DMM and KD- SHP2 affect the ECM metabolic markers and paraptosis levels. A significant increase in MMP13 and CHOP expression was observed in the cartilage of the DMM group, that decreased after KD- SHP2, whereas COL2A1 and Alix showed a reverse trend (H–I). Intriguingly, in contrast to Sham group, rats subjected to DMM surgery displayed decreased mechanical thresholds, which were alleviated following KD- SHP2, indicating that KD- SHP2 effectively mitigated pain in OA rats (Additional file 1:). Next, we used the TreadScan gait analysis system to measure gait abnormalities and footprint disruptions. We analyzed three gait parameters: stance time, average print area, and stance pressure. The results showed that both stance time and average print area of the DMM group were significantly shorter than Sham group, while KD- SHP2 could partially improve these metrics (Additional file 1:), suggesting a positive effect of KD- SHP2 on gait abnormalities caused by OA. Collectively, these results demonstrated that KD- SHP2 attenuated the cartilage degeneration in the DMM model and alleviated the level of paraptosis in vivo.
title: SHP2-mediated ROS activation induces chondrocyte paraptosis in osteoarthritis and is attenuated by low-intensity pulsed ultrasound
section_title: SHP2 knockdown alleviates cartilage degeneration in post-traumatic OA rats

text: For the purpose of determining the optimal intensity of LIPUS intervention for inflammatory chondrocytes, we applied diverse intensities of the intervention. Intensities of 30 mW/cm 2, 45 mW/cm 2, and 60 mW/cm 2 were applied for 20 min to chondrocytes. The results demonstrated that while 30 mW/cm 2 LIPUS showed limited suppression of iNOS expression, it significantly alleviated inflammation and maintained ECM homeostasis by enhancing Aggrecan expression, a core cartilage ECM component, and reducing COX2 levels, a key inflammatory enzyme, highlighting its integrated therapeutic efficacy. Furthermore, 30 mW/cm 2 LIPUS treatment for 20 min also attenuated ER stress, as evidenced by decreased protein levels of p-PERK and CHOP (A and Additional file 1:). These findings suggested that LIPUS intervention at 30 mW/cm 2 for 20 min considerably restored the ECM homeostasis of chondrocytes and inhibited ER stress. For the subsequent experiments, an intensity of 30 mW/cm 2 for 20 min was selected as the intervention condition. The qPCR analysis confirmed that LIPUS was effective in inflammatory chondrocytes (B). The IF assay also showed the same results as above, as evidenced by an increase in COL2A1 fluorescence intensity following LIPUS treatment compared to IL-1β intervention, while a decrease in MMP13 fluorescence intensity (C–F). According to the research, SHP2 plays a vital role in the polarity orientation and force response within the rigid cellular matrix. SHP2 may perceive and respond to mechanical stimulation brought by LIPUS, thereby exerting a series of biological effects in chondrocytes. Therefore, firstly, we explored the effect of LIPUS on SHP2. We evaluated the expression of SHP2 and MAPK pathway-related markers. The findings revealed that IL-1β treatment elevated p-SHP2, p-MEK1/2, and p-ERK1/2, whereas LIPUS application significantly reduced the phosphorylation of both SHP2 and MEK1/2 (G and Additional file 1:). Further research was conducted using LIPUS to elucidate the therapeutic effects of LIPUS on OA through regulation of SHP2. Results showed that when oe- SHP2 and IL-1β were combined, COL2A1 expression was further reduced while MMP13, COX2, and iNOS expression increased compared to chondrocytes exposed to oe- SHP2 or IL-1β alone (H and Additional file 1:). Based on these findings, LIPUS effectively restored the balance of ECM homeostasis in chondrocytes and mitigated the inflammatory progression induced by SHP2 overexpression. Next, we preliminary deliberated on the effects of LIPUS on the paraptosis of chondrocytes. We implemented LIPUS intervention on inflammatory chondrocytes in the context of overexpression of SHP2 and examined the MAPK pathway and ER stress levels implicated in paraptosis. The results demonstrated that, compared to the IL-1β group, SHP2 overexpression augmented p-MEK1/2 and p-ERK1/2, and enhanced p-PERK, ATF4, and CHOP, while LIPUS exhibited therapeutic effect and precluded the upregulation of these proteins. In addition, Alix, a key protein for inhibiting paraptosis, was significantly down-regulated after OE- SHP2, and LIPUS significantly reversed this adverse result (I and Additional file 1:). Interestingly, cytoplasmic vacuolization was not alleviated immediately after the imposition of the LIPUS intervention, but was significantly suppressed at 24 h of the intervention (J). Moreover, 20 min of LIPUS intervention followed by 36 h of culture alleviated IL-1β-induced cell death in chondrocytes (K).
title: SHP2-mediated ROS activation induces chondrocyte paraptosis in osteoarthritis and is attenuated by low-intensity pulsed ultrasound
section_title: LIPUS relieves chondrocytes paraptosis via SHP2 and MAPK pathway

text: In addition, Alix, a key protein for inhibiting paraptosis, was significantly down-regulated after OE- SHP2, and LIPUS significantly reversed this adverse result (I and Additional file 1:). Interestingly, cytoplasmic vacuolization was not alleviated immediately after the imposition of the LIPUS intervention, but was significantly suppressed at 24 h of the intervention (J). Moreover, 20 min of LIPUS intervention followed by 36 h of culture alleviated IL-1β-induced cell death in chondrocytes (K). Collectively, these data implied that LIPUS exerted a notable therapeutic effect on inflammatory chondrocytes by modulating SHP2 and possibly alleviating paraptosis.
title: SHP2-mediated ROS activation induces chondrocyte paraptosis in osteoarthritis and is attenuated by low-intensity pulsed ultrasound
section_title: LIPUS relieves chondrocytes paraptosis via SHP2 and MAPK pathway

text: As LIPUS promotes cartilage repair, we investigated its effects on OA in vivo. First, rats were intra-articularly injected with AAV9-OE- SHP2 to increase expression of SHP2, while a control group received AAV-Vector. The rats were either operated on with Sham or DMM three weeks after injection. Following this, LIPUS treatment was initiated 2 weeks post-surgery and continued for a duration of 6 weeks (A). A statistically significant difference in body weight was not observed between the groups (Additional file 1:). The results confirmed that AAV effectively transduced chondrocytes in the articular cartilage, significantly increasing SHP2 expression (B–C). Furthermore, the micro-CT image of the tibial plateau showed that the subchondral bone surface in the Sham group and the group treated with LIPUS alone was smooth, while the surface in the DMM group was rough, with numerous scattered holes of various sizes. More severe wear and destruction occurred after SHP2 overexpression, which was alleviated by LIPUS treatment (D). Meanwhile, the H&E and Safranin O/Fast Green staining results demonstrated a marked reduction in cartilage degeneration after LIPUS treatment, as reflected by a lower OARSI score compared to the DMM group or the DMM + OE- SHP2 group (E–F). Similarly, immunohistochemistry data showed that p-SHP2, MMP13, and CHOP levels were further aggravated in AAV-OE- SHP2 -treated rats, but markedly suppressed in LIPUS treatment. Conversely, the expression of COL2A1 and Alix exhibited the opposite trend (G and Additional file 1:). Additionally, we investigated the levels of inflammatory factors and discovered that DMM surgery and SHP2 overexpression elevated serum IL-1β and TNF-α, while LIPUS treatment resulted in a reduction of these inflammatory factors (Additional file 1:). We also evaluated the mechanical pain in the rats. Among the groups, there were no significant differences in baseline mechanical pain. Compared with the Sham group, rats undergoing DMM surgery exhibited reduced mechanical thresholds, while LIPUS intervention inhibited the DMM-induced decrease in mechanical thresholds (Additional file 1:). Continuing with the previously mentioned gait analysis method, we observed that the DMM group exhibited significant gait abnormalities. In the DMM group, the affected side exhibited significant reductions in stance time (%) and average print area (sq.mm) compared to the Sham group, whereas LIPUS partially attenuated these reductions induced by DMM and OE- SHP2 (Additional file 1:). In summary, these results suggest that LIPUS treatment alleviated cartilage degeneration, reduced paraptosis, and diminished inflammation in rats with post-traumatic OA.
title: SHP2-mediated ROS activation induces chondrocyte paraptosis in osteoarthritis and is attenuated by low-intensity pulsed ultrasound
section_title: LIPUS protects against DMM-induced cartilage degeneration via SHP2

text: Paraptosis is implicated in a range of physiological and pathological processes, including embryogenesis, the progression of neurodegenerative diseases, and the advancement of cancer. However, the precise role of paraptosis in OA onset and progression remains poorly understood. Our study demonstrated that IL-1β can induce paraptosis in chondrocytes by promoting excessive ROS production, with SHP2 identified as a potential target. Additionally, low-intensity pulsed ultrasound (LIPUS) was shown to slow the progression of OA by reducing SHP2 levels and suppressing paraptosis (see mechanism diagram). In the context of OA, inflammatory factors such as IL-1β can activate a variety of intracellular signaling pathways and enhance ROS production. Numerous lines of evidence indicate that elevated ROS levels can be detrimental to chondrocytes, acting as signaling intermediaries that facilitate chondrocyte destruction, and that modulating ROS levels has emerged as a strategy for combating OA. In our study, we reported that IL-1β induces ROS in cultured chondrocytes. Previous studies showed that SHP2 plays a pivotal role in regulating the generation of ROS and modulating the cellular response to oxidative stress. SHP2 can trigger alterations in cellular metabolism by activating specific signaling pathways, such as ERK activation in macrophages, which enhances ROS production, and inhibiting p-JNK and NOX4 in gastric cancer cells, which modulates ROS levels. Additionally, SHP2 may augment mitochondrial metabolism, leading to increased mitochondrial ROS production and subsequent oxidative stress. Furthermore, SHP2 affects the function of cellular antioxidant defense systems. For example, SHP2 affects NADPH in endothelial progenitor cells via the PI3K-Akt pathway, and S-glutathionylation of critical residues of SHP2 drives ROS1 activity and affects GPX1 function. Both NADPH and GPX1 functions are integral to managing oxidative and reductive stress, and disruption of this balance may lead to elevated ROS levels. In our study, IL-1β triggered ROS production in chondrocytes, and SHP2 exacerbated ROS accumulation, which is consistent with recent studies emphasizing ROS targeting to chondrocytes and the influence of SHP2 on redox status. A key finding of our study is that IL-1β is capable of inducing chondrocyte paraptosis. Although some characteristics have been described, including the accumulation of ROS, the activation of MAPK, ionic homeostasis disruption, disruption of protein synthesis, and ER stress, the underlying mechanisms of paraptosis are still not clear. Here, we systematically elaborated on the aforementioned process in the context of IL-1β-induced paraptosis. ROS accumulation is known to be associated with paraptosis, and our findings indicate that elevated ROS levels in inflammatory chondrocytes act as the initiating factor for paraptosis activation. Increased ROS levels have been demonstrated to inhibit proteases, resulting in the accumulation of misfolded proteins and ER stress. ER stress has been implicated in the progression of paraptosis, and we identified multiple indicators of ER stress in both IL-1β-treated and SHP2-overexpressing chondrocytes. The vacuolization witnessed during paraptosis is considered to be an osmotic imbalance elicited by the accumulation of misfolded proteins in the ER, resulting in water influx from the cytoplasm and thereby expanding the luminal space of the ER into vacuoles, which indicates that ER stress might contribute to the process of cell death.
title: SHP2-mediated ROS activation induces chondrocyte paraptosis in osteoarthritis and is attenuated by low-intensity pulsed ultrasound

text: ER stress has been implicated in the progression of paraptosis, and we identified multiple indicators of ER stress in both IL-1β-treated and SHP2-overexpressing chondrocytes. The vacuolization witnessed during paraptosis is considered to be an osmotic imbalance elicited by the accumulation of misfolded proteins in the ER, resulting in water influx from the cytoplasm and thereby expanding the luminal space of the ER into vacuoles, which indicates that ER stress might contribute to the process of cell death. Here, we also explored the function of MAPK in paraptosis. First, the MEK1/2 inhibitor effectively prevented IL-1β-induced ER stress, ER-derived vacuoles, and paraptosis in chondrocytes. Second, the use of six datasets enabled the identification of the MAPK pathways-activated factor SHP2 as an important target of IL-1β, which was reported to regulate the process of paraptosis. Knocking down SHP2 or MAPK pathway inhibitors can significantly reduce chondrocyte paraptosis. Nevertheless, the contribution of intracellular mitochondrial dysfunction and ionic imbalance to IL-1β-induced chondrocyte death cannot be excluded, as these mechanisms have been demonstrated in other disease models. A key finding of this study is that inflammatory chondrocytes undergo paraptosis, with SHP2 gene expression regulation playing a crucial role, offering important insights into the pathogenesis of OA. Research has shown that LIPUS can slow the progression of OA and other inflammatory conditions. It has been documented that LIPUS can down-regulate the phosphorylation of ERK1/2 within the MAPK signaling pathway, thereby facilitating cartilage repair in OA. Additionally, LIPUS can mitigate ER stress by attenuating the unfolded protein response, facilitating the enhancement of osteogenic capacity, and alleviating periodontal inflammation. Our study found that LIPUS treatment attenuated the MAPK signaling pathway, ER stress, and ER-derived vacuoles in chondrocytes, all of which play significant roles in paraptosis. Our attention is also concentrated on the mechanical shift of LIPUS. According to the mechanobiological transduction theory, LIPUS influences cell structure and movement, inducing mechanotransduction and cavitation effects, which initiate cellular and molecular signaling events that determine biological responses and cell fate. Mechanosensitive receptors convert mechanical signals into biological signals; further identification of mechanosensitive proteins will help fully elucidate the mechanotransduction mechanisms mediated by LIPUS. Notably, SHP2 is a key molecule in mechanotransduction, responding to mechanical stimuli by sensing external forces exerted on the cell and converting them into biological signals that influence cellular functions. However, it has not been reported whether LIPUS modulates OA progression through SHP2. In this context, our novel finding is that LIPUS suppresses SHP2 phosphorylation and promotes its degradation by modulating mechanical stress on chondrocytes. Furthermore, LIPUS inhibits paraptosis via the SHP2/MAPK pathway.We propose that LIPUS exerts its effects through several mechanisms. First, it modulates cellular signaling pathways, such as SHP2/MAPK, affecting protein synthesis, metabolic responses, and downstream cellular processes. Second, LIPUS may gradually alleviate vacuolization by regulating the ER stress response and activating repair mechanisms like autophagy.
title: SHP2-mediated ROS activation induces chondrocyte paraptosis in osteoarthritis and is attenuated by low-intensity pulsed ultrasound

text: In this context, our novel finding is that LIPUS suppresses SHP2 phosphorylation and promotes its degradation by modulating mechanical stress on chondrocytes. Furthermore, LIPUS inhibits paraptosis via the SHP2/MAPK pathway.We propose that LIPUS exerts its effects through several mechanisms. First, it modulates cellular signaling pathways, such as SHP2/MAPK, affecting protein synthesis, metabolic responses, and downstream cellular processes. Second, LIPUS may gradually alleviate vacuolization by regulating the ER stress response and activating repair mechanisms like autophagy. Third, it may play a role in restoring cellular energy metabolism and mitochondrial function by modulating pathways involved in oxidative stress, such as reducing ROS levels. Given that these regulatory processes require time to activate and exert their effects, this may explain why cytoplasmic vacuolization was significantly alleviated 24 h post-LIPUS intervention, rather than immediately after treatment. Nevertheless, more specific experiments are required to validate the effect of LIPUS on paraptosis. This study has certain limitations. First, the induction of paraptosis typically depends on broad cellular stress responses, and no completely specific inducers have been identified. Therefore, we cannot compare the differences between IL-1β-induced paraptosis and that induced by specific inducers, highlighting an important area for future investigation. Second, while we explored the paraptosis of chondrocytes induced by LIPUS via the influence of SHP2, we suspect that other unknown mechanisms may also be at play, such as mitochondrial dysfunction and ion imbalance. The precise mechanisms involved need to be clarified through further detailed studies.
title: SHP2-mediated ROS activation induces chondrocyte paraptosis in osteoarthritis and is attenuated by low-intensity pulsed ultrasound

text: In the present study, we demonstrated that IL-1β induced elevated ROS levels in chondrocytes, triggering chondrocyte paraptosis. SHP2 exacerbated redox imbalance, increased the production of misfolded proteins through the SHP2/MAPK axis, induced ER stress and ER-derived cytoplasmic vacuolization, and further triggered OA chondrocyte paraptosis. Furthermore, the application of LIPUS at specific intensities and durations regulated SHP2, suppress cartilage cell inflammation, and paraptosis. These findings have significant implications for understanding the pathogenesis and potential treatment of OA.
title: SHP2-mediated ROS activation induces chondrocyte paraptosis in osteoarthritis and is attenuated by low-intensity pulsed ultrasound

text: Atherosclerosis (AS) is a chronic and progressive inflammatory disorder with high morbidity and mortality worldwide, potentially resulting in serious clinical complications such as myocardial infarction and strokes. AS is characterized by the accumulation of fibrofatty lesions within the intima. The development of AS is influenced by various risk factors, including elevated low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, aging, hyperglycemia, and nicotine exposure. Within atherosclerotic lesions, three primary cell types have been identified: vascular endothelial cell (VEC), vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMC), and macrophage. It is worth mentioning that when monocytes, VSMC, and other cells phagocytose large amounts of lipids, their cytoplasm becomes filled with lipid droplets. Under a light microscope, these cells exhibit a foamy appearance, so they are named foam cells. Nevertheless, as of the present date, the mechanisms through which specific cell types contribute to the pathogenesis of AS remain inadequately elucidated. This lack of understanding has considerably complicated efforts to prevent and manage the condition. Cell death plays a pivotal role in maintaining homeostasis in all living organisms. Dysregulation of cell death, whether through excessive or insufficient process, can contribute to a range of human diseases, including cancer, neurodegenerative disorder, autoimmune diseases, and infections. The Nomenclature Committee on Cell Death (NCCD) classifies cell death into two categories: accidental cell death (ACD) and regulated cell death (RCD). RCD is often referred to as programmed cell death (PCD) under physiological conditions. ACD is characterized by the immediate and destructive death of cells due to unforeseen assaults or injuries, whereas RCD is governed by specific molecular mechanisms. Therefore, RCD can be considered a core event in various pathophysiological processes. And RCD presents a promising target for pharmacological interventions in therapeutic applications, which has attracted the attention of an increasing number of researchers. Numerous studies have revealed that various types of RCD are involved in the onset and advancement of AS. This review aims to provide a thorough overview of different types of RCD that are implicated in the key cellular components involved in AS, specifically VEC, VSMC, and macrophages. The objective is to deepen the understanding of the cellular mechanisms underlying AS and to explore potential pharmacotherapeutic strategies for its prevention and management.
title: Distinct types of regulated cell death in atherosclerosis

text: Apoptosis represents a well-characterized type of RCD, which can be categorized into intrinsic and extrinsic pathways. The intrinsic pathway, mediated by mitochondrial mechanisms, is activated by a variety of stimuli including cytokine, hypoxia, radiation, growth factor deprivation and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress. These stimuli upregulate the expression of pro-apoptotic proteins such as BH3-interacting domain death agonist (Bid), B-cell lymphoma 2 (BCL-2) modifying factor (BMF), p53 upregulated modulator of apoptosis (PUMA), BCL-2-interacting mediator of cell death (BIM), and BCL-2 associated agonist of cell death (BAD). These pro-apoptotic protein interact with anti-apoptotic proteins such as BCL-2 and BCL2 related protein A1 (BCL2A1), resulting in the release BCL-2 antagonist/killer (BAK) and BCL-2-associated X protein (BAX) to promote mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization (MOMP) and the subsequent release of pro-apoptotic factors, including cytochrome c (Cyto-C), second mitochondrial activator of caspases (SMAC) and high-temperature requirement A serine peptidase 2 (HTRA2), apoptosis-inducing factor (AIF) and endonuclease G (EndoG). In detail, Cyto-C binds to apoptotic peptidase activating factor 1 (APAF1) and pro-Caspase-9, leading to the formation of apoptosome, which activates Caspase-9 and the executioner Caspases-3/6/7, eventually initiating the apoptotic process. Concurrently, SMAC exacerbates apoptosis by repressing the X-linked inhibitor of apoptosis (XIAP), an anti-apoptotic protein that can attenuate the activity of executioner Caspases-3/6/7. It's important to note that these executioner caspases facilitate apoptosis by activating DNase and Rho-associated protein kinase 1 (ROCK-1), which are responsible for chromatin condensation and DNA fragmentation, and membrane blebbing, respectively. Following these events, apoptotic cells are fragmented into smaller structure known as apoptotic bodies (ABs). Additionally, instead of depending on caspases, AIF and EndoG can induce apoptosis independently of caspase by translocating to the nucleus, where they cleave DNA, thereby contributing to the apoptotic process. The extrinsic apoptotic pathway is predominantly mediated by two types of receptors on the cell surface. One is death receptors (DRs), which recruit adaptor proteins via death domains (DDs) and then bind pro-Caspase-8 to form a death-inducing signaling complex (DISC), culminating in the activation of Caspase- 8. The other is pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), which interact with pathogen associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) to activate Caspases-9/12. Both receptors ultimately trigger the activation of executioner Caspases-3/6/7. Importantly, accumulating evidence revealed that AS is associated with apoptosis across various cell types, including VEC, VSMC, and macrophages.
title: Distinct types of regulated cell death in atherosclerosis

text: Previous research has demonstrated that VEC apoptosis is involved in the early stages of AS. High glucose (HG) upregulates cyclooxygenase 2 (COX2) through phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)/Akt-nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) signaling pathway to activate Caspase-3 and induce endothelial cell (EC) apoptosis. Furthermore, oxidized low-density lipoprotein (ox-LDL), which is recognized by DRs, promotes EC apoptosis via NF-κB/lectin-type oxidized LDL receptor 1 (LOX-1) pathway. Moreover, exposure to radiation causes DNA fragment, which activates the ataxia telangiectasia-mutated (ATM) gene and DNA-dependent protein kinase (PK), leading to the phosphorylation of p53 and subsequent cell cycle arrest and ultimately EC apoptosis. Additionally, radiation can also provoke the generation of ceramide derived from sphingomyelin, facilitated by active tumor necrosis factor (TNF) and extracellular acidic sphingomyelinase. The process subsequently result in cell membrane dysfunction and EC apoptosis through activating stress-activated protein kinase 1 (SEK1), c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) and c-Jun. Although the specific role of EC apoptosis during the above-mentioned event remains unclear, it is reasonable to hypothesize that the accumulation of apoptotic cells may contribute to a diminished capacity for self-renewal and AS. Under physiological conditions, minor endothelial damage is typical repaired through the recruitment of white blood cells, which facilitate the formation of a fibrin network, thereby preventing leukocytes accumulation within the tunica intima. Nevertheless, under pathogenic circumstances, instead of ameliorating injuries, ECs are more susceptible to rupture and hemorrhage, leading to the formation of thrombosis. While small blood clots are generally resolved through digestion and dissolution, larger thrombi can obstruct blood flow, affecting capillaries, veins, aorta and other blood vessels. This obstruction can result in serious conditions, including cerebral infarction and myocardial infarction, which are classified as acute symptoms of advanced AS. The thrombosis associated with EC apoptosis is triggered by relocating phosphatidylserine (PtdSer) to the cell surface to enhance pro-coagulant properties while diminishing anticoagulant factors. What's worse, exposure to pathogenic factors lead to the upregulation of leukocyte adhesion molecules, such as intercellular cell adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1) and vascular cell adhesion molecule-1 (VCAM-1), on the cell surface of EC. This up-regulation facilitates the adhesion of circulating monocytes, neutrophils and lymphocytes. In addition, sustained damage to EC results in the loss of vascular integrity and the increase of vascular endothelium permeability, thereby ox-LDL and monocytes gain access to the tunica intima, where monocytes differentiate into fully developed macrophages, which subsequently engulf excess ox-LDL and transform into foam cells. Foam cells, as characteristic pathological cells found in atherosclerotic plaques, play a crucial role in the onset and progression of AS, contributing to the formation, development, and instability of plaques. Additionally, the proliferation and migration of VSMC from tunica media to tunica intima, along with the formation of extracellular matrix (ECM), are driven by growth factors and active components secreted by dysfunctional VEC. The evidence mentioned above suggest that apoptosis can affect the structure and function of VEC, thus participating in the occurrence and progression of AS.

Additionally, the proliferation and migration of VSMC from tunica media to tunica intima, along with the formation of extracellular matrix (ECM), are driven by growth factors and active components secreted by dysfunctional VEC. Research has demonstrated that Caspase-8 deletion leads to a reduction in apoptosis. Moreover, the loss of endothelial Caspase-8 causes hemorrhage, not by triggering apoptosis, but instead by eliciting mixed lineage kinase domain-like protein (MLKL)-dependent necroptosis. Due to the pharmacological or genetic inactivation or depletion of caspases, there is a shift from apoptosis to necroptosis in VEC. However, whether solely inhibiting apoptosis is an effective therapeutic approach for the treatment of AS requires further research.

text: The protective fibrous cap of atherosclerotic plaques is primarily composed of VSMC and a relatively intensive ECM containing elastin, proteoglycans and collagen. The collagen present in the fibrous cap is predominantly synthesized by VSMC, which are essential for preserving the stability of AS plaques and offering protection against AS. In VSMC, ox-LDL promotes the translocation of Fas to the cell membrane, further inducing apoptosis. In addition, the interactions between VSMC and EC, as well as between VSMC and macrophages, also contribute to VSMC apoptosis. Mechanically, nitric oxide (NO) produced by EC interacts with reactive oxygen species (ROS) to generate peroxynitrite, which subsequently leads to mitochondrial dysfunction, caspases activation, and apoptosis in VSMC. Furthermore, NO derived from macrophage enhances the interactions between Fas and Fas ligand (FasL), thereby promoting VSMC apoptosis. The complex interactions may trigger a cascade of reactions throughout the development of AS. This underscores the critical importance of early intervention in this process. Evidence has revealed a correlation between VSMC apoptosis and the progression of AS. Over time, the initial fatty streaks consisting of VSMC evolve into fibroatheromas characterized by a cell-free lipid core, indicating an increase in the number of apoptotic VSMC as AS lesions advance. What's more, VSMC apoptosis is preferentially observed in inflammatory environments. In contrast to other cell types, VSMC exhibits a heightened resistance to Fas-elicited apoptosis due to the initial sequestration of Fas/tumor necrosis factor receptor (TNFR) 1 by the Golgi apparatus. Upon exposure to inflammatory cytokines such as interleukin (IL)-1β, TNF-α, interferon (IFN)-γ, ox-LDL and NO, Golgi apparatus facilitates the translocation of Fas to the cell membrane to promote apoptosis. This process can initiate a detrimental cycle, as the accumulation of apoptotic VSMC may trigger secondary necrosis and the release of additional inflammatory cytokines. The consequences of VSMC apoptosis are evident in the structural integrity of AS plaques, which are characterized by thinner fibrous caps due to reduced collagen production, larger necrotic cores, increased plaque vulnerability, and calcification. Vascular calcification is observed in the tunica intima, tunica media and cardiac valves, with calcification in tunica intima being particularly associated with atherosclerotic diseases. This calcification contributes to the instability of atherosclerotic plaques and the formation of microcalcifications, which can exacerbate plaque rupture by compromising the mechanical integrity of the fibrous cap. In sum, the inhibition of VSMC apoptosis represent a promising therapeutic strategy for AS. However, it is important to recognize that excessive suppression of apoptosis may lead to abnormal VSMC proliferation, which could exacerbate AS by facilitating hyperplasia in the tunica intima. Therefore, due to the complexities involved in accurately regulating the degree of VSMC apoptosis, the endeavor to target VSMC apoptosis as a treatment modality for AS remains a considerable challenge.
title: Distinct types of regulated cell death in atherosclerosis

text: In the early stages of AS, macrophage apoptosis contributes to the reduction of lesion size and the suppression of inflammation, a process that is largely supported by the proficient phagocytic functions of these immune cells. However, as the disease advances, the phagocytic capacity, commonly referred to as efferocytosis, diminishes within mature plaques. This decline, coupled with the accumulation of apoptotic cells, exacerbates inflammation, ultimately leading to plaque necrosis or rupture, which is often observed in cases of acute luminal thrombosis. That is to say, macrophage apoptosis plays a significant role throughout the progression of AS, encompassing initiation, growth, rupture, and calcification. Various stimuli can induce macrophage apoptosis, with ox-LDL being the most prevalent trigger. Ox-LDL enters macrophages via pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), including scavenger receptor class A (SRA), CD36, and LOX-1, or through the CD36/toll-like receptor (TLR) 4/TLR6 trimer complex. Within the lysosome, the cholesterol ester component of LDL can be hydrolyzed into free cholesterol by lysosomal acid lipase (LAL). In the context of AS, free cholesterol accumulates in the lysosome, leading to the formation of cholesterol crystals, which activate NLR family pyrin domain-containing protein 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome. This activation induces ER stress, subsequently transforming macrophages into foam cells. Additionally, ferrylhemoglobin can induce macrophage apoptosis through its interaction with cluster of differentiation 163 (CD163), which also triggers ER stress. To mitigate ER stress, the unfolded protein response (UPR) is activated to decrease the synthesis of misfolded proteins. However, prolonged exposure to ER stress can result in abnormal UPR activation, ultimately leading to the activation of caspases and the induction of apoptosis. The elucidation of the distinct mechanisms of action associated with various stimuli will promote the implementation of targeted interventions, ultimately contributing to the postponement or mitigation of AS. A significant complication associated with AS is vascular calcification, which is also linked to the apoptosis of macrophages. Similar to VSMC, apoptotic macrophages release extracellular vesicles (ECVs), including ABs and MVs. These ECVs, which are situated within ECM, can interact with collagen and bind to hydroxyapatite through electrostatic forces. Additionally, they can facilitate the formation of HA via a membrane complex involving annexin V, PtdSer, and S100A9/MRP14, which promotes the entry of inorganic phosphate (Pi) and calcium into the ECVs. Furthermore, VSMCs that exhibit osteoblast-like characteristics are indicative of vascular calcification. Notably, the transformation of VSMC into an osteoblast-like phenotype during ER stress can be induced by osteogenic factors secreted by macrophage-derived foam cells. As macrophage apoptosis may initially serve a protective role in early AS lesions, inhibiting macrophage apoptosis in advanced plaques becomes necessary due to the compromised efferocytosis and the accumulation of apoptotic cells as AS progresses. Taken together, the upstream regulatory mechanisms of apoptosis and the crosstalk between different types of cells during AS are complex. Moreover, the apoptosis of VEC, VSMC, and macrophages in AS should not be viewed as isolated events; rather, they are interrelated processes. It is essential to consider the interactions among these cell types when identifying potential therapeutic targets for the management of AS.

text: Autophagy is responsible for the degradation and recycling of damaged organelles, misfolded proteins, and various forms of cellular debris. Autophagy is classified into four distinct types: macroautophagy, chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA), microautophagy, and crinophagy. Among these, macroautophagy, commonly referred to simply as autophagy, is the most extensively researched form. It involves the formation of a double-membrane structure known as the autophagosome, which encapsulates cytoplasmic constituents, including damaged organelles and misfolded proteins. Subsequently, the autophagosome fuses with a lysosome to create an autolysosome, wherein the contents are subjected to degradation and recycling. This mechanism is vital for maintaining cellular homeostasis and facilitating responses to stress. CMA represents a selective autophagic process wherein specific proteins that possess a KFERQ-like motif are recognized by chaperone proteins, such as heat shock cognate 70 (Hsc70). These proteins are then translocated directly across the lysosomal membrane via the lysosomal-associated membrane protein 2A (LAMP-2A) receptor. CMA is critical for the degradation of particular cytosolic proteins and plays a significant role in cellular quality control and stress response. Microautophagy, on the other hand, entails the direct engulfment of small portions of the cytoplasm by the lysosome through invagination or protrusion of the lysosomal membrane. This process is characterized by its less selective nature compared to macroautophagy and is integral to the continuous turnover of cytoplasmic components, thereby contributing to cellular homeostasis and the response to nutrient deprivation. Compared of the extensively study with macroautophagy and CMA, microautophagy has received much less attention. Lastly, crinophagy is a specialized form of autophagy that involves the direct fusion of secretory granules with lysosomes for degradation. This process is particularly significant in endocrine and exocrine cells, as it aids in regulating the turnover of secretory granules and maintaining cellular homeostasis. Crinophagy ensures the efficient degradation and recycling of excess or aged secretory granules. In short, autophagy is an essential cellular mechanism that contributes to the maintenance of cellular homeostasis. In the absence of specific clarification, the term "autophagy" typically denotes macroautophagy.

text: Under conditions of nutrient-rich, the active mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) inhibits autophagy by obstructing the interaction between AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) and unc-51 like autophagy-activating kinase 1 (ULK1), thereby hindering the formation and maturation of autophagosomes. Conversely, during periods of glucose starvation, AMPK is activated, which facilitates autophagy by inhibiting mTOR and directly phosphorylating ULK1. It suggested that autophagy in VEC plays a vital role in preserving endothelial function and mitigating inflammation, both of which are critical components in the initial phases of AS. Research indicates that autophagy modulates inflammatory responses through the degradation of damaged mitochondria, thereby preventing the release of mitochondrial DNA, which has the potential to trigger inflammation. Enhanced autophagy has been shown to significantly reduce chronic vascular inflammation, diminish plaque area, and inhibit AS. Additionally, partial inhibition of glycolysis in VEC results in a decrease in the expression level of adhesion molecules, such as VCAM-1 and ICAM-1, in an autophagy-dependent manner, thus providing a protective effect against AS. That is to say, the regulation of autophagy has the potential to impact both inflammation and endothelial function, thereby influencing the onset and progression of AS.
title: Distinct types of regulated cell death in atherosclerosis

text: Similarly, AMPK is also activated in VSMC with glucose starvation. Then, activated AMPK modulates the activity of beclin-1, a pivotal regulator of autophagy to facilitate the formation of autophagosomes. Specifically, autophagy serves to protect VSMC from apoptosis triggered by oxidized lipids and various stressors, thereby contributing to the stability of atherosclerotic plaques. In a study involving ApoE -/- mice, the knockout of the autophagy-related gene (ATG) 7 in VSMC, following exposure to 7-ketocholesterol, resulted in increased VSMC apoptosis, enhanced plaque growth, medial disruption, and the formation of aneurysms. In short, autophagy in VSMC plays a critical role in ensuring cell survival and maintaining plaque stability. However, autophagy induced by platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) leads to a loss of the contractile phenotype in VSMC, which is crucial for their migration and proliferation. Additionally, it has been observed that nicotine activates the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs)/ROS/NF-κB signaling pathway in VSMC, which subsequently upregulates beclin-1, initiates autophagosome formation, and accelerates the transition from a contractile to a synthetic phenotype, ultimately promoting the progression of AS. It is evident that mitigating excessive autophagy in VSMC is significantly advantageous in postponing the advancement of AS.
title: Distinct types of regulated cell death in atherosclerosis

text: The macrophage-specific overexpression of transcription factor EB (TFEB), which serves as a master regulator of autophagy and lysosome biogenesis, has been shown to confer atheroprotection by ameliorating autophagy dysfunction and decreasing overall plaque burden. Consistently, ox-LDL activates the mTOR pathway, thereby inhibiting the nuclear translocation of TFEB, which results in the downregulation of ATG5 and a subsequent reduction in autophagic activity. Furthermore, arsenic trioxide has been found to induce autophagy in macrophages through the promotion of ROS generation, which facilitates the nuclear translocation of TFEB and the inhibition of the PI3K/Akt/mTOR signaling pathway, a critical regulator of autophagy. Research has demonstrated that arsenic trioxide effectively reduces early atherosclerotic lesions in ApoE -/- mice by enhancing macrophage autophagy, thereby suggesting its potential as a therapeutic agent in the treatment of AS. These studies demonstrated that autophagy in macrophages plays a protective role in the context of AS. Existing research indicates that under normal CMA, the NLRP3-Hsc70 complex is subject to degradation by lysosomes through the LAMP-2A receptor. In instances of defective CMA, this degradation process is compromised, resulting in the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome and subsequent secretion of IL-1β and IL-18, which contribute to inflammation and the progression of AS. Notwithstanding, the involvement of CMA in AS remains inadequately understood. In sum, autophagy exhibits a dual function, serving both protective and harmful roles contingent upon the disease's progression and the particular cell types involved. A comprehensive understanding of these mechanisms may offer valuable insights for the development of therapeutic strategies aimed at modulating autophagy pathways in AS.

text: Necroptosis, a form of regulated necrosis, is initiated by diverse stimuli, including TNF-α, FasL, TLR ligands, TNF-related apoptosis-inducing ligand (TRAIL), and IFN. Notably, the necroptosis pathway executed by MLKL in response to TNF-α is considered the canonical pathway. The interaction of TNF-α with its receptor, TNFR, activates the receptor and facilitates the recruitment of receptor-interacting protein kinase (RIPK) 1 and TNF receptor type 1-associated death domain (TRADD). TRADD subsequently recruits TNF receptor-associated factor (TRAF)-2/5 and cellular inhibitors of apoptosis (cIAP)-1/2, leading to the formation of complex I. This complex significantly influences cellular outcomes, including cell survival, apoptosis, and necroptosis, highlighting its crucial role in AS. Cell survival is associated with RIPK1 ubiquitination, which promotes the release of NF-κB, thereby activating inflammatory and prosurvival genes. In instances where cIAP-1/2 are inhibited, RIPK1 undergoes de-ubiquitination and dissociates from complex I. The transition from cell survival to either apoptosis or necroptosis is contingent upon the activation or inhibition of Caspase-8, which is closely linked to the formation of complex IIa and complex IIb, respectively. The second outcome, commonly referred to as complex IIa-mediated apoptosis, involves a complex comprising RIPK1, fas-associated death domain (FADD), TRADD, pro-Caspase-8, and the cellular FLICE-like protein long isoform (c-FLIP) heterodimer, as well as pro-Caspase-8 homodimer. Interestingly, complex IIb, consisting of RIPK1, RIPK3, c-FLIP, pro-Caspase-8, and FADD, also plays a role in promoting apoptosis following the activation of RIPK1 and Caspase-8. In contrast, the inhibition of Caspase-8 leads to the induction of necroptosis. Specifically, when both c-FLIP and Caspase-8 are inhibited, self-phosphorylated RIPK1 interacts with RIPK3 through the RIP homotypic interaction motif, resulting in RIPK3 phosphorylation. This phosphorylation subsequently activates and oligomerizes MLKL, which exposes its helical bundle. Ultimately, the phosphorylated MLKL oligomers translocate to the plasma membrane, where they facilitate the opening of calcium and sodium channels. Furthermore, the N-terminal four-helix bundle structural domain of MLKL contributes to plasma membrane permeability by altering osmotic pressure and membrane potential, leading to the formation of cellular micropores and ultimately resulting in necroptosis characterized by cell swelling, disruption, and lysis. Concurrently, the release of damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) and cytokines from necroptotic cells through these pores significantly exacerbate the inflammatory response. As of the present time, the precise mechanisms by which these three distinct fates are regulated remain ambiguous. This uncertainty has presented significant challenges for a comprehensive understanding of the implications of various types of cell death in pathological contexts, as well as for the advancement of innovative therapeutic strategies aimed at targeting these processes. Interestingly, the RIPK3/Ca 2+ -calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII) signaling pathway represents a novel mechanism of necroptosis. Instead of modifying MLKL, RIPK3 activates CaMKII through the phosphorylation of the Thr287 residue or by enhancing the activity of glycogen phosphorylase, glutamate-ammonia ligase, and glutamate dehydrogenase 1. This activation leads to an increased production of ROS and the subsequent oxidation of the Met281/282 residues of CaMKII.

text: Interestingly, the RIPK3/Ca 2+ -calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII) signaling pathway represents a novel mechanism of necroptosis. Instead of modifying MLKL, RIPK3 activates CaMKII through the phosphorylation of the Thr287 residue or by enhancing the activity of glycogen phosphorylase, glutamate-ammonia ligase, and glutamate dehydrogenase 1. This activation leads to an increased production of ROS and the subsequent oxidation of the Met281/282 residues of CaMKII. Furthermore, both oxidized CaMKII (ox-CaMKII) and phosphorylated CaMKII (p-CaMKII) promote calcium influx by phosphorylating ryanodine receptor 2, a principal calcium release channel located on the sarcoplasmic reticulum, as well as the mitochondrial calcium uniporter. This results in mitochondrial calcium accumulation and dysfunction, which subsequently decrease adenosine triphosphate (ATP) synthesis and increase ROS generation, further instigating necroptosis, characterized by significant organelle swelling. It is important to note that MLKL membrane pore formation is not involved in this process. Therefore, CaMKII activation by phosphorylated RIPK3 elevates mitochondrial Ca 2+ levels, ultimately resulting in the necroptosis of VSMC and contributing to the pathogenesis of cardiovascular diseases.
title: Distinct types of regulated cell death in atherosclerosis

text: In VEC, hypoxia induced SUMOylation of FADD promotes the FADD-RIPK1-RIPK3 complex formation and necroptosis. In VSMC of atherosclerotic plaques, there is an increase in the expression of necroptotic proteins and the release of inflammatory cytokines. Recent findings have identified a novel mechanism whereby cigarette tar induces ER stress, subsequently resulting in cytoplasmic Ca 2+ overload. This overload triggers VSMC necroptosis through the Ca 2+ /CaMKII-RIPK3 pathway. In macrophages, ox-LDL accumulates in the sub-endothelial space, which subsequently promotes the expression of RIPK3 and MLKL via enhancing ROS, leading to an increase in the formation of a necrotic core, heightened plaque vulnerability, and ultimately, plaque rupture. Notably, dihydrotanshinone I (DHT) has been shown to effectively counteract the effects of ox-LDL by mitigating oxidative stress, thereby inhibiting RIPK3-mediated necroptosis in macrophages and contributing to the stabilization of vulnerable plaques. Stimulation with lipopolysaccharide (LPS)/IFN-γ leads to the activation of hypoxia-inducible factor 1α, which in turn causes mitochondrial dysfunction and depletion of ATP, thereby promoting macrophage necroptosis and accelerating the progression of AS. The elevated levels of RIPK1, RIPK3, and MLKL observed in atherosclerotic plaques and various cellular types, as previously mentioned, consistently indicate that necroptosis may be involved in different stages of AS.
title: Distinct types of regulated cell death in atherosclerosis
section_title: Necroptosis of VEC, VSMC, and macrophages in AS

text: Research has shown that RIPK1 is significantly up-regulated in both early and less advanced atherosclerotic lesions in humans and murine models. Inhibition of RIPK1 has been associated with a reduction in plaque size and stabilization of plaques in ApoE-deficient mice. It is also important to highlight that RIPK1 primarily enhances the inflammatory response through the NF-κB signaling pathway. Thus, the downregulation of RIPK1 has potential ability to mitigate the progression of atherosclerotic lesions by suppressing inflammation during the early stages of the disease. Furthermore, the inhibition of necroptosis through the application of necrostatin-1 (Nec-1) or GSK872 significantly enhances the viability of tar-induced VSMC. RIPK3 siRNA, rather than RIPK1, is responsible for reversing the decrease in VSMC viability induced by cigarette tar. In addition, research has indicated that in ApoE/RIPK3 double-knockout mice, inflammation within atherosclerotic plaques is diminished, advanced atherosclerotic lesions and necrotic core areas are reduced, and life expectancy is prolonged. However, these effects are not observed during the earlier stages of plaque development. Given that both the knockdown and knockout of RIPK3 confer protection against AS, it appears that RIPK3 represents a promising target for therapeutic intervention in AS. Additionally, MLKL is integral to initiate necroptosis and inflammatory response. MLKL deficiency in advanced plagues attenuated necroptosis and necrotic cores, whereas lipid content was still increased in the lesion, which might mainly be attributed to accumulated lipid and defective efferocytosis in macrophage. Therefore, targeting MLKL, the executors of necroptosis, may exhibit a protective role against AS. In terms of targeting CaMKII, contrary to the prevailing belief that CaMKII functions downstream of RIPK3, one study revealed that the inhibition of CaMKII significantly reduced the levels of RIPK3, MLKL, and phosphorylated MLKL (p-MLKL), thereby enhancing necroptosis in tar stimulated VSMC. This finding suggests that CaMKII may act as an upstream kinase, highlighting the complex role of CaMKII in its interactions and its ambiguous effects on RIPK3. GRP78, a marker of ER stress, was found to be up-regulated in VSMC derived from the aortic roots of tar-treated mice. ER stress inhibitor 4PBA improved cell viability by downregulating RIPK3, MLKL, and p-MLKL, indicating that tar-induced ER stress is a critical factor in VSMC necroptosis and the progression of AS. Given that ER stress can lead to Ca 2+ overload in both mitochondria and the cytoplasm, CaMKII may be activated by elevated Ca 2+ level to initiate necroptosis. Therefore, it is reasonable to hypothesize that the inhibition of either CaMKII or ER stress could be advantageous in mitigating AS by reducing necroptosis. In sum, the upstream regulatory mechanisms and the downstream effects of the necroptosis during AS are not known well. Nonetheless, necroptosis plays a crucial role in the inflammatory processes associated with AS and should be considered when developing strategies to target necroptosis executors for the protection against AS.
title: Distinct types of regulated cell death in atherosclerosis
section_title: Targeting the executors of necroptosis to attenuate AS

text: RCD and the efficient removal of dead and dying cells, a process referred to as efferocytosis, are essential for maintaining homeostasis in multicellular organisms. Impairments in efferocytosis can exacerbate the progression of AS, resulting in plaque enlargement, plaque rupture, acute coronary syndromes, and even stroke. The process of efferocytosis can be delineated into four distinct stages: the 'find-me' phase, the bridging phase connecting effector cells with target cells, the 'eat-me' phase, and the resolution phase. During the 'find-me' phase, apoptotic cells release chemoattractants, known as find-me signals, which include low, approximately equimolar concentrations of ATP, uridine triphosphate, and soluble fractalkine. These signals serve to attract circulating monocytes and macrophages to the vessel wall. Infiltrated macrophages subsequently engage in the efferocytosis of apoptotic cells through the utilization of efferocytosis receptors, such as MerTK, which interact with PtdSer present on the surface of apoptotic cells, either directly or via bridging molecules like growth arrest-specific 6 (GAS6). Furthermore, the process of engulfment can be enhanced by the interaction of LDL receptor-related protein 1 (LRP1) with calreticulin. The resolution phase encompasses a variety of processes, including the ingestion of apoptotic cells, suppression of inflammation, and preparation for ongoing efferocytosis. Specifically, following the ingestion of apoptotic cells, macrophages release anti-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-10 and transforming growth factor-β (TGFβ) which serve to inhibit leukocyte migration, thereby establishing a negative feedback loop. Additionally, LRP1 is known to activate peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-γ (PPARγ), facilitating the efflux of the ingested material. The four stages mentioned above have crosstalk through complex mechanisms, which poses great challenges to the exploration of targeted interventions. To enhance the process of efferocytosis, macrophages increase intracellular glucose and promote a transition from cytoplasmic arginine to putrescine, which results in actin polymerization, a necessary step in efferocytosis. Numerous potential mechanisms contributing to impaired efferocytosis in AS have been identified, including dysfunctional phagocytes and/or apoptotic cells that exhibit reduced susceptibility to efferocytosis.
title: Distinct types of regulated cell death in atherosclerosis

text: The pathophysiology of AS is characterized by an accumulation of lipids in the sub-endothelium, which heightens the incidence of apoptotic and necrotic cell death, thereby triggering an inflammatory cascade that exacerbates atherosclerotic disease. This complex process is influenced by various factors, such as excessive ATP signaling, as well as diminished levels of MerTK, GAS6, and 'eat-me' signals (e.g., calreticulin) associated with efferocytosis. In short, the ability of phagocytes, primarily macrophages, to engage in efferocytosis is impaired, resulting in the accumulation of apoptotic and necrotic tissue within the atherosclerotic plaque. This accumulation contributes to the expansion of the necrotic core, exacerbates luminal stenosis, heightens plaque inflammation, and increases the risk of plaque rupture or erosion.
title: Distinct types of regulated cell death in atherosclerosis

text: Specifically, the modulation of macrophage metabolism through the inhibition of ATP citrate lyase has been shown to enhance efferocytosis and promote apoptosis, thereby contributing to the stabilization of atherosclerotic plaques. Furthermore, statins, inhibitors of 3-hydroxy-3-methyl glutaryl coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase, not only reduce cholesterol level and inflammation but also inhibit RhoA, a negative regulator of efferocytosis that is overexpressed in atherosclerotic lesions. Additionally, it has been reported that myeloid cluster of differentiation 147 (CD147) enhances the secretion of proinflammatory cytokines and late apoptosis through the TRAF6-inhibitor of κB kinase (IKK)-interferon regulatory factor 5 (IRF5) signaling pathway, while simultaneously inhibiting efferocytosis by repressing the phosphorylation of signal transducer and activator of transcription (STAT) 6 to suppress GAS6 in response to LPS/IFN-γ stimulation. These mechanisms contribute to the expansion of necrotic cores and the exacerbation of AS. Notably, the experiment conducted in ApoE -/- mice with humanized CD147 transgenic expression exhibits atheroprotective effects comparable to those of traditional lipid-lowering therapies. Above research implies that enhancing efferocytosis presents a viable pharmacological strategy for the treatment of AS. Concurrently, necrotic cells upregulate 'don't-eat-me' signals (e.g., CD47) to evade macrophage-mediated efferocytosis. Additionally, ox-LDL competes with calreticulin for binding to LRP1. Furthermore, 7-ketocholesterol present in ox-LDL inhibits the catabolism of phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate [PtdIns(4,5)P2] and actin polymerization, thereby obstructing macrophage efferocytosis and exacerbating inflammation, which further propels the progression of AS. Although anti-CD47 antibodies have demonstrated potential in decreasing plaque burden, their clinical use is limited by possible adverse effects. As a result, research has increasingly focused on signal regulatory protein α (SIRPα), whose deletion has been associated with atheroprotective effects without the aforementioned complications. The mechanisms and roles of efferocytosis during the process of AS have been illustrated. It indicates that focusing on efferocytosis may present certain limitations, including inadequate specificity, a high incidence of adverse reactions, and restricted efficacy in combating AS. Future research must address these challenges to achieve significant advancements in this field.
title: Distinct types of regulated cell death in atherosclerosis

text: Ferroptosis represents a form of PCD that is predominantly initiated by the iron overload, lipid peroxidation, and disturbances in redox homeostasis. This phenomenon is marked by a loss of plasma membrane integrity, swelling of the cytoplasm and organelles, shrinkage of mitochondria, and a decrease in the number of mitochondrial cristae, whereas the morphology of the nucleus remains relatively intact. Iron uptake by cells occurs through two primary mechanisms. The first mechanism involves the interaction of Fe 3+ -transferrin with transferrin receptor (TfR) located on the cell surface. The second mechanism entails the diffusion of Fe 2+ into the cell, facilitated by small molecules such as ATP, citrate, and ascorbate. Concurrently, excess iron can be exported into the plasma via ferroportin (Fpn) to maintain iron homeostasis. Fpn can be internalized and degraded by hepcidin, which may result in iron overload. These processes collectively contribute to an increase in the labile iron pool (LIP) level. From a physiological perspective, ferritin, which has the capacity to store up to 4500 Fe(III) atoms, oxidizes Fe 2+ to Fe 3+, thereby preventing the accumulation of ferrous iron in the cytosol and the growth of the LIP. However, when the buffering capacity of ferritin is exceeded or when lipid peroxides are not effectively cleared, polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs), which serve as lipid mediators and are essential components of membrane lipids, become susceptible to lipid peroxidation. The continuous oxidation and depletion of PUFAs can compromise membrane integrity, ultimately resulting in plasma membrane rupture and ferroptosis. In other words, interfering with iron ions can regulate ferroptosis and thus may have an impact on a variety of pathophysiological processes. The processes involved in the formation and propagation of lipid peroxidation mediated by iron encompass both nonenzymatic and enzymatic pathways. The nonenzymatic pathway is characterized by a series of free radical-driven reactions that are initiated by the Fenton reaction, which occurs in the presence of Fe 2+ sourced from LIP and hydrogen peroxide (H 2 O 2) released from mitochondria. This sequence ultimately leads to the generation of phospholipid hydroperoxide (PLOOH) and lipid radicals (PL·), thereby facilitating the amplification of the radical chain reaction. Concurrently, the enzymatic pathways involve various enzymes, including lipoxygenases, acyl-CoA synthetase long-chain family member 4 (ACSL4), and lysophosphatidylcholine acyltransferase 3 (LPCAT3), among others. Notably, during the process of ferroptosis, the acyl chains of Phospholipids undergo oxidation. Specifically, arachidonic acid (AA), a member of PUFAs, is located in the membrane of phosphatidylethanolamine (PE), and can be released as free AA after stimulation. ACSL4 facilitates the synthesis of AA-CoA derivatives, and then LPCAT3 is responsible for the conjugation of PE-AA. Subsequently, lipoxygenases in conjunction with ROS catalyze the peroxidation of PE-AA, resulting in the formation of PE-AA-OOH, which contributes to the intensification of ferroptosis. Additionally, the degradation of PLOOH can produce reactive and toxic aldehydes, such as 4-hydroxy-2-nonenal (4-HNE) or malondialdehyde (MDA), further promoting ferroptosis. Overall, there are numerous molecules involved in the process of ferroptosis, which brings challenges to subsequent drug research and development as well as mechanism exploration.
title: Distinct types of regulated cell death in atherosclerosis

text: Subsequently, lipoxygenases in conjunction with ROS catalyze the peroxidation of PE-AA, resulting in the formation of PE-AA-OOH, which contributes to the intensification of ferroptosis. Additionally, the degradation of PLOOH can produce reactive and toxic aldehydes, such as 4-hydroxy-2-nonenal (4-HNE) or malondialdehyde (MDA), further promoting ferroptosis. Overall, there are numerous molecules involved in the process of ferroptosis, which brings challenges to subsequent drug research and development as well as mechanism exploration. Specifically, coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) is reduced to ubiquinol by ferroptosis suppressor protein-1 (FSP-1). Ubiquinol subsequently captures lipid peroxyl radicals, thereby inhibiting the formation of lipid peroxides. Furthermore, glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), a member of the selenium-dependent glutathione peroxidase family, also plays a crucial role in antioxidation by converting toxic lipid hydroperoxides into less harmful lipid alcohols. However, the activity of GPX4 can be compromised by a reduction in its substrate, glutathione. Therefore, it is important to recognize that redox imbalance significantly contributes to the accumulation of lipid peroxidation and the initiation of ferroptosis. The synthesis of GSH depends on cystine/glutamate antiporter (system Xc −), which comprises the light chain SLC7A11 (also known as xCT) and the heavy chain SLC3A2 (4F2hc), facilitating the import of extracellular cystine and the export of intracellular glutamate. Additionally, GSH can be regenerated from oxidized glutathione with the assistance of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate hydrides (NADPH). Research has demonstrated that (1S,3R)-RAS-selective-lethal compound 3 (RSL3) inhibits GPX4, leading to the induction of lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis. Concurrently, erastin, a well-established trigger of ferroptosis, not only inhibits GSH production by targeting system Xc − but also enhances membrane permeability and mediates NADPH oxidation through voltage-dependent anion channels 2/3. This cascade results in ROS production and mitochondrial damage, ultimately culminating in ferroptosis.
title: Distinct types of regulated cell death in atherosclerosis

text: Emerging evidence suggests that ferroptosis observed in VEC, VSMC, and macrophages may be involved in AS In mouse aortic ECs, inhibiting ferroptosis may alleviate AS by attenuating lipid peroxidation and improving endothelial function. In VSMC, cigarette smoke extract, a well-established inducer of AS, has been found to induce ferroptosis, accompanied with augmented atherosclerotic inflammatory factors. In macrophages, an imbalance in iron metabolism induces ferroptosis, thereby exacerbating the progression of AS. More and more evidence demonstrates that ferroptosis is involved in AS, which has brought new ideas for the prevention and treatment of AS.
