section_title: Ferroptosis of VEC, VSMC and macrophages in AS

text: TfR1, functioning in iron uptake and ferritin synthesis, has been shown to be significantly elevated in foamy macrophages derived from the intimal lesions of human carotid atheromas. This increase contributes to the progression and rupture of atherosclerotic plaques. The silencing of TfR1 has been demonstrated to inhibit ferroptosis, while a reduction in the expression of ferritin or Fpn is likely to facilitate the occurrence of ferroptosis. Furthermore, hepcidin has been implicated in elevating intracellular iron concentrations and exacerbating inflammatory AS by promoting iron storage, which in turn induces ferroptosis. Additionally, iron chelators such as desferrioxamine (DFO) facilitate the removal of iron overload through effective transport and excretion, resulting in a reduction of the pro-inflammatory factor monocyte chemotactic protein-1 (MCP-1) and a decrease in macrophage markers such as CD68. This action confers a protective effect against AS without altering total cholesterol and triglyceride levels in ApoE -/- mice. Furthermore, an imbalance in iron homeostasis has been shown to accelerate AS formation through ferroptosis in macrophages. It is noteworthy that DFO is a Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved, naturally occurring iron chelator commonly used to treat transfusion-induced iron overload. Previous studies have confirmed that iron overload exacerbates AS, and support the clinical applications of iron restriction in iron-loaded individuals to mitigate iron-aggravated AS. Therefore, administrating DFO to regulate the concentration of iron ions might be a direct and effective strategy for the treatment of AS, which requires further clinical evidence.

section_title: Targeting iron overload during ferroptosis to attenuate AS

text: Ferrostatin-1 (Fer-1) and liproxstatin-1 (Lip-1) have been recognized as effective inhibitors of ferroptosis, functioning by trapping chain-carrying peroxyl radicals and mitigating inflammatory responses to decrease lipid hydroperoxides, rather than inhibiting 15-lipoxygenase-1. In contrast, other antioxidant agents, such as tocopherols and tocotrienols (vitamin E), counteract ferroptosis through the suppression of lipoxygenase activity. Collectively, these antioxidants have been demonstrated to confer protective effects against AS by reducing lipid peroxidation. Apparently, by regulating lipid peroxidation, an important pathway through which ferroptosis causes cell death, it will be beneficial to alleviate various cell damages and delay AS.
title: Distinct types of regulated cell death in atherosclerosis
section_title: Targeting lipid peroxidation during ferroptosis to attenuate AS

text: Research has indicated that there is a reduction in GPX4 level in AS. Conversely, the overexpression of GPX4 has been shown to mitigate ferroptosis by effectively scavenging lipid peroxidation and reducing the size of atherosclerotic lesions in ApoE -/- mice. Additionally, Fer-1, a lipid ROS scavenger, has been identified as a compound that counteracts both ferroptosis and AS in high-fat diet-fed ApoE -/- mice by enhancing the levels of xCT and GPX4. Furthermore, prenyldiphosphate synthase subunit 2, an essential enzyme involved in the synthesis of CoQ10, has been found to activate the nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway, thereby inhibiting ROS production and reducing iron level, which ultimately alleviates ferroptosis and AS. These data suggested that regulating the redox imbalance in the process of ferroptosis will have a potential protective effect on AS.

section_title: Targeting redox imbalance during ferroptosis to attenuate AS

text: Nrf2, an antioxidant transcription factor, maintains redox homeostasis by regulating a variety of downstream antioxidant target genes. A study demonstrated that the administration of Micheliolide (MCL), the active metabolite of parthenolide, significantly reduced plaque area and lipid deposition while increasing collagen level, thereby providing protection against AS. This protective effect is attributed to MCL's ability to competitively bind to the Arg483 site of Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (KEAP1), promoting the dissociation of KEAP1 from Nrf2. Consequently, Nrf2 enhances the expression of GPX4 and xCT by binding to their respective promoters, leading to a reduction in iron content and lipid ROS level in KEAP1 wild-type (KEAP1-WT) macrophages compared to those with the Arg483 mutation (KEAP1-R483S, where Arg is mutated as Ser). Actually, recent studies have confirmed that Nrf2 activation significantly inhibits ferroptosis by regulating antioxidant-related genes in VEC, VSMC, and macrophages. These researches suggests that the inhibition of ferroptosis through Nrf2-mediated genetic regulation may help prevent AS. However, one study found that Nrf2 knockout reduced ROS level and iron overload in the substantia nigra and striatum of aging mice by regulating ferroportin 1 expression of brain microvascular ECs. The inconsistent results may be attributed to various factors, including different cell types, animal strains, modeling methods, and the extent of damage. These contradictory findings suggest that Nrf2 may have a dual role in iron-induced ferroptosis, creating uncertainty regarding the efficacy of targeting Nrf2 and ferroptosis for the treatment of AS. Taken together, iron overload, lipid peroxidation, and redox imbalance are implicated in ferroptosis, presenting a promising target for combating AS.

section_title: Targeting genetic regulation during ferroptosis to attenuate AS

text: Pyroptosis represents a specific type of regulated necrosis that is initiated by PAMPs or DAMPs including viral cytosolic double-stranded DNA (dsDNA), LPS, ATP, cholesterol crystals, mitochondrial ROS and DNA, as well as ER stress and particulate matter. The process of pyroptosis is governed by two primary molecular mechanisms. The first is the Caspase-1-mediated canonical pathway, which involves an inflammasome composed of sensor proteins, the adaptor protein apoptosis-associated speck-like protein containing a CARD (ASC), and the effector protein Caspase-1. Among the sensor proteins, NLRP3 is the most extensively studied; it features a pyrin domain (PYD) at its N-terminus. ASC also contains a PYD structure along with a caspase-recruitment domain (CARD), while Caspase-1 possesses a CARD structure. Upon detection of stimuli, NLRP3 binds to ASC, which subsequently recruits and activates Caspase-1. Under physiological conditions, NLRP3 is maintained in an inactive ubiquitinated form, which is inadequate for the assembly of the canonical inflammasome. The activation of inflammasomes requires two distinct signals: the priming signal, which is initiated by IFN signaling and TLR ligands, leads to the upregulation of inflammasome components (pro-IL-1β, pro-IL-18, NLRP3, ASC, pro-Caspase-1) through the NF-κB pathway. Concurrently, the deubiquitination of NLRP3, facilitated by the Lys63-specific deubiquitinase BRCA1/BRCA2-containing complex subunit 3 (BRCC3), represents an additional priming mechanism. The activating signal, which can be triggered by various stimuli such as potassium efflux, calcium influx, and ROS, promotes the assembly and activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome. Upon activation of Caspase-1, this enzyme not only processes inactive precursors of IL-1β and IL-18 into their mature forms but also cleaves gasdermin D (GSDMD) into its active N-terminal fragment (GSDMD-N). The GSDMD-N fragment subsequently translocates to the cell membrane, where it oligomerizes to form membrane pores, leading to cell swelling and rupture, thereby facilitating the secretion of mature IL-1β and IL-18, as well as potassium ions, which further amplifies the inflammatory response. Additionally, there exists a non-canonical pathway mediated by Caspase-11 in mice and Caspase-4/5 in humans. In this pathway, LPS directly activates Caspase-4/5/11, which then cleaves GSDMD into GSDMD-N. Beyond its previously mentioned functions, GSDMD-N also serves to activate the NLRP3 inflammasome, thereby enhancing the Caspase-1-dependent canonical pathway. Actually, pyroptosis ultimately boosts the inflammatory level of the body, thus affecting the progression of various diseases. Recent research has identified novel pathways in pyroptosis that can be categorized based on their dependence on caspases. Investigations have demonstrated that various stimuli, such as chemotherapy agents, TNF-α, bacterial infections, activate apoptotic caspases, which subsequently cleave gasdermin proteins to trigger pyroptosis. Furthermore, nerve injury-induced protein 1 (Ninj1), previously recognized as a small adhesion molecule involved in inflammation and tumor suppression, has been implicated in the execution of pyroptosis. Although moderate pyroptosis plays a beneficial role in bacterial immunity, excessive pyroptosis can lead to the aberrant activation of inflammasomes, which in turn may result in the over-activation of Caspase-1.

text: Furthermore, nerve injury-induced protein 1 (Ninj1), previously recognized as a small adhesion molecule involved in inflammation and tumor suppression, has been implicated in the execution of pyroptosis. Although moderate pyroptosis plays a beneficial role in bacterial immunity, excessive pyroptosis can lead to the aberrant activation of inflammasomes, which in turn may result in the over-activation of Caspase-1. This excessive activation can trigger a significant inflammatory response, potentially contributing to the onset and progression of various diseases, including AS.

text: In VEC, pyroptosis exists in the initial phase of the disease, resulting in the release of inflammatory cytokines, which facilitate the recruitment of monocytes. In VSMC, pyroptosis promotes the release of procoagulant molecules, diminishes the integrity of the fibrous cap, and further destabilizes the plaque to cause the complications associated with AS. In macrophages, pyroptosis exists in the advanced stages of AS, exacerbating inflammation and contributing to the formation of a necrotic core, thereby compromising plaque stability. The substantial body of evidence indicates that pyroptosis plays a significant role in the pathogenesis of AS.
title: Distinct types of regulated cell death in atherosclerosis
section_title: Pyroptosis of VEC, VSMC, and macrophages in AS

text: A recent study has demonstrated that forkhead box P1 (Foxp1), a modular transcriptional repressor with high expression in VEC, experiences a significant decrease in atherosclerotic and athero-susceptible endothelium. This reduction in Foxp1 correlates with an upregulation of components associated with the endothelial inflammasome, such as NLRP3, Caspase-1, and IL-1β, which are known to influence the expression of adhesion molecules like VCAM-1. Consequently, this leads to the adhesion and migration of macrophages to the vascular wall, thereby contributing to the progression of AS. The data first verify an atheroprotective role of endothelial Foxp1, identifying it as a novel regulator of endothelial inflammasome activation in atherogenesis. Consequently, this discovery offers opportunities for therapeutic intervention of atherosclerotic diseases. Furthermore, Rho family GTPase 3 (Rnd3) has been shown to inhibit EC pyroptosis induced by ox-LDL through the Rnd3/TRAF6/NF-κB/NLRP3 signaling pathways. Specifically, Rnd3 inhibits the ubiquitination of K63-linked TRAF6 while promoting the ubiquitination of K48-linked TRAF6 which results in the suppression of NF-κB activation and the degradation of TRAF6. In macrophages, tranilast has been reported to modulate NLRP3 ubiquitination, thereby antagonizing the assembly and activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, which ultimately protects against vascular inflammation and AS. Additionally, VX-765, a Caspase-1 inhibitor, significantly reduces pyroptosis and IL-1β production in VSMC challenged by ox-LDL during atherogenesis, alleviating AS without affecting plasma lipoprotein level. Moreover, Tongxinluo (TXL), a commonly utilized traditional Chinese medicine, counteracts the pro-atherosclerotic effects of ox-LDL by inhibiting pyroptosis through the down-regulation of Caspase-1, leading to decreased levels of cleaved-Caspase-1, pro-GSDMD, cleaved GSDMD, NLRP3, IL-18, and IL-1β in mouse aortic ECs. Lastly, IRF1 is crucial in plaque instability and vulnerability, as it activates Caspase-1 to modulate macrophage pyroptosis. Since pyroptosis is usually triggered by the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, interventions aimed at this molecule have demonstrated promising outcomes in alleviating AS.
title: Distinct types of regulated cell death in atherosclerosis
section_title: Targeting NLRP3 inflammasome during pyroptosis to attenuate AS

text: The AIM2 inflammasome has been found to facilitate the induction of pyroptosis through the ASC-Caspase-1 pathway, which exacerbates the burden of atherosclerotic lesions. Furthermore, the nuclear dsDNA released from necrotic cells also activates the AIM2 inflammasome, leading to an increased secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines in macrophages, thereby contributing to the destabilization of atherosclerotic lesions. Further research has demonstrated that tauroursodeoxycholic acid (TUDCA) inhibits the activation of the protein kinase RNA-like ER kinase (PERK)-α-subunit of the eukaryotic elongation factor 2 (eIF-2α)-activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4)-AIM2 pathway, thus alleviating AS and enhancing cholesterol efflux capacity of macrophages. Since the effects after inhibition of the NLRP3 inflammasome or the AIM2 inflammasome are roughly the same, it indicates that the inflammasome may be a more effective target and is worthy of in-depth research in the future.
title: Distinct types of regulated cell death in atherosclerosis
section_title: Targeting absent in melanoma 2 (AIM2) inflammasome during pyroptosis to attenuate AS

text: GSDMD is predominantly expressed in atherosclerotic macrophages and plaques. The absence of GSDMD has been shown to mitigate AS in high-fat diet-fed ApoE -/- mice through the mitochondrial-the stimulator of interferon genes (STING)-IRF3/NF-κB signaling pathway. Mechanistically, upon activation by ox-LDL, Caspase-1 not only activates GSDMD, leading to the cleavage of GSDMD into GSDMD-N, but also facilitates the disruption of mitochondria in macrophages. This disruption results in the release of mitochondrial DNA, which is subsequently detected by cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS). This recognition activates STING, leading to the phosphorylation of IRF3 and NF-κB, thereby promoting the transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines. This cascade amplifies the inflammasome response and exacerbates AS. Furthermore, another study has indicated that ox-LDL-induced GSDME-mediated pyroptosis in macrophages also contributes to the progression of AS, with STAT3 playing a crucial role in the upregulation of GSDME expression during this process. The findings suggest that gasdermin proteins-mediated pyroptosis may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for addressing AS progression.
title: Distinct types of regulated cell death in atherosclerosis
section_title: Targeting gasdermin proteins during pyroptosis to attenuate AS

text: Quercetin, a well-known natural antioxidant, exhibits anti-atherosclerotic properties by competitively binding to the Arg483 site of KEAP1, which activates Nrf2. This activation leads to the transcription of various antioxidant genes, consequently mitigating oxidative stress and inhibiting macrophage pyroptosis. Additionally, sinapic acid, another natural antioxidant, has been shown to downregulate long noncoding RNA (lncRNA) metastasis-associated lung adenocarcinoma transcript 1 (MALAT1), thereby inhibiting macrophage pyroptosis. Moreover, circular RNAs (circRNAs), a novel class of ncRNAs, have also been implicated in AS, although their functions remain poorly understood. One study reported that ox-LDL significantly upregulated hsa_circ_0029589 in VSMC. Another investigation demonstrated that IRF1 enhanced the N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modification of circ_0029589, promoting macrophage pyroptosis in AS. Above evidence has increasingly indicated that targeting noncoding RNAs (ncRNAs) during pyroptosis regulates gene expressions that are implicated in the pathogenesis of AS. Collectively, pyroptosis is a critical process in the development of AS. The mechanisms and roles of pyroptosis during the process of AS have been illustrated. In addition to targeting key proteins associated with pyroptosis, it is essential to target transcription factors, ncRNAs, and mitochondrial function for the treatment of AS.
title: Distinct types of regulated cell death in atherosclerosis
section_title: Targeting ncRNAs during pyroptosis to attenuate AS

text: Parthanatos, which refers to poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase 1 (PARP-1) dependent cell death, represents a novel form of PCD characterized by DNA excessive damage and the overactivation of PARP-1. The overactivation of PARP-1 leads to the cleavage of NAD + into nicotinamide and ADP-ribose, the latter of which accumulates through a process known as poly (ADP-ribosyl)ation (PARylation), resulting in the formation of poly (ADP-ribose) (PAR). This accumulation subsequently facilitates the translocation of PAR, prompting the release of AIF from the mitochondria into the cytoplasm. In the cytoplasm, AIF combines with the macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF). Afterwards, the AIF/MIF complex translocates into the nucleus, resulting in chromatin condensation and extensive DNA fragmentation, ultimately leading to parthanatos. Existing evidence indicates a significant increase in oxidative DNA damage and PARP-1 activity across all cell types present in human atherosclerotic plaques, including VEC, VSMC, and macrophages. Notably, the overactivation of PARP-1 is recognized as a defining characteristic of parthanatos. Consequently, it is reasonable to hypothesize that parthanatos may play a role in AS.
title: Distinct types of regulated cell death in atherosclerosis

text: Research indicates that pro-atherosclerotic factors, such as ROS, ox-LDL, angiotensin II (Ang II), and hyperglycemia, induce DNA extensive damage and PARP-1 overactivation, resulting in parthanatos in EC. Specifically, ox-LDL-induced activation of PARP-1 leads to the upregulation of arginase II (Arg II), which competes with endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS), thereby reducing NO production and impairing VEC function. Notably, these detrimental effects were mitigated following the deletion of PARP-1. Given that ECs play an important role in maintaining the normal functions of blood vessels, it is obvious that parthanatos of ECs is involved in the occurrence and development of AS.
title: Distinct types of regulated cell death in atherosclerosis

text: A recent study utilizing an in vitro system designed to replicate plaque dynamics has revealed a correlation between AS and parthanatos. Specifically, the depletion of PARP-1 was found to enhance the viability of VSMC and confer protection against cell death induced by H 2 O 2, TNF-α, or ox-LDL. However, there is a paucity of research that has established a definitive link between parthanatos of VSMC and AS, and a comprehensive examination of the distinct characteristics of parthanatos has yet to be conducted. As a result, the occurrence of parthanatos within VSMC remains uncertain.
title: Distinct types of regulated cell death in atherosclerosis

text: 10.13039/100028438 Elevated level of 7,8-dihydro-8-oxoguanine (8-oxoG), a marker of oxidative 10.13039/100026054 DNA damage, along with substantial quantities of fragmented 10.13039/100026054 DNA strands observed in both human and experimental plaques, support the notion that peroxynitrite generated in advanced plaques leads to extensive 10.13039/100026054 DNA damage. This damage is associated with PARP1 overactivation, particularly in macrophage-derived foam cells within the plaques. These findings indicated that parthanatos in plaque macrophages was responsible for AS. Additionally, PARP1 deficiency may inhibit the translocation of NF-κB into the nucleus, thereby diminishing the expression of inflammatory mediators such as VCAM-1 and MCP-1, which in turn affects monocyte recruitment and results in insufficient plaque formation, as evidenced by the deteriorated plaque development in ApoE -/- mice. Additionally, the stability of the plaques appears to improve under these conditions. Recent findings further suggest that parthanatos may facilitate the calcification of atherosclerotic plaques, thereby exacerbating AS. In PARP1-deficient diabetic ApoE -/- mice, there is a notable reduction in the number of calcium nodules within atherosclerotic lesions and a decrease in total calcium content in the aorta. Moreover, under hyperglycemic conditions, PARP1 mediates calcification and inflammation by promoting the transition of VSMC from a contractile to a synthetic phenotype, as well as the differentiation of macrophages into pro-inflammatory and osteoblast-like macrophages through the STAT1-Runt-related transcription factor-2 (RUNX2) signaling pathway. The deletion of PARP-1 has been shown to reverse these processes and mitigate AS. The mechanisms and roles of parthanatos during the process of AS have been illustrated. It implies that parthanatos may also represent a critical mechanism underlying AS, and PARP-1 could serve as a potential target for therapeutic intervention aimed at atheroprotection.
title: Distinct types of regulated cell death in atherosclerosis

text: Cuproptosis is a novel form of cell death characterized by cell death resulting from copper dyshomeostasis. Specifically, copper has been shown to directly bind to lipoylated components and promote their oligomerization within the tricarboxylic acid cycle, leading to the aggregation of lipoylated proteins. Additionally, copper dyshomeostasis can result in the loss of iron-sulfur (Fe-S) cluster proteins, which induces proteotoxic stress and ultimately culminates in cell death. Both excess and deficiency of copper have been associated with the pathogenesis of AS through mechanisms involving mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, inflammation, and endothelial dysfunction. Recent studies have identified several key cuproptosis genes and cuproptosis-related genes associated with AS, which may serve as potential diagnostic biomarkers and aid in the identification of molecular subtypes for AS. Consequently, cuproptosis may represent a potential pathogenic mechanism in AS, and therapeutic strategies targeting cuproptosis could provide valuable insights for the management of AS. Lysosome-dependent cell death (LDCD) is a biological process characterized by lysosomal membranes permeabilization (LMP) and the subsequent release of cathepsins. Research indicates that ox-LDL exhibits resistance to hydrolysis within lysosomes, and the accumulation of inadequately hydrolyzed ox-LDL within these organelles contributes to the formation of cholesterol crystals. The presence of cholesterol crystals can trigger LMP, the release of cathepsins, and inflammatory responses. Furthermore, the induction of lysosomal biogenesis in macrophages via TFEB has been shown to mitigate atherosclerotic lesion size, inflammation, and instability. It suggested that induction of a lysosomal biogenesis program based on LDCD in macrophages has antiatherogenic effects. NETotic cell death is characterized by NADPH oxidase-mediated ROS production, histones citrullination, and excessive neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) release in response to infection or injury. The enzyme peptidyl arginine deiminase 4 (PAD4) plays a crucial role in this process by catalyzing the conversion of arginine residues to citrulline in histones. PAD4 deficiency effectively inhibits NETosis in experimental models of atheroma, thereby preventing endothelial injury and thrombus formation, which suggests a protective effect against AS. It suggests that targeting PAD4 to regulate NETosis may be a potential ideal means to delay the progression of AS. Paraptosis is a nonapoptotic form of cell death mediated through the insulin-like growth factor I receptor (IGFIR) and mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling pathways. This process is subsequently influenced by Ca 2+ imbalances resulting from the transport of Ca 2+ between ER and mitochondria. Various factors, such as impaired proteostasis and imbalanced ion homeostasis, can initiate paraptosis, which is characterized by large vacuoles formation derived from both dilated ER and mitochondria, ultimately leading to the loss of plasma membrane integrity and subsequent cell death. One study has identified paraptosis as a critical regulator of intracellular heme level, endothelial cell homeostasis, and angiogenesis. The direct evidence on endothelial cell implies that paraptosis may play a relevant role in the pathophysiology of AS. Alkaliptosis, defined as a process of intracellular alkalinization leading to pH-dependent cell death, is triggered by alkaline agents such as ammonia, sodium hydroxide, or high-pH buffers.
title: Distinct types of regulated cell death in atherosclerosis

text: One study has identified paraptosis as a critical regulator of intracellular heme level, endothelial cell homeostasis, and angiogenesis. The direct evidence on endothelial cell implies that paraptosis may play a relevant role in the pathophysiology of AS. Alkaliptosis, defined as a process of intracellular alkalinization leading to pH-dependent cell death, is triggered by alkaline agents such as ammonia, sodium hydroxide, or high-pH buffers. The underlying mechanisms involve the inhibition of carbonic anhydrase 9 (CA9) via NF-κB, and the assembly of the ATPase H + transporting V0 subunit D1 (ATP6V0D1) with STAT3, and then cause lysosomal acidification and cytosolic alkalinization. But so far, the exact relationship between alkaliptosis and AS has not been clarified. Oxeiptosis is a caspase-independent and ROS-induced cell death type, characterized by dissociation of phosphoglycerate mutase 5 (PGAM5) from KEAP1, subsequently leading to PGAM5 translocation into the nucleus, where it interacts with and dephosphorylates apoptosis-inducing factor mitochondria-associated 1 (AIFM1). This signaling pathway plays a pivotal role in the modulation of oxidative stress and inflammation, both of which are critical contributors to the initiation and advancement of AS. Entotic cell death is a regulated form of cell death in which one viable cell engulfs and subsequently degrades another viable cell, which may be either homotypic or heterotypic, predominantly occurring under conditions of matrix detachment. The underlying mechanisms involve the promotion of junction formation between the engulfing and entotic cells by E-cadherin and catenin α1. Additionally, Rnd3 activates the RhoA-ROCK-Actomyosin pathway, thereby facilitating the internalization of cells. Following this process, the engulfed cells may undergo division, release, or degradation. Moreover, to date, there is a lack of data concerning the role of entotic cell death in AS. PANoptosis is a unique form of cell death that is characterized by a multifaceted mechanism, which simultaneously activates pyroptosis (GSDMD-N), apoptosis (Caspase-3/7), and necroptosis (p-MLKL), yet cannot be exclusively categorized by any single one of these cell death modalities. Research has demonstrated that AIM2 interacts with pyrin and Z-DNA-binding protein 1 (ZBP1) to promote the formation of the PANoptosome, a structure that plays a crucial role in mediating PANoptosis and bolstering host defense mechanisms. Recent investigations have shown that, despite the variability in the responses of ox-LDL-treated macrophages, human umbilical vein endothelial cell (HUVEC) and VSMC, PANoptosis-based genes exhibit upregulation in atherosclerotic tissues. This observation implies a potential involvement of PANoptosis in the pathophysiological processes underlying AS. However, it is important to note that this conclusion is based on mRNA expression data rather than protein expression level. Therefore, further research employing techniques such as co-immunoprecipitation is necessary to clarify the potential pathways implicated in PANoptosis within the context of AS. Taken together, multiple types of RCD have been confirmed to be involved in AS, and there are also many other types of RCD that may be related to it but still lack strong evidence, suggesting the diversity of cell death types in AS. Therefore, comprehending the various mechanisms of RCD in AS may yield novel insights into therapeutic approaches designed to stabilize vulnerable plaques and enhance the effectiveness of current anti-atherosclerotic interventions.
title: Distinct types of regulated cell death in atherosclerosis

text: As above indicated, various forms of RCD are crucial in the pathogenesis of AS. An increasing body of literature suggests that modulating the signaling pathways associated with cell death could herald a novel approach to the treatment of AS. Currently, numerous drugs and compounds have been found to play a significant role in the prevention and treatment of AS by targeting RCD.
title: Distinct types of regulated cell death in atherosclerosis
section_title: Drugs or compounds targeting RCD for the treatment of AS

text: Equol, a metabolite derived from daidzein, activates the Nrf2 signaling pathway, thereby alleviating ER stress, which in turn reduces EC apoptosis and mitigates the progression of AS. Ellagic acid, a polyphenolic compound, exhibits anti-apoptotic properties in ox-LDL-stimulated HUVEC by activating the PI3K/Akt/eNOS signaling pathway, as well as upregulating BCL-2 and downregulating Caspase-3. Additionally, paeonol, an active compound extracted from traditional Chinese medicine, protects endothelial cells from apoptosis induced by ox-LDL by reducing LOX-1 expression, decreasing ROS overproduction, inhibiting p38 MAPK phosphorylation, and lowering Caspase-3 level, while simultaneously increasing BCL-2 level. Actually, there are a great many drugs or compounds that can regulate apoptosis, but their anti-AS effects are far from satisfactory, and further in-depth investigations are needed.
title: Distinct types of regulated cell death in atherosclerosis

text: Curcumin, a natural polyphenol derived from the turmeric spice, has been shown to inhibit mTOR activity, enhance TFEB-mediated autophagy, and attenuate inflammation by suppressing P300 and bromodomain-containing protein 4 (BRD4) in AS. The compound 3PO (3-[3-pyridinyl]-1-[4-pyridinyl]-2-propen-1-one), which partially inhibits glycolysis, has been found to increase ATG7 expression and reverse the TNF-α-induced upregulation of adhesion molecules such as VCAM-1 and ICAM-1 through an autophagy-dependent mechanism, thereby providing an atheroprotective effect. Additionally, miR-100, often referred to as an "anti-athero-miR," inhibits both mTOR and raptor, promotes endothelial autophagy, reduces NF-κB activity, and decreases plaque area. Since autophagy has a double-edged effect, various factors such as the concentration, time window of application, duration of administration as well as the individual's baseline health status and disease condition all have widely varying impacts on autophagy during the progression of AS. This variability presents substantial challenges in developing therapeutic strategies targeting autophagy for the treatment of AS.
title: Distinct types of regulated cell death in atherosclerosis

text: The RIPK1 inhibitor Nec-1 inhibits formation of the RIPK1 and RIPK3 complex, which subsequently leads to a decrease in phosphorylated MLKL level. This mechanism results in a reduction of the necrotic core area within lesions and an increase in the area occupied by smooth muscle actin, indicating that the modulation of necroptosis may enhance the stability of atherosclerotic plaques. Additionally, miR-223-3p has been shown to inhibit RIPK3-mediated necroptosis in macrophages, exhibiting a similar pro-atherosclerotic effect as Nec-1. Unfortunately, the types of compounds that can inhibit necroptosis are currently limited. Therefore, the potential benefits of targeting necroptosis for AS rely on the development and optimization of novel and efficient necroptosis inhibitors.
title: Distinct types of regulated cell death in atherosclerosis

text: Magrolimab, an anti-CD47 monoclonal antibody, has been shown to restore efferocytosis and mitigate inflammation within atherosclerotic lesions. Fer-1, a specific inhibitor of ferroptosis, has been demonstrated to reduce iron accumulation and lipid peroxidation while simultaneously upregulating the expression of SLC7A11 and GPX4. This mechanism contributes to the alleviation of atherosclerotic lesions in ApoE -/- mice subjected to a high-fat diet. Tranilast has been shown to enhance K63-linked ubiquitination of NLRP3, which subsequently inhibits the assembly and activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, as well as the production of IL-1β, ultimately ameliorates vascular inflammation and AS. Tetracyclines, a class of antimicrobial agents, have been found to impede parthanatos by inhibiting PARP1. This action mitigates inflammatory responses within atherosclerotic lesions, prevents the thinning of the fibrous cap, and enhances the stability of atherosclerotic plaques. Cl-amidine, a haloacetamidine-derived PAD inhibitor, exhibits a preferential affinity for PAD4, effectively inhibiting NETotic cell death and mitigating the progression of AS and arterial thrombosis in ApoE -/- mice. All these studies suggest that intervening in one specific RCD will bring more or less a certain protective effect on AS. In contrast to direct interventions targeting inflammatory pathways, the deficiency or inhibition of the PANoptosis component has been associated with a reduction in the levels of IL-1β and IL-18 within atherosclerotic lesions, while not adversely affecting the overall immune response. Considering that AS actually involves multiple types of RCD, regulating AS by influencing PANoptosis has more translational prospects.
title: Distinct types of regulated cell death in atherosclerosis
section_title: Drugs targeting other types of RCD

text: The targeting of RCD as a therapeutic strategy for AS is challenging, primarily due to the complex interactions among various forms of cell death. The therapeutic modulation of cell death pathways is complicated by the phenomenon in which the inhibition of one type of cell death may inadvertently activate another. For instance, research has demonstrated that Caspase-8 not only initiates extrinsic apoptosis but also inhibits necroptosis mediated by RIPK3-MLKL and pyroptosis mediated by ASC/Caspase-1. Evidence suggests that only in the absence of Caspase-8, MLKL, and ASC/Caspase-1, embryonic lethality and premature death can be completely rescued. Caspase-8 deficiency in mice has been associated with exacerbated AS, characterized by larger necrotic cores and an increased number of dead cells. Inhibiting caspase-8 in macrophages exposed to ox-LDL or oxysterols results in a transition from apoptosis to necroptosis. It has also been reported that the induction of necroptosis provides priming signals for the NLRP3 inflammasome by upregulating the transcription of NLRP3 via TLR activation. Additionally, RIPK1-RIPK3 pathway induces the activation of NLRP3 inflammasome, indicating a close relationship between necroptosis and pyroptosis. Collectively, there is significant overlap and cross-talk among the pathways of pyroptosis, apoptosis, and necroptosis. The dual role of autophagy is particularly significant in ferroptosis. Enhanced autophagy has been observed in various cell types in response to ferroptosis activators, such as erastin and RSL3. Although autophagy likely evolved as a pro-survival mechanism, excessive autophagy coupled with impaired lysosomal activity, may lead to iron accumulation and lipid peroxidation, both of which are critical factors in the initiation of ferroptosis. Taken together, these interactions highlight the intricate molecular dialogues and crosstalk among various forms of RCD, presenting significant challenges for the targeted regulation of RCD in the treatment of AS.
title: Distinct types of regulated cell death in atherosclerosis
section_title: Complex interactions among various forms of RCD

text: The role of RCD varies across different stages of AS progression and may exhibit contrasting effects. For instance, in the early stages of AS, apoptosis of macrophages is beneficial as it reduces lesion cellularity and slows plaque progression. However, in the advanced stages of AS, driven by pro-inflammatory factors, macrophages undergo increased apoptosis coupled with impaired efferocytosis, which contributes atherosclerotic plaque formation. Similarly, in the early stages of AS, exposure of VSMCs to moderate concentrations of ox-LDL, autophagy acts as a protective mechanism by promoting cell survival and enhancing plaque stability. Conversely, in the advanced stages of AS, elevated concentrations of ox-LDL reduce the protective effects of autophagy, leading to other types of cell death (e.g. ferroptosis) and plaque destabilization. This indicates a dysfunctional stress response once a critical threshold of cellular injury is exceeded. In summary, the paradoxical roles of RCD at different stages of AS highlight the importance of stage-specific modulation of RCD in AS therapy. However, given the various types of RCD, further investigation is warranted to determine whether other types exhibit opposing effects at different stages of AS.
title: Distinct types of regulated cell death in atherosclerosis
section_title: The role of RCD varies across different stages of AS

text: Although previous research has elucidated the roles of various RCD in AS, most studies remain confined to the cellular or animal models, with relatively limited clinical evidence. The outcomes of preclinical experiments may not accurately reflect the actual conditions in humans, creating a translational barrier between basic research and clinical application. Moreover, current research often overlooks the influence of individual factors on RCD and AS, complicating the development of personalized and precise diagnosis and treatment strategies for AS.
title: Distinct types of regulated cell death in atherosclerosis
section_title: Lack of clinical evidence for targeting RCD to attenuate AS

text: In addition, reliable and sensitive biomarkers that can accurately indicate the occurrence of specific cell death modalities in the context of AS remain unidentified. Furthermore, given the critical role of RCD in maintaining physiological homeostasis, it is imperative to determine the effective thresholds for targeting these pathways to prevent the exacerbation of AS. Lastly, emerging forms of cell death, such as alkaliptosis, have been associated with inflammation and oxidative stress—known risk factors for AS—yet their direct relationship with the disease remains poorly understood. Consequently, further investigations are warranted to clarify the potential roles and mechanisms of diverse cell death pathways in AS.
title: Distinct types of regulated cell death in atherosclerosis

text: Several forms of RCD are crucial in the initiation and progression of AS. Pharmacological approaches that targeting RCD show promise in managing AS. However, challenges arise due to the complexity of cell death pathways. There is a notable absence of reliable biomarkers to identify specific types of cell death associated with AS, and data regarding the roles of different cell death modalities at various stages of AS is limited. It is imperative to comprehend effective thresholds for targeting RCD pathways to prevent exacerbation of AS. Additionally, emerging forms of cell death, such as alkaliptosis, have been associated with inflammation and oxidative stress, yet their relationship with AS remains poorly understood. Future research should concentrate on the effective regulation of RCD to mitigate the detrimental effects of cell death and to delay or prevent the progression of AS.

text: Despite significant medical advances, atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, a lipid-driven chronic inflammatory disease of large arteries, remains the leading cause of mortality worldwide. While most atherosclerotic risk factors (e.g. hypercholesterolemia, hypertension) are systemic, atherosclerotic plaques form at specific sites in the arterial circulation exposed to disturbed blood flow, such as arterial branch points, curvatures, and bifurcations. Endothelial cells sense the frictional force generated by blood flow, termed shear stress, and cell culture models demonstrate that shear stress generated by unidirectional laminar flow promotes an atheroprotected endothelial phenotype, whereas shear stress from disturbed flow promotes endothelial cell activation, a state in which endothelial cells adopt a proinflammatory, pro-oxidative phenotype that promotes barrier dysfunction, adhesion molecule expression (e.g. vascular cell adhesion molecule-1 (VCAM-1), intracellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1)), and leukocyte adhesion. In addition to shear stress, endothelial activation is further exacerbated by local proinflammatory mediators such as oxidized low-density lipoprotein (oxLDL). Preventing endothelial activation, through deletion of proinflammatory transcription factors (e.g. nuclear factor κ B (NF-κB)) or adhesion molecules (e.g. VCAM-1) is sufficient to reduce early atherogenic inflammation and atherosclerotic plaque formation. In addition to hemodynamics, atherogenic endothelial activation highly depends on the content of the subendothelial matrix. In early atherogenesis, the subendothelial extracellular matrix at atheroprone sites undergoes significant changes, shifting from a laminin- and collagen IV-rich basement membrane to a provisional matrix enriched in fibronectin, an extracellular matrix protein deposited during vascular injury and inflammation. While laminar flow prevents fibronectin deposition, disturbed flow creates a permissive environment for fibronectin deposition, which is exacerbated by proinflammatory stimuli such as oxLDL. In addition, matrix composition also regulates the response to shear stress and oxLDL, as both stimuli induce the activation of endothelial cell integrins, heterodimeric receptors for extracellular matrix proteins containing α and β subunits. Integrin activation results in a conformation change that enhances affinity for ligand and stimulates ligation-associated integrin signaling. Integrin signaling differs based on the specific αβ heterodimer, and signaling through the fibronectin-binding integrins α5β1 and αvβ3 promote oxLDL and shear stress-induced proinflammatory signaling (NF-κB, c-jun N-terminal kinase (JNK)) and gene expression (e.g. VCAM-1). Furthermore, inhibitors of α5β1 (e.g. ATN-161) and αvβ3 (e.g. S247) and endothelial-specific deletion of the α5 and αv integrin subunits limit early endothelial activation and atherosclerotic plaque formation in mouse models. In addition to integrin signaling, both shear stress and oxLDL stimulate endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, with ER stress promoting endothelial inflammation and atherosclerotic plaque formation. Under normal conditions, the ER maintains protein homeostasis by regulating folding, maturation, and trafficking of nascent proteins. title: Integrin-specific signaling drives ER stress-dependent atherogenic endothelial activation

text: In addition to integrin signaling, both shear stress and oxLDL stimulate endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, with ER stress promoting endothelial inflammation and atherosclerotic plaque formation. Under normal conditions, the ER maintains protein homeostasis by regulating folding, maturation, and trafficking of nascent proteins. Under conditions of metabolic or inflammatory stress, disruptions in this balance triggers the unfolded protein response (UPR), a signaling network that attempts to restore ER function. The UPR is initiated by three ER-resident sensors: inositol-requiring enzyme 1α (IRE1α), protein kinase RNA-like ER kinase (PERK), and activating transcription factor 6 (ATF6). These sensors typically remain inactive through their association with the chaperone binding immunoglobulin protein (BiP). However, upon accumulation of misfolded proteins, BiP dissociates from the sensors, with each arm of the UPR activating distinct but overlapping pathways. Although transient UPR activation supports cell survival, prolonged or dysregulated signaling can promote inflammation, oxidative stress, and apoptosis. Atheroprone sites in vivo show gene expression patterns associated with ER stress and activation of UPR sensors. While matrix composition regulates multiple aspects of endothelial activation at atheroprone sites, the contribution of extracellular matrix composition to ER stress regulation remains unknown. Therefore, we sought to assess whether matrix composition regulates ER stress in early atherogenesis using endothelial culture and endothelial-specific knockout model systems.

After treatment, cells were lysed for Western blot analysis to assess puromycin incorporation. TPE-MI staining – TPE-MI staining was performed as previously described. Briefly, TPE-MI was dissolved in DMSO to prepare a 1 mM stock solution, which was stored at −20 °C and protected from light. For experiments, the stock was diluted in pre-warmed culture medium to a final concentration of 50 μM. Following stimulation with oxLDL or exposure to oscillatory shear stress (OSS), cells were incubated with TPE-MI for 30 min at 37 °C. Samples were then washed and counterstained with an anti-lamin antibody to visualize nuclear envelope structures. Superoxide production was measured using dihydroethidium (DHE; Invitrogen). Cells were incubated with 5 μM DHE for 30 min at 37 °C in the dark, washed with PBS, and lysed. DHE oxidation to 2-hydroxyethidium, a superoxide-specific oxidation product, was quantified using HPLC with fluorescent detectors in the LSU Health Shreveport CoBRE Redox Molecular Signaling Core (RRID:SCR 024778), and superoxide levels were normalized to protein concentration, expressed as nmol/mg of total protein. After blocking nonspecific binding with 5 % (w/v) nonfat dry milk in TBS/0.1 % (v/v) Tween 20, the membranes were incubated with primary antibodies (see Supplemental Table 1 for details) at 4 °C overnight. After secondary antibody incubation and chemiluminescence, densitometry was analyzed using NIH ImageJ software. For each Western blot, protein levels were quantified using ImageJ. First, the GAPDH signal from each condition (i) was normalized to the GAPDH signal from the control lane (NormGAPDH(ᵢ) = GAPDH(ᵢ)/GAPDH(control)). text: Previous studies have shown that the subendothelial matrix composition enhances endothelial activation in response to disturbed flow and oxLDL. To determine whether ER stress is similarly regulated by matrix composition, we cultured human aortic endothelial cells on fibronectin or basement membrane proteins and exposed them to either OSS or oxLDL. Western blot analysis showed that oxLDL selectively activated multiple branches of the UPR in endothelial cells cultured on fibronectin, but not on basement membrane (A–F). IRE1α undergoes autophosphorylation and activates its endoribonuclease activity, which splices X-box binding protein 1 (XBP1) mRNA to produce a potent transcription factor (XBP1s) that drives expression of ER chaperones such as BiP. Treatment with oxLDL (100 μg/ml) stimulated XBP1s expression in endothelial cells on fibronectin but not in cells on basement membrane proteins (A and B). The PERK pathway phosphorylates eukaryotic initiation factor 2α (eIF2α), leading to selective translation of activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4), which upregulates genes involved in protein folding, redox balance, and apoptosis, including BiP. Treatment with oxLDL increased phosphorylation of eIF2α and upregulated ATF4 (A, C/D). Expression of BiP, a downstream chaperone, and the nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (NRF2), a redox-sensitive transcription factor, was also higher following oxLDL treatment in cells on fibronectin compared to basement membrane proteins (A, E/F). In contrast, no detectable ATF6 cleavage bands were observed after oxLDL treatment (data not shown), indicating that this branch of the UPR was not activated under these conditions. Like oxLDL, mimicking disturbed flow conditions by treating endothelial cells with OSS (± 5 dyn/cm 2 with 1 dyne forward flow for 24 h) induced a similar pattern, with increased activation of the IRE1α pathway (XBP1s), the PERK pathway (p -eIF2α, ATF4), and downstream induction of BiP and NRF2 in endothelial cells on fibronectin, whereas cells on basement membrane showed minimal or no induction of these markers (G–L). No difference in ATF6 cleavage was observed between cells on fibronectin and those on basement membrane (Sup A and B). Immunocytochemistry further supported these findings, revealing enhanced XBP1s staining in cells cultured on fibronectin after oxLDL and OSS stimulation, compared to basement membrane (M and N). Furthermore, cells transfected with fluorescent reporters for the IRE1α arm (XBP1s-mNeonGreen) and PERK arm (ATF4-mScarlet) confirmed this matrix-specific response, showing stronger fluorescence on fibronectin relative to basement membrane after oxLDL and OSS stimulation (O–R), consistent with increased activation of both UPR branches in endothelial cells on fibronectin.
title: Integrin-specific signaling drives ER stress-dependent atherogenic endothelial activation

text: Endothelial cells interact with fibronectin through several integrins, including α5β1, αvβ3, and αvβ5. Previous studies have identified α5β1 and αvβ3 as key mediators of proinflammatory signaling in response to oxLDL and disturbed flow. Both oxLDL and OSS stimulate integrin activation, a conformation shift to a high affinity state, and subsequent ligation of α5β1 and αvβ3 in cells on fibronectin activates proinflammatory signaling responses following oxLDL and OSS treatment. To investigate whether integrin activation is also required for oxLDL- and OSS-induced ER stress, we used mouse lung endothelial cells expressing the talin1 L325R mutation, which disrupts integrin activation without affecting adhesion. Western blot analysis showed that talin1 L325R cells failed to induce the IRE1α (XBP1s) and PERK (phosphorylated eIF2α) arms of the UPR in response to oxLDL or OSS (A–F). However, these cells maintained a normal ER stress response to tunicamycin (Sup A–C), indicating that the UPR machinery remained intact and that integrin activation was specifically required for ER stress induced by mechanical or metabolic stressors. To test whether integrin activation alone is sufficient to trigger ER stress, we stimulated endothelial cells with CHAMP peptides, which target the transmembrane domains of integrin α subunits. Activation of α5 or αv integrins using CHAMP peptides robustly stimulated the IRE1α (XBP1s) and PERK (phosphorylated eIF2α) arms of the UPR, demonstrating that direct integrin activation is sufficient to initiate ER stress signaling (G–K). To determine whether fibronectin-induced ER stress reflected changes in global translation, we assessed global translation rate using puromycin incorporation. However, no significant differences in puromycin incorporation into newly translated proteins were detected between endothelial cells on fibronectin or basement membrane proteins after oxLDL and OSS stimulation, indicating that total protein synthesis likely does not drive the UPR response on fibronectin and does not diminish in response to the activated UPR on fibronectin (Sup A–D). Similarly, labeling with the thiol-reactive probe TPE-MI revealed no increase in unfolded protein burden in fibronectin-cultured cells after oxLDL and OSS stimulation, suggesting that matrix-specific ER stress activation does not result from protein misfolding (Sup E and F). Finally, to assess the role of oxidative stress, we measured superoxide production by treating cells in the presence of dihydroethidium (DHE) and assessing the superoxide-specific oxidation product 2-hydroethedium by HPLC. Endothelial cells on fibronectin showed no increase in superoxide production following OSS treatment, and scavenging superoxide by pretreatment with TEMPOL, a cell-permeable superoxide scavenger, did not attenuate ER stress following integrin activation (Sup G and H). Together, these results demonstrate that activation of fibronectin-binding integrins by oxLDL and OSS stimulates ER stress in endothelial cells by activating specific arms of the UPR in response to mechanical and metabolic stressors, independent of global translation and oxidative stress.
title: Integrin-specific signaling drives ER stress-dependent atherogenic endothelial activation
section_title: Integrin sctivation is required and sufficient for fibronectin-dependent ER stress

text: Integrins αvβ3 and α5β1 mediate proinflammatory responses to disturbed flow, including proinflammatory signaling (NF-κB, JNK) and adhesion molecule expression. While α5β1 has been specifically implicated in oxLDL-induced endothelial activation, its role in regulating ER stress remains unclear. To determine whether fibronectin-binding integrins differentially regulate ER stress, we used siRNA to selectively deplete the α5 or αv subunits in endothelial cells prior to exposure to OSS. Knockdown of the αv subunit, which can pair with multiple β subunits including β3 and β5, significantly reduced flow-induced expression of ER stress markers in response to OSS (A–C). To further assess the specific role of αvβ3, we depleted the β3 subunit, and similarly observed a strong reduction in ER stress activation in response to OSS (D–F). While knockdown of α5, which forms the α5β1 heterodimer, did not attenuate ER stress after OSS (A–C), α5 depletion prevented the UPR activation in response to oxLDL treatment (G–I). These findings demonstrate that among fibronectin-binding integrins, αvβ3 plays a predominant role in mediating endothelial ER stress in response to mechanical stress, whereas α5β1 promotes ER stress in response to metabolic stimuli in vitro.

text: To evaluate the role of fibronectin-binding integrins in ER stress in vivo, previously validated inducible endothelial cell–specific knockout mice for αv (iEC-αv KO) and α5 (iEC-α5 KO) were used. Mice were fed a high-fat diet (HFD) for 2 or 8 weeks, and ER stress markers were assessed in the aortic arch and brachiocephalic artery (A and B). After 2 weeks of HFD, immunostaining of aortic arch sections showed significant XBP1s staining the lesser curvature of the aortic arch (exposed to disturbed flow), whereas the XBP1 staining was absent from the greater curvature of the arch exposed to atheroprotective laminar flow (B). Consistent with in vitro models suggesting a role for α5 and αv integrins in ER stress in response to disturbed flow and oxLDL, XBP1s expression was reduced at atheroprone sites in both iEC-αv KO and iEC-α5 KO mice compared to iEC- WT controls (B and C). As a secondary readout for ER stress, we assessed BiP staining in the brachiocephalic arteries after 8 weeks of HFD feeding. Like XBP1s, expression of the chaperone protein BiP was elevated at atheroprone sites in vivo, whereas BiP expression was significantly decreased in the endothelial layer of iEC-αv KO and iEC-α5 KO mice (E and F). These results confirm that endothelial αv and α5 integrins contribute to ER stress activation in vivo under proatherogenic conditions.

section_title: Deletion of fbronectin-binding integrins in endothelium blocks ER stress in mice

text: To gain a broader understanding of the transcriptional effects of ER stress in response to OSS, we performed RNA sequencing on HAECs pretreated with the ER stress inhibitor TUDCA, followed by OSS exposure. Principal component analysis revealed clear transcriptional separation between TUDCA-pretreated and untreated groups (A), supporting distinct transcriptomic profiles. Using a cutoff of log2 fold change (log2FC) ≥ |1| and a false discovery rate (FDR)-adjusted p-value <0.05, we identified 518 differentially expressed genes (DEGs), including 230 downregulated and 288 upregulated genes (B). Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment analysis of the downregulated genes revealed significant suppression of pathways related to metabolism, lipid handling, and inflammation, including “Lipid and atherosclerosis,” “Fluid shear stress and atherosclerosis,” and “TNF signaling pathway” (C), indicating that ER stress may broadly amplify atherogenic signaling. To refine our focus, we curated a subset of 32 downregulated genes associated with inflammatory and endothelial activation pathways for heatmap visualization (D). This list was selected based on prior biological relevance and overlap with curated gene lists for vascular inflammation. Notably, VCAM-1 emerged among the most strongly repressed targets. To validate this observation at the protein level, we assessed VCAM-1 and ICAM-1 expression by Western blotting under oxLDL or OSS stimulation, with or without TUDCA. In both contexts, TUDCA markedly inhibited VCAM-1 induction (E–H), whereas ICAM-1 expression remained largely unaffected, suggesting selective transcriptional regulation. These findings position VCAM-1 as an ER stress–sensitive effector of fibronectin-dependent endothelial activation. Leukocyte–endothelial interactions are a fundamental component of the inflammatory response and are tightly controlled under physiological conditions. To investigate the involvement of ER stress in inflammation triggered by OSS and oxLDL, we pretreated HAECs with the chemical chaperone TUDCA prior to exposure to either OSS or oxLDL. Monocyte adhesion assays were then performed. As expected, both OSS and oxLDL significantly increased THP-1 monocyte attachment to endothelial cells. However, pretreatment with TUDCA markedly reduced this monocyte adhesion (Sup A–D), indicating that ER stress contributes to the pro-inflammatory effects of OSS and oxLDL on endothelial activation and highlight the therapeutic potential of ER stress inhibition in vascular inflammation.
title: Integrin-specific signaling drives ER stress-dependent atherogenic endothelial activation
section_title: Blocking ER stress inhibits fibronectin-specific oxLDL and disturbed flow-mediated endothelial inflammation

text: To investigate how ER stress contributes to endothelial inflammation, we assessed whether preventing ER stress with TUDCA treatment affected any of the pathways classically induced downstream of fibronectin-binding integrins, including the NF-κB and JNK pathways. Pretreatment with TUDCA effectively blocked JNK phosphorylation in HAECs stimulated with either oxLDL (A and B) or OSS (D and E), while NF-κB activation by either oxLDL (A and C) or OSS (D and F) remained unaffected, indicating that ER stress selectively regulates the fibronectin-associated JNK signaling. Consistent with ER stress-dependent JNK activation, phosphorylation of c-Jun, a major downstream effector of JNK, was induced by both oxLDL and OSS and inhibited by TUDCA treatment (G and H). JNK inhibition reduces VCAM-1 expression in response to low flow in vitro and at atheroprone sites in vivo, and we demonstrated significantly reduced VCAM-1 expression in response to either oxLDL (I and J) or OSS (K and L) in HAECs treated with the JNK inhibitor SP600125, confirming that JNK is necessary for ER stress–associated endothelial activation on fibronectin. To further validate the role of c-Jun in ER stress-associated VCAM-1 expression, we transfected HAECs with a dominant-negative FLAG-tagged mutant of c-Jun (TAM67) and measured VCAM-1 expression by Western blotting. Disruption of c-Jun function prevented oxLDL- (M and N) and OSS-induced (O and P) VCAM-1 expression, providing strong evidence that c-Jun is a critical downstream effector linking ER stress to endothelial inflammation. To validate the relevance of this pathway in vivo, we examined aortic tissues from endothelial-specific α5 and αv knockout mice (A). Both p -JNK and p -cJun levels were markedly diminished at atheroprone sites in these mice compared to controls (B–E). These findings support the conclusion that fibronectin-binding integrins are essential upstream activators of the ER stress–JNK/c-Jun signaling axis and its inflammatory consequences during atherogenesis. Together, these results establish a mechanistic and physiological link between fibronectin–integrin engagement, ER stress, and JNK/c-Jun–dependent endothelial activation.
title: Integrin-specific signaling drives ER stress-dependent atherogenic endothelial activation
section_title: ER stress promotes endothelial activation via JNK/c-jun signaling

text: Fibronectin–integrin signaling as a driver of endothelial ER stress in atherogenesis. ER stress has been consistently observed in atheroprone regions of the vasculature, particularly in arterial sites exposed to disturbed flow, both in murine and porcine models of atherosclerosis. In contrast, ER stress markers are largely absent in regions experiencing laminar flow. However, the upstream cues that spatially pattern ER stress in the endothelium have remained poorly defined. In this study, we identify the extracellular matrix protein fibronectin and its integrin receptors as central mediators of endothelial ER stress in response to atherogenic stimuli such as oxLDL and OSS. Our findings reveal that fibronectin, a key component of the provisional ECM deposited early in atherogenesis, selectively promotes activation of the IRE1α and PERK branches of the UPR. These effects were dependent on the fibronectin-binding integrins α5β1 and αvβ3, which showed stimulus-specific roles in mediating ER stress activation. Notably, the observed ER stress was independent of traditional triggers such as oxidative stress, global protein misfolding, or translational attenuation—suggesting a non-canonical mode of UPR engagement. These observations position matrix-integrin signaling not only as a spatial cue but also as a biochemical regulator of ER stress in vascular endothelial cells, offering a novel mechanistic insight into the early molecular events of atherogenesis. Matrix remodeling and UPR activation: A bidirectional axis. Matrix remodeling is one of the earliest atherogenic changes observed at sites of disturbed flow. In healthy vessels, the subendothelial matrix is composed primarily of basement membrane proteins such as laminin and collagen IV. However, during atherogenesis, this composition shifts toward a provisional matrix enriched in fibronectin, fibrinogen, and other glycoproteins. Fibronectin is essential for endothelial activation in response to both disturbed flow and oxLDL. Our study extends these findings by demonstrating that fibronectin-rich matrices also trigger ER stress, providing a direct link between mechanical and metabolic perturbations, ECM remodeling, and UPR signaling. This expands the known repertoire of fibronectin's influence on endothelial cell fate and suggests that its role is not limited to canonical pathways such as NF-κB or MAPK signaling. Interestingly, basement membrane proteins failed to elicit similar ER stress responses, emphasizing the specificity of this effect. However, published reports suggest that this may be a bidirectional system, with the UPR response promoting matrix remodeling as well. In renal epithelial cells, PERK signaling promotes ECM deposition under hyperglycemic conditions, while in hepatocytes and lens epithelial cells, ER stress drives TGF-β–dependent fibrotic remodeling. Furthermore, the IRE1α-XBP1 axis promotes fibronectin-rich matrix deposition during viral infection, and calreticulin-mediated ER stress facilitates TGF-β signaling and ECM assembly in fibrotic tissues. In the context of our findings, these reports suggest that ER stress is not merely a consequence of matrix remodeling but may act as an upstream signal that regulates endothelial matrix composition. Integrin specificity and signal routing: α5β1 vs. αvβ3. While α5β1 and αvβ3 are the principal fibronectin-binding integrins expressed in endothelial cells, our study reveals a division of labor between these receptors in mediating ER stress in response to different atherogenic stimuli.
title: Integrin-specific signaling drives ER stress-dependent atherogenic endothelial activation

text: In the context of our findings, these reports suggest that ER stress is not merely a consequence of matrix remodeling but may act as an upstream signal that regulates endothelial matrix composition. Integrin specificity and signal routing: α5β1 vs. αvβ3. While α5β1 and αvβ3 are the principal fibronectin-binding integrins expressed in endothelial cells, our study reveals a division of labor between these receptors in mediating ER stress in response to different atherogenic stimuli. Signaling through α5β1 promotes ER stress in response to oxLDL, whereas αvβ3 mediates the response to disturbed flow. This specificity was confirmed through loss-of-function approaches using integrin-activation deficient mutants, siRNA knockdowns, and small molecule inhibitor studies, whereas studies with CHAMP peptides suggest that activation of either integrin is sufficient to induce the ER stress response. Prior studies have shown that αvβ3 drives shear-induced endothelial activation, whereas α5β1 contributes to both shear-induced and oxLDL-induced NF-κB signaling and vascular inflammation. However, α5β1 also drives fibronectin deposition, suggesting that inhibiting α5β1 could reduce signaling through αvβ3 indirectly. Mechanistically, the downstream pathways linking integrin activation to UPR engagement remain incompletely understood. While canonical ER stress typically involves unfolded protein accumulation or oxidative damage, our data indicate that integrin signaling can initiate UPR activation in the absence of oxidative stress, global protein misfolding, or translational attenuation. Potential mechanisms may include focal adhesion–mediated calcium flux, cytoskeletal tension affecting ER architecture, or misfolding-independent phosphorylation of UPR sensors. Integrin ligation can initiate focal adhesion–mediated calcium influx and ER calcium release through IP3 receptors, which can be sufficient to trigger UPR signaling in the absence of proteotoxic stress. Alternatively, cytoskeletal tension transmitted through RhoA/ROCK pathways may distort ER membrane architecture. In addition to calcium- and force-dependent mechanisms, UPR sensors such as PERK and IRE1α can also be activated through direct phosphorylation by kinases including PAK and c-Abl, independently of protein misfolding, suggesting additional modes of transactivation at the ER membrane. Additional studies will be necessary to define the molecular mechanisms by which integrin signaling drives the endothelial UPR during atherogenic endothelial activation. Implications for endothelial metabolism and inflammatory gene expression. In addition to its effects on adhesion molecule expression, ER stress appears to regulate broader transcriptional programs in endothelial cells. Our RNA-seq data show that inhibiting ER stress in cells exposed to disturbed flow suppresses multiple inflammatory and metabolic pathways, including those involved in lipid handling and cholesterol biosynthesis. This finding highlights a potential role for the UPR in modulating endothelial lipid metabolism. Given that endothelial cells actively participate in lipoprotein uptake, transcytosis, and cholesterol transport, alterations in ER function could directly influence vascular lipid homeostasis and atherogenic lipoprotein retention. ER stress activates sterol regulatory element-binding proteins, promoting lipid synthesis and uptake, which may exacerbate intracellular lipid accumulation and endothelial dysfunction.
title: Integrin-specific signaling drives ER stress-dependent atherogenic endothelial activation

text: This finding highlights a potential role for the UPR in modulating endothelial lipid metabolism. Given that endothelial cells actively participate in lipoprotein uptake, transcytosis, and cholesterol transport, alterations in ER function could directly influence vascular lipid homeostasis and atherogenic lipoprotein retention. ER stress activates sterol regulatory element-binding proteins, promoting lipid synthesis and uptake, which may exacerbate intracellular lipid accumulation and endothelial dysfunction. These effects are compounded by ER–mitochondria crosstalk, as disruption of mitochondrial-associated ER membranes impairs ATP production and increases apoptotic signaling. Together, these observations suggest that the UPR is a key integrator of metabolic stress and matrix remodeling across multiple organ systems, and that targeting ER stress may have pleiotropic benefits in vascular disease. JNK as a selective effector of ER stress–driven inflammation. Our data further demonstrate that ER stress promotes VCAM-1 expression via activation of the JNK–AP-1 (c-Jun) pathway, without affecting ICAM-1 levels. This specificity is consistent with prior reports showing that VCAM-1 transcription requires both NF-κB and AP-1, whereas ICAM-1 is largely regulated by NF-κB alone. Given this selective upregulation of VCAM-1, one would expect downstream consequences on leukocyte recruitment. Indeed, integrins α5β1 and αvβ3 have been shown to critically regulate endothelial inflammatory responses and leukocyte adhesion. For instance, oxLDL enhances monocyte adhesion to fibronectin-adherent endothelial cells via α5β1 and FAK signaling, and blockade of α5β1 reduces both VCAM-1 expression and monocyte binding. Similarly, inhibition of αvβ3 integrins reduces NF-κB activation and VCAM-1 expression in endothelial cells exposed to oscillatory shear stress. Additionally, αvβ3 integrin has been shown to promote monocyte motility and transmigration through interactions with β2 integrins. Moreover, ligands targeting αvβ3 integrin have been found to suppress TNF-α–induced VCAM-1 expression in HUVECs, further implicating this integrin in regulating endothelial inflammation and monocyte recruitment. Consistent with these reports, our findings show that blunting ER stress with TUDCA reduces monocyte adhesion under oxLDL and OSS conditions. Importantly, JNK activation in our model is matrix-dependent, as fibronectin—but not basement membrane proteins—promotes its phosphorylation under stress conditions. Furthermore, in vivo studies have previously shown that disturbed flow activates JNK and promotes atherosclerosis. These findings integrate several key signaling axes—matrix composition, integrin engagement, ER stress, and JNK activation—into a unified framework for endothelial inflammatory activation. Disturbed flow and oxLDL converge on fibronectin–integrin interactions, which initiate non-canonical UPR signaling and downstream JNK-mediated transcriptional programs. This pathway offers a molecular explanation for how spatial and mechanical cues in the vascular microenvironment translate into localized proinflammatory gene expression and lesion formation. Our data place ER stress as an upstream modulator of this pathway in the endothelium, expanding the current understanding of how biomechanical forces interact with cellular stress responses to shape vascular pathophysiology.
title: Integrin-specific signaling drives ER stress-dependent atherogenic endothelial activation

text: In summary, our findings identify fibronectin–integrin interactions as key regulators of endothelial ER stress in response to atherogenic stimuli such as disturbed flow and oxidized LDL. This matrix-dependent mechanism involves selective activation of the IRE1α and PERK arms of the UPR, independent of oxidative stress or protein misfolding, and promotes inflammation via JNK/c-Jun signaling. These results provide new insight into how extracellular matrix composition and integrin signaling shape vascular stress responses and augments proinflammatory responses. Targeting this pathway may offer new therapeutic opportunities for early intervention in atherosclerosis. Broader significance and therapeutic implications. The integrin–ER stress axis identified in this study offers several potential opportunities for therapeutic intervention. Pharmacological targeting of UPR components (e.g., PERK or IRE1α inhibitors), modulation of integrin signaling, or strategies aimed at restoring normal ECM composition could attenuate early inflammatory responses and slow plaque progression. Furthermore, because our findings identify distinct integrin receptors responsible for ER stress in response to different stimuli, it may be possible to develop targeted therapies that selectively disrupt proatherogenic signaling without impairing physiological integrin functions. More broadly, our study highlights the importance of considering matrix context in vascular disease research. Understanding how provisional matrix components like fibronectin interact with mechanotransduction and metabolic cues will be critical for designing next-generation interventions for atherosclerosis and other chronic inflammatory diseases. Limitations and future directions. While this study provides new insight into the molecular pathways linking matrix remodeling to ER stress and inflammation, several questions linger. First, the precise molecular events linking integrin activation to IRE1α and PERK signaling remain to be elucidated. Second, it will be important to determine how long-term ER stress influences endothelial turnover, permeability, and senescence—features relevant to plaque vulnerability. Finally, the role of each of the UPR branches in regulating endothelial phenotype remains to be explored. Future studies should utilize single-cell approaches to dissect endothelial heterogeneity in ER stress responses across vascular beds and disease stages.
title: Integrin-specific signaling drives ER stress-dependent atherogenic endothelial activation

text: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), the most prevalent interstitial lung disease, is characterized by a gradual and progressive decline in pulmonary function over time. Due to the absence of effective diagnostic methods and treatments, patients with IPF often face a bleak prognosis. In Asia, the incidence of IPF is 0.35–1.30 per 10,000 people, and carries a heavy economic burden on families and society. Additionally, IPF is not curable at present. Hence, it is imperative to unveil the molecular mechanisms underlying the pathogenesis of IPF and to explore effective therapeutic interventions aimed at slowing or reversing its progression. According to previous studies, excessive alveolar epithelial cells (AECs) apoptosis contribute to fibrosis, and inhibiting apoptosis was reported to relieve IPF. Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress is frequently found in lung tissues in patients with IPF and continuous ER stress contributes to fibrosis via apoptosis-mediated pathways. Modulating ER stress might be a method to alleviate apoptosis and slow down the process of IPF. Due to the capacity of self-renew and multi-differentiating potential, Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) have emerged as a dependable source in biotherapy, renowned for their robust therapeutic potential across a spectrum of diseases due to their paracrine properties. Several studies revealed that MSCs primarily mitigate lung fibrosis through their paracrine effects. We previously found MSCs alleviated lung fibrosis by modulating ER stress in a bleomycin-treated mouse IPF model. Notably, although MSCs exert several amazing therapeutic effects, some limitations, such as cell senescence, malignant transformation, tumor formation and strict transportation conditions, restrict their application in clinical cell therapy. Thus, how to maximize the beneficial effects of MSCs while avoiding their disadvantages is a research hotspot. Interestingly, MSC-derived exosomes (MSC-Ex) are considered as a key mediator for the paracrine effects of MSCs. MSC-Ex refers to the small bilayer vesicles containing small RNAs and proteins. MSC-Ex have similar biological characteristics and functions to MSCs. Data from numerous studies suggest that MSC-Ex might be a promising treatment modality for cell-free MSC-based therapies with less risk. MSC-Ex could alleviate lung injury and pulmonary fibrosis by inhibiting ER stress, inflammation, ROS and apoptosis. However, the detailed molecular mechanisms of MSC-Ex on reducing alveolar epithelial cell apoptosis remains unstudied. Therefore, we questioned whether MSC-Ex could reduce AEC apoptosis via the ER stress pathway and hypothesized that ER stress is an important target in MSC-Ex-mediated alleviation of apoptosis in IPF models.

text: SPF-grade lineC57BL/6 mice were kept at the Guizhou University of Traditional Chinese Medicine animal center, following the guidelines outlined in the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals. The mice were kept individually in single cages within the animal care facility at a suitable temperature range of 21–25 °C and humidity levels of 50–70 %, with a 12-h light/dark cycle. According to the principle of random allocation based on body weight, 15 C57BL/6 mice (male, 8w old) were randomly divided into 3 groups. The IPF model was established by intratracheal injection of BLM (3.5 mg/kg) in mice (n = 10). On the second day after surgery, 5 mice were randomly selected from the model group and administered MSC-Ex (400 μg/mouse, once every 2 weeks for 4 weeks) via tail vein injection according to the results of prior studies. The remaining mice were injected with an equal volume of PBS (A). The anesthesia and euthanasia procedures for the mice were conducted in accordance with the ethical standards and approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) at University of Traditional Chinese Medicine. Mice were euthanized with an overdose of sodium pentobarbital (150 mg/kg i.p.). Each experimental result in the animal study included data values from all mice in the group (n = 5).

section_title: ER stress contributes to BLM-induced apoptosis in A549 cells

text: To further investigate whether the inhibitory effect of MSC-Ex on apoptosis is associated with the modulation of ER stress, we introduced tauroursodeoxycholic acid (TUDCA), an ER stress inhibitor. TUDCA (100 μM) alleviated ER stress, as evidenced by decreased BiP and CHOP expression compared with the BLM group (A). Interestingly, TUDCA restored cell viability (B), reduced the ratio of apoptotic cells and Bax protein level while increasing Bcl-2 protein expression (C and D), indicating that the amelioration of BLM-induced apoptosis in A549 cells is associated with the inhibition of ER stress. Next, we assessed the regulatory effect of MSC-Ex on ER stress using the ER stress inducer thapsigargin (TG). The results demonstrated that MSC-Ex markedly attenuated TG (100 μM)-induced ER stress in A549 cells (E), highlighting the potent capacity of MSC-Ex to modulate ER stress. Furthermore, MSC-Ex reduced the ratio of apoptotic cells compared to BLM group, whereas TG attenuated this effect (F). Taken together, these findings suggest that ER stress inhibition contributes to the anti-apoptotic effect of MSC-Ex.
