text: Having established the suitability of compounds in 2D monolayer cell culture settings, the efficacy of ZnL2 probe was investigated on 3D multicellular cancer spheroids (MCTSs). MCTSs have gained prominence as an in vitro model for gauging the therapeutic potential of drugs. This study’s advantage lies in the fact that 2D cell cultures struggle to replicate 3D physiological conditions, leading to the failure of numerous anticancer agents to transition positively from 2D monolayer cells found in 96 well plates to in vivo mouse models. Tumours that exist within living organisms are distinguished by complex structures consisting of multiple layers, which provide intricate connections between cells. These interactions pose a significant challenge to the effective delivery of drugs. MCTSs, akin to their in vivo counterparts, exhibit analogous viable cellular interactions including tight junctions and extracellular matrix deposition. Moreover, they exhibit constraints on the diffusion of drugs. Moreover, akin to tumors in living organisms, multicellular tumor spheroids (MCTSs) exhibit the formation of a necrotic core in conjunction with hypoxic areas, hence playing a role in the development of drug resistance during cancer treatment. In aggregate, these characteristics make MCTSs a valuable in vitro model for a more accurate assessment of medication efficacy compared with 2D monolayer cells. Consequently, we generated MCTSs using MCF-7 cells with an approximate diameter of 400–500 μm to assess the cytotoxic impact of ZnL2. c and d illustrates the ZnL2-induced inhibition in MCTS growth. After 72 h, control MCTSs exhibited a 62% growth rate, whereas those treated with ZnL2 displayed an approximately 17% growth rate analyzed by ImageJ software. Nevertheless, when we conducted a morphological assessment of the MCTSs, it became evident that the boundaries of the MCTSs exhibited signs of structural disruption over time. This observation suggests that the drug treatment indeed had a discernible impact on the MCTSs.

text: The overall efficacy of metal-based anticancer drugs is influenced by their internalization into cellular structures. In our study, we observed that the cytotoxic effects of a zinc complex were more pronounced in MCF-7 cells compared with other cell types. Consequently, MCF-7 cells were selected as the subject of investigation for the intracellular uptake of this zinc complex (referred to as ZnL2) and zinc chloride (ZnCl 2) using inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS). Following an 8 h treatment of MCF-7 cells with ZnL2, a significant increase in intracellular zinc content was observed in comparison to both the control group and cells treated with the metal salt ZnCl 2. The order of cellular uptake was as follows: ZnL2 > ZnCl 2 > control. These findings clearly demonstrate that the overall cellular uptake of the zinc complex, characterized by tert -butyl groups at positions R1 and R3 of salicylaldehyde, is notably higher than that of ZnCl 2. Moreover, the results from cytotoxicity assays and cellular uptake measurements suggest a correlation between the antiproliferative activity of ZnL2 and its cellular uptake efficiency.

text: Our mechanistic study illustrates the role of intracellular copper ions on the cytotoxicity of the Zn(II) complexes. While the zinc complexes are not redox active, availability of Cu(II) ion in our biological system could easily transmetallate to show enhanced cytotoxicity. During this process, it becomes interesting to determine whether the inhibitory property of these SIRTi’s analogues is retained. Thus, to determine the inhibitory constant, protein–ligand docking of NAD + -dependent protein deacetylase SIRT1 and SIRT2 with HL3 and Cu(L3) 2 was performed using CB-Dock2, incorporating template-independent docking with AutoDock Vina. The crystal structures of SIRT1 (PDB 4KXQ, Uniprot ID: Q96EB6) and SIRT2 (PDB 4RMJ, Uniprot ID: Q8IXJ6) were obtained from the RCSB PDB database. − For SIRT1, HL3 was observed to bind within a cavity with a volume of 3554 Å 3 (a). Docking calculations were performed using a 23 × 32 × 29 Å grid, centered at coordinates (30, −17, 4) Å in the x, y, and z directions, respectively. The resulting docked complex exhibited a Vina score of −9.6 kcal/mol, indicating a favorable binding energy. Analysis of the protein–ligand interactions revealed specific contact residues, including GLY261, ALA262, PHE273, ARG274, TYR280, PHE297, ILE316, GLN345, ASN346, ILE347, HIS363, ILE411, VAL412, PHE413, PHE414, LEU418, SER441, SER442, VAL445, and ARG446. Notably, the ligand interacted with HIS363, a key residue at the active site, as well as GLY261, ALA262, GLN345, PHE273, ARG274, and ILE347 residues involved in NAD+ binding. The K i value for the HL3 was calculated to be 0.091 μM. Similarly, Cu(L2) 2 was found to bind within another cavity with a volume of 553 Å 3, exhibiting a slightly weaker binding affinity with a Vina score of −9.0 kcal/mol compared to the ligand (c). The grid dimensions for the metal complex docking were set to 24 × 24 × 24 Å, centered at coordinates (22, −26, −3) Å in the x, y, and z directions, respectively. Analysis of the protein-metal complex interactions revealed contact residues, including GLN361, GLY364, SER365, ALA367, THR368, LYS375, TYR376, LYS377, GLU410, GLU416, ASN417, LEU418, PRO419, GLU420, GLN421, and ARG424. The K i value calculated for Cu(L3) 2 was 0.25 μM, indicating a comparatively lower binding affinity compared to the HL3 ligand. For SIRT2, which is a homomeric dimer in its biologically functional form, HL3 was observed to bind within a cavity located in Chain B of the protein, with a volume of 3609 Å 3 (b). Docking calculations were performed using a grid size of 23 × 29 × 23 Å autogrid points, with the grid centered at coordinates (13, −11, −62) Å in the x, y, and z directions, respectively. The resulting docked complex exhibited a Vina score of −9.5 kcal/mol, indicating a favorable binding energy. Analysis of the protein–ligand interactions revealed specific contact residues in Chain B, including GLY84, ALA85, ILE93, PRO94, PHE96, ARG97, TYR104, PHE119, LEU138, GLN167, ASN168, ILE169, ASP170, HIS187, ILE232, VAL233, PHE234, THR262, SER263, LEU264, GLN265, and VAL266. Notably, the ligand interacted with HIS187, a key residue located at the active site, as well as ASN168, ILE169, ALA85, PHE96, THR262, GLN167, and ARG97 residues involved in NAD+ binding. text: Collectively, The research described in this article addresses (i) de novo synthesis of Zn(II) complexes of SIRT i 1/2 analogues and (ii) that undergo transmetalation with Cu(II) ions to generate redox-active copper complexes and generate ROS. (iii) They have proven to amplify the mitochondrial oxidative stress by causing depolarization in the mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨ m) and depletion in ATP generation. (iv) The mechanistic profile exhibits a ROS mediated paraptosis cell-death pathway, and (v) the computational docking analysis establishes this new class of paraptosis inducer to simultaneously inhibit SIRT1/2 protein. Apoptosis is the primary mechanism by which most anticancer medications induce cell death, there are cases where alternate forms of programmed cell death (PCD) are detected in response to standard therapeutic regimens. Certain anticancer medications exhibit limited effectiveness in eliminating malignant cell lines that possess compromised apoptotic pathways. In such cases, paraptosis emerges as a viable mechanism for inducing cell death, thereby presenting a novel and promising approach for cancer treatment. This is the first study that demonstrates Zn(II) complexes of SIRT i 1/2 analogues that undergo transmetalation with redox active Cu(II) ions. Moreover, our study explores the uptake of the paraptosis mediated cell death pathway, which distinguishes it from other SIRT inhibitors that induce cell death through the p53 dependent pathway. The results of our study indicate that the initiation of paraptosis through Zn(II) complexes is linked to the disruption of mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) and the decline of ATP levels. Additionally, we conducted experiments to assess the effectiveness of our complexes in 3D multicellular tumor spheroids (MCTSs), which provide a more accurate means of evaluating the efficacy of drugs compared to 2D monolayer cells. The study’s focus on the rational design of a new class of paraptosis inducer as therapeutic agent that aligns perfectly with the new avenues in the field of cancer therapeutics.

text: Proteostasis maintains the stable status of protein biogenesis through a network of expression, folding, trafficking, and degradation. Aberrant proteostatic control has been implicated in aging and various diseases, including cancer and neurodegenerative disorders. In cancer cells, elevated genomic instability and metabolic demands cause severe proteotoxic stress, their reliance on protein quality control makes cancer cells highly vulnerable to proteasome inhibition. Despite the effectiveness of proteasome inhibitors in inducing cell death, cancer cells exhibit significant adaptability in evading apoptosis through various resistance mechanisms. Consequently, while proteasome inhibitors such as bortezomib and carfilzomib are successful in multiple myeloma, their clinical efficacy remains limited, necessitating novel strategies to address this challenge. The recognition of alternative cell death mechanisms has contributed to overcoming apoptosis resistance. Paraptosis is a form of regulated cell death closely linked to proteostasis disruption and the activation of unfolded protein responses (UPRs) during ER stress. It is de novo translation-dependent and is characterized by extensive cytoplasmic vacuolation involving mitochondrial and ER swelling. Unlike apoptosis, paraptosis does not require caspase activation and is unaffected by overexpression of anti-apoptotic proteins or caspase inhibitors. It typically relies on MAPK family members such as JNK1, p38, and MEK-2, while negatively regulated by the multifunctional adapter protein AIP-1/Alix. Recent studies indicate that paraptosis is a bona fide immunogenic cell death in that dying cancer elicits an immune response to recognize and attack residual malignant cells. Thus, identifying inducers of ER stress and paraptosis is of significant interest. We envision that the cytosolic presence of abiotic, hydrophobic macromolecules will be detected and trigger a similar stress response. However, most preformed polymers and nanoparticles are trapped in endosomes post-endocytosis, – so such a hypothesis cannot be easily tested. We propose that intracellular synthesis of polymers, i.e. in situ polymerization, can be utilized to access intracellular space. This chemical approach relies on cell-permeable monomers that polymerize upon endogenous or exogenous cues, which can be achieved in supramolecular and covalent fashions. – The former primarily includes the self-assembly of peptides through the co-ops of intermolecular non-covalent interactions. Covalent polymers have been synthesized through photo-induced – or metal-catalyzed radicals, oxidative processes, and enzymatic reactions. Several studies demonstrated that intracellular abiotic polymers can elicit cell death, but the precise cell death mechanisms remain poorly defined with some ascribed to apoptosis. In addition, these in situ polymerizations may require harsh conditions (e.g. high monomer concentration, toxic metal catalyst) and face inhibition from endogenous biomolecules, for example, glutathione (at 0.5–10 mM in cells) can potently inhibit polymerization reactivity. In this study, we designed a small, cell-permeable monomer that undergoes intracellular polymerization to form hydrophobic poly(luciferin) polymers nanoaggregates at low μM concentrations. Key features of our design include: (i) dual-caging of the monomer, enabling spatiotemporal control via light and glutathione (GSH), and (ii) a biocompatible condensation reaction between cysteine (Cys) and 2-cyanobenzothiazole (CBT), which occurs inside cells.

text: In this study, we designed a small, cell-permeable monomer that undergoes intracellular polymerization to form hydrophobic poly(luciferin) polymers nanoaggregates at low μM concentrations. Key features of our design include: (i) dual-caging of the monomer, enabling spatiotemporal control via light and glutathione (GSH), and (ii) a biocompatible condensation reaction between cysteine (Cys) and 2-cyanobenzothiazole (CBT), which occurs inside cells. As we sought to investigate the biological consequences, we discovered that intracellular poly(luciferin) aggregates potently and persistently activated ER stress, particularly activating the BiP-PERK-CHOP axis of UPR. This led to Ca 2+ ion and redox dysregulation, resulting in a regulated cell death consistent with paraptosis. Notably, unlike other paraptosis inducers, the cell death induced by poly(luciferin) was independent of translation inhibition, suggesting that the hydrophobic polymer aggregates, rather than misfolded proteins, triggered ER stress. Furthermore, dying cells emitted danger-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), indicative of an immunogenic cell death process. This work provides the first mechanistic characterization of in situ synthesized polymers mimicking insoluble misfolded protein aggregates to induce cellular stress, highlighting the potential of this approach to exploit the proteotoxic vulnerabilities of cancer cells.

text: Stemmed from the biosynthesis of D-luciferin, the Cys/CBT condensation reaction exhibits a rapid reaction rate comparable to that of the popular copper-catalyzed azide-alkyne cycloaddition (CuAAC) reaction (second-order rate constant: 10 M −1 s −1),, and biocompatible notably demonstrated by the intracellular synthesis of D-luciferin for bioluminescence imaging. – Molecules containing both CBT and Cys have been characterized to undergo intra- or intermolecular condensation yielding macrocyclic products that self-assemble into nanoaggregates, which has been successfully demonstrated as a contrast mechanism for in vivo molecular imaging. – Despite the wide use of CBT/Cys condensation for imaging applications, little is known about how cells react to the formed nanoaggregates. To probe the response of cellular machinery to intracellular in situ synthesized polymer aggregates, we introduced photocaging to the Cys/CBT condensation chemistry. Previous examples of Cys-CBT conjugates decorated with peptide cages and linkers are generally not membrane-permeable. To achieve efficient intracellular polymerization, we thus explored photo uncaging that uses a small caging group and provides precise spatial and temporal control in cells. As shown in, monomer 1 is designed with L-Cys and CBT groups directly coupled through an amide bond; the Cys N -terminal amino group caged by 1-(2-nitrophenyl)ethyl carbamate; and the thiol group of the Cys side-chain is protected by a disulfide bond. We envisioned that monomer 1 would possess optimal membrane permeability and be controlled by an AND-logic gate involving light and glutathione (GSH) to polymerize in live cells. Compound 2, featuring S -methylated L-Cys, serves as a non-polymerizable control compound. Characterization of all compounds was performed using nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS), and high-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS), as detailed in the. Both 1 and 2 were stable in the dark, showing minimal degradation after 24 h in aqueous buffer (phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) at pH 7.4). A hand-held 6W lamp at 365 nm was used for photouncaging. The time-dependent conversion of both compounds was monitored by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) (&). The full conversion was achieved after approximately 15 min of irradiation at room temperature, yielding 1a and 2a as the sole products, respectively. To “trap” the reactive intermediate after disulfide deprotection, the subsequent reduction was performed in a 2-(N -morpholino)ethanesulfonic acid (MES) buffer at an acidic pH of 5.0. As expected, upon the addition of tris(2-carboxyethyl)phosphine (TCEP, 1 mM), 1a was fully converted to reactive intermediate 1b, whereas 2a remained unchanged. We next tested the light- and reduction-induced polymerization of 1. In PBS buffer at pH 7.4 (containing 10% DMSO), upon sequential irradiation and addition of TCEP (5 mM), the solution of 1 (100 μM) gradually changed from a clear homogenous solution to a white suspension in the time course of 1 h. Larger particles were sedimented when the reaction was allowed to settle for 24 hours. The insoluble product was isolated from the aqueous phase by repeated centrifugation and washing with pure water to remove all the soluble components, followed by lyophilization to dryness. The product exhibits limited solubility in all the common organic solvents tested (e.g. THF, chloroform, methanol, toluene, trichlorobenzene, and DMF).

The product exhibits limited solubility in all the common organic solvents tested (e.g. THF, chloroform, methanol, toluene, trichlorobenzene, and DMF). We managed to acquire the 1 H NMR spectrum of the solid product in DMSO- d 6 (, full spectrum in). In comparison to the spectrum of photo-uncaged monomer 1a (TFA salt), the chemical shifts of the product showed the most obvious shifts in the protons at the α-position (from 4.27 to 5.58 ppm) and the β-position (from 3.28 to 3.85 ppm) of the L-Cys group, which are attributed to the condensation reaction with the CBT and formation of a structure that resembles firefly luciferin. The product spectrum showed characteristic peak broadening of polymers with the shorter T 2 relaxation due to restricted bond rotations. Efforts to measure the molecular weight of the polymer product using mass spectrometry including MALDI-TOF were unsuccessful due to its poor solubility and ionization. We, therefore, pursued to calculate the number of repeating units of luciferin in the polymer by analyzing the NMR peak integrals of the polymer product, which were estimated to be 10 (Refer to for details), affording the average molecular weight (M n) of the poly(luciferin) to be 2990 Da. Under the aqueous reaction condition, the extensive hydrophobic and aromatic structure of poly(luciferin) would further drive the self-assembly into higher-order polymeric aggregates. To monitor the aggregation process, we employed Thioflavin-T (ThT), a rotor-based fluorescence dye for staining amyloid fibrils and other protein aggregates. We rationalize that the potential hydrophobic and π-π interactions with poly(luciferin) can cause the dye to bind and fluoresce. In the presence of ThT (10 μM) in PBS buffer, after photolysis (15 min) and reduction with TCEP (1 mM), the reactions containing 1 showed an increase in the ThT fluorescence signal when the concentration of 1 was as low as 10 μM. The fluorescence increased exponentially as a function of the concentration of 1 (exponential fit, R 2 = 0.9412). In contrast, the reaction containing 2 did not show any significant fluorescence increase compared to the blank. The polymerization and aggregation kinetics were monitored by the ThT fluorescence assay in real-time: no increase in the ThT fluorescence was observed after irradiation of 1 until the reduction, and the addition of TCEP or GSH gave a rapid rise in the ThT fluorescence which reached a plateau around 1 h. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and dynamic light scattering (DLS) confirmed the formation of polymeric nanoaggregates made of amorphous spherical particles with sizes ranging from 100–500 nm depending on the monomer concentration. These data establish the AND-logic gate control of polymerization and de novo construction of insoluble polymeric nanoaggregates by photoactivation and reduction of monomer 1.

text: We next tested if the AND-logic gate control of polymerization and de novo construction of large insoluble polymeric nanoaggregates could occur in living cells. Intracellularly abundant GSH serves as an activation trigger for polymerization upon photoactivation. We first confirmed the cell permeability of monomer 1 across the plasma membrane. The CBT group exhibits weak blue fluorescence when excited at 405 nm. Murine mammary carcinoma 4T1 cells were treated with 10 μM of 1 for 15 min, monitored by time series of confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM) imaging. When imaged by a 405 nm excitation laser, a gradual increase in fluorescence signals was observed in the cytosol of cells after the addition of 1, which reached a plateau within 10 min. The fluorescence signal of 1 was excluded from the nucleus and not localized in lysosome and mitochondria, although there was substantial overlap with the widespread endoplasmic reticulum (ER) network. These results suggest that monomer 1 can rapidly diffuse through the plasma membrane. To improve subcellular imaging, we installed additional bioorthogonal handles on monomer 1, which permits late-stage or post-polymerization “click” labeling. Instead of adding a linker between Cys and CBT which would confer macrocyclization, we installed azide and alkyne functionalities at the C4’-position on the benzothiazole ring to make 1-N 3 and 1-alk, respectively. From 1-N 3, 1-biotin was obtained by CuAAC with biotin-PEG 4 -alkyne. As outlined in, human breast adenocarcinoma MDA-MB-231 cells were treated with a full medium containing 1-biotin for 2 h at 37 °C in the dark to allow complete uptake and disulfide reduction by GSH, then exposed to light for 10 min for photo-uncaging to initiate the polymerization. Fresh medium was replaced, and cells were fixed 2 h later with ice-cold methanol which also removed soluble contents. Prominent fluorescence puncta were observed in the cells labeled with AF647-conjugated streptavidin (Strep-AF647) at the 10 μM concentration of 1-biotin that resembles the formation of polymer aggregates. The fluorescence signals increased with the concentration of 1-biotin. In contrast, cells kept in the dark showed no fluorescence signals when compared to cells treated with 1-biotin (20 μM) and exposed to light (, lower left), suggesting that the accumulation of fluorescence puncta is light-dependent. An additional 3-dimensional image confirmed that the large puncta were located inside the cells (, inset Z-stack). Consistent concentration-dependent accumulation of puncta was also observed when the cells were treated with 1-alk, followed by staining the fixed cells with sulfoCy3 azide mediated by CuAAC. To further probe the cellular location of the aggregates, we co-stained cells with protein markers specific for mitochondria, lysosome, endosome, endoplasmic reticulum, autophagosome, actin filament, peroxisome, and Golgi apparatus. The fluorescence signals of 1-biotin aggregates (red) did not fully merge with any organelle markers (green). The Pearson’s correlation coefficient (PCC) values between the fluorescence signals from 1-biotin aggregates and the different organelles were found to be generally low (< 0.4) except for ER which was a slightly higher–0.58. We also stained the cells with streptavidin conjugated to both 5 nm colloidal gold and AF488 (Strep-Au 5 -AF488). Under CLSM, green fluorescence puncta were observed in cells treated with 1-biotin (20 μM).

text: To explore the cellular responses to intracellular insoluble polymer aggregates, we evaluated the cytotoxicity of 1 in 4T1 cells. Compounds 1a and CBT were tested to examine the impact of the photocage and L-Cys moieties, respectively, and 2 as a non-polymerizing control. At 10 μM, monomer 1 effectively reduced cell viability only in the presence of photo-irradiation. At the same concentration, all three control compounds have minimal effect on cell growth irrespective of light irradiation. Full concentration-response curves of all compounds against 4T1 cells with or without light exposure revealed that the combined treatment of 1 and light was highly effective in inhibiting 4T1 cell proliferation with a half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC 50) of 8.1 μM. Without irradiation, the IC 50 of 1 was more than 100 μM; this inhibitory effect in the dark might be attributed to some spontaneous hydrolysis of the caging group. The control monomer 2 and CBT moiety alone were ineffective in reducing the growth of 4T1 cells irrespective of light irradiation. Similar results were observed with other cell lines (&) including murine colon cancer (CT26) and human non-cancerous HEK293T, cancers of the breast (MDA-MB-231), prostate (PC3), cervical (HeLa), and lung (A549) and with derivatives of 1 – 1-N 3, 1-alk, and 1-biotin in the presence of light. To our surprise, 1a exhibited poor potency. We discovered that the majority of 1a in the extracellular medium was converted to CBT following incubation with cells. This activity was presumably caused by a promiscuous aminopeptidase that can recognize cysteine derivates. On the other hand, the photocaging group protected the compound 1 from aminopeptidase degradation. We tested if the cell death occurred through apoptosis by performing a PI and Annexin V (AF488 conjugated) staining assay. Upon treated with 1 (10 μM) and light, 4T1 cells were stained and analyzed by flow cytometry (&), showing that the total PI+ cells increased from 29% at 4 h to 55% at 8 h, 68% at 12 h, and 84% at 24 h, indicating an early onset of cell death. Yet, the subset of cells that were PI-negative and Annexin V-positive remained low (3–10%), indicating the involvement of an alternative cell death pathway to apoptosis. Confocal microscopy imaging of 4T1 cells showed double staining of PI (nucleus, red) and Annexin V (membrane, green) at 24 h after treatment of 1 and light, and a swelling phenotype that is typically associated with necrosis due to the rupture of the plasma membrane. Furthermore, a significantly higher amount of intracellular enzyme lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) was released to the cell culture medium from 4T1 cells treated with 1 (10 μM) and light, but not from cells treated with 2 (10 μM) regardless of light or 1 (10 μM) in the dark. This necrotic cell death cannot be prevented by co-treatment with specific cell death inhibitors, the RIPK inhibitor nectrostatin-1 (Nec1) for necroptosis, pan-caspase inhibitor z-VAD-fmk (zVAD) for apoptosis, or iron chelator deferoxamine (DFO) for ferroptosis. Accordingly, western blot analysis validated that signaling cascades involved in these death pathways, alongside pyroptosis, remained unchanged under treatment conditions in MDA-MB-231 cells. These results suggest that cell death induced by intracellular polymer aggregates does not occur through apoptosis, necroptosis, ferroptosis, or pyroptosis.

text: To gain further insight into the death mechanism, we employed RNA sequencing to globally assess the impact of in situ polymerization on cells at the transcriptome level. MDA-MB-231 cells were subjected to incubation of 1 and light irradiation, then RNA was harvested at 8 and 24 h. Comparing the vehicle group and the treatment group (with 1 (10 μM) and light) at 8 h revealed a large number of significantly differentially expressed genes: 1297 up-regulated and 716 down-regulated; threshold of log 2 (Fold Change) ≤ 1, −log 10 (p-value) ≥ 1.3. Controls where cells treated with 2 (10 μM) and light or 1 (10 μM) kept in the dark displayed small degrees of changes at 8 h when compared to vehicle controls. Among the most upregulated transcripts were several heat shock proteins (HSPs) including HSP70 family members (HSPA6, HSPA7, HSPA1A, and HSPA1B) and HSP40 (DNAJB1). HSPs are molecular chaperones that play important roles in assisting protein folding and degradation to prevent the formation of misfolded protein aggregates and are upregulated in response to cellular stress. In breast cancer, inducible HSP70 has been associated with apoptosis and senescence suppression. This may partially explain the non-apoptotic cell death induced by poly(luciferin), despite the upregulation genes encoding several pro-apoptotic mediators (BAK, NOXA, PUMA). HSP70 and HSP40 have also been shown to cooperatively bind to hydrophobic unfolded polypeptides in an ATP-dependent manner to solubilize protein aggregates implicated in neurogenerative disorders. To identify significantly regulated pathways, we performed the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analysis, which revealed enrichment in MAPK signaling and pathways in cancer that broadly encompass proliferation-governing genes. Our attention was particularly drawn to protein processing in ER as it was enriched in 8 h, suggesting the genes involved are associated with early stress response induced by poly(luciferin). Indeed, many genes involved in proteostasis regulations were upregulated, such as HSPA5 encoding the ER chaperone BiP and SQSTIM1 encoding an autophagosome cargo protein p62. The unfolded protein response (UPR) is a signaling system that detects misfolded proteins within the ER and coordinates a cellular response to restore protein homeostasis. Misfolded protein aggregates are sequestered by chaperones and directed toward degradation through ER-associated degradation (ERAD) in proteosomes and autophagy in lysosomes. The ER chaperone BiP plays a central role as a sensor of hydrophobic aggregates and a negative regulator of UPR. Upon binding to aggregates, BiP dissociates from UPR activators to give rise to three separate branches of response. PERK (PPP1R15A) and IRE1α (ERN1) are the two ER-resident transmembrane UPR activators that undergo dimerization or oligomerization and autophosphorylation, leading to UPR activation. We performed western blotting to validate the upregulation and activation of the UPR at the protein level. After the cells were treated with 1 (10 μM) and irradiation, time-dependent upregulations and post-translational modifications of the key proteins were observed. Specifically, BiP level was increased as early as 2 h and sustained up to 24 h. Robust PERK phosphorylation was observed simultaneously, suggesting a dominating ER stress overcoming the negative regulation by BiP. In contrast, IRE1α appeared to be phosphorylated at a later time point (8 h), as resolved by the reported method using the Phos-tag system.

text: After the cells were treated with 1 (10 μM) and irradiation, time-dependent upregulations and post-translational modifications of the key proteins were observed. Specifically, BiP level was increased as early as 2 h and sustained up to 24 h. Robust PERK phosphorylation was observed simultaneously, suggesting a dominating ER stress overcoming the negative regulation by BiP. In contrast, IRE1α appeared to be phosphorylated at a later time point (8 h), as resolved by the reported method using the Phos-tag system. In principle, PERK phosphorylation of eIF2α attenuates protein translation and activates transcription of ATF4 that regulates genes involved in autophagy and redox homeostasis. On the other hand, IRE1α serves as an endoribonuclease to splice mRNA encoding XBP1, which induces the expression of target genes involved in ERAD and lipid biogenesis. Immunoblotting indeed showed increased levels of chaperones and autophagy components. After irradiation of cells treated with 1, both HSP90 and HSP70 levels heightened within 2 h. We also observed the accumulation of p62 and conjugation of LC3 to phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) to form LC3-II in a time-dependent manner, indicating an increase in autophagy flux. These results collectively prove that ER stress is an early cellular response to the formation of polymer aggregates. The activation of UPR, ERAD, and autophagy serve as mitigation mechanisms to resolve the stress. However, we found induction of transcription factor CHOP (DDIT3) during 2 to 8 h, which signifies sustained ER stress rendering cancer cells vulnerable.
title: Light-controlled Intracellular Synthesis of Poly(luciferin) Polymers Induces Cell Paraptosis
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
section_title: Intracellular Poly(luciferin) Aggregates Induce Early ER Stress Responses

text: Next, we sought to characterize the programmed death of cells undergoing ER stress induced by polymer aggregates. As shown in, MDA-MB-231 cells treated with 1 and light showed a distinct cellular morphology characterized by extensive cytoplasmic vacuolization and retaining adhesion. TEM analysis also validated the cytosolic vacuoles, which are enclosed by a single lipid layer. These alterations are consistent with the induction of paraptosis, a caspase-independent programmed cell death characterized by cytoplasmic vacuolation and ER swelling in response to disrupted proteostasis and ion homeostasis. Paraptosis is associated with different mechanisms that involve the MAPK signaling pathways, which were significantly altered as revealed in our transcriptomic data. Although the detailed biochemical signals regulating paraptosis remain unclear, ER stress has been established as an essential contributor. It is often accompanied by the acute release of Ca 2+ ions stored in the ER lumen. As shown in, irradiated cells treated with 1 had augmented cytosolic Ca 2+ concentration as imaged by the Ca 2+ indicator Fluo-4. Simultaneously, these treated cells had depolarized mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨ m) as revealed by JC-1 and augmented reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels, specifically, mitochondria-generated superoxide anion (O 2 •−), detected by MitoSox. These changes occurred in a time-dependent manner that was in line with the induction of UPR, with a surge in the O 2 •− level at 24 h. The observation that Ca 2+ overloading causes mitochondria dysfunction that potentiates ROS generation is well-matched with the catastrophic processes reported in paraptosis. To identify the molecular determinant leading to paraptosis, we applied a variety of inhibitors to pharmacologically perturb individual steps of cell death induced by intracellular polymer aggregation. Canonical paraptosis has been considered highly dependent on de novo translation, where the accumulation of misfolded proteins acts as the main source of ER stress. An inhibitor of de novo translation, cycloheximide (CHX), has been shown effective in preventing paraptosis by reducing protein synthesis. However, pre-treatment MDA-MB-231 cells with CHX did not alleviate the toxicity induced by poly(luciferin), suggesting that aggregates rather than misfolded proteins caused ER stress. Remarkably, the cell viability was significantly rescued by the co-treatment of a potent PERK kinase inhibitor AMG44, recapitulating the PERK-eIF2α-ATF4-CHOP axis as the critical UPR pathway leading to paraptosis. Autophagy inhibitor chloroquine (CQ), intracellular calcium chelator BAPTA-AM, and superoxide anion scavenger FeTMPyP all failed to prevent the loss of viability, suggesting these events are downstream of the ER stress. Interestingly, a high concentration of N-acetylcysteine (NAC) was found effective in reducing cell death. Although NAC is well recognized as a generic antioxidant, the primary mechanism of action is proposed to act as a prodrug of L-Cys by deacetylation. We reason the rescuing effect of NAC might be due to the elevated cellular L-Cys that competes for the CBT on the monomer to prevent polymerization. Finally, recent literature has demonstrated the mechanistic connections between ER stress and immunogenic cell death (ICD), in particular the PERK branch of UPR. In vitro, a panel of danger-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) emitted by dying cells can serve as hallmarks of ICD.

text: Cancer cells are inherently vulnerable to proteostatic stress because of their high demand for protein synthesis to support rapid growth and proliferation. This increased protein load puts stress on the cellular machinery responsible for maintaining proteostasis. Therapeutic strategies targeting proteostasis in cancer include inhibition of the proteasome and unfolded protein response (UPR) to induce the accumulation of misfolded proteins and thus cellular stress and cell death. This work explores an alternative strategy by chemically synthesizing polymer mimics of insoluble misfolded protein aggregates to induce cellular stress. This strategy circumvents the limitation of endosomal entrapment faced by traditional nanoparticles and polymers, providing a new means of perturbing intracellular proteostasis. Both supramolecular and covalent chemistries have been explored for in situ polymerization. However, due to the poor membrane permeability of monomers, some formed polymers are reported to reside in endosomal and lysosomal vesicles. Harsh conditions (e.g. high monomer concentration) are often required and endogenous biomolecules, for example, glutathione can potently inhibit polymerization reactivity. More importantly, the underlying death mechanism induced by the synthesized polymer aggregates has not been elucidated. Our study presents a novel in situ polymerization platform leveraging photocaging and biocompatible reactions to enable intracellular polymerization. Photocage and disulfide moieties provide a dual-locked monomer and allow the temporal and spatial control of the synthesis of poly(luciferin) featuring luciferin repeating units at low μM concentrations. The photocage also served as a protecting group against aminopeptidase. In addition, replacing L-Cys moiety into D-Cys should improve the monomer stability. The resulting poly(luciferin) was found to be prone to aggregate and form nanoparticles. Notably, we discovered that the formation of insoluble polymer aggregate induces cytotoxicity in a caspase-independent manner. We demonstrated potent cytotoxic effects against various cancer cell lines, with monomers exhibiting low micromolar IC 50 potency. Questions remain about whether polymerization alone is sufficient to induce stress, otherwise, aggregation into nanostructure is essential to drive cancer cell death. This issue coincides with the controversial views in neurodegenerative diseases that oligomeric aggregates of certain sizes are the most toxic species,, while the cell death mechanisms in neurons are still not well defined. In elucidating the mechanism of cell death, we identified that the insoluble poly(luciferin) aggregates triggered ER stress and elicited UPR. These findings uncovered the interactions between the in situ synthesized polymer and the endogenous cellular machinery. Intriguingly, a recent landmark study observed that the ER region surrounding the inclusion bodies of protein aggregates showed significantly reduced membrane dynamics, accumulation of ERAD factors, and ER chaperones that indicate ER stress. These findings are consistent with our data and preceding discoveries that intracellular aggregates compromise ER function and also perturb Ca 2+ signaling and redox state, – suggesting that poly(luciferin) aggregate resembles pathological misfolded proteins that occur in proteinopathies. Whether any specific interaction exists between poly(luciferin) aggregates and cellular organization remains to be determined.

Whether any specific interaction exists between poly(luciferin) aggregates and cellular organization remains to be determined. Furthermore, we uncovered paraptosis to be the programmed cell death pathway of TNBCs induced by poly(luciferin). Despite that paraptosis is less known and characterized, it holds promise in overcoming apoptosis-resistance cancer cells and potentially bolstering anticancer immunity via ICD. Future investigations will focus on validating the ICD effect induced by polymer aggregates through gold-standard prophylactic vaccination experiments in syngeneic mouse models. We envision further structural derivatization would evolve our understanding of cell death mechanisms induced by polymerization and aggregation. While light is used to trigger in situ polymerization, other means like tumor-specific enzymes (e.g. nitroreductase in hypoxic tumors) and radiation can be explored, in synergy with the ICD effect, for in vivo applications. The newly synthesized CBT cores containing click handles provide a convenient site for attaching other drug molecules in combined therapy. This study represents important insights toward understanding and harnessing intracellular polymerization to target proteostasis for cancer therapy.

text: Paraptosis, a form of programmed cell death, is distinguished by unique morphological and biochemical features that set it apart from apoptosis and necrosis. Unlike apoptosis, which involves cellular shrinkage, DNA fragmentation, and the formation of apoptotic bodies, paraptosis is characterized by extensive cytoplasmic vacuolization, mitochondrial swelling, and the absence of caspase activation or DNA fragmentation. This form of cell death is typically accompanied by protein and Ca 2+ homeostasis disruption and activation of the unfolded protein response of the endoplasmic reticulum (UPR ER). Paraptosis is usually mediated through signaling pathways involving mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPKs). Despite the heterogeneity of its activation mechanisms, a few studies have reported specific paraptosis-inducing targets like the insulin-like growth factor I receptor (IGF1R),, GDP-dissociation inhibitor beta (GDI2), and UBP10 (USP10), a member of the ubiquitin-specific protease family of cysteine proteases. Recently, VCP/p97 (SVIP) has been recognized as a paraptosis target and its inhibition triggers ER vacuolation. Understanding paraptosis is crucial for elucidating its role in development, disease, and therapy, − as it provides alternative mechanisms for cell death that could be harnessed for therapeutic interventions, particularly in cancer treatment where traditional apoptosis pathways are often dysregulated. Unlike other cell death mechanisms (i.e., apoptosis, necrosis, ferroptosis, and pyroptosis), paraptosis is controlled, noninflammatory, and independent of apoptotic pathways. These characteristics make it especially appealing for therapeutic applications, particularly in cancer and neurodegenerative disorders. Its unique morphological and molecular features complement other forms of cell death, broadening the scope of therapeutic strategies. Exploiting paraptosis for therapeutic purposes requires the development of effective chemical probes. Various compounds have been reported to induce paraptosis in cancer cell lines at concentrations ranging from 0.5 to 40 μM, with incubation periods between 6 and 72 h −. However, the high concentrations and prolonged exposure required to trigger paraptosis highlight the low potency of current compounds. Moreover, many of these compounds are natural products with complex chemical structures, which complicates structure–activity relationship studies. Therefore, identifying new, structurally simple molecules with improved potency and selectivity targeting paraptosis-related proteins is crucial to explore the therapeutic potential of this cell-death mechanism. In this context, hemicyanine compounds emerge as promising candidates due to their structural simplicity, biological compatibility, and ability to interact selectively with biomolecules and respond to changes in the cellular environment. − Their strong fluorescence, good biocompatibility, and ability to penetrate cells make them ideal candidates for bioimaging and biosensing. Additionally, their photosensitive properties enable their use in photodynamic and photothermal therapies, contributing to advancements in cancer treatment and other disease-targeted applications. We recently observed that hemicyanine compounds (1–5, A) induced varying levels of cytoplasmic vacuolation and exhibited significant cytotoxicity. Among them, compound 2 induced extensive vacuolation and cytotoxicity across three different cell lines.
title: Potent Inducers of Paraptosis through Electronic Tuning of Hemicyanine Electrophiles

Additionally, their photosensitive properties enable their use in photodynamic and photothermal therapies, contributing to advancements in cancer treatment and other disease-targeted applications. We recently observed that hemicyanine compounds (1–5, A) induced varying levels of cytoplasmic vacuolation and exhibited significant cytotoxicity. Among them, compound 2 induced extensive vacuolation and cytotoxicity across three different cell lines. Herein, we demonstrate that compound 2 triggers hallmark features of paraptosis, including mitochondrial swelling, ER dilation, increased superoxide production, and reactivity with cysteine residues. Proteomic analysis identified Sec23 homologue A (SEC23A) and GDP-dissociation inhibitor alpha (GDI1) as targets of compound 2 and potential activators of this nonapoptotic cell death pathway. These findings establish compound 2 as a potent activator of paraptosis and highlight its potential as a lead compound for further development.

text: We hypothesized that hemicyanine compounds 1 – 5 would display varying degrees of electrophilicity owing to the electronic properties of the substituent R in the indolenine fragment (A). These compounds were synthesized following a published procedure and characterized by 1 H-, 13 C NMR, and HRMS (Figures S17–S49). The half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC 50) of these compounds was determined in HEK293 (embryonic kidney), HeLa (cervical cancer), and MDA-MB-231 (triple-negative breast cancer) human cells at different time points by the dimethylthiazol tetrazolium (MTT) assay (B; Figure S1). The toxicity of the compounds was significantly influenced by changes in the electronegativity of the R substituent (C3). As the electronegativity of the substituent increased, the compounds displayed higher cytotoxicity, showing a consistent trend across all cell lines. Given that hemicyanines are Michael acceptors, we interpreted this trend as an indication that the toxicity of these compounds is related to their electrophilicity. Thus, compounds 1 - 5 may act as covalent ligands for nucleophilic residues in proteins such as cysteine (vide infra). Additionally, we investigated the influence of oxygen and nitrogen atoms at the C14 position. To explore this effect, we synthesized compound 2-NH 2 by replacing the hydroxyl (−OH) group in compound 2 with an amine (−NH 2) group. The nitrogen-containing compound 2-NH 2 is less cytotoxic than its oxygen-containing analog 2. This difference could be explained considering that the oxygen in compound 2 with a p K a of 7.0 ± 0.2 is largely deprotonated at neutral pH, giving an overall neutral molecule. In contrast, compound 2-NH 2 cannot be deprotonated within the biologically relevant range of pH values and has a positive charge. This change in total charge decreases the membrane permeability of 2-NH 2 and affects its subcellular localization, as confirmed by fluorescence microscopy and colocalization analysis. We observed that even though compound 1 should be more electrophilic than compound 2, it exhibits similar cytotoxicity across the three cell lines (B). This seemingly counterintuitive observation can be explained by considering that with increased electrophilicity, compound 1 is also more prone to reaction with glutathione (GSH) than compound 2. Thus, compound 2 displays sufficient electrophilicity to potentially modify protein residues, but not enough to be substantially trapped by abundant GSH in the cell. Given its potency and favorable properties, we chose compound 2 to characterize the biological effects and identify the molecular targets of this class of electrophilic compounds.

text: Cytoplasmic vacuolation has been widely associated with nonapoptotic mechanisms. To determine whether compound 2 triggered a nonapoptotic mechanism, we evaluated apoptosis induction by measuring caspase-3/7 activation in HeLa cells treated with compound 2. Caspase-3/7 cleavage was detected using the fluorescent probe CellEvent TM Caspase-3/7 Green, alongside the nucleic acid stain SYTO TM Deep Red. Staurosporine (STS), a well-established apoptosis inducer, served as the positive control, while DMSO was used as the negative control, and zVAD-FMK as a pan-caspase inhibitor. Cells treated with compound 2 exhibited no significant caspase-3/7 activation compared to the controls (A and Figure S6). As expected, cells pretreated with zVAD-FMK followed by STS did not display caspase activation (A and Figure S6). In the same experiment, we evaluated cell shrinkage and nuclear fragmentation, both well-characterized hallmarks of apoptosis. Our findings demonstrated that, in contrast to STS treatment, compound 2 did not induce nuclear fragmentation or cellular shrinkage (B). Overall, these results indicate that compound 2 does not trigger caspase activation, nuclear fragmentation, or cellular shrinkage, suggesting the involvement of nonapoptotic pathways.

text: We next evaluated the morphological changes of the ER and mitochondria in the three cell lines induced by compound 2. HEK293, HeLa, and MDA-MB-231 cells were incubated with 2 for 2 h and stained with ER-Tracker TM Green. Cytoplasmic vacuolation was observed in all three cell lines (A). Additionally, the vacuole membranes were stained with ER-Tracker TM Green, suggesting their ER origin. To further evaluate the origin of the vacuoles, we transfected the cells with a fluorescent protein targeted to the ER lumen using the KDEL retention sequence (KDEL-mTurquoise2) and incubated them with compound 2 for 2 h. Confocal time-lapse microscopy revealed that these vacuoles contain the fluorescent protein, confirming that they originate from ER dilation (B). ER dilation is often accompanied by mitochondria swelling. Thus, we monitored morphological changes in mitochondria and their role in vacuole formation by incubating compound 2 with HeLa cells stained with the mitochondrial probe PKmito DEEP RED (C). The morphology changes were evident starting at 5 min after the addition of compound 2 and a characteristic donut-shaped morphology was observed (C), indicating mitochondrial stress. After 15 min, the PKmito DEEP RED probe began to leak to the cytosol, indicating mitochondrial depolarization. Importantly, we observed that vacuolation did not involve mitochondria as they surround the vacuoles and no PKmito DEEP RED was observed in the vacuoles.

text: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are primarily generated in mitochondria and they have an important role in cell death mechanisms. Previous studies have shown that superoxide (O 2 •‑) is closely associated with paraptosis induction. Therefore, we assessed the production of this radical anion in HeLa cells treated with compound 2. We used a derivative of the fluorescent probe HKSOX-1 (HKSOX-1*) to detect intracellular O 2 •– as shown in A. We employed Antimycin A, an inhibitor of cytochrome c reductase that increases the intracellular concentration of O 2 •– as the positive control, and DMSO as the negative control. Cells treated with compound 2 displayed a significantly higher O 2 •– accumulation compared to cells treated with the controls and this increase was dose-dependent (B, C, and S9).

text: Paraptosis is a process that does not involve caspase activation and the vacuolation process can be suppressed by the protein synthesis inhibitor cycloheximide (CHX). We evaluated the effect of the pan-caspase inhibitor zVAD-FMK and CHX on vacuole formation induced by compound 2. This effect was evaluated by confocal microscopy in HeLa cells expressing KDEL-mTurquoise2. DMSO was used as a negative control and compound 2 in the absence of inhibitors as a positive control. The percentage of vacuolated cells was quantified and compared against controls. After 2 h of treatment with compound 2, zVAD-FMK (20 μM) was unable to rescue cells from ER vacuolation (A and B). On the other hand, pretreatment with CHX (20 μM) partially prevented vacuole formation as evidenced by a smaller percentage of vacuolated cells (A and B). These results confirm that vacuolation is a caspase-independent process and that ER dilation is driven by the accumulation of proteins. However, this response seems to be faster than the onset of the unfolded protein response in the ER (UPR ER) because upregulation of BiP/GRP78, an established indicator of UPR ER, is not observed at this time point. These observations are consistent with a paraptotic cell-death mechanism. We next questioned whether ER dilation and mitochondrial damage are related. We first assessed the role of O 2 •‑ accumulation in the formation of vacuoles by pretreating the cells with the O 2 •– scavenger Tiron (100 μM). Prior treatment with the scavenger did not impact the process of vacuole formation, as indicated in. This observation suggests that the increase in O 2 •– does not play a part in the formation of the vacuoles. We next tested whether ER dilation affects mitochondrial morphology. We transfected HeLa cells with the KDEL-mTurquoise2 plasmid and prestained them with PKmito DEEP RED. After a 2 h preincubation with CHX (20 μM), the cells were coincubated with compound 2 for an additional 2 h. Confocal time-lapse microscopy revealed that all cells displayed mitochondrial damage irrespective of whether they contained ER vacuoles or not. This lack of correlation between vacuolation and mitochondrial damage suggests that these processes are independent.

text: Compound 2 is a competent electrophile that can react with thiol-based nucleophiles such as GSH. We next assessed whether this reactivity extends to cysteine residues in proteins by gel-based, qualitative activity-based protein profiling (ABPP). We purified the soluble proteome from the lysate of HeLa cells and treated it with compound 2. Next, we labeled the ligandable cysteines using the reactive probe ATTO 620 maleimide. A control proteome was treated with ATTO 620 maleimide only. Separation of these proteomes by sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) revealed that cysteine labeling by ATTO 620 maleimide (5 μM) is blocked by compound 2 in some proteins in a dose-dependent manner (10–200 μM, A). This observation strongly suggests that compound 2 reacts with ligandable cysteine residues in proteins, blocking these sites. We posited that paraptosis triggered by compound 2 may be correlated to the covalent modification of free thiol groups of intracellular protein targets, leading to the disruption of thiol proteostasis. To test this hypothesis, we performed the competitive ABPP experiment described before for all hemicyanines 1 – 5 (B). This experiment revealed that the extent of cysteine labeling correlates qualitatively with the electrophilicity of the compound, its toxicity, and its ability to induce ER vacuolation (C). A recent study found that nearly all cysteine-modifying covalent ligands induce the formation of stress granules. To verify whether this is also the case for compound 2, we transfected HeLa cells with fluorescently labeled G3BP1 protein, a validated nucleator of stress granules. We observed that indeed compound 2 induced the formation of stress granules, further validating its role as a cysteine covalent modifier.
title: Potent Inducers of Paraptosis through Electronic Tuning of Hemicyanine Electrophiles

text: We hypothesized that compound 2 interacts with specific thiol-containing proteins involved in paraptosis. To identify these protein targets, we employed mass-spectrometry-based ABPP, − and synthesized a biotinylated probe derived from compound 2 (2-biotin, A). Additionally, to identify targets potentially unrelated to thiol modification, we used a biotinylated probe based on compound 5 (5-biotin, A), which is a structural analog of 2 with diminished electrophilicity and lack of paraptosis-inducing activity. Finally, to identify general targets of electrophilic probes, we used a biotinylated iodoacetamide (IA-biotin, A) probe, which is a broad-spectrum cysteine-reactive compound. Importantly, treatment of cells with IA did not induce ER vacuolation and therefore serves as a valuable control in the identification of targets that are specifically engaged by compound 2 and are involved in vacuolation. We treated cell lysates with 2-biotin, 5-biotin, or IA-biotin for ABPP-based target enrichment. The enriched proteins were subsequently identified through proteomic analysis using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). Proteins captured upon treatment of cell lysates with DMSO were used as a negative control, while 2-biotin, 5-biotin, and IA-biotin were used to identify specific interactors. We employed SAIN T express software to identify significant targets, which we defined as those with a Bayesian false discovery rate (BFDR) threshold of 0.05 and an empirical fold-change score (EFC) threshold of 2 (log 2 (EFC) ≥ 1, Figure S13). Nearly 3000 proteins were enriched using either 2-biotin or IA-biotin. These results suggest that 2-biotin is a powerful electrophile capable of reacting with many proteins at the concentration used (10 μM). However, 2-biotin did not react indiscriminately with nucleophilic cysteines, e.g., while protein disulfide isomerases PDI3–6 were efficiently enriched using IA-biotin, they were not detected in the fraction enriched by 2-biotin. Since IA does not induce ER vacuolation and paraptosis, we posited that proteins that react with 2-biotin but not with IA-biotin might be involved in the induction of this phenotype. We set thresholds of log 2 (EFC) and -log 10 (BFDR) of >3 for 2-biotin and <1 for IA-biotin (B) and identified 13 proteins that were strongly enriched by 2-biotin but not by IA-biotin (B and Table S2). In our ABPP experiment, we treated whole cell lysate with the biotinylated probes, and therefore the whole soluble proteome was exposed to the electrophiles. Live-cell imaging revealed that compound 2 was notably enriched in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), as indicated by colocalization with ER-specific markers; therefore, from the subset of 13 proteins, we focused only on those known to localize to the ER. Based on these considerations, three proteins emerged as potential drivers of ER vacuolation: Sec23 homologue A (SEC23A), GDP-dissociation inhibitor alpha (GDI1), and oxysterol-binding protein 1 (OSBP). SEC23A is a critical component of COPII-coated vesicles, which transport secretory proteins from the ER to the Golgi apparatus. Interestingly, fibroblasts from individuals carrying mutant SEC23A exhibit ER dilation, confirming its role in vacuolation. GDI1 is a protein that regulates Rab GTPase activity and plays a key role in vesicular trafficking. Although direct inhibition of GDI1 has not been associated with cytoplasmic vacuolation, its isoform GDI2, which shares similar functions, has been previously linked to paraptosis and ER vacuolation.

text: SEC23A is a critical component of COPII-coated vesicles, which transport secretory proteins from the ER to the Golgi apparatus. Interestingly, fibroblasts from individuals carrying mutant SEC23A exhibit ER dilation, confirming its role in vacuolation. GDI1 is a protein that regulates Rab GTPase activity and plays a key role in vesicular trafficking. Although direct inhibition of GDI1 has not been associated with cytoplasmic vacuolation, its isoform GDI2, which shares similar functions, has been previously linked to paraptosis and ER vacuolation. Moreover, previous efforts to generate a GDI1 / GDI2 double knockout in U2OS cells were unsuccessful, likely due to impaired cell survival and proliferation. OSBP is a lipid transporter that delivers sterol to the Golgi complex in exchange for phosphatidylinositol 4-phosphate, which is degraded by the SAC1/SACM1L phosphatase in the ER. OSBP inhibition has been associated with disruption of the Golgi apparatus and impaired retrograde trafficking. Although genetic depletion of OSBP has not been reported to significantly affect cell viability, some small-molecule inhibitors of OSBP exhibit cytotoxic effects, leading to cell death in specific cell lines. Notably, OSBP does not appear to be directly involved in ER vacuolation or paraptosis, as knockdown experiments have failed to induce the characteristic vacuolation. Based on this precedent, we conclude that hemicyanine 2 induced ER vacuolation and paraptosis primarily through inhibition of SEC23A, with a potential contribution from GDI1. The proteins discussed above are likely to contribute to paraptosis activation but the cytotoxic effects of compound 2 may involve additional interactions. For instance, mitochondrial proteins aspartate aminotransferase (GOT2) and mitochondrial import receptor subunit TOMM70 may lead to the observed increase in superoxide production, contributing to cell death. Additionally, thioredoxin reductase 1 (TXNRD1) was enriched in both 2-biotin and IA-biotin treatments. TXNRD1 contains a highly reactive selenocysteine residue, making it particularly susceptible to electrophilic compounds. Thus, increasing the selectivity of compound 2 for SEC23A, while decreasing its overall electrophilicity, will be crucial to develop a probe that can be used to study the induction of paraptosis independently from other potentially confounding sources of cytotoxicity.

section_title: Compound 2 Binds to Potential Regulators of Paraptosis

text: Paraptosis serves as an alternative cell death pathway when apoptosis is ineffective, offering a potential therapeutic avenue in diseases where apoptosis is dysregulated. However, the high concentration and prolonged exposure needed to trigger paraptosis highlight the limited potency of current compounds. In this study, we introduced hemicyanine compounds as novel paraptosis activators. Among them, compound 2 effectively induces paraptosis in various cell lines by covalently interacting with free cysteine residues in cellular proteins triggering hallmark features of paraptosis, including extensive vacuolation of the ER. Through ABPP analysis, we identified key protein targets of compound 2, including SEC23A and GDI1, which are associated with vesicle trafficking and ER vacuolation. Notably, compound 2 displayed some degree of selectivity, with minimal interaction with highly nucleophilic PDIs, underscoring its potential as a chemical probe. These findings position compound 2 as a promising lead for developing selective, targeted probes to study paraptosis, with potential applications in the development of therapeutics in cancers where traditional apoptotic pathways are impaired. Future studies will focus on optimizing the structure–activity relationships of compound 2 to enhance its potency and selectivity.
