A scientist studying death of a cell can be compared with a forensic physician investigating a crime scene. However, in contrast to forensic physicians who focus on identifying the cause of a murder, scientists focused on cell death are primarily interested in understanding the mechanisms and types of PCD, that is, cell suicide. However, understanding the processes and types of cell death is important to fully comprehend the manner in which cells resolve internal disharmony and maintain balance. Therefore, scientists interested only in cell suicide will play an increasingly important role in the cellular universe, similar to forensic scientists investigating crime scenes in the macroscopic world.
title: Diversity and complexity of cell death: a historical review

text: Transmembrane B cell lymphoma 2-associated X protein (BAX) inhibitor motif-containing (TMBIM) 6, also known as Bax inhibitor 1 (BI-1), was identified as an anti-apoptotic protein that predominantly localizes to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). TMBIM6 structure remains unknown but is predicted to be a 6 or 7-transmembrane protein who’s N terminus (TMBIM6 N trm) interacts with pro-survival binding partners including cardiolipin (CP), phosphatidylserine (PS), Bcl-2, Bcl-xL and anti-apoptotic bacterial effector proteins [ – ]; but seemingly lacks direct functionality with relation to TMBIM6 activity. TMBIM6 C-terminus (TMBIM6 C trm) is directly involved in TMBIM6 function and regulates ER stress [ – ], reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, actin cytoskeletal dynamics [, – ], metabolism, cell survival, and cytosolic Ca 2+ concentration [ – ] through interaction with numerous binding partners. TMBIM6 has environmental detection sites that detect variations in pH and Ca 2+ [ – ]. TMBIM6’s functional diversity is key in the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative disease (Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease), ischemic-reperfusion injury, viral and bacterial infection, heart disease, liver disease, wound healing, aging, traumatic brain injury, and cancer [ – ]. Within cancer, TMBIM6 expression varies greatly, with breast, glioma, prostate, uterine, and ovarian cancers over-expressing TMBIM6 two-fold or more whereas stomach, colon, kidney, lung, and rectal cancers downregulate TMBIM6 expression two-fold or more. Within breast, ovarian and uterine cancers TMBIM6 knockdown, using siRNA (TMBIM6 kd), either induced spontaneous apoptosis or, where spontaneous apoptosis did not occur, increased cellular stress and heightened sensitivity to pro-apoptotic stimulants. Recently, a TMBIM6 antagonist, BIA, was shown to inhibit tumor growth and, for some cancers, reduced tumor size and volume. BIA acted by inhibiting TMBIM6 interaction with mTORC2, thereby blocking mTORC2 complex formation with RICTOR and RPL19, resulting in the inhibition of Akt phosphorylation; cellular metabolism; cancer cell migration; and tumor invasion. The TMBIM6 interaction site for BIA was not elucidated nor was the type of cell death (i.e., apoptosis, anoikis, etc.) or cellular changes (i.e., nuclear condensation, caspase activation, etc.). Our results show TMBIM6 activates specific functions in response to distinct IntraCellular Environmental (ICE) changes, with TMBIM6 Ntrm modulating TMBIM6 response. ICE changes are fundamental to disease/injury progression and regulation dictates disease outcome. We show, following disease/injury-induced ICE change, TMBIM6 Ntrm modulation can overcome the effects of toxins, viral infection, excitotoxicity observed in brain injury, and promote wound healing. Yet in cancer, we reveal TMBIM6 has pro-death capabilities, inducing paraptotic cell death. However, TMBIM6 Ntrm modulation had no effect on non-cancerous/non-stressed cells even at high doses. We observed that TMIBM6 induces paraptosis in non-canonical manner and did not involve ER stress signaling, p38 MAPK pathways, proteasomal or autophagosomal pathways, and protein synthesis is not required. TMBIM6 paraptotic induction occurred due to elevated cytosolic ROS and Calcium which activated lysosomal-mediated ER degradation. This was universal across all cancers tested and was not dictated by the level of TMBIM6 expression or variations in the genotype/phenotype of the cancer.
title: TMBIM6/BI-1 is an intracellular environmental regulator that induces paraptosis in cancer via ROS and Calcium-activated ERAD II pathways

text: However, TMBIM6 Ntrm modulation had no effect on non-cancerous/non-stressed cells even at high doses. We observed that TMIBM6 induces paraptosis in non-canonical manner and did not involve ER stress signaling, p38 MAPK pathways, proteasomal or autophagosomal pathways, and protein synthesis is not required. TMBIM6 paraptotic induction occurred due to elevated cytosolic ROS and Calcium which activated lysosomal-mediated ER degradation. This was universal across all cancers tested and was not dictated by the level of TMBIM6 expression or variations in the genotype/phenotype of the cancer. In mice models, TMBIM6 Ntrm modulation had no toxic effects, even at doses >400 mg/kg, and induced significant reduction (> 95%) in tumor size and volume in breast and ovarian models. In summary, we highlight the therapeutic potential of ICE regulation through TMBIM6 modulation across multiple diseases, injuries, and cancers.
title: TMBIM6/BI-1 is an intracellular environmental regulator that induces paraptosis in cancer via ROS and Calcium-activated ERAD II pathways

text: TMBIM6 modulating therapeutics were identified via high-throughput screening (HTS) using materials from ChEMBL, proprietary peptide/chemical libraries, and known TMBIM6 binding partners described in. Small molecules and peptides that bind to TMBIM6 and modulate its activity were identified. This paper focuses on MQT, a chemically synthesized peptide, that binds to TMBIM6 Ntrm modulating its function (Supplementary Fig) and is described in patent PCT/US2019/048414. MQT had no effect on cell survival in normal cells (HMEC, HOSEpC, HUF, and MRC-5) (Supplementary Fig), however, in cells challenged with apoptosis-inducing toxins, MQT significantly promoted cell survival (MQT blocked apoptotic characteristics including caspase-3 activation, nuclear condensation, mitochondrial hyper-permeabilization and activation of the ER stress-associated transcription factor CREB3 (Interestingly, MQT pre-treatment, prior to toxin challenge, had no effect on cell survival (Supplementary Fig) and did not inhibit apoptotic characteristics when challenged with toxins. Knockdown of TMBIM6 negated MQT effect indicating TMBIM6 is essential for MQT activity (The anti-apoptotic effects of TMBIM6 modulation by MQT were blocked by ABT-737 (Bcl-2, Bcl-xL, and Bcl-w inhibitor) for ER stress-inducing toxins, tunicamycin (TUN) and brefeldin A (BFA), but only marginally impacted FasL and had no impact on staurosporine (StS); indicating anti-apoptotic BCL-2 members are required for TMBIM6 to inhibit ER stress induced cell death. A key step in the Fas-mediated death pathway, is Akt phosphorylation which TMBIM6 regulates. Following FasL challenge, MQT greatly increased Akt phosphorylation in the first hour but had no effect prior to Fas challenge (Fig. time 0). The data indicates MQT modulates TMBIM6 post stress to significantly enhance its activity. The only measured, pre-stress effect of MQT on healthy cells was increased ERK phosphorylation (TMBIM6 induces ERK phosphorylation to promote cell survival, indicating MQT likely activates this TMBIM6 function. However, as pre-treatment of cells with MQT did not negate toxin effects, then pre-activation of the ERK pathway was not key in promoting cell survival. Therefore, non-ERK activating TMBIM6 activities are more important in promoting TMBIM6-mediated cell survival to different stresses. TMBIM6 is important in real-world stresses such as brain injury [ – ], viral infection, and wound healing. To assess the therapeutic potential of TMBIM6 modulation on these diseases/injuries, we used MQT or the TMBIM6 antagonist BIA on translational models; specifically excitotoxicity challenge of neuronal cells; viral challenge assays with Influenza A (Panama/2007/99 (H3N2) and A/X-31 (H3N2)), RSV (strain A2), Adenovirus (type 5), and the beta-coronavirus (OC43); and wound healing as described in. TMBIM6 modulation significantly; overcame excitotoxicity (p < 0.001); protected cells to viral challenge against all viruses tested (Fig. with Influenza A infection responding most profoundly (p < 0.001); and promoted wound healing (p < 0.05) (BIA mildly inhibited wound healing (p < 0.05) but no impact on viral assay or excitotoxicity (Again, pre-treatment of cells with MQT or BIA, prior to challenge with excitotoxicity, infection or injury had no effect. Toxin challenge, brain injury, viral infection, and wound healing impose unique stresses, yet TMBIM6 Ntrm modulation could overcome them.
title: TMBIM6/BI-1 is an intracellular environmental regulator that induces paraptosis in cancer via ROS and Calcium-activated ERAD II pathways
section_title: TMBIM6 modulating peptides act via TMBIM6 N terminus to promote cell survival to a broad range of cell stresses, including injury/disease

text: TMBIM6 has diverse pro-survival activity [ – ] and our data shows it can respond to unique stresses. We hypothesized TMBIM6 must be capable of detecting unique IntraCellular Environmental (ICE) change that induce conformational change to activate specific TMBIM6 functions. Using circular dichroism (CD), we estimated TMBIM6 structure to be 45% helix, 18% sheet, 11% turn and 27% disordered at pH7.4 (MQT induced a 91% decrease in TMBIM6 sheets, 67% increase in turns and 24% increase in disorder (This conformational change could be the reason for MQT induced ERK phosphorylation (BIA had no impact on TMBIM6 conformation. To date, there is no data showing BIA directly interacts with TMBIM6. Therefore, we assessed BIA-TMBIM6 interaction via BLI and SPR. Neither approach confirmed direct BIA-TMBIM6 interaction. We hypothesize BIA might only interact with TMBIM6 when in the mTORC2 complex, as described in. As there is no data supporting direct TMBIM6 interaction we did not use BIA as a future control. Next, we assessed if environmental stimuli (pH, Ca2+, and ROS) impact TMBIM6 conformation. At low pH (≤6.5) TMBIM6 was 55% helix, 3.3% sheet, 13% turn and 29% disordered, showing a shift to a more helical state relative to TMBIM6(pH 7.4) (MQT addition to TMBIM6(pH 6.5) reduced helices by 37% and increased sheets >400%, indicating a more alpha-beta formation (MQT pre-treatment of TMBIM6(pH 7.4), then lowering pH to ≤6.5, had no impact, with TMBIM6 adopting its pH6.5 conformation (To assess the effect of intracellular Ca2+ changes we used 500 nM Ca2+. At this concentration, mitochondria actively uptake Ca2+ and several physiological changes occur. TMBIM6(500 nM Ca2+) was 74% helix, 3.9% sheet, 9.3% turn and 13.3% unstructured, indicating a highly helical structured state that bears a strong resemblance to the TMBIM6 bacterial homolog BsYetJ. Adding MQT to TMBIM6(500 nM Ca2+) reduced helices by 24%, increased sheets by 123%, increased turns 48%, and increased disorder by 64% (MQT pre-treatment of TMBIM6 followed by 500 nM Ca2+ decreased the degree of TMBIM6 conformational change, relative to 500 nM Ca2+ in the absence of MQT (ROS (H2O2) had little impact on TMBIM6 conformation, only slightly reducing helical and sheet structures whilst increasing disorder (Neither treatment nor pre-treatment, with MQT impacted TMBIM6 conformation. CD data shows a complex picture with at least five TMBIM6 conformations (normal, ERK activating, H+ regulating, Ca2+ regulating and ROS regulating). However, detailed structural analysis is required to understand these distinct changes and assess the impact on binding partner interaction. TMBIM6 structure has not been experimentally determined, therefore, to assess the conformational changes we used the AlphaFold2 model. AlphaFold2 (AF2) predicts TMBIM6 is a seven-transmembrane protein composed largely of helical structures, with the C-terminus residing in the ER intraluminal space. To validate this model, we carried out immunofluorescence analysis in cells overexpressing N or C terminal HA-tagged TMBIM6. Both N-HA-TMBIM6 and TMBIM6-HA-C were detected by immunofluorescence indicating both the N and C termini project into the cytosol. This aligns to the results in, which also contradict the AlphaFold2 model. However, the tags themselves may have affected TMBIM6 folding. The AlphaFold2 model is seemingly greatly influenced by BsYetJ, to which TMBIM6 identity is 23.77% (BLASTp). BsYetJ acts primarily, or exclusively, as a Ca2+ channel and reacts to H+ to create open and closed forms that regulate Ca2+ efflux.

text: Both N-HA-TMBIM6 and TMBIM6-HA-C were detected by immunofluorescence indicating both the N and C termini project into the cytosol. This aligns to the results in, which also contradict the AlphaFold2 model. However, the tags themselves may have affected TMBIM6 folding. The AlphaFold2 model is seemingly greatly influenced by BsYetJ, to which TMBIM6 identity is 23.77% (BLASTp). BsYetJ acts primarily, or exclusively, as a Ca2+ channel and reacts to H+ to create open and closed forms that regulate Ca2+ efflux. Our CD data shows TMBIM6(500 nM Ca2+) adopts a high helical form, which fully aligns to the AlphaFold2 model (We hypothesized the AlphaFold2 model represents TMBIM6 in a high Ca2+ environment. For this reason, we assessed if TMBIM6(500 nM Ca2+)/AlphaFold2 model reacts to acidification in a manner like that of BsYetJ. To achieve this, we used the TMBIM6(500 nM Ca2+)/AlphaFold2 model and titrated three amino acids (Asp, Glu and His) to perform 100-ns constant pH molecular dynamic simulations (CpHMD) at pH6.5 and pH7.5 (CpHMD allows the protonated state of the titrated residues to change during the simulation considering the interaction with surrounding residues. This enables exploration of where the protein has pH-dependent structural features. At pH6.5, the radius of gyration indicated TMBIM6(500 nM Ca2+) becomes more compact relative to pH7.5 (To further evaluate this, we selected Transmembrane (TM) helices 1, 4 and intra-membrane (TM7) as reference structures for alignment of CpHMD trajectories, to calculate the root mean square deviation (RMSD) of the non-reference TMBIM6 structures. RMSD results show significant variations for TM2, 3, 5 and 6 at pH6.5 versus 7.5 with DSSP analysis showing TMs 2, 3 and 5 have increased helical or turn structures (Our data shows TMBIM6(500 nM Ca2+)/AlphaFold2 model behaves like BsYetJ as described in, with acidification (pH6.5) inducing TM5 into an ‘open’ conformation with amino acids 151–159 being exposed to the solvent region; this is closed at pH7.5. In support, we identified a hydrophobic pocket which becomes larger at low pH, suggesting a potential site for Ca2+ efflux/influx and showing how TMIBM6 could regulate Ca2+ levels. This data further supports the idea that TMBIM6 can detect ICE change, which induces structural conformational change. Several publications indicate TMBIM6 aspartic acid-213 (D213) is key for ICE detection [ – ]. To assess this, we created TMBIM6 KD cells using CRISPR, and ectopically expressed TMBIM6 D213A or wild-type TMBIM6. MQT had no effect on TMBIM6 KD or TMBIM6 D213A cells but promoted cell survival in cells reverted to wild type, indicating the anti-apoptotic effect was both due to TMBIM6 ICE detection and MQT modulation of TMBIM6 Ntrm. Altogether, this data shows TMBIM6’s ability to detect ICE change is key in dictating the function it needs to perform. This explains TMBIM6’s high importance in response to different injuries and diseases, such as cancer, where significant ICE change occurs and TMBIM6 relevance has been well researched.

text: TMBIM6 expression has been extensively linked to cancer survival, metastasis, chemoresistance and growth, with most research focusing on breast and lung cancers. TMBIM6 mRNA expression analysis in cancer biopsies from the NCBI/GEO database (Human Protein Atlas; www.proteinatlas.org) indicate higher TMIBM6 expression significantly correlates (p < 0.05) with reduced patient survival in breast, head and neck, melanoma, glioma, and lung cancers (However, for colorectal, urothelial, and renal cancers higher TMBIM6 expression correlated with higher patient survival (p < 0.05) (Three cancers (breast, head and neck, and renal) indicated high significance (p < 0.001) between patient survival and TMBIM6 expression. In breast cancer patients (n = 1,075) the median patient survival was strikingly different for cancers with high (7.85 yrs) versus low (12.21 yrs) TMBIM6 expression (This was also true for head and neck cancers (n = 499) where the median survival was 2.96 years for high and 5.49 years for low TMBIM6 expression (However, renal cancers (n = 877) inverted this trend as median survival was >15 yrs for high TMBIM6 expression, whereas low TMBIM6 expression resulted in median survival of 5.4 yrs (We postulated MQT modulation of TMBIM6 Ntrm, where pro-survival partners bind, offers insight into key pathways that promote cancer cell survival and tumorigenesis. We focused on breast cancers, where patient data indicated the strongest relationship between TMBIM6 expression and patient survival. Initially, we assessed TMBIM6 expression in three highly characterized breast cancer cell lines; luminal A (MCF-7 and T47D) and triple negative (MDA-MB-231). We observed significant differences in the level of TMBIM6 expression, with MDA-MB-231 expressing significantly lower TMBIM6. TMBIM6 knockdown resulted in significant cell death of MDA-MB-231, which had the lowest levels of TMBIM6 expression, but not that of MCF-7 or T47D cell lines; however, we did observe MCF-7 and T47D became sensitive to stress. Based on this data, TMBIM6 expression alone does not dictate patient survivability, as TNBCs have lower survivability yet the representative TNBC cell line, MDA-MB-231, had the lowest level of TMBIM6 expression. To assess the importance of TMBIM6 Ntrm we treated 8 breast cancer cell lines (ATCC 30–4500 K) with MQT; each cell line represents a breast cancer sub-type with key genetic variations/mutations (Non-cancerous breast cell line HMEC was used as a control. MQT (5 μM) reduced cancer cell viability ≥50% in 24 h across all cancerous cell lines tested, this continued to >97% over 96 h (No change in cell viability of control cell lines relative to untreated. This suggests the genotype/phenotype of the cancerous cell did not affect how TMBIM6 Ntrm modulation decreased cell viability (Cell detachment assays corroborated cell viability data, with MQT (5 μM) inducing ≥45% loss in cancer cell attachment in 24 h rising to >90% over 96 h across all cancer cell lines (There was no change in the attachment of control cells relative to untreated. text: Cancer cell death induced by TMBIM6 modulation was unexpected, so we investigated the mechanism by which this occurs. TMBIM6 is a regulator of apoptosis, therefore we assessed early, mid, and late-stage apoptotic markers. Externalization of annexin-V (early apoptotic marker) did occur but only late-stage in rounded cells, many of which were floating. Adherent cells did not exhibit Annexin-V externalization but had cytosolic vacuolation (Fig. pre-rounding), indicating vacuolation occurred prior to cell rounding and Annexin-V externalization. Caspase-3 activation (early apoptotic marker) also did not occur when assessed via IF (This was validated using Caspase-Glo 3/7 (Promega) which showed no caspase 3/7 activation in MQT-treated cells, confirming caspase-independent cell death. We assessed if any caspase activation was necessary for cancer cell death using pan-caspase inhibitor Z-VAD-fmk prior to the addition of 5 μM MQT. Z-VAD-fmk did not block cancer cell death or the observed cytosolic vacuolation (Mitochondrial permeabilization (early apoptotic marker) was observed in cancer cells treated with MQT, but not in control cells (MCF-10A), indicating loss of mitochondrial viability. Late-stage characteristics of apoptosis; nuclear condensation, DNA fragmentation, formation of apoptotic bodies, and cell membrane blebbing were not observed. However, MQT did induce a form of ‘nuclear condensation’ in >50% of cancer cells (24 h), rising to >97% (96 h). (No apoptotic markers, early or late, were observed in non-cancerous cell lines. Taken together, TMBIM6 Ntrm modulation did not promote cancer survival but had the opposing effect irrespective of cancer’s genotype or phenotype. Furthermore, cancer cells were not dying via apoptotic-related pathways. The absence of apoptotic characteristics and cytosolic vacuolation were unexpected. To determine where MQT localizes, we used Myc-tagged MQT in MCF-7 cells and immunostained with calnexin (ER), DAPI (nuclei), anti-Myc (MQT), and actin. The observed vacuoles were in the ER with MQT localizing around the vacuoles (ER vacuolation was also observed in ovarian, uterine, lung, and colorectal cancers. To determine the importance of TMBIM6 for ER vacuolation, TMBIM6 knockdown (TMBIM6 kd) was done on MCF-7 and MCF-10F cells. In addition, to determine the importance of TMBIM6 environmental detection site (TMBIM6 D213) for ER vacuolation TMBIM6 antisense (TMBIM6 kd) was used on MCF-7 and MCF-10F cells, before ectopically expressing TMBIM6 D213A. In both MCF-7 TMBIM6 kd and TMBIM6 D213A cells TMBIM6 modulation by MQT had no effect, confirming the importance of both TMBIM6 and its environmental detection capabilities for ER vacuolation and cell viability (ER vacuolation is not an apoptotic characteristic. To assess its formation, we performed live-cell time series analysis. Small vacuoles were observed as early as 1 hr post TMBIM6 modulation in breast, ovarian and uterine cancers; however, in lung and colorectal cancer small vacuoles did not occur until ~3 h. Smaller vacuoles were observed to combine into larger vacuoles between 6–12 h (8–12 h after TMBIM6 modulation we observed cell rounding, but the plasma membrane was maintained. Cell detachment occurred after 18–24 h with no loss in cell membrane integrity. The data suggests a similarity between different cancers as the genotypes and phenotypes varied significantly between the cancers tested, yet all underwent the same form of cell death.

Prior data (Figs.) shows MQT does not act prophylactically and requires TMBIM6 and its environmental detection capabilities. Structural data (Figs.) also indicated TMBIM6’s ability to detect ICE change is key in dictating the function it needs to perform. This supports our prior hypothesis that cancers share similar intracellular environment characteristics i.e., ER burden, elevated cytosolic ROS, elevated cytosolic H+, increased metabolism, etc. These common changes would explain why MQT affected diseased/injured cells, where ICE change occurred. However, there was no effect on healthy cells where no ICE change was present and TMBIM6 was ‘inactive’. Owing to the absence of apoptotic characteristics yet extensive ER vacuolation, which progressed over time, we believe TMBIM6 modulation induces paraptosis. reviews the features of paraptosis relative to other forms of cell death. The morphological features of paraptosis are all observed in MQT treated cancer cells and include occurrence in a single cell, intact cytomembrane (Fig. – actin,), presence of cytoplasmic vacuoles, dilatation of mitochondria (indirectly shown – Fig show dilated mitochondria using MitoTracker) and endoplasmic reticulum, and irregular chromatin aggregation. We observed vacuolation intensity increases with smaller vacuoles fusing to form larger ones, ruling out methuosis. Larger vacuolation formation progressed to chromatin condensation and finally intact cell rounding/detachment. Paraptotic induction occurs via several distinct mechanisms summarized in the most widely reported being via the MAPK/ERK/JNK pathway. To identify the paraptotic mechanism involved we conducted time-course analysis on SK-OV-3 and MCF-7 cells treated with MQT, with pathway-specific activation assessed via western blot. No activation or downstream consequences of the p38 MAPK pathway were detected (Alix, a known inhibitor of p38 MAPK-mediated paraptosis, was not elevated and showed a reduction in expression. JNK and ERK pathway analysis showed decreased expression and phosphorylation of Ask1 and cRAF (However, their downstream targets, MKK4 and MEK1/2 respectively, showed slightly increased phosphorylation at 2 h, with significant phosphorylation occurring after 3.5 h; this was also the case for ERK and p90RSK phosphorylation. However, significant JNK phosphorylation occurred within the first 2 h, indicating it is activated via non-MKK4 routes. Unusually, the downstream effects of JNK phosphorylation, i.e., c-Jun phosphorylation, followed the same pattern as that of MKK4. Morphologically, paraptotic characteristics (i.e., ER vacuolation) occurred within 45 min. These findings imply the MAPK/ERK/JNK pathways are not directly associated with paraptotic features, like ER vacuolation, induced by TMBIM6 within the first hour of MQT treatment.

text: Each disease/injury induces a unique stress and change in the IntraCellular Environment (ICE) which is essential for disease/injury pathogenesis. For example, excitotoxicity induces an intracellular surge of cytosolic Ca2+ and promotes cell death [ – ]. In contrast, influenza infection induces ROS to favor viral gene replication. TMBIM6 can detect unique ICE changes to activate specific functions that overcome the imposed disease/injury stress. In the aforementioned examples, TMBIM6 alone could overcome excitotoxicity, and secondary TBI events, as well as stop influenza infection. This study shows TMBIM6 Ntrm can be modulated to overcome toxin exposure, excitotoxicity in neurodegenerative disease, viral infection, and promote wound healing. Current TMBIM6 understanding could explain these results. For example, TMBIM6 is localized to the ER (cells’ main store of Ca2+) and functions, in part, as a Ca2 + /H+ channel to regulate cytosolic Ca2+ and acidification; both of which are key in regulating mitochondrial function. During excitotoxicity, TMBIM6 directly blocks Ca2+ channels, such as the IP3 receptor (IP3R). IP3R is a major ER Ca2+ efflux pump and is activated by IP3. IP3 is released by MetabR upon glutamate binding triggering a significant increase in cytosolic Ca2+, in turn contributing to mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and cell death. To block this, TMBIM6 directly inhibits IPR3 but also interacts with anti-apoptotic BCL-2 members (i.e., Bcl-2/Bcl-xL) localizing them to the ER/mitochondria. Doing so allows Bcl-2/xL to bind IP3R and inhibit IP3R Ca2+ efflux. Localized Bcl-2/xL could also interact with any pro-death proteins i.e., BAX/BID that were released from MOMP to promote cell survival. TMBIM6’s ability to localize Bcl-2/xL could explain how MQT overcame ER stress-inducing toxins TUN and BFA. By inhibiting Ca2+ efflux pumps, via different mechanisms, TMBIM6 asserts itself as the major [Ca2+] cytosolic controller in the cell. TMBIM6 can now directly regulate cytosolic Ca2+ thereby controlling [Ca2+] cytosolic levels. As such TMBIM6 can block/minimize downstream effects of high [Ca2+] cytosolic, stopping excitotoxicity-induced cell death. In the viral challenge, TMBIM6 inhibits influenza gene replication by blocking and reverting virally elevated ROS via the mechanisms described in. Our data aligns to publications that show TMBIM6 overcomes viral infection, reverts/stops brain injuries [ –, – ], promotes wound healing, and can slow/stop aging. However, our data shows modulation of TMBIM6 Ntrm alone was insufficient to treat disease/injury, without TMBIM6 first sensing and reacting to ICE change. Our data indicates TMBIM6 is only activated in a cell where disease/injury ICE change occurs. Structural assessment supports this, showing TMBIM6 has distinctly different conformations dictated by the environment i.e., low pH form, high Ca2+ form, etc. It is highly likely that each TMBIM6 conformation enables unique partner interaction to regulate and overcome the ICE change i.e., NPR interaction to regulate ROS, IRE1 interaction to regulate ER stress, mTOR interaction for pro-survival, etc. In cancer, ICE changes are a byproduct of the disease and not necessary for its pathogenesis. text: It is highly likely that each TMBIM6 conformation enables unique partner interaction to regulate and overcome the ICE change i.e., NPR interaction to regulate ROS, IRE1 interaction to regulate ER stress, mTOR interaction for pro-survival, etc. In cancer, ICE changes are a byproduct of the disease and not necessary for its pathogenesis. For example, cancers have increased glucose uptake, preferential use of lactate, and constitutive aerobic glycolysis (Warburg effect). These produce detrimental byproducts such as increased Ca2+, ROS and acidification; which confer cancer benefits by promoting metastasis and cell motility, activating pro-survival pathways (i.e., Akt, NFκB), enhancing chemoresistance, and promoting gene expression [ – ]. However, if ICE byproducts are unregulated, by regulators such as TMBIM6, they will quickly result in cell death. Interestingly, there is significant variation in TMBIM6 expression between cancers, which impacts patient survivability and portrays a complicated picture. However, this picture must be contextualized by the large variations in ICE severity between different cancers. Those ICE variations occur due to differences in cancer growth rates, metabolic burdens, and expression of other proteins i.e., XIAP, Bcl-2, etc. These variations in ICE severity create different degrees of TMBIM6 dependency i.e., cancers with severe ICE change/cellular burden impose more dependence on TMBIM6. Consistent with published data, we found the TMBIM6 Ntrm to be pro-survival, enabling the cell to overcome stresses imposed by toxins, excitotoxicity, etc. Surprisingly in cancer, the opposite was observed, with TMBIM6 Ntrm modulation inducing a unique form of cell death; paraptosis. Paraptotic induction did not occur via common pathways involving MAPK, JNK, ERK, proteasomal, autophagocytic, caspase-9, or UPR. Instead, TMBIM6-paraptotic induction occurred by inducing ICE change, elevating both cytosolic Ca2+ and ROS. TMBIM6 is a well-researched regulator of [Ca 2+ ] cytosolic that can seize [Ca 2+ ] cytosolic control by blocking major ER Ca2+ efflux channels i.e., IP3R. TMBIM6 directly regulates [Ca 2+ ] cytosolic via oligomerization, to form a Ca 2+ pore, or via its C-terminal ER-membrane-dipping domain to release ER Ca 2+. In high [Ca2+] our structural data show TMBIM6 adopts a conformation akin to BsYetJ, the bacterial TMBIM6 homolog that acts as a Ca2+ channel. Our model shows TMBIM6-Ca2+ release is regulated by acidification, which induces an ‘open’ conformation to increase cytosolic Ca2+. TMBIM6 Ntrm modulation in cancer increased [Ca 2+ ] cytosolic 3-fold and was required for paraptotic induction. Elevated [Ca 2+ ] cytosolic affects cationic balance through continuous leakage of Ca 2+ from the ER. This would activate H + -associated transporter systems, in turn, increasing cytoplasmic H +. We show scavenging [Ca 2+ ] cytosolic with BAPTA-AM stopped TMBIM6-induced paraptosis and blocked paraptotic characteristics (i.e., ER vacuolation). However, it did not prevent lysosomal recruitment to the ER, indicating a second player is involved. Elevated [ROS] cytosolic occurred in tandem with elevated [Ca 2+ ] cytosolic. Signaling analysis showed increased expression of ERO1α and PDI, which are heavily involved in ROS formation at the ER. However, increased ERO1α and PDI does not occur until ≥3.5 h following TMBIM6 Ntrm modulation, yet paraptotic characteristics and lysosomal recruitment occur within the first 1–2 h.

text: However, it did not prevent lysosomal recruitment to the ER, indicating a second player is involved. Elevated [ROS] cytosolic occurred in tandem with elevated [Ca 2+ ] cytosolic. Signaling analysis showed increased expression of ERO1α and PDI, which are heavily involved in ROS formation at the ER. However, increased ERO1α and PDI does not occur until ≥3.5 h following TMBIM6 Ntrm modulation, yet paraptotic characteristics and lysosomal recruitment occur within the first 1–2 h. Assessing other mechanisms for ROS formation, TMBIM6 negatively regulates ROS production at the ER by disrupting the microsomal monooxygenase (MMO) system or increasing expression of ROS scavengers i.e., heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1). The MMO is known to increase tumor progression, tumorigenesis, metastasis, and cancer risk. TMBIM6 Ntrm modulation increased [ROS] cytosolic ~2-fold within the first 2 h, indicating loss of TMBIM6 inhibition of the MMO. Increased ROS was required for TMBIM6 paraptotic induction, as ROS scavengers i.e., NAC and Trolox blocked/inhibited paraptotic characteristics (i.e., ER vacuolation) and cell death. Interestingly, blocking increased [ROS] cytosolic stopped ER lysosomal recruitment, implying elevating [ROS] cytosolic is necessary to recruit lysosome to the ER. Our data shows that TMBIM6 Ntrm modulation in cancer induces significant ICE change and cellular stress within 2 h. Therefore, the observed signaling changes that occur from 3.5 h onwards are not the causative factors in elevating cytosolic ROS and Ca2+. In alignment, we showed eIF2 phosphorylation, which occurs in response to environmental stress (i.e., ICE change) occurred within the first 2 h. p-eIF2 globally inhibits translation and transcription factor expression (i.e., CHOP) to halt protein synthesis in response to ICE change. This acts to conserve energy and enable reprogramming of gene expression/signaling pathways to restore environmental balance. This supports our data showing ICE change i.e., increased [ROS] cytosolic and [Ca2+] cytosolic, and paraptotic characteristics (i.e., ER vacuolation) occur in the first 2 h and do not depend on ‘canonical’ paraptotic routes involving signaling cascades We observed lysosomal recruitment to the ER also occurred within the first 1-2 h, with lysosome staining showing an increase in number and intensity; indicating lysosomal biogenesis is occurring. Studies show TMBIM6 increase lysosomal activity and induce lysosome biogenesis, either via local release of Ca2+ or by stimulating the lysosomal V-ATPase by elevating cytosolic H + and Ca2+. We showed lysosome recruitment, but not biogenesis, occurred in cells where [Ca2+] cytosolic was scavenged by BAPTA-AM. Indicating ROS to be key in recruiting lysosome, however, despite lysosomal recruitment their intensity did not increase. In contrast, loss of ROS using scavengers showed no lysosomal recruitment or biogenesis. Taken together, the data shows ROS must be involved in TMBIM6 recruitment of lysosome to the ER, but not in lysosomal biogenesis. Indicating elevation in [Ca2+] cytosolic must be required for lysosomal biogenesis. Furthermore, ER vacuolation and death did not occur in Ca2+/ROS scavenger experiments indicating both are essential for TMBIM6-induced paraptosis. Our data shows TMBIM6-induced paraptosis occurs via elevation of [ROS] cytosolic and [Ca2+] cytosolic to induce ERAD II lysosome-mediated pathways. These effects can be explained with the current TMBIM6 understanding.
title: TMBIM6/BI-1 is an intracellular environmental regulator that induces paraptosis in cancer via ROS and Calcium-activated ERAD II pathways

text: Taken together, the data shows ROS must be involved in TMBIM6 recruitment of lysosome to the ER, but not in lysosomal biogenesis. Indicating elevation in [Ca2+] cytosolic must be required for lysosomal biogenesis. Furthermore, ER vacuolation and death did not occur in Ca2+/ROS scavenger experiments indicating both are essential for TMBIM6-induced paraptosis. Our data shows TMBIM6-induced paraptosis occurs via elevation of [ROS] cytosolic and [Ca2+] cytosolic to induce ERAD II lysosome-mediated pathways. These effects can be explained with the current TMBIM6 understanding. Modulation of TMBIM6 Ntrm could relinquish TMBIM6 control of the MMO, which would elevate [ROS] cytosolic and have a dual effect. Firstly, it would activate H + -associated transporter systems, increasing cytoplasmic H + and lowering pH. Lowering pH would activate lysosome by stimulating their V-ATPase, which TMBIM6 can also activate. Secondly, acidification promotes the ‘open’ TMBIM6 Ca2+ channel conformation and enables its Ca2 + /H+ anti-porter activity. Both lysosomal activation and TMBIM6-Ca2+ regulation response is to lower intracellular pH. However, this acts to create a perfect storm as activated lysosomes would be forced into biogenesis as TMBIM6 would increase [Ca2+] cytosolic. TMBIM6-Ca2+ release would also have an additive effect, as elevated [Ca 2+ ] cytosolic affects cationic balance through continuous leakage of Ca 2+ from the ER. This further activates H + -associated transporter systems. This TMBIM6-induced ICE change would recruit and activate nearby lysosome, promote their biogenesis via Ca2+ release, and initiate ER vacuolation and paraptosis via the ERAD II lysosome-mediated pathway. An artefact of TMBIM6 Ntrm modulation, actin recruitment, supports this conclusion. TMBIM6 has an actin-binding LxxL motif on its C-terminus, actin is recruited to TMBIM6 in the presence of increased, localized [Ca2+] cytosolic. Actin was recruited to the site of the ER vacuolation, indicating TMBIM6 Ntrm modulation was indeed promoting localized Ca2+ release. This artefact also indicates the C-terminus of TMBIM6 must be cytosolic facing as it would not be able to recruit actin if it was within the ER transmembrane space. TMBIM6 actin polymerization is a function that is manipulated by cancers to promote metastasis by increasing cell adhesion, as exemplified in non-small lung cell carcinomas. The induction of paraptosis is poorly characterized but is gaining considerable attention within cancer research. Taken together, we believe TMBIM6 exhibits novel cancer-killing qualities by mis-regulation of cytosolic Ca2+, H+, and ROS to promote lysosome formation, culminating in paraptosis. We showcased how TMBIM6 modulation can treat breast, ovarian, lung, colorectal, and uterine cancerous cells. Irrespective of their different genotypes and phenotypes, we saw the same morphological changes and loss of cell viability. However, the timeframe this occurred changed depending on the cancer, which we hypothesize is due to the differences in severity of ICE change. The absence of toxicity and broad therapeutic potential is centralized around the activation of TMBIM6 in response to severe ICE change. Severe ICE change only occurs in diseased/injured cells. Beyond cancer, TMBIM6 modulation can overcome toxin challenge, excitotoxicity, viral challenge and promote wound healing.

The sample was centrifuged (1,500 rpm, 10 min, 4 C) and the supernatant collected, representing the non-specifically bound (NSB) fraction. The beads were resuspended in 1 ml lysis buffer and incubated and pelleted as previous, the supernatant collected represented a washed fraction. Elution of the recombinant protein occurred stepwise using 1 ml elution buffer (50 mM Tris, 10 mM Reduced Glutathione, pH8.0) per fraction with the sample being incubated, centrifuged, and the supernatant collected as previous, resulting in 3 final eluted fractions. For orthotopic injection, Female BALB/c mice were inoculated with the cell resuspension in the mammary fat pads under anesthesia via Matrix VMS anesthesia machine (Midmark Corporation) by continuous inhalation of 2% isoflurane gas for 5–10 min. Tumor length (L) and width (W) were measured twice weekly using calipers, and tumor volume (V) was calculated as [V = (L x W2)/2]. In the studies, tumor-bearing mice were treated daily for 5 days with PBS, Control, or MQT at a dose of 10 mg/kg (3.4 μMol/kg). Tumor volume was determined three times a week. Body weights were measured twice weekly. Mice were sacrificed on day 20 due to the significant reduction in tumor size and volume of MQTS-treated mice. Significance (P < 0.001) between control groups and MQTS-treated groups was determined using a series of mixed-model analyses as described in Statistical Methods. text: Aberrantly activated mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling exists in over 85% of the cancers and accounts for more than 40% of cancer cases. MAPK pathway inhibitors are under laboratory and clinical investigation to identify their efficacy against various tumors, but MAPK signal reactivation could invariably develop and lead to treatment failure. Interestingly, cancer cells that acquire drug resistance are used to an optimal level of MAPK signaling, and enhancing MAPK activity in these cells has antitumor effects. For example, acute MAPK inhibitor withdrawal or ERK2 overexpression in drug-addicted resistant cells results in excessive MAPK signaling, which causes cytotoxicity. Knockout of negative MAPK regulators protein phosphatase 6 catalytic subunit (PPP6C) or dual specificity phosphatase 4/6 (DUSP4/6) results in MAPK overactivation and selectively impairs the viability of melanoma cells with increased baseline levels of MAPK. Maladjusted MAPK could even reportedly cause apoptosis, slow-cycling, senescence, and parthanatos-related cell death in resistant melanoma cells. These phenomena indicate that cancer cells require a finely tuned MAPK fitness zone, which will not be tolerated above a certain threshold. Epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC), the most lethal gynecological cancer, often evades early detection and defies treatment. As screenings are not recommended in average-risk asymptomatic women, most EOCs (>80%) are diagnosed at an advanced stage. For the last two decades, debulking surgeries followed by adjuvant platinum/taxane-based chemotherapy have been the standard treatment for EOC, with encouraging clinical response in newly diagnosed patients. Unfortunately, most EOCs become incurable due to the emergence of chemoresistance. Recently, poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPi) have revolutionized EOC management. However, acquired resistance to PARPi is still inevitable. In EOC, MAPK activation has been proven to weaken the efficacy of platinum, taxane, and PARPi. – Specifically, microtubule-associated serine/threonine kinase 1 (MAST1) induced MAPK activation contributes to platinum insensitivity and is associated with shortened survival in EOC. Upregulation of the RAF/MEK/ERK pathway downregulates FoxM1 to engender paclitaxel resistance. Increased RAS/MAPK activities lead to impaired response to PARPi by regulating the FOXO3a-BIM cascade. Therefore, introducing agents capable of eradicating resistant tumor cells is an essential avenue to improved outcomes of EOC. Paraptosis is a specific form of programmed cell death (PCD) accompanied by massive cytoplasmic vacuoles involving the dilation of endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and/or mitochondria. Paraptosis is caspase-independent and lacks the typical morphological changes of apoptosis, but requires transcription and translation. Thus, inhibition of protein synthesis by cycloheximide (CHX) could effectively block paraptosis, while apoptosis inhibition such as caspase inhibitors shows no affection. In most cases, paraptosis is mediated by MAPKs, such as MEKs or JNKs. Thus, paraptosis can be rescued by specific inhibition of these kinases, including inhibitors or siRNAs, and can also be specifically blocked by AIP-1/Alix (apoptosis-linkedgene-2-interacting protein-1, also known as Alix). We hypothesized that by inducing MAPK activation-mediated paraptosis, drug-resistant cancer cells with intrinsically increased MAPK signaling could be preferentially eliminated.
title: Elaiophylin triggers paraptosis and preferentially kills ovarian cancer drug-resistant cells by inducing MAPK hyperactivation

text: In most cases, paraptosis is mediated by MAPKs, such as MEKs or JNKs. Thus, paraptosis can be rescued by specific inhibition of these kinases, including inhibitors or siRNAs, and can also be specifically blocked by AIP-1/Alix (apoptosis-linkedgene-2-interacting protein-1, also known as Alix). We hypothesized that by inducing MAPK activation-mediated paraptosis, drug-resistant cancer cells with intrinsically increased MAPK signaling could be preferentially eliminated. Here, we demonstrated that elaiophylin, a natural C 2 -symmetric macrodiolide antibiotic isolated from Streptomyces melanosporus, induced ER-derived vacuolization and consequent paraptosis through the hyperactivation of MAPK pathway. More importantly, MAPK activation in platinum-, taxane-, or PARPi-resistant cancer cells, which endowed them with survival advantages against cytotoxic drugs, simultaneously increased their susceptibility to elaiophylin and became an exploitable therapeutic target for refractory EOC.

text: Previously, we identified elaiophylin as a late-stage autophagy inhibitor based on functional screening of 540 natural compounds of microbial origin. Meanwhile, we noticed that, unlike the typical morphological characteristics of apoptosis, the death of elaiophylin-treated ovarian cancer cell lines was preceded by the formation and accumulation of massive cytoplasmic vacuoles in the vicinity of the nucleus. Vacuoles fused and enlarged when moving towards the cell periphery (The same phenomena were observed in primary ovarian cancer cells and cell lines of other cancers (A549, MDA-MB-231, SiHa, and SW480) treated with elaiophylin (Supplementary Fig. S -). Transmission electron microscopy was used to reveal the ultrastructural characteristics of this process, showing single-membrane vacuoles surrounding intact nuclei in elaiophylin-treated SKOV3 cells (To determine whether the elaiophylin-induced vacuoles were related to autophagy, we used SKOV3 cells expressing GFP-LC3B, and found the vacuoles did not colocalize with GFP-LC3B (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. S a). Furthermore, the addition of the autophagy inhibitors chloroquine (CQ) or 3-methyladenine (3-MA) was not able to block elaiophylin-induced vacuoles (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. S b, c). To investigate the relevance between elaiophylin-induced cell death and several established forms of cell death, we examined the hallmarks of apoptosis (cleavage of caspase 3 and PARP), pyroptosis (cleavage of GSDMD or GSDME), necroptosis (phosphorylation of RIPK1 and MLKL), and ferroptosis (lipid peroxidation). We only observed the cleavage of caspase 3 and PARP after 12 h of elaiophylin treatment and positive Annexin V/PI staining, indicating that apoptosis was involved in elaiophylin-induced cell death (Supplementary Fig. S a–e). However, the apoptosis inhibitor Z-VAD-FMK could not block the formation of vacuoles (Supplemental Fig. S f). In addition, no obvious cell cycle arrest was observed in elaiophylin-treated cells (Supplemental Fig. S g). To investigate the origin of vacuoles in elaiophylin-treated cells, we transfected them with a fluorescent mitochondrial marker (GFP-Mito) or an ER marker (DsRed-ER). Vacuoles colocalized precisely with DsRed-ER fluorescence rather than GFP-Mito fluorescence (Taken together, these data demonstrate that elaiophylin-induced vacuoles originate from the ER.

text: We next explored whether elaiophylin-induced ER stress in ovarian cancer cells. Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) conducted on the microarray data of SKOV3 cells treated with elaiophylin for 0, 3, 6, or 12 h found a significant enrichment of gene sets involved in unfolded protein response, such as DDIT3 (CHOP), ATF3, and HERPUD1, which were further confirmed by real-time PCR (Besides, elaiophylin caused phosphorylation of IRE1 and upregulated the protein levels of ATF4 and CHOP, suggesting that elaiophylin-induced ER stress in SKOV3 cells (Paraptosis is a nonapoptotic PCD featured by ER stress and extensive cytoplasmic vacuoles originated from the ER. To further investigate whether elaiophylin induces paraptosis, we pretreated SKOV3 and OVCAR8 cells with CHX, which blocks paraptotic vacuoles, and found that CHX pretreatment effectively diminished elaiophylin-induced vacuoles and ER dilatation (Consistently, CHX pretreatment attenuated elaiophylin-induced upregulation of ATF4, p-IRE1, and CHOP, indicating that elaiophylin-induced ER stress was alleviated (Furthermore, CHX pretreatment partially rescued the decrease in cell viability induced by elaiophylin (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. S). In addition, exogenous overexpression of Alix in SKOV3 cells alleviated ER stress, cytoplasmic vacuolization, and elaiophylin-induced cell death (Supplementary Fig. S). Altogether, these data indicate that elaiophylin induces paraptotic cell death in ovarian cancer cells.

text: MAPK activation has been reported to be another feature of paraptosis. GSEA indicated that the MAPK signaling pathway was significantly enriched in the elaiophylin-treated groups (The phosphorylation levels of ERK1/2 and MEK1/2 markedly increased in elaiophylin-treated SKOV3 cells (eIF4E, the translation initiator acting downstream of MAPKs,, was also significantly phosphorylated, indicating that elaiophylin-induced MAPK activation promoted nascent protein synthesis. These data further confirm the paraptotic cell death induced by elaiophylin. Next, U0126, a MEK1/2 inhibitor, was used to investigate whether MEK/ERK activation was responsible for elaiophylin-induced ER stress and paraptosis. We observed that U0126 distinctly diminished elaiophylin-induced vacuolization in SKOV3 and OVCAR8 cells (The elaiophylin-induced ER dilatation observed in SKOV3-DsRed-ER cells was also markedly eliminated by U0126 (Western blotting revealed that ERK1/2 and eIF4E were less phosphorylated and the ER stress indicator CHOP was less upregulated in the presence of U0126 in elaiophylin-treated SKOV3 cells (Additionally, U0126 partially attenuated elaiophylin-induced cell death (Furthermore, simultaneous knockdown of MEK1/2 (MAP2K1 / MAP2K2, mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase 1/2) or ERK1/2 (MAPK3 / MAPK1, mitogen-activated protein kinase 3/1) both occluded elaiophylin-induced vacuolization, ER stress, and cell viability loss (Supplementary Fig. S). In summary, these results suggest that elaiophylin-induced paraptosis is mediated by MAPKs.

text: To identify the critical genes involved in elaiophylin-induced paraptosis, we performed genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 knockout library screening. SKOV3-Cas9 cells were transduced with the Human GeCKO v2 Library. After puromycin selection, cells expressing gRNAs were split into duplicates and treated with dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) or elaiophylin. After 10 days of treatment, the surviving cells were collected, gRNAs were amplified, and amplicons were sequenced (The top ten candidates were identified for positive selection (Positive selection identified candidate genes whose deletions led to elaiophylin resistance, indicating that these genes were potential targets of elaiophylin. Among these, PTPRM (protein tyrosine phosphatase receptor type M) and PTPN11 (protein tyrosine phosphatase non-receptor type 11, encoding SHP2, Src homology 2 domain-containing tyrosine phosphatase 2) are related to MAPK signaling. To determine the direct target of elaiophylin, we performed a cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA) to evaluate the binding affinity of elaiophylin towards PTPRM or SHP2 protein. Elaiophylin treatment shifted the SHP2 melting curve to the right, rather than the PTPRM melting curve, implying direct binding between elaiophylin and SHP2 protein. Next, we employed surface plasmon resonance (SPR) to further confirm that elaiophylin bound to the recombinant SHP2 protein in a dose-dependent manner (SHP2 activates the RAS/MAPK pathway by promoting RAS conversion from the inactive GDP-bound form to the active GTP-bound form via SOS1 (Son of sevenless homolog 1). In the meantime, SOS1 itself is activated by RAS, forming a positive feedback loop between SOS1 and RAS, which upregulates RAS/MAPK signaling (Next, we investigated whether elaiophylin activated SHP2. In elaiophylin-treated cells, the phosphorylation of Tyr542/580 of SHP2 was markedly increased, with increased expression of SOS1, indicating that elaiophylin may activate the MAPK pathway by SHP2 (To further validate whether SHP2 is necessary for elaiophylin-induced paraptosis, siRNAs against PTPN11 were used. PTPN11 knockdown distinctly attenuated elaiophylin-induced vacuolization in SKOV3 and OVCAR8 cells (PTPN11 knockdown also prevented the elaiophylin-induced increase in p-ERK1/2, p-eIF4E, CHOP, and viability loss (To further verify that SHP2/SOS1/MAPK pathway activation was required for elaiophylin-induced paraptosis, we used SHP099 (SHP2 inhibitor) and BAY293 (SOS1/RAS interaction inhibitor). As expected, SHP099 and BAY293 effectively decreased vacuolization and cell death in elaiophylin-treated cells (Supplementary Fig. S a–d). Moreover, SHP099 and BAY293 prevented the elaiophylin-induced increase in p-ERK1/2, p-eIF4E, and CHOP (Supplementary Fig. S e, f). In addition, the salvage effects of paraptosis-related inhibitors CHX, SHP099, and BAY293 were more prominent than those of the apoptosis inhibitor Z-VAD-FMK (Supplementary Fig. S a, b). Meanwhile, PTPN11 knockdown, SHP099, and BAY293 partially eliminated the cleavage of caspase3 and PARP (Supplementary Fig. S c, d). Collectively, our results suggest that SHP2 is a critical target for elaiophylin-induced paraptosis.

text: As elaiophylin is an autophagy inhibitor, we sought to explore the relationship between paraptosis and autophagy. First, ATG7 and ULK1, two critical autophagy genes, were knocked down using siRNAs to test the impact of autophagy regulation on elaiophylin-induced paraptosis. ATG7 or ULK1 knockdown did not prevent ERK1/2 phosphorylation and CHOP increase in response to elaiophylin (As mentioned above, elaiophylin-induced ER stress occurred earlier than autophagy inhibition in the temporal gradient assay (Therefore, we hypothesized that blocked autophagic flux was the outcome of paraptosis. To test this hypothesis, we regulated paraptosis using siRNAs against PTPN11 and the inhibitors used above to examine their impacts on autophagy. As expected, PTPN11 knockdown decreased SQSTM1 accumulation following elaiophylin treatment (Similarly, the addition of CHX, U0126, SHP099, or BAY293 partially eliminated SQSTM1 accumulation in elaiophylin-treated SKOV3 cells, implying that autophagy inhibition was partially restored by downregulated paraptosis. Previously, we proved that elaiophylin inhibited autophagy by disrupting lysosomal function. We then tested whether paraptosis was responsible for elaiophylin-induced lysosomal dysfunction. First, PTPN11 knockdown or the addition of CHX, U0126, SHP099, and BAY293 rescued the decrease in LysoTracker Deep Red fluorescence in SKOV3 cells exposed to elaiophylin, suggesting that the volume loss of the acidic compartment was restored. On the other hand, lysosomal dysfunction manifested as reduced enzymatic activity of cathepsin B (CTSB) and cathepsin D (CTSD). Consistently, PTPN11 knockdown or addition of CHX, U0126, SHP099, and BAY293 partially rescued the impaired activity of CTSB and CTSD (Collectively, these data suggest that paraptosis at least partially contributes to elaiophylin-induced autophagy inhibition by impairing lysosomal function (

text: Using an ovarian cancer patient-derived xenograft (PDX) model, we validated the significant antitumor effects of elaiophylin, which could be counteracted by SHP099 (Besides, the IHC staining of PDX models phenocopied in vitro studies. Specifically, elaiophylin increased the expression of p-SHP2 Tyr 542, p-ERK1/2, CHOP, SQSTM1, cleaved caspase 3, and decreased Ki67 expression, which were reversed by combination with SHP099 (In addition, cathepsin activity assays conducted on tumor tissues revealed a significant decrease in CTSB and CTSD enzymatic activity in the elaiophylin treatment group, which was also rescued by SHP099, indicating that SHP2 inhibition partially abolished elaiophylin-induced paraptosis, lysosomal dysfunction, autophagy inhibition, and apoptosis in vivo. Next, we assessed the antitumor effect of elaiophylin in an immunocompetent ID8 murine ovarian cancer model. Similarly, elaiophylin activated the SHP2/SOS1/MAPK pathway and induced ER stress and cytoplasmic vacuoles in ID8 cells (Supplementary Fig. S a–c). Gradient doses of elaiophylin (2, 4, and 6 mg/kg) showed powerful antineoplastic capabilities, as evidenced by decreased tumor volumes and weights (Supplementary Fig. S d). In addition, tumor specimens from the elaiophylin treatment group demonstrated dose-dependent vacuolization and ER dilation in tumor cells (Supplementary Fig. S e, f). IHC analysis of ID8 tumors demonstrated that p-SHP2 Tyr 542, p-ERK1/2, CHOP, SQSTM1, and cleaved Caspase3 were increased in elaiophylin-treated tumors, but p-MLKL, 4-HNE, GPX4, and HMOX1 staining presented no upregulation, indicating decreased Ki67 expression in elaiophylin treatment group was associated with the induction of paraptosis, apoptosis and autophagy inhibition rather than ferroptosis or necroptosis (Supplementary Fig. S g, h). Furthermore, cathepsin activity assays conducted on tumor tissues revealed a dose-dependent decrease in CTSB and CTSD enzymatic activity (Supplementary Fig. S i, j). Moreover, there was no weight loss or evident organ toxicities in mice treated with 2, 4, and 6 mg/kg elaiophylin (Supplementary Fig. S), indicating that these doses were tolerable in vivo. These data confirm that elaiophylin is also effective in immunocompetent mouse model.
title: Elaiophylin triggers paraptosis and preferentially kills ovarian cancer drug-resistant cells by inducing MAPK hyperactivation
section_title: Elaiophylin induces paraptosis and consequent autophagy inhibition in vivo

text: Since elaiophylin triggers paraptotic cell death by activating the MAPK pathway, we set out to explore the impact of MAPK basal levels on elaiophylin-induced paraptosis by using iKRAS G12D cells, a KRAS-inducible cell line where RAS/MAPK activation was inducible with doxycycline (DOX). Interestingly, elaiophylin-treated DOX-on iKRAS cells exhibited more extensive cytoplasmic vacuolization, significantly higher p-ERK1/2 and CHOP expression, and more viability loss than their DOX-off counterparts. In addition, normal cells were less affected by elaiophylin than cancer cells (Supplementary Fig. S). Furthermore, a significant positive correlation was observed between the basal levels of MAPK and elaiophylin-induced cell death in the eight cancer cell lines used in this study (Supplementary Fig. S), suggesting that elaiophylin-induced paraptosis was highly dependent on basal levels of MAPK signaling activity. Given that MAPKs are often aberrantly activated during drug resistance acquisition in multiple cancers, we wondered whether elaiophylin would be more effective against drug-resistant ovarian cancer. To validate this hypothesis, we used the cisplatin-sensitive cell line OV2008 and its cisplatin-resistant derivative C13* cells (Supplementary Fig. S a). In addition, taxane-resistant OVCAR8 clones (Supplementary Fig. S b) and PARPi-resistant A2780 clones were generated (Supplementary Fig. S c) by culturing the cells in the presence of paclitaxel or olaparib for three months. These drug-resistant cell lines exhibited higher basal levels of MAPK than their parental cells. Elaiophylin treatment displayed increased cytotoxicity and autophagy inhibition in drug-resistant derivatives than in parental cells (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. S), indicating that as ovarian cancer cells became resistant to platinum, taxane, or PARPi, they simultaneously became hypersensitized to elaiophylin. Next, the antitumor effects of elaiophylin were investigated in vivo using three drug-resistant models: platinum-resistant C13* xenografts, taxane-resistant OVCAR8 xenografts, and PARPi-resistant A2780 xenografts. In these models, chemotherapy or PARPi failed to suppress tumor growth, whereas 2 mg/kg elaiophylin significantly controlled tumor growth (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. S a–i). H&E staining of tumor sections showed typical features of vacuolization in the elaiophylin-treated groups (Supplementary Fig. S j). Immunofluorescence analysis of tumor sections demonstrated that p-SHP2 Try542, p-ERK, and CHOP expression were strikingly increased, accompanied by moderately increased TUNEL staining in elaiophylin-treated xenografts compared with the other groups (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. S), suggesting that elaiophylin fully activated the SHP2/MAPK pathway and induced ER stress in chemotherapy- and PARPi-resistant tumors. IHC analysis of markers of cell death and proliferation in drug-resistant tumors phenocopied those in ID8 tumors after elaiophylin treatment (Supplementary Figs. S). Taken together, we conclude that elaiophylin-induced paraptosis overcomes chemotherapy resistance and PARPi resistance by exploiting MAPK activation as a vulnerability factor in ovarian cancer.
title: Elaiophylin triggers paraptosis and preferentially kills ovarian cancer drug-resistant cells by inducing MAPK hyperactivation
section_title: Elaiophylin exploits MAPK activation as a vulnerability in drug-resistant ovarian cancer

text: Inducing nonapoptotic cell death in cancer cells is regarding as a promising antitumor strategy. – In this study, we revealed that elaiophylin could induce excessive ER stress, ER-derived vacuolization, and consequent paraptosis in ovarian cancer cells. An unbiased genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 knockout library screening, CETSA, and SPR identified the direct interaction between elaiophylin and SHP2, and overactivation of the SHP2/SOS1/MAPK pathway as the underlying mechanism. Most importantly, increased MAPK levels in drug-resistant ovarian cancers, which offered them survival advantage against chemotherapy and PARPi, became an Achilles’s heel for elaiophyin to unleash cytotoxicity by inducing MAPK overactivation (Supplementary Fig. S). Previously, we screened and identified elaiophylin as a late-stage autophagy inhibitor, which was later confirmed in multiple tumor models. Initiated by massive cytoplasmic vacuoles not overlaying autophagosomes, we unveiled the capability of elaiophylin to provoke paraptosis. Although apoptosis accounted for a part of elaiophylin-induced cell death, the weak rescue of the apoptosis inhibitor suggested that apoptosis was not the principal mechanism of action. Consistent with our findings, autophagosome accumulation is frequently observed in cancer cells treated with several other paraptosis inducers,, whereas the correlation between these two vital biological processes has not been fully elucidated. Our previous article provided a thorough justification to certify that elaiophylin blocks autophagic flux at the late stage by attenuating lysosomal function. Accordingly herein, we found paraptosis, at least partially, responsible for elaiophylin-induced lysosomal dysfunction and resulting autophagy inhibition, revealing the detailed relationship between paraptosis and autophagy. The induction of paraptotic cell death is emerging as a potential direction for antitumor therapy. To date, numerous natural compounds have been identified as paraptosis inducers, such as curcumin and celastrol. In addition, some synthetic compounds could also induce paraptosis, such as benzo[a]quinolizidine analogs and nanomedicines made from Cu 2+ -responsive HQ-releasing micelles (Cu(HQ) 2). However, the mechanisms underlying paraptosis are insufficiently understood, although some features including activation of MAPKs, de novo protein synthesis, and ER stress have been described. Here, we systematically explored the role of MAPKs in elaiophylin-induced paraptosis. First, MEK inhibitors, or siRNAs targeting MEK1/2 or ERK1/2 effectively abrogated elaiophylin-induced ER stress, ER-derived vacuoles, and paraptotic cell death. Second, using genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 knockout library screening, SHP2 (encoded by PTPN11), an RAS/MAPK pathway activator, was identified as an essential target of elaiophylin-induced paraptosis. Inhibition of the SHP2/SOS1/MAPK pathway by siRNAs directed against PTPN11 or pharmacological inhibitors distinctly attenuates paraptosis. Third, activation of the RAS/MAPK pathway with DOX in iKRAS G12D cells sensitizes the cells to elaiophylin-triggered paraptosis. The different reactivities of paired cells with different basal MAPK levels profoundly reflected the decisive nature of MAPKs in paraptotic cell death. Over the past two decades, numerous pathways or targets have been regarded as loss-of-control mechanisms of cancer, such as DNA replication stress, reactive oxygen species, driver mutations, and metabolic reprogramming.
title: Elaiophylin triggers paraptosis and preferentially kills ovarian cancer drug-resistant cells by inducing MAPK hyperactivation

text: Third, activation of the RAS/MAPK pathway with DOX in iKRAS G12D cells sensitizes the cells to elaiophylin-triggered paraptosis. The different reactivities of paired cells with different basal MAPK levels profoundly reflected the decisive nature of MAPKs in paraptotic cell death. Over the past two decades, numerous pathways or targets have been regarded as loss-of-control mechanisms of cancer, such as DNA replication stress, reactive oxygen species, driver mutations, and metabolic reprogramming. Traditional therapeutics aim to curb or even reverse these hallmarks, that is, “shutting off the engine”. In contrast, a sophisticated concept is to “fuel the engine” to an unsustainable extent until cancer cells collapse. Consistent with this concept, in the present study, we demonstrated that elaiophylin directly acted on SHP2 and hyperactivated MAPK signaling, thus triggering paraptosis. MAPK activation liberated ovarian cancer cells from cytotoxicity of platinum, taxane and PARP inhibitors, but contemporaneously became a vulnerability to elaiophylin-induced paraptosis. Thus, a thorough understanding of cellular homeostasis management reveals the potential of such novel approaches in overcoming resistance by turning the advantages of malignancies into fatal flaws. In summary, we demonstrated that elaiophylin triggers paraptosis by hyperactivating the SHP2/SOS1/MAPK pathway, inducing excessive ER stress and ER-derived vacuolization. Exploiting the elevated basal MAPK levels in drug-resistant cells, elaiophylin overcame platinum, taxane, and PARPi resistance in ovarian cancer. The notable effects and safety of elaiophylin in mouse models observed in this study support the further investigation of elaiophylin in clinical trials and strengthen the idea that paraptosis inducers might represent a novel treatment approach, especially in drug-resistant tumors with enhanced MAPK activities.

text: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER), an organelle in most eukaryotic cells, is the foundation for synthesizing several essential substances, including proteins, lipids, and sugars, in addition to nucleic acids. Furthermore, the ER consists of a series of lamellar vesicles and tubular lumens, forming a continuous reticular system that links the nucleus, cytoplasm, and cell membrane, thereby facilitating the transport of substances. Almost all proteins originate in the cytoplasmic matrix and are shortly thereafter translocated to the ER. Specifically, most secreted and transmembrane proteins, including those involved in synthesis, folding, and maturation, begin traveling within the ER lumen. Once appropriately modified, these proteins are either transported to their specific destinations within the cell or released outside through the cell membrane. However, the process of generating proteins does not necessarily proceed in the right direction, and a variety of intrinsic and extrinsic factors may induce ER stress, which is characterized by excessive accumulation of misfolded or unfolded proteins as well as dysregulation of sterol and lipid levels. Mild ER stress can be restored to protein homeostasis by some intracellular processing capacity. Nevertheless, if stress persists beyond the adaptive capacity of the cell, ER stress will activate the unfolded protein response (UPR). This adaptive signaling pathway reduces the burden on unfolded or misfolded proteins, thereby restoring the balance of proteins. When ER stress is extremely severe or persists for too long, it exceeds the adaptive capacity of the cell and may initiate an apoptotic program. Although ER stress usually triggers the UPR, whether the UPR promotes cellular adaptation back to normal or initiates cell death depends on various factors. Researchers have used ER stress in clinical applications to treat numerous types of diseases because of an understanding of its mechanisms. Growing evidence suggests that the ER stress response can influence the cellular phenotypes critical for cancer onset, progression, and treatment. On the one hand, if the ER stress response that persists in tumor cells is targeted to be induced, leading to their death, this would help prevent cancer progression. On the other hand, inhibiting UPR signaling to enhance antitumor immune responses could make the ER stress response system a potential target for cancer immunotherapy. Cardiovascular diseases are often affected by the accumulation of unfolded or misfolded proteins in the ER, leading to cellular damage that causes cardiovascular dysfunction. Cardiovascular disease is triggered by an imbalance in ER homeostasis, which in turn disrupts the function of the secretory pathway, leading to exacerbation of the ER stress response. ER stress is a critical contributor to the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases, as it disrupts protein folding and impairs neuronal survival. This stress activates the UPR, which, when overwhelmed, leads to neuronal apoptosis and neuroinflammation. The resulting cellular dysfunction is closely associated with cognitive decline and neurodegeneration. ER stress plays a pivotal role in the dysregulation of lipid and glucose homeostasis in metabolic diseases, leading to insulin resistance (IR) and metabolic dysfunction. The accumulation of misfolded proteins within the ER triggers the UPR, further exacerbating metabolic disturbances. This interplay contributes to the progression of various metabolic diseases and associated complications.

ER stress plays a pivotal role in the dysregulation of lipid and glucose homeostasis in metabolic diseases, leading to insulin resistance (IR) and metabolic dysfunction. The accumulation of misfolded proteins within the ER triggers the UPR, further exacerbating metabolic disturbances. This interplay contributes to the progression of various metabolic diseases and associated complications. ER stress is also implicated in the pathogenesis of autoimmune diseases, where it can increase the activation of immune cells and promote the secretion of proinflammatory cytokines. The UPR is activated in response to ER stress, increasing antigen presentation and autoimmune reactivity. This process ultimately results in tissue damage and the exacerbation of autoimmune responses. Therefore, given the role of ER stress in disease pathogenesis, understanding its complex mechanisms in cells of various tissues is important for studying disease pathogenesis and therapeutic strategies. This review systematically focuses on characterizing ER stress in multiple disease states and explores therapeutic strategies to target ER stress. First, we describe the major research findings in the relevant fields. Next, ER stress-related regulators and their functional mechanisms are described in detail. We subsequently investigated the role of ER stress in five typical disease categories, namely, cancer, cardiovascular disease, neurodegenerative disease, metabolic disease, and autoimmune disease. In addition, we emphasize the feasibility of targeting ER stress as a therapeutic agent and the current status of clinical trials. Finally, we profile several novel drugs for treating ER stress and suggest possible gaps in the current research. We believe that this review will deepen our understanding of the mechanisms of ER stress and elucidate its regulatory functions in human cells during disease progression, thereby improving the efficacy of therapies targeting ER stress.

text: ER stress is an important mechanism by which cells respond to environmental changes and physiological stress. As an important organelle in the cell, the ER is responsible for synthesizing, folding, and modifying proteins and is also involved in lipid synthesis and calcium storage functions. When cells encounter unfavorable environments (e.g., hypoxia, nutritional deficiencies, pathogen infections, etc.) or intrinsic defects (e.g., protein-folding errors), the function of the ER may be impaired, leading to ER stress. It affects cell survival and is closely related to the occurrence and development of many diseases. In 1977, scientists first discovered glucose-regulated protein 78 (GRP78), also known as binding immunoglobulin protein (BiP), and focused on characterization in the ER. Research on ER stress began in the 1990s, with initial studies focusing on how ER dysfunction affects the physiological state of cells. In 1992, the discovery of transcription factors associated with ER stress opened the study of the UPR. Three key proteins involved in the UPR were successively discovered in mammalian cells from 1998--1999. – These discoveries laid the foundation for subsequent studies revealing the important effects of ER stress on processes such as cell survival, death, and autophagy. Immediately afterward, the first functional study linking ER stress to neurodegenerative diseases reported that neurons are less tolerant to ER stress and that sustained activation is closely associated with neuronal apoptosis. In 2002, with further research, the role of ER stress in cancer was gradually recognized. Tumor cells usually experience high levels of ER stress in the microenvironment because they need to synthesize large amounts of proteins for rapid proliferation. The UPR helps tumor cells adapt to this stress to some extent, but prolonged ER stress may lead to cell death. Therefore, many researchers have focused on promoting tumor cell death by regulating the ER stress response. Research in this area has provided new ideas for cancer treatment. In 2004, research on ER stress made significant advances in a variety of diseases. First, ER stress was found to be a central feature of peripheral insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes mellitus, which play important roles in insulin secretion and fat metabolism. Metabolic diseases can lead to ER dysfunction and affect insulin synthesis and secretion. Research in this area has provided new ideas for the treatment of metabolic diseases such as diabetes, suggesting that improving ER function may help to restore a normal metabolic state. In addition, ER stress is associated with cardiovascular diseases, and long-term stress can lead to cardiomyocyte apoptosis during the progression from cardiac hypertrophy to failure, suggesting that regulating ER stress may be a therapeutic strategy for cardiovascular diseases. Furthermore, ER stress was first found to be associated with autoimmune diseases by studying the antibody response to the human stress protein BiP in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA). Studies have shown that ER stress is involved in inflammatory responses and immune cell dysfunction and may lead to autoantigen exposure, which triggers an autoimmune response. In 2006, drugs targeting ER stress-related pathway inhibitors were first developed, such as 4-phenyl butyric acid (4-PBA), which was used to treat Parkinson’s disease (PD). In 2007, Lin’s team revealed differences in the dynamics of different signaling branches in the ER stress-triggered UPR.

text: Studies have shown that ER stress is involved in inflammatory responses and immune cell dysfunction and may lead to autoantigen exposure, which triggers an autoimmune response. In 2006, drugs targeting ER stress-related pathway inhibitors were first developed, such as 4-phenyl butyric acid (4-PBA), which was used to treat Parkinson’s disease (PD). In 2007, Lin’s team revealed differences in the dynamics of different signaling branches in the ER stress-triggered UPR. The activities of IRE1 and ATF6 decrease under sustained stress, whereas the PERK pathway, including the sustained expression of the proapoptotic factor CCAAT/enhancer-binding protein homologous protein (CHOP), remains active, leading to a shift in the cellular response from protection to apoptosis. Cell survival was significantly enhanced by artificially prolonging IRE1 activity, suggesting that temporal regulation of UPR signaling is critical in determining cell life and death. In 2008 and 2009, two studies revealed a novel mechanism linking ER stress to obesity. Overnutrition triggers obesity by inducing ER stress in the hypothalamus and activating the IKKβ/NF-κB signaling pathway, leading to central insulin and leptin resistance. Reducing ER stress through genetic intervention or chemical chaperones (e.g., PBA and TUDCA) significantly restores leptin sensitivity and ameliorates obesity, and these studies suggest that targeting ER stress is a novel strategy for the treatment of obesity and related metabolic diseases. In 2010, new progress was made in the application of ER stress in tumor therapy. In the hypoxic environment of tumors, ER stress transcriptionally activates the autophagy genes MAP1LC3B and ATG5 through the PERK/CHOP signaling axis, which enhances the hypoxia tolerance and radioresistance of tumor cells. In 2011, a novel IRE1 small molecule inhibitor, STF-083010, was developed for the treatment of multiple myeloma (MM) and has shown significant antitumor activity. In 2012, a PERK inhibitor, GSK2606414, and two IRE1 inhibitors, 4μ8C and MKC3946, were developed for the treatment of cancer. – In 2014, two more IRE1 inhibitors were manufactured, with B-I09 showing significant therapeutic efficacy in a variety of hematologic tumors and KIRA6 playing a role in the treatment of metabolic diseases. In 2015, AMG-44 was developed as a highly potent and selective PERK inhibitor that targets and alleviates ER stress-associated pathological processes by sensing the UPR and inhibiting its activity, providing novel tool compounds for the treatment of diseases such as cancer. In 2017, a major breakthrough was made in the treatment of type 1 diabetes by targeting ER stress; attenuating IRE1 reduces pancreatic β-apoptosis and reverses type 1 diabetes (T1D). The IRE1 inhibitor KIRA8 was also effective in reversing established diabetes by preserving the physiological function of β-cells. In 2019, the IRE1-specific inhibitor MKC8866 strongly inhibited prostate cancer tumor growth and showed synergistic antitumor effects with current drugs. In 2021, a novel pancreatic cancer therapeutic agent, YUM70, was developed with the primary function of inducing ER stress-mediated apoptosis in tumor cells by inhibiting GRP78. In 2022, a breakthrough in tumor therapy was achieved when a novel tumor vaccine against ER stress began to be put into clinical trials as an active immunotherapy.
