section_title: mtDSN enhances tumor immunogenicity via fostering ICD cascade

text: The ICD induction by mtDSN-2 in vitro motivated us to assess whether mtDSN-2 could promote tumor immunogenicity in vivo by investigating the prophylactic vaccination response in immunocompetent BALB/c mice. Certain chemotherapeutic agents (e.g., doxorubicin) stimulate immune-dependent antitumor responses by inducing ICD and secreting numerous bioactive molecules—including DAMPs—that interact with the immune system,. Therefore, we exposed murine 4T1 cancer cells to mtDSN-2 or chemotherapy (doxorubicin or non-ICD drugs, i.e., paclitaxel and cisplatin), and vaccinated mice with a subcutaneous injection of dying cells into the right flank. Two weeks later, we orthotopically injected live 4T1 cells to assess the immune protection from tumorigenesis provided by the vaccination regimen (We interpreted the rejection of the orthotopic tumor growth as a sign of antitumor vaccination. Mice immunized with doxorubicin- or mtDSN-2-pretreated 4T1 cells displayed better cancer cell rejection features than other mice, namely a high tumor-free rate and extended survival (4T1 breast cancer is poorly immunogenic but highly invasive and metastatic to distant organs. Interestingly, vaccination with mtDSN-2-exposed cells significantly restrained the metastatic burden to draining lymph nodes as well as to distal lung and liver (Fig. and To better understand the mechanism of mtDSN-mediated immunization, we examined the activation of immunological responses. Specifically, we looked at the T-cell activation-associated cytokines interleukin 12 (IL-12), tumor necrosis factor α (TNF-α), and interferon γ (IFN-γ) by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) before and after vaccination. The immunization with mtDSN-2-treated tumor cells significantly increased the levels of these cytokines compared with conventional paclitaxel or cisplatin regimens (Dendritic cell maturation plays a pivotal role in antigen presentation to T lymphocytes, and initiates adaptive immunity response. Flow cytometry analysis of the tumor-draining lymph nodes indicated that mtDSN-2 vaccination facilitated dendritic cell maturation, increasing the frequency of CD11c + CD80 + CD86 + cells from 9.9% (in saline-treated mice) to 34.8%. The proportion of MHC II + dendritic cells also increased by 2.4 folds (Fig. and Moreover, the mtDSN-2- and doxorubicin-treated cancer cell-based vaccines converted naive T cells to the active phenotype and to the effector memory T-cell (T EM) phenotype (CD3 + CD4/8 + CD62L − CD44 +) in vivo (Fig. and These results suggest that mtDSN-2-treated cancer cell-based vaccination generated T-cell memory response in mice, accounting for the long-term rejection of rechallenged viable tumor cells.
title: Mitochondrial rewiring with small-molecule drug-free nanoassemblies unleashes anticancer immunity
section_title: mtDSN-2-pulsed tumor cells are immunogenic and serve as prophylactic vaccine

text: Encouraged by the cancer vaccine effect, we next tested whether local mtDSN treatment could elicit abscopal antitumor immune responses against distant tumor lesions. To this end, we established a bilateral 4T1 tumor model in BALB/c mice, and only treated the primary tumor with mtDSN (Two intratumoral injections of mtDSN-2 to the right flank tumors significantly inhibited the growth of both the treated and untreated tumors and improved mouse survival (Immunofluorescence staining also evidenced the expansion of tumor-infiltrating CD8 + T cells at contralateral tumors after mtDSN-2 treatment compared with saline-treated mice, supporting the induction of a systemic immune response by mtDSN-2 (mtDSN therapy was well tolerated and showed negligible toxicity (To probe the specificity of the T-cell responses, we used unrelated CT26 colorectal cancer cells instead of 4T1 breast cancer cells as the contralateral tumor (In that case, mtDSN-2 suppressed the local tumor but exerted no abscopal tumor control, as contralateral CT26 tumors displayed rapid growth kinetics comparable to those of saline-treated mice (These results indicate that tumor-specific immunity is responsible for the observed antitumor activity. Cytotoxic CD8 + T lymphocytes (CTL) are crucial for the abscopal effect. To further explore the specificity of mtDSN-mediated T-cell priming, we analyzed the CTL status in both TME and spleens in ovalbumin (OVA)-expressing or OVA-negative B16F10 mouse models (mtDSN-2 therapy increased the frequency of OVA 257-264 (SIINFEKL)-specific tumor-infiltrating CD8 + T-cell expansion (detected using H-2K b -OVA tetramer staining) than saline treatment (Fig. and As expected, mtDSN-2 treatment produced almost no OVA-specific CD8 + T cells in OVA-deficient B16F10 tumors, demonstrating the stimulated OVA-specific T-cell responses (Moreover, B16F10-OVA tumors displayed higher frequencies of IFN-γ-secreting OVA tetramer + CTLs than B16F10 tumors did after mtDSN-2 vaccination, further highlighting the potential of mtDSN as an in situ vaccine for priming effector T-cell responses (CTL profiling of splenocytes also supported the results observed in the TME (Together, these results support the premise that the mtDSN scaffold initiates ICD-induced tumor-specific T-cell activation, thereby driving abscopal antitumor immunity.
title: Mitochondrial rewiring with small-molecule drug-free nanoassemblies unleashes anticancer immunity
section_title: Intratumoral injection of mtDSN induces abscopal antitumor effect

text: Toll-like receptors are pattern recognition receptors that play a fundamental role in activating innate immunity. The TLR4 agonist monophosphoryl lipid A (MPLA) is a lipopolysaccharide derivative that can serve as an adjuvant enhancing the efficacy of cancer treatments. The intratumoral combination of mtDSN-2 with MPLA improved the tumor-suppressive effect and mouse survival extension of mtDSN-2 monotherapy, and led to abundant infiltration of CD8 + T cells in subcutaneous 4T1 tumors (Additionally, mtDSN-2 synergized with clinically used ICB therapy (e.g., anti-PD-1 antibody) (The histological analysis of mouse lungs revealed that mtDSN-2 alone or combined with anti-PD-1 significantly attenuated metastatic tumor burden, as shown by the markedly low numbers of metastatic foci (Fig. and However, the combination with MPLA was less efficient than that with anti-PD-1 for inhibiting tumor metastasis (Previous studies suggested a link between TLR4 activation and augmented metastatic phenotypes of cancer cells. TLR4 activation also was associated with local and systemic inflammation, creating the TME (e.g., reconstructed tumor-associated lymphatic and blood vessels) that favors tumor recurrence and metastasis,. Hence, these effects of TLR4 agonist MPLA may account for the impaired metastatic inhibition of mtDSN-2. Having shown this synergy, we then assessed the effect of mtDSN-2 against a murine colorectal cancer MC38 tumor model established in syngeneic C57BL/6 mice. This model is generally considered hypermutated and harbors a microsatellite-instable phenotype, contributing to a T-cell-inflamed TME. Three intraperitoneal doses of anti-PD-1 antibody indeed notably dampened tumor growth, and four out of nine treated mice showed complete MC38 tumor regression, indicating robust ICB therapy responses (Treatment with mtDSN-2 induced tumor regression and, even more encouragingly, synergized with the PD-1 blockade, yielding highly potent antitumor activity. The combination therapy cured 89% of the mice, with tumor remission sustained for over 60 days, and the mice had a 100% survival rate (Immunofluorescence analysis revealed that mtDSN-2 treatment substantially promoted the recruitment of tumor-infiltrating CTLs, supporting the ICD-induced immune activation (We then rechallenged naive mice and mice cured from MC38 tumors by mtDSN-2 treatment by subcutaneously injecting them with MC38 cells. Interestingly, all cured mice but not naive mice persistently rejected tumor growth, suggesting that mtDSN treatment established systemic antitumor memory. Next, we performed flow cytometry profiling of peripheral blood monocytes (PBMCs) to examine the mechanism underlying immune memory response. Compared with vehicle control, mtDSN-2 markedly increased the CD4 + and CD8 + effector memory T-cell subsets (CD44 + CD62L −, T EM) in cured mice, which may contribute to the long-term immune protection from recurring tumors (Fig. and Additionally, spleens of mice treated with the combined therapy had higher proportions of both central memory T cells (CD62L + CD44 +, T CM) and T EM than control after rechallenge, further supporting an evoked protective antitumor immune memory (
title: Mitochondrial rewiring with small-molecule drug-free nanoassemblies unleashes anticancer immunity
section_title: mtDSN-2 synergizes with immunotherapies to control tumor growth

text: Despite the compelling clinical benefits of PD-1 blockade in various types of malignant cancer, patients eventually develop acquired resistance to this therapy after an initial response. To address this, we established an anti-PD-1-resistant MC38 tumor model through the repeated administration of anti-PD-1 antibodies followed by serial implantation (Although PD-1 blockade exhibited significant tumor-suppressive activity in S0 (parental) tumors, serially implanted S3 tumors (termed MC38/R) were refractory to anti-PD-1 therapy (Immunostaining also revealed notable CTL exclusion and macrophage polarization from antitumorigenic M1-like to protumorigenic M2-like in MC38/R tumors (Supplementary Fig.) compared with that in parental tumors, confirming the immune desertification of the TME and the acquired resistance established in this model. Subsequently, we assessed the effects of mtDSN-2 on proinflammatory remodeling of the TME and its synergism with anti-PD-1 therapy to increase immune response in this clinically relevant tumor model. The mtDSN-2 therapy caused significant MC38/R tumor regression and extended mouse survival (Notably, M2-to-M1-like repolarization of macrophages (Supplementary Fig.), abundance of intratumoral dendritic cells, and remarkable increase in tumor-infiltrating CTLs supported the hypothesis that mtDSN-2 exerts immunomodulatory effects on tumors. More significantly, the combined mtDSN and anti-PD-1 regimen displayed a synergistic effect, with complete antitumor responses in six of nine mice and a striking increase in mice survival rate over 60 days (Most patients with colorectal cancer have a mismatch repair-proficient or microsatellite-stable phenotype, and they rarely respond to anti-PD-1 monotherapy. Therefore, we then evaluated the combination therapy in a nonhypermutated/microsatellite-stable CT26 tumor model. As shown in Fig. CT26 subcutaneous tumors were highly proliferative and aggressive, with only an 8-day median survival time. Additionally, the negligible antitumor efficacy of anti-PD-1 alone compared with saline control confirmed the primary resistance to anti-PD-1 therapy. By contrast, intratumoral mtDSN-2 exposure was effective and further synergized with PD-1 blockade, extending mouse survival and eradicating two out of the ten tumors. Immune profiling also showed that mtDSN-2 transformed immunologically silent TME into an inflamed one, as manifested by the enrichment in dendritic cells and increased recruitment of infiltrating CD8 + T cells into CT26 tumors, consistent with the long-lasting antitumor response in the combination regimen. Overall, these preclinical results support that mtDSN-2-increased immunogenicity can potentiate the response to anti-PD-1 therapy, which may represent a promising strategy for treating ICB-refractory cancers.

section_title: mtDSN inflames the tumor microenvironment to enhance the ICB response

text: Finally, to document how mtDSN therapy impacts the phenotype of tumor-infiltrating immune cells, we performed single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) on the established anti-PD-1-resistant MC38 tumors with immune exclusion of CTLs. We projected discrete clusters of tumor-associated cell populations using t -distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t -SNE) analysis and annotated them based on the expression of canonical cell marker genes (Notably, mtDSN-2 treatment induced large shifts in the frequency and transcriptional state of numerous immune subsets, including a significant increase in the overall TILs (We then identified distinct T-cell states and found that TILs from mtDSN-2-treated tumors were highly enriched in activated effector T-cell subsets, which were assigned primarily to exhausted (Tex) and effector memory (T EM) states (Fig. and mtDSN-2 treatment decreased the proportion of regulatory T cells (Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) analysis revealed that the gene sets and pathways affected by mtDSN-2 were correlated with immune activation (Consistently, relative to vehicle control, TILs from mtDSN-2-treated tumors were featured by higher expression of Ifng, Gzmk, and Gzmb, suggesting an augmented effector function and cytolytic capacity (These findings provide compelling evidence that mtDSN-2 potentiates tumor cell immunogenicity, which unleashes CD8 + T-cell-mediated effector functions. Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) in tumor tissues are closely associated with cancer progression and metastasis. Indeed, mtDSN-2 notably reduced the population of CAFs in tumors (In particular, it significantly decreased the number and percentage of myofibroblastic CAFs (myCAFs)—which are associated with matrix-induced immune exclusion—as evidenced by the CAF landscape profiling (Further inspection of the DEGs showed that, compared with vehicle control, CAFs from mtDSN-2-treated tumors expressed remarkably lower levels of Vegfa, Vegfb, and Vegfc, associated with tumor angiogenesis; Tgfbr1, Tgfbr2, Tgfbr3, and Tgfb3, associated with myCAF matrix production and function; while higher levels of cytokines such as IL1a, IL1b, CCL2, and CCL5, indicating the effects of therapy to induce inflamed TME. We also examined the impact of mtDSN-2 therapy on tumor-associated macrophages (TAM) and found that the treatment substantially reduced TAM infiltration (Further profiling unveiled that mtDSN-2 promoted the polarization of macrophages from the protumorigenic M2-like to antitumorigenic M1-like phenotype (Fig. and Supplementary Fig.), manifested by decreased Mrc1 expression and increased Nos2, IL1a, and IL1b expression. GSEA identified several top hallmark pathways altered by mtDSN-2 treatment, among which the ROS production and proinflammatory pathways were upregulated in macrophages (Furthermore, mtDSN-2 treatment significantly increased the number of tumor-associated neutrophils (TANs) (Of note, the expression of arginase-1 (Arg1), a pivotal enzyme contributing to tumor immune evasion, was substantially reduced in neutrophils clusters following mtDSN-2 therapy (The enrichment analysis revealed that mtDSN-2 stimulated the specific pathways of TANs related to proinflammatory immune activation (Fig. and Supplementary Fig.), with IL1a, IL1b, and IL15 particularly upregulated (Additionally, mtDSN-2 upregulated CD274 (PD-L1) expression across tumor and immune cells (Supplementary Fig.), further supporting the rationale of improving immunotherapy efficacy with ICB inhibitors.

section_title: mtDSN transforms immunosuppressive and anti-PD-1-resistant tumors into “hot” tumors

text: Developing therapeutic strategies able to promote an immunogenic tumor phenotype and increase response to ICB therapy with minimal systemic inflammation and toxicity remains a central challenge for effective immunotherapy. Recent evidence has highlighted that mitochondria are a critical hub for boosting the antitumor immune response via the inflammation of immune-desert tumors. For example, mitochondrial DNA released upon disruption of mitochondria, besides acting as a DAMP and activating the NLRP3 inflammasome and TLR9 to induce an inflammatory response may also activate the stimulator of interferon genes signaling pathway,. In addition, mitochondrial biogenesis, dynamics, and ROS production regulate the function of some subsets of tumor-infiltrating immune cells, and also have roles in T-cell activation,. All these findings indicate that mitochondria are a potential target for enhancing tumor immunogenicity or to synergize with current immunotherapies. Here, we conceived a small-molecule-based dynamic nanosystem to target this cellular organelle, whose cytotoxic mechanism differs from conventional chemotherapy. Very interestingly, we observed aggregation-induced cytotoxicity, and the dissociation of the nanoassemblies attenuated this activity, hopefully indicating that these nanoassemblies could become low-toxicity and traceless cancer therapy. Indeed, mtDSN-2 was less cytotoxic on hepatocytes than on cancer cells observed in in vitro assays (Intratumoral administration of mtDSN-2 did not impart any side effects on major healthy tissues (Supplementary Fig.) while inducing extensive apoptotic cell death in tumors (Supplementary Fig.), suggesting its favorable safety profile for the preclinical use. Morphological observation by TEM and SEM suggested that these nanoassemblies act as nanobombs directly disrupting the mitochondrial membrane and causing lethal damage on mitochondria. Although further studies are warranted to elucidate the underlying molecular mechanisms, we hypothesize that incorporating massive amounts of exogenous polyunsaturated fatty acids into mitochondrial membrane phospholipids disrupts the mitochondrial stability and permeability, leading to deformed membrane structure. Mechanistic experiments revealed that the mtDSN platform substantially impeded mitochondrial biogenesis in tumor cells. The overwhelming mitochondrial stress, induced by mtDSN-2, also perturbed ER homeostasis through excessive ROS production and potential imbalance in substance exchanges, leading to irreversible ER stress. This pronounced ER stress facilitated the activation of subsequent cellular death programs through both paraptosis and apoptosis pathways. Additionally, we observed that stressed and injured tumor cells emitted various DAMPs, including surface-exposed CRT, passively released HMGB1, and secreted ATP. These danger signals stimulated immunological responses by eliciting the ICD cascade and converted immunologically silent tumors into inflamed ones. So far, various ICD inducers (including chemotherapeutic agents, such as doxorubicin and oxaliplatin) have been reported to incite antitumor immunity. In addition, cancer cells treated ex vivo with these agents and then implanted subcutaneously function as a vaccine, yielding potent anticancer immunity. Compared with chemotherapy-based bona fide ICD inducers (e.g., doxorubicin), mtDSN-2 induced notable ICD efficiency but demonstrated fewer side effects in vivo (published elsewhere), presumably due to its aggregation-dependent cytotoxic potential.
title: Mitochondrial rewiring with small-molecule drug-free nanoassemblies unleashes anticancer immunity

text: So far, various ICD inducers (including chemotherapeutic agents, such as doxorubicin and oxaliplatin) have been reported to incite antitumor immunity. In addition, cancer cells treated ex vivo with these agents and then implanted subcutaneously function as a vaccine, yielding potent anticancer immunity. Compared with chemotherapy-based bona fide ICD inducers (e.g., doxorubicin), mtDSN-2 induced notable ICD efficiency but demonstrated fewer side effects in vivo (published elsewhere), presumably due to its aggregation-dependent cytotoxic potential. After performing their antitumor activity, these noncovalent assemblies should dissociate into nontoxic small molecules, thereby contributing to the favorable safety profile of this platform in animals. mtDSN treatment converted injured cancer cells into either a prophylactic vaccination regimen or therapeutic vaccine and also triggered a localized inflammatory antitumor immune cascade in multiple syngeneic models, including those refractory to PD-1 blockade. Last, a high-dimensional interrogation of tumors with scRNA-seq revealed that this mtDSN platform profoundly remodeled the TME, enlisting activated effector T-cell populations executing a cell-killing activity highly hinged on IFN-γ and granzyme expression, and reducing TAM infiltration while clearly shifting the macrophage phenotype from M2-like to the proinflammatory M1-like. TANs can exert dual functions; they either promote tumor progression by driving angiogenesis, metastasis, and immunosuppression, or mediate antitumor responses by directly killing cancer cells. Unexpectedly, mtDSN exposure increased neutrophils recruitment while transforming neutrophils into antitumor phenotype on the basis of TANs plasticity. Consistently, the expression of the proinflammatory chemokine CXCL2, which is responsible for neutrophil recruitment in mice, was widely upregulated in all cells (Moreover, the profound S100A8/A9 overexpression throughout the tumors might also account for neutrophil accumulation and proinflammatory cytokine secretion, whose high levels are characteristic for leukocyte recruitment and inflammatory conditions (Accumulating evidence showed that exposure to proinflammatory cytokines, such as IFN-γ, TNF-α, and interleukins, could trigger the adaptive expression of PD-L1, thereby promoting the immune escape of tumor cells. Indeed, we found that mtDSN-treated tumors featured considerable PD-L1 upregulation and tested the feasibility of combining mtDSN with ICB therapy in animal models. In summary, we have described the example of nontherapeutic small molecular ICD nanoinducer and identified its mechanism of mitochondria/ER-associated ICD induction that substantially potentiated tumor immunogenicity and unleashed the full potential of T-cell based therapy. As a traceless therapy, this mitochondria-targeting and rewiring platform has established its high safety profile and warrants further investigations for stimulating anticancer immune responses.

text: Tumor cells were seeded in 96-well plates and incubated at 37 °C overnight. Then, the cells were incubated with different agents at serially diluted concentrations for 48 or 72 h. At the end of the incubation period, 30 μl of 3-[4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl]-3,5- diphenyl tetrazolium bromide (MTT) solution (5 mg ml −1) was added and incubated at 37 °C for 4 h. Afterwards, the MTT solution was replaced with 100 μl dimethyl sulfoxide to dissolve the purple MTT-formazan crystals. The absorbance in each individual well was then measured at 490 nm using a microplate reader (Multiskan FC, Thermo Scientific). The viability of untreated cells was defined as 100%. IC 50 was calculated with the following formula: Y = 100/[1 + [[ X /IC 50 ]^ P ]]. Herein, Y represents cell viability, X is the compound concentration, and the initial value of P is 0.05.

text: For TEM analysis, solutions of mtDSNs were dipped into a carbon-coated 300-mesh copper grid for 3 min. Then, the solution was removed with filter paper. Two wt% aqueous uranyl acetate solution was used to stain the samples before observation. Tumor cells were treated with different agents (5 μM) and fixed with 2.5% glutaraldehyde overnight at 4 °C. After further fixation in 1% osmium tetroxide for 1 h and 2% uranyl acetate for 0.5 h, we dehydrated the cells in a graded solvent series (50, 70, 90, and 100% ethanol for 15 min each time and 100% acetone twice for 20 min). Samples were further permeated, and underwent fixation in embedding medium. Ultrotome V (LKB) ultramicrotome was used to prepare Ultrathin sections (60–70 nm). Finally, we counterstained the sections using uranyl acetate and lead citrate. The images were obtained using TEM (Talos L120C, Thermo) at an acceleration voltage of 120 kV. For SEM characterization, mitochondria isolated from tumor cells were incubated at 4 °C for 30 min with or without 0.5 μM mtDSN-2, then fixed with 2.5% glutaraldehyde at room temperature for 2 h, followed by overnight at 4 °C. Subsequently, the cells were washed three times with PBS, fixed with 1% osmium tetroxide, dehydrated through a graded series of ethanol concentrations (30, 50, 70, 80, 90, and 95% for 15 min each time and 100% for 20 min twice). After vacuum drying, the samples were coated with gold/palladium and analyzed by SEM using a Nova Nano 450 (Nova Nano 450, Thermo).

text: BMDCs were prepared according to the reported protocol. In brief, bone marrow was flushed from isolated femurs of C57BL/6J mice using PBS. After RBC lysis, bone marrow cells were seeded in petri dishes and cultured with dendritic cell medium (Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium supplemented with 10% heat-inactivated fetal bovine serum, 1% penicillin–streptomycin, 20 ng ml −1 murine granulocyte macrophage colony-stimulating factor and 5 ng ml −1 interleukin-4). Half of the culture medium volume was refreshed on day 2. Non-adherent and loosely adherent immature BMDCs were collected on day 4, and we determined their phenotype by assessing CD11c expression (60–80% CD11c + cells were routinely obtained). Tumor cells were treated with different agents (5 μM) for 6 h, and then the culture medium was replaced by fresh medium followed by further incubation for 36 h. Afterwards, the medium supernatant of tumor cells was collected and used to incubate BMDCs for 24 h before flow cytometry analysis.

text: For immune cell profiling, peripheral blood monocytes (PBMCs), spleens, lymph nodes and tumors were harvested for assays. To isolate splenocytes, the spleens were mechanically homogenized and resuspended in red blood cell (RBC) lysis buffer (Solarbio, China) for RBCs removal. Tumors were cut into pieces and resuspended in medium containing collagenase D (1 mg ml −1, Sigma-Aldrich) followed by incubation in a shaking incubator for 30 min at 37 °C. After washing, suspensions of PBMCs, lymph node cells, splenocytes and tumor cells were stained with various antibodies. For memory T cell analysis, PBMCs, splenocytes and tumor cells were stained with Zombie Aqua™ (Biolegend, cat. no. 423102), blocked with CD16/32 antibody and further stained with fluorophore-labeled antibodies against CD45, CD3, CD4, CD8a, CD44, and CD62L at 4 °C. For dendritic cell analysis, BMDCs and lymph node cells were stained with Zombie Aqua™, blocked with CD16/32 antibody and further stained with fluorophore-labeled antibodies against CD45, CD11c, CD80, CD86, and MHC II at 4 °C. For OVA-specific T-cell analysis, splenocytes and tumor cells were stimulated by cell activation cocktail with brefeldin A (Biolegend, cat. no. 423304) at 37 °C for 6 h. Subsequently, cells were stained with Zombie Aqua™, blocked with CD16/32 antibody, and further stained with fluorophore-labeled antibodies against CD45, CD3, CD8a, IFN-γ, and T-Select H-2K b OVA tetramer-SIINFEKL-PE (MBL Life Science, cat. no. TS-5001-1C) at 4 °C. Then, the cells were washed twice with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) and filtered through a 70-µm nylon cell strainer before subjected to flow cytometry analysis.

text: We exposed 4T1 cells to distinct chemotherapeutic agents and induced ~70% ± 10% cell death. Then, the dying 4T1 cells were subcutaneously injected into right flank of the immunocompetent BALB/c mice. Control mice received sterile saline instead of this cancer cell vaccine. After immunization with the corresponding cancer vaccines (containing 2 × 10 6 cells in 100 μl sterile phosphate-buffered saline) twice on day 0 and day 7, mice were then orthotopically rechallenged with 5 × 10 5 live 4T1 cells into the fifth mammary fat pad on day 14. The tumor growth, metastasis and the survival rate were monitored throughout the whole study. On day 59, lymph nodes (axillary and inguinal), lungs and livers were collected from mice bearing established 4T1 tumors in each group, and subjected to H&E staining for tumor metastasis analysis. Immune profiling was performed by ELISA and flow cytometry analysis.

text: To test the specific abscopal antitumor effect, bilateral tumor models were established. Briefly, 1 × 10 6 4T1 tumor cells were subcutaneously inoculated into both flanks of BALB/c mice, or 1 × 10 6 4T1 cells and 5 × 10 5 CT26 cells were subcutaneously inoculated into the right and left flanks of BALB/c mice, respectively. Seven days after tumor inoculation, intratumoral injection of mtDSN-2 (1 mg kg −1) was performed on the right tumor every other day twice. The growth of tumors on both flanks was monitored at various time points. Representative tumors were harvested for immunofluorescence staining to assess CD8 + T-cell infiltration on day 8. Mice were defined as dead and sacrificed when tumor volume exceeded 1500 mm 3. To measure the effects on cancer metastasis, 4T1 tumor cells were transplanted into the right flank of BALB/c mice. When the resulting tumors reached ~150 mm 3, the mice received intratumoral injections on day 0 and 2 of one of the treatment formulations: saline, mtDSN-2 (1 mg kg −1), mtDSN-2 (1 mg kg −1) plus MPLA (50 μg kg −1), and mtDSN-2 (1 mg kg −1) plus anti-PD-1 (1 mg kg −1). The tumor volume was monitored. Representative tumors were harvested for immunofluorescence staining to assess CD8 + T-cell infiltration on day 8. Mice were sacrificed and lungs were collected when tumor volume exceeded 1500 mm 3 or at the endpoint of the experiment. Metastatic burden of lungs was assessed on the basis of the H&E staining. To assess the therapeutic effect on colorectal cancer, 2 × 10 6 MC38 tumor cells were subcutaneously inoculated on C57BL/6 mice. Treatment started when the tumor volumes reached ~100 mm 3 with one of the formulations: saline (intratumoral), anti-PD-1 (10 mg kg −1, intraperitoneal), mtDSN-2 (1 mg kg −1, intratumoral), and mtDSN-2 (1 mg kg −1, intratumoral) plus anti-PD-1 (10 mg kg −1, intraperitoneal). On day 15, representative tumors were photographed and subjected to immunohistochemical analysis. For the MC38 rechallenge study, cured mice were subcutaneously injected with 2 × 10 6 MC38 cells 67 days after the first injection of MC38 cells. Healthy mice received the same injection as a control. At the end of the experiment, PBMCs and splenocytes were collected for flow cytometry analysis. To assess the antitumor effect on anti-PD-1-resistant tumors, mice bearing MC38 tumors were repeated administrated with anti-PD-1 antibodies at a low dose (5 mg kg −1) followed by the serial transplantation of low-response tumors into different mice according to the indicated experiment schema. After three cycles of anti-PD-1-resistance induction, mice bearing anti-PD-1-resistant MC38 tumors were treated with one of the formulations: saline (intratumoral), anti-PD-1 (10 mg kg −1, intraperitoneal), mtDSN-2 (1 mg kg −1, intratumoral), and mtDSN-2 (1 mg kg −1, intratumoral) plus anti-PD-1 (10 mg kg −1, intraperitoneal). Tumor volume was monitored and the survival time was recorded. On day 15, representative tumors were photographed and subjected to immunohistochemical analysis. To build another anti-PD-1-resistant tumor model, 1 × 10 6 CT26 tumor cells were subcutaneously inoculated into BALB/c mice. These mice underwent the same treatment protocol as MC38-bearing mice.

text: Mice bearing anti-PD-1-resistant MC38 tumors received intratumoral injections of vehicle (saline containing 5% DMSO) or mtDSN-2 (1 mg kg −1) every 3 days. After a total of three doses, tumors were collected, minced and dissociated (n = 3 mice or samples were pooled to control for biological variability). The cell suspension was prepared according to general protocols and loaded into Chromium microfluidic chips with 3’ (v3.1) chemistry and barcoded with a 10X Chromium Controller (10X Genomics). RNA from the barcoded cells was subsequently reverse-transcribed. The sequencing libraries were constructed using a Chromium Single Cell 3’ (v3.1) reagent kit (10X Genomics) (Novogene). Illumina NovaSeq 6000 PE150 was used for sequencing following the manufacturer’s instructions. Raw reads were demultiplexed and mapped to the reference genome by 10X Genomics Cell Ranger pipeline using default parameters. After mapping with Cell Ranger (v7.0.0) on the mouse reference, downstream single-cell analyses were further performed using Seurat (v4.3.0). In silico doublet prediction and removal were performed using DoubletFinder. Cells with number of genes detected per cell >8500 or <200, and percentage of mitochondrial genes >30% were removed from the dataset before the downstream analysis. After this initial filtering, we normalized the gene expression of each cell by the total expression before performing log-transformation. In the log-normalized data, we identified the top 2000 most highly variable genes and included them in principal component analysis and clustering analysis. Scaling was carried out by centering the expression of each gene before dividing the mean-centered expressions by the standard deviation. Cell cluster annotations were performed by manual annotation based on selected canonical markers via unsupervised clustering. Based on filtered gene expression matrix by Seurat, differential expression analysis between samples was performed using the edgeR package for acquiring zone-specific marker genes. GO enrichment and KEGG pathway analyses of marker genes were conducted using the cluster Profiler R package, where gene length bias was corrected. GSEA was used to test for enrichment of a specific gene set. A normalized enrichment score (NES) was specified for each GSEA. For the differential gene-expression, a significant result was defined as an unadjusted P value lower than 0.05.

text: Graphs were generated and statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism v.8 unless stated otherwise. The data are represented as mean ± s.d., and values of P < 0.05 were considered statistically significant. Comparison between two unpaired groups was performed using a two-tailed Student’s t test. For multiple comparisons involving one variable, one-way ANOVA was used with Tukey’s or Bonferroni’s multiple comparison test when SDs were equal; Brown-Forsythe and Welch ANOVA with Dunnett’s T3 multiple comparisons test was used when SDs were not equal. Two-way ANOVA with Tukey’s or Sidak’s multiple comparison test was used for simultaneous analysis of two variables (tumor growth over time) among multiple groups. Survival curves were obtained using the Kaplan-Meier method and compared by the log-rank test. Sample sizes of in vivo studies were designed based on previous experience of the experimental models, and thus no statistical method was used to predetermine sample size. Mice were randomized to different groups, carefully examined daily, and humanely euthanized at defined study endpoints. Data collection during experiments was performed blinded to ensure the consistency of measurements across all groups. No data were excluded from the analyses. Besides, the histological examination was performed blinded to avoid biased assessment.

text: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER), the largest organelle in eukaryotic cells, is responsible for lipid and protein biosynthesis, providing locales for modifying and folding nascent integral membranes and secreted proteins. Overload of protein folding or perturbations in cellular metabolism instigate ER stress, which disrupts essential cellular processes leading to serious human diseases (such as Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s syndrome, diabetes, and even cancer) and plant diseases (e.g., rice blast and bacterial diseases) –. Therefore, the detection of ER stress is highly important for disease prevention and treatment. Both the plasma membrane (PM) and organelle membrane, two types of membrane systems, are crucially involved in the perception and transmission of stress induced by both internal and external stimuli –. The response to ER stress is initiated by the activation of Ire1, an ER membrane protein, by oligomerization and autophosphorylation, which leads to the induction of the transcriptional activator Hac1 by variable shear stress, followed by the subsequent regulation of the expression of downstream stress-responsive genes through entry into the nucleus –. These genes reduce protein misfolding and induce membrane synthesis, upon which ER function is enhanced, and ER stress is alleviated. The unfolded protein response (UPR), the stress-sensing and response from the ER to the nucleus, which is initiated by Ire1 at the ER membrane, is the most well-characterized response to ER stress. Ire1 is considered one of the most important ER stress sensors present in various species, including mammals, plants, and fungi –. However, the critical role of the PM structure, where stress-sensing and signal transduction start, in this internal stress response remains uncertain. PM proteins play crucial roles in the perception of biotic and abiotic stresses across various species, thereby increasing their adaptive capacity –. Magnaporthe oryzae, the causative agent of devastating fungal blast disease in rice, requires the perception of rice surface signals by plasma membrane proteins as a prerequisite for the formation of its essential infection structure, the appressorium. Multiple PM proteins in M. oryzae, including MoPth11, MoSho1, MoMsb2, and MoRgs7, are critical for recognizing hydrophobic signals, waxes, cutin, and other surface cues from rice –. Upon perceiving diverse signals, these receptors undergo state changes (such as phosphorylation) or modulate their interaction networks, thereby initiating intracellular signal transduction pathways, including the cAMP and MAPK cascades, to relay signals downstream and regulate the expression of genes associated with appressorium formation and consequently modulating pathogenicity. Although several PM proteins that are involved in stress signal perception and pathogenicity have been identified in M. oryzae, only a few of these proteins have been thoroughly characterized in terms of their mechanistic actions, specific signal responses, and comprehensive regulatory networks. Our previous study demonstrated a regulatory mechanism under ER stress conditions, which is essential for appressorium function and virulence, in which a core autophagy-related protein kinase, MoAtg1, directly targets the MAPKK kinase MoMkk1, phosphorylates it, and activates the cell wall integrity pathway independently of the conserved upstream MAPKKK kinase. title: Magnaporthe oryzae MoPh1 perceives ER stress and promotes adaptive responses via a plasma membrane-to-vacuole pathway

text: Our previous study demonstrated a regulatory mechanism under ER stress conditions, which is essential for appressorium function and virulence, in which a core autophagy-related protein kinase, MoAtg1, directly targets the MAPKK kinase MoMkk1, phosphorylates it, and activates the cell wall integrity pathway independently of the conserved upstream MAPKKK kinase. Given the unprecedented nature of this regulatory mechanism wherein a protein substitutes for MAPKKK function under ER stress, it appears that M. oryzae employs regulatory modalities and networks to respond to ER stress, warranting further investigation. In this study, we further investigated putative key PM proteins involved in the ER stress response through comparative membrane proteomic profiling. Combined with expression analysis and subcellular localization assessment, we identified a pleckstrin homology (PH) domain-containing protein, MoPh1. MoPh1 is localized to the PM under non-stress conditions, whereas upon ER stress, it perceives stress signals through inter-organellar communication mediated by the ER-PM contact site regulatory protein MoTcb1 and is subsequently phosphorylated by the protein kinase MoDbf2, leading to its dissociation from the PM. Phosphorylated MoPh1 then targets autophagosomes and interacts with key autophagy-related proteins, including the core scaffold protein MoAtg11 and the autophagosome-vacuole fusion-related protein MoYpt7, to promote the initiation and progression of autophagy, thereby facilitating cellular stress adaptation. Concurrently, MoPh1 enhances the efficiency of phase-separated droplet formation by interacting with Ire1, a key sensor in the canonical ER stress response pathway, thereby amplifying the activity of the classical stress response machinery. Surprisingly, this PM-to-vacuole stress response pathway mediated by MoPh1 does not depend on conventional stress sensors or the classical response pathway; however, it increases the intensity of the classical pathway and appears to be specific to PH domain-containing proteins in M. oryzae. Overall, our study not only identified a PM-localized ER stress sensor, MoPh1, in both microorganisms and plants but also elucidated a distinct response model in which it activates autophagy via a non-canonical PM-to-vacuole pathway to mitigate internal stress, enhance fungal fitness, and promote pathogenicity, providing new perspectives for exploring internal stress perception and response in biological systems.

text: We initially examined the changes in key factors involved in the ER stress response in M. oryzae at the hyphal stage following treatment with ER stress stimulators [dithiothreitol (DTT) and tunicamycin (TM)]. The results revealed that these treatments significantly increased the phosphorylation level of Ire1, the ratio of spliced Hac1, and the expression of downstream target genes involved in the unfolded protein response (UPR), indicating the promotion of ER stress accumulation and response by these agents. The changes in ER stress levels at various time points during the formation of the appressorium, a crucial structure of infection by M. oryzae, were subsequently examined. The accumulation of ER stress during the period of appressorium formation showed a fluctuating trend, peaking after 8 h of treatment, followed by a gradual decrease, indicating that ER stress could be induced not only exogenously but also naturally in a fluctuating manner during the development of its infectious structures. To further investigate whether the dynamics of stress during appressorium formation are associated with fungal pathogenicity, 4-PBA was introduced as an inhibitor of ER stress, while DTT and TM were used as stimulators to treat fungal conidia at different concentrations to interfere with the accumulation of stress. According to our findings, DTT, TM, and 4-PBA treatments interfered with the germination of fungal conidia, which delayed the germination process and appressoria formation rate and led to lower turgor pressure than that of wild-type Guy11 (Further determination of the pathogenicity of these treated conidia on rice leaves revealed that either excessive stimulation or inhibitory stress led to reduced fungal pathogenicity and disease area (Similarly, infection assays on rice leaf sheaths also revealed that at 24 h post-inoculation, conidia treated with DTT, TM, or 4-PBA either failed to form infective appressoria or produced only short primary invasive hyphae. By 48 h, only limited invasive hyphae restricted to initially infected cells were observed, whereas the wild-type and solvent (DMSO) control groups presented extensive hyphal expansion into neighboring cells (These results suggest that the accumulation of ER stress and an appropriate response are required for appressorium formation and pathogenicity in M. oryzae. In addition to its role in fungal pathogenicity, we were also curious about whether the ER stress response is essential for fungal viability under stress. Thus, the survival rate of fungal conidia under ER stress after the application of two ER stress response inhibitors in the wild-type Guy11 strain, including the dual inhibitor of the kinase and RNase activities of Ire1, GSK2850163, and the sole inhibitor of Ire1 RNase activity, STF-083010 was determined. The results revealed a significant reduction in the survival rate of the conidia and mycelia caused by an abnormal ER stress response under Ire1 inhibitor treatment (We also obtained an Ire1 knockout mutant in a specialized KU80 background, which does not impair the developmental processes or pathogenicity of M. oryzae but increases the frequency of targeted gene replacement and evaluated its virulence and sensitivity to ER stress. The results revealed that deletion of the MoIRE1 -encoding gene led to a similar reduction of survival rate, the ratio of spliced Hac1 and pathogenicity of M. oryzae (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. A,), suggesting that an appropriate response to ER stress is crucial for not only fungal infection but also fundamental survival.

section_title: Endoplasmic reticulum stress perception and response are vitally important for both fungal survival and pathogenicity

text: As one of the key components in perceiving various stress signals, plasma membrane (PM) sensors play crucial roles in both recognizing and transducing signals. During the perception and response process, these sensors might undergo some protein modifications and localization alterations. To investigate the putative PM proteins that are critical for the ER stress response, we conducted a quantitative membrane proteomics analysis to identify differentially expressed membrane proteins in both the absence and presence of ER stress (DTT + TM co-treatment). Through further screening and analysis, we focused more on the candidate proteins with PM-associated domains whose gene expression significantly increased but whose membrane protein content decreased (Fig. Supplementary Fig. and Data S), which might be more likely to be associated with the ER stress response. Two putative proteins with the lowest p value attracted our attention since they both contain a pleckstrin homology (PH) domain (MGG_03558 and MGG_11259). Further protein localization screening confirmed the localization of MoPh1 (MGG_11259) to the PM in the absence of stress and its significant response to ER stress (To elucidate the role of the PM protein MoPh1 in the stress response, we generated deletion mutants of MoPH1 (Δ Moph1 #6, Δ Moph1 #8) via homologous recombination and examined their ER stress response. The results revealed that a significant defect in the ER stress response caused by the deletion of the MoPH1 gene occurred under both the DTT and TM treatments and during appressorium formation (Supplementary Fig. A,), including the ratio of spliced MoHAC1 and the expression of downstream UPR target genes, but not during the phosphorylation of MoIre1. The deletion of MoPh1 also concurrently increased the susceptibility of the pathogen to ER stress, which caused a marked reduction in its survival rate and inhibition rate of mycelia in the presence of DTT or TM (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. A,), indicating the possible role of MoPh1 in regulating the ER stress response. Since deletion of MoPh1 did not affect the phosphorylation, it seems that its function might be independent of the classical ER stress sensor Ire1. Furthermore, as a pathogenic fungus, we examined the phenotypic effects of MoPH1 deletion on appressorium function and pathogenicity. The loss of MoPh1 significantly reduced the infection and virulence of the pathogen in both rice and barley (Fig. and Supplementary Fig.), and the appressorium turgor pressure in the mutant strains were markedly lower than that in the wild-type and complemented strains (Δ Moph1/MoPH1) (Consistent with the pathogenicity results, infection assays on rice leaf sheaths and barley leaf abaxial epidermis revealed that at 24 h post-inoculation, the MoPH1 deletion mutant either failed to penetrate the plant epidermis or produced only a minimal infection peg. In contrast, the wild-type and complemented strains generated extensive invasive hyphae with branching within the infected cells. When the infection period was extended, the MoPh1 deletion mutant still produced only limited invasive hyphae, whereas the wild-type and complemented strains fully colonized the initially infected cells and expanded into adjacent cells (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. C,). These findings indicated that MoPh1 was essential for appressorium function and pathogenicity in M. oryzae and that the pathogenicity defect observed in the deletion mutant was likely associated with the impaired appressorium function.

text: Further observation of MoPh1 localization under different stress conditions revealed that it was localized to the PM under non-stress conditions. Upon short-term ER stress (0.5 and 1 h), a portion of MoPh1 formed punctate aggregates inside the cells. This aggregation process could be inhibited by the endocytosis inhibitor latrunculin B (Supplementary Fig.), indicating that MoPh1 could enter the cytoplasm via endocytosis under stress conditions. When the ER stress treatment was prolonged (2 and 5 h), the internalized MoPh1 further localized to autophagosomes and vacuoles. Notably, unlike artificial ER stress treatment during the hyphal stage, MoPh1 constantly maintained partial PM localization under the natural fluctuations of ER stress during appressorium formation (However, the proportion of MoPh1 internalized into the cells exhibited similar fluctuating changes in response to variations in stress levels: a gradual increase in the proportion of intracellular MoPh1 co-localized with autophagosomes was recorded within the initial 0-8 h of conidial germination, and subsequently declined (These results suggest that synchronous variation in MoPh1 localization corresponds to different levels of ER stress. Combined with the findings that MoPH1 gene expression was induced by ER stress and that the loss of MoPh1 severely impaired the stress response and tolerance, we concluded that MoPh1 might serve as a PM sensor capable of sensing and responding to ER stress.

text: Autophagy is an evolutionarily conserved process that plays a role in degrading and recycling the cytosol and organelles in eukaryotic cells by delivering the materials destined for degradation to lysosomes or vacuoles,. Given that MoPh1 can target autophagosomes and vesicles under ER stress, we wondered whether this stress response initiated from the PM leads to the activation of autophagy to help relieve stress. Thus, we first examined the number of autophagosomes in the wild-type and mutant strains under ER stress using transmission electron microscopy and detected a significant reduction in the number of autophagosomes in the MoPh1 deletion mutant (The intensity of both selective (marked with MoSec61) and non-selective (marked with MoAtg8) autophagy in M. oryzae under ER stress was examined, and both were found to be significantly induced in the presence of ER stress in the wild-type strain Guy11 and largely influenced in the absence of MoPh1, indicating the role of MoPh1 in the regulation of selective and non-selective autophagy triggered by ER stress. To elucidate the mechanisms involved in the entry of MoPh1 into autophagosomes and its regulatory impact on autophagy, MoPh1 was used as bait, and its interaction patterns under ER stress were screened. Our findings revealed the specific potential MoPh1-interacting proteins involved in several biological processes, including the plasma membrane, autophagy, vesicular transport and protein modification, during this stress (Fig. and Data S). Among the processes related to autophagy, MoPh1 was found to interact directly with MoAtg11, which is a key scaffold protein that plays a role in autophagy, specifically in autophagosome formation under ER stress, under both DTT treatment at the hyphal stage and appressorium formation stage (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. A–). Notably, the deletion of MoPh1 disrupted the localization of MoAtg11 to the autophagosome (Fig. and Supplementary Fig.) and also led to an aberrant interaction strength between MoAtg11 and another core autophagy regulator, MoAtg9 (Supplementary Fig.), manifested as the enhancement of MoAtg11-MoAtg9 under ER stress compared with that in the wildtype, which resulted in a marked reduction in the characteristic punctate distribution of Atg9 but accumulation in large aggregates (Fig. and Supplementary Figs. and A,). Furthermore, the analysis of MoPh1-interacting proteins revealed the interaction of MoPh1 with MoYpt7 (Supplementary Fig. A,), which is responsible for regulating the fusion of autophagosomes with the vacuolar membrane, and the deletion of MoPH1 affects the aggregation of MoYpt7 in vesicles in the context of ER stress (Fig. and Supplementary Figs. and A,). Additionally, MoYpt7 serves as a marker of late endosomes during the processes associated with endocytosis, which corroborates our previous finding that the entry of MoPh1 into the cytoplasm via endocytosis. text: To investigate how MoPh1, a PM-localized protein, receives signals from the ER, which induce the subsequent initiation of the relevant response, we reanalyzed the data of MoPh1-interacting proteins and identified an interesting component, MoTcb1, which functions in regulating the contact between the ER and the PM. ER-PM contact sites (EPCSs) are formed that allow the exchange of material and information between these two structures –. Here, MoSec61 was used as an ER marker, and FM4-64 was used to label the PM. We observed that under normal conditions without ER stress, the ER predominantly exhibited a regular, continuous tubular network that was relatively independent of the PM (In contrast, under ER stress conditions, the ER displayed not only a tubular morphology, but also a more dispersed distribution, with a significantly increased proportion of regions closely apposed to the PM, especially under relatively short-term ER stress (0.5 and 1 h), indicating that frequent ER-PM contacts during the response to ER stress in M. oryzae and that the ER might transmit signals to the PM through these contact sites. Notably, following prolonged ER stress (2 and 5 h), the proportion of dispersed ER structures in close proximity to the PM gradually decreased, while the regular ring-like ER morphology became increasingly predominant. This dynamic redistribution suggested that the stress-induced ER remodeling and its close association with the PM represent a transient signaling phase rather than a sustained state (Localization tracking revealed that MoTcb1 localized to the PM with punctate aggregation under normal conditions (Supplementary Fig.), whereas the puncta-MoTcb1 on the PM were significantly enriched near the ER-PM contact sites and partially co-localized with them under ER stress, indicating that MoTcb1 could localize to the ER-PM contact sites during stress conditions. Concurrently, a fraction of MoTcb1 internalized and co-localized with autophagosomes and vacuoles under stress conditions (We then confirmed the interaction between MoTcb1 and MoPh1 and found that this interaction occurred specifically under short-term ER stress, as puncta on the PM closely coincided with the distribution pattern of ER-PM contact sites but did not interact under long-term ER stress or normal conditions (Fig. and We further generated a MoTCB1 deletion mutant (Δ Motcb1) and introduced GFP-tagged MoPh1 into this background. The results revealed that MoPh1 failed to dissociate from the PM under ER stress in the Δ Motcb1 mutant (Fig. and Supplementary Fig.), along with the significant impairment of ER stress-induced autophagy (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. A,), confirming the generation of ER stress signals perceived by MoPh1 from EPCSs through MoTcb1. In addition, most PM receptors undergo modifications before and after they sense signals –. Our mass spectrometric analysis of MoPh1 phosphorylation led to the identification of two specific phosphorylation sites (S226 and S230) under ER stress (We then validated the authenticity of these two phosphorylation sites using Phos-tag analysis and found that, constitutively unphosphorylated MoPh1 S226, 230A still maintained the localization on the PM even under ER stress, whereas the constitutively activated MoPh1 S226, 230D internalized spontaneously without stress treatment (Fig. and Supplementary Figs. and), suggesting that the phosphorylation of MoPh1 was essential for its dissociation from the PM.

Notably, among the proteins that specifically interact with MoPh1 under ER stress, we identified a potential PM-localized, mitosis-related protein kinase, MoDbf2 (Supplementary Fig.), and verified the specific interaction on the PM under stress conditions through BiFC, Co-IP and Y2H assays (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. D–). The validation of phosphorylation was performed both in vivo and in vitro to verify whether MoDbf2 can directly phosphorylate MoPh1 at two specific phosphorylation sites (S226 and S230) (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. A,). Consistent with these findings, MoPh1 also failed to dissociate from the PM in the MoDBF2 deletion mutant (Δ Modbf2), which was similar to the constitutively unphosphorylated MoPh1 S226,230A (Fig. and These results together demonstrated that the specific phosphorylation of MoPh1 by MoDbf2 was also a prerequisite for its dissociation from the PM. text: Considering that both the classical ER-to-nucleus response pathway mediated by the ER membrane sensor MoIre1 and the PM-to-vacuole response pathway mediated by the PM sensor MoPh1 influence the fungal response to ER stress and survival, we investigated the relationship between these two pathways. We thus impaired the classical response pathway through different Ire1 enzymatic inhibitors and a MoIRE1 deletion mutant and examined whether the MoPh1-mediated response was affected. The results revealed that neither the inhibition of Ire1 enzymatic activity nor the deletion of MoIRE1 affected the interaction between MoTcb1 and MoPh1 under ER stress, the dynamic changes in MoPh1 localization, or the autophagy process (Fig. and Supplementary Figs. A, and), indicating that the MoPh1-mediated response does not depend on the classical ER stress sensor. However, we previously reported that the deletion of MoPh1 affects the splicing of Hac1 and the response of downstream UPR target genes in the classical ER stress response pathway but not Ire1 phosphorylation, suggesting that these two pathways function relatively independently but exhibit crosstalk at specific nodes. We therefore sought to further identify the crosstalk node between these two pathways. A recent study demonstrated that mammalian Ire1α can form efficient Ire1 machinery after oligomerization and autophosphorylation through the formation of phase-separated droplets, which enhances Ire1 splicing efficiency and consequently improves the response capacity to stress. title: Magnaporthe oryzae MoPh1 perceives ER stress and promotes adaptive responses via a plasma membrane-to-vacuole pathway
section_title: The PM-to-vacuole ER stress response pathway mediated by MoPh1 is relatively conserved in both fungi and plants

text: Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress occurs when there is an accumulation of unfolded or misfolded proteins due to the overwhelming demand on the cellular folding machinery under severe environmental stress conditions. To counteract the detrimental effects of ER stress, cells have evolved a conserved degradation pathway from the ER to the nucleus, known as the unfolded protein response (UPR). In mammals, the initiation of the UPR and monitoring of ER stress are carried out by three ER transmembrane sensors: IRE1α, PERK, and ATF6. In yeast, this process is solely managed by IRE1, whereas in plants, it is mediated by two types of ER membrane proteins: IRE1 and bZIP28,. In these diverse eukaryotes, stress-activated sensor proteins transduce signals via oligomerization and autophosphorylation to orchestrate nuclear gene expression and promote protein folding, ultimately restoring proteostasis by balancing folding capacity with demand, basically following an ER-to-nucleus transcriptional regulatory model. However, it remains unclear whether plasma membrane (PM) sensors, as critical factors in stress perception and response, are involved in sensing and responding to such internal stresses. Here, our study identified a stress-induced PM protein, MoPh1, whose subcellular localization changed dynamically in response to ER stress levels, and its deletion severely impaired stress perception and response, indicating its potential role as an ER stress sensor. Under ER stress, the ER itself undergoes morphological changes, increasing its proximity and contact sites with the PM, which enables stress signals to be transmitted from ER-PM contact sites via the regulatory protein MoTcb1 to MoPh1. MoPh1 subsequently altered its phosphorylation status and dissociated from the PM, targeted the autophagosomes, and initiated autophagy to facilitate stress alleviation. Interference with the classical response pathway demonstrated that this PM-to-vacuole response mediated by the PM sensor MoPh1 operated independently of the classical ER stress sensors. Nevertheless, it reinforces the classical pathway by influencing the formation of Ire1 phase-separated condensates and simultaneously utilizes its unique ability to regulate autophagy to alleviate ER stress at the protein degradation level, thereby increasing an organism’s adaptability to ER stress (Like the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress response, most reported mechanisms for perceiving and responding to internal stresses follow an “internal stress, intracellular solution” paradigm, whereby internal sensors directly initiate intracellular response processes upon stress detection. For example, M. oryzae employs a turgor-sensing histidine-aspartate kinase, Sln1, localized in the appressorium pore, to monitor appressorial turgor pressure in real time. Once a critical threshold is reached, it promotes host penetration and facilitates pathogenicity. In human embryonic kidney 293 (HEK293) cells, the cytosolic apoptosis signal-regulating kinase 3 (ASK3) senses internal osmotic stress, quickly forms liquid-demixing condensates, and modulates its own enzymatic activity to regulate cellular homeostasis. Additionally, the cysteine-rich Keap1 protein in human cells detects oxidative stress, releases bound Nrf2, and activates the expression of antioxidant genes to counteract oxidative stress. Unlike these situations, for internal ER stress, we identified a distinct PM-to-vacuole response pathway that functions from the surface to the innards.
title: Magnaporthe oryzae MoPh1 perceives ER stress and promotes adaptive responses via a plasma membrane-to-vacuole pathway

text: In human embryonic kidney 293 (HEK293) cells, the cytosolic apoptosis signal-regulating kinase 3 (ASK3) senses internal osmotic stress, quickly forms liquid-demixing condensates, and modulates its own enzymatic activity to regulate cellular homeostasis. Additionally, the cysteine-rich Keap1 protein in human cells detects oxidative stress, releases bound Nrf2, and activates the expression of antioxidant genes to counteract oxidative stress. Unlike these situations, for internal ER stress, we identified a distinct PM-to-vacuole response pathway that functions from the surface to the innards. This response pathway operates independently of classical intracellular stress sensors at its initiation. Instead, it relies on stress-induced contact between the ER and PM, through which the stress signal is transmitted via the ER-PM contact sites, regulating proteins to the PM sensor MoPh1 and subsequently triggers downstream autophagy processes to alleviate stress. This discovery not only enriches our understanding of the strategies organisms employ to cope with intracellular stress but also provides new perspectives on the role of the PM in the response to internal stresses. Conventionally, stress-sensing sensor proteins undergo not only changes in expression levels but also alterations in post-translational modifications upon stress perception. Phosphorylation is a common feature of characterized PM sensors following stress perception –. We found here that the PM-located MoPh1 remained in an unphosphorylated state in the absence of ER stress. Upon receiving stress signals from the ER-PM tethering protein MoTcb1, it is specifically phosphorylated at two sites (S226 and S230) by MoDbf2, a cell cycle-associated protein kinase with partial PM localization. Neither the MoDBF2 deletion nor the constitutively unphosphorylated mutant of MoPh1, MoPh1, failed to dissociate from the PM even under ER stress, indicating that phosphorylation of MoPh1 is essential for the propagation of stress signals. Furthermore, MoPh1 could also not be phosphorylated under ER stress in the Δ Motcb1 mutant, demonstrating that phosphorylation of MoPh1 by MoDbf2 occurred after it received stress signals from MoTcb1. Consistent with this finding, the interaction between MoTcb1 and MoPh1 under stress was unaffected in the Δ Modbf2 mutant, indicating that the transmission of the stress signal to MoPh1 preceded its phosphorylation and subsequent dissociation from the PM. Additionally, the interaction strength of MoTcb1-MoPh1 under ER stress remained unchanged in the MoIRE1 deletion mutant, further confirming that the MoPh1-mediated response pathway operates independently of the classical ER stress sensor. title: Magnaporthe oryzae MoPh1 perceives ER stress and promotes adaptive responses via a plasma membrane-to-vacuole pathway

text: Multiple PM proteins in M. oryzae are crucial for appressorium formation and pathogenicity, –, and MoPh1 is no exception. We found that the absence of MoPh1 significantly reduced the survival rate of the pathogen under ER stress, accompanied by markedly decreased appressorial turgor pressure and abnormal infection rates, which were likely the primary reasons for the severe impairment of pathogenicity in the mutant. Studies have indicated that the autophagy process is essential for appressorium function and pathogenicity in M. oryzae, –, and MoPh1 is localized to autophagosomes and vacuoles after dissociating from the PM under ER stress, where it interacts with the core autophagy scaffold protein MoAtg11 and promotes its scaffolding function and facilitates autophagosome formation, suggesting that the impaired autophagy level in the absence of MoPh1 leads to the aberrant appressorium function and pathogenicity. Atg11, as one of the two core scaffold proteins (along with Atg17) involved in autophagy, plays an essential role not only in initiating autophagosome formation but also in organizing and activating selective autophagy pathways by interacting with selective autophagy receptors. However, little is known about the function of Atg11 and its related regulatory network in M. oryzae. According to previous studies, Atg11 itself does not enter the vacuole and degraded during autophagy, possibly because the recruitment of Vam7 to the autophagosome might help with the release of Atg11 from the Atg11-autophagy receptor complex and the elimination of this complex. Nevertheless, our results revealed that MoAtg11 co-localized with MoAtg8 in vacuoles during appressorium formation in M. oryzae and that this process was significantly disrupted in the MoPh1 deletion mutant. Under ER stress, substantial amounts of MoAtg11 accumulate near the Atg8-marker autophagosome/vacuole, indicating a unique regulatory role for MoPh1 in modulating MoAtg11 during ER stress-induced autophagy in M. oryzae. Furthermore, as one of the key interacting partners of MoAtg11, the interaction between MoAtg9 (the only transmembrane protein among the core autophagy machinery) and MoAtg11 was abnormally enhanced in the absence of MoPh1, led to a similar abnormal accumulation around autophagosomes and vacuoles just like MoAtg11, indicating that MoPh1 promoted the maintenance of the dynamic punctate localization of MoAtg9 during ER stress-induced autophagy through preventing the combination of MoAtg9-MoAtg11. Additionally, MoPh1 also interacted with MoYpt7, a key protein regulating autophagosome-vacuole fusion, and facilitated its targeting to vacuoles. Therefore, through influencing multiple aspects of the autophagy process, MoPh1 regulates both selective and non-selective autophagy under ER stress conditions, thereby ensuring proper appressorium function, successful host infection, and pathogenicity. The pleckstrin homology (PH) domain is a common domain found in the human proteome and is known primarily for its ability to target cellular membranes by specifically binding to phosphoinositides. As cognition intensifies, PH domains have diverse functions beyond phosphoinositide binding, including interactions with small G proteins. Although PH domains are prevalent in proteins and are associated with both the ER stress response and autophagy processes, few reports exist on their clear mechanism for linking these two essential biological processes, and there are no reports on their ability to function as stress sensors to activate autophagy to help relieve stress.
title: Magnaporthe oryzae MoPh1 perceives ER stress and promotes adaptive responses via a plasma membrane-to-vacuole pathway

text: As cognition intensifies, PH domains have diverse functions beyond phosphoinositide binding, including interactions with small G proteins. Although PH domains are prevalent in proteins and are associated with both the ER stress response and autophagy processes, few reports exist on their clear mechanism for linking these two essential biological processes, and there are no reports on their ability to function as stress sensors to activate autophagy to help relieve stress. Few studies have shown that PH domain-containing proteins participate in the ER stress response, and most of them are limited to the transcriptional level –. Similarly, investigations into the role of PH domain proteins in autophagy have focused mainly on their interactions with the protein sorting (HOPS) complex, Rab family members, and finite core Atg proteins such as Atg8 and Atg5 –. In this study, we identified a PM-localized PH domain-containing protein, MoPh1, that perceives and responds to stress through precise protein interactions, which target the key scaffold protein Atg11 on autophagosomes and promote the autophagy process and alleviate stress, thereby expanding the known functional repertoire of PH domain proteins. While M. oryzae encodes nearly 20 PH domain-containing proteins, our examination of 11 randomly selected proteins, along with the recently reported MoVast2, revealed that none exhibited PM localization or dynamic relocation under ER stress comparable to that of MoPh1, indicating that the function of MoPh1 as an ER stress receptor might be specific to this pathogen. Furthermore, we found that the MoPh1-mediated stress response likely also occurred in A. thaliana, suggesting that this “surface-to-innards” response mechanism for internal stress might possess a certain degree of universality across species. Considering that a limited number of receptors and sensors have been identified in the top ten plant pathogenic fungi, including M. oryzae, the identification of MoPh1 as an essential component for the stress response and fungal virulence is highly valuable. Moreover, since membrane proteins constitute the main category of known drug targets for pharmaceuticals, MoPh1 represents a promising target for potential drug development in the future, with the aim of better controlling the destructive diseases caused by the fungus on rice, which is still by far the most essential and staple food for more than half of the human population worldwide.

text: In eukaryotic cells, a large fraction of secretory and membrane proteins needs to be translocated into the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), where they are processed and modified post-translationally to obtain the correct conformation. Overburden of the ER with unfolded proteins, a condition called ER stress, may result in ER and cell dysfunction. To cope with this, cells initiate the unfolded protein response (UPR) by activating three sentinels—IRE1α, PERK, and ATF6—that localize on the ER membrane. IRE1α undergoes trans-autophosphorylation and oligomerization, switching on its endo-ribonuclease activity to initiate the splicing of a specific mRNA, XBP1, creating a transcription factor, XBP1s. PERK decreases protein translation globally by phosphorylating eIF2α, meanwhile accelerating the translation of a transcription factor, ATF4. ATF6 translocates to the Golgi apparatus, where it is cleaved by proteases to release the N-terminal fragment, ATF6(N), as a transcription factor. By so doing, signals are transduced to the cytosol and the nucleus to reduce ER protein import and upregulate expression of genes that are involved in protein folding, ER expansion, and misfolded protein degradation in order to restore the protein homeostasis in the ER. We call these signals the adaptive UPR. The intensity of the UPR signals needs tight control, not only because the UPR is energy-consuming but also because either overreaction or inertness of the UPR can be detrimental to the cell. On the one hand, constitutive activation of both IRE1α and PERK branches is known to contribute to programmed cell death, herein referred to as the terminal UPR. IRE1α oligomers can recruit TRAF2, promoting JNK phosphorylation and apoptosis, or degrade selective microRNAs that normally repress programmed cell death,. Sustained PERK activation increases the expression of pro-apoptotic protein CHOP and its downstream factors, death receptor 5 and Bim,. On the other hand, repression of the adaptive UPR under unresolved ER stress may exacerbate ER stress insult. For example, the IRE1α-XBP1 signal is attenuated during prolonged ER stress, allowing the translation of death receptor 5 downstream of PERK, inducing apoptosis,. A complicated regulatory system has evolved in the cell to tailor the UPR signals so as to adapt to different conditions, making the live-death decision largely based on the duration time and the strength of ER stress. A short-term ER stress, for example, a transient protein overload in the ER that may occur under normal physiological conditions, could be buffered by existing ER-localized chaperones without fully activating the UPR. This can be achieved by BIP ampylation/de-ampylation and PDI phosphorylation,. In the case that the UPR is activated, an increase in protein folding capacity at transcriptional and translational levels would soon resolve ER stress, accompanied by the UPR signals turning off. Switch-off of the UPR may also happen if cells are overwhelmed by irremediable ER stress. To date, several mechanisms have been reported to explain the inactivation of the UPR, yet it remains unclear whether these mechanisms apply to the conditions when ER stress is resolved or still unmitigated. Examples of these mechanisms include, but are not limited to, de-phosphorylation of eIF2α and IRE1α, reduction of IRE1α by PDIA6, S-nitrosylation of IRE1α, and degradation of IRE1α and ATF6 through ER-associated degradation –. How do cells deal with constitutive but non-lethal ER stress?
title: Calcium-mediated calreticulin-IRE1α interaction drives dynamic fluctuation of IRE1α activity under chronic endoplasmic reticulum stress

text: Switch-off of the UPR may also happen if cells are overwhelmed by irremediable ER stress. To date, several mechanisms have been reported to explain the inactivation of the UPR, yet it remains unclear whether these mechanisms apply to the conditions when ER stress is resolved or still unmitigated. Examples of these mechanisms include, but are not limited to, de-phosphorylation of eIF2α and IRE1α, reduction of IRE1α by PDIA6, S-nitrosylation of IRE1α, and degradation of IRE1α and ATF6 through ER-associated degradation –. How do cells deal with constitutive but non-lethal ER stress? Conceivably, this could happen under physiological and pathophysiological conditions, for example antibody secretion in plasma cells and nutrient/oxygen deprivation in tumor tissues. So far, we still lack a satisfactory answer to this question, partly because it was difficult to clarify whether ER stress is resolved or not in cells that are maintained in conditions that can theoretically induce ER stress. Recently, we developed a fluorescence-based reporter that enables live-cell imaging of unfolded protein accumulation in the ER lumen. With this tool, we hereby defined conditions that correspond to transient, constitutive but non-lethal, and lethal ER stress, and monitored the UPR under each conditions along the time. A fluctuation in the IRE1α signal under constitutive ER stress, tuned by BIP and calreticulin (CALR) that interact with IRE1α competitively in a calcium-dependent manner, was discovered.
