text: To mimic different intensities of ER stress, we cultured HeLa cells under a series of concentrations of tunicamycin (Tm). This led to a dose-dependent increase of cell apoptosis. In particular, while with 1 μg/mL of Tm the apoptotic level remained at around 20%, A dramatic surge of the apoptotic level occurs when the concentration of Tm was elevated from 1 μg/mL to 2 μg/mL, which became even more apparent with time extended (We then monitored the unfolded protein accumulation in the ER lumen—defined as ER stress—by using our recently developed reporter, and found that the fluorescence puncta of the reporter—a sign of ER stress—remained in HeLa cells during the 48 h treatment with Tm at 1 μg/mL, yet disappeared with Tm at 250 ng/mL, suggesting a recovery from ER stress at only low dose (250 ng/mL) of Tm (We then defined the condition under Tm treatment at 250 ng/mL as mild ER stress, which was finally resolved by the cell and did not cause cell apoptosis. The condition with Tm at 5 μg/mL was defined as severe ER stress, as it ultimately killed almost all of the cell. The condition with 1 μg/mL of Tm was regarded as intermediate ER stress, as the unfolded proteins persist in the ER lumen without causing significant cell death. XBP1 splicing has been reported to be diminished after it reaches the plateau under prolonged ER stress. In agreement with this, the maximum splicing ratio occurred at 4–8 h under mild ER stress, then gradually disappeared, roughly matching the dynamic change of unfolded protein accumulation level (Fig. –D). This up-and-down pattern was also seen in cells under intermediate and severe ER stress (Interestingly, under intermediate and severe ER stress, a second wave of XBP1 splicing came up at about 36 h, further increasing till 48 h (The signal of GFP-tagged IRE1α clustering, a reflection of the oligomerization and activation of IRE1α, also fluctuated in the same pace as XBP1 splicing ratio under intermediate ER stress (Such re-initiation of XBP1 splicing was also seen in three additional types of cells, including human breast cancer cell line MDA-MB-231, human embryonic kidney cell line 293 T, primary mouse embryotic fibroblast (MEF), and mouse skeletal muscle myoblast (C2C12), albeit at different concentrations of Tm and with crest and trough at different time points due to different sensitivity of the cells to ER stress (There were even two to three waves of XBP1 splicing ratio in MEF cells (Treating HeLa with another ER stress inducer, thapsigargin (Tg), at low dose (5 nM), also recapitulated the resurgence of XBP1 splicing (However, such phenomenon was not seen at higher concentration of Tg, probably due to high severity of ER stress induced by Tg that disrupted the UPR modulation capacity of the cell (We measured several signals of the three UPR arms. Similar to XBP1 splicing, the phosphorylation level of IRE1α and the protein amount of XBP1s plateaued at 8–12 h and then diminished under all of mild, intermediate, and severe ER stress conditions, surging up again only under intermediate and severe ER stress (The protein level of ATF6(N) (the active form of ATF6) reached an unobvious peak at 4–8 h under mild and intermediate ER stress possibly due to transcription upregulation, and dramatically increased at late time points (36–48 h) under intermediate and severe ER stress in spite of a constant level of full-length ATF6.
title: Calcium-mediated calreticulin-IRE1α interaction drives dynamic fluctuation of IRE1α activity under chronic endoplasmic reticulum stress
section_title: UPR fluctuation under prolonged ER stress

text: Similar to XBP1 splicing, the phosphorylation level of IRE1α and the protein amount of XBP1s plateaued at 8–12 h and then diminished under all of mild, intermediate, and severe ER stress conditions, surging up again only under intermediate and severe ER stress (The protein level of ATF6(N) (the active form of ATF6) reached an unobvious peak at 4–8 h under mild and intermediate ER stress possibly due to transcription upregulation, and dramatically increased at late time points (36–48 h) under intermediate and severe ER stress in spite of a constant level of full-length ATF6. This can be explained by irreversible cleavage of ATF6 that results in accumulation of ATF6(N) if ER stress persists (Transcription level of BIP and CHOP, downstream of ATF6 and PERK, respectively, also showed fluctuation under severe ER stress, but only came up one time within 48 h under mild and intermediate ER stress (The transcription level of BIP reached the first crest at 12 h, later than the XBP1 splicing ratio did (Such time lag was more obvious at the protein level, with expression of XBP1s peaked at 8–12 h whereas BIP at 24–36 h (After reaching the plateau, the protein level of BIP neither decreased as much as its mRNA level did under mild and intermediate ER stress (at 24–36 h), nor recovered as mRNA level did under severe ER stress (at 48 h), probably because BIP is a long-lived protein and that its translation efficiency is dampened under prolonged, severe ER stress. As for PERK pathway, we saw slight band-shift of PERK protein, indicating its phosphorylation, and the expression of the downstream proteins ATF4 and CHOP, which peaked at about 8–12 h followed by decrease (Re-upregulation of ATF4 and CHOP, at 36–48 h, only occurred under severe ER stress, similar to that of CHOP mRNA. The transcription level of TXNIP, one of the terminal UPR markers previously reported to be downstream of IRE1α, did not show a fluctuation pattern but continuously increased only under severe ER stress (Similarly, JNK phosphorylation and caspase-3 cleavage, signatures of terminal UPR, were activated only at the late stage (36-48 h) of severe ER stress (These results, together with the fact that resurgence of CHOP solely happened under severe ER stress, echoing the observation that pronounced apoptosis occurred under severe but not intermediate ER stress (In summary, under prolonged ER stress, cells exhibit a fluctuation pattern of IRE1α-XBP1 signal (adaptive UPR), which is re-activated under both intermediate and severe ER stress but not mild ER stress. ATF6-BIP signal (adaptive UPR) is activated behind XBP1 splicing, and remains stable under mild, intermediate, and severe ER stress. PERK-CHOP signal is quickly initiated and diminishes similar as IRE1α-XBP1 signal does, and resurges up only when cells experience severe ER stress, accompanied by JNK phosphorylation, TXNIP upregulation, and caspase-3 cleavage that irreversibly lead to cell death (terminal UPR) (It should be noted that the temporal dynamics of any of the above signals shall not be considered as being regulated by a single UPR pathway, since the regulation of the UPR is a highly complicated process with multiple feedbacks and cross-talks among IRE1α, PERK, and ATF6 branches.
title: Calcium-mediated calreticulin-IRE1α interaction drives dynamic fluctuation of IRE1α activity under chronic endoplasmic reticulum stress
section_title: UPR fluctuation under prolonged ER stress

text: The different pattern of the temporal dynamics of the three arms of the UPR suggests a complicated regulation of the UPR that may play important roles in life-and-death decisions of the cell. We are particularly interested in the UPR signal dynamics under intermediate ER stress, a condition where unfolded proteins remain in the ER but do not induce significant cell apoptosis. To this end, transcriptomic change under prolonged ER stress was systematically investigated in HeLa cells that were challenged with intermediate ER stress for different times. Totally 11,520 genes were ranked according to the correlation coefficient between their expression level and XBP1 splicing ratio, and the top 2000 positive-correlated genes and 2000 negative-correlated genes were picked up and subjected to weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) (Fig. For the top 2000 positively and 2000 negatively correlated genes, 11 and 7 gene modules were identified, respectively, based on how the expression level of each gene was correlated with the XBP1 splicing ratio. Among these modules, the grey modules exhibited the highest positive or negative correlation values with XBP1 splicing ratio (Fig. The most positive-correlated genes within the grey module included DDIT3, PTP4A3 and FBXW4 that may be involved in phosphorylated protein regulation, GOLPH3, IFT46, UVRAG, and TMEM167B that may participate in protein transport, STC2 that regulates calcium and phosphate homeostasis, and UPR markers XBP1 and DDIT3, among others (The most negative-correlated genes within the grey module included ALG8, B3GNT2, and FUT8 that catalyze protein glycosylation, GEMIN6, DDX17, and HNRNPH3 that are related to RNA splicing, CERK, B4GALT5, and DGAT2 that catalyze sphingolipid and glycolipid biosynthesis, and chaperones/co-chaperones DNAJB4, HSPA8, and FKBP4, among others (While hub genes identified from the 11 modules of 2000 most positive-correlated genes are highly connected, the ones from 7 modules of 2000 most negative-correlated genes are mainly isolated (KEGG analysis of the hub genes revealed that genes positively correlated with XBP1 splicing ratio were predominantly associated with protein processing in the endoplasmic reticulum, circadian rhythm, and autophagy, whereas genes negatively correlated with XBP1 splicing ratio were primarily linked to osteoclast differentiation, IL-17 signaling pathway, and N-glycan biosynthesis (These findings highlight the diverse biological processes regulated by XBP1 splicing during cellular stress responses. We also examined genes that were previously reported to be downstream of the three UPR arms. Many genes downstream of IRE1α-XBP1 branch exhibited expression fluctuation pattern similar to XBP1 splicing ratio, including those encoding ER-localized heat shock proteins and chaperones (DNAJB9, FICD, HSPA13, and PDIA5), protein translocation and transport-related genes (SEC23B, SEC61A1, SSR3, and SRP19), and ER-associated-degradation-related gene EDEM2 (Genes belonging to the PERK/ISR arm showed different expression dynamics: PPP1R15A (GADD34), WARS1, GADD45A, TRIB3, and CBX4 fluctuated similar to those under the IRE1α-XBP1 arm, whereas some genes (including DDIT3 that encodes CHOP) did not recover after the first wave. The elevation of ATF4 mRNA level became apparent only at 48 h, in agreement with the fact that the upregulation of ATF4 at the early stage of ER stress is at the translational level rather than the transcriptional level.

section_title: Systematic mapping of UPR dynamics reveals fluctuation of the IRE1α-XBP1 branch under intermediate ER stress

text: Among the three UPR arms, IRE1α signals exhibited the most apparent fluctuation pattern under intermediate to severe ER stress. We then focused on the IRE1α pathway and tried to disclose the regulatory mechanism of its signal fluctuation. To this end, proteomic analysis was performed on IRE1α-interacting proteins that were co-immunoprecipitated from HeLa cells treated with intermediate or severe ER stress for 24 h and 48 h. Under intermediated ER stress, 202 (UP) and 218 (DOWN) proteins showed increased and decreased bindings with IRE1α, respectively, at 48 h compared to 24 h (The DOWN group enriched proteins related to ribosome biogenesis in eukaryotes and RNA transport, among others, which had no direct link with the ER (As for the UP group, we noticed enrichment in protein processing in ER (These proteins included ER-shaping protein CKAP4, protein disulfide isomerase family member PDIA3, heat shock proteins HSP90B1, HSP90AA1, and HYOU1, Ca 2+ -binding proteins calreticulin (CALR) and calnexin (CANX), ER-associate protein degradation-related protein VCP, and glucosidase (GANAB), as well as the previously reported IRE1α-interacting protein TRAF2 (We also compared the abundance of IRE1α-interacting proteins in cells under severe ER stress for 24 h and 48 h. Again, prolonged stress enriched proteins involved in RNA transport in the DOWN-regulated group, and proteins involved in protein processing in the ER in the UP-regulated group (Under both intermediate and severe ER stress, eight proteins involved in protein processing in the ER were identified to have more interaction with IRE1α at 48 h compared to 24 h: CALR, CANX, GANAB, HSP90AA1, HSP90B1, HYOU1, PDIA3, and VCP (We were particularly interested in CALR, a Ca 2+ -binding protein in the ER that plays an important role in the quality control of glycoproteins, but has not been reported to bind to and regulate IRE1α. Under basal conditions, CALR interacted with IRE1α. As a positive control, BIP also showed interaction with IRE1α (Under intermediate or severe ER stress, the interaction between CALR and IRE1α increased at 8 h, then decreased at 24 h, and went up again at 48 h, well correlated with the phosphorylation level of IRE1α and XBP1s protein amount (Fig. Notably, the decrease (at 24 h) and recovery (at 48 h) of CALR-IRE1α interaction negatively correlated with the interaction between IRE1α and BIP, the master regulator of the UPR (Fig. The same trend of CALR-IRE1α and BIP-IRE1α interactions was observed in C2C12 cells (We did not see decrease of BIP-IRE1α interaction at 8 h, probably because the cell has already passed the early response stage. The fluctuation of CALR-IRE1α interaction did not match the total amount of CALR, which barely changed under intermediate ER stress and slightly increased under severe ER stress, suggesting that other factors, instead of CALR expression itself, drives the fluctuation of CALR-IRE1α interaction intensity (Fig. The interaction between CALR and IRE1α is ER stress-dependent, since (1) it is relatively weak under basal condition compared with that under ER stress, and (2) it did not revive when cells recovered from mild ER stress (In other words, the zigzag form of CALR-IRE1α interaction intensity was seen only if cells had not yet recovered from ER stress, which inversely correlated with BIP-IRE1α interaction intensities.
title: Calcium-mediated calreticulin-IRE1α interaction drives dynamic fluctuation of IRE1α activity under chronic endoplasmic reticulum stress
section_title: Zigzag of BIP-IRE1α interaction that negatively correlated with calreticulin-IRE1α interaction under intermediate and severe ER stress, but not mild ER stress

text: The inverse correlation of BIP-IRE1α and CALR-IRE1α interaction suggested that BIP and CALR bind with IRE1α competitively. Pull-down assay using recombinant proteins confirmed the direct interaction of IRE1α lumenal domain (IRE1α(LD)) with CALR and BIP (Fig. Notably, addition of CALR interrupted the interaction between IRE1α(LD) and BIP in a concentration-dependent manner (Similarly, increasing BIP concentration also reduced the amount of CALR that bound to IRE1α(LD) (Next, we examined whether BIP competed with CALR in IRE1α binding in the cell. Overexpressing BIP or CALR decreased the interaction of IRE1α with CALR or with BIP, respectively (These results support a competitive relationship between BIP and CALR in IRE1α binding, which could explain why higher IRE1α-CALR interaction is accompanied by lower IRE1α-BIP interaction, and vice versa. The IRE1α-BIP interaction has been well studied, with two lumenal regions (residues 313-338, aka. loop, and residues 391-444, aka, tail) of IRE1α being known to be important for interaction with BIP. We generated IRE1α(LD)ΔΔ that had both the loop and the tail deletion (The deletion of these two regions reduced the ability of IRE1α to bind with BIP, similar to that was previously reported (Notably, the CALR-IRE1α(LD)ΔΔ binding level was reduced by BIP to a less extent compared to CALR-IRE1α(LD) (Considering that BIP is an ATPase, whether ATP regulates the competition between BIP and CALR in IRE1α interaction is an interesting question. We found that the addition of ATP increased the IRE1α(LD)-BIP interaction, but had no effect on the IRE1α(LD)-CALR interaction. In addition, BIP reduced the amount of CALR that bound to IRE1α(LD) more potently if ATP is added (Thus, ATP potentiates IRE1α-BIP interaction and favors BIP over CALR in IRE1α binding competition. So far, how CALR binds to IRE1α is unknown. To study this, we generated a series of truncated CALR mutants and examined their interactions with IRE1α(LD) (Fig. Mutants that contain the N domain could bind with IRE1α(LD), while N domain-deleted mutants could not. Interestingly, mutants that lack the C domain showed greater IRE1α-binding ability than full-length CALR (Such interaction is specific, as it was barely seen with GFP antibody pull-down, ruling out the possibility that C domain-truncation disrupted the global conformation of CALR and led to nonspecific interactions with other proteins (Furthermore, the N domain alone reduced IRE1α-BIP interaction more strongly than full-length CALR (Thus, the N domain is necessary and sufficient for CALR interacting with IRE1α, and the C domain may negatively regulate its interaction with IRE1α. CALR is a master protein that assists glycoprotein folding and quality control in the ER. IRE1α(LD) expressed in E. coli that lacks N-glycosylation can still be recognized by CALR. To further clarify whether the carbohydrate-binding capacity of CALR is necessary for its recognition of IRE1α, we replenished CALR -knockout (KO) cells with wild-type CALR or the CALR(Y92A) mutant that lacks the oligosaccharide moiety binding site. CALR KO elevated the amount of BIP that bound to IRE1α under both basal condition or prolonged intermediate conditions. Exogenously expressed CALR and CALR(Y92A) bound to IRE1α to a similar level under ER stress, and showed similar ability in repelling BIP (These results further demonstrate the competition relationship between BIP and CALR, and suggest that IRE1α is not a typical glycoprotein substrate of CALR.
title: Calcium-mediated calreticulin-IRE1α interaction drives dynamic fluctuation of IRE1α activity under chronic endoplasmic reticulum stress
section_title: CALR and BIP interact with IRE1α in a competitive way

text: The above results suggested a conformational change in CALR that may regulate the interaction between CALR and IRE1α. CALR is a calcium-binding protein and is regulated by calcium. Inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) showed that each purified CALR molecule bound with two Ca 2+ ions, whereas CALR(N) did not (Chelating Ca 2+ with EDTA altered the sedimentation coefficient of CALR, indicating a conformational change (Moreover, EDTA sensitized CALR to proteinase K digestion, suggesting that removal of Ca 2+ led to an “open” conformation of CALR, exposing the binding site for IRE1α (Notably, incubation with EDTA greatly enhanced IRE1α interaction with CALR but not CALR(N) (In addition, the equilibrium dissociation constant (Kd) of IRE1α-CALR interaction was greater than that of IRE1α-CALR(N) interaction, but was reduced by EDTA, further demonstrating that CALR had much weaker interaction with IRE1α than CALR(N), but could be strengthened by EDTA (Thus, IRE1α-CALR interaction is negatively regulated by calcium. On the contrary, addition of either Ca 2+ or EDTA did not alter the IRE1α-BIP interaction level, suggesting that such interaction is not sensitive to Ca 2+, although BIP is a Ca 2+ -binding protein (To further demonstrate that IRE1α-CALR interaction is regulated in a Ca 2+ -dependent manner, we generated CALR(DEL52), a disease-relevant mutant of CALR. With the loss of Ca 2+ -binding residues in the C-domain, this mutant has been shown to activate the IRE1α/XBP1 pathway and drive myeloproliferative neoplasms progression. Notably, CALR(DEL52) exhibited much higher ability in binding with IRE1α(LD) compared to CALR (Fig. We asked whether perturbation of calcium in the ER lumen could strengthen CALR-IRE1α interaction. A quick depletion of lumenal calcium with a low dose of Tg increased the amount of CALR that co-precipitated with IRE1α (This change happened so quickly that unfolded proteins in the ER had not increased (Next, we measured Ca 2+ concentration in the ER lumen ([Ca 2+ ] ER) under chronic intermediate ER stress. Remarkably, [Ca 2+ ] ER decreased at 8 h, partially recovered at 24 h, and then decreased again at 48 h, nicely correlated with the dynamic changes of IRE1α-BIP and IRE1α-CALR interactions (The [Ca 2+ ] ER fluctuation was also seen under Tg treatment at low dose, negatively correlated with XBP1 splicing ratio (Supplementary Fig. We did not see [Ca 2+ ] ER fluctuation in cells treated with higher concentration of Tg, consistent with the result that XBP1 splicing ratio did not recover (Supplementary Fig. These results suggested that fluctuation of [Ca 2+ ] ER could happen under prolonged ER stress, and may be one reason why BIP and CALR seesawed with each other in IRE1α binding.
title: Calcium-mediated calreticulin-IRE1α interaction drives dynamic fluctuation of IRE1α activity under chronic endoplasmic reticulum stress

text: Next, we investigated whether the fluctuation in IRE1α activity could be attributed to the competition between BIP and CALR that alternatively bind to IRE1α. The CALR-IRE1α interaction co-fluctuated with IRE1α phosphorylation and XBP1 splicing, suggesting that CALR promoted IRE1α activation. Indeed, knocking down CALR with shRNA compromised IRE1α phosphorylation and reduced the amount of XBP1s. This was more obvious during prolonged ER stress, as the recovery of IRE1α-XBP1 signal was abandoned in CALR-deleted cells at 48 h with Tm treatment. Importantly, replenishment of CALR restored the re-activation of IRE1α (CALR is important for IRE1α re-activation under both intermediate and severe ER stress (This does not require CALR’s glycan binding capacity, as CALR(Y92A) was also able to activate IRE1α (Fig. compare lanes 7 & 8 in Input samples). BIP is a known repressor of IRE1α, but whether it suppresses IRE1α activity during prolonged ER stress has not been tested. To study this, we transfected HeLa cells with a BIP-expressing vector at 24 h after Tm treatment, at which time the IRE1α signal had decreased but not yet resurged. We found that overexpression of BIP suppressed the re-activation of IRE1α as well as the re-induction of XBP1s expression (To further confirm this, we used BIX to induce BIP expression starting at 24 h during Tm treatment. Although BIX only slightly increased the BIP amount (possibly because the expression level of BIP had already been elevated during prolonged ER stress), it significantly suppressed the recovery of XBP1s at 48 h under both intermediate and severe ER stress (Taken together, CALR and BIP regulate IRE1α activity at opposite directions, and their switch in IRE1α binding contributes to the fluctuation of IRE1α signal intensities during prolonged ER stress.

text: We then investigated the physiological significance of IRE1α signal fluctuation under chronic ER stress. Inhibition of IRE1α, no matter starting at the beginning or at 24 h right before its re-activation, sensitized cells to intermediate ER stress, evidenced by increased levels of cell apoptosis and decreased mitochondrial membrane potential. This was even the case under severe ER stress, demonstrating that IRE1α protects cells from prolonged ER stress insult (Knockdown of CALR, consistent with its effect of suppressing IRE1α re-activation, enhanced caspase-3 cleavage, which was reduced again by CALR re-expression (In addition, CALR knockdown increased cell death, whereas re-expression of CALR reduced apoptosis under prolonged intermediate ER stress (Similarly, knocking out CALR also sensitized cells to intermediate ER stress, and CALR supplementation protected cells against apoptosis (Remarkably, re-expression of CALR(N), a mutant that retains IRE1α-binding capacity but lacks the P domain that binds function-specific chaperones, also suppressed ER stress-induced apoptosis, highlighting the importance of the anti-apoptosis effect of CALR-IRE1α interaction (Fig. K, L). text: Finally, we asked whether the fluctuation of CALR-IRE1α interaction intensities exists under physiological conditions in the mouse model. A basal roughly 12 hr period rhythmic activation of the IRE1α pathway has been reported in mouse liver, but with the driving force undetermined. Similarly, we observed an oscillation of IRE1α phosphorylation level in mouse liver, which peaked at zeitgeber time (ZT) 12 and remained low at ZT0 and ZT22 (Remarkably, the intensity of calreticulin-IRE1α interaction fluctuated keeping pace with IRE1α phosphorylation level, same as what happened in Tm-treated cells. text: Possessing both pro-adaptation and pro-death properties, the UPR needs to be tightly controlled so as to accommodate to a spectrum of ER stress intensities. This task is relatively easy when ER stress is either transient and mild, where adaptive UPR is taken, or long-lasting and severe, where terminal UPR will be ignited. In many cases, however, a threat of ER stress is chronic but non-lethal, posing a dilemma to the cell in making the life-and-death decision. In this study, we discovered that the IRE1α signal fluctuates under such circumstances. We think this may represent a transitional status of the cell, where cells struggle to combat long-term ER stress and meanwhile prepare to adjust to the upcoming stress (While IRE1α reactivation does not always succeed in protecting the cell from apoptosis, it signifies a meaningful attempt of the cell to survive under prolonged intermediate ER stress. Due to difficulties in long-time cell culture, we only observed the second activation phase of IRE1α in HeLa cells. However, we did see a third round of XBP1 splicing in MEF cells, indicating a continuous fluctuation of the IRE1α signal under prolonged ER stress. Compared to the basal level, the IRE1α-XBP1 signal remained partially activated during the deactivation phase, suggesting that under prolonged ER stress, the UPR was attenuated but not fully inactivated. It is possible that the remaining, partially activated UPR could be more readily to be re-activated, enabling prompt response and accommodation to alterations in ER stress conditions. In addition, partial activation of IRE1α may also be due to cellular heterogeneity. It would be interesting to monitor the UPR signals at single cellular level. Mechanistically, we discovered that CALR binds with IRE1α. Higher interaction level correlates with elevated IRE1α activity, suggesting that CALR promotes IRE1α activation. This was confirmed by CALR KO and overexpression. CALR and calnexin (CANX) are lectins that, together with PDIA3 (also known as ERp57), constitute the CALR/CANX cycle that assists the folding and quality control of glycoproteins. Interestingly, both CANX and PDIA3 had more interactions with IRE1α under intermediate ER stress at 48 h compared with 24 h, and CANX showed a similar pattern of IRE1α-binding fluctuation as CALR did under all of mild, intermediate, and severe ER stress (Fig. and Supplementary Fig.), raising the possibility that IRE1α acts as a glycoprotein substrate for CALR. However, this hypothesis needs to be taken with caution. We found that CALR could interact with recombinant IRE1α(LD) expressed in E. coli that does not produce glycoproteins, suggesting that IRE1α glycosylation, if there is, is not necessary for CALR binding. In addition, CALR(Y92A), which was unable to bind with oligosaccharides could still interact with IER1α. Furthermore, while both the N and P domains in CALR are thought to be involved in glycoprotein binding by recognizing the glucose moiety and recruiting ER chaperones (PDIA3, cyclophilin B, and ERp29), respectively, CALR(ΔP) that lacks the P domain interacted with IRE1α at a level similar to full-length CALR. Thus, CALR may bind with IRE1α and glycoprotein substrates in different ways. CALR has been shown to bind directly to non-glycosylated hydrophobic proteins and suppress their aggregation,. We postulate that under ER stress, the lumenal domain of IRE1α becomes partially unfolded, exposing hydrophobic residues to interact with CALR.
title: Calcium-mediated calreticulin-IRE1α interaction drives dynamic fluctuation of IRE1α activity under chronic endoplasmic reticulum stress

text: Thus, CALR may bind with IRE1α and glycoprotein substrates in different ways. CALR has been shown to bind directly to non-glycosylated hydrophobic proteins and suppress their aggregation,. We postulate that under ER stress, the lumenal domain of IRE1α becomes partially unfolded, exposing hydrophobic residues to interact with CALR. In such a scenario, CALR may act as a chaperone to prevent amorphous aggregation of IRE1α, paving the way for its oligomerization in a controlled manner. This could be the reason why CALR activates IRE1α. Both full-length CALR and CALR(N) exhibited anti-apoptosis function, suggesting that CALR can protect cells through activating IRE1α independent of its canonical role in the CALR/CANX cycle. To characterize the CALR binding site(s) on IRE1α and the conformational change of IRE1α upon CALR binding will help to better understand the mechanism by which CALR activates IRE1α, and how CALR competes with BIP to bind to IRE1α. CALR and BIP bind with IRE1α competitively. BIP is a well-known negative regulator of IRE1α, PERK, and ATF6 –. Its disassociation from IRE1α promotes IRE1α dimerization/oligomerization and activation. This can happen within minutes when cells encounter ER stress. We found that at 8 h of ER stress, the amount of CALR that co-precipitated with IRE1α increased, while the amount of IRE1α-interacting BIP did not decrease. This result indicates that (1) the dissociation of BIP is transient, accounting for the early stage of IRE1α activation well before 8 h, (2) CALR binding is able to activate IRE1α even if the basal level of BIP binding remains, and (3) basal-to-slightly-increased level of BIP-IRE1α interaction could co-exist with increased level of CALR-IRE1α interaction. Nevertheless, a dramatically increasing amount of BIP that interacted with IRE1α at 24 h repulsed CALR from IRE1α, and re-binding of CALR at 48 h dismissed excessive BIP from IRE1α, suggesting that simultaneous binding of a high amount of BIP and CALR to IRE1α is disallowed. Importantly, both BIP and CALR are highly expressed in cells, especially during prolonged ER stress, enabling their competition in IRE1α binding that may not be noticeable if any of them is of low concentration. Thus, besides BIP, CALR provides an additional layer of regulation on IRE1α activities throughout prolonged ER stress when the amount of IRE1α-bound BIP remains exceeding the basal level. Calcium adds another layer of IRE1α regulation through dictating CALR-IRE1α interaction. CALR bears a highly acidic C-terminal region that binds with Ca 2+ with high capacity. We found that depletion of Ca 2+ rendered IRE1α(LD) more sensitive to proteinase K digestion, and increased the IRE1α-binding capacity of CALR but not CALR(N). Since CALR(N) had higher IRE1α-binding capacity than full-length CALR, these results suggest that Ca 2+ -unbound CALR adopts an “open” conformation with the N domain more accessible to IRE1α than that in the Ca 2+ -bound form. Similarly, Ca 2+ has been shown to protect CALR from trypsin digestion. Another piece of evidence supporting Ca 2+ -regulated conformational change of CALR is that Ca 2+ depletion enhanced CALR oligomerization. Not only this, but both C-terminal region deletion and Ca 2+ depletion were able to enhance the binding of CALR to deglycosylated substrates (major histocompatibility complex class I heavy chains) and enhance CALR’s chaperone activity.

text: Similarly, Ca 2+ has been shown to protect CALR from trypsin digestion. Another piece of evidence supporting Ca 2+ -regulated conformational change of CALR is that Ca 2+ depletion enhanced CALR oligomerization. Not only this, but both C-terminal region deletion and Ca 2+ depletion were able to enhance the binding of CALR to deglycosylated substrates (major histocompatibility complex class I heavy chains) and enhance CALR’s chaperone activity. Taken together, we reckon that at normal [Ca 2+ ] ER, CALR prefers binding with glycoprotein substrates, adopting a conformation in which the C-terminal region hinders IRE1α interaction. When [Ca 2+ ] ER decreases, CALR undergoes a conformational change to expose the N domain that binds with IRE1α, acting as a chaperone to facilitate IRE1α oligomerization. Ca 2+ may mediate a role switch of CALR between the CALR/CANX cycle and UPR activation. [Ca 2+ ] ER –mediated regulation of IRE1α activity has its specialties. First, fast [Ca 2+ ] ER alteration enables quick binding of CALR to IRE1α. We observed increased amount of IRE1α-bound CALR under Tg treatment for 5 min, earlier than the unfolded protein increase in the ER. This could result in a quick activation of IRE1α if it is needed. Second, [Ca 2+ ] ER can change within a wide range, which could generate robust and complex signals. In contrast, protein-binding-mediated regulation of IRE1α depends on the ratio of protein concentration change. This could be efficient when the regulator proteins are at low concentrations. However, prolonged ER stress usually generates large amounts of BIP and unfolded proteins. Other ER-localized regulators of IRE1α, for example, CALR and previously reported PDIA1, PDIA6, and ERp47, among others, are usually highly expressed; thus, their concentration change ratios are normally subtle and may not be enough to influence IRE1α activity. On the other hand, many ER-resident IRE1α regulators, for example, BIP, PDIA1, and our newly discovered CALR, are Ca 2+ -bound proteins and have functions regulated by Ca 2+, –. In such a scenario, Ca 2+ -mediated UPR regulation is important and perhaps more efficient than alteration of protein concentrations of those UPR regulators. The same principle may also apply to post-translational modifications of IRE1α regulators, which have been shown to play important roles in IRE1α activation/deactivation, –. It is possible that Ca 2+ signal and post-translational modification drives IRE1α activation/deactivation, whereas chaperones and unfolded proteins buffer such alterations. Third, feedback regulation of [Ca 2+ ] ER can theoretically cause [Ca 2+ ] ER fluctuation that drives IRE1α signal fluctuation. When [Ca 2+ ] ER decreases, extracellular Ca 2+ flows into the cell to refill intracellular store and restore [Ca 2+ ] ER through store-operated calcium entry (SOCE). SOCE is tuned by [Ca 2+ ] ER, resulting in a negative feedback loop in [Ca 2+ ] ER regulation. IRE1α at the monomer status could interact with IP3R and render Ca 2+ release from the ER independent of IRE1α enzymatic activity. CALR binding at low [Ca 2+ ] ER may shut down this process so that [Ca 2+ ] ER can be recovered. Although the mechanism of [Ca 2+ ] ER fluctuation during prolonged ER stress is still unknown, this negative feedback is a theoretically possible reason, which deserves further investigation. Finally, while [Ca 2+ ] ER decrease activates IRE1α, [Ca 2+ ] ER elevation could also activate IRE1α.

text: IRE1α at the monomer status could interact with IP3R and render Ca 2+ release from the ER independent of IRE1α enzymatic activity. CALR binding at low [Ca 2+ ] ER may shut down this process so that [Ca 2+ ] ER can be recovered. Although the mechanism of [Ca 2+ ] ER fluctuation during prolonged ER stress is still unknown, this negative feedback is a theoretically possible reason, which deserves further investigation. Finally, while [Ca 2+ ] ER decrease activates IRE1α, [Ca 2+ ] ER elevation could also activate IRE1α. This is reported in a recent study where [Ca 2+ ] ER overload due to TMCO1 depletion led to BIP dissociation from IRE1α and IRE1α activation. It seems that the UPR is sensitive to [Ca 2+ ] ER alteration, and an appropriate range of [Ca 2+ ] ER should be kept to maintain a proper function of the ER. The unique high [Ca 2+ ] environment in the ER lumen, together with multiple Ca 2+ -binding chaperones, enables sophisticated regulation of the UPR signals via diverse mechanisms. Ca 2+ - and CALR-regulated IRE1α signal fluctuation that we discovered in cell culture with prolonged ER stress induced by Tm may also apply to animals under physiological conditions. Clock-controlled rhythmic lipid metabolism has been reported to cause a 12 h period rhythmic activation of IRE1α in mouse liver. Lipid bilayer stress can activate the UPR and can also induce ER calcium depletion –. Rhythmic lipid metabolism may possibly cause lipid bilayer stress, leading to [Ca 2+ ] ER fluctuation and consequent periodical IRE1α activation. We found that in mouse liver, CALR binds to IRE1α with a rhythmic pattern in concert with IRE1α phosphorylation. It will be interesting to see if [Ca 2+ ] ER also expresses a similar fluctuation in hepatocytes under basal conditions. Not only this, XBP1s-governed, circadian clock-independent rhythm of gene expression has been shown to regulate ER and mitochondria homeostasis in mouse liver, some of which is evolutionarily conserved in crustaceans and nematodes. It is possible that these gene expression rhythms are also regulated by [Ca 2+ ] ER signals and CALR-IRE1α interaction. So far, little is known about the temporal dynamics of the ER protein status and the UPR signals under conditions marked with UPR activation, for example, plasma cell differentiation, neuron degeneration, and tumor growth –. Dramatic alteration of proteome, extensive protein burden, and harsh external environment under these conditions could very likely induce long-term ER stress without causing immediate cell death. Switching between UPR-active and UPR-attenuated status could be an ideal strategy for cells to cope with such a dilemma, giving them more time to adjust themselves epi-genetically or genetically, and broadcast the stress signals bodywide. Finally, Ca 2+ - and CALR-regulated IRE1a signaling may also apply to physiological processes that relate to [Ca 2+ ] ER change, for example, insulin secretion, glucose transportation, and virus infection that happen in minute-to-hour scale, with repetitive stimulations and feedback that further generate long-term signal fluctuation. Further studies under physiological and pathophysiological conditions are needed.
