Further confirmation of such activation came from the demonstration of a moderate but significant increase in the Xbp1 spliced/unspliced ratio during the transition between PND25 and PND32 in obese female mice. The factor Xbp1 is first transcribed as an unspliced Xbp1-u isoform that, following ER stress activation, is transformed into the spliced Xbp1-s variant, which is active and contributes to the induction of UPR. Hence, this mRNA ratio is a proxy marker of enhanced IRE1α activity and serves as quantitative index of ER stress levels. Altogether, these mRNA changes point out the activation of ER stress in Kiss1 ARC neurons in conditions of obesity in pubertal mice, which is in line with the observed induction of some ER stress markers (e.g., p-PERK and its downstream, p-eIF2α) in the MBH of obese female rats with accelerated puberty. Interestingly, the changes in ER stress markers detected in Kiss1 ARC were not observed in Kiss1 AVPV neurons. This is congruent with the contention that Kiss1 neurons in the AVPV are likely less sensitive than Kiss1 ARC neurons to metabolic distress. Admittedly, the contribution of ER stress in other key neuronal populations, such as GnRH neurons, to obesity-induced pubertal acceleration cannot be discarded based on our data. In addition, given the correlative nature of our expression data, the effector mechanism whereby activation of ER stress in Kiss1 ARC neurons may lead to accelerated puberty is yet to be defined and warrants future investigation. Notably, maternal obesity has been reported to induce hypothalamic ER stress in the early postnatal period in the offspring, affecting the development of melanocortin circuits. Given the proven interplay between melanocortin (POMC) and Kiss1 ARC neurons in the metabolic control of puberty, it is plausible that at least part of the effects of hypothalamic ER stress activation on the Kiss1 system in conditions of early obesity may stem from perturbation of such POMC-Kiss1 neuronal interplay. Early obesity is a worrying condition linked to long-term adverse health outcomes, such as cardiometabolic, musculoskeletal, gynecological, and psychological disorders, as well as increased risk of some forms of cancers and reduced life expectancy. Hence, elucidation of the underlying mechanisms is mandatory in order to design more appropriate strategies for prevention and treatment. Together with previous data pointing out the hypothalamic roles of specific cell energy sensors and lipid mediators, such as ceramides, in conveying the effects of obesity on pubertal timing, our current study uncovers a previously unsuspected role of hypothalamic ER stress, which contributes to pubertal acceleration in conditions of obesity; a phenomenon which is centered mainly at the ARC and might involve, at least in part, Kiss1 neurons.

text: Female rat model of ON: A rat model of early overnutrition (ON) was generated by rearing female rats in small litters, containing four pups per dam, from PND1 until weaning at PND21. text: Statistical analyses were performed using Prism software (GraphPad Prism 9.0 for Macintosh, GraphPad Software, La Jolla, CA, www.graphpad.com). Data distribution was examined to ensure the selection of appropriate statistical methods. Normality tests were performed using the Shapiro–Wilk test. Student t test for parametric or Mann–Whitney for nonparametric data was used to compare the two groups. The differences between several groups were analyzed by One-way ANOVA followed by the Tukey multiple comparison test for parametric or Kruskal–Wallis test followed by Dunn’s multiple comparison test for nonparametric data. Two-way ANOVA followed by Sidak’s multiple comparisons test was performed to compare the influence of two different independent variables. A minimal group size of n = 7 animals per group was established (unless otherwise indicated for operational reasons), since these sample sizes should provide at least 80% power to detect effect sizes. For physiological experiments, group sizes usually exceeded this threshold. However, based on standard procedures, while phenotypic and hormonal analyses were applied to all available samples, more complex molecular and histological analyses were implemented in a representative subset of randomly assigned samples. Hormonal determinations were performed in duplicate with a minimal total number of 6 to 9 determinations per group, RNA analyses were performed in duplicate from at least five independent samples per group, and WB analysis was conducted in at least 5 to 6 samples per group. As general rule, no data were excluded from the analysis, unless in rare occasions when objective scientific (outlier identification based on Grubbs tests or statistical GraphPad Prism software) or animal welfare reasons demanded exclusions. Outliers are identified in data source files. All data are expressed as mean ± SEM; a P value <0.05 was considered statistically significant.

text: Copper is one of the essential trace elements and acts as a cofactor in various key enzymes, including electron transport chain complex IV, Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase, ceruloplasmin, and dopamine monooxygenase. Therefore, copper plays a crucial role in various physiological processes in the body, including mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, oxidative stress, apoptosis, and cell survival. Copper absorption primarily occurs in the duodenum and small intestine, with the liver serving as the main storage site. Excess copper is predominantly excreted through bile and eventually eliminated via feces. A portion of copper is secreted into the gastrointestinal tract, and a small amount is excreted through urine. Copper maintains a dynamic equilibrium throughout its absorption, transport, and excretion processes, a balance known as copper homeostasis. The intracellular copper level should be maintained within an appropriate range, both copper deficiency and copper overload can result in cellular damage. An expanding body of research suggests that imbalance in copper homeostasis is associated with the onset and progression of various diseases. Copper deficiency can impair the activity of essential metalloenzymes, leading to cellular dysfunction and the onset of diseases such as Menkes disease, anemia, and cardiovascular disorders. Excessive accumulation of copper in the body can lead to various diseases, such as Wilson’s disease, neurodegenerative disorders, cardiovascular diseases, kidney diseases, and cancer. The kidney is recognized as a crucial target organ for copper accumulation. Numerous studies have shown that copper can instigate nephrotoxicity through inducing a series of programmed cell death, oxidative damage, energy deficiency and metabolic disorders. However, research on the pathological mechanisms of copper in various kidney diseases is still in its early stages. We mainly focus on the kidney diseases: acute kidney injury (AKI), chronic kidney disease (CKD) and diabetic kidney disease (DKD). Epidemiologic studies show that about 13 million people worldwide suffer from AKI each year. Due to its high incidence and poor prognosis, it has gradually become a hot topic of current research. The global prevalence of CKD is 9.1%, and it is expected that by 2040 it will become the fifth leading cause of death worldwide. Diabetes is one of the most common causes of CKD, with DKD being a form of CKD. The International Diabetes Federation estimates that by 2035, there will be 592 million diabetic patients worldwide and DKD is an important complication in diabetic patients, manifesting early clinical symptoms of proteinuria. As the disease progresses, renal failure and uremia develop, and dialysis becomes necessary for treatment. The multifaceted pathogenesis of renal disease involves various triggering factors, and currently, there is no specific clinical intervention. Therefore, the development of novel therapeutic targets for kidney diseases is particularly crucial. This review centers on exploring the relationship between the development of kidney diseases and copper homeostasis and summarizing the connections between them. In addition, we delve into the potential mechanisms linking copper to the progression of kidney diseases in terms of several common cell death, aiming to enhance our understanding of kidney diseases pathogenesis. In addition, therapeutic drugs that can reduce copper-induced nephrotoxicity are summarized and offer novel insights for the treatment of kidney diseases.
title: Copper-instigated modulatory cell mortality mechanisms and progress in kidney diseases

text: Extracellular copper ions are present in the small intestine as divalent copper ions. Cu 2+ cannot be absorbed directly by intestinal cells and needs to be reduced to Cu + by the six-transmembrane epithelial antigen of prostate (STEAP) family members, a group of metal reductases. Cu + is primarily transported into the cell through solute carrier family 31 member 1/copper transporter 1 (SLC31A1/CTR1) and solute carrier family 31 member 2/copper transporter 2 (SLC31A2/CTR2). In addition, under copper overload, Cu 2+ enters the cytoplasm via a nonspecific divalent metal transporter 1(DMT1).

text: When copper enters the cell, it is immediately bound by copper chaperone proteins or non-protein ligands such as glutathione (GSH) and other non-protein anionic copper ligands (CuL), which are assembled into functional proteins that mediate different cellular processes. Metallothionein (MT) is a family of low molecular weight protein that binds intracellular copper via sulfhydryl (SH) in cysteine residues. Intracellularly, GSH binds to copper ions through its sulfhydryl to form stable GSH-Cu complexes. Besides, in the cytoplasm, after copper binds to CuL, it needs to be triggered by solute carrier family 25 member 3 (SLC25A3) for its transport to the mitochondrial matrix, where copper is stored in its ligand-bound form, and stromal copper can be transported from the mitochondrial matrix to the intermembrane space of mitochondria (IMS), but the pathway remains unclear. When copper is conveyed to IMS, it has the potential to engage with numerous copper enzymes, about one-fourth of them being employed by the mitochondrial most crucial copper enzyme, cytochrome c oxidase (CcO). As the terminal enzyme of the mitochondrial respiratory chain, CcO is responsible for transferring electrons from cytochrome C to molecular oxygen while pumping protons from the matrix to the IMS, generating a proton gradient essential for fueling mitochondrial adenosine triphosphate (ATP) synthesis. The transportation of copper to CcO involves a sophisticated process facilitated by copper chaperone proteins. These proteins can be broadly classified into two types, distinguished by their roles in the function of the CcO assembly factors: (1) Copper-metal chaperone proteins: e.g. cytochrome C oxidase assembly protein: COX17, COX11 and SCO1, which directly bind and deliver copper through specific protein-protein interactions. The transport of copper ions to CcO relies predominantly on COX17. After forming coordination with Cys residues in COX17, copper is subsequently transferred to SCO1, SCO2 and COX11. SCO1/SCO2 facilitate the incorporation of copper into the Cu A site of COX2 in CcO, while COX11 is responsible for delivering copper to the Cu B site of COX1 in CcO. (2) Cofactors: such as cytochrome oxidase assembly factor 6 (COA6) and SCO2, which do not transfer copper per se but facilitate the process. Copper chaperone proteins bind copper because their cysteines exist in a reduced form, allowing them to effectively bind with copper ions. This function is provided by SCO2 and COA6, which have been shown to function as disulfide bond reductases of the SCO1 and COX2. Another important copper enzyme in mitochondria is superoxide dismutase (SOD). SOD2 is the major superoxide dismutase in the mitochondrial matrix, but SOD1 is essential for controlling oxidative stress in the IMS. Copper chaperone for superoxide dismutase (CCS) can bind to copper and is a key mediator of Cu + binding in SOD1. On one hand, following the transportation of copper to the cytoplasm by CTR1, CCS facilitates the transfer of copper to SOD1 in the cytoplasm. On the other hand, 5–10% SOD1 enters IMS by crossing the outer membrane of mitochondria, where it plays a role in neutralizing superoxide generated by the mitochondrial respiratory chain. Research indicates that CCS has the ability to control the allocation of SOD1 between the IMS and cytoplasm, thereby maintaining the stability of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in vivo.

text: Since the consumption of copper in the diet (about 1 mg copper per day) is much less than the renewal of copper in our bodies (a few milligrams copper), the primary regulatory mechanism for copper homeostasis is through the excretion of copper rather than its absorption. When copper enters the cell via CTR1, copper is transported by the copper chaperone gene antioxidant 1 (ATOX1) to the ATPase copper transporting polypeptide 1(ATP7A) and ATPase copper transporting beta polypeptide (ATP7B) located at the trans-Golgi network (TGN) or the plasma membrane, which expel the copper to the external of the cell. ATP7A, widely found in various tissues, transports copper to the extracellular matrix. Upon entering the bloodstream, copper binds to α2- macroglobulin, albumin and other ligands, then gets transported to the liver; whereas ATP7B moves copper out of hepatocytes and directs it into the bile, ultimately leading to its excretion from the body. It has been found that urinary copper excretion is increased by small copper carriers (SCC) in the blood in a mouse model lacking ATP7A. SCC is secreted into the blood (possibly by liver and intestinal cells) and the bloodstream filters them into the urine, thus providing an alternative method of excreting excess copper. In addition, a recent study has shown that the lysosomal copper transporter protein SLC46A3 can regulate intracellular copper level by chelating copper into lysosomes, suggesting a new copper-regulated pathway in cell.
title: Copper-instigated modulatory cell mortality mechanisms and progress in kidney diseases

text: Copper plays a vital role as a trace element within biological systems, sustaining the function of intracellular metalloenzymes and consequently influencing cellular activity. However, excessive copper can induce oxidative stress damage in cells through the Fenton reaction and by promoting the production of hydroxyl radicals, leading to cellular DNA double-strand breaks, cell cycle arrest, mitochondrial dysfunction, lipid peroxidation, and protein modification. Consequently, a range of programmed cell death pathways is activated, including apoptosis, paraptosis, pyroptosis, ferroptosis, cuproptosis, autophagy and necroptosis. visually summarizes the connection between copper and programmed cell death.
title: Copper-instigated modulatory cell mortality mechanisms and progress in kidney diseases

text: Apoptosis is a form of programmed cell death that is highly regulated in metabolic processes. It is distinguished by chromatin condensation, DNA cleavage and apoptotic vesicle morphology. The mechanisms of apoptosis are complex and are mainly divided into endogenous and exogenous pathways. The apoptotic exogenous pathways comprise two mechanisms: the Fas Ligand (FasL)/Fas receptor (FasR) model and the tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α)/TNF receptors 1 (TNFR1) model. In these pathways, FasL binds to FasR and TNF α bind to TNFR1, leading to the recruitment of Fas-associated via death domain (FADD) for the binding with caspase-8. Once caspase-8 is activated, the subsequent activation of downstream effectors, namely caspase-3 and caspase-7, initiates the terminal phase of apoptosis. The endogenous pathway is a mitochondrial pathway initiated by mitochondrial damage signals, such as those induced by DNA damage, hypoxia and metabolic disorders. The BH3 protein undergoes upregulation, attaching to the anti-apoptotic protein BCL-2, resulting in the liberation of BAX and BAK, thereby augmenting the permeability of the mitochondrial outer membrane. Consequently, cytochrome c or apoptosis-inducing factor (AIF) is released. These proapoptotic factors play a pivotal role in activating the caspase cascade, ultimately causing the cleavage of numerous proteins and culminating in the induction of apoptosis. P53 is another important apoptotic regulator transcribed and P53 activation increases BAX expression, leading to the increase of the mitochondrial permeability. Excess copper ions can induce apoptosis through several mechanisms. Firstly, copper engages in the Fenton reaction, producing ROS. ROS disrupts mitochondrial function and triggers endogenous pathway, leading to the initiation of apoptosis. Secondly, it was discovered that copper has the capability to enhance the expression of P53, leading to apoptosis. Moreover, numerous research studies have indicated that the accumulation of copper within the nucleus can bind the DNA, causing DNA damage and subsequently triggering apoptosis. Similarly, copper enzymes, copper transporter proteins, and copper chaperone proteins (e.g. ATP7A, ATP7B, and CCS) strictly regulate intracellular copper homeostasis. Dysregulation of these proteins may lead to aberrant intracellular copper distribution, thereby affecting apoptotic signaling pathways. For example, ATP7B mutation, such as those found in Wilson’s disease, results in the accumulation of copper in the liver and brain, leading to cell death and tissue damage. In addition, copper can inactivate proteasome subunits, such as copper can inhibit 20S proteasome or 19S proteasome deubiquitinase activity. The ubiquitin-proteasome system is an important intracellular protein degradation system that promotes apoptosis by targeting apoptosis inhibitory factors. Therefore, copper provides a new strategy for tumor therapy by inhibiting the ubiquitin-proteasome system.
title: Copper-instigated modulatory cell mortality mechanisms and progress in kidney diseases

text: In 2000, Sperandio et al. identified a death phenotype distinct from apoptosis, which does not rely on the activation of caspase, defined as paraptosis. Paraptosis is characterized by cytoplasmic vacuolization, swelling of the endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria and a lack of apoptotic features (for example, the formation of apoptotic bodies). When endoplasmic reticulum stress occurs, the endoplasmic reticulum is unable to absorb cytoplasmic Ca 2+, resulting in a deficiency of Ca 2+, causing the accumulation of misfolded proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum lumen, leading to the swelling of the endoplasmic reticulum, inducing intracellular Ca2+ imbalance. And then, excessive accumulation of Ca 2+ in mitochondria results in mitochondrial swelling, causing the uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation and disruptions in metabolic processes. Recently, Ca 2+ depletion in the endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondrial Ca 2+ overload have been shown to play key roles in apoptosis induced by a variety of natural products and Chemicals, such as curcumin, raffinose, hesperidin, morusin, Oligomer procyanidins and others. Furthermore, the initiation of paraptosis can be triggered by the activation of mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPK), disturbances in protein homeostasis, disruptions in ion level and oxidative stress. Therefore, paraptosis-inducing signals are nonspecific. Recently, it has been discovered that copper complexes can induce paraptosis in vitro, and the mechanism is that copper complexes can inhibit proteasome activity. This inhibition results in the buildup of unfolded proteins and cause functional impairment in the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway, which triggers endoplasmic reticulum stress and swelling, ultimately leading to paraptosis. Besides, copper acts as a caspase-3 inhibitor, forcing the cell into caspase-independent paraptosis. Copper-induced paraptosis offers new potential approaches for anti- tumor therapy.
title: Copper-instigated modulatory cell mortality mechanisms and progress in kidney diseases

text: Pyroptosis is a form of programmed cell death, characterized by persistent cell swelling, leading to eventual rupture of the cell membrane, accompanied by the activation of inflammasome and the release of inflammatory factors such as interleukin IL-1β and IL-18. The pathway of pyroptosis has traditionally been divided into a classical pathway activated by caspase-1 and a non-classical pathway activated by caspase −4/5. Classical pathway suggests that infection and other signals induce the formation of NLR family pyrin domain containing 3 (NLRP3), and NLRP3 activates caspases, which break down gasdermin D (GSDMD) into a C-terminal inhibitory domain and an N-terminal effector domain. The N-terminal of GSDMD is highly aggregated and is able to bind membrane lipids, leading to changes in cellular osmotic pressure, ultimately resulting in the rupture of the cell membrane. In the non-classical pathway, caspase-4/5 can be activated by intracellular LPS, leading to cleavage of GSDMD, promoting pyroptosis. Some studies have demonstrated that copper is the key factor in NLRP3 inflammasome assembly and subsequent activation of pyroptosis. Copper-induced ROS production may also lead to pyroptosis. Research indicates that exposure to copper increases the expression of caspase-1 and genes associated with pyroptosis, including IL-1β, GSDMD and caspase-1, and induces NLRP3 inflammasomes activation through multiple cascade pathway.
title: Copper-instigated modulatory cell mortality mechanisms and progress in kidney diseases

text: Ferroptosis is the oxidation of polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA) on lipid membranes by reactive oxygen species in cells in the presence of iron to produce lipid peroxides, causing membrane damage and cell death. Ferroptosis can be divided into endogenous and exogenous pathways. The exogenous pathway is mediated by the inhibition of cell membrane transport proteins such as cystine/glutamate reverse transporter protein (System xc-), System xc- constitutes a vital intracellular antioxidant system, comprising two subunits, SLC7A11 and SLC3A2, which transports glutamate out of the cell and cystine into the cell, facilitating subsequent synthesis of glutathione, a substrate for a variety of enzymes that scavenge ROS and an essential cofactor for glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4). GPX4 is capable of concomitantly transforming reduced GSH into oxidized GSH (GSSG) while concurrently diminishing lipid peroxidation and suppressing ferroptosis. Endogenous pathways include the ferroptosis suppressor protein 1(FSP1)/Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) pathway. CoQ10 is an important substrate of FSP1 that prevents lipid and protein peroxidation. FSP1 catalyzes the regeneration of CoQ10 via NADPH reductase and reduces the generation of ROS, thus inhibiting cells from undergoing ferroptosis. Beyond the pathway mentioned above, one is the GTP cyclohydrolase-1 (GCH1)/5,6,7,8-tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4)/dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) pathway: Kraft et al. used a genetic screen revealed that GCH1 and BH4 are specific for inhibiting ferroptosis and are not dependent on GPX4 signaling pathway. It was found that GCH1 expression in cell promotes the biosynthesis of BH4, which pairs with dihydrobiopterin (BH2) to form a redox cycle to reduce endogenous oxidative free radicals and protect lipid membranes, thereby inhibiting ferroptosis, and dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) controls BH4 production. The other pathway involves dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH)/dihydroubiquione (CoQH2), with DHODH situated in the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM), catalyzing the ubiquitin-mediated oxidation of dihydroorotate (DHO) to orotate (OA), which linked to the reduction of CoQ to CoQH2, reducing the oxidative stress and thus inhibiting ferroptosis. Although previous studies have shown that iron is the only metal that induces ferroptosis, there is growing evidence showing that copper can promote ferroptosis under certain circumstances. A study found that the copper ion carrier elesclomol promotes ferroptosis. Elesclomol can stimulate the breakdown of ATP7A, leading to an elevation in cellular copper level. However, ATP7A safeguards SLC7A11 against degradation. Therefore, the degradation of ATP7A triggered by elesclomol can lead to downregulation of SLC7A11, which reduces intracellular transport of cysteine, inhibits GSH synthesis, promotes oxidative stress and further induces ferroptosis. In addition, Cu 2+ was found to bind directly to the C107 and C148 cysteine residues of the GPX4 protein, inducing GPX4 protein aggregation. The autophagy receptor Tax1 binding protein 1 (TAX1BP1) identified and targeted the aggregates, leading to their degradation through the autophagy pathway, ultimately resulting in ferroptosis. In addition, intracellular copper can stabilize hypoxia-inducible factor 1 subunit α (HIF-1α) protein by inhibiting prolyl hydroxylase (PHD) in hepatocellular carcinoma cells and upregulate lipid metabolism-related genes to inhibit ferroptosis.
title: Copper-instigated modulatory cell mortality mechanisms and progress in kidney diseases

text: When excess Cu 2+ enters the cell, it is translocated into the mitochondria and reduced to Cu +. Tsvetkov et al. discovered that none of the cell death inhibitors using apoptosis, necroptosis, and ROS prevented Cu from continuing to induce cell death, naming it cuproptosis, a new type of programmed cell death. Excessive intracellular copper induces aggregation of dihydrolipoctamide S-acetyltransferase (DLAT), which is associated with the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, leading to proteotoxic stress and further inducing cell death. Copper-induced death involves the process of protein lipoicylation, a lysine post-translational modification that occurs in four metabolic enzymes: pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH), α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (KDH), branched chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase (BCKDH), and glycine cleavage system (GCS). These enzymes are directly or indirectly involved in the TCA, and when combined with copper ions, they cause thioctylated protein aggregation, which hinders the TCA; the subsequent loss of iron-sulfur cluster proteins leads to metabolic dysfunction in the mitochondria, proteotoxic stress, and ultimately, cell death. The loss of iron-sulfur cluster proteins leads to mitochondrial metabolic dysfunction, proteotoxic stress and ultimately cell death. Ferredoxin 1 (FDX1), a core regulatory gene for copper-induced cell death, has a strong reducing ability to reduce Cu 2+ to the more toxic form Cu +, and lipoylates four specific enzymes in mitochondria, such as: DLAT, dihydrolipoctamide S-succinyltransferase (DLST), glycine cleavage system protein H (GCSH) and dihydrolipoctamide branched chain transacylase E2 (DBT), which inhibits mitochondrial respiration and causes proteotoxic stress, ultimately leading to cell death.
title: Copper-instigated modulatory cell mortality mechanisms and progress in kidney diseases

text: Autophagy reduces reactive oxygen species and removes damaged, denatured or senescent proteins and organelles from the cell. Under the regulation of autophagy associated gene (ATG), the outer membrane of autophagosome is fused with lysosome, which digests and degrades it. Autophagy plays an important role in maintaining intracellular homeostasis and synthesis, degradation and recycling of cellular products; however, excessive autophagy may lead to the degradation of cellular components and even cause cell death. Mechanistic targets for initiating cellular autophagy include activation of adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK) or inhibition of mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR). When cellular energy metabolism is impaired, ATP level is low, AMPK can be phosphorylated, and then phosphorylated AMPK (p-AMPK) can phosphorylate mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1), unc-51-like kinase 1 (ULK1), type III phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase-vacuolar protein-sorting 34 (PIK3C3/VPS34) and Beclin 1 (BECN1) to promote autophagy. mTORC1 inhibits autophagy by directly phosphorylating ULK1 to inhibit AMPK-ULK1 interactions. Under pathological conditions, such as energy deficiency and metabolic disorders, mTOR activity can be inhibited. Inhibition of mTOR activity reduces energy expenditure and activates autophagy. Studies have shown that there is a complex and tight connection between cellular energy level and autophagy. Autophagy can be triggered by various stress states, such as oxidative stress, metabolic disorders and starvation. Copper can produce ROS, causing ROS accumulation, oxidative damage and apoptosis. Copper can cause autophagy by increasing the expression of ATG, sequestosome 1 (SQSTM1) and microtubule associated protein 1 light chain 3 (MAP1LC3), affecting the AMPK-mTOR pathway, or inducing oxidative stress. In addition, studies have clarified that copper can trigger the autophagic response by affecting mTOR activity. Further studies have revealed that excess copper causes disturbances in intracellular energy metabolism, autophagy can occur via the AMPK-mTOR pathway, leading to kidney injury in broiler chickens.
title: Copper-instigated modulatory cell mortality mechanisms and progress in kidney diseases

text: Necroptosis is a regulated form of necrosis, characterized by swelling of organelles, rupture of cell membranes, and breakdown of cytoplasm and nuclei. The necroptosis process is initiated by the activation of cell surface death receptors (e.g. ttumor necrosis factor receptor 1 (TNFR1), interferon receptor (IFNR), Toll-like receptors (TLRs), RIG-like receptors (RLRs) and FasRs), and is critically dependent on the phosphorylation of mixed spectrum kinase structural domain-like Proteins (MLKLs) by receptor interacting kinase-1 (RIPK1) and RIPK3. Tumor necrosis factor receptor-associated death structural domain (TRADD), tumor necrosis factor receptor-associated factor 2 (TRAF2), apoptosis inhibitory protein 1 (cIAP1), and cIAP2 are the components of complex I, which is quickly formed by TNFR. cIAP1/2 ubiquitinates RIPK1, which can activate NF-κB and promote the expression of anti-apoptotic proteins; complex I becomes cytoplasmic complex II when NF-κB is inhibited by Smac mimics, where FADD and caspase-8 are drawn in, and caspase-8 is activated to induce apoptosis. If caspase-8 or FADD is destroyed, RIPK1 phosphorylates and activates RIPK3, and activated RIPK3 phosphorylates the MLKL, which breaks the integrity of the plasma membrane, leading to cell swelling and cell lysis. Autophagy and necroptosis interact with each other, in a recent study, copper was shown to activate ULK1 to phosphorylate RIPK1, inhibiting RIPK1-mediated cell death. In addition, the autophagy protein ATG16L1 was shown to protect intestinal epithelial cells from necroptosis by blocking the RIPK1, RIPK3 or MLKL.
title: Copper-instigated modulatory cell mortality mechanisms and progress in kidney diseases

text: The content of copper in the body mainly depends on the dynamic balance between small intestine absorption and bile excretion, and the kidney is one of the pathways for copper excretion. When the body is exposed to high level of copper, the function of kidney cells is impaired, leading to kidney damage. As mentioned above, numerous studies have shown that excess copper can trigger cell death. The mechanism of copper-induced nephrotoxicity is still not well studied, and the exploration of the mechanism of copper in AKI, CKD, DKD and other renal diseases provides guidance for the treatment of renal diseases.
title: Copper-instigated modulatory cell mortality mechanisms and progress in kidney diseases

text: The renal tubular epithelium is the main target of copper-induced kidney injury, according to earlier research. Copper accumulation in renal tissues can lead to inflammatory damage and oxidative stress in renal tubular epithelial cells. Copper has been shown to overexpress caspase-3, downregulate Bcl-2, and activate the NF-κB signaling pathway, which promotes inflammation, oxidative stress and apoptosis, resulting in kidney injury. Copper-induced renal injury involves a variety of mechanisms and the mitochondrial dysfunction may be one of the main causes of renal tubular injury. It was shown that copper exposure induced BNIP3/NIX dependent mitochondrial autophagy in renal tubular epithelial cell, and inhibition of ­mitochondrial autophagy aggravated copper-induced mitochondrial dysfunction, causing ATP production is reduced and oxidative phosphorylation is impaired, leading to damage to cell. Additionally, as copper concentration increased in kidney, the mRNA levels of mitochondrial function-related genes COX4, sirtuin1 (SIRT1), mitofusin 2 (MFN2) and optic atrophy 1 (OPA1) were decreased, resulting in mitochondrial dysfunction, and ultimately causing kidney injury. Research has found that in cisplatin induced acute kidney injury, SLC31A1 is activated, causing an imbalance in intracellular copper homeostasis, leading to mitochondrial dysfunction, inducing cuproptosis, and exacerbating kidney injury. Therefore, urinary copper can be utilized as a novel biomarker for early acute kidney injury detection, according to Gardner et al.’s conclusion. Moreover, targeting copper transporters to reduce copper accumulation in the body may become a potential therapeutic target for AKI.
title: Copper-instigated modulatory cell mortality mechanisms and progress in kidney diseases

text: Around 9.1% of people worldwide currently have CKD, and this number is rising quickly. A typical progression from CKD to end-stage renal disease is renal fibrosis. Diabetes, high blood pressure and environmental pollution have been linked to the onset and development of CKD, while the exact cause of the disease is still unclear. A growing number of studies have shown the connection between the accumulation of copper and fibrosis. A cross-sectional study demonstrated that copper exposure was significantly associated with the prevalence of CKD. Elevated blood copper level can lead to a decrease in glomerular filtration rate, further impairing renal function and accelerating the progression of CKD. Niu et al. firstly explored the potential mechanism of copper in renal fibrosis and discovered that Smad transcription factors (Smad2/3) phosphorylation was induced by TGF-β, a major factor in renal fibrosis. The phosphorylated Smad2/3 was then transferred to the nucleus and directly bound to the promoter of CTR1, increasing intracellular accumulation of copper. And then, the copper activated lysyl oxidase (LOX), increasing the cross-linking of collagen and elastin and promoting renal cellular damage. The team later demonstrated again that COX17 improves mitochondrial function by maintaining mitochondrial copper homeostasis to restore complex IV activity, thereby ameliorating renal fibrosis. Moreover, excessive copper can cause mitochondrial oxidative stress, induce autophagy and apoptosis, cause renal cell damage, produce nephrotoxicity, and gradually progress to CKD. In addition, it was found that using copper chelators to inhibit the expression of copper transporter proteins and LOX may be a potential way to attenuate renal fibrosis.
title: Copper-instigated modulatory cell mortality mechanisms and progress in kidney diseases

text: The number of patient with CKD is estimated to reach 700 million globally, with 20–40% of these being caused by DKD. DKD carries a risk of cardiovascular events and it may finally lead to end-stage renal disease. Reducing cardiovascular events, increasing patient survival, and improving quality of life all depend on early prevention and diagnosis as well as slowing down the progression of DKD. Some studies conclude that there is a strong correlation between copper level and the diabetes. On the one hand, copper has a significant impact on copper and zinc SOD activity and is closely correlated with zinc level. For the regulation of oxidative/antioxidant balance, these two micronutrients must be in balance, and an increased serum Cu/Zn ratio speeds up the development of DKD. On the other hand, insulin resistance can result from copper shortage because copper has the capacity to activate insulin signaling. Moreover, copper shortage reduces insulin level because copper inhibits the activity of the insulin-degrading enzyme (IDE). And then, an excessive amount of copper promotes the generation of ROS, which raises oxidative stress and eventually results in diabetes. Moreover, intracellular copper accumulation may activate transcription factor 3 (ATF3) and proto-oncogene (SPI1), thereby promoting the upregulation of SLC31A1 and inducing cuproptosis. Furthermore, more and more studies have found that patients with DKD had higher serum copper level and higher urine copper excretion. The extent of urinary copper excretion is associated with different stages of DKD. Patients who have severe proteinuria have greater urinary copper/ceruloplasmin and copper/albumin ratios, which decrease as renal disease develops. However, a clinical study found no difference in serum copper level between DKD patients and the healthy control group. Therefore, the correlation between blood copper level and DKD still needs to be verified.
title: Copper-instigated modulatory cell mortality mechanisms and progress in kidney diseases

text: Copper chelators mainly bind excess copper in the body, reducing the accumulation of copper in kidney and thus reducing the damage of copper to kidney cells. Copper ­chelators commonly used in clinical and experimental settings include triethylenetetramine (TETA), ammonium tetrathiomolybdate (TM), ethylene diamine tetraacetic acid (EDTA) and clioquinol (CQ). At first, when penicillamine was intolerable to patients with Wilson’s illness, TETA was used as a second-line treatment option. TETA has the potential to bind surplus copper in tissues, thereby diminishing oxidative stress and cellular damage and may ameliorate diabetic renal fibrosis by inhibiting TGF- β/Smad4 signaling. A recent study revealed that TETA increased the enzymatic activity of the mitochondrial copper enzymes CcO and SOD1, maintained the expression of the copper chaperone proteins COX17, COX11 and CCS, and restored the expression of the mitochondrial regulator of biogenesis, peroxisome proliferator- activated receptor γ coactivator 1-alpha (PGC-1α) expression, thereby contributing to the maintenance of cellular homeostasis through the regulation of copper homeostasis. Moreover, TM can mitigate organ damage associated with ischemia-reperfusion by lowering copper level and reducing mitochondrial oxidative stress. According to recent research, TM protects against cisplatin-induced AKI by activating the Nrf2 pathway in renal tubular epithelial cells and reducing oxidative stress. EDTA chelates with metals and is able to reduce vascular toxic metal load, which may reduce endothelial dysfunction, ROS and atherosclerosis. In addition, it has been demonstrated in animal models that copper chelators, including disulfiram (DSF), TM, and CQ reduce LOX, leading to reduced collagen deposition and protecting the kidney from progressive kidney injury and fibrosis.
title: Copper-instigated modulatory cell mortality mechanisms and progress in kidney diseases

text: In addition to copper chelators, which inhibit copper-induced oxidative stress, studies have found that there are other plant extracts play a similar role. Many chemicals found in sage, including as rosmarinic acid, silymarinic acid, and silybinol, have anti-inflammatory and antioxidant qualities. These compounds may help reduce inflammation and oxidative stress. Houcine et al. found that sage might protect against copper-induced damage in mouse liver and kidney through its antioxidant characteristics and by lowering the production of pro-inflammatory factors and inhibiting the reduction in the activities of SOD, catalase (CAT) and acetylcholinesterase (AChE)-related enzymes. The ethanolic extracts of vernonia amygdalina plant, a small shrub that grows mainly in tropical Africa, were found to ameliorate copper-induced damage to the liver and kidney through an effective antioxidant mechanism. Cinnamon, belonging to the camphoraceae family, is a plant frequently employed in traditional medicine, showcasing a diverse range of bioactive impacts. Its high polyphenol content gives it the title of a natural antioxidant with ROS scavenging and metal chelating effects, which may attenuate copper-induced nephrotoxicity. In addition to its antioxidant activity, cinnamon has other pharmacological effects such as anticancer, hypotensive, antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, insecticidal and cholesterol lowering. In summary, the aforementioned drugs inhibit copper-induced oxidative stress, thus preventing copper-induced cell damage, though their precise mechanisms of action remain unclear. However, research indicates that curcumin activates the Nrf2/HO-1 pathway, suppressing oxidative stress and apoptosis, and protect against copper-induced nephrotoxicity. Furthermore, probiotics, a microorganism that promotes host health by regulating the balance of intestinal flora. In past studies, probiotics have been found to bind and remove heavy metals from the body such as cadmium and lead. A recent study found that probiotics provide nephroprotection against copper sulfate induced nephrotoxicity in broiler chickens by modulating oxidative stress, inflammation, and apoptosis.
title: Copper-instigated modulatory cell mortality mechanisms and progress in kidney diseases

text: The mitochondria serve as the energy center of the cell and is also the main storage site of copper in the cell. Excessive or insufficient copper concentrations can have a negative effect on the cell, making it crucial to maintain copper homeostasis. So far, research has shown a strong connection between programmed cell death and copper metabolism. This review summarizes the mechanisms by which copper mediates different cell death through the activation of various signaling pathways and illustrates the current state of research on copper homeostasis and common kidney diseases. In general, the role of copper homeostasis in kidney disease is one of the current research hotspots, and as an important pathogenesis of kidney disease, studying the role of copper metabolic balance in kidney disease is a new direction to study the pathogenesis of kidney disease. With the continuous development of copper chelators and other drugs in the treatment of kidney diseases, it is expected to become an adjuvant treatment for kidney diseases in the future.
title: Copper-instigated modulatory cell mortality mechanisms and progress in kidney diseases

text: Breast cancer is the most common cancer among women with the five-year survival rate for breast cancer approaching 90%. As patients with breast cancer are living longer, the long-term complications associated with treatment and surgery are increasingly becoming evident. 19.5% to 21.8% of breast cancer survivors experience persistent moderate to severe pain. Compared with their pain-free counterparts, breast cancer survivors dealing with chronic pain report significantly worse scores on assessments of mental health, social functioning, and vitality. Prevalence of post-breast cancer pain has a substantial impact on daily activities and overall quality of life. Addressing these issues is crucial for improving the long-term well-being of breast cancer survivors. Cancer pain arises not only from the direct effects of tumors but also as a consequence of surgical and pharmacological interventions. Effective pain management remains a critical component of cancer care, as it directly impacts patients’ quality of life. Among analgesics, opioids have received particular attention due to their dual role in pain control and potential effects on tumor behavior. Several preclinical and retrospective clinical studies have reported an association between perioperative opioid administration, perioperative immunosuppression, and cancer progression. This proposed risk is supported by observations that the μ-opioid receptor is overexpressed in several human cancers, including breast cancer, where it may contribute to enhanced tumor growth and metastasis. Nevertheless, the relationship between opioid exposure and cancer progression appears to be complex and context-dependent. Preclinical evidence also indicates that certain opioids can exert antitumor effects. For instance, prolonged morphine treatment has been shown to suppress the proliferation of BT474 human breast cancer cells by modulating the ErbB signaling network. Likewise, opioid ligands acting on distinct receptor subtypes have demonstrated dose-dependent inhibitory effects on the growth of MCF-7 breast cancer cells – an effect reversed by co-administration of the opioid receptor antagonist naloxone. Clinically, emerging evidence suggests that intraoperative opioid administration may even confer protective benefits, such as improved recurrence-free survival in patients with triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). Postoperative administration of tramadol has been associated with a lower incidence of cancer recurrence and mortality in patients undergoing breast cancer surgery. Tramadol is a centrally acting analgesic widely accepted for treating moderate postoperative pain. It is commonly used for acute pain management following breast cancer surgery, alongside with a lower risk of tolerance, dependence, and respiratory depression. Tramadol exerts its analgesic effects through dual mechanisms: it binds to μ-opioid receptors and inhibits the reuptake of noradrenaline and serotonin. Both tramadol and its principal metabolite, O -desmethyltramadol (M1), exhibit opioid-like effects by binding to μ-opioid receptors in the central nervous system. However, the binding affinity of tramadol for μ-opioid receptors is approximately 6,000 times lower than that of morphine, whereas the affinity of M1 is approximately 20 times lower. Recent studies have demonstrated that tramadol has anticancer effects on breast cancer both in vitro and in vivo simultaneously. Notably, clinical reports indicate that the postoperative use of tramadol is associated with a reduced risk of breast cancer recurrence.
title: Tramadol induced hypoxia signaling and paraptosis-like cell death in breast cancer cells via HIF-1α and ATF4 dependent pathways
journal: Redox Report: Communications in Free Radical Research

text: However, the binding affinity of tramadol for μ-opioid receptors is approximately 6,000 times lower than that of morphine, whereas the affinity of M1 is approximately 20 times lower. Recent studies have demonstrated that tramadol has anticancer effects on breast cancer both in vitro and in vivo simultaneously. Notably, clinical reports indicate that the postoperative use of tramadol is associated with a reduced risk of breast cancer recurrence. Tramadol combined with doxorubicin demonstrated synergistic anticancer effects in MDA-MB-231 cells, a model of TNBC, as well as specific synergistic outcomes in MCF-7 cells, which are estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer cells. Furthermore, tramadol was found to induce mitochondrial dysfunction in endometrial cancer cells, leading to a decrease in the oxygen consumption rate and an increase in the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS). Although these findings are promising, the precise molecular mechanisms underlying the antitumor effects of tramadol in breast cancer remain largely unexplored. Many studies have shown that while chemotherapy can temporarily induce apoptosis in cancer cells, cancer cells may survive and repopulate due to incomplete or inefficient apoptosis. These findings also indicate that apoptosis does not represent a strict point-of-no-return, as the process can reverse even at advanced stages. Once nuclear fragmentation occurs, apoptosis becomes irreversible. Furthermore, both intrinsic resistance to apoptosis and acquired resistance after treatment (for example, the development of multidrug resistance following breast cancer chemotherapy) present significant challenges in effective cancer therapy. Therefore, identifying alternative cell death mechanisms could be a key to overcoming apoptosis resistance. There are two main types of alternative cell death pathways: caspase-dependent and caspase-independent, including anoikis, autosis, ferroptosis, pyroptosis, necroptosis, and paraptosis. Recent studies have shown that several natural compounds can trigger paraptosis in different tumor cell lines, including breast cancer cell lines. Paraptosis was recently described as a form of programmed cell death (PCD) characterized by features distinct from those of apoptotic cell death. The hallmark of paraptosis is extensive cellular vacuolization, which is generated from either endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress or mitochondrial swelling. It is well established that increased ROS production contributes to mitochondrial dysfunction and/or ER stress, which is a prerequisite for the formation of paraptotic vacuoles. ER stress is known to accumulate as part of the unfolded protein response (UPR) and is a primary driver of ROS production and autophagy. Three primary UPR pathways are involved: inositol-requiring enzyme-1α (IRE1), activating transcription factor 6 (ATF6), and protein kinase RNA-like endoplasmic reticulum kinase (PERK). Each pathway plays a distinct role in managing cellular stress. Activated ATF6 functions as a transcription factor, promoting the expression of ER chaperones and XBP1. When activated, IRE1 splices XBP1 mRNA to produce the spliced XBP1 protein (XBP1s), which translocates to the nucleus to regulate the transcription of ER-resident chaperones and genes involved in lipogenesis and ER-associated degradation. Moreover, PERK activation leads to the phosphorylation of eukaryotic initiation factor 2α (p-eIF2α), which inhibits general protein synthesis while selectively allowing the translation of activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4).
title: Tramadol induced hypoxia signaling and paraptosis-like cell death in breast cancer cells via HIF-1α and ATF4 dependent pathways
journal: Redox Report: Communications in Free Radical Research

text: Activated ATF6 functions as a transcription factor, promoting the expression of ER chaperones and XBP1. When activated, IRE1 splices XBP1 mRNA to produce the spliced XBP1 protein (XBP1s), which translocates to the nucleus to regulate the transcription of ER-resident chaperones and genes involved in lipogenesis and ER-associated degradation. Moreover, PERK activation leads to the phosphorylation of eukaryotic initiation factor 2α (p-eIF2α), which inhibits general protein synthesis while selectively allowing the translation of activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4). ATF4 then moves to the nucleus, where it drives the transcription of various genes essential for ER quality control. The ER and mitochondria are closely connected organelles through mitochondria-associated membranes. Numerous studies have confirmed that ER stress triggers mitochondrial dysfunction. Hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs) are transcription factors that serve as key regulators of oxygen homeostasis, orchestrating various adaptive responses to hypoxic conditions. The HIF-α subunit acts as the primary hypoxia sensor. HIFs function as heterodimers, comprising a hypoxia-sensitive HIF-α subunit and a constitutively expressed HIF-β subunit. The stability of HIF-α proteins is regulated post-translationally by prolyl hydroxylase domain (PHD)-containing enzymes. Under normoxic conditions, HIF-1α and HIF-2α are continuously hydroxylated by PHDs at specific proline residues, marking them for rapid degradation via the von Hippel-Lindau (pVHL)-ubiquitin-proteasome pathway. In mild hypoxia, PHD activity is inhibited, allowing HIF-α proteins to escape pVHL-mediated degradation, stabilize, translocate to the nucleus, and dimerize with HIF-β. This forms the HIF transcriptional complex, which binds to hypoxia response elements (HREs) in target gene promoters. HIF-regulated target genes play crucial roles in cellular and systemic adaptations to hypoxia, including metabolic reprogramming, resistance to apoptosis, angiogenesis, invasion, and metastasis. Overexpression of HIF-1α has been linked to poor prognosis in several cancers, including breast, cervical, oropharyngeal, ovarian, and endometrial cancers. However, recent studies have reported an association between HIF-1α overexpression and reduced mortality in patients with head and neck squamous cell carcinoma and non-small-cell lung cancer. This apparent discrepancy may stem from the limitations of current clinical methods used to assess protein levels in cancer cells. Immunohistochemical analysis, the most common technique for measuring protein expression, does not provide information on potential mutations or post-translational modifications that could influence HIF-1α functions. As a result, variations in HIF-1α activity rather than expression alone may contribute to its differing prognostic significance across cancer types. Hence, in this study, we aimed to clarify which type of cell death is induced by tramadol in breast cancer cells, to investigate whether this effect may involve a nonapoptotic form of cell death such as paraptosis, and to determine the underlying molecular mechanisms, particularly the involvement of HIF-1α and ATF4 dependent signaling. Understanding these mechanisms could provide valuable insights into the potential of tramadol as a therapeutic agent in breast cancer and its ability to increase the efficacy of existing treatments.

text: To assess the cytotoxic potential of tramadol, we first evaluated cell viability in MCF-7, MDA-MB-231, and non-tumorigenic MCF-10A breast epithelial cells using MTT assays. A dose-dependent suppression of metabolic activity was observed in both cancer cell lines, with MCF-7 cells exhibiting approximately 1.5-fold greater susceptibility than MDA-MB-231 cells. In contrast, MCF-10A cells exhibited relative resistance to tramadol, indicating a potential therapeutic window for cancer-selective cytotoxicity (A). To explore the molecular basis of tramadol's cytotoxicity, RNA-seq analysis was performed on tramadol-treated MCF-7 and MDA-MB-231 cells. Differential expression analysis revealed extensive transcriptomic remodeling: 319 genes were significantly upregulated and 95 were downregulated in MDA-MB-231 cells, while MCF-7 cells displayed 210 upregulated and 195 downregulated genes (B). Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) further identified consistent enrichment of pathways related to hypoxia response, the unfolded protein response (UPR), and reactive oxygen species (ROS) signaling in both cell types (C).

text: To verify whether tramadol could elicit hypoxia-like cellular responses, we utilized a hypoxia-sensitive probe that emits fluorescence in the presence of nitroreductase activity, a biochemical hallmark of hypoxic environments. Flow cytometric analysis showed a concentration-dependent elevation in hypoxia-associated fluorescence following tramadol exposure in both MDA-MB-231 and MCF-7 cells, implying that tramadol induced a pseudo-hypoxic state despite ambient oxygen levels (A). Our prior work had demonstrated that tramadol increases HIF-1α protein expression in normoxic breast cancer cells. To determine whether this upregulation resulted from enhanced protein stability, we inhibited translation using cycloheximide (CHX) and monitored the degradation kinetics of HIF-1α protein. In both breast cancer cell lines, tramadol treatment significantly extended HIF-1α half-life, supporting the conclusion that it impedes normoxic degradation of the protein (B). As HIF-1α exerts its function by regulating gene transcription within the nucleus, we examined its intracellular distribution following tramadol treatment. Immunofluorescence staining revealed strong nuclear localization of HIF-1α in tramadol-treated breast cancer cells, marked by intensified nuclear red signals in both MDA-MB-231 and MCF-7 cells (C). These observations were further validated by nuclear and cytoplasmic fractionation followed by western blotting, which confirmed increased nuclear accumulation of HIF-1α protein upon tramadol exposure (D). These results suggest that tramadol not only stabilized HIF-1α under normoxia but also promoted its translocation into the nucleus, an essential step for its transcriptional activity. To assess whether nuclear HIF-1α retained its transcriptional function, we performed quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) analysis to evaluate expression levels of known downstream targets, including BHLHE40, HMOX1, and VEGFA. Tramadol treatment led to a dose-dependent increase in the expression of all three genes in both MDA-MB-231 and MCF-7 cells (E). To determine the dependency on HIF-1α activity, we employed PX-478, a pharmacological inhibitor that blocks HIF-1α-mediated transcription. Pre-treatment with PX-478 significantly reduced tramadol-induced upregulation of these genes, indicating that the gene expression changes were indeed mediated through HIF-1α. These data showed that tramadol under normoxia activated HIF-1α signaling by promoting its nuclear localization and target gene expression.

text: To investigate the specific UPR pathways activated by tramadol-induced ER stress in breast cancer cells, we performed western blotting to assess the involvement of the three primary UPR pathways. Our western blot results demonstrated that tramadol induced the expression of the IRE1, ATF6, and PERK proteins in MCF-7 cells but downregulated the expression of those proteins in MDA-MB-231 cells. However, the expression of the components of the p-eIF2α/ATF4/CHOP signaling pathway, which is activated by the UPR, was detected in both cell types (A). ATF4 also induced the expression of the C/EBP homologous protein (CHOP) transcription factor (A). Next, we confirmed through nuclear–cytoplasmic fractionation that tramadol-induced ATF4 translocated to the nucleus (B) in both breast cancer cell lines. This translocation is crucial, as it enables ATF4 to function as a transcription factor and regulate the expression of genes involved in the cellular response to ER stress. We then performed qPCR to validate the expression of ATF4 downstream target genes identified in our RNA-seq analysis. The expression of the genes encoding glutathione-specific gamma-glutamylcyclotransferase 1 (CHAC1), ATF3, and Jun dimerization protein 2 (JDP2), which was upregulated following treatment with tramadol, as shown in c, exhibited a consistent increasing trend (C). These findings suggested that tramadol triggered an ATF4-mediated transcriptional response, activating genes crucial for adapting to ER stress. Since ATF4 and CHOP cooperatively stimulate the expression of genes involved in protein synthesis, the reactivation of translation can lead to ROS overproduction, potentially triggering cell death. Studies have shown that the forced expression of ATF4 and CHOP increases protein synthesis, leading to ATP depletion and oxidative stress, ultimately resulting in cell death. Furthermore, our previous GSEA revealed that treatment with tramadol significantly activated the ROS pathway in the MDA-MB-231 and MCF-7 breast cancer cell lines (D). In subsequent experiments, we assessed whether tramadol affects ROS levels in breast cancer cells. The results revealed that tramadol significantly increased cytosolic ROS levels in both MDA-MB-231 and MCF-7 cells, with a notable increase in mitochondrial ROS levels observed only in MDA-MB-231 cells (D). This cell-specific mitochondrial ROS response suggested that, compared with MCF-7 cells, MDA-MB-231 cells may be more susceptible to mitochondrial oxidative stress under tramadol treatment.

text: Next, we investigated whether tramadol-induced breast cancer cell death could be rescued by various inhibitors of ROS (N-acetylcysteine, NAC), PERK (GSK260414), ferroptosis (Fer-1), autophagy (3-MA), necroptosis (Nec-1), and apoptosis (Z-VAD-FMK) and to clarify the type of cell death involved. The results indicated that in MDA-MB-231 cells, tramadol-induced cell death could be rescued by the ROS scavenger NAC (A). In contrast, in MCF-7 cells, cell death was rescued by NAC and GSK260414. Notably, none of the inhibitors targeting ferroptosis, autophagy, necroptosis, or apoptosis prevented tramadol-induced cell death in either cell line. Vacuolation, a defining morphological feature, aligns with paraptosis, which is characterized by cytoplasmic vacuolization from the ER and mitochondrial swelling. Interestingly, phase-contrast microscopy revealed notable morphological changes in breast cancer cells following treatment with tramadol. In both MDA-MB-231 and MCF-7 cells, numerous cytoplasmic vacuoles (black arrows indicate cytoplasmic vacuoles) were observed, which increased in number with higher doses and longer treatment times (B). These vacuoles eventually merged into larger vacuoles, and this accumulation led to cell death, suggesting that tramadol may have a cytotoxic effect on breast cancer cells. Similar observations have been reported in human hepatocellular carcinoma, where sorafenib induces ER dilation, UPR pathway activation, and cytoplasmic vacuolation associated with nonapoptotic cell death. To further examine these vacuoles, we utilized transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to observe their morphology at higher magnification (selection by yellow squares). In tramadol-treated MDA-MB-231 and MCF-7 cells, there were numerous vacuoles (C). These included autophagic vacuoles containing intracellular material (indicated by blue arrows) and empty lipid droplets (indicated by green LD). Under ER stress, an enlarged ER membrane (indicated by pink ER) contributes to autophagosome formation. The mitochondria (shown as yellow M) in the control cells maintained a fusion state, whereas in the tramadol-treated cells, most of the mitochondria were in a fission state. To further assess lipid droplets, we employed BODIPY staining to visualize their distribution. The results revealed an increase in lipid droplets in response to 0.25 and 0.5 mg/ml tramadol, with a punctate distribution within the cells (A). At 1 mg/ml, however, the lipid droplets became more uniformly distributed throughout the cells. Flow cytometry validated these findings, indicating that tramadol significantly increased lipid droplet accumulation in both MDA-MB-231 and MCF-7 cells (B).

text: Oxidative stress and ER stress are significant contributors to cell death, often resulting from mitochondrial permeability transition and impaired autophagy. Autophagy is a highly conserved cellular process that involves the degradation and recycling of cellular components, including damaged proteins and organelles. This process is essential for maintaining cellular homeostasis and promoting cell survival under stress conditions. During autophagy, cytoplasmic components are sequestered into double-membraned structures called autophagosomes, which subsequently fuse with lysosomes for degradation. Acridine orange (AO) is a cell-permeable green fluorophore that can be protonated and trapped in acidic vesicular organelles (AVOs). Under AO staining, the cytoplasm and nucleoli fluoresce green, whereas acidic compartments, such as lysosomes or autophagolysosomes, fluoresce bright red or orange red with blue-light excitation. To investigate whether tramadol induces autophagy in breast cancer cells, we conducted AO staining and analyzed the fluorescence images presented in A. The results revealed that in both MDA-MB-231 and MCF-7 cells, the red fluorescence representing AVOs (squares indicate representative regions shown as enlarged areas) increased in both size and quantity as the tramadol dose increased. This observation suggested that treatment with tramadol enhanced the formation of acidic vesicles, indicating increased autophagic activity. In addition to AO staining, we utilized DALGreen, a dye that selectively integrates into the autophagosome membrane upon autophagosome formation, in conjunction with flow cytometry to assess autophagy in live cells. This approach allows for the quantitative measurement of autophagic activity by analyzing the fluorescence intensity associated with autophagosomes. The results indicated that treatment with tramadol significantly enhanced autophagic activity in both MDA-MB-231 and MCF-7 cells in a dose-dependent manner (B). LC3-I is converted into LC3-II during autophagy; LC3-II is associated with the autophagosomal membrane and is considered a crucial marker of autophagy. To elucidate the effects of tramadol on autophagy, we performed Western blotting to assess the protein expression levels of LC3B. The results indicated that treatment with tramadol significantly induced LC3B II protein expression in both MDA-MB-231 and MCF-7 cells (C). Collectively, these findings provide compelling evidence that tramadol induces autophagy in breast cancer cells.

section_title: Tramadol induced autophagy in breast cancer cells

text: The morphology of mitochondria is regulated primarily by the processes of fusion and fission, which are essential for maintaining mitochondrial function and ensuring strict quality control. To investigate whether tramadol affects mitochondrial morphology, we used MitoTracker to label mitochondria. Among MDA-MB-231 cells, those in the control group presented a tubular distribution of mitochondria throughout the cell; however, following treatment with tramadol, the mitochondria clustered together, emitting stronger red fluorescence (A). In MCF-7 cells, the control group also exhibited a tubular distribution of mitochondria; however, after treatment with tramadol, the distribution of mitochondria was less widespread. These findings indicated that tramadol significantly altered mitochondrial morphology in breast cancer cells. To investigate the effects of tramadol on the mitochondrial membrane potential in breast cancer cells, JC-1 dye was used. This dye is particularly useful because it can indicate changes in the mitochondrial membrane potential, specifically highlighting the phenomenon of mitochondrial membrane potential loss. Our results revealed that in both MDA-MB-231 and MCF-7 cells, the loss of the mitochondrial membrane potential increased in a dose-dependent manner with increasing doses of tramadol (B). These findings suggest that tramadol not only affects mitochondrial morphology but also disrupts mitochondrial membrane potential, a critical aspect of mitochondrial function. Next, we employed the Seahorse XF Cell Mito Stress Test to assess mitochondrial bioenergetic function more comprehensively. This assay allows the real-time measurement of key parameters of mitochondrial bioenergetic functions, including the oxygen consumption rate (OCR), basal respiration, ATP production, and maximal respiratory capacity of cells. The results from this analysis confirmed that treatment with tramadol significantly impaired mitochondrial OCR (C) and decreased basal respiration, maximal respiration, spare respiratory capacity, nonmitochondrial respiration, proton leakage, and ATP production in both MDA-MB-231 and MCF-7 cells (C). Collectively, these findings indicate that tramadol induces both morphological and functional changes in mitochondria, which may contribute to its cytotoxic effects on breast cancer cells.

text: Cell death pathways are classified on the basis of their signaling dependencies, morphological characteristics, and molecular mechanisms. Our data revealed that tramadol might induce paraptosis-like cell death in breast cancer cells, as indicated by distinct cellular responses, such as ER stress, ROS generation, autophagy, mitochondrial dysfunction, and extensive vacuole formation. Notably, paraptosis represents a distinct, nonapoptotic form of PCD that occurs independently of caspase activation. Mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) components, i.e. p38 MAPK, JNK (c-Jun N-terminal kinase), and ERK (extracellular signal-regulated kinase), play critical roles in mediating stress responses within the cell, and their abnormal activation is essential for driving paraptotic cell death. The first natural inhibitor of paraptosis identified was ALG-2-interacting protein X (Alix), a protein that was initially cloned from apoptosis-linked gene 2 (ALG-2), a calcium-binding protein involved in T cell receptor-induced cell death. To investigate the molecular changes induced by tramadol, we treated both MDA-MB-231 and MCF-7 cells with tramadol followed by Western blot analysis. In the context of caspase-dependent apoptosis, poly(ADP–ribose) polymerase (PARP) is cleaved by caspase 3, a hallmark of this apoptotic pathway. Our results revealed that tramadol did not induce PARP cleavage, which suggests that tramadol does not activate the caspase cascade, indicating a lack of apoptotic signaling through this pathway. Additionally, our analysis revealed that tramadol activated the p38 and ERK signaling pathways in both MDA-MB-231 and MCF-7 cells. Moreover, we observed a significant decrease in Alix protein expression, specifically in MDA-MB-231 cells, following treatment with tramadol.
title: Tramadol induced hypoxia signaling and paraptosis-like cell death in breast cancer cells via HIF-1α and ATF4 dependent pathways

section_title: Tramadol induced paraptosis in MDA-MB-231 and MCF-7 cells

text: Finally, we conducted knockout experiments targeting the HIF-1α, ATF4 and the programmed cell death 6 interacting protein (PDCD6IP) gene, which encodes the Alix protein, to investigate their roles in tramadol-induced cell death in breast cancer cells. To investigate the functional contribution of ATF4, HIF-1α, and Alix to tramadol-mediated cytotoxic effects, we analyzed the morphological outcomes in MDA-MB-231 cells following gene-specific knockout using CRISPR/Cas9 technology. Successful knockout of HIF-1α, ATF4, and PDCD6IP (Alix) was confirmed by qPCR, which showed markedly reduced mRNA expression levels, indicating efficient gene disruption (A-B). To assess the role of HIF-1α in tramadol-induced cytotoxicity, we measured cell viability following tramadol treatment in HIF-1α knockout cells. At 750 µg/mL tramadol, both sgHIF-1α constructs conferred protection against cell death, with sgHIF-1α−2 exhibiting a more substantial protective effect than sgHIF-1α−1 (C), underscoring the involvement of HIF-1α in the cellular stress response to tramadol. Notably, ATF4 knockout also markedly attenuated tramadol-induced cytotoxicity in MDA-MB-231 cells, suggesting that ATF4 is a key mediator of tramadol’s cell-killing effects (D). In contrast, deletion of PDCD6IP enhanced the cytotoxicity of tramadol, indicating that Alix may function as a protective factor under tramadol-induced stress. Upon tramadol exposure, control cells expressing non-targeting sgRNA (sgNT) exhibited a dose-dependent increase in cytoplasmic vacuole formation and cell enlargement (E). In ATF4 -deficient cells (sgATF4), the extent of vacuolization was notably diminished, implicating ATF4 as a key driver of this phenotype. Conversely, HIF-1α knockout cells (sgHIF1α−1 and sgHIF1α−2) displayed vacuolization levels similar to those of control cells; however, these cells maintained a more intact morphology with fewer instances of detachment and rounding. This suggests that while HIF-1α may not directly influence vacuole formation, it plays a protective role in sustaining cell integrity under tramadol-induced stress. Interestingly, loss of PDCD6IP resulted in pronounced morphological deterioration following tramadol treatment. Cells lacking Alix exhibited extensive rounding and detachment, indicating heightened vulnerability to tramadol-induced cytotoxicity and suggesting a protective function for Alix in this context. Together, these findings suggest that ATF4 facilitates cytoplasmic vacuolization (red arrows), HIF-1α contributes to cellular resilience, and Alix functions as a negative regulator of tramadol-induced cell death in MDA-MB-231 cells.

text: This study uncovered that tramadol impaired cancer cell viability through two mechanistically linked but separate processes: the stabilization of HIF-1α under normal oxygen conditions and the activation of paraptotic cell death driven by oxidative stress and ER dysfunction. These findings shed light on previously unrecognized cellular effects of tramadol, suggesting potential applications beyond its traditional use as a pain reliever. In cancer treatment, the resistance of cancer cells to apoptosis poses a significant challenge and contributes to numerous cancer-related deaths. A promising strategy to overcome this resistance involves targeting cancer cells through the induction of paraptosis, a recently identified alternative caspase-independent cell death pathway. This study elucidated the molecular mechanisms by which tramadol exerts its anticancer effects and induces paraptosis, a nonapoptotic form of programmed cell death, in MDA-MB-231 and MCF-7 breast cancer cells. Paraptosis induced by tramadol involves the coordinated activation of ROS, hypoxia signaling, and ER stress, all converging on the p-eIF2α/ATF4/CHOP axis. In parallel, autophagy disruption, mitochondrial impairment, and lipid droplet buildup contribute to extensive cytoplasmic vacuolization, a defining feature of paraptotic cell death. Paraptosis is a distinct type of nonapoptotic cell death characterized by dilation of the ER and/or mitochondria. Unlike apoptotic cells, paraptotic cells do not exhibit features such as cell shrinkage, DNA fragmentation, or caspase activation. Instead, paraptosis involves disruptions in cellular protein and ion balance, particularly concerning calcium ion transport. This form of cell death can be triggered by various pharmacological agents, including natural compounds, metal complexes, proteasome inhibitors, and specific ion regulators. Key pathways that initiate paraptosis include MAPK activation via insulin-like growth factor-I receptor (IGFIR), ER stress resulting from proteasome inhibition or other factors, osmotic stress due to ROS production, and impaired mitochondrial function. The literature also indicates that downregulation of the phosphorylation of MAPK signaling pathways inhibits tumor bone metastasis and osteoclastogenesis in breast cancer, suggesting that MAPK signaling plays a critical role not only in paraptosis but also in cancer progression and metastatic regulation. Furthermore, imbalances in ion homeostasis can lead to ER and mitochondrial swelling. In contrast, certain genes, such as PDCD6IP, heme transporter 1 (FLVCR1), and thioredoxin reductase 1 (TXNRD1), are known to inhibit paraptosis. Although apoptosis and paraptosis were initially thought to function independently, emerging research suggests a potential connection between the two, with the tumor proteins p53 (TP53) and MAPK acting as key mediators. In situations where TP53 is deficient, MAPK-driven apoptosis and paraptosis may interact in either a synergistic or competitive manner. For example, fusaric acid, a mycotoxin found in food, can induce either apoptosis or paraptosis in a dose-dependent manner in human peripheral blood mononuclear cells and THP-1 cells. While paraptosis is generally considered a caspase-independent form of regulated cell death, caspase 9 has been implicated in regulating both apoptosis and paraptosis, with paraptotic cell death becoming more pronounced when apoptosis is inhibited. Therefore, targeting paraptosis represents a promising strategy for overcoming the resistance to apoptosis commonly observed in cancer cells.

text: For example, fusaric acid, a mycotoxin found in food, can induce either apoptosis or paraptosis in a dose-dependent manner in human peripheral blood mononuclear cells and THP-1 cells. While paraptosis is generally considered a caspase-independent form of regulated cell death, caspase 9 has been implicated in regulating both apoptosis and paraptosis, with paraptotic cell death becoming more pronounced when apoptosis is inhibited. Therefore, targeting paraptosis represents a promising strategy for overcoming the resistance to apoptosis commonly observed in cancer cells. Our previous study primarily investigated the interaction between tramadol and doxorubicin; however, the possibility that tramadol may also modulate the cytotoxic effects of other chemotherapeutic drugs remains an important direction for future research. Given tramadol’s pleiotropic mechanisms – including ROS generation, ER stress induction, and modulation of HIF-1α and ATF4 signaling – it is plausible that its impact on drug efficacy could vary according to the molecular mechanisms of individual chemotherapeutic agents. For example, drugs such as paclitaxel and cisplatin, which also induce oxidative and ER stress responses, might exhibit additive or synergistic effects when combined with tramadol. In contrast, agents that act primarily through DNA intercalation or topoisomerase inhibition may display distinct patterns of interaction. Potential pharmacokinetic interference should also be taken into account, as tramadol metabolism via CYP2D6 could influence systemic drug exposure or toxicity profiles. Furthermore, since our findings were derived from in vitro experiments in breast cancer cell lines, in vivo pharmacodynamic interactions and tumor microenvironmental influences remain to be elucidated. From a translational standpoint, the identification of tramadol as a modulator of the HIF-1α/ATF4 axis provides new insights into therapeutic strategies targeting stress-adaptive pathways in resistant breast cancer subtypes. The dual involvement of HIF-1α stabilization and ATF4 activation suggests that tramadol may exploit the cellular stress network to drive nonapoptotic paraptotic death, offering a potential route to overcome apoptosis resistance commonly observed in TNBC. Pharmacological or genetic inhibition of this adaptive axis has been proposed to restore drug sensitivity in hypoxic tumors, and our findings imply that tramadol or its derivatives might achieve similar outcomes through partial pathway modulation. Future studies integrating tramadol with targeted inhibitors or conventional chemotherapeutics could clarify whether these effects translate into improved therapeutic efficacy in vivo. Tramadol differentially affected three primary UPR pathways – IRE1, ATF6, and PERK – in MDA-MB-231 and MCF-7 breast cancer cells. Specifically, tramadol induced the expression of the IRE1, ATF6, and PERK proteins in MCF-7 cells but decreased their expression in MDA-MB-231 cells. However, the expression of components of the p-eIF2α/ATF4/CHOP signaling pathway, which is activated by the UPR, was observed in both cell types. MCF-7 and MDA-MB-231 cells are both invasive ductal breast carcinoma cells but differ significantly in their phenotypic and genotypic profiles. MCF-7 cells are hormone dependent, estrogen receptor positive, progesterone receptor positive, and HER2 negative, whereas MDA-MB-231 cells are triple negative. The absence of hormone receptors in MDA-MB-231 cells renders them unresponsive to antiestrogen and targeted therapies, such as tamoxifen or anti-HER2 therapies.
