text: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease characterized by persistent inflammation and damage to the colonic mucosa, significantly impacting patients’ quality of life. One of the hallmarks of UC pathogenesis is the disruption and damage to the intestinal epithelium, which serves as a critical barrier to maintain gut homeostasis and protect against pathogens and inflammatory insults. When this epithelial barrier is compromised, it leads to increased intestinal permeability, further driving inflammation and disease progression. Current research indicates a close relationship between endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and the pathogenesis of various intestinal disorders, including UC. ER stress, which arises from the accumulation of misfolded proteins in the ER, triggers the unfolded protein response (UPR) to restore homeostasis. However, prolonged or unresolved ER stress can lead to cellular apoptosis via CHOP-dependent or independent induction of Bcl2-like11 (Bcl2L11), NADPH oxidase activator (NOXA), and p53 unregulated apoptosis modulator (PUMA),, contributing to the exacerbation of inflammatory responses and tissue damage in UC. In particular, the inositol-requiring enzyme 1 (IRE1)-X-box binding protein 1 (XBP1) axis of the UPR plays a pivotal role in mitigating ER stress by promoting XBP1 mRNA splicing. This spliced form of XBP1 enhances the production of ER chaperones and other proteins that help alleviate ER stress, thus protecting epithelial cells from stress-induced apoptosis. Genetic variants in XBP1, which lead to spontaneous enteritis, were identified to have link to increased risk of both Crohn’s disease and UC. Recent studies have highlighted the promise of mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs), particularly those derived from umbilical cord tissues, in modulating inflammation and promoting tissue repair. In preclinical and clinical studies, MSCs and their derived exosomes have demonstrated beneficial effects in treating UC, primarily by reducing inflammation and enhancing mucosal healing. However, the specific impact of MSC therapy on ER stress in UC has not yet been fully elucidated. Here, we hypothesize that human umbilical cord–derived MSCs (hUC-MSCs) alleviate UC by targeting the IRE1/XBP1 axis to resolve ER stress and inhibit epithelial apoptosis. Using a DSS-induced murine colitis model and TNF-α-stimulated colon epithelial cells, we investigate whether hUC-MSCs restore ER homeostasis through XBP1 splicing, thereby bridging the gap between MSC therapy and ER stress modulation in UC. This study not only elucidates a novel mechanistic pathway but also highlights the translational potential of hUC-MSCs for clinical UC management.

text: Female-specific pathogen-free (SPF) C57BL/6 mice (6–8 weeks old) were purchased from Beijing Vital River Laboratory Animal Technology Co. Ltd (Beijing, China) and housed in the Animal Facility at Shanxi Medical University. The experimental mice were randomly divided into three groups: DSS+PBS, DSS+MSCs, and control groups (n = 6 per group for survival analysis and histological examination, n = 3 per group for RNA sequencing). Starting from day 0, mice in the DSS + PBS and DSS + MSCs groups were administered with 4% DSS (molecular weight 36–50 kDa; MP Biomedicals, CA, USA) in drinking water for 7 days, followed by regular water. Mice in the control group received regular water throughout the experiment. For therapeutic studies, mice in DSS + MSCs group were injected with uc-MSCs (1.0 × 10 6 cells per mouse, 100 μL) intraperitoneally on days 3, 5, and 7, while mice in DSS + PBS and the control groups received 100 μL of PBS via same route and on the same schedule. For survival analysis, body weight, disease activity index (DAI), and survival rate were monitored daily over a period of 14 days. For RNA-sequencing and histological examination, mice were euthanized on day 8. After euthanasia, colons were excised, rinsed with PBS, and measured for length. Portions of colon were used for myeloperoxidase (MPO) activity assay and RNA isolation. Tissue for histological examination was stored in 10% formalin.

text: Formalin-fixed colon tissues were embedded in paraffin routinely. Paraffin sections, 5 μm thick, were stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E). Inflammatory scores were determined using a score system as follows: Epithelium (E) score: 0, normal morphology; 1, loss of goblet cells; 2, loss of goblet cells in large areas; 3, loss of crypts; 4, loss of crypts in large areas. Infiltration (I) score: 0, no infiltration; 1, infiltrate around crypt basis; 2, infiltrate reaching to lamina muscularis mucosa layer; 3, extensive infiltration reaching the muscularis mucosa with abundant edema; and 4, infiltration of the submucosa layer. The histological score was calculated as the sum of these two parameters (total score = E + I).

text: To investigate the therapeutic efficacy of intraperitoneal injection of hUC-MSCs against ulcerative colitis, we established a preclinical model by administering a solution of 4% DSS in drinking water to mice for 7 days (ure). At the end of this period, mice are taken back to normal water. DSS-induced colitis mice were intraperitoneally injected with 1.0 × 10 6 hUC-MSCs on day 3, day 5, and day 7, and the disease activity, body weight, and survival rate of the mice were monitored. Upon DSS administration, regardless of hUC-MSC injection, DAI values began to increase, peaking on day 7 or 8, followed by a gradual decline. However, after the recovery of normal water, the DAI decreased more rapidly in the presence of hUC-MSCs. The body weight of mice sharply declined from day 4 to day 9 post-DSS administration, but recovery was faster in the hUC-MSC-treated group after day 9. Consistent with these findings, the survival rate was significantly improved in the presence of hUC-MSCs. On day 8 after DSS treatment, colon length was measured before histological examination. Shortening of the colon, which is the characteristic pathological feature of colitis, was substantially inhibited by hUC-MSCs treatment. MPO level, a commonly used biomarker of colitis, is a neutrophil granule constituent, where its level is proportional to the number of migrated neutrophils. In the MSCs treated group, the MPO activity in colon tissues decreased by 45% compared to the PBS–treated mice, implying that hUC-MSCs treatment suppressed the infiltration of neutrophils. The expression of TNF-α, the major cytokine involved in ulcerative colitis, was markedly reduced in the MSCs treated mice. Collectively, MSCs showed preventive and therapeutic effects in the acute colitis models.

section_title: Intraperitoneal hUC-MSCs treatment alleviated the DSS-induced colitis in mice model

text: In the DSS-induced colitis model, administration of DSS disrupts the intestinal epithelial barrier. Histological analysis revealed loss or shortening of crypts and marked infiltration of inflammatory cells in both the lamina propria and muscularis mucosa, accompanied by significantly increased histopathological scores. Previous studies have suggested that DSS exerts direct cytotoxic effects on intestinal epithelial cells in the basal crypts, leading to increased epithelial apoptosis. Consistent with this, immunohistochemical analysis showed that DSS treatment increased the number of active caspase (Casp)-3-positive cells in colonic tissues and reduced the number of Ki67-positive cells, indicating enhanced epithelial cell apoptosis and impaired proliferation, respectively. Compared to the DSS+PBS group, colonic tissues in the DSS+MSC group exhibited more intact crypts, reduced infiltration of inflammatory cells, and significantly lower histopathological scores. Immunohistochemical analysis further demonstrated that hUC-MSC treatment markedly reduced epithelial apoptosis. Moreover, hUC-MSC treatment significantly restored Ki67 expression levels, indicating a reversal of colon epithelial cells loss. To determine the specific localization of transplanted MSCs, Dil-labeled hUC-MSCs were intraperitoneally injected into DSS-induced colitis mice. The labeled hUC-MSCs were detected in the inflamed colonic tissues 24 h post-injection. Interestingly, hUC-MSCs were observed in both the epithelium and lamina propria of the inflamed colon, with a higher accumulation in the epithelium. These findings indicate that hUC-MSC treatment reduces epithelial injury in DSS-induced colitis by alleviating apoptosis, promoting colon epithelial cells regeneration, and preferentially localizing to and accumulating in the colonic epithelium.

text: We next investigated the genetic regulatory network regulated by hUC-MSC in colitis. Total RNA was extracted from colons of three NC group mice, three DSS+PBS group mice, and three DSS+MSC group mice. RNA sequencing data demonstrated that 1491 upregulated and 940 downregulated differentially expressed genes (DEGs, P -adjust <.05, absolute log 2 [fold change] > 1) induced by DSS treatment, respectively. However, much less genes were regulated (558 genes were upregulated and 485 genes were downregulated) with hUC-MSC treatment with the same criteria compared to untreated. Further analyses found that 526 and 872 genes were upregulated and downregulated in DSS-MSC group when compared to DSS-PBS group mice, respectively. Principal component analysis also showed that the mRNA expression profile in the colon of DSS-MSC group mice was separated from DSS-PBS group mice but closed to NC group mice. Hierarchical clustering analysis also indicated distinguishable transcription patterns between the DSS+PBS and DSS+MSC groups. Various chemokines and their receptors (Cxcl11, Cxcl13, and Ccr1), cytokines and their receptors (Csf3, IL1r2, Il6ra, and Il7r), as well as inflammation-related genes (Saa3, Tlr5, S100a8, and S100a9) were upregulated upon DSS induction but downregulated with MSC treatment. Of note, Nlrp10 (a multifunctional negative regulator of inflammation and apoptosis) and Cldn4 (an intestinal barrier-related gene) were detected to be downregulated upon DSS induction, but were upregulated in hUC-MSC treated mice as compared to the DSS + PBS group. We further compared the DEGs induced by DSS with the “Inflammatory bowel disease” gene set in the GeneCards database, and 832 genes overlapped. However, only 343 genes overlapped the “Inflammatory bowel disease” gene set among the DEGs between DSS + MSC group and NC group. These RNA-seq data uncover that hUC-MSC treatment regulates the pro-inflammatory transcriptional profile in DSS-induced colitis. We estimated the enrichment of innate immune cells and epithelial cells in the colon using the xCell algorithm applied to the RNA-seq data. The xCell enrichment scores, which estimate the proportion of cell types for each sample, indicated that the levels of macrophages, monocytes, neutrophils, and dendritic cells (DC) were significantly higher in the colons of DSS + PBS group mice compared to NC group. hUC-MSC treatment reduced the enrichment of these innate immune cells in the colon to varying degrees; however, the differences were not statistically significant. In contrast, intestinal epithelial cells (IEC) were almost completely depleted by DSS induction. Remarkably, hUC-MSC treatment significantly restored IEC enrichment.

text: The induction of ER stress is a hallmark of colitis and contribute to the progression of inflammation by triggering IEC death. To investigate the involvement of ER stress in hUC-MSC treatment for UC, we analyzed the overlap between the “Response to endoplasmic reticulum stress (RERS)” gene set and DEGs induced by DSS + PBS or DSS + MSC. Specifically, compared to healthy controls, DSS induction significantly altered the expression of 29 RERS genes, 21 of which were restored to near-normal levels following MSC treatment (and, see for a color version of this Functional annotations of these DSS induced RERS-related DEGs via Gene Ontology (GO) analyses revealed enrichment in biological processes such as response to ER stress, response to topologically incorrect protein, response to unfolded protein, autophagy, intrinsic apoptotic signaling pathway in response to ER stress, regulation of inflammatory response, positive regulation of apoptotic signaling pathway, and IRE1-mediated unfolded protein response. The PPI network of the DSS-induced RERS-related DEGs was shown in. The expression levels of the key RERS genes were further validated in colon tissues from DSS + PBS and DSS + MSC group mice. Casp12, a caspase family member specifically activated by ER stress, was upregulated in the DSS + PBS group but returned to baseline levels with MSC treatment. Similarly, Nupr1, an ER stress-inducible transcription factor,, was significantly upregulated in the DSS + PBS group but was reversed in the DSS + MSC group. The expression of interferon-γ (IFN-γ), a key cytokine involved in IBD, was markedly reduced in the hUC-MSC treated mice compared to only DSS-induced mice. In both human and mice, anterior gradient 2 (Agr2) deficiency is associated with mucus barrier defect, impaired ability to mitigate ER stress, and infantile-onset IBD. Consistent with these findings, Agr2 expression was downregulated in DSS-induced colitis model, whereas MSC treatment restored its expression. Bcl2l1, a key mediator of ER stress–induced apoptosis, was upregulated at both mRNA and protein levels in the DSS + PBS group but was restored to baseline levels following MSC treatment. During ER stress, IRE1 activation induces splicing of Xbp1 mRNA, generating spliced Xbp1 (Xbp1 -S), which plays a critical role in damage repair. Compared with DSS-induced colitis model group, hUC-MSC treatment increased IRE1 Ser-724 phosphorylation levels, enhanced Xbp1- S mRNA abundance, and Xbp1-S protein expression, while reducing unspliced Xbp1 (Xbp1- U)mRNA levels. These findings suggest that MSC transplantation mitigates ER stress-induced intestinal injury by promoting Xbp1 splicing.

section_title: hUC-MSC treatment suppressed pathological ER stress induced by DSS

text: The predominant colitogenic cytokine, TNF-α, has been reported to serve as a physiological ER stress inducer in IECs. We analyzed the overlap between the “RERS” gene set and DEGs in IECs from TNF-α treated mice (GSE268933). Specifically, TNF-α induction significantly altered the expression of 20 RERS genes compared to healthy controls, including Bcl2l11, Nupr1, and Cebpb, which were also upregulated in DSS-induced colitis in mice. Recent studies have increasingly highlighted that the therapeutic efficacy of MSC transplantation is primarily mediated through paracrine signaling. To further explore this mechanism, we investigated the protective effects of MSC-conditioned medium (MSC-CM) on TNF-α-induced intestinal epithelial cell damage in vitro. Apoptosis analysis revealed that MSC-CM effectively suppressed TNF-α-induced cell apoptosis. qPCR and Western blotting analyses showed MSC-CM inhibited TNF-α-induced BCL2L11 expression. Mechanically, both IRE1 phosphorylation and Xbp1 mRNA splicing were promoted by MSC-CM treatment. However, the protective effects of MSC-CM were abrogated upon addition of the Xbp1 splicing-specific inhibitor 4μ8C. These findings suggest that MSC-CM exerts its protective effects on TNF-α-induced intestinal epithelial cell apoptosis by promoting Xbp1 mRNA splicing, thereby alleviating ER stress and reducing cell death.

section_title: hUC-MSC inhibited TNF-α-induced ER stress and intestinal epithelial cell apoptosis via paracrine signaling

text: MSCs derived from various tissue origins or administered through different transplantation routes have exhibited distinct therapeutic potentials in different disease models. This study revealed the therapeutic efficacy of hUC-MSC, delivered via intraperitoneal injection, in mitigating epithelial injury and inflammation in a DSS-induced colitis model. hUC-MSCs’ treatment significantly alleviated the disruption of the intestinal epithelial barrier, restored crypt structure, and reduced inflammatory cell infiltration, as evidenced by histological and immunohistochemical analyses. Previous studies have shown the potentials of MSCs and MSC-derived products in the treatment of UC. The therapeutic mechanisms include immunomodulation, promotion of intestinal epithelial cell regeneration, and normalization of the intestinal microbiome. In this study, hUC-MSCs were demonstrated to modulate ER stress pathways by promoting Xbp1 mRNA splicing, thereby reducing the expression of key pro-apoptotic genes such as Bcl2l11(Bim). These effects were observed both in DSS-induced UC mouse model and in vitro TNF-α-induced ER stress and apoptosis in cultured intestinal epithelial cells. Collectively, these findings provide novel insights into the mechanisms by which hUC-MSCs and their secreted factors alleviate ER stress–induced epithelial injury and inflammation, offering a promising therapeutic strategy for UC. The XBP1 pathway is critical for maintaining gut barrier function and immune balance. The pathogenesis of UC is thought to result from a complex interplay of genetic, environmental, microbial, and immune factors. Genetic variants in XBP1 increase the risk of UC, while certain microbial or dietary compounds—such as trierixin from Streptomyces —can suppress its normal activity in epithelial cells. Animal studies show that loss of Xbp1 in intestinal epithelial cells triggers spontaneous inflammation and worsens colitis. Additionally, the IRE1/XBP1 pathway contributes to intestinal homeostasis by augmenting cytokine production in group 3 innate lymphoid cells (ILC3s), a key cell type for mucosal defense; disrupting this pathway in ILC3s reduces the expression of protective cytokines like Il22, leading to increased vulnerability to infections and colitis. Earlier network analyses found that XBP1 levels are increased in UC and correlate with more severe disease and higher macrophage infiltration, but with fewer CD8 + T cells. However, these studies did not account for differences between the spliced (active) and unspliced forms Xbp1. Because these forms have distinct roles in epithelial versus immune cells, overlooking this distinction may explain the inconsistencies among previous studies. In this study, intraperitoneal injection of hUC-MSCs significantly increased Xbp1 mRNA splicing in intestinal epithelial cells, which may play a critical protective role against UC pathogenesis. This finding demonstrates the importance of Xbp1 splicing levels and cell type–specific functions in UC and reveals a novel mechanism for MSC therapy in treatment of colitis. In active UC, the rate of apoptosis of epithelial cells is significantly elevated. DSS results in the death of epithelial cells, leading to the disruption of the epithelial monolayer lining. This disruption allows the entry of luminal bacteria and associated antigens into the mucosa and causes an altered mucosal immune response.

text: This finding demonstrates the importance of Xbp1 splicing levels and cell type–specific functions in UC and reveals a novel mechanism for MSC therapy in treatment of colitis. In active UC, the rate of apoptosis of epithelial cells is significantly elevated. DSS results in the death of epithelial cells, leading to the disruption of the epithelial monolayer lining. This disruption allows the entry of luminal bacteria and associated antigens into the mucosa and causes an altered mucosal immune response. Mucosal healing has become a key therapeutic goal for treatment of patients with UC suggested by its strong association with improved clinical outcomes and long-term disease remission. A recent Immunity study further demonstrated that XBP1 safeguards the intestinal mucus barrier and suppresses necroptosis-induced colitis, underscoring its essential role in maintaining epithelial homeostasis and barrier function. Together with our findings, these data highlight the multifaceted protective effects of XBP1 signaling in colitis. Compared to conventional anti-inflammatory therapies, targeting downstream inflammatory mediators, hUC-MSCs offer a more effective therapeutic strategy by addressing both epithelial damage and immune dysregulation, a promising treatment for UC.

text: This study also has limitations. The DSS-induced colitis model, although widely used, does not fully recapitulate the chronic relapsing nature and multifactorial pathogenesis of human UC. Furthermore, our experiments were limited to preclinical models, and the therapeutic efficacy of hUC-MSCs in human UC patients requires careful evaluation in clinical settings. These caveats should be acknowledged when interpreting our findings. From a translational perspective, while MSC-based therapies hold promise, several challenges remain before clinical application. Critical considerations include ensuring the long-term safety of MSC administration, determining optimal dosing regimens, and assessing the durability of therapeutic benefits. Potential risks such as immunogenicity, tumorigenicity, and unintended differentiation must be addressed in future studies. Additionally, regulatory and manufacturing challenges, including standardization of MSC isolation and expansion protocols, will influence the feasibility of clinical translation. Addressing these issues will be essential for advancing hUC-MSC therapy from experimental models to clinical practice.

text: Our current study revealed that intraperitoneally injection of hUC-MSC alleviated DSS-induced colitis in mice. In vivo tracking experiment demonstrated that injected MSCs can homing to both the epithelium and lamina propria of the inflamed colon. RNA-sequencing and subsequent qPCR and western blotting analysis confirmed that hUC-MSCs confer protection in UC through the modulation of ER stress and promotion of Xbp1 splicing in colon epithelial cells. Our study has strongly suggested the clinical potential of hUC-MSCs in management of UC. It also suggested targeting ER stress in developing future therapeutic strategies for UC.

text: Corneal wound healing is a highly orchestrated and intricate process that progresses through several overlapping phases: inflammation, proliferation, migration, and remodeling. A notable early event following corneal epithelial injury is the rapid onset of keratocyte apoptosis, occurring within minutes to a few hours post‐injury. This apoptosis response appears to be a key initiating factor in the corneal wound healing process, particularly after injury or refractive surgical procedures. Although keratocyte apoptosis occurs during the inflammatory phase of wound healing, its biological role remains unclear, as apoptosis is generally regarded as a non‐inflammatory form of cell death. Pyroptosis is characterized by the release of inflammatory cytokines, such as IL‐1 and IL‐18, which may serve a functional role during the early inflammatory phase of wound healing. Notably, keratocyte death has been identified using TUNEL assays, a method that detects DNA fragmentation, which includes events seen in both apoptotic and pyroptotic cell death, suggesting a potential overlap between these mechanisms in early corneal wound responses. Recently, two studies have reported pyroptosis in human corneal fibroblasts. In both cases, pyroptosis was confirmed by measuring intracellular markers such as cleaved IL‐1β and GSDMD. Zheng et al. further demonstrated cell membrane disruption in human keratocytes, indicative of pyroptosis. However, we argue that additional data are needed to solidify these conclusions. For instance, the release of cleaved IL‐1β should be measured, and typical morphological changes such as nuclear condensation and bubble‐like cell bursts, which are hallmarks of pyroptosis, should be documented. Nigericin, an antibiotic derived from Streptomyces hygroscopicus, is a well‐established reagent for inducing pyroptosis. It acts as an ionophore, causing potassium efflux from cells, which leads to NLRP3 inflammasome activation and subsequent pyroptosis. NLRP3 inflammasome activation is a key player in the immune response to bacterial infections. This process mimics certain aspects of bacterial infection during corneal injury, as many bacterial pathogens produce toxins that disrupt ion homeostasis and membrane integrity. Examining the response of exposing keratocytes to nigericin, offers a valuable approach to study the potential role of pyroptosis in the inflammatory phase of wound healing. Paraptosis, unlike pyroptosis, is a non‐inflammatory form of cell death characterized by large vacuoles arising from the swelling of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and mitochondria. While the precise origin of these vacuoles remains unclear, paraptosis is distinguished by molecular markers such as increased autophagic markers beclin‐1 and LC3BII, caspase‐independent pathways, and increased ER stress. A study has found that cobalt (CoCl2)‐induced hypoxia causes human corneal epithelial cell (HCE) death by paraptosis. Attenuating paraptosis in HCE cells promoted corneal wound healing. No studies have investigated paraptosis in keratocytes, highlighting the need for further research to understand its role in corneal wound healing. Keratocytes are crucial for maintaining corneal transparency and structure. While their response to injury often involves apoptosis, a well‐characterized process in corneal wound healing, the role of alternative cell death pathways, such as pyroptosis and paraptosis, remains poorly understood. Investigating these pathways could provide insights into corneal wound healing mechanisms and potential therapeutic targets.
title: Nigericin Induces Paraptosis‐Like Cell Death Instead of Pyroptosis in Corneal Keratocytes

text: No studies have investigated paraptosis in keratocytes, highlighting the need for further research to understand its role in corneal wound healing. Keratocytes are crucial for maintaining corneal transparency and structure. While their response to injury often involves apoptosis, a well‐characterized process in corneal wound healing, the role of alternative cell death pathways, such as pyroptosis and paraptosis, remains poorly understood. Investigating these pathways could provide insights into corneal wound healing mechanisms and potential therapeutic targets. This study aims to identify the occurrence of pyroptosis and paraptosis in keratocytes in vitro and to explore the underlying mechanisms.

text: The procedure for isolating and culturing primary keratocytes was carried out following the methods described earlier. Human corneal tissue was obtained from the Tissue Establishment, Eye Bank Umeå, at the University Hospital of Umeå, Sweden. The tissue was donated by deceased individuals who had, prior to their passing, consented to donate their corneas for both transplantation and research in accordance with Swedish law. Corneal grafts that were either unused for transplantation or leftover tissue from successful transplant surgeries were provided to the laboratory for research purposes. All these samples were anonymized; only labeled with the donors' sex and age. The protocol was reviewed by the Regional Ethical Review Board in Umeå, who deemed it exempt from requiring approval (2010‐373‐31 M). This research adhered to the guidelines of the Declaration of Helsinki. The isolation and culturing of cells were conducted following previously outlined methods. To eliminate any residual epithelial or endothelial cells, corneal samples were scraped with a sterile scalpel and subsequently washed using sterile Hanks' balanced salt solution (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA). The remaining stromal tissue was then sectioned into small pieces (1–2 mm 2) with a scalpel and digested overnight at 37°C with collagenase (1 mg/mL; Sigma, St. Louis, MO, USA). After digestion, the cell suspension was centrifuged, and the pellet was cultured in DMEM/F‐12 medium (Gibco, Carlsbad, CA, USA) containing 2% fetal bovine serum (FBS; Gibco, Carlsbad, CA, USA), and maintained in a humidified incubator at 37°C with 5% CO 2. The culture medium was refreshed every 3 days until the cells reached full confluence. Once confluent, the cells were harvested using 0.05% Trypsin–EDTA and subcultured at a 1:3 ratio. Cells were passaged up to passage 2, after which they were cryopreserved in liquid nitrogen. In this study, different donor cells were used for each experiment, with passages 3 to 7 employed for experimental procedures. The cultured cells maintained their keratocyte phenotype, as validated by our previous studies.

text: The chemicals were purchased from different sources: Nigericin from InvivoGen (USA), Cycloheximide (CHX) solution from Sigma‐Aldrich (St. Louis, MO, USA), Caspase Inhibitor Z‐VAD‐FMK from Promega (Fitchburg, WI, USA), ER stress inhibitor 4‐Phenylbutyric acid (4‐PBA) and autophagy inhibitory 3‐Methyladenine (3‐MA) from Medchemexpress (NJ, USA). text: To quantify IL‐1β levels in cell culture supernatants, we utilized the Human IL‐1β/IL‐1F2 DuoSet ELISA kit (R&D Systems, DY201). Cell culture supernatants were collected and centrifuged at 1000 × g for 10 min to remove cellular debris. The clarified supernatants were then aliquoted and stored at −80°C until analysis. The ELISA procedure was conducted according to the manufacturer's instructions. Briefly, 96‐well microplates were coated with the capture antibody and incubated overnight at room temperature. Following a blocking step, standards and samples were added to the wells and incubated for 2 h. After washing, a biotinylated detection antibody was added and incubated for 2 h. Streptavidin‐HRP was then added, followed by substrate solution. The reaction was terminated with stop solution, and absorbance was measured at 450 nm with wavelength correction at 540 nm using a microplate reader. IL‐1β concentrations in the samples were interpolated from the standard curve using a four‐parameter logistic (4‐PL) curve fit.

text: Keratocytes were seeded into 96‐well plates at a density of 5000 cells per well. After 24 h of incubation, the cells were cultured in DMEM/F‐12 media (Gibco, Carlsbad, CA), supplemented with 2% FBS (Sigma‐Aldrich, 0001648078, USA), and treated with different concentration of Nigericin (InvivoGen) for 24 h. Following treatment, 50 μL of XTT mix from the Cell Proliferation Kit II (Roche, 11 465 015 001, Germany) was added to the wells, and absorbance was measured at 480 and 690 nm after 3 h. The difference in absorbance between 480 and 690 nm was used to calculate the cell viability. The cell viability in Nigericin treated groups was calculated by dividing its absorbance by that of the untreated group.

text: Nigericin‐treated keratocytes were analyzed for their cell live/dead ratio using the LIVE/DEAD Cell Imaging Kit (488/570) (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, USA), following the manufacturer's guidelines. In brief, keratocytes were exposed to different concentrations of Nigericin for 24 h; the Live Green and Dead Red reagents were mixed to prepare a 2× stock solution, which was then applied to the cells at room temperature for 15 min. Fluorescence imaging was performed using the Incucyte S3 Live‐Cell Analysis System (Sartorius, Ann Arbor, MI, USA). Cells with green fluorescence were identified as live cells, while those with red fluorescence were categorized as dead. Images from five random fields per well were captured using a fluorescence microscope, and at least 500 cells per condition were counted across three independent experiments.

text: The mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP) in keratocytes was assessed using tetramethylrhodamine, methyl ester (TMRM, ThermoFisher, I34361), a dye that is cell‐permeable and selectively accumulates in mitochondria with functional membrane potentials, as per the manufacturer's guidelines. In summary, keratocytes were cultured in a 6‐well plate for observation. The cells were then incubated with TMRM for 30 min at 37°C in the absence of light, followed by three washes with PBS. Fluorescence imaging was performed using the Incucyte S3 Live‐Cell Analysis System (Sartorius, Ann Arbor, MI, USA). All imaging parameters (e.g., laser power, exposure time, gain) were maintained constant across all samples to ensure comparability. For image analysis, acquired images were processed using ImageJ/Fiji. Regions of interest (ROIs) were delineated manually. The mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) within each ROI was measured to represent the mitochondrial TMRM signal, which correlates with MMP. Data from at least three independent biological replicates were collected.

text: For western blot analysis, 1 × 10 5 keratocytes were seeded into 6‐well plates in DMEM/F‐12 medium supplemented with 2% FBS. At the end of the experiment, the cells were washed with PBS and frozen at −80°C before extraction (three experimental replicates per group). Cells were freeze‐thawed and further lysed in RIPA (radioimmunoprecipitation) lysis buffer (Thermo Fisher, Waltham, MA, USA) with added protease and phosphatase inhibitors (Sigma, St. Louis, MO, USA, #P1860). Total protein concentration was measured using the BCA assay (Thermo Fisher, Waltham, MA, USA). Protein samples (20 μg) were separated on SDS‐polyacrylamide gels and transferred onto PVDF membranes (Thermo Fisher, Waltham, MA, USA). Membranes were blocked in 5% bovine serum albumin in TBS‐T for 1 h before staining with primary antibodies overnight at 4°C. After rinsing, secondary HRP‐conjugated antibodies were applied for 1 h at room temperature, followed by incubation in ECL solution, and analyzed using the Odyssey Fc Dual‐Mode Imaging System (LI‐COR Biotechnology, Nebraska, USA). Image J software (NIH) was used for densitometric analysis. β‐actin served as an internal control, and the analysis was conducted by dividing the intensity of the target protein by the intensity of β‐actin. text: Keratocytes were seeded at a density of 0.5 × 10 4 per well into an 8‐chamber polystyrene treated glass slide (Falcon ref. 354 108) in DMEM/F‐12 medium supplemented with 2% FBS, and cultured overnight. After treatment with 10 μM Nigericin for 6 h, the culture medium was removed from the wells, followed by two washes with PBS. Cells were then fixed in 3.7% Formaldehyde in PBS for 10 min at room temperature. After washed in PBS, cold methanol was used to permeabilize the cells. Blocking was achieved by adding 3% FBS and incubating for 15 min at room temperature. For staining, cells were incubated with Alexa Fluor 555 MG130 antibody (1:10 dilution) per well and TGN46 antibody (1:200 dilution) per well for 1 h at room temperature. In the MG130 staining, the use of a secondary antibody is not necessary, as the primary antibody is directly conjugated to the fluorescent dye. For TGN46 staining, secondary IgG conjugated with Alexa Fluor 555 (1:300 dilution) was applied for 1 h at room temperature. After a final wash, counter‐stain the nuclei by adding Hoechst solution 33 342 (Sigma‐Aldrich Cat. No. B2261). Finally, cells were washed and images were captured using the Leica Thunder Widefield Microscope (Leica AG, Heerbrugg, Switzerland). All antibodies used are summarized in Table.

text: Proteomics analysis was conducted following our established protocols, encompassing sample preparation, protein separation, identification, and validation. Raw data was searched against the homo sapiens UniProt FASTA (proteome identifier [ID] UP000005640) using FragPipe(version 18), LFQ‐MBR workflow was employed for label‐free quantification. Proteins identified from contaminants and decoys were removed. Only proteins that quantified in more than one replicate in each group were retained for further analysis. R (version 4.2.2) was used for statistical analysis and volcano plots. To reduce technical variation, data was normalized using the vsn package. Protein differential expression was evaluated using the limma package. Differences in protein abundances were statistically determined using the Student's t‐test moderated by Benjamini–Hochberg's method. Differences in expression between proteins were considered to be statistically significant if they exhibited a minimum two‐fold change in abundance (i.e., a fold change ≥ 2 or ≤ 0.5) and an adjusted p ‐value ≤ 0.05.

text: Morphologically, we observed pyroptosis‐like cell death in keratocytes cultured in vitro. Using time‐lapse microscopy, we captured rapid cell lysis characterized by membrane rupture and nuclear condensation (Video). This cell death was accompanied by a rapid loss of mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP) in cells exhibiting pyroptotic morphology, indicating potential mitochondrial dysfunction (Furthermore, analysis of the culture supernatants from cell cultures with pyroptotic cells revealed significantly elevated levels of cleaved IL‐1β, supporting the activation of a pyroptosis‐like pathway (To further study the mechanisms involved, we aimed to establish a reproducible model to study this form of cell death in keratocytes. Pyroptosis‐like cell death events were sporadically observed in our live cell imaging experiments, occurring in approximately 10% of cases. These events were seen in both control and treated keratocytes using the Incucyte system. We investigated several potential triggers, including serum concentration, hypoxia, mechanical loading, and surface stiffness, but none consistently induced pyroptosis‐like death. Additionally, a standard protocol involving LPS priming followed by ATP stimulation was applied, yet it also failed to reliably elicit pyroptosis‐like cell death in keratocytes.

text: Nigericin is a known pyroptosis inducer. We found that nigericin induces keratocyte cell death in a dose‐dependent manner, with the highest dose (30 μM) showing the most significant cell death, as confirmed by XTT viability assays and live‐dead cell staining (Distinct morphological changes in keratocytes were observed, notably extensive vacuolation visible under light microscopy (Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) further verified the presence of pronounced intracellular vacuolation, while scanning electron microscopy (SEM) imaging revealed corresponding changes in the cell membrane (The holes seen in the SEM images represent intracellular vacuolation rather than actual cell membrane ruptures, as they were artifacts introduced during SEM sample preparation. Importantly, the cell membrane remained intact during vacuole formation, as evidenced by Figure (1 μM nigericin treatment), Figure (1–6 h with 10 μM nigericin), and Figure (TEM images).

text: The morphological changes induced by nigericin in keratocytes suggested a paraptosis‐like cell death pathway. To confirm this, several molecular markers of paraptosis were analyzed. First, nigericin treatment did not result in caspase‐3 cleavage, and cells treated with the pan‐caspase inhibitor z‐VAD‐fmk remained susceptible to nigericin‐induced cytotoxicity, confirming a caspase‐independent process (Despite paraptosis often being associated with endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, nigericin treatment did not elevate the ER stress marker BiP, nor did the ER stress inhibitor 4‐PBA prevent vacuole formation (Cell viability assay confirmed that 4‐PBA did not rescue nigericin‐induced cell death (As positive controls, ER stress inducers Thapsigargin (2.5 μg/mL) and Tunicamycin (0.05 μM) effectively induced BiP expression in keratocytes (Additionally, nigericin treatment significantly increased autophagy marker LC3‐II levels, while Beclin‐1 expression remained unchanged, indicating that autophagy initiation was not activated (Using 3‐MA, a specific autophagy inhibitor, did not rescue cell viability, as measured by cell confluency 24 h after treatments (Interestingly, inhibiting protein synthesis with cycloheximide (CHX) significantly reduced the cytotoxic effects of nigericin on keratocytes (This observation further suggests the involvement of a paraptosis pathway, as CHX has been reported to effectively inhibit paraptosis. We observed disorganized mitochondrial cristae in keratocytes treated with nigericin, as shown in the TEM images (Figure, upper panel). This structural alteration was accompanied by a significant loss of mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP) in the treated cells, further supporting mitochondrial dysfunction as part of the cellular response to nigericin exposure (Figure, lower panel, To further validate our observation of nigericin‐induced paraptosis, we treated keratocytes with xanthohumol (XN), a compound we previously confirmed to induce paraptosis in cells. Similar to nigericin, XN treatment led to dose‐dependent cell death, extensive vacuolization, and an increased accumulation of LC3‐II in keratocytes (

text: To address why nigericin, a known pyroptosis inducer, instead induces paraptosis‐like cell death in keratocytes, we conducted proteomic profiling on keratocytes from five donors. The data revealed that, while keratocytes express GSDME, three out of five donors lacked detectable expression of GSDMD, and for all donors NLRP3, ASC, and caspase‐1 were below the limit of detection (These findings were corroborated by western blot analysis. Western blot analysis confirmed these results; whereas NLRP3, ASC, and caspase‐1 could be robustly detected in macrophage lysates, they remained undetectable in keratocyte samples, ruling out technical failure of the antibodies and validating their true absence in keratocytes. To rule out the possibility that inflammasome components, such as NLRP3 and ASC, require stimulation, keratocytes were pretreated with LPS and IL‐1β, but no detectable expression of NLRP3 or ASC was observed (data not shown). Corresponding to the proteomics data, expression of uncleaved Caspase‐3 and GSDME in keratocytes were confirmed by western blot. However, neither of them was cleaved upon nigericin treatment, suggesting that the pyroptosis pathway mediated by Caspase‐3 and GSDME was not active. As a positive control, we confirmed that nigericin successfully induces pyroptosis in macrophages, as evidenced by characteristic morphological changes and the cleavage of Caspase‐3, and GSDME (Notably, cleavage of Caspase‐3 and GSDME was absent at later time points (3 h and 6 h post‐treatment) when pyroptosis occurred. This may be due to the loss of pyroptotic macrophages from the culture, as these cells are rapidly eliminated during the process. Consequently, the cell lysates used for western blot analysis were likely derived from surviving cells that did not undergo pyroptosis and therefore contained predominantly uncleaved Caspase‐3 and GSDME.

section_title: Keratocytes Lack the Canonical Executors of Pyroptosis

text: Nigericin has been shown to mediate NLRP3 inflammasome activation via disruption of the trans‐Golgi network. In line with these observations, we found that nigericin not only caused dramatic disruption of the trans‐Golgi network but also affected the cis‐Golgi bodies in keratocytes (Additionally, we observed multilamellar vesicles within the vacuoles of keratocytes. Upon nigericin treatment, the structure of these vacuoles became enlarged and dispersed, with a noticeable reduction in the number of layers compared to untreated cells (This suggests that the multilamellar vesicles are one of the sources of the vacuoles induced by nigericin. Lysosomes display a clustered distribution within the cytoplasm in untreated cells. In contrast, lysosomes in the nigericin‐treated group are more dispersed, suggesting that nigericin treatment influences lysosomal dynamics and possibly reflects cellular responses to lysosomal stress.
title: Nigericin Induces Paraptosis‐Like Cell Death Instead of Pyroptosis in Corneal Keratocytes
section_title: Nigericin‐Induced Disruption of Membrane Structures in Cellular Organelles

text: Consistent with previous studies reporting pyroptosis in keratocytes, we observed pyroptosis‐like changes in keratocytes. Our findings provide additional evidence supporting that keratocytes can undergo pyroptosis, as indicated by the release of IL‐1β and characteristic morphological changes. However, our western blot and proteomics analyses revealed that human keratocytes lack canonical pyroptosis executors, such as GSDMD and Caspase‐1. This suggests that keratocytes may utilize alternative pathways to undergo pyroptosis. Further studies are needed to uncover these alternative pathways. While nigericin can effectively induce pyroptosis in macrophages, our study shows that it fails to do so in keratocytes. Research has shown that nigericin‐induced Golgi network dispersion is crucial for activating the NLRP3 inflammasome and pyroptosis. We observed similar Golgi network dispersion in keratocytes treated with nigericin. However, the keratocytes we examined lack the necessary components to fully execute pyroptosis. There is a possibility that unexplored signaling pathways are responsible for the pyroptosis‐like cell death observed in cultured keratocytes. Nigericin is widely recognized for its ability to induce NLRP3 inflammasome activation, which mirrors a key aspect of the host immune response during bacterial infections. In corneal injury, the innate immune system often responds to microbial components and toxins by activating the NLRP3 inflammasome, leading to the release of pro‐inflammatory cytokines like IL‐1β. While the keratocytes of our study lacked key components of the pyroptotic pathway, the use of nigericin can still provide valuable insight into the cellular stress and inflammatory responses that occur during bacterial infections in corneal wounds. Although we observed a paraptosis‐like form of cell death, rather than pyroptosis, the disruption of the Golgi network and induction of vacuolization in keratocytes treated with nigericin may reflect cellular responses to bacterial invasion. The observed increase in LC3‐II levels, without a corresponding change in Beclin‐1 expression, suggests that nigericin treatment may affect autophagic flux at the level of autophagosome processing rather than initiation. Typically, Beclin‐1 is involved in the early stages of autophagy, particularly autophagosome formation. The lack of Beclin‐1 upregulation, alongside increased LC3‐II and disrupted lysosome organization, points to a possible disruption in autophagosome‐lysosome fusion, leading to LC3‐II accumulation. This impaired autophagic flux may contribute to cellular stress responses, aligning with the paraptosis‐like vacuolization observed in keratocytes under nigericin treatment. Given that 3‐MA primarily inhibits early stages of autophagy, it is possible that nigericin induces LC3‐II accumulation through a pathway that bypasses the initial steps impacted by 3‐MA, further supporting the hypothesis of impaired autophagic flux, rather than enhanced autophagic initiation. This observation underscores the need for further studies into the impact of nigericin on autophagy‐related pathways in keratocytes. We found that nigericin‐treated cells exhibit more prominently visible and condensed mitochondrial cristae. This enhanced visibility is likely a result of nigericin's impact on mitochondrial morphology and function. Acting as a K + /H + antiporter, nigericin disrupts ion homeostasis across the mitochondrial inner membrane, which can induce structural alterations.
title: Nigericin Induces Paraptosis‐Like Cell Death Instead of Pyroptosis in Corneal Keratocytes

text: This observation underscores the need for further studies into the impact of nigericin on autophagy‐related pathways in keratocytes. We found that nigericin‐treated cells exhibit more prominently visible and condensed mitochondrial cristae. This enhanced visibility is likely a result of nigericin's impact on mitochondrial morphology and function. Acting as a K + /H + antiporter, nigericin disrupts ion homeostasis across the mitochondrial inner membrane, which can induce structural alterations. Supporting this, we observed a significant reduction in mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP) in nigericin‐treated cells, indicative of mitochondrial dysfunction. In contrast, untreated cells displayed a strong MMP signal, consistent with normal mitochondrial activity. Therefore, although the cristae in nigericin‐treated cells appear more defined, this likely reflects pathological remodeling rather than preserved mitochondrial integrity. Our study demonstrated paraptosis‐like cell death in the absence of significant ER stress markers, a notable finding given the frequent association between ER stress and paraptosis in previous studies. Other key observations, including a lack of caspase‐3 activation, impaired autophagy, and characteristic morphological changes, further support a paraptotic cell death pathway. The absence of ER stress markers in this context suggests that while ER stress often accompanies paraptosis, it may not be an essential trigger. Rather, ER stress could be a secondary response to paraptotic events, highlighting a more nuanced relationship between ER stress and paraptotic cell death.
title: Nigericin Induces Paraptosis‐Like Cell Death Instead of Pyroptosis in Corneal Keratocytes

text: In summary, our findings indicate that nigericin induces paraptosis‐like cell death in keratocytes, rather than the expected pyroptosis. The absence of key inflammasome components, such as NLRP3, ASC, as well as pyroptosis executor GSDMD, coupled with the distinct morphological changes observed, suggest that keratocytes may employ alternative cell death pathways in response to stressors like nigericin. This study opens new avenues for exploring non‐canonical mechanisms of cell death in corneal wound healing and highlights the need for further studies into the signaling pathways that govern these processes. Understanding the precise nature of keratocyte death could lead to novel therapeutic strategies aimed at improving wound healing outcomes and mitigating excessive inflammation in corneal diseases.
title: Nigericin Induces Paraptosis‐Like Cell Death Instead of Pyroptosis in Corneal Keratocytes

text: While our study provides valuable insights into the mechanisms of nigericin‐induced cell death in keratocytes, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, our experiments were conducted in vitro using cultured human keratocytes, which may not fully recapitulate the complex microenvironment of the cornea in vivo. The absence of immune and inflammatory responses in our model may influence the observed cell death pathways, potentially differing from those occurring in a physiological setting. Second, although our proteomics and western blot analyses identified the lack of canonical pyroptosis executors, further functional validation using genetic knockout or knockdown models would strengthen these findings. Additionally, while we observed LC3‐II accumulation, the precise mechanisms linking autophagy dysregulation to paraptosis‐like cell death remain to be fully elucidated. Future studies using real‐time autophagic flux assays could provide deeper mechanistic insights. Moreover, other features of paraptosis—including the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), proteasome inhibition, calcium overload, and activation of kinases such as MAPK or JNK—were not fully explored in our study. Additional experiments assessing these hallmarks in nigericin‐treated keratocytes would help to better define the paraptosis pathway. In particular, studying whether nigericin treatment leads to activation of MAPK or JNK kinases would be valuable. Furthermore, testing whether inhibition or silencing of MAPK, JNK, or SHP2 (an upstream regulator of the MAPK cascade and previously linked to paraptosis) can rescue the cytotoxic effects of nigericin, as described in other paraptosis studies, could provide critical mechanistic insights. Lastly, our study primarily focuses on morphological and molecular markers of cell death; however, exploring upstream signaling pathways that trigger this process could further refine our understanding of nigericin‐induced cytotoxicity in keratocytes.

text: As one of the redox-active metal ions essential for human survival, copper maintains a dynamic equilibrium in the human body. Environmental factors can induce abnormal copper homeostasis, which is copper deficiency or copper overload, and imbalance in copper homeostasis can induce abnormal cellular autophagy, cytotoxicity, etc. Recently, the team of Peter Tsvetkov and Todd R. Golub at the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard University has proposed for the first time a novel mode of cell death, copper-induced cell death, which occurs mainly by the mechanism of excess copper ions The main mechanism for this is that excess copper ions bind to thioredoxin in the tricarboxylic acid cycle pathway, resulting in abnormal levels of thioredoxin and loss of iron-sulfur cluster proteins, thereby triggering a proteotoxic stress response and ultimately causing cell death. Evidence suggests that although copper-induced cell death is distinct from the known regulated cell death (RCD) modalities such as apoptosis, autophagy, cell scorching and iron death, it still shares common hallmarks and characteristics of different forms of RCD, such as induction of reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, inhibition of the ubiquitin-proteasome system The RCD is a common marker and characteristic of different forms of RCD, such as induction of ROS, inhibition of the ubiquitin-proteasome system, etc. Because copper is involved in a variety of biological activities in the body, including oxidative stress, lipid metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis, imbalances in copper homeostasis are closely associated with the development of many diseases, including neurodegenerative disorders, diabetes, and tumors. Wilson‘s disease, for example, is caused by copper overload due to ATP7B deficiency, which induces other system dysfunctions such as liver and nervous system. α-Ssynuclein aggregation is thought to be an important participant in the pathogenesis of Parkinson’s disease, so it has been proposed that when copper is overloaded, it causes neuronal cell death and α-synuclein aggregation, inducing Parkinson’s disease. Besides, Zn deficiency and simultaneous increase in Cu levels is associated with elevated levels of oxidative stress, which may exacerbate diabetic microangiopathy. While increased levels of free Cu ions may be associated with glycosylation and the release of Cu ions from the Cu-binding sites of proteins, so the application of Zn supplements and selective Cu chelators may help to alleviate oxidative stress and prevent further exacerbation of diabetic retinopathy. Cancer, a difficult disease for current medicine to overcome, has been a hot topic in the field of research. Recently, it has been found that elevated copper levels are closely associated with the development of several malignant tumors. Therefore, adjustment of copper homeostasis has also become one of the strategies to combat tumors. Currently, there are 2 main mechanisms, one is to use copper complexes to reduce copper ion content and inhibit tumor cell proliferation; the other is to transfer copper ions from extracellular to intracellular via its carrier, which increases intracellular Cu 2 + levels and induces oxidative stress, resulting in tumor cell death. Thus, the use of copper-induced cell death as a target or the use of copper therapy is expected to be a new way of cancer treatment. The mechanism of copper metabolism and copper-induced cell death is still unclear.
title: Knowledge mapping of copper-induced cell death: A bibliometric study from 2012 to 2022

text: Currently, there are 2 main mechanisms, one is to use copper complexes to reduce copper ion content and inhibit tumor cell proliferation; the other is to transfer copper ions from extracellular to intracellular via its carrier, which increases intracellular Cu 2 + levels and induces oxidative stress, resulting in tumor cell death. Thus, the use of copper-induced cell death as a target or the use of copper therapy is expected to be a new way of cancer treatment. The mechanism of copper metabolism and copper-induced cell death is still unclear. Therefore, it is of great significance and prospect to further study the mechanism of copper metabolism homeostasis and related signaling pathways. The application of copper chelators is expected to become an important part of adjuvant therapy for a variety of diseases. As the concept of copper-induced cell death has just been introduced, researchers are still in an imperfect state in terms of previous research in the field, so it is a major challenge for researchers to effectively sort through the past literature and further explore the deeper research directions in the field. As a discipline that efficiently counts the current status and evolution of the literature in the field and predicts cutting-edge trends, bibliometrics can effectively capture the overall trends in the field and provide insights into the hotspots of research, thus showing researchers the latest research trends. Many researchers have used bibliometrics to explore the content of research in this field. To date, no bibliometrics study on copper induced-cell death has been conducted, so this study aims to evaluate the literature on copper-induced cell death in the last decade using Cite Space software. The analysis will be carried out in 5 areas: annual publications, countries/regions and institutions, co-cited journals, literature co-citation and literature emergence, and keywords, in order to describe the current status of research in the field and outline the trends in the field, with the hope of providing a reference for researchers in the field to choose their research direction and an objective basis for further research in the field.
title: Knowledge mapping of copper-induced cell death: A bibliometric study from 2012 to 2022

text: The data for this study were obtained from the Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC) with the search term set to TS = copper-induced cell death. The Time-slicing was set from January 1st, 2012 to April 8th, 2022. The language was limited to English. The limitation of literature type only included article. After excluding non-medical subjects such as fisheries and water resources, the remaining 832 articles were de-duplicated and excluded, resulting in the inclusion of 770 articles. All data in the text were extracted on the same day, April 8th, 2022, to avoid bias due to daily updates of the database. Each data entry was downloaded as a complete record in plain text format. text: Co-cited documents are documents that are frequently cited by other publications. A knowledge base is a collection of documents frequently referred by relevant research groups, which is not exactly the same as highly cited literature. The top 10 literature co-cited in this field are presented in Table S3 through a bibliometric analysis of the literature related to copper-induced cell death. In 2014, the first co-cited paper was published in Chemical Reviews by 6 authors, led by Santini C, as a collaborative review entitled Advances in copper complexes as anticancer agents, demonstrating its outstanding contribution to the study of copper-induced cell death. This paper describes a form of cell death that is distinct from apoptosis. A specific class of copper complexes, in particular the thioxotriazole copper(II) complex [Cu(L49)Cl2], are potent inhibitors of CT-L protease activity, which allowed scientists to explore a new mode of cell death. The second co-cited paper was published by Denoyer D in Metallomics in 2015. This paper describes the involvement of copper in angiogenesis, cancer growth and metastasis, and the finding of elevated copper levels in malignant tumors, laying the theoretical foundation for the subsequent investigation of the involvement of copper overload in the pathogenesis of diseases such as cancer. The third co-cited paper was published by Skrott Z et al In 2017 in Nature, titled Alcohol-abuse drug disulfiram targets cancer via p97 segregase adaptor NPL4. The paper explored the anticancer potential of disulfiram (tetraethylthiuram disulfide, DSF) and NPL4 was identified as the molecular target of tumor inhibition, and found that the antitumor effects of DSF could be enhanced by the presence of Cu. All in all, the top 10 co-cited literature focused on reviews (7 reviews were published from 2009 to 2018), involving relevant mechanisms including Oxidative Stress, Autophagy, and genotoxic potential. The authors also published reviews on biomarkers such as p97 and NPL4, as well as diseases related to copper-induced cell death, such as cancer, Cardiovascular disease, and Huntington’s disease. These have provided a solid foundation for future research in the emerging field of copper-induced cell death.

text: The burst detection results suggest hotspots of research in this field. The current analysis shows that the hotspots of research in this field focus on mechanisms, including induced apoptosis, aggregation, autophagy, endoplasmic reticulum stress, induced oxidative stress, and inflammation. Parkinson’s disease and cancer are 2 diseases that are closely related to copper-induced cell death. The literature on Parkinson’s disease has mostly explored its pathogenesis concerning copper-induced cell death, while the literature on cancer has explored chiefly the use of copper complexes in cancer therapy. It is noteworthy that in 2020, the fastest growth in the number of articles in this field may be related to the term nanoparticle, which was the most popular in that year. Inflammation, biological evaluation, nanoparticle, and cu(ii)) have become popular research topics in the last 4 years. This article may suggest that future research will continue to focus on improving the biological evaluation of tumors, thus broadening the ideas of tumor therapy in the form of copper complexes. An analysis of the dynamics of this field with keyword co-occurrence analysis and burst word detection reveals scholars focused on the mechanism in the early stage, and gradually presented the trend of parallel research on the mechanism and clinical diseases in the late stage. Since the clinical application of cisplatin-based drugs has many limitations, and copper complexes can better avoid their shortcomings, researchers have carried out many studies on copper complexes, drawing on their previous experience in mechanistic research, which has laid a solid foundation for effectively solving clinical problems. It is evident that mechanistic studies have been the focus of research in the field of copper-induced cell death. The proliferation of clinical problems has led researchers to explore further the mechanisms associated with cancer, which is currently the focus of research in this field. In recent years, research on copper-induced cell death and human disease is still relatively scarce, probably because this field is still in its infancy. More studies have focused on the therapeutic application of copper complexes, suggesting that their primary mechanism of action is the induction of DNA damage. However, this anti-proliferative mechanism sometimes does not exert a selective cytotoxic effect on cancer cells, thus making searching for other intracellular targets problematic. Therefore, the deeper the exploration of the mechanism of copper-induced cell death, the more rational the design of therapeutic drugs for cancer and other diseases, and the better the role of copper complexes in overcoming drug resistance. The 8 clusters of keywords presented in this paper illustrate 8 research frontiers in this field, which to some extent represent 8 significant aspects of research in it, mostly related to the mechanisms involved in cancer treatment. Copper is considered a limiting factor in cancer progression, including growth, angiogenesis, and metastasis. As a result, copper complexes are of great interest for cancer therapy, with mechanisms such as endoplasmic reticulum stress, DNA cleavage, paraptosis, glutamate, and ROS. Specifically, for example, a phosphine copper(I) complex, [Cu(thp)(4)][PF(6)] (CP), was found to induce endoplasmic reticulum stress by inhibiting 26S proteasome activities, a novel mechanism for CP-induced cancer cell death is revealed: a possible association with a signaling pathways involved in paraptosis.

text: Copper is considered a limiting factor in cancer progression, including growth, angiogenesis, and metastasis. As a result, copper complexes are of great interest for cancer therapy, with mechanisms such as endoplasmic reticulum stress, DNA cleavage, paraptosis, glutamate, and ROS. Its influence on the field is evident as it continues into 2019. More importantly, of the top 25 literature with the highest citation bursts, 8 literature are still in bursts. text: Meningiomas represent the most prevalent primary tumors of the central nervous system in adults, constituting approximately 40.8% of all primary CNS tumors in the United States and 56.2% of “nonmalignant” primary brain tumors. These tumors primarily originate from arachnoid cap cells located in the arachnoid granulations. Although the majority of meningiomas are histologically benign, their incidence increases with age, and a subset of tumors demonstrates aggressive behavior, including local invasion and recurrence, which can significantly impair neurological function and quality of life. The clinical presentation of meningiomas varies depending on their anatomical location and may manifest as headaches, seizures, visual disturbances, or other focal neurological deficits. Current standard treatments include surgical resection, radiotherapy, and pharmacological interventions. In individuals with recurrent or progressive meningiomas, current therapeutic strategies demonstrate limited effectiveness in managing invasive or recurrent lesions, as indicated by elevated recurrence rates and the emergence of therapeutic resistance. These difficulties may be ascribed to tumor heterogeneity and the restrictive function of the blood–brain barrier in impeding drug delivery. Given these challenges, the identification of molecular biomarkers linked to the pathogenesis and progression of meningiomas is crucial. Such biomarkers not only provide insights into the underlying mechanisms driving tumor development but also offer potential targets for personalized therapeutic strategies, ultimately contributing to improved clinical outcomes for patients with meningiomas. Paraptosis is a distinct form of programmed cell death characterized by cytoplasmic vacuolization, mitochondrial swelling, and endoplasmic reticulum dilation, differing from apoptosis as it is caspase-independent and lacks typical apoptotic features such as chromatin condensation or DNA fragmentation. Biologically, paraptosis plays a crucial role in cellular homeostasis, defense against malignant transformation, and regulation of cellular responses to stress, with its mechanisms primarily involving dysregulation of intracellular ion homeostasis, mitochondrial dysfunction, and protein aggregation. Unlike apoptosis, which is well-studied and widely recognized, paraptosis remains relatively underexplored, particularly in the context of tumorigenesis. Recent research has indicated a possible association between paraptosis and cancer, suggesting that paraptosis-related genes (PRGs) may play a role in influencing tumor cell proliferation, survival, invasion, and resistance to conventional therapies. Nonetheless, the precise function and underlying mechanisms of PRGs in the context of meningioma are not yet fully understood. The swift progression of contemporary bioinformatics technologies has underscored the critical importance of integrating multi-omics data-encompassing genomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics-in meningioma research for the identification of paraptosis-related biomarkers. This integrative approach not only elucidates the mechanistic role of paraptosis in the tumorigenesis and progression of meningioma but also enhances early disease diagnosis and aids in the identification of novel therapeutic targets. This study employs a novel integration of comprehensive bioinformatics and experimental validation to identify biomarkers associated with paraptosis in meningioma.
title: Identification and experimental validation of biomarkers associated with paraptosis in meningioma

text: This integrative approach not only elucidates the mechanistic role of paraptosis in the tumorigenesis and progression of meningioma but also enhances early disease diagnosis and aids in the identification of novel therapeutic targets. This study employs a novel integration of comprehensive bioinformatics and experimental validation to identify biomarkers associated with paraptosis in meningioma. By utilizing meningioma-related datasets from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database, we performed differential expression analysis, protein–protein interaction (PPI) analysis, and gene expression analysis to identify potential molecular targets implicated in the development and progression of meningioma. The expression levels of these biomarkers were subsequently validated in clinical samples using reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR). To elucidate their functional roles, we conducted functional enrichment analysis to identify key pathways, constructed detailed regulatory networks involving transcription factors (TFs) and noncoding RNAs, and performed drug prediction analyses to identify potential therapeutic compounds. These analyses reveal the molecular basis of meningioma, offering new insights into its pathophysiology and suggesting novel strategies for better treatment, particularly for invasive or recurrent cases.
title: Identification and experimental validation of biomarkers associated with paraptosis in meningioma

text: Transcriptome data for meningioma were gained from GEO database (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/). In particular, the GSE43290 dataset (GPL96 platform) included 47 meningioma tumor and 4 control tissue samples. While the GSE77259 dataset (GPL6244 platform) consisted of 14 meningioma tumor tissue samples, and the data of 3 control tissue samples were from http://www.affymetrix.com/support/technical/sample_data/gene_1_0_array_data.affx. Additionally, a total of 66 PRGs were acquired from the literature (Table S1, Supplemental Digital Content, https://links.lww.com/MD/R126). During data processing, raw data were first downloaded using the getGEO tool, from which the expression matrix and sample information were extracted. After converting probe IDs in the expression matrix to gene symbols, the na.omit function was applied to directly remove probes containing missing values. For duplicate genes that appeared after conversion, the probe with the highest mean expression level was retained. Finally, group labeling was completed according to sample types.

text: PCA was conducted to examine the dispersion and correlation between tumor and control samples in GSE43290 dataset. After, differentially expressed genes (DEGs; tumor vs control) were ascertained via “limma” package (v 3.52.4) (|log 2 Fold change (FC)| > 0.50 and P <.05). Subsequently, the acquired DEGs were clearly visualized through a volcano plot and heatmap. The volcano plot was generated with “ggplot2” (v 3.3.6), in which the top 10 upregulated genes and top 10 downregulated genes ranked by log 2 FC were labeled. Meanwhile, the heatmap was produced employing the “ComplexHeatmap” package (v 2.18.0) to display the expression patterns of the above-mentioned top 10 upregulated DEGs and top 10 downregulated DEGs in tumor samples and control samples.

text: Candidate genes were ascertained by intersecting DEGs and PRGs employing the “ggvenn” package (v 0.1.10; https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=ggvenn). Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) analyses were then executed to explore the functions roles and pathways related to these candidate genes, utilizing the “clusterProfiler” package (v 4.7.1.3) (adj. P <.05). Additionally, to examine protein interactions among the candidate genes, a PPI network was built employing STRING database (https://string-db.org/) with a confidence threshold of 0.4. After removing outlier genes, the PPI network was clearly visualized employing Cytoscape software (v 3.9.0). Notably, key module within the PPI network was ascertained by clustering employing the MCODE plugin in Cytoscape (v 3.9.0; degree cutoff = 2, k -core = 2, node score cutoff = 0.2, and max. depth = 100). Ultimately, the genes within the key module were defined as candidate biomarkers for meningioma.
title: Identification and experimental validation of biomarkers associated with paraptosis in meningioma
section_title: 2.3. Function analysis of candidate genes and identification of candidate biomarkers

text: To further evaluate and verify the expression of candidate key genes, based on candidate biomarkers, the Wilcoxon test was employed to perform gene expression analyses between tumor and control samples in the GSE43290 and GSE77259 datasets. Genes demonstrating statistically notable differences (P <.05) and consistent expression patterns across both datasets were ascertained as biomarkers. Subsequently, GeneMANIA (https://genemania.org/) was employed to ascertain genes functionally linked to these biomarkers, facilitating the construction of a gene–gene interaction network. Furthermore, to further explore the biological roles linked to the biomarkers, gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) was carried out on the GSE43290 dataset. In particular, Spearman coefficients between the biomarkers and other genes were calculated and subsequently ranked in descending order employing the “psych” package (v 2.2.9). The “c2.cp.kegg.v7.0.symbols.gmt” gene set was gained from the Molecular Signatures Database (MSigDB, http://software.broadinstitute.org/gsea/msigdb) as the background set. GSEA was subsequently performed employing the “clusterProfiler” package (v 4.7.1.3), with significance criteria established at an adjusted P -value of <.05 and an absolute normalized enrichment score (|NES|) >1. The top 5 enriched pathways were ascertained and ranked according to their adjusted P -values in ascending order.
title: Identification and experimental validation of biomarkers associated with paraptosis in meningioma

text: To determine the chromosomal locations of the biomarkers, the “RCircos” package (v 1.2.0) was applied for visualization. Furthermore, to explore the subcellular distribution situation of the ascertained biomarkers, FASTA files of the biomarker sequences were retrieved from the Gene database on the NCBI website (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/gene/). The mRNALocater database (http://www.rnalocate.org/) was then employed to determine the subcellular localization of these biomarkers.

text: ChEA3 database (https://amp.pharm.mssm.edu/ChEA3) was applied to predict TFs targeting the ascertained biomarkers. The top 20 TFs with the highest scores were selected to construct and visualize a TF-biomarker network using Cytoscape (v 3.9.0). Additionally, the miRDB (http://mirdb.org) and TargetScan (http://www.targetscan.org) databases were applied to fully predict miRNAs that targeted the biomarkers. Key miRNAs were identified by overlapping predictions from both databases using the “ggvenn” package (v 0.1.10). Subsequently, the starBase database (http://starbase.sysu.edu.cn/index.php) was chosen to predict lncRNAs targeting the key miRNAs (clipExpNum > 25). These relationships were organized to construct and visualize a lncRNA-miRNA–mRNA network employing Cytoscape (v 3.9.0). Furthermore, the DisGeNET database (https://www.disgenet.org/) was applied to predict diseases associated with the biomarkers, and a biomarker-disease network was built and clearly visualized employing Cytoscape (v 3.9.0). As treatment strategies for meningioma based on biomarkers might impact multiple organs and tissues, the BioGPS database (https://biogps.org) was employed to obtain mRNA expression data of the biomarkers across various organs and tissues. A biomarker-tissue/organ network was then visualized employing Cytoscape (v 3.9.0).
title: Identification and experimental validation of biomarkers associated with paraptosis in meningioma

text: Drug-Gene Interaction Database (DGIdb, http://www.dgidb.org) was employed to fully predict drugs targeting specific biomarkers, with a combined score threshold of >10,000. A biomarker-drug interaction network was then built and visualized employing Cytoscape (v 3.9.0). To assess the binding potential of the identified drugs to the biomarkers, drugs with the highest combined score for each biomarker were selected for further molecular docking analysis. The 3D structures of the biomarkers (serving as receptors) were mined from Protein Data Bank (PDB, https://www.rcsb.org/), while the 3D molecular structures of the drugs (acting as ligands) were retrieved from PubChem database (https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/). Following this, molecular docking was carried out employing CB-Dock (https://cadd.labshare.cn/cb-dock/php/blinddock.php), and binding affinities were calculated. The final results were visualized employing PyMOL software (v 3.0.3). Generally speaking, a binding energy lower than −5.0 kcal/mol is typically regarded as a strong indicator of an effective binding conformation.
title: Identification and experimental validation of biomarkers associated with paraptosis in meningioma

text: To better validate the expression situation of biomarkers in clinical samples, RT-qPCR analysis was performed. Specifically, a total of 10 samples (5 controls and 5 cases) were acquired from the clinic in The First Hospital of Lanzhou University. All participants were given informed consent. The study had the approval of the First Hospital of Lanzhou University ethics committee (approval number: LDYYLL2025-801). Total RNA was fully extracted from the 10 tissue samples employing the TRIzol reagent (Ambion, Austin) in accordance with the manufacturer’s protocol. Subsequently, RNA concentrations were clearly measured with a NanoPhotometer N50. Complementary DNA (cDNA) was fully synthesized via reverse transcription employing the SureScript First-Strand cDNA Synthesis Kit, with the reverse transcription process conducted on an S1000TM Thermal Cycler (Bio-Rad). Primer sequences are detailed in Table S2 Supplemental Digital Content, https://links.lww.com/MD/R126. Quantitative PCR (qPCR) assays were carried out employing the CFX Connect Real-Time Quantitative Fluorescence PCR Instrument (Bio-Rad) under the following conditions: initial denaturation at 95°C for 1 minute, followed by 40 cycles of denaturation at 95°C for 20 seconds, annealing at 55°C for 20 seconds, and extension at 72°C for 30 seconds. The relative quantification of mRNA levels was determined employing the 2 −ΔΔCT method. Ultimately, the RT-qPCR results were initially exported to Excel and subsequently imported into GraphPad Prism 5 (https://www.graphpad.com/) for statistical analysis and visualization.

For RT-qPCR analysis, a t -test was employed for statistical comparisons (P <.05). Notably, **** represented P <.0001, *** represented P <.001, ** represented P <.01, * represented P <.05, and ns represented P >.05.
