text: PCA analysis revealed a clear distinction between tumor and control samples in the GSE43290 dataset. In this dataset, a total of 5753 DEGs were identified, including 439 up-regulated and 5314 down-regulated genes in tumor samples (Fig. B, C). Subsequently, 26 candidate genes were selected by intersecting the 5753 DEGs with 66 PRGs. Overall, this analysis successfully highlighted candidate genes that might play significant roles in the pathophysiology of meningioma.

text: The 26 candidate genes were enriched in 99 GO terms, including 90 biological processes and 9 molecular functions, as well as 112 KEGG pathways. Noteworthy GO terms included “cellular response to biotic stimulus” (biological process) and “cysteine-type endopeptidase activity involved in apoptotic process” (molecular function), etc. In the KEGG analysis, these candidate genes were predominantly involved in pathways related to “pathways of neurodegeneration – multiple diseases,” “lipid and atherosclerosis,” and “prion disease”. Furthermore, after excluding 9 outlier genes, a PPI network was constructed. Within this network, HSPA5 was found to interact closely with several genes, including PDCD6IP and HSPB8. The key module of the PPI network was identified using the MCODE plugin, and the 10 genes in this key module were considered as candidate biomarkers.

section_title: 3.2. Function and pathways of candidate genes were explored

text: In the GSE43290 and GSE77259 datasets, 3 genes-ITPR3, MAPK1, and MAPK8-demonstrated statistically significant expression differences (P <.05) with consistent trends, as illustrated in Figure A and B. Notably, ITPR3 was upregulated in tumor samples, while MAPK1 and MAPK8 were markedly downregulated in these samples. Based on these findings, ITPR3, MAPK1, and MAPK8 have been proposed as potential biomarkers for meningioma, highlighting their significance in the advancement of targeted therapeutic strategies. Notably, RT-qPCR validation demonstrated that ITPR3 exhibited significantly elevated expression levels in tumor samples, whereas MAPK1 and MAPK8 were markedly more expressed in control samples (P <.05; Fig. C). Furthermore, GeneMANIA analysis identified 20 genes functionally associated with these biomarkers, uncovering significant interactions, including those between MAPK1 and MAP3K1, MAPK8 and MAP2K7, as well as ITPR3 and JUN. These interactions were involved in important processes such as the “Fc receptor signaling pathway” and the “stress-activated MAPK cascade”. GSEA further revealed that ITPR3 was significantly enriched in pathways related to “olfactory transduction” and “basal transcription factors”, MAPK1 in pathways related to “lysosome” and “ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis”, and MAPK8 in pathways related to “neuroactive ligand-receptor interaction” and “olfactory transduction,” etc. These findings highlighted the potential involvement of ITPR3, MAPK1, and MAPK8 in key biological pathways, providing valuable insights into their roles in the progression of meningioma.
title: Identification and experimental validation of biomarkers associated with paraptosis in meningioma

text: Chromosomal localization analysis indicated that ITPR3 was located on chromosome 6, MAPK1 on chromosome 22, and MAPK8 on chromosome 10. Additionally, subcellular localization analysis revealed that ITPR3 and MAPK8 were mainly present in the cytoplasm, while MAPK1 was predominantly localized in the nucleus. These results provided important insights into the genomic and cellular positioning of these biomarkers, enhancing our understanding of their functional roles.
title: Identification and experimental validation of biomarkers associated with paraptosis in meningioma
section_title: 3.4. The localization of biomarkers was explored

text: A total of 130, 138, and 123 TFs were predicted to target ITPR3, MAPK1, and MAPK8, respectively. Utilizing the top 20 TFs with the highest scores, a TF-mRNA interaction network was constructed, which revealed that SMAD3 co-targets all 3 biomarkers. Furthermore, the miRDB and TargetScan databases were queried, resulting in the identification of 267 and 166 miRNAs targeting these biomarkers, respectively. The intersection of these miRNAs led to the identification of 57 key miRNAs. Additionally, 11 long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) targeting these key miRNAs were predicted, facilitating the development of a lncRNA–miRNA–mRNA network. For instance, interactions such as MAPK1-“hsa-miR-130a-3p”-MIR17HG, MAPK8-“hsa-miR-32-5p”-NORAD, and ITPR3-“hsa-miR-506-3p”-MALAT1 were identified. Furthermore, a disease-biomarker network was constructed based on disease associations from the DisGeNET database, which identified 6, 59, and 17 diseases linked to ITPR3, MAPK1, and MAPK8, respectively. Notably, 5 diseases, including stomach neoplasms, schizophrenia, hyperalgesia, trigeminal neuralgia, and extrahepatic cholestasis, were co-associated with MAPK1 and MAPK8. Regarding tissue expression, all 3 biomarkers were observed to be expressed in CD34+ cells, cardiac myocytes, and testis seminiferous tubules. Collectively, these findings provide significant insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying meningioma and suggest that these biomarkers may be instrumental in the development of targeted therapeutic strategies.
title: Identification and experimental validation of biomarkers associated with paraptosis in meningioma
section_title: 3.5. Regulatory networks of biomarkers were constructed

text: A comprehensive search of the DGIdb database revealed the identification of 8, 57, and 57 pharmacological agents targeting ITPR3, MAPK1, and MAPK8, respectively. Notably, the identical set of 57 compounds was found to target both MAPK1 and MAPK8. Furthermore, 8 compounds, including tamoxifen, and menadione were identified as co-targeting all 3 biomarkers. Significantly, tamoxifen achieved the highest aggregate score across the 3 biomarkers, positioning it as a promising candidate for additional research. Consequently, tamoxifen was chosen for molecular docking analysis. The docking results indicated that tamoxifen demonstrated a favorable binding energy of −9.0 kcal/mol with ITPR3, with critical interactions involving the residue Lys236. For MAPK1, tamoxifen showed a binding energy of −5.9 kcal/mol, with key interactions involving the residue Asp173. Similarly, in the case of MAPK8, tamoxifen displayed a binding energy of −6.2 kcal/mol, with key interactions involving the residue Ser307. Overall, these findings highlighted the potential of tamoxifen as a candidate for targeted therapies involving ITPR3, MAPK1, and MAPK8, offering valuable insights for future research and clinical applications.

text: Meningiomas pose significant diagnostic challenges due to their frequent incidental detection and heterogeneous biological behavior, with some cases exhibiting malignant potential despite being histologically classified as typically benign tumors. The discovery of novel biomarkers that facilitate early detection and serve as therapeutic targets is both a research priority and a technical challenge in the field of neuro-oncology. Among the various mechanisms of programmed cell death, apoptosis and paraptosis have emerged as critical regulatory nodes in tumor biology. This study addresses the existing knowledge gap by systematically characterizing paraptosis-associated biomarkers through bioinformatics analysis and experimental validation. In doing so, it elucidates the pathogenic role of paraptosis dysregulation in the genesis of meningiomas and identifies new targets for diagnosis and treatment. Utilizing extensive bioinformatics analysis complemented by in vitro validation, we have identified, for the first time, 3 pivotal biomarkers – ITPR3, MAPK1, and MAPK8 – that demonstrate significantly altered expression patterns in meningioma tissues compared to normal controls. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying meningioma and facilitate the advancement of novel therapeutic strategies. ITPR3 is upregulated in tumors, while MAPK1 and MAPK8 are downregulated. As a calcium channel protein on the endoplasmic reticulum, ITPR3 is vital for intracellular calcium signaling and cancer-related processes like apoptosis and tumor cell survival. Its upregulation is linked to poor prognosis in cancers such as bladder, colorectal, and pancreatic cancer. In bladder cancer, ITPR3 promotes proliferation and metastasis via the NF-κB/CD44 pathway; in colorectal cancer, it aids metastatic colonization with RELB; and in pancreatic cancer, its overexpression is tied to poor survival. PTEN and FBXL2 regulate ITPR3 degradation, and stabilizing ITPR3 in PTEN-deficient cancers may enhance sensitivity to photodynamic therapy. ITPR3 is increasingly seen as a prognostic biomarker and therapeutic target due to its role in calcium homeostasis and cancer progression. MAPK1 (ERK2) serves as a pivotal intracellular signaling molecule that is integral to cellular processes such as proliferation, differentiation, migration, and apoptosis, and it holds a significant role in the pathogenesis of various cancers. The hyperactivation of MAPK1 is intricately linked to tumor initiation, metastasis, and invasion, particularly in malignancies such as breast, pancreatic, and bladder cancers. [ – ] MAPK1 facilitates tumor cell growth and metastasis through the activation of downstream effectors, including BTRC and IQGAP1. Additionally, MAPK1 contributes to the tumor microenvironment by modulating immune and inflammatory responses. Given its critical functions, MAPK1 represents a promising therapeutic target, with inhibitors demonstrating potential in curtailing tumor growth and metastasis. Furthermore, MAPK8 (JNK1), another essential member of the MAPK family, plays a crucial role in mediating cellular responses to stress, inflammation, apoptosis, and differentiation. MAPK8 is activated by signals like inflammatory cytokines and stress, playing a role in cellular processes such as proliferation and survival. In cancer, it aids tumor progression by influencing cell cycle control, metastasis, and chemotherapy response. For instance, in colorectal cancer, the PVT1/miR-152-3p/E2F3/MAPK8 axis enhances tumor growth by activating MAPK8.
title: Identification and experimental validation of biomarkers associated with paraptosis in meningioma

text: Furthermore, MAPK8 (JNK1), another essential member of the MAPK family, plays a crucial role in mediating cellular responses to stress, inflammation, apoptosis, and differentiation. MAPK8 is activated by signals like inflammatory cytokines and stress, playing a role in cellular processes such as proliferation and survival. In cancer, it aids tumor progression by influencing cell cycle control, metastasis, and chemotherapy response. For instance, in colorectal cancer, the PVT1/miR-152-3p/E2F3/MAPK8 axis enhances tumor growth by activating MAPK8. In bladder cancer, MAPK8 collaborates with other MAPKs to affect TFs, impacting cell cycle arrest and proliferation. Targeting MAPK8 could inhibit tumor growth, reduce metastasis, and improve cancer treatment efficacy. Although ITPR3, MAPK1, and MAPK8 have been extensively investigated in various other cancers, our study identifies distinct expression patterns and potential functional roles for these genes in meningioma, highlighting the significance of tissue-specific research. These observed differences may stem from the unique molecular landscapes or microenvironmental interactions characteristic of meningioma, thereby emphasizing the necessity for further research to elucidate their mechanisms and therapeutic potential. In terms of mechanisms, functional enrichment analysis indicates a significant involvement of ITPR3 and MAPK8 in the olfactory transduction pathway and MAPK1 in the lysosome pathway, suggesting that these pathways may be critical in the progression of meningioma. The olfactory transduction pathway, traditionally associated with odor detection, involves G protein-coupled receptors and downstream calcium signaling. Dysregulation of calcium homeostasis, mediated by key components such as ITPR3, has been implicated in tumor growth, invasion, and resistance to apoptosis. The lysosomal pathway plays a pivotal role in intracellular degradation and autophagy, significantly impacting tumor progression by modulating cellular stress responses and survival mechanisms. MAPK1, as a key component, may affect tumor cell survival and metastasis through lysosome-mediated autophagy and apoptosis. This study underscores the involvement of the lysosomal pathway in meningioma invasion and recurrence, with a particular emphasis on lysosomal proteases and their inhibitors. Meningioma invasiveness is linked to lysosomal proteases Cathepsin B and L, with elevated levels, especially Cathepsin B, distinguishing invasive from noninvasive cases. While Cathepsin B activity correlates with cell invasiveness, its expression doesn’t predict prognosis. However, its inhibitor, Stefin B, is a key predictor of recurrence. Alkaline phosphatase activity increases with meningioma grade, aiding diagnosis. Endogenous cysteine protease inhibitors like Stefin A, Stefin B, and Cystatin C are more active in benign meningiomas but decrease in malignant ones. The imbalance between proteases and inhibitors likely drives increased invasiveness. The lysosomal pathway contributes to meningioma invasion and recurrence through this protease-inhibitor balance, offering crucial insights for future diagnostic and treatment research. To better understand the roles of these biomarkers, we analyzed their subcellular localization. ITPR3 and MAPK8 are mainly in the cytoplasm, indicating a role in cytoplasmic signaling, while MAPK1 is mostly in the nucleus, suggesting involvement in transcriptional regulation and DNA damage response. These patterns provide insights into their functions and potential for targeted therapies.

text: The lysosomal pathway contributes to meningioma invasion and recurrence through this protease-inhibitor balance, offering crucial insights for future diagnostic and treatment research. To better understand the roles of these biomarkers, we analyzed their subcellular localization. ITPR3 and MAPK8 are mainly in the cytoplasm, indicating a role in cytoplasmic signaling, while MAPK1 is mostly in the nucleus, suggesting involvement in transcriptional regulation and DNA damage response. These patterns provide insights into their functions and potential for targeted therapies. Additionally, TF analysis identified SMAD3 as a common TF co-targeting all 3 biomarkers, which could shed light on their transcriptional regulation. SMAD3, in particular, is crucial in meningioma growth, invasion, and grading via the TGF-β signaling pathway. Phosphorylated SMAD3 (p-SMAD3) has been identified in nearly all meningioma specimens, with elevated expression levels noted in higher-grade tumors, such as grades II and III, underscoring its importance in tumor progression. TGF-β signaling, which is mediated via SMAD3, frequently exhibits alterations in high-grade meningiomas, characterized by a marked reduction in the expression of TGF-β receptor III (TGF-βRIII), potentially contributing to enhanced tumor invasiveness. Although TGF-β is capable of activating SMAD3 and downstream signaling molecules such as p38 MAPK and p44/42 MAPK, its growth-inhibitory effects are often diminished in higher-grade tumors, indicating a disruption of its regulatory functions. SMAD3 may serve as a central regulator of ITPR3, MAPK1, and MAPK8, influencing calcium signaling and balancing cell proliferation and stress responses. Disruption of this network in meningioma could lead to tumor progression. Targeting SMAD3 to restore its tumor-suppressive function, possibly by enhancing TGF-βRIII or modulating SMAD3 activation, offers a potential treatment strategy. Investigating the interactions between ITPR3, MAPK1, and MAPK8 may reveal new tumorigenesis mechanisms and therapeutic targets for meningioma. This study highlights ITPR3, MAPK1, and MAPK8 as promising meningioma biomarkers and suggests tamoxifen as a potential treatment targeting these markers. Known for its use in breast cancer treatment, tamoxifen shows strong binding to these biomarkers, suggesting its potential repurposing for meningioma therapy. Molecular docking reveals tamoxifen’s specific binding to key residues in these proteins, indicating it may modulate their activity. Additionally, tamoxifen appears to reduce meningioma risk, especially in breast cancer patients on long-term or high-dose treatment, likely due to its inhibition of estrogen receptors and modulation of growth factor pathways. Immunohistochemical analysis of ER and PKC can identify patients who may benefit. Further studies are required to refine its use and develop personalized treatments.

text: Despite the partial external validation supporting our findings, this study has several limitations that should be acknowledged. Chief among these is the reliance on publicly available genomic data from the GEO database, without subsequent validation in independent clinical cohorts. This may constrain the generalizability and translational relevance of our results. To address this, future studies involving larger prospective clinical samples are warranted to further verify and refine our conclusions. Furthermore, integration of multi-omics approaches – such as metabolomic and proteomic profiling – could provide a more comprehensive understanding of the molecular pathogenesis of meningiomas. Such efforts would help elucidate underlying mechanisms and identify novel therapeutic targets, thereby enriching the biological context of our findings. Finally, the identification of biomarkers such as ITPR3 opens promising avenues for targeted drug development. Advancing these molecules toward personalized therapeutic strategies could enhance treatment precision and improve clinical outcomes for patients with meningioma.

text: This study identified TPR3, MAPK1, and MAPK8 as novel biomarkers for meningiomas, highlighting their roles in disease pathways like “olfactory transduction” and “lysosome.” SMAD3 was found to regulate these biomarkers, and tamoxifen emerged as a potential treatment based on drug prediction and molecular docking. These insights could enhance personalized meningioma treatments, though further multi-omics analyses and clinical validations are needed to understand molecular mechanisms and discover more therapies. This research advances meningioma study and targeted therapy development.

text: Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide, with its incidence and mortality rates rising sharply in recent years. According to the World Health Organization Classification of Thoracic Cancers 2021, lung cancer (LC) classification primarily relies on morphological assessment, followed by immunohistochemistry and molecular biology techniques. Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), comprising approximately 85% of all LC cases, is the most common form, with lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) being its most prevalent subtype. [ – ] The incidence of LUAD continues to increase. LUAD is characterized by invasive growth, transitioning from a tumor that preserves alveolar structure to one that remodels and invades lung tissue. Recent advances in understanding LUAD’s molecular pathogenesis have led to the development of several precision therapies. While the prognostic significance of genes like NPM1 and EMG1 has been demonstrated, considerable knowledge gaps persist. LUAD is highly heterogeneous, with its pathogenesis driven by numerous genetic mutations, epigenetic changes, and the aberrant activation of signaling pathways. However, the full scope of these complex regulatory networks remains poorly understood. Additionally, despite advances in diagnostics and treatments, the 5-year survival rate for LUAD remains dismally low at 10% to 20%, highlighting the urgent need for novel biomarkers beyond current therapeutic targets. Furthermore, the role of the tumor microenvironment (TME) in LUAD, particularly in disease progression and resistance to treatment, remains incompletely elucidated, with a focus on the interactions between immune cells and tumor cells. Finally, although paraptosis has demonstrated anti-tumor effects in various cancers, its specific mechanisms in LUAD and the function of paraptosis-related genes (PRGs) have yet to be fully explored, necessitating further research for therapeutic applications. Programmed cell death (PCD) is a fundamental regulatory mechanism in living systems, playing a critical role in maintaining intracellular stability both in health and disease. Apoptosis, one of the key forms of PCD, is vital to various diseases, including cancer. Paraptosis, another significant form of PCD, is characterized by cytoplasmic vacuolization and differs from apoptosis in several crucial aspects. Paraptosis represents a therapeutically exploitable death mechanism, induced in cancers by natural compounds and metal complexes. Members of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) family have been shown to be essential for the induction of paraptosis. Additionally, studies suggest that the activation of the MAPK/ERK signaling pathway facilitates LUAD proliferation and metastasis. Both paraptosis and LUAD are linked to the MAPK pathway. Paraptosis signaling is also involved in other cancers, including colorectal cancer, glioblastoma, and pancreatic cancer, [ – ] and may similarly impact LUAD. A recent study identified 24 PRGs, including CDKN3, TP53, and PHB, that are highly up-regulated in tumor tissues and play critical roles in LUAD treatment and prognosis. Despite this, the expression patterns, prognostic significance, and molecular functions (MFs) of PRGs in LUAD remain underexplored, and the associated molecular mechanisms are not fully understood. Consequently, the development of therapeutic strategies, early diagnosis, and prognosis for patients with LUAD relies heavily on the identification of novel and more reliable biomarkers.

text: The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA)-LUAD dataset, comprising 511 LUAD cases and 59 normal lung tissue samples, was obtained from the TCGA database (http://cancergenome.nih.gov/) for use as the training set. This dataset included raw data for patients with LUAD, such as RNA-seq data, clinical details, and survival information. The validation set, GSE13213 (platform: GPL6480), was sourced from the Gene Expression Omnibus (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/), containing 117 lung tissue samples from patients with LUAD along with clinical information, including age, gender, pathological stage, and survival data. Additionally, 66 PRGs were compiled from existing literature.

text: For differential gene expression analysis, the DESeq2 package (version 1.38.0) was employed to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between LUAD and control groups in the training set. The thresholds were set to |log 2 fold change (FC)| > 0.5 and P.adj <.05. Volcano and heat maps of DEGs were generated using the “ggplot2” (version 3.4.1) and pheatmap (version 1.0.12, https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=pheatmap) packages, respectively, with the top 10 up- and down-regulated DEGs labeled.

text: To identify DEGs related to PRGs in LUAD, the intersection of DEGs and PRGs was obtained using the ‘ggvenn’ package (version 0.1.9, https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=ggvenn) to generate the CGs. To explore the biological functions and signaling pathways associated with CGs, Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analyses were performed using the “ClusterProfiler” package (version 4.7.1.3). GO analysis encompassed biological process (BP), cellular component (CC), and MF. The analyses were performed with a P -value threshold of <.05, and the top 15 most significant enriched functions were visualized in dendrograms.

text: Univariate Cox regression analysis (P <.05) was conducted on CGs in LUAD samples from the training set using the coxph function in the ‘survival’ package (version 3.5.3, https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=survival) to identify genes with prognostic value. These genes were further tested for the proportional hazards (PH) assumption (P >.05). Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) regression, implemented via the “glmnet” package (version 4.1.4), was used to perform feature selection and control model complexity through L1 regularization. LASSO is particularly effective for handling high-dimensional data and constructing concise models, especially when key variables must be clearly defined. The optimal model was determined when lambda was minimized. Prognostic genes were selected from the LASSO model for constructing the LUAD risk model: r i s k s c o r e = ∑ n i = 1 (β g e n e × c o e f i).
title: Identification and validation of paraptosis-related prognostic biomarkers in lung adenocarcinoma: An observational study based on transcriptomics and clinical outcomes

text: A risk model was constructed based on prognostic genes, with risk scores calculated for each patient with LUAD in the training set using the aforementioned formula. LUAD samples were then divided into high- and low-risk cohorts based on the median risk score. The distribution of risk scores and survival status for patients with LUAD were visualized. The difference in overall survival (OS) between the 2 risk cohorts was assessed using the log-rank test (P <.05) and displayed with Kaplan–Meier (K–M) curves, generated via the ‘survminer’ package (version 0.4.9, https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=survminer). Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves were plotted using the ‘survivalROC’ package (version 1.0.3.1, https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=survivalROC) to predict OS in patients with LUAD at 1, 3, and 5 years, with the area under the curve (AUC) calculated to indicate predictive accuracy (AUC > 0.6).
title: Identification and validation of paraptosis-related prognostic biomarkers in lung adenocarcinoma: An observational study based on transcriptomics and clinical outcomes

text: To validate the generalizability of the model, the risk model was applied to LUAD data from the validation set. Similar high- and low-risk cohorts were established, and the distribution of risk scores and patient survival status were displayed. ROC curve analysis further assessed the model’s accuracy.
title: Identification and validation of paraptosis-related prognostic biomarkers in lung adenocarcinoma: An observational study based on transcriptomics and clinical outcomes

text: To verify the reliability of the risk model, LUAD samples from the training set were grouped based on clinical characteristics such as age (≤60 years, >60 years), gender (male, female), TNM.stage (stage I, stage II, stage III, and stage IV), T-stage (T1–4), N-stage (N0–2), and M-stage (M1, M2). Survival analysis was conducted between high- and low-risk cohorts within each clinical subgroup, with the results presented via K–M curves (P <.05). The distribution of risk scores across these clinical characteristics was examined using the Wilcoxon test (for 2 groups) and Kruskal–Wallis test (for multiple groups) (P <.05).
title: Identification and validation of paraptosis-related prognostic biomarkers in lung adenocarcinoma: An observational study based on transcriptomics and clinical outcomes

text: To investigate whether the risk score serves as an independent prognostic factor for LUAD, univariate Cox regression analysis was performed on the significantly different clinical characteristics and risk score from the training set. Potential independent prognostic factors with hazard ratios (HR) ≠ 1 and P <.05 were selected. These factors were further tested for PH assumption (P >.05). Factors that passed the PH test were then analyzed using multivariate regression analysis through the “survival” package to determine final independent prognostic factors (P <.05). A nomogram was developed using the ‘rms’ package (version 6.2-0, https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=rms), with each factor scored according to its impact on LUAD prognosis (i.e., regression coefficient). The total points were calculated to predict 1-, 3-, and 5-year survival probabilities for patients with LUAD. To assess the accuracy of the nomogram, a calibration curve was plotted, with results closer to the reference line (true probability) indicating greater reliability. Finally, ROC curve analysis was performed using the “survivalROC” package, with an AUC > 0.6 validating the independent prognostic factors.
title: Identification and validation of paraptosis-related prognostic biomarkers in lung adenocarcinoma: An observational study based on transcriptomics and clinical outcomes

text: To understand the biological processes underlying the significant enrichment observed in high- and low-risk patients with LUAD, GSEA was performed on the 2 risk cohorts in the training set. Initially, differences between the 2 cohorts (high-risk vs low-risk) were analyzed using the “DESeq2” package, with log 2 FC values calculated and ranked by magnitude. GSEA was subsequently executed using the “ClusterProfiler” package, with reference gene sets taken from the Molecular Signatures Database: “c2.cp.v2023.2.Hs.symbols.gmt” and “c5.all.v2023.2.Hs.symbols.gmt.” A threshold of P.adjust <.05 and |normalized enrichment score (NES)| > 1 was applied. The top 3 positively and negatively enriched KEGG pathways and GO functions were displayed based on NES rankings.

text: To investigate immune infiltration in LUAD, the xCell algorithm was used to calculate immune cell infiltration scores for 64 immune cell types across the high- and low-risk cohorts in the training set. The distribution of immune cell proportions was visualized. The Wilcoxon test was then applied to identify immune cells with significantly different infiltration scores between the 2 cohorts (P <.05). Correlation analyses were performed to assess the relationships between immune cell infiltration, risk score, and prognostic genes. This analysis was conducted in the LUAD training set using the ‘psych’ package (version 2.2.9, https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=psych), with correlation coefficients (| r |) > 0.3 and P <.05 considered significant.

text: To identify potential drugs targeting the prognostic genes, the CellMiner database was queried. Drug–gene pairs with | r | > 0.4 and P <.05 were retained for further analysis. The drug–prognostic gene interaction network was visualized using the “ggalluvial” package (version 0.12.5). To assess the binding potential of the drugs with the prognostic genes, molecular docking simulations were conducted using CB-Dock and visualized with Pymol software. First, the protein structures of prognostic genes were retrieved from the Protein Data Bank. Next, top-ranked drugs correlated with the prognostic genes were obtained from the PubChem database. Finally, molecular docking was performed for key drugs and their respective prognostic genes, with binding energy values of <−1.2 kcal/mol considered significant.

text: The expression levels of prognostic genes were validated in 5 LUAD and control samples via RT-qPCR. The clinical samples of this study were collected from Shenzhen Hospital, Southern Medical University with written informed consent obtained from all participants. The study protocol received ethics approval (Approval No.: NYSZYYEC2024K072R001) from the Institutional Review Board of Shenzhen Hospital, Southern Medical University. Total RNA was isolated from the 10 samples with TRIzol reagent (Ambion, USA) in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. The RNA concentration was measured using a NanoPhotometer N50. cDNA was generated via reverse transcription with the SureScript-First-strand-cDNA-synthesis-kit, and the reverse transcription process was conducted using an S1000TM Thermal Cycler (Bio-Rad, USA). qPCR experiments were executed with a CFX Connect real-time quantitative fluorescence PCR instrument (Bio-Rad, USA) under the following conditions: initial denaturation for 1 minute at 95°C, followed by 40 cycles of 20 seconds at 95°C, 20 seconds at 55°C, and 30 seconds at 72°C. GAPDH was used as the reference gene, and relative expression levels of prognostic genes were calculated using the 2 -ΔΔCT method.

text: Differential expression analysis identified a total of 8857 DEGs, including 5639 up-regulated and 3218 down-regulated DEGs in the LUAD group (Fig. A and B). The intersection of these 8857 DEGs and 66 PRGs resulted in 27 CGs. For these 27 CGs, 307 GO biological functions were enriched, including 243 BPs, 28 MFs, and 36 CCs. The most significantly enriched GO functions included “BP: ER overload response,” “MF: calcium-release channel activity,” and “CC: smooth endoplasmic reticulum”. Additionally, the CGs were significantly enriched for 21 KEGG pathways, with the highest enrichment observed for the “MAPK signaling pathway,” “small cell LC,” and “P53 signaling pathway”.

text: Univariate Cox regression analysis of the 27 CGs revealed 6 genes with prognostic value (HR ≠ 1, P <.05), all of which passed the PH assumption test (P >.05) (Fig. A and Table S2, Supplemental Digital Content, https://links.lww.com/MD/R386). Subsequently, LASSO analysis was performed on these 6 prognostic genes using LUAD samples from the training set. The optimal model, identified when lambda.min = 0.01504096, included 4 prognostic genes: CDKN3, PEBP1, TNFRSF19, and PHB. The resulting risk score formula was as follows: risk score = (0.1835 × CDKN3) + (−0.2506 × PEBP1) + (−0.1042 × TNFRSF19) + (0.0746 × PHB). The LUAD samples in the training set were divided into high- and low-risk cohorts based on the median risk score, resulting in 255 high-risk and 256 low-risk samples. The distribution of risk scores and patient survival status for the 2 cohorts were displayed (Fig. C and D). K–M curves demonstrated that low-risk patients with LUAD had significantly longer survival compared to high-risk patients (P <.0001). The ROC curve showed AUC values of 0.63, 0.65, and 0.65 at 1, 3, and 5 years, respectively, confirming that the constructed risk model effectively serves as a prognostic tool for LUAD. In the validation set, risk scores for each patient with LUAD were calculated based on the prognostic risk model, and the patients were divided into high- and low-risk cohorts, with 58 high-risk and 59 low-risk patients (Fig. A and B). K–M curves again indicated a significant survival difference between the 2 cohorts (P =.00074). In the ROC curves of OS on in LUAD patients, the AUCs were all above 0.6, indicating that the constructed prognostic risk model is effective. However, it did not exceed 0.7, and external validation in a clinical setting was still required.

text: GSEA results revealed significant enrichment in 541 GO functions and 368 KEGG pathways for the high- and low-risk cohorts in the training set (Fig. A and B). Among the top findings, the most significantly enriched KEGG pathways and GO functions, ranked by positive and negative NES scores, included “spindle elongation” and the “medicus reference cenpe interaction with NDC80 complex,” both of which were notably active in the high-risk cohort. text: To explore the immune characteristics during the development of LUAD, the xCell algorithm was 1st used to calculate the infiltration scores of 64 types of immune cells in LUAD patients in the high/low-risk groups, and the distribution proportions of different immune cell types were observed. A comparison of infiltration scores between the 2 risk cohorts revealed 40 immune cell types with significant differences, including adipocytes, astrocytes, and CD4+ memory T cells (Figure S2, Supplemental Digital Content, https://links.lww.com/MD/R386). Correlation analysis showed strong associations between risk score, prognostic genes (CDKN3, TNFRSF19, PHB, and PEBP1), and most differential immune cells. Notably, both risk score and CDKN3 were strongly negatively correlated with hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) and positively correlated with Th2 cells. TNFRSF19 exhibited the strongest negative correlation with Th1 cells and the strongest positive correlation with neurons. PHB showed the strongest negative correlation with HSC and the strongest positive correlation with megakaryocyte–erythroid progenitors (MEP). PEBP1 had a robust negative correlation with keratinocytes and a strong positive correlation with neurons. We speculated that these prognostic genes might exert relevant functions through aforementioned immune cells.

text: Drug analysis of the 4 prognostic genes revealed no predicted drugs for CDKN3, 8 for PEBP1, 3 for TNFRSF19, and 3 for PHB. These results were integrated into a drug–prognostic gene interaction network. Since TNFRSF19 and PHB lacked available protein structures, molecular docking was performed using the PEBP1 protein structure. The top-ranked drugs, vorinostat and raloxifene, were selected for docking. Molecular docking results showed that PEBP1 bound to vorinostat with a docking score of −7.3 kcal/mol and to raloxifene with a score of −9.0 kcal/mol, with both interactions involving hydrogen bonds (Fig. B and C). These findings suggest strong binding affinities between PEBP1 and both drugs, indicating potential molecular interactions. However, these in silico results require experimental validation to confirm their therapeutic efficacy in LUAD.

title: Identification and validation of paraptosis-related prognostic biomarkers in lung adenocarcinoma: An observational study based on transcriptomics and clinical outcomes

text: NSCLC accounts for approximately 85% of all LC cases, with LUAD being the most common subtype, representing approximately 50% of all LCs. Consequently, LUAD is a leading cause of cancer-related deaths globally. The complex pathophysiology of LUAD involves genetic mutations, epigenetic alterations, and other factors. Despite advances in targeted therapy and immunotherapy, the prognosis for LUAD remains poor, with a 5-year survival rate of approximately 10% to 20%. Consequently, there is an urgent need to identify novel biomarkers and therapeutic targets to improve patient outcomes. Paraptosis, an unconventional form of PCD, is characterized by cytoplasmic vacuolization, often accompanied by endoplasmic reticulum and/or mitochondrial enlargement. Unlike apoptosis, paraptosis induces cell death by disrupting protein, redox, and ion homeostasis, and does not rely on cysteine caspase activation. While paraptosis has demonstrated anti-tumor effects in several cancers, its role in LUAD remains unclear. The 4 prognostic genes (CDKN3, PEBP1, TNFRSF19, and PHB) identified in this study were all selected from PRGs. Their expression and prognostic value in LUAD are potentially linked to paraptosis mechanisms. Regarding core features of paraptosis, it depends on MAPK pathway activation and is accompanied by cytoplasmic vacuolation. Consistently, KEGG enrichment analysis in this study revealed that these CGs were significantly enriched in the “MAPK signaling pathway,” suggesting they may influence LUAD progression by regulating this key proptosis pathway. Given that the mechanistic contribution of PRGs to tumorigenesis is poorly understood, exploring their role in LUAD may reveal new therapeutic strategies. For instance, Zhuo and Song employed bioinformatics analysis to delineate the prognostic characteristics of 2 distinct molecular subtypes in LUAD and validated the prognostic biomarker CDKN3. However, that study involved fewer prognostic markers and did not encompass predictive analysis of therapeutic agents. In contrast, the present study 1st identified 27 DEGs in LUAD using bioinformatic approaches and further refined these to obtain 4 prognostic genes (PEBP1, TNFRSF19, CDKN3, and PHB) with enhanced clinical specificity. Subsequently, an independent prognostic model was constructed to enable risk stratification. Finally, significant associations among risk scores, the prognostic genes, and differentially expressed immune cells were established, and potential drug targets were screened (e.g., vorinostat and raloxifene demonstrated high binding affinity for PEBP1). Furthermore, this study systematically explored the potential mechanistic roles of these 4 genes in LUAD progression and therapeutic targeting. CDKN3, located at the 14q22 locus, plays a significant role in cancer development and progression by encoding the CDKN3 protein. Identified as a tumor suppressor in several malignancies, CDKN3 has emerged as a potential biomarker and therapeutic target in LUAD. Its expression is up-regulated during LUAD progression and is involved in critical biological processes, including the cell cycle, cell division, and cell proliferation. Previous studies have used CDKN3 as a metabolism-related gene to develop predictive models, demonstrating that high CDKN3 expression is associated with poor prognosis in patients with LUAD. Additionally, CDKN3 knockdown significantly reduces tumor cell invasion, migration, and proliferation, as supported by previous studies.
title: Identification and validation of paraptosis-related prognostic biomarkers in lung adenocarcinoma: An observational study based on transcriptomics and clinical outcomes

text: Its expression is up-regulated during LUAD progression and is involved in critical biological processes, including the cell cycle, cell division, and cell proliferation. Previous studies have used CDKN3 as a metabolism-related gene to develop predictive models, demonstrating that high CDKN3 expression is associated with poor prognosis in patients with LUAD. Additionally, CDKN3 knockdown significantly reduces tumor cell invasion, migration, and proliferation, as supported by previous studies. This study confirmed significant CDKN3 overexpression in LUAD (HR = 1.3, univariate Cox regression), identifying it as a prognostic risk factor. Among 40 immune cell types analyzed in the LUAD microenvironment, CDKN3 was found to correlate with 34, showing the strongest negative association with HSC and the strongest positive association with Th2 cells. It has been reported that HSC expression is decreased in the high-risk LUAD group. Moreover, glycolysis in patients with LUAD has been strongly linked to poor prognosis and resistance to immunotherapy, potentially driven by Th2 cell infiltration, which aligns with our findings. These results suggest that CDKN3 plays a biologically significant role in LUAD therapy and warrants further investigation. PEBP1, also known as Raf kinase inhibitory protein, inhibits cell metastasis in NSCLC by blocking the Raf/ERK/STAT3 signaling pathway. In NSCLC, PEBP1 mRNA expression is significantly down-regulated, and lower expression levels are associated with poorer differentiation and more advanced clinical TNM staging in patients. PEBP1 can also inhibit paracellular apoptosis, and in LUAD, PEBP1 regulates iron mutation in LUAD cells. The transcription factor NFYA inhibits this mutation by transcriptionally down-regulating PEBP1 expression, highlighting PEBP1’s significant impact on LUAD initiation and progression, making it a promising therapeutic target. In immune infiltration studies, PEBP1 expression was positively correlated with resting mast cells, potentially linked to PEBP1’s negative regulation of mast cell activation. Univariate Cox regression analysis revealed that PEBP1 serves as a protective factor for LUAD prognosis, with an HR of 0.71. PEBP1 was associated with 21 out of 40 immune cell types in the LUAD immune microenvironment. These immune cells showed the strongest positive correlation with neuronal cells and the strongest negative correlation with keratinocytes. The role of neuronal cells in LUAD, as well as the impact of PEBP1 on keratinocytes, warrants further investigation to understand their contribution to LUAD onset and progression. Additionally, the high-affinity binding of vorinostat and raloxifene to PEBP1 suggests their potential use in LUAD treatment. TNFRSF19, also known as TAJ/TROY, is an orphan member of the TNF receptor family primarily expressed in skin and lung tissue cells. It plays a pivotal role in maintaining the correct phenotype of postnatal human lung tissue. TNFRSF19’s distinct structural domain can induce apoptosis without caspase involvement, and overexpression of this protein results in non-apoptotic cell death with paraptosis-like morphology. In LC studies, TNFRSF19 expression was found to be significantly lower in tumor tissues compared to paraneoplastic tissues. Its expression level was negatively correlated with survival time and tumor stage, suggesting that TNFRSF19 serves as a key tumor suppressor gene in lung tissue.

text: It plays a pivotal role in maintaining the correct phenotype of postnatal human lung tissue. TNFRSF19’s distinct structural domain can induce apoptosis without caspase involvement, and overexpression of this protein results in non-apoptotic cell death with paraptosis-like morphology. In LC studies, TNFRSF19 expression was found to be significantly lower in tumor tissues compared to paraneoplastic tissues. Its expression level was negatively correlated with survival time and tumor stage, suggesting that TNFRSF19 serves as a key tumor suppressor gene in lung tissue. Furthermore, TNFRSF19 has been closely linked to LUAD prognosis, and its inclusion in risk scoring and prognostic models for patients with LUAD has been explored. Given that TNFRSF19 is underexpressed in LUAD, it is considered a protective factor for LUAD prognosis. Analysis of 40 immune cell types in the LUAD immune microenvironment revealed that TNFRSF19 was associated with 32 of these cells, with the strongest negative correlation to Th1 cells and the strongest positive correlation to neuronal cells, mirroring the association seen with PEBP1. TNFRSF19 has been identified as a component of the Nogo receptor complex, with its expression elevated in human glioma tissues and cells. Inhibition of TNFRSF19 expression in vivo and in vitro slows glioma progression, raising the possibility that this finding may be relevant to its positive correlation with neuronal cells in LUAD. Further research is needed to explore this relationship in the context of LUAD. PHB encodes prohibitin, a protein primarily localized to mitochondria, where it plays a critical role in maintaining mitochondrial function and preventing cellular aging. It is highly conserved and functions as a scaffolding protein essential for cancer cell proliferation and survival. PHB interacts with the MAPK signaling pathway to promote cancer cell proliferation and tumor formation, particularly in colorectal cancer cells. PHB1 has been found to be widely expressed in NSCLC, correlating with a low survival rate and chemoresistance, making PHB1 inhibition a promising therapeutic approach for kras-mediated NSCLC. In this study, PHB was significantly expressed in LUAD, consistent with earlier findings. Univariate Cox regression analysis revealed an HR of 1.3 for PHB, identifying it as a prognostic risk factor for both LUAD and CDKN3. In an analysis of 40 immune cell types in the LUAD immune microenvironment, PHB was found to correlate with 28 of the 40 cell types, showing the strongest negative correlation with HSC, similar to CDKN3, and the strongest positive correlation with MEP. The significant relationship between PHB, HSC, and MEP in LUAD suggests that further investigation is needed to understand how PHB mediates changes in HSC and MEP levels in LUAD, and to elucidate PHB’s specific role in these processes. Additionally, the functional divergence or convergence of PHB-CDKN3 antagonism in HSCs and its mechanistic basis warrant further exploration. Although this study established a prognostic risk model using TCGA-LUAD data and successfully identified 4 genes (CDKN3, PEBP1, TNFRSF19, and PHB) with significant prognostic value, laying a foundation for LUAD treatment, several limitations remain. First, the sample size used for RT-qPCR validation was relatively small. While the results were consistent with TCGA/Gene Expression Omnibus analyses, this limited size may restrict the generalizability of the findings.
title: Identification and validation of paraptosis-related prognostic biomarkers in lung adenocarcinoma: An observational study based on transcriptomics and clinical outcomes

text: Although this study established a prognostic risk model using TCGA-LUAD data and successfully identified 4 genes (CDKN3, PEBP1, TNFRSF19, and PHB) with significant prognostic value, laying a foundation for LUAD treatment, several limitations remain. First, the sample size used for RT-qPCR validation was relatively small. While the results were consistent with TCGA/Gene Expression Omnibus analyses, this limited size may restrict the generalizability of the findings. Second, despite constructing the prognostic model, the specific biological functions and clinical applicability of these PRGs in LUAD require further investigation. Third, although the model’s AUC values all exceeded 0.6, indicating some predictive capability, they did not reach the commonly used threshold of 0.7, necessitating further research to enhance accuracy. Fourth, this study only examined a subset of PRGs; future studies are needed to identify other relevant genes and pathways in LUAD. Furthermore, the predicted potential drugs, vorinostat and raloxifene, currently lack supporting clinical trial data or pharmacological studies confirming their efficacy in LC, rendering their therapeutic potential for LUAD speculative. Finally, the latest (9th edition) Lung Cancer TNM (LCTNM) staging system subdivides N2 LC into N2a and N2b; however, our dataset lacked this granular information, necessitating analysis of more detailed data. Future work will incorporate additional genes, clinical variables, and more detailed staging criteria to refine the model. Validation will be strengthened by performing RT-qPCR on larger, multi-center clinical cohorts. Concurrently, in vitro and in vivo experimental techniques (e.g., gene knockout, overexpression) will be employed to verify these findings and elucidate the precise regulatory mechanisms of the prognostic genes in LUAD. Finally, pharmacological studies on vorinostat and raloxifene will be pursued. This will involve assessing efficacy through post-treatment cell viability assays and therapeutic experiments in animal disease models, along with mechanistic exploration, prior to evaluating their clinical potential.

text: This study successfully identified 4 genes with significant prognostic value (CDKN3, PEBP1, TNFRSF19, and PHB) and developed a prognostic risk model by extensively analyzing the role of PRGs in LUAD. RT-qPCR analysis of 5 LUAD samples and matched controls provided preliminary validation of the prognostic gene expression. The model demonstrated strong predictive capability in both the training and validation sets, offering a novel tool for assessing LUAD prognosis. Additionally, by identifying paraptosis-associated genes and mapping immune cell distributions within the TME, this study highlighted potential therapeutic agents that may target these genes, paving the way for new treatment strategies in LUAD.

text: In several multicellular organisms, stem cells maintain tissue integrity through proliferation Brunet et al. Specifically, in the skin, a stratified epithelium that protects organisms from insults and infections, stem cells in the basal layer of the epidermis can self‐renew and play essential roles in constant cell turnover and wound repair Simpson et al. During aging, epidermal stem cells undergo exhaustion and lose their proliferative capacity, which leads to a decline in their ability to maintain tissue homeostasis and repair damaged tissues (Goodell and Rando; Liu et al. Inomata et al. Although the mechanisms controlling epidermal stem cell activity and skin aging have been extensively studied, it is not well understood how intrinsic cellular signaling changes affect cell proliferation during aging. In addition to stem cell exhaustion, the loss of proteostasis is a hallmark of tissue aging (López‐Otín et al.). Proteostasis refers to the system that maintains protein homeostasis within cells by overseeing protein synthesis, ensuring protein quality control, and employing adaptive mechanisms to mitigate the accumulation of unfolded and misfolded proteins, thereby preventing abnormal protein aggregation and supporting tissue homeostasis Hipp et al. The ubiquitin‐proteasome and lysosome‐autophagy systems are major players in proteostasis maintenance, eliminating unfolded proteins from cells through proteolysis, and the activities of both systems decrease with aging (Kaushik and Cuervo). In addition to cytosolic proteostasis, the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress‐response system also contributes to proteostasis in organelles. ER plays a central role in the synthesis and correct folding of approximately one‐third of the cellular proteome (Braakman and Bulleid). Under conditions such as hypoxia, nutrient deprivation, increased protein oxidation, or disruptions in secretory pathways, the ER may excessively accumulate misfolded proteins, leading to a condition known as ER stress (Walter and Ron). ER stress activates three canonical pathways to prevent misfolded protein accumulation: inositol‐requiring enzyme 1 (Ire1)–X‐box binding protein‐1 (Xbp1), PKR‐like ER kinase (Perk)–activating transcription factor 4 (Atf4), and activating transcription factor 6 (Atf6) pathways (Hetz). In the Ire1–Xbp1s pathway, ER stress stimulates the dimerization and subsequent trans‐autophosphorylation of Ire1 and thereby facilitates RNase activity of Ire1. Activated Ire1 splices a 26‐nucleotide intron from Xbp1 mRNA to produce the transcription factor Xbp1s (spliced Xbp1). Xbp1s stimulates the expression of a cluster of genes related to protein folding and quality control mechanisms (Hetz). Previous studies in model organisms have revealed alterations in ER stress‐response activity during aging (Martínez et al.). In C. elegans, the ability to respond to pharmacological inducers of ER stress is lost with age (Ben‐Zvi et al., whereas in the Drosophila intestine, the Ire1‐Xbp1s pathway is activated during aging, which induces abnormal proliferation of aged intestinal cells Wang et al. Several studies in mice have shown that the ER stress‐response is activated during aging (Martínez et al.). Increased levels of Atf4 and Xbp1s were found in aged mouse osteocytes compared to young adults Chalil et al. Similarly, adipose stromal cells in aged mice show elevated levels of Atf6 and phosphorylated Ire1 Ghosh et al. These results suggest that ER stress and its response pathways are dysregulated with age and are associated with the progression of tissue aging.
title: ER Stress Ire1‐Xbp1s Pathway Maintains Youthful Epidermal Basal Layer Through the Regulation of Cell Proliferation

text: Several studies in mice have shown that the ER stress‐response is activated during aging (Martínez et al.). Increased levels of Atf4 and Xbp1s were found in aged mouse osteocytes compared to young adults Chalil et al. Similarly, adipose stromal cells in aged mice show elevated levels of Atf6 and phosphorylated Ire1 Ghosh et al. These results suggest that ER stress and its response pathways are dysregulated with age and are associated with the progression of tissue aging. Changes in the ER stress‐response have been considered to be linked to aging progression, but it is still poorly understood how these changes affect the vertebrate aging process, in part because the age‐dependent alteration of the ER stress‐response has been examined only in limited organs and cells. To uncover this, analyzing the dynamics and roles of the ER stress‐response throughout the vertebrate lifespan would be effective. However, the long lifespan of conventional vertebrate models (approximately 3 years for mice and zebrafish) has hampered our understanding. To overcome this hurdle, we utilized the African turquoise killifish, Nothobranchius furzeri, which is an extremely short‐lived (several months) small vertebrate Harel et al., to investigate the spatial dynamics and roles of ER stress‐response activity during the aging process.

text: We showed the aging‐associated dynamics and an unexpected role of the ER stress‐response pathway in regulating epidermal tissue homeostasis and aging using N. furzeri and human cell cultures. Previous studies have reported that the age‐dependent unfolded protein accumulation‐mediated ER stress and sustained activation of the ER stress‐response are linked to various aging‐associated diseases (Chen et al. Boslem et al. Lefebvre and Staels). Consistent with these observations, our qPCR and reporter analyses revealed that the ER stress‐response Ire1‐Xbp1s pathway is upregulated in various tissues of N. furzeri, including the liver and heart, with age. Surprisingly, Ire1‐Xbp1s was highly activated in the young N. furzeri epidermal basal layer and downregulated during aging. In young skin, the Ire1‐Xbp1s pathway maintains cell proliferation by activating the cell cycle regulator, Vcp. The activation of Ire1‐Xbp1s in the epidermal basal layer is driven by glucose metabolism, which also declines during aging. The glucose‐Ire1‐Xbp1s‐VCP axis also positively regulates the proliferation of human skin cell cultures. These results indicate that the ER stress‐response may control epidermal cell aging by sustaining its proliferative activity. ER stress has been regarded as detrimental; however, its beneficial effects are not well understood. In addition, studies on Ire1‐Xbp1s have focused on its role as an adaptive mechanism against misfolded protein aggregation stress; however, its other functions remain unclear. Although recent studies show that the Ire1‐Xbp1s pathway can promote proliferation of cancer cells in vitro Ji et al. and satellite cells in mouse injured muscle Roy et al., and pharmacological activation of ER stress stimulates β cell proliferation in vitro, the mechanism connecting ER stress response and cell proliferation remains unclear Sharma et al. Our reporter and spatial transcriptome analyses revealed a previously unrecognized role for ER stress signaling in the positive regulation of epidermal cell proliferation through Ire1‐Xbp1s to maintain skin homeostasis. We also demonstrated that age‐dependent downregulation of Ire1‐Xbp1s activity correlates with aging phenotype in the epidermal basal layer, whereas previous studies proposed that age‐dependent upregulation of the ER stress response is a driver of aging (Martínez et al. Wang et al. Ghosh et al. Furthermore, we successfully reactivated aged skin epidermal cells by pharmacologically activating ER stress. It is well understood that organismal aging is affected by surrounding environmental stimuli, including cellular stress (Kourtis and Tavernarakis). Previous studies on C. elegans have shown that oxidative stress during the larval stage may induce a hormesis state that enhances stress resistance and longevity Bazopoulou et al. Similarly, the ER stress‐response was recently shown to regulate cellular responses in human hematopoietic stem cells, where, under ER stress, human hematopoietic HSCs upregulated the pro‐survival Ire1‐Xbp1s branch to survive (van Galen et al. This indicates the possibility that moderate ER stress signaling and specific activation of the Ire1‐Xbp1s pathway could be beneficial for maintaining tissue homeostasis. Additionally, our observation that cytoplasmic ubiquitination was not detected in young epidermal basal layers suggests that strong Ire1‐Xbp1s activity in the young epidermal basal layer may be independent of unfolded protein;
title: ER Stress Ire1‐Xbp1s Pathway Maintains Youthful Epidermal Basal Layer Through the Regulation of Cell Proliferation

text: This indicates the possibility that moderate ER stress signaling and specific activation of the Ire1‐Xbp1s pathway could be beneficial for maintaining tissue homeostasis. Additionally, our observation that cytoplasmic ubiquitination was not detected in young epidermal basal layers suggests that strong Ire1‐Xbp1s activity in the young epidermal basal layer may be independent of unfolded protein; however, it is also important to note that activation of Ire1‐Xbp1s, to some extent, may reduce the accumulation of unfolded protein. Interestingly, the young brain mesencephalic region also shows strong Ire1‐Xbp1s activity, which declines with age, suggesting that Ire1‐Xbp1s activity may contribute to the maintenance of youthfulness in the epidermal basal layer, and this decline drives aging not only in the skin but also in other tissues. In contrast, the intestinal crypt Ire1‐Xbp1s activity tended to increase with age. The increase in Ire1‐Xbp1s activity in aged N. furzeri intestinal crypts might indicate abnormal cell proliferation, similar to findings in Drosophila intestines, where the Ire1‐Xbp1s pathway upregulation during aging causes abnormal intestinal cell proliferation Wang et al. Further investigation of various tissues is necessary to better understand the roles and significance of the Ire1‐Xbp1s pathway‐mediated control of cell proliferation in tissue homeostasis. The application of PIC, a novel spatial transcriptomics method, enabled the analysis of transcriptomes specific to the epidermal basal layer of N. furzeri and identify glucose metabolism and Vcp as upstream and downstream mediators of the Ire1‐Xbp1s pathway, respectively, in epidermal cell proliferation. Vcp has been well studied as a positive regulator of the cell cycle and cancer progression Meyer et al.; however, its roles and regulation in tissue homeostasis and cell proliferation are poorly understood. This study revealed that Vcp activity is essential for Ire1‐Xbp1s‐mediated N. furzeri epidermal cell proliferation. Notably, Vcp is also a known mediator of protein degradation during ER‐associated degradation (ERAD) which is activated during the ER stress‐response (Wolf and Stolz). In young skin epidermal basal layer, it is possible that Vcp plays a role not only in cell cycle control but also in protection from proteotoxic insults downstream of the Ire1‐Xbp1s ER stress‐response. Several studies have reported that reduced glucose metabolism correlates with an aging phenotype. For example, in Drosophila, aging leads to a reduction in the expression of glycolytic genes in the muscle and brain, and the forced expression of glycolytic genes extends a healthy lifespan (Ma et al. Oka et al. Glycolysis is also impaired in aged human brain and aged mouse endothelial cells Kiesworo et al. In this study, we showed that glucose promotes N. furzeri epidermal cell proliferation by activating the Ire1‐Xbp1s pathway and that age‐dependent reduction of glucose metabolism may downregulate the Ire1‐Xbp1s pathway to promote N. furzeri epidermal cell aging. Even though glucose‐dependent activation of Ire1‐Xbp1s was also observed in pancreatic β‐cells Sharma et al., it remains unclear how glucose stimulates Ire1‐Xbp1s via its metabolism.

In this study, we showed that glucose promotes N. furzeri epidermal cell proliferation by activating the Ire1‐Xbp1s pathway and that age‐dependent reduction of glucose metabolism may downregulate the Ire1‐Xbp1s pathway to promote N. furzeri epidermal cell aging. Even though glucose‐dependent activation of Ire1‐Xbp1s was also observed in pancreatic β‐cells Sharma et al., it remains unclear how glucose stimulates Ire1‐Xbp1s via its metabolism. A study on hepatoma cells suggested that the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, a metabolic pathway downstream of glucose, could stimulate ER stress through Idh2 ‐mediated mitochondrial NADPH production and glutathione redox Gansemer et al., indicating the possibility that glucose might activate Ire1‐Xbp1s activity through this TCA cycle‐mediated mechanism in N. furzeri skin. A previous study also showed that inhibiting lactate production by knocking out Ldh, an enzyme that produces lactate, suppressed stem cell proliferation in hair follicles, suggesting that increased production of lactate or other associated metabolites from glycolysis is essential for stem cell activation Flores et al. Thus, it might also be possible that lactate or other Ldh ‐associated metabolites are involved in the ER stress‐mediated epidermal cell activation Sun et al. Further elucidation of the relationship between cell metabolism and the ER stress response is necessary to uncover the cause of declining proliferation in epidermal cells. Importantly, the human public data also showed an age‐dependent reduction in the expression of ER stress‐response‐related genes, Vcp, and glycolysis‐related genes in human skin, similar to N. furzeri Schneider et al. These findings suggest that the glucose‐Ire1‐Xbp1s‐Vcp axis may contribute to the maintenance and aging of young human epidermal cells. Further understanding of the roles and regulation of Ire1‐Xbp1s activity in mammalian and human epidermal stem cells may lead to the discovery of promising therapeutic strategies for promoting healthy skin aging in humans.

text: Spinal cord injury (SCI) usually results in a large range of sensorimotor and autonomic nerve injury and remains a serious public health problem worldwide. SCI affects approximately 273 000 people in the United States, and there are some 12 000 new cases each year. Therefore, SCI brings severe economy burdens and psychological pressure to patients. However, there are currently no effective therapies for SCI clinically, and an effective treatment is awaited. This is due mainly to the molecular mechanisms of SCI remain elusive. The pathological process of SCI is known as a complex process, which can be classified into two phases: Primary injury is the direct mechanical damage of spinal cord tissue and includes demyelination and necrosis of neurons and axons; and the secondary injury is composed of a variety of pathophysiologic mechanisms, including local haemorrhage, ischaemia, oedema, ionic imbalance, free radical stress and inflammatory responses. This complex pathological process of SCI may explain the difficulty in finding a suitable and effective therapy. Therefore, understanding the molecular mechanisms of SCI is critical for the development of therapeutic strategies. Cell death is known as the final stage of cells and it can be resulted from cytotoxicity from exogenous or endogenous substances. In 1842, cell death was first posed by Carl Vogt, and lots of molecules are considered to be involved in this irreversible process to support the maintenance of cellular homeostasis. Cell death was initially divided into two types, necrosis and apoptosis. Necrosis is considered as a passive and accidental cell death, which can be resulted from environmental perturbations and the large amounts of release of inflammatory cellular contents. Apoptosis is considered as an active, programmed process of autonomous cellular dismantling without the release of cytoplasmic content to the extracellular space. In recent years, various forms of programmed cell death (PCD) were discovered, including autophagy, necroptosis, pyroptosis and ferroptosis. Unlike necrosis, PCD is known as an active cell death mediated by a cascade of gene expression events, commonly found in organisms. PCD is important for elimination unnecessary and damaged cells, and it can also represent a defence mechanism. As research has progressed, more and more researches showed that PCD was involved in central nervous system (CNS) development, neurodegenerative disorders, psychiatric disorders and CNS injury. More recently, there still is a lack of the study on PCD in SCI, and increasing evidence shows that PCD play significant roles following SCI. In this review, we summarized and explored the recent advances in the roles of PCD in SCI in order to know the molecular mechanisms underlying SCI.
title: Programmed cell death in spinal cord injury pathogenesis and therapy

text: As a type of PCD, apoptosis is the most common form of PCD, it was extensively studied and could be defined as programmed self‐killing simply. Apoptosis has been considered as an immunologically silent form of PCD since cell corpses are cleared by phagocytes, and it can arise from the extrinsic (death receptor initiated) and the intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathways. Excitotoxins, free radicals and inflammatory mediators are known as the factors that initiate cell death and stimulate necrosis or apoptosis. Apoptosis is known as a naturally occurring physiological process and may play a key role in secondary SCI. The secondary injury following SCI is considered to be due to the continuation of cellular destruction through apoptosis, and the long‐term neurological deficits following SCI might result from a large range of apoptosis of neurons and oligodendrocytes in the injured spinal cord, so a better understanding of apoptosis following SCI will lead to novel strategies for therapeutic interventions. Apoptosis can be found in the injured spinal cord of animal models and humans. Injury‐induced apoptosis could be observed in neurons, astrocytes, oligodendroglia and microglia in rat spinal cord after injury, and the apoptotic oligodendrocytes mainly located in the longitudinal tracts of the white matter. Apoptosis in neurons was detected at 4 hours and peaked at 8 hours after injury; apoptosis in glial cells was detected at 4 hours after injury, and peaked at 24 hours after injury; apoptosis in oligodendrocytes was detected in the white matter at 24 hours and reached to the highest at 8 days after injury. Apoptosis in microglia was relatively rare at 24 hours and 5 days, but gradually increased in numbers and peaked at 8 days post‐injury. Furthermore, most of apoptotic cells could be observed in the rim of surviving tissue around the centre of the injured spinal cord, and this may help explain why the lesion area expand, progressively. Apoptosis can also be detected in oligodendrocytes in white matter tracts showing Wallerian degeneration, which is a significant characteristic in chronic phase of SCI. In recent years, more and more studies occur to investigate the role of apoptosis after SCI. Apoptosis is a caspase‐dependent cell death modality, and this programme was primarily regulated by the caspase family of cysteine proteases. Upstream and downstream components of the caspase‐3 apoptotic pathway have proved to be activated after SCI in rats and play a vital role in the process of apoptosis. Previous studies showed that activation of the Fas death receptor pathway played a key role in neuronal, oligodendrocyte and microglia apoptosis in animal models following SCI. The interaction of Fas and Fas receptor (FasR) initiates apoptosis via the activation of the cysteine proteases resulting in proteolysis and DNA cleavage by effector caspases culminating in cell death. Some key signalling pathways, including SIRT1/AMPK signalling pathway, Wnt/β‐catenin signalling pathway and E2F1/CDK1 pathway, have already proved to be involved in regulating apoptotic activity in SCI. Furthermore, recent studies revealed that microRNAs (miRNAs) and long non‐coding RNAs (lncRNAs) may have an important effect on the pathogenesis of SCI including cell apoptosis. A previous study revealed that miR‐137 could inhibit apoptosis after SCI via targeting MK2. Gu et al found that knockdown of long coding RNA XIST played a critical role in inhibiting neuronal apoptosis after SCI by competitively binding miR‐494 and regulation on PTEN/AKT/mTOR pathway.

text: Furthermore, recent studies revealed that microRNAs (miRNAs) and long non‐coding RNAs (lncRNAs) may have an important effect on the pathogenesis of SCI including cell apoptosis. A previous study revealed that miR‐137 could inhibit apoptosis after SCI via targeting MK2. Gu et al found that knockdown of long coding RNA XIST played a critical role in inhibiting neuronal apoptosis after SCI by competitively binding miR‐494 and regulation on PTEN/AKT/mTOR pathway. Another study showed that PI3K/Akt/mTOR signalling pathway took part in the apoptosis of neurons after SCI and this pathway could induce apoptosis by activation of the mitochondrial pathway. Having an in‐depth knowledge of the molecular and cellular mechanisms of apoptosis can help us screen out the specific drug targets. Liu et al used proteomics analysis to find a key protein, endoplasmic reticulum protein 29 (ERp29), which could regulate a group of genes related with cell survival and apoptosis including caspase and Erk and improve locomotor function in spinal cord transection rats. Furthermore, minocycline, antibody blockade of the CD95 (FAS) ligand and the blockade of glycosphingolipid‐induced iNOS have already proved to suppress the apoptosis of neurons and glia cells, and it is accompanied by improvement in neurological outcomes, and increase the efficacy of cell transplantation strategies. In another recent study, CARD6, Caspase recruitment domain family member 6, was shown to be a key molecular which could inhibit apoptosis by decreasing Cyto‐c release to cytosol from mitochondria and inhibition of Caspase‐3 signalling pathway. Zhang et al firstly performed a rat model of SCI, and upregulated p38 was related to inflammation and apoptosis after SCI. Zhang et al also suggested that p38 inhibitor SB203580 treatment could alleviate secondary SCI by suppressing inflammation and apoptosis. The deficiency of progranulin, a 593 amino acid secreted glycoprotein, is not conducive to SCI recovery via promotion of cellular apoptosis and neuroinflammation. In a recent study, metformin was found to increase the expressions of β‐catenin and brain derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), inhibit neuron apoptosis and inflammatory response, and promote motor functional recovery in rats after SCI. In the above research results, it has been shown that apoptosis contributed to the tissue damage following SCI. Finding the way to inhibit apoptosis after SCI may have important clinical implications for the further treatment. Although more and more studies focus on the intrinsic or extrinsic signals which are associated with apoptosis following SCI, there are more problems still need to be studied, including the detailed mechanisms causing apoptotic death of neurons, astrocytes, oligodendroglia and microglia after SCI.
title: Programmed cell death in spinal cord injury pathogenesis and therapy

text: Apoptosis was known as the only form of PCD traditionally, however, more and more studies showed that necrosis can be induced in a similar manner to apoptosis, which is termed ‘programmed necrosis’ or ‘necroptosis’. Necroptosis can be regulated by the caspase‐independent pathway and shows the morphological characteristics of necrosis (early loss of plasma membrane integrity, gain in cell volume and swelling organelles). In recent years, necroptosis has been found to contribute to many diseases including neurodegenerative diseases, ischaemic brain injury and viral myocardial infarction. The most widely studied pathway causing necroptosis results from binding of Tumour necrosis factor‐α (TNF‐α) to TNF‐R1. Various studies have shown that necroptosis are involved in intracellular signalling cascade transduced by receptor‐interacting protein 1/3 (RIP1/3) and mixed lineage kinase domain‐like protein (MLKL). RIP1 kinase activity has been verified to be essential for the activation of necroptosis. In recent research, the author found that overexpress and knockdown PSMB4 could regulate the MLKL and RIP3 pathway in TNF‐α induced necroptosis cell model. Furthermore, Wang et al found that necrostatin‐1 (Nec‐1), inhibitor of necroptosis, could improve and protect the physiological function by inhibiting necroptosis via inhibition of RIP1/3–MLKL recruitment. In another research, the results also revealed that necroptosis could contribute to neural cell death, and Nec‐1 could reduce histopathological and functional deficits after SCI in mice. Therefore, Nec‐1 could be a potential target for treating SCI. Moreover, accumulating evidences revealed that necroptosis is bound up with inflammation following SCI. Fan et al found that endoplasmic reticulum of necroptotic microglia/macrophages could be manipulated for regulating inflammation following SCI. Then their subsequent study showed that reactive astrocytes could undergo M1 microglia/macrophages‐induced necroptosis through TLR/MyD88 signalling pathway. Shao et al found that Smurf1 could facilitate necroptosis of neurons after LPS‐induced neuroinflammation, and Smurf1 may be a potential target for treatment. Necroptosis was already considered as a critical and emerging mode of PCD following SCI. It has been previously demonstrated that activation of necroptosis leads to neuronal and glial cell death after SCI. Activation of necroptosis has been found to lead to cell loss and tissue damage in central nervous system injury, including SCI. Although some work has been done to explore the molecular mechanism of necroptosis after SCI, the understanding of necroptosis is still inadequate. Therefore, identification of the role of necroptosis in the pathological processes of SCI is necessary to find the therapeutic target for secondary injury.
