section_title: ER ‐Stress Initiated Apoptosis and Its Mitigation by EMPA

text: Despite several attempts to prevent and treat DIC, the rate of its development in the cancer population has not improved over the years. Although traditional therapies including RAS antagonists and beta blockers are used in the management of heart failure, no drug has been approved specifically for the treatment of DIC and heart failure. Even though EMPA has been approved as guideline directed medical therapy for heart failure, little is known of its potential role in the setting of DIC. In this study using a chronic in vivo model of DIC, we found that prophylactic and concurrent treatment with EMPA can prevent adverse cardiovascular remodelling. Specifically, there were adverse changes in the structure and function of the myocardium in rats treated with Dox, which were rescued by EMPA treatment. Additionally, we recorded activation of all three ER transmembrane proteins, but not chaperones, indicating a switch from the adaptive response to apoptosis following Dox treatment. EMPA was able to maintain ER homeostasis in our in vivo DIC model through initiation of the ER adaptive response, upregulated chaperone expression and downregulated ER‐initiated apoptosis proteins.

text: SGLT2i are the latest addition to guideline‐directed medical therapy in the management of heart failure as they have the potential to improve cardiovascular remodelling. Previous murine studies have evaluated the role of EMPA, a SGLT2i, in the prevention of DIC. Bariş et al. administered 18 mg/kg BW Dox to Sprague Dawley rats on Days 2, 4, 8,10, 12 and 14 alongside 10 mg/kg BW EMPA daily during this 2‐week period. They observed that Dox‐only treated rats had an increase in LV volumes with a depressed LVEF of 35% at the 2‐week study end point. Conversely, rats concurrently treated with EMPA + Dox had a significant reduction in LV volumes with an improved LVEF of 74%. Additional studies have confirmed dapagliflozin (DAPA), another SGLT2i, in the improvement of LVEF in rats treated with DAPA + Dox. In their study, Chang et al. reported that prophylactic treatment with DAPA 10 mg/kg BW daily for 6 weeks followed by 4 weeks of Dox at 20 mg/kg improved LVEF to 85% as compared to 75% in the Dox only group. Similarly, Hseih et al. also showed a significant improvement in LVEF to 75% when DAPA was administered 0.1 mg/kg daily for 4 weeks concurrently with 12 mg/kg BW weekly injections of Dox compared to 50% LVEF in the Dox only group. All of the aforementioned studies used a SGLT2i in either the prophylactic setting or concurrent treatment with Dox. In our preclinical study, we mimicked a clinically relevant chronic in vivo DIC model in SD rats with EMPA being administered before, during and after Dox therapy. Our 6‐week study demonstrated that Dox + EMPA significantly improved LV remodelling with a decrease in LV cavity dimensions by approximately 20% as compared to the Dox‐only treated group. There was also a significant improvement in LVEF of 66% in the Dox + EMPA treated rats as compared to a LVEF of 50% in the Dox only group which corroborates the findings of the previous aforementioned studies. It is worth noting that significant BW reduction can influence cardiac function. However, severe or rapid weight loss accompanied by ascites is often associated with worsened cardiac outcomes in Dox‐treated groups. In our study, although the Dox + EMPA group exhibited significant weight loss, this was accompanied by improved cardiac markers and absence of abdominal edema, suggesting that EMPA's cardioprotective effects extend beyond the impact of weight change alone. Overall, SGLT2i used in both the prevention and treatment settings can prevent adverse cardiovascular remodelling in preclinical models of DIC.

text: In addition to LV cavity dilation and LV systolic dysfunction, loss of myocardial integrity is an established side effect of Dox. Several preclinical studies using a chronic DIC model have reported myofibril fragmentation, mitochondrial swelling, loss of ER reticular network and vacuolisation of the cytoplasm. Recently, EMPA was shown to be beneficial in preserving myocardial ultrastructure in several preclinical studies in either a diabetic cardiomyopathy or postmyocardial infarction model. In the DIC model, Bariş et al. observed that a SGLT2i can maintain mitochondrial integrity with preserved myofibrils in Dox + EMPA treated rats using EM. Our study also demonstrated the cardioprotective effects of EMPA in preserving cardiomyocyte ultrastructure using EM. In our comprehensive study, we also performed light microscopy which confirmed that EMPA was able to reduce cardiac fibrosis in the Dox + EMPA group. Two previous studies have reported similar findings that EMPA mitigates Dox induced fibrosis in a C57BL/6 mouse model. The effects of EMPA on reducing cardiac fibrosis has been previously reported in other disease models as well including hypertension, diabetes and postmyocardial infarction. Overall, SGL2Ti, including EMPA, reduce cardiac fibrosis and preserve mitochondrial integrity and myofibrils in a DIC model.

text: The intermediary role of ER‐stress leading to cardiac dysfunction and apoptosis has been previously proposed as an important mechanism of DIC by our group and others. Since EMPA has been reported to reduce OS and inflammation which can trigger UPR and ER‐initiated apoptosis, we investigated the potential effects of EMPA in reducing ER‐stress and subsequently DIC. We observed the activation of all three ER transmembrane proteins following Dox treatment indicating the initiation of ER‐stress. A significant upregulation of ATF6 and IRE1α under Dox treatment was previously reported by our group and others, in both in vitro and in vivo models of DIC. Although EMPA treatment in the Dox + EMPA group did not have any significant effect on ATF6 activity, IRE1α and its downstream molecule unspliced XBP1 were significantly upregulated. Additionally, a significant increase in IRE1α expression in the Dox + EMPA group played a pivotal role in restoring ER homeostasis and promoting cell survival under Dox‐induced stress. This is supported by the restored morphological and functional aspects of the heart observed in our experiments (Figures and). While previous reports have identified general ER stress reduction by SGLT2 inhibitors, our data uniquely reveal that EMPA promotes adaptive UPR signalling via enhanced XBP1 unspliced protein, thereby distinguishing its mechanism from broader ER stress modulators. Additionally, unspliced XBP1 forms a complex with spliced XBP1 to suppress its function and promote ER‐stress recovery. In EMPA group, our findings suggest that EMPA initially activates PERK signalling to induce protective chaperones, followed by a resolution phase characterised by downregulation of PERK and sustained IRE1α/XBP1 activity in Dox + EMPA group. This temporal modulation aligns with models proposed by Hetz and Papa, where dynamic UPR signalling determines cell fate under chronic ER stress. EMPA‐induced inhibition of PERK and subsequent autophagy has been reported in an ischemia/reperfusion myocardial injury model as well. On the other hand, other studies reported an increase in autophagy following EMPA treatment that helped in attenuating ER stress and subsequent apoptosis. Similar contradictory results were found in our study as EMPA treatment alone increased PERK expression and possibly cardioprotective autophagy. Although we observed overexpression of all three UPR proteins in the Dox group, the expression of the ER chaperone GRP78 was significantly low in the Dox treated group. GRP78 in the whole heart is essential in downregulating overall ER stress and inhibiting ER‐initiated apoptosis. In our study, EMPA upregulated the expression of the ER chaperone, GRP78, in the Dox + EMPA group which may play an essential role in cardioprotection via assisting protein folding and inhibiting overall ER stress. We also measured ER‐linked apoptotic protein expression in different treatment groups. ER‐resident caspase‐12 is activated by cleavage and leads to cleavage of caspase‐3 and links ER‐initiated apoptosis to mitochondrial apoptosis. Both caspase‐12 and 3 were highly upregulated in the Dox group and EMPA treatment was able to rescue apoptosis in the Dox + EMPA group. In addition to activation of caspases, we also observed phosphorylation of JNK which has been reported as one of the key players in Dox‐induced apoptosis that can be activated by both ER‐dependent and ER‐independent pathways. The activation of these cell executioners in the Dox group led to myocardial loss as confirmed by histology.

text: Both caspase‐12 and 3 were highly upregulated in the Dox group and EMPA treatment was able to rescue apoptosis in the Dox + EMPA group. In addition to activation of caspases, we also observed phosphorylation of JNK which has been reported as one of the key players in Dox‐induced apoptosis that can be activated by both ER‐dependent and ER‐independent pathways. The activation of these cell executioners in the Dox group led to myocardial loss as confirmed by histology. The role of EMPA in attenuating apoptosis has been reported in multiple studies in several disease models. However, the effects of EMPA on procaspase‐12 downregulation to block ER‐initiated apoptosis are very important in attenuating cardiomyocyte death and promoting healthy myocardium. In conclusion, our results indicate that EMPA induced IRE1α/XBP1 signalling helped manage the overall ER‐stress and aided in ER‐stress recovery in the Dox + EMPA group. Our findings also suggest that early administration may offer cardioprotective benefits to DIC. However, further clinical studies are needed to determine the safety and efficacy of EMPA before such an approach can be integrated into standard clinical care.

text: Our study demonstrates the involvement of IRE1 in maintaining ER homeostasis and attenuating ER‐initiated apoptosis in in vivo settings. There are a few chemical IRE1 inhibitors available such as STF‐083010, ORIN1001 and toxoflavin that can be utilised to better understand and to compare the role of IRE1 in Dox‐induced ER stress‐initiated apoptosis and to compare the role of EMPA in inducing its cardioprotective effects via IRE1 adaptive response. Additionally, siRNA‐mediated knockdown of IRE1α or XBP1 could be used to evaluate their critical roles in EMPA‐mediated cardio protection and to further elucidate the underlying molecular pathways. Future studies should also incorporate more comprehensive morphological assessments, including gross and histological evaluation of cardiac dilation, to further support the functional and hemodynamic findings. In addition, histological staining of heart sections for markers of apoptosis and necrosis would provide spatial evidence of cellular injury and further strengthen the mechanistic understanding of the cardioprotective effects observed.

text: Photodynamic therapy (PDT) involves the use of photosensitizing agents that target specific sub-cellular loci. Irradiation at wavelengths corresponding to an absorbance band of a photosensitizer can trigger pathways to cell-death. A study involving tumor cells derived from patients with head and neck cancer explored response patterns to ionizing radiation (IR) vs. photodynamic therapy (PDT) using benzoporphyrin derivative (BPD, Visudyne) as the photosensitizing agent. Tumor cells derived from patients infected with the human papilloma virus (HPV) showed an enhanced response to IR but an impaired response to PDT when compared with cells from uninfected patients. The poor response to PDT in HPV(+) tumor cells could not be attributed to impaired BPD accumulation or reduced reactive oxygen species (ROS) formation associated with PDT. While apoptosis was impaired in HPV(−) cells, such cells can be killed via photodamage directed at the ER: this leads to a non-apoptotic death pathway termed paraptosis. We now provide further information on determinants of PDT efficacy as a function of sub-cellular PDT targets and the HPV status of the patient from whom tumor was derived.

text: Infection with HPV tends to enhance the clinical response of head and neck cancer to ionizing radiation [ – ]. An earlier study involving cell cultures revealed that a line (UP154) derived from a patient with an HPV infection was less responsive to PDT (with BPD as photosensitizer) than another cell line (WSU12) that came from an HPV(−) patient. depicts survival as a function of HPV status after exposure to PDT. We interpret these data, combined with more recent studies, to suggest that an HPV infection promotes the apoptotic response to IR but impairs the effects of ER/mitochondrial photodamage to initiate both apoptosis and paraptosis. Effects of lysosomal photodamage mimic IR: apoptotic death is more readily evoked in HPV(+) cells. Effects of PDT using BPD vs. NPe6 reflect differences in the target(s) for photodamage. BPD is known to partition to ER and mitochondria, a pattern that can lead to apoptosis and paraptosis, whichever is available. With apoptosis impaired in WSU12 cells, paraptosis becomes the pathway to cell death after ER photodamage. Photodamage to lysosomes leads to only apoptosis. Compared with ER/mitochondrial targeting by BPD the lethality of NPe6-directed PDT was greater in HPV(+) cells, since apoptosis is an available death mechanism. Because of an impaired apoptotic pathway, WSU12 cells were less responsive to the effects of lysosomal photodamage) (. While the UP154 cell line did show a greater phototoxic response than WSU12, photokilling after lysosomal photodamage was limited even at a relatively high light dose. Prior studies had shown the PDT dose-response curve for WSU12 had a prominent shoulder, consistent with the cytoprotective effect of autophagy. No such shoulder was observed for UP154. There is no evidence of impaired BPD accumulation by UP154 cells. Moreover, the rate of formation of singlet molecular oxygen during irradiation was similar in both lines. A summary of information relating to responses of these cell lines to IR vs. PDT is shown in. Determinants of PDT efficacy have yet to be fully explored. Casas et al summarized a collection of potential factors. These include [a] impaired photosensitizer accumulation, [b] altered sub-cellular localization, [c] enhanced capacity for DNA repair, [d] variation in induction of early-response genes and signal transduction pathways, [e] quenching of reactive oxygen species, [f] altered expression of heat shock proteins, [g] resistance mediated by NO formation or survivin. With regard to cell lines examined here, prior results rule out [a], [b] and [e]. Effects of an HPV infection on the other pathways remain to be explored. Tasso et al reported a correlation between rates of photobleaching vs. photodamage to artificial membranes. These authors reported finding no correlation between PDT efficacy and ROS formation and therefore proposed that the extent of photobleaching might be a more pertinent determinant of efficacy. Since no examples of actual photokilling were examined, it is not clear that these results reflect the role of PDT as a means to tumor eradication. Several studies have indicated that hypoxia can limit photokilling, indicating that ROS formation is required. Affinity of photosensitizing agents for sub-cellular membranes is, however, a determinant of efficacy since ROS formed during irradiation will have a very limited lifetime. There are metabolic effects associated with an HPV infection that could affect the ability of photodamage to eradicate a cell population.

text: Since no examples of actual photokilling were examined, it is not clear that these results reflect the role of PDT as a means to tumor eradication. Several studies have indicated that hypoxia can limit photokilling, indicating that ROS formation is required. Affinity of photosensitizing agents for sub-cellular membranes is, however, a determinant of efficacy since ROS formed during irradiation will have a very limited lifetime. There are metabolic effects associated with an HPV infection that could affect the ability of photodamage to eradicate a cell population. These include decreased glucose metabolism and more dependence on mitochondrial respiration. There was also a report that infection with Epstein/Barr and HPV can lower both glutathione peroxidase and superoxide dismutase levels which would be expected to promote photokilling. No data was acquired from cells lacking both infections, so there the ‘base-line’ values were missing. The potential role of such metabolic differences in the lethality of both ionizing radiation and PDT remains to be explored. Lockshin has postulated that a lethally damaged cell will take any available pathway to death. Examples shown in this report relating to apoptosis and paraptosis provide further evidence for this proposal. In reviews of PDT efficacy in clinical studies, there have been no reports of decreased responsiveness when there is a concurrent HPV infection [ – ]. The ability of PDT to affect multiple factors related to tumor survival may account for this observation. In addition to direct cell killing, PDT can also shut down the tumor vasculature and stimulate antitumor immunologic responses.
title: Characteristics of an Impaired PDT Response

text: Photodynamic therapy (PDT) is a procedure for the selective eradication of neoplastic cells. This involves a photosensitizing agent that preferentially localizes in such cell types, light at a wavelength that corresponds to an absorbance band of the photosensitizer and molecular oxygen. Because of tissue optics, wavelengths at 630 - 750 nm are needed for this purpose. At shorter wavelengths, photons will be scattered and absorbed and tissue penetration is limited. Successful PDT involves both direct tumor killing, shutdown of the tumor vasculature and immunologic effects. Death pathways are examined here using the phenothiazine EtNBS to selectively photosensitize lysosomes and BPD (benzoporphyrin derivative, Visudyne) to target ER > mitochondria. The pathway to cell death is a function of sites of sub-cellular photodamage. The principal consequences of PDT are apoptosis, paraptosis, necrosis and autophagy, with the latter generally considered to be cytoprotective. Necrosis can also occur at higher PDT doses. The latter is usually associated with loss of tissue specificity since most ‘normal’ cell types will also accumulate levels of photosensitizing agents sufficient to cause photodamage at high light doses. We have shown that paraptosis can be a pertinent death pathway even when apoptosis is impaired. More recently, data was obtained indicating that PDT doses required for tumor eradication, i.e., in the LD 90 to LD 99 range, can shift the mechanism of paraptosis from the ‘canonical’ pathway, i.e., the route initiated by certain drugs or biochemical manipulations [ - ]. What can be termed the ‘non-canonical’ route to paraptosis is found at the higher, more clinically-relevant PDT doses required for tumor eradication. Unlike the drug-induced pathway, ‘non-canonical’ paraptosis does not require a brief interval of protein synthesis or action of kinases that are involved in the ‘canonical’ route. At very high PDT doses, sufficient to result in cross-linking of ER proteins, we have observed that paraptosis can be impaired with cell death then associated with apoptosis and/or necrosis.

text: Canine mammary tumours (CMT) are the most common tumours in female dogs, with malignancy and prognosis influenced by reproductive status. Although early ovariohysterectomy reduces CMT risk, nearly half of the cases in intact females are malignant and late‐spayed dogs face a similar risk of developing malignant tumours as intact females. These malignancies pose significant therapeutic challenges. Standard treatments including surgery and chemotherapy are often limited in effectiveness, especially against malignant tumours that are resistant or recur. Moreover, conventional chemotherapy with cytotoxic agents is commonly associated with adverse effects, including gastrointestinal disturbances, bone marrow suppression, and systemic toxicity, all of which can impact the patient's quality of life. This highlights the need for new therapeutic approaches in veterinary oncology that can effectively target treatment‐resistant malignant CMT with minimal side effects. Drug repurposing involves identifying new therapeutic uses for existing drugs beyond their original medical indications. This strategy is a promising approach to accelerate the development of new treatments, as it leverages known safety profiles and clinical data from approved drugs. Auranofin (AF) is an FDA‐approved drug initially used for human rheumatoid arthritis. In veterinary medicine, AF is used to treat idiopathic polyarthritis and pemphigus complex in dogs and cats, with oral doses of 0.05–0.3 mg/kg every 12 h. Recently, AF has demonstrated significant anticancer effects both in vitro and in vivo in various human cancers, including chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) and osteosarcoma. In addition, AF has shown in vitro efficacy against classical Hodgkin lymphoma, non‐small cell lung cancer, and breast cancer. AF's anticancer effects are linked to its ability to inhibit thioredoxin reductase (TrxR), an enzyme that helps maintain redox balance in cancer cells. By inhibiting TrxR, AF increases oxidative stress, leading to stress in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and cell death. Given its demonstrated effects on human breast cancer and established use in animals, AF warrants further investigation into its anticancer potential in CMT. Paraptosis is a distinct mode of programmed cell death different from apoptosis, characterised by large vacuoles in the cytoplasm originating from a swollen ER or mitochondria. Since paraptosis is not inhibited by standard apoptotic blockers, it could serve as an effective alternative cell death pathway in cancers resistant to apoptosis‐driven therapies. In human breast cancer cells, AF has been shown to induce paraptosis through dual inhibition of TrxR and the proteasome. However, to our knowledge, paraptosis has not been described in canine cancer cells. Recent research has examined AF's effects on CMT cells, demonstrating its ability to induce apoptosis via the PI3K/AKT pathway. While this study provided valuable insights, it primarily focused on apoptosis and did not explore alternative mechanisms of cell death. Therefore, this study aims to investigate the effects of AF on CMT cells, with a focus on its potential to suppress TrxR activity, induce ER stress‐mediated apoptosis, and paraptosis‐like cell death.

text: To examine AF's mechanisms in AF‐sensitive CMT cell lines, CMT‐U27, CHMm, and CHMp cells were treated with increasing AF concentrations, and the expression of proteins associated with ER stress, proteasome inhibition, and apoptosis was analysed. Western blot analysis revealed a concentration‐dependent ER stress response, with IRE1α expression rising up to 2 μM AF, followed by ATF4 induction at higher concentrations. Proteasome inhibition was indicated by the accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins, noticeable at 3 μM and more pronounced at 4 μM. Additionally, a dose‐dependent decrease in pro‐caspase‐3 and increases in cleaved PARP and Bax suggest AF induces apoptosis in these cell lines. In summary, 0.5–2 μM AF effectively induced ER stress‐mediated apoptosis in AF‐sensitive cells, while concentrations exceeding 3 μM led to near‐complete cell death through additional proteasome inhibition. These results indicated that AF induces anticancer effects in AF‐sensitive CMT cells through ER stress, proteasome inhibition, and apoptosis.

text: When observing morphological changes over time in AF‐resistant CMT cell lines (CIPp and CIPm) treated with 2 μM AF and 16.7 nM Bz, small cytoplasmic vacuoles appeared in some cells after 8 h. By 24 h, most cells exhibited extensive cytoplasmic vacuolization, and vacuoles became larger at 32 h. Eventually, cells began to detach and float with intact vacuoles inside. Massive cytoplasmic vacuolization is a hallmark of paraptosis, a form of non‐apoptotic cell death that requires active protein synthesis. To determine whether the observed vacuolation was indicative of paraptosis, we pretreated AF‐resistant CMT cell lines with CHX, a protein synthesis inhibitor known to prevent paraptosis. Vacuolation was absent with AF alone and occurred in less than 20% of cells treated with Bz alone, with random analysis of over 300 cells showing vacuoles in 16.8% of CIPp and 5.8% of CIPm cells after 24 h (In contrast, the combination (AF + Bz) induced extensive vacuolation in nearly all cells, while CHX pretreatment completely inhibited vacuolation and partially restored cell viability (These findings support a paraptosis‐like mechanism and a potential association connecting vacuole formation with reduced cell viability. Paraptosis is characterised by vacuoles originating from a swollen ER or mitochondria. To trace the origin of the vacuoles observed in AF + Bz‐treated cells, we stained the cells with ER‐Tracker Green and Hoechst 33342. Live‐cell staining revealed the vacuoles primarily co‐localised with the ER, suggesting the AF + Bz‐induced vacuoles originate from ER swelling and indicating a likely involvement of ER stress in this process. Collectively, AF + Bz‐induced cell death exhibits features of paraptosis: (1) extensive vacuolation, (2) ER‐originating vacuoles, and (3) suppression of vacuolation and cytotoxicity by CHX. However, cleaved PARP expression suggests concurrent apoptosis, as also observed in sensitive cell lines (Thus, this cell death is classified as paraptosis‐like rather than typical paraptosis.

text: To elucidate the mechanism underlying AF + Bz‐induced paraptosis‐like cell death in AF‐resistant CMT cells, TrxR activity assays and Western blot analyses were performed. Consistent with previous findings, 2 μM AF effectively inhibited TrxR activity (AF + Bz inhibited TrxR activity to a level similar to AF alone at 2 μM, showing that TrxR inhibition is primarily driven by AF, while Bz alone has no effect on TrxR activity. In contrast, Bz alone or combined with AF increased ubiquitinated protein levels, highlighting its role in proteasome inhibition, whereas 2 μM AF had no effect on proteasome activity in AF‐resistant cell lines (AF + Bz also elevated IRE1α expression more than either agent alone, suggesting that the combination induces ER stress more effectively than single‐agent treatments. In cells pretreated with CHX, the AF + Bz‐induced increases in both IRE1α and ubiquitinated proteins were suppressed. These findings demonstrate that CHX prevents cytoplasmic vacuolation and restores cell viability by reducing proteasome dysfunction and ER stress. Collectively, these results indicate the AF + Bz combination induces paraptosis‐like cell death by inhibiting TrxR activity through AF and proteasome activity through Bz, leading to ER stress of CMT cells. This highlights that combining AF with Bz in resistant cell lines effectively mimics the impact of lethal doses (≥ 3 μM) of AF in sensitive cell lines, resulting in pronounced cancer cell death.

section_title: AF + Bz Induces Paraptosis‐Like Cell Death via TrxR Inhibition, Proteasome Inhibition, and ER Stress

text: This study provides new insights into the cytotoxic mechanisms of AF in malignant CMT cells, expanding beyond previous research that primarily focused on apoptosis. In veterinary oncology, AF's anticancer effects have been largely associated with apoptosis, with an in vitro study in canine lymphoma, in vitro and xenograft models of osteosarcoma, and a clinical pilot study in dogs with osteosarcoma. Similarly, a recent study revealed AF's role in inducing apoptosis in CMT cells but did not examine other mechanisms. In contrast, our study expands this understanding by exploring the multifaceted mechanisms underlying AF's cytotoxic effects, including TrxR inhibition, proteasome inhibition, ER stress, and paraptosis‐like cell death. TrxR is critical for maintaining cellular redox balance by reducing thioredoxin (Trx), which regulates reactive oxygen species (ROS) generated during metabolism. In cancer cells, high metabolic demands increase reliance on TrxR for redox homeostasis. Our study demonstrated that AF‐sensitive CMT cell lines showed greater reductions in TrxR activity at lower AF concentrations, likely contributing to their heightened sensitivity to AF. In contrast, AF‐resistant CMT cell lines exhibited resilience to TrxR inhibition, potentially due to compensatory redox pathways. This aligns with findings in human lung cancer cells, where AF resistance is associated with alternative mechanisms such as glutathione reductase (GSR) and NAD(P)H quinone dehydrogenase 1 (NQO1), which help mitigate oxidative stress in resistant cells. The proteasome is essential for maintaining cellular proteostasis by degrading misfolded or damaged proteins. Proteasome inhibition results in the accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins, inducing proteotoxic stress and activating ER stress pathways such as the unfolded protein response (UPR) and integrated stress response (ISR). In human breast cancer cells, 5 nM Bz has been shown to cause similar levels of ubiquitinated protein accumulation as observed with 4–5 μM AF. However, in the AF‐sensitive CMT cell line CHMp, ubiquitinated protein accumulation at 10 nM Bz did not significantly differ from the control group (This suggests that CMT cells may exhibit higher resistance to proteasome inhibition than human breast cancer cells, requiring higher Bz concentrations to achieve effective proteasome inhibition. ER stress occurs when the ER's protein‐folding capacity is overwhelmed, leading to an accumulation of misfolded or unfolded proteins. This activates the UPR and ISR, which restores proteostasis or induces cell death under prolonged stress. The UPR plays a central role in managing ER stress, with IRE1α as a key mediator. IRE1α drives the expression of genes that alleviate the protein‐folding burden. Complementing the UPR, the ISR integrates various stress signals, such as ER stress, nutrient deprivation, and oxidative stress. ISR activation promotes the translation of stress‐responsive transcripts like ATF4. ATF4 regulates genes involved in programmed cell death, with persistent ISR activation often marking the transition from adaptation to cell death. In AF‐sensitive CMT cells, IRE1α expression initially increased, indicating early UPR activation aimed at restoring ER proteostasis. With increasing concentrations of AF treatment, IRE1α expression decreased while ATF4 expression rose, reflecting a shift from UPR‐mediated adaptation to ISR activation. This transition indicates that the stress exceeded the tolerance of sensitive cells, leading them to initiate programmed cell death.
title: Auranofin Induces ER Stress‐Mediated Apoptosis, and Its Combination With Bortezomib Elicits Paraptosis‐Like Cell Death in Malignant Canine Mammary Tumour Cells

text: ATF4 regulates genes involved in programmed cell death, with persistent ISR activation often marking the transition from adaptation to cell death. In AF‐sensitive CMT cells, IRE1α expression initially increased, indicating early UPR activation aimed at restoring ER proteostasis. With increasing concentrations of AF treatment, IRE1α expression decreased while ATF4 expression rose, reflecting a shift from UPR‐mediated adaptation to ISR activation. This transition indicates that the stress exceeded the tolerance of sensitive cells, leading them to initiate programmed cell death. Conversely, in AF‐resistant CMT cells treated with AF + Bz, IRE1α expression was increased, whereas ATF4 expression remained unchanged. This suggests that the full transition from UPR to ISR has not yet occurred. Interestingly, paraptosis‐like cell death was observed despite the absence of ATF4 upregulation, highlighting that this process can occur independently of ATF4 upregulation. In contrast, ATF4 upregulation has been identified as a critical regulator of proteotoxic stress and paraptosis in human breast cancer cells. These differences may reflect higher baseline proteasome activity in CMT cells and corresponding variations in their ER stress response pathways. Paraptosis is a distinct form of programmed cell death characterised by cytoplasmic vacuolation originating from the ER and/or mitochondria. In our study, AF‐resistant cells treated with a combination of AF and Bz exhibited extensive cytoplasmic vacuoles primarily originating from the ER, a hallmark feature of paraptosis. Additionally, pretreatment with CHX, known as a paraptosis inhibitor, effectively reversed the vacuolation and partially restored cell viability. These findings suggest that vacuole formation is not a resistance mechanism but rather contributes to reduced viability, supporting the induction of a paraptosis‐like mechanism by AF + Bz. Considerable evidence connects ER stress and proteasome inhibition to the induction of paraptosis. Since Bz alone can induce ER stress, its combination with AF amplifies this stress, leading to paraptosis‐like cell death. In this study, AF‐resistant cell lines treated with AF + Bz demonstrated a marked accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins and pronounced elevations in ER stress markers. These findings indicate significant disruption of proteostasis and the resulting overburden of misfolded proteins in the ER. The accumulation of misfolded proteins in the ER can exacerbate osmotic imbalances, potentially driving water influx and the formation of vacuoles within the ER. This mechanism may explain our observation of extensive cytoplasmic vacuolation in AF‐resistant cells treated with AF + Bz. In contrast, AF‐sensitive cell lines did not display cytoplasmic vacuolation even when treated with lethal AF doses inhibiting proteasome activity (Figures and). This suggests that AF‐sensitive cells may undergo apoptosis before vacuolation develops, highlighting potential differences in cell death pathways between AF‐sensitive and AF‐resistant cell lines. Further investigation into these two distinct cell death pathways and differing sensitivity to AF across CMT cell lines could provide valuable insights for the development of targeted therapeutic strategies. Several studies have investigated the pharmacokinetics and safety profile of AF in humans and animals, supporting its potential application in CMT. In dogs, a single oral dose of 0.1 mg/kg AF produced a blood gold (Au) maximum concentration of approximately 0.2 μM (40 ng Au/mL).
title: Auranofin Induces ER Stress‐Mediated Apoptosis, and Its Combination With Bortezomib Elicits Paraptosis‐Like Cell Death in Malignant Canine Mammary Tumour Cells

text: Further investigation into these two distinct cell death pathways and differing sensitivity to AF across CMT cell lines could provide valuable insights for the development of targeted therapeutic strategies. Several studies have investigated the pharmacokinetics and safety profile of AF in humans and animals, supporting its potential application in CMT. In dogs, a single oral dose of 0.1 mg/kg AF produced a blood gold (Au) maximum concentration of approximately 0.2 μM (40 ng Au/mL). Since each AF molecule contains one gold atom, the molar concentrations of AF and Au are equivalent. Oral AF doses up to 6 mg/kg/day were well tolerated in dogs without excessive emesis, and prenatal development studies in rats established a no‐observed‐adverse‐effect level (NOAEL) of 5 mg/kg/day for maternal and fetal toxicity. The therapeutic strategies proposed in this study include using up to 2 μM AF as monotherapy in AF‐sensitive cells and combining 2 μM AF with Bz to treat resistant cells. Proportional extrapolation suggests that achieving a 2 μM maximum plasma concentration (C max) in dogs would require single oral doses of approximately 1 mg/kg. This dose is higher than the current oral clinical dose in dogs but remains well below the NOAEL. Furthermore, prolonged administration could potentially achieve similar levels even with lower doses. For instance, in human clinical settings, AF is typically administered orally at a dose of 6 mg/day and a simulation study indicated that this regimen over 14 days achieves a steady‐state blood gold concentration of 0.42 μg/mL (2.03 μM). Additionally, FDA‐approved trials (NCT01419691) for CLL allowed daily doses up to 21 mg, with patients tolerating up to 12 mg/day for 28 days. With regard to tolerance in dogs, AF demonstrated a favourable safety profile when administered orally at a dosage of 9 mg (for dogs ≥ 15 kg) or 6 mg (for dogs < 15 kg) every 3 days in a study involving dogs with osteosarcoma, where treatment was continued until relapse or death. Unlike conventional chemotherapy, which is often accompanied by severe side effects, AF showed no significant abnormalities in blood screen metrics, and no unexpected symptoms or behavioural changes were reported by the owners. These findings suggest that achieving a blood C max near 2 μM of AF in dogs is feasible, and AF demonstrates advantages in safety and tolerability compared to conventional chemotherapy, positioning it as a promising treatment option for CMT. In conclusion, our study demonstrates that AF induces ER stress‐mediated apoptosis in AF‐sensitive CMT cells, and its combination with Bz induces paraptosis‐like cell death in AF‐resistant CMT cells. These findings suggest that AF, alone or in combination with Bz, represent a promising therapeutic strategy for malignant CMT, highlighting paraptosis‐like cell death as a potential alternative approach to target canine tumour cells.
title: Auranofin Induces ER Stress‐Mediated Apoptosis, and Its Combination With Bortezomib Elicits Paraptosis‐Like Cell Death in Malignant Canine Mammary Tumour Cells

text: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is a prevalent and rapidly growing chronic liver condition, affecting ~30% of the global population or nearly 2 billion people. MASLD encompasses a disease continuum, ranging from simple hepatic steatosis (SLD) to the more severe metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), characterized by hepatocellular injury, chronic inflammation, and fibrosis. Without effective intervention, MASH can progress to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), making it a major health burden worldwide (–). Metabolic stress induced by prolonged high-fat diet (HFD) consumption plays a pivotal role in MASLD development and its progression to MASH and HCC. This metabolic stress elicits extensive gene expression reprogramming, which has been predominantly studied at the transcriptional level. Transcriptomic analyses have revealed widespread alterations in mRNA abundance in response to HFD-induced stress, resulting from a complex interplay between transcriptional regulation and mRNA stability remodeling. However, the direct functional consequences of these changes at the level of protein synthesis and their impact on liver disease progression remain largely unexplored. As a key metabolic organ, the liver is constantly exposed to nutrient fluctuations, triggering circadian-regulated stress responses, including the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress response, which activates the unfolded protein response (UPR) to restore homeostasis (–). Under normal physiological conditions, acute and transient ER stress induces the canonical UPR, mediated by the eIF2α kinase PERK, which suppresses global protein synthesis while selectively allowing the translation of specific mRNAs containing short upstream open reading frames (uORFs). This acute UPR is essential for maintaining daily liver function. However, if the stress is prolonged and cannot be resolved, then the UPR transitions from a protective to a proapoptotic program, ultimately promoting cell death. Therefore, chronic metabolic stress, such as persistent HFD exposure, renders the acute-UPR insufficient to sustain liver function, needing the activation of a distinct and much less studied chronic ER stress response. We have recently shown that HFD triggers the synthesis of cytoplasmic polyadenylation element binding protein 4 (CPEB4), encoded by a uORF-containing mRNA, to mediate adaptive-UPR in hepatocytes subjected to chronic ER stress while preventing the proapoptotic effects mediated by CHOP synthesis induced by acute UPR. CPEB4 is an RNA binding protein (RBP) that regulates poly(A) tail length, modulating the stability and translation of a subset of mRNAs containing a cytoplasmic polyadenylation element (CPE) motif in their 3′ untranslated region (–). While CPEB4’s role in oocyte maturation has been well established (–), its broader function in the translational reprogramming during chronic ER stress adaptation remains largely unexplored, particularly in the context of prolonged metabolic stress and MASLD progression. In this study, we investigated the mechanisms underlying hepatocyte dysfunction in chronic MASLD/MASH, with a particular focus on the translational regulatory network governed by the CPEB4-dependent branch of chronic ER stress. Using a combination of ribosome profiling, genome-wide polyadenylation analysis, and transcriptomic approaches in a mouse model with hepatocyte-specific deletion of CPEB4, we characterized the gene expression reprogramming driven by the chronic ER stress response.
title: Posttranscriptional reprogramming controls MASLD progression through chronic ER stress adaptation

text: In this study, we investigated the mechanisms underlying hepatocyte dysfunction in chronic MASLD/MASH, with a particular focus on the translational regulatory network governed by the CPEB4-dependent branch of chronic ER stress. Using a combination of ribosome profiling, genome-wide polyadenylation analysis, and transcriptomic approaches in a mouse model with hepatocyte-specific deletion of CPEB4, we characterized the gene expression reprogramming driven by the chronic ER stress response. Our results reveal that, although prolonged exposure to HFD induces transcriptomic alterations in hundreds of genes, only ~30% of these changes are directly reflected at the protein level. These transcripts primarily encode proteins involved in metabolic adaptation to the HFD. In contrast, the remaining 70% of diet-induced gene expression changes are subject to substantial translational regulation. Within this subset, the CPEB4-dependent branch of the chronic ER stress response is responsible for the selective translational activation of mRNAs associated with liver regeneration, as well as immune and inflammatory responses. We further demonstrate that HFD-induced translational activation predominantly affects mRNAs that are typically expressed at low levels, exhibit limited translational efficiency, and are characterized by suboptimal codon usage. These transcripts also display a balanced distribution of CPEs and AU-rich elements (AREs), suggesting a finely tuned regulatory interplay between mRNA polyadenylation and deadenylation processes displaced by HFD. Loss of CPEB4 impairs the hepatocellular adaptive response to chronic ER stress, resulting in heightened inflammation, enhanced fibrogenesis, and increased tumorigenic potential. Collectively, our findings establish CPEB4 as a key regulator of hepatic adaptation to chronic ER stress and propose that therapeutic strategies aimed at restoring or enhancing CPEB4 function may represent a promising avenue for halting MASLD progression and preventing liver carcinogenesis.
title: Posttranscriptional reprogramming controls MASLD progression through chronic ER stress adaptation

text: To determine whether CPEB4 expression changes during the progression of MASLD, we analyzed liver samples from obese patients diagnosed with either SLD or MASH. Liver tissue from nonobese individuals without liver disease served as controls. Immunohistochemical staining revealed minimal CPEB4 protein levels in normal livers. In contrast, livers from patient with SLD exhibited a significant overexpression of CPEB4, coinciding with mild to moderate hepatic steatosis, low-grade inflammation, and the absence of fibrosis or abnormal serum transaminase levels. However, increased severity of the disease (MASH) correlated with lower levels of CPEB4 expression, showing a 92% reduction in patients with advanced MASH compared to those with SLD. Notably, obese individuals with low hepatic CPEB4 levels exhibited more severe histopathological features, including extensive steatosis, hepatocellular ballooning, lobular inflammation, and fibrosis. Liver function tests confirmed a significant deterioration, with elevated serum levels of alanine aminotransferase (ALT; >68 U/liter), aspartate aminotransferase (AST; >40 U/liter), gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT; >45 U/liter), and bilirubin (>0.8 mg/dl). No significant differences in body mass index (BMI) or age were detected between patients with SLD and MASH, suggesting that CPEB4 reduction is associated with disease severity rather than general patient characteristics. These findings establish a strong correlation between increased CPEB4 levels upon SLD and HFD-stress and CPEB4 down-regulation and the histopathological progression of MASLD, implicating CPEB4 deficiency as a potential contributor to disease worsening. To explore causality and further define the role of CPEB4 in disease progression, we next used a liver CPEB4 knockout mouse model.
title: Posttranscriptional reprogramming controls MASLD progression through chronic ER stress adaptation
section_title: Lower levels of CPEB4 are associated with progression from steatosis to MASH in the human liver

text: To assess the causal role of CPEB4 deficiency in MASLD and MASH progression, we generated hepatocyte-specific CPEB4 knockout mice (CPEB4 LKO) using Cre-recombinase driven by the albumin promoter, with wild-type (WT) Cpeb4 +/+ Cre T/+ littermates as controls. Beginning at 6 weeks of age, these mice were fed either an HFD or a normal diet (ND) for 30 weeks. As expected, prolonged HFD exposure induced obesity and hepatic steatosis, evidenced by increased body weight, elevated hepatic lipid accumulation (Oil Red staining;), and hepatocyte cytoplasmic vacuolation [hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining; and fig. S1G] compared to ND-fed mice. Notably, CPEB4 LKO mice exhibited increased susceptibility to HFD-induced MASH, displaying more severe steatosis (, and fig. S1G), hepatomegaly, and fibrosis (Masson’s trichrome staining;) than their WT counterparts. Moreover, CPEB4-deficient livers showed increased hepatic inflammation, with marked infiltration of CD3-positive T lymphocytes and F4/80-positive macrophages (fig. S1, G and I), confirming the development of steatohepatitis in HFD-fed CPEB4 LKO mice. In parallel, these mice exhibited significantly higher serum levels of triglycerides and cholesterol than HFD-fed WT controls. Liver damage was further exacerbated, as evidenced by a ~54% increase in serum ALT levels in HFD-fed CPEB4 LKO mice compared to HFD-fed WT mice, suggesting enhanced hepatic injury in the absence of CPEB4 under metabolic stress conditions. As expected, combining HFD with phenobarbital further exacerbated MASH-associated liver injury (fig. S1, M to O). Under these conditions, CPEB4 LKO and WT mice developed hepatic steatosis to a similar extent (fig. S1, N and O), suggesting that CPEB4 deficiency primarily influences MASH progression rather than initial lipid accumulation. These findings from both human patients and murine models establish a strong connection between hepatic CPEB4 deficiency and increased vulnerability to MASLD and MASH progression. In a hepatocyte-derived cell line, we observed that tunicamycin-induced ER stress could be efficiently rescued by tauroursodeoxycholic acid (TUDCA) in both WT and CPEB4-depleted cells, indicating that CPEB4 dependence is ER stress specific (fig. S1, P and Q). To further dissect the mechanisms driving this phenotype, we investigated whether CPEB4 loss compromises chronic ER stress adaptation in hepatocytes, leading to widespread dysregulation of gene expression at both the transcriptional and posttranscriptional levels. To address this, we conducted a comprehensive transcriptomic and translatomic analysis, integrating data on genome wide cytoplasmic polyadenylation and translational regulation in CPEB4-deficient and WT livers under MASLD and MASH conditions.
title: Posttranscriptional reprogramming controls MASLD progression through chronic ER stress adaptation
section_title: Hepatic loss of CPEB4 promotes the progression of diet-induced MASLD in mice

text: To assess how HFD influences steady-state mRNA levels, resulting from combined alterations in transcription and mRNA stability, and to determine whether these changes are modulated by the chronic adaptive ER stress response (measured by CHOP expression and Xbp1s/Xbp1t unbalance, fig. S1R), we performed a comparative transcriptomic analysis of WT and CPEB4 LKO mice fed either ND or HFD. In WT mice, HFD induced widespread transcriptomic remodeling, with 2362 genes up-regulated [7.09% at 5% false discovery rate (FDR)] and 802 genes down-regulated (3.62% at 5% FDR) (, left, and fig. S2A). These alterations are consistent with previous studies examining HFD-induced hepatic transcriptomic changes (–). Notably, lowly expressed genes were preferentially up-regulated, while highly expressed genes exhibited down-regulation, suggesting a compensatory transcriptional response (, left). A similar pattern was observed in CPEB4 LKO mice, with 4.89% of genes up-regulated and 2.08% down-regulated (5% FDR). Transcriptomic changes induced by HFD in WT and CPEB4 LKO mice were highly correlated (Spearman’s Rho = 0.8) (, left). Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) revealed distinct biological responses in metabolic adaptation and immune response genes. These findings suggest that HFD-induced transcriptional and mRNA stability alterations, affecting more than 10% of the liver transcriptome, are primarily independent of CPEB4, a modulator of the chronic ER stress response. Given that variations in mRNA levels do not necessarily correlate with changes in protein expression, we next performed ribosome profiling to measure ribosome-protected fragments (RPFs) as an indicator of protein synthesis and translation efficiency (TE; RPFs normalized to mRNA levels). In WT mice, HFD induced significant translational remodeling, with 886 genes up-regulated and 781 genes down-regulated at the translatome level (, middle). A similar trend to the transcriptome was observed, where lowly translated genes were up-regulated, while highly translated genes were down-regulated (, middle). In CPEB4 LKO mice, HFD-induced 856 genes up-regulated (4.22%) and 612 genes down-regulated (3.02%) at the translatome level. However, the correlation between HFD-induced TE changes in CPEB4 LKO and WT mice (Spearman’s Rho = 0.76) was lower than the correlation observed at the transcriptome level (, middle). This suggests that chronic ER stress exerts a greater regulatory effect on translation than on transcription or mRNA stability in MASLD. To integrate transcript-level and translation-level changes, we categorized differentially expressed genes (DEGs) on the basis of their behavior in mRNA abundance and ribosome occupancy (RPFs) in both WT and CPEB4 LKO livers. Following the criteria established by Tebaldi et al., we classified genes into three regulatory categories (, left). Homodirectional changes (green) were observed in genes that exhibited matching up-regulation or down-regulation in both mRNA levels and RPFs, indicating that their regulation occurs primarily at the transcriptional or mRNA stability level, with no major impact on TE. In contrast, a subset of genes was regulated predominantly at the translational level (yellow), as evidenced by significant changes in RPFs resulting from increased (TU) or decreased (TD) TE, without significant changes in mRNA levels. Last, a third group of genes exhibited translational buffering (blue), where opposing changes in TE counteracted variations in mRNA abundance.
title: Posttranscriptional reprogramming controls MASLD progression through chronic ER stress adaptation
section_title: Posttranscriptional regulation of gene expression in MASLD

text: In contrast, a subset of genes was regulated predominantly at the translational level (yellow), as evidenced by significant changes in RPFs resulting from increased (TU) or decreased (TD) TE, without significant changes in mRNA levels. Last, a third group of genes exhibited translational buffering (blue), where opposing changes in TE counteracted variations in mRNA abundance. Within this category, some genes displayed buffering up (BU), in which reduced mRNA levels were offset by increased TE, whereas others underwent buffering down (BD), where elevated mRNA levels were counteracted by reduced TE. In WT livers under HFD conditions, only 30% of DEGs exhibited homodirectional regulation (green), whereas 70% displayed TE adjustments. Notably, 41% of DEGs exhibited TE-driven buffering (blue), and 27% showed translational regulation independent of mRNA changes (yellow) (, middle). However, in CPEB4 LKO mice, the disruption of the chronic ER stress branch in HFD-induced MASLD (, right) resulted in a significantly altered distribution of gene regulatory modes. The proportion of genes with homodirectional transcript and RPF changes increased to 34%, while translational buffering was reduced to 30% and purely translationally regulated genes increased to 34% (, right). This shift indicates that CPEB4 is essential for maintaining translational homeostasis under chronic metabolic stress. Notably, the most pronounced differences between WT and CPEB4 LKO mice were observed in three key categories: genes exhibiting increased translation efficiency (TU), genes undergoing buffering up (BU), and genes experiencing buffering down (BD) (and fig. S2, E and F). These findings underscore that CPEB4 deficiency perturbs the chronic ER stress adaptation program, shifting translational regulation patterns and exacerbating MASLD-associated gene expression reprogramming by HFD.
title: Posttranscriptional reprogramming controls MASLD progression through chronic ER stress adaptation
section_title: Posttranscriptional regulation of gene expression in MASLD

text: Gene Ontology analysis revealed that genes translationally up-regulated by HFD in WT mice, but not in CPEB4 LKO, were primarily associated with cell cycle regulation and organelle biogenesis (, top). This suggests that these processes play a crucial role in the chronic ER stress response, facilitating cellular adaptation under metabolic stress and potentially contributing to liver regeneration. Conversely, genes buffered down by HFD in WT, but not in CPEB4 LKO, due to increased transcript levels and reduced TE, were linked to signal transduction, cell differentiation, and cell junction maintenance. In contrast, genes buffered down by HFD in CPEB4 LKO mice, but not in the WT, were predominantly associated with immune responses (, middle and bottom; and fig. S2, F and G), suggesting that CPEB4 deficiency triggers key regulatory pathways involved in inflammation and disrupts tissue remodeling during MASLD progression. Certain cellular adaptations to HFD appeared independent of chronic ER stress regulation (fig. S2, F and G). Processes such as nucleoside and ribonucleoside synthesis, energy production pathways, mitochondrial function (translation down), metabolic adaptation, catabolic and biosynthetic pathways, extracellular matrix remodeling, and collagen formation (homodirectional regulation) were not reliant on CPEB4-mediated chronic ER stress adaptation. However, the complement cascade buffering (BU) was significantly dependent on CPEB4, further supporting its role in translational control of stress-related pathways. These findings are consistent with CPEB4’s established function in cytoplasmic poly(A) tail length regulation, which governs mRNA translation and stability. To directly assess the impact of CPEB4-mediated poly(A) tail length regulation on mRNA stability and translation, we performed poly(A) tail length measurements using poly(U) chromatography, and RNA immunoprecipitation (RIP) to determine CPEB4-mRNA interactions. In WT mice, HFD exposure led to the elongation of poly(A) tails in 1015 genes and shortening in 848 genes (5.7 and 4.7% of total transcripts, respectively). Genes were ranked according to log 2 fold change (, right). A clear trend emerged, where mRNAs with long basal poly(A) tails underwent deadenylation in response to HFD, while transcripts with shorter basal poly(A) tails exhibited increased polyadenylation (, right). Comparative analyses between WT and CPEB4 LKO mice revealed no correlation in HFD-induced polyadenylation changes (Spearman’s Rho = 0.0) (, right), indicating that poly(A) tail length alterations in response to MASLD/MASH are strictly dependent on CPEB4. Furthermore, the relationship between HFD-induced changes in TE and poly(A) tail length was markedly altered in CPEB4 LKO mice, with a negative correlation (Spearman’s Rho = −0.18) compared to a positive correlation in WT mice (Rho = 0.29). These findings confirm that CPEB4 is required to coordinate translational activation through poly(A) tail elongation under metabolic stress conditions. To further define CPEB4-regulated transcripts, we performed RIP in ND- and HFD-fed WT mice, identifying 1327 direct CPEB4 target genes (P < 0.05) (, and fig. S3A). Among these, 568 genes were ND specific, 148 were HFD specific, and 611 were common to both conditions. These mRNAs were significantly enriched in CPE motifs (fig. S3, B and C) and were associated with key biological processes such as cell division, differentiation, and immune/inflammatory responses.
title: Posttranscriptional reprogramming controls MASLD progression through chronic ER stress adaptation
section_title: Translatome changes in hepatocytes are critical for MASLD progression and severity

text: To further define CPEB4-regulated transcripts, we performed RIP in ND- and HFD-fed WT mice, identifying 1327 direct CPEB4 target genes (P < 0.05) (, and fig. S3A). Among these, 568 genes were ND specific, 148 were HFD specific, and 611 were common to both conditions. These mRNAs were significantly enriched in CPE motifs (fig. S3, B and C) and were associated with key biological processes such as cell division, differentiation, and immune/inflammatory responses. Integration of CPEB4 target mRNAs with polyadenylation and TE data further revealed that mRNAs with short poly(A) tails under ND conditions underwent elongation in response to HFD, correlating with increased TE. This poly(A) tail elongation–mediated translational activation was entirely lost in CPEB4 LKO livers, reinforcing the role of CPEB4 as a key mediator of translation control in MASLD/MASH progression. Together, these data support that the activation of the CPEB4-dependent branch of the chronic ER-stress response promotes poly(A) tail elongation of CPE-containing mRNAs. In turn, this elongation results in mRNA stabilization and/or translational activation affecting genes implicated in key cellular functions during the MASLD/MASH progression, such as cell cycle regulation and organelle biogenesis (TU in WT, but not in KO), immune responses (BD in KO, but not in WT), and complement cascade (BU in WT, but not in KO). On the other hand, metabolic adaptation to HFD appears to be regulated mainly at the transcriptional level independently of the ER stress responses.
title: Posttranscriptional reprogramming controls MASLD progression through chronic ER stress adaptation
section_title: Translatome changes in hepatocytes are critical for MASLD progression and severity

text: Although the most prominent differences between WT and CPEB4 LKO mice in response to HFD were observed in the polyadenylation and TE of direct CPEB4-target mRNAs, not all CPEB4-bound transcripts followed a uniform regulatory pattern. This suggests that additional mRNA features influence translation/stability in the context of chronic ER stress. To investigate these factors, we searched for regulatory elements that might explain the differential translation of CPEB4-bound mRNAs observed under HFD-induced stress. The presence of short uORFs, a key feature in transcripts regulated during acute ER stress, did not exhibit a differential distribution among DEGs at either the transcript or TE level. This finding suggests that chronic ER stress relies on alternative regulatory mechanisms distinct from those governing acute stress adaptation. Given that HFD-regulated mRNAs tended to have short poly(A) tails, low basal levels, and minimal TE before CPEB4 activation, we focused on two additional features known to influence poly(A) tail shortening and TE: AREs, which are recognized by ARE-binding proteins, such as tristetraprolin (TTP), and contribute to mRNA decay; and codon optimality, a well-known determinant of translation rates. Analyzing the differential polyadenylation and TE of mRNAs in response to HFD based on their CPE and ARE content revealed a negative correlation between the presence of these elements and basal translation levels (RPFs). Intriguingly, the number of CPEs and AREs showed a positive correlation with poly(A) tail elongation and increased TE upon HFD. mRNAs that lacked both CPEs and AREs remained unresponsive to HFD, as did those carrying only one of the regulatory elements, irrespective of their abundance. In contrast, transcripts that contained a balanced number of CPEs and AREs exhibited an enhanced response, with TE and polyadenylation increasing proportionally to the cumulative number of these motifs. Notably, this correlation was lost in CPEB4 LKO mice, reinforcing the essential role of CPEB4 in orchestrating these regulatory events. Specifically, transcripts that contained a predominant enrichment of only one motif (Low CPE, Low A+C, CPE, and Low ARE) displayed translational buffering, whereas those containing a balanced number of both elements (A+C) exhibited increased TE and polyadenylation without accompanying changes in mRNA levels in response to HFD. The relationship between codon optimality and TE for CPEB4-bound mRNAs (depicted in red) further underscores the functional significance of this coregulation. For CPEB4-targets, a strong negative correlation was observed between codon optimality and HFD-induced changes in TE (HFD-DTE) in WT animals (Spearman’s Rho = −0.48), which was reduced in CPEB4 LKO mice (Rho = −0.39). Additionally, a negative correlation was identified between codon optimality and HFD-induced polyadenylation of CPEB4-bound transcripts (Rho = −0.30), which was completely lost in CPEB4 LKO mice (Rho = 0.18). These results suggest that mRNAs undergoing polyadenylation and translational activation by CPEB4 in response to HFD tend to have low codon optimality. Consistently, a direct anticorrelation was observed between codon optimality and the presence of CPEs and AREs, further supporting the idea that transcripts containing balanced numbers of these motifs generally exhibit lower codon optimality.
title: Posttranscriptional reprogramming controls MASLD progression through chronic ER stress adaptation
section_title: Translatome changes in hepatocytes during MASLD are driven by a dynamic interplay between the RBPs CPEB4 and AREBPs

text: These results suggest that mRNAs undergoing polyadenylation and translational activation by CPEB4 in response to HFD tend to have low codon optimality. Consistently, a direct anticorrelation was observed between codon optimality and the presence of CPEs and AREs, further supporting the idea that transcripts containing balanced numbers of these motifs generally exhibit lower codon optimality. Interrogating the distribution of CPE and ARE motifs among the six regulatory categories defined in revealed that mRNAs containing a balanced number of CPEs and AREs were significantly enriched in the two categories characterized by increased TE and polyadenylation upon HFD (TU and BU), an association that was completely lost in CPEB4 LKO mice. Conversely, transcripts that lacked both regulatory motifs (No_Reg), which underwent deadenylation upon HFD exposure, were strongly associated with the category of translational down-regulation (TD). This latter correlation was independent of CPEB4, indicating that mRNAs not polyadenylated by CPEB4 in response to the HFD activation of chronic ER stress undergo translational inhibition during MASLD progression. To validate these observations, we selected three candidate mRNAs from the A+C category for further analysis: hyaluronan and proteoglycan link protein 1 (Hapln1), gasdermin E (Gsdme), and lysocardiolipin acyltransferase 1 (Lclat1) (figs. S5, A to C, and S6). As predicted, Hapln1 and Gsdme exhibited increased translation in response to HFD in WT mice. Furthermore, we confirmed that the translation of all three genes was significantly reduced in the absence of CPEB4 under HFD conditions compared to WT mice (and fig. S5C). Notably, these differences were not due to changes in mRNA levels. Additionally, in an HCC cell line, we also validated the increase of translation of Gsdme and Hapln1 mRNAs upon ER stress, which was abrogated in the CPEB4 KO cells, supporting the conclusion that CPEB4 regulates these targets at the translational level via poly(A) tail control. To assess the relevance of these findings in a clinical setting, we performed immunohistochemistry analysis on liver tissues from patient with MASLD. A notable overlap in the spatial distribution of LCLAT1 and CPEB4 was observed in pericentral hepatocytes, providing further evidence for CPEB4-dependent regulation of LCLAT1 expression. Consistently, a pronounced reduction in both LCLAT1 and CPEB4 levels was evident in liver tissues from patients with advanced MASH, mirroring the observations in CPEB4 LKO mice. These results underscore the clinical relevance of CPEB4-mediated translational control and suggest that its loss contributes to MASLD/MASH progression by impairing the stress-adaptive translatome.
title: Posttranscriptional reprogramming controls MASLD progression through chronic ER stress adaptation
section_title: Translatome changes in hepatocytes during MASLD are driven by a dynamic interplay between the RBPs CPEB4 and AREBPs

text: Given that CPEB4 regulates mRNAs encoding factors involved in inflammation, cell proliferation, and differentiation, in addition to its role in modulating the chronic ER stress response, we investigated whether its depletion influences HFD-driven liver cancer development. The disruption of CPEB4-dependent mechanisms has been shown to impair liver homeostasis under metabolic stress, suggesting that its loss might exacerbate MASLD-associated tumorigenesis. To address this, we used a murine MASLD-liver cancer model in which HFD-fed mice were exposed to diethylnitrosamine (DEN) and phenobarbital to promote hepatocarcinogenesis. Comparing CPEB4 LKO and WT mice under these conditions, we observed similar increases in body weight, liver weight, hepatic steatosis (; Oil Red and H&E stainings in), and liver fibrosis (; Sirius Red staining in). Additionally, serum transaminase levels were comparable between HFD-fed CPEB4 LKO and WT mice, indicating that CPEB4 depletion does not affect overall liver injury at this stage. However, after 50 weeks, HFD-fed CPEB4 LKO mice exhibited a significantly increased tumor burden compared to their WT counterparts, as evidenced by a higher tumor incidence and tumor number. Moreover, histological analysis revealed that liver tumors in HFD-fed CPEB4 LKO mice were more aggressive, displaying a greater proportion of adenocarcinomas and adenomas. These findings indicate that hepatic CPEB4 loss under HFD conditions promotes the appearance of primary liver tumors. Notably, CPEB4 ablation in mice maintained on a ND had no significant impact on tumor incidence, number, or profile compared to WT littermates, reinforcing the idea that CPEB4 function is particularly critical under chronic metabolic stress. A bioinformatic analysis was performed to determine the association between CPEB4 and oncogenesis, with a specific focus on HCC drivers. Enrichment analysis in the IntOgen database found CPEB4 targets to be significantly overrepresented among both PanCancer driver genes (P = 1.89 × 10 −16) and specific HCC driver genes (P = 5.41 × 10 −15; data S2). In parallel, Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analysis further confirmed this oncogenic link by showing a significant overrepresentation of CPEB4 targets in the “Pathways in cancer” category (P = 1.55 × 10 −5; data S2). Overall, these results reinforce the potential role of CPEB4 in tumorigenesis. These results support the conclusion that the CPEB4-dependent chronic ER stress response is essential not only for the recovery of hepatocytes subjected to HFD-induced stress but also for preventing the transition from fatty liver to liver cancer. By regulating the adaptive response to chronic metabolic challenges, CPEB4 plays a pivotal role in protecting against MASLD-driven tumorigenesis. To provide further mechanistic support for the role of CPEB4 in liver cancer progression, we established WT and CPEB4-knockout (CPEB4 KO) liver tumor cell lines derived from HFD-DEN–induced tumors in C57BL/6 mice (fig. S7, A and B). To evaluate their tumorigenic potential in vivo, we performed both subcutaneous and orthotopic xenograft assays. In immunocompromised and immunocompetent host settings, CPEB4 KO cells exhibited a significantly higher tumor-initiating frequency and accelerated tumor growth compared with WT counterparts (fig. S7, C to E), demonstrating that CPEB4 loss enhances malignant progression in vivo. We next assessed whether these differences were associated with cell-autonomous malignant phenotypes in vitro.

text: The liver plays a central role in energy metabolism, blood homeostasis, detoxification, and lipid regulation. In MASLD, excessive lipid accumulation leads to metabolic stress, hepatocyte injury, and disease progression, ultimately increasing the risk of HCC. A key feature of this process is the activation of the UPR, an adaptive mechanism that helps the liver cope with stress. However, if metabolic stress is sustained, then the failure to adapt can promote hepatocyte death, fibrosis, and tumorigenesis. The UPR initially functions as a protective response, reducing global translation and enhancing protein folding and degradation pathways to restore cellular homeostasis. If these mechanisms fail, then prolonged stress triggers apoptosis through CHOP activation. CPEB4 expression, from a uORF-containing mRNA, is induced as part of the acute UPR and initiates a secondary wave of translation of CPE-containing mRNAs that contributes to chronic adaptation, independently of CHOP-mediated apoptosis. Prolonged HFD exposure triggers widespread transcriptomic remodeling, affecting metabolism, inflammation, extracellular matrix remodeling, and cell survival pathways. These changes are highly conserved across human and murine models of MASLD and liver cancer. However, the assumption that transcriptional regulation directly determines protein abundance is challenged by the concept of translational offsetting or buffering, where mRNA fluctuations are counterbalanced by opposing changes in ribosome occupancy and by mRNAs whose translation is regulated in the absence of significant transcript differences (–). Here, we show that HFD induces extensive changes in transcription and mRNA stability, as well as a major independent remodeling of the translatome. We identify CPEB4 as a key mediator of this posttranscriptional regulation, orchestrating an adaptive response to chronic metabolic stress in MASLD progression. Unexpectedly, only 30% of transcriptomic alterations result in direct protein synthesis changes, primarily affecting metabolic pathways and extracellular matrix remodeling, but independent of chronic UPR modulation. The remaining 70% of transcriptomic shifts are regulated at the translational level, with 30% of genes exhibiting translation-dependent regulation and 40% undergoing buffering effects, where TE counteracts mRNA level fluctuations. We further demonstrate that CPEB4-dependent TE increases under HFD conditions are associated with poly(A)-mediated mRNA stabilization, highlighting poly(A) tail remodeling as a key regulatory mechanism of chronic adaptation. However, not all CPEB4 targets were sensitive to HFD, as HFD-induced translational activation predominantly affected lowly expressed, poorly translated mRNAs with low codon optimality. Additionally, these mRNAs exhibited a balanced number of CPEs and AREs, suggesting a dynamic regulatory equilibrium between polyadenylation and deadenylation. This CPE/ARE regulatory balance is tightly controlled by RBPs. TTP, an ARE-binding protein, promotes mRNA deadenylation via CCR4/not recruitment, while HuR counteracts TTP to enhance mRNA stability. Notably, disrupting CCR4/not recruitment by TTP has been shown to protect against HFD-induced obesity and hepatosteatosis, while HuR depletion exacerbates MASLD. Conversely, liver-specific TTP knockout improves glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity, underscoring the intricate interplay between AREBPs and metabolic regulation.

text: This CPE/ARE regulatory balance is tightly controlled by RBPs. TTP, an ARE-binding protein, promotes mRNA deadenylation via CCR4/not recruitment, while HuR counteracts TTP to enhance mRNA stability. Notably, disrupting CCR4/not recruitment by TTP has been shown to protect against HFD-induced obesity and hepatosteatosis, while HuR depletion exacerbates MASLD. Conversely, liver-specific TTP knockout improves glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity, underscoring the intricate interplay between AREBPs and metabolic regulation. The subset of mRNAs regulated by CPEB4 through the CPE/ARE interplay includes genes encoding cell cycle and differentiation regulators, which are critical for cancer development. Accordingly, disrupting the chronic adaptation pathway mediated by CPEB4 not only worsened MASLD progression but also increased liver cancer risk, in agreement with our recent findings. These results reveal a tumor-protective role for CPEB4 in the liver, in contrast to its protumorigenic function in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas and melanomas, where it is required for tumor cell proliferation. All our datasets in the hepatic context consistently support a tumor-restraining function for CPEB4. Here, we show that CPEB4-KO liver cancer cells exhibit enhanced anchorage-independent growth and increased migratory capacity, indicating that loss of CPEB4 promotes key malignant traits at the cellular level. These results are fully consistent with the in vivo xenograft assays, in which CPEB4-deficient cells display higher tumor-initiating frequency and accelerated tumor growth in both subcutaneous and orthotopic models. Moreover, in the in vivo HFD + DEN hepatocarcinogenesis model, hepatocyte-specific deletion of CPEB4 markedly accelerates tumor development under metabolic stress, reinforcing a tumor-suppressive role for CPEB4 in the liver. Together, these findings underscore that the function of CPEB4 is highly tissue and context dependent, shaped by the cellular environment and stress landscape with the features of the cell of origin. Our findings demonstrate that CPEB4 is critical for sustaining liver homeostasis during MASLD progression, acting as a regulatory hub that integrates translational control mechanisms to mitigate metabolic stress and prevent disease exacerbation. This suggests that CPEB4 function extends beyond late-stage tumorigenesis, playing a key role in protecting hepatocytes from metabolic insults that drive MASLD-associated liver dysfunction and cancer development. These results have important therapeutic implications for the treatment of MASLD, MASH, and liver cancer. Given the crucial role of CPEB4 in maintaining hepatic homeostasis under chronic metabolic stress, strategies aimed at reactivating the chronic adaptive response via CPEB4 activation may represent a promising approach to prevent NASH progression and MASLD-associated hepatocarcinogenesis.

text: Human liver tissue samples were obtained from patients diagnosed with MASLD undergoing bariatric surgery at the St. Franziskus Hospital Cologne, Germany. The diagnosis of SLD and MASH was based on histopathological evaluation of H&E-stained liver sections by expert histopathologists, as well as clinical and biochemical parameters, including age, BMI, ALT, AST, GGT, and bilirubin levels. Histological assessments included steatosis, hepatocyte ballooning, lobular inflammation, and fibrosis scoring. Liver samples were fixed in formalin and embedded in paraffin for immunohistochemical analysis. All participants provided written informed consent, acknowledging that clinical data and biological samples would be used for research purposes. The study was approved by the Ethical Committees of the Medical Chambers of Westfalen-Lippe and Nordrhein, Germany (reference numbers 2022-734-f-S and 2017110, respectively). Paraffin-embedded normal human liver tissue blocks were commercially obtained from OriGene Technologies (Rockville, MD, USA).

text: To generate Cpeb4 conditional knockout mice (Cpeb4llox/lox), mouse embryonic stem cells carrying a βgeo (β-galactosidase-neomycin resistance) cassette in Cpeb4 intron-1 and loxP sites flanking exon-2 (clone EPD0060_4_E10; Sanger Institute, Cambridge, UK) were microinjected into blastocysts. The resulting chimeric mice (Cpeb4 + /loxfrt) were crossed with C57BL6/J mice to establish germline transmission. To remove the βgeo-cassette, Cpeb4 + /loxfrt mice were bred with FlpO recombinase-expressing transgenic mice (Tg.pCAG-Flp), generating Cpeb4lox/lox conditional knockout animals. To generate hepatocyte-specific CPEB4 knockout mice (CPEB4LKO), Cpeb4llox/lox mice were crossed with albumin-Cre transgenic mice, resulting in CPEB4 deletion specifically in hepatocytes within the liver (Cpeb4lox/lox; Alb-Cre, referred to as CPEB4LKO throughout this study). To ensure genetic homogeneity, offspring were backcrossed for five generations onto the C57BL/6J background. Routine genotyping was performed by polymerase chain reaction (PCR).
