section_title: ER stress induces vascular endothelial dysfunction ex vivo

text: Reduced Niban phosphorylation has also been associated with heightened ER stress. To determine if increasing Niban phosphorylation would mitigate endothelial dysfunction induced by ER stress, isolated rat aortas were treated with TM in the presence of NiPp. NiPp treatment mitigated the effects of TM on endothelium-dependent relaxation (EC 50 [CCH]: TM = 2.744 × 10 −7 M vs TM + NiPp = 1.546 × 10 −7 M, p = 0.05;).
title: Mitigating sepsis-induced vascular endothelial dysfunction through Niban phosphorylation
section_title: NiPp mitigates vascular endothelial dysfunction induced by an ER stressor ex vivo

text: Sepsis-induced vascular dysfunction arises from the complex interplay of inflammation and oxidative stress, which can both influence and be exacerbated by ER stress, collectively contributing to endothelial dysfunction. Niban is an ER stress-inducible protein that may be a regulator of the ER stress pathways with pro-survival functions. Previous findings indicating that the downregulation of Niban phosphorylation is associated with vascular injuries suggest a potential link between ER stress and Niban regulation in sepsis, highlighting the possibility that restoring Niban phosphorylation could improve sepsis-induced endothelial dysfunction. Using a polymicrobial CS sepsis model, the current study identified an association between impaired vascular function, reduced Niban phosphorylation, and heightened ER stress during sepsis. Moreover, we demonstrated that increasing Niban phosphorylation attenuated vascular endothelial dysfunction in septic aorta associated with the CS model of sepsis, as well as in ex vivo endothelial dysfunction induced by individual mediators of sepsis or ER stress. Specifically, we employed NiPp, a cell-permeant phosphopeptide mimetic designed to recapitulate the functional effects of phosphorylated Niban, to establish the physiologic relevance of Niban in vascular homeostasis. NiPp has been shown to improve endothelial function after P2X7R activation, a DAMP-responsive receptor, and acidosis, both of which are associated with sepsis. In this study, we demonstrated that NiPp not only improved endothelium-dependent relaxation in septic aortic rings but also in normal aortic rings exposed to LPS, IL-1β, and CFH, key drivers of endothelial injury in sepsis. These mediators represent the inflammatory and oxidative stress conditions characteristic of sepsis,, and our findings suggest that modulating Niban phosphorylation may be a relevant therapeutic target. In addition, these data demonstrate the broad applicability of NiPp in addressing endothelial dysfunction in sepsis. Moreover, the elderly population is particularly susceptible to sepsis, in part due to vascular complications associated with age-related endothelial dysfunction. – In a previous publication, we demonstrated that NiPp can restore endothelial function in aged human saphenous veins, highlighting the potential importance of Niban regulation in this vulnerable population. The concentration of NiPp chosen for the current study was based on the dose–response study in which 50 μM did not show salutary effects on IL-1β-induced impairments of endothelium-dependent function. Together with our previous studies using a higher NiPp dose (500 µM) on different vascular injuries, it suggests that there is a range of ex vivo pharmacologic efficacy for NiPp that is likely to be context-dependent. Furthermore, the Scr3NiPp control peptide, which contains a scrambled cargo sequence of NiPp, failed to confer protection against inflammatory insult, reinforcing the specificity of NiPp. Scr3NiPp also failed to affect P2X7R-induced endothelium dysfunction (data not shown), further corroborating the specificity of NiPp. Collectively, these results underscore the therapeutic relevance of Niban phosphorylation in mitigating sepsis-induced vascular endothelial dysfunction and the utilization of NiPp for exploring new molecular mechanisms underlying vascular dysfunction. The current study also demonstrated impaired vascular reactivity to KCl and PE in septic rat aortas, reflecting hyporesponsiveness to vasoconstrictors characteristic of sepsis-induced vasoplegia.
title: Mitigating sepsis-induced vascular endothelial dysfunction through Niban phosphorylation

text: Scr3NiPp also failed to affect P2X7R-induced endothelium dysfunction (data not shown), further corroborating the specificity of NiPp. Collectively, these results underscore the therapeutic relevance of Niban phosphorylation in mitigating sepsis-induced vascular endothelial dysfunction and the utilization of NiPp for exploring new molecular mechanisms underlying vascular dysfunction. The current study also demonstrated impaired vascular reactivity to KCl and PE in septic rat aortas, reflecting hyporesponsiveness to vasoconstrictors characteristic of sepsis-induced vasoplegia. Briefly, KCl-induced contraction relies on smooth muscle depolarization and calcium influx, while PE-induced contraction depends more on adrenergic receptor activation and downstream calcium signaling. However, both processes are modulated by endothelium-derived vasoconstrictors or vasodilators. During sepsis, endothelial damage caused by inflammatory mediators and oxidative stress disrupts these endothelial signals. Previous rat studies have demonstrated similar reductions in vasoreactivity to KCl and PE during sepsis, linking the impairments to endothelial dysfunction. – Sepsis-induced endothelial cell death may also further impair endothelial signaling, calcium uptake, and release of various vasoconstrictive factors. Notably, the preserved SNP-induced relaxation in septic aortas indicates that nitric oxide-mediated smooth muscle responsiveness remains intact in this sepsis model despite a reduction in eNOS phosphorylation. This suggests that the impairments in KCl- or PE-induced contraction are likely due to a loss of endothelium-derived vasoconstrictors, adrenergic receptor dysfunction, or impaired calcium handling rather than altered nitric oxide signaling in smooth muscle cells. Alternatively, reduced responses to KCl may be a result of cell death caused by the complex circulating septic milieu in vivo. The observation that acute treatment of septic aorta with NiPp did not restore responses to KCl or PE suggests that Niban regulation does not interfere with PE signaling pathways, or that NiPp may selectively impact endothelial vasodilatory signaling rather than the molecular mechanisms that drive endothelium-derived vasoconstriction or smooth muscle-mediated vasoreactivity in the septic rat aorta. Nevertheless, the improvement in endothelial responses implicates a role for Niban in endothelial homeostasis, a crucial aspect of sepsis-induced vascular dysfunction and the development of vasoplegia. Building on established knowledge that sepsis impairs vascular homeostasis through inflammation and oxidative stress, our study highlights the role of ER stress as a key mediator of the pathologic endothelial response in sepsis, with Niban activation emerging as a potential regulator of ER stress responses in this context. Specifically, we observed elevated protein levels of GRP78, a well-established marker of ER stress linked to both sepsis and vascular dysfunction, along with a trend toward increased phosphorylation of eIF2α, a critical component of one of the three UPR branches. – These findings suggest that sepsis induced by CS promotes ER stress, which is accompanied by reduced Niban phosphorylation in septic aortas. The observed increase in GRP78, without corresponding changes in the transcriptional regulation of eIF2α, provides new mechanistic insights into our sepsis model.
title: Mitigating sepsis-induced vascular endothelial dysfunction through Niban phosphorylation

text: Specifically, we observed elevated protein levels of GRP78, a well-established marker of ER stress linked to both sepsis and vascular dysfunction, along with a trend toward increased phosphorylation of eIF2α, a critical component of one of the three UPR branches. – These findings suggest that sepsis induced by CS promotes ER stress, which is accompanied by reduced Niban phosphorylation in septic aortas. The observed increase in GRP78, without corresponding changes in the transcriptional regulation of eIF2α, provides new mechanistic insights into our sepsis model. Together, these results suggest that vascular ER stress in sepsis may primarily result from dysregulation of the other branches of UPR signaling and impaired degradation of misfolded proteins. Alternatively, this discrepancy may reflect the timing and sequential activation of ER stress pathways, wherein GRP78 upregulation occurs in the earlier phase, and eIF2α phosphorylation occurs later. This latter interpretation would align more favorably with previous findings linking decreased Niban levels to increased eIF2α phosphorylation in models of ER stress. Whereas GRP78 levels were not directly measured following NiPp treatment, the observed improvements in endothelium-dependent relaxation for septic aortas and those treated with the ER stressor, TM, suggest that modulating Niban phosphorylation could mitigate the downstream effects of sepsis-induced ER stress. These findings raise important questions about the time course and mechanisms through which Niban phosphorylation influences endothelial stress responses, including whether Niban directly regulates ER stress pathways like the UPR, or acts indirectly through upstream signaling cascades. Further elucidation of how Niban affects ER stress and vascular function will be critical for understanding its broader role in maintaining vascular homeostasis. Sepsis progression involves multiple cellular and molecular mechanisms that contribute to vascular dysfunction, including dysregulated inflammatory responses, oxidative injury, and altered endothelial-derived vasoactive mediators such as nitric oxide, prostanoids, endothelin, and endothelium-derived hyperpolarizing factor (EDHF). These mechanisms collectively respond to the surrounding physiological environment and may compensate for the absence of endothelial nitric oxide and prostacyclins. Various signaling pathways, such as nuclear factor-κB, MAPKs, and hypoxia-induced factor 1α, are activated and the interplay can trigger detrimental effects. For example, ER stress plays a pivotal role in downregulating eNOS, leading to impaired NO synthesis, which is vital for maintaining endothelial function. Similarly, ER stress, excessive inflammation, and oxidative stress activate p38 MAPK, further reducing eNOS activity. In the CS-induced septic aortae, we found reduced eNOS phosphorylation, which likely contributes to the impaired endothelium-dependent relaxation. Although p38 MAPK activation is often anticipated during cellular stress in sepsis, because many circulating mediators (including those used in our ex vivo model) activate p38 MAPK, – no difference in p38 MAPK phosphorylation was observed 24 hours after sepsis induction. This may be explained by the timing of vascular p38 MAPK regulation, either through direct activation by sepsis-associated mediators or as downstream ER stress signaling.

text: In the CS-induced septic aortae, we found reduced eNOS phosphorylation, which likely contributes to the impaired endothelium-dependent relaxation. Although p38 MAPK activation is often anticipated during cellular stress in sepsis, because many circulating mediators (including those used in our ex vivo model) activate p38 MAPK, – no difference in p38 MAPK phosphorylation was observed 24 hours after sepsis induction. This may be explained by the timing of vascular p38 MAPK regulation, either through direct activation by sepsis-associated mediators or as downstream ER stress signaling. Previous studies have reported reduced p38 MAPK phosphorylation in skeletal muscle in a chronic intra-abdominal septic abscess rat model, whereas increased phosphorylation has been observed in the lungs and brain after cecal ligation puncture-induced sepsis in mice. These findings highlight the complexity of the septic environment, where various pathological stimuli elicit dynamic and organ-specific responses during the progression of endothelial dysfunction. Further research into the temporospatial regulation and interplay between Niban and ER stress responses in vascular function will be critical to understanding their broader role in maintaining vascular homeostasis. The inclusion of multiple mediators of sepsis-induced endothelial injury, alongside a polymicrobial rat model of sepsis, strengthens the translational relevance of this study. LPS, IL-1β, CFH, and TM represent distinct but interconnected drivers of vascular dysfunction during sepsis. By evaluating NiPp across these mediators, our study demonstrates its ability to target multiple pathways relevant to sepsis pathology. Furthermore, the protective effects of NiPp in septic rat aortae indicate that Niban phosphorylation has the potential to modulate systemic vascular dysfunction in sepsis, extending beyond its effects on individual mediators. Importantly, this finding suggests that restoring Niban phosphorylation after a septic insult counteracts the complex, synergistic vascular insults present in polymicrobial sepsis and provides clinical relevance to further interrogation of the potential of NiPp as a rescue therapy in humans. This multitargeted approach offers a promising avenue for addressing the vascular complications of sepsis and potentially other conditions characterized by endothelial injury. Moreover, ex vivo examination of septic aorta also allows for the investigation of endogenous cellular and molecular defects and the discovery of salutary therapeutic mechanisms that improve vascular functions. Despite these advances, there are several limitations in this study that warrant consideration. The ex vivo nature of our experiments using intact aortic tissues in a muscle bath system provided a controlled environment to isolate vascular effects and evaluate endothelial dysfunction induced by sepsis or its mediators. This approach eliminated systemic influences such as inflammatory mediators, hemodynamics, or multiorgan interactions, – as well as confounding variables related to targeted drug delivery, metabolism, cellular uptake, or optimized dosing. However, it does not allow for assessment of the systemic impact of NiPp, including its effects on survival and multiorgan dysfunction in sepsis.

text: This approach eliminated systemic influences such as inflammatory mediators, hemodynamics, or multiorgan interactions, – as well as confounding variables related to targeted drug delivery, metabolism, cellular uptake, or optimized dosing. However, it does not allow for assessment of the systemic impact of NiPp, including its effects on survival and multiorgan dysfunction in sepsis. Though the aortic ring model enabled a focused evaluation of endothelial function and the differentiation between endothelium-dependent and endothelium-independent relaxation, it does not account for the heterogeneity of vascular beds throughout the body (i.e., the complexity and differences between macrovascular and microvascular dysfunction), both of which are critical for tissue oxygenation and perfusion during sepsis,, potentially limiting its applicability to broader physiological contexts. Further, only female rats were utilized in this study, which may limit the generalizability of the findings, as sex differences in vascular reactivity and endothelial function during sepsis have been well documented. – The use of a single sex was intended to provide initial insights into the cellular mechanisms associated with Niban regulation in a controlled setting. Investigating the systemic effects of NiPp on vascular function across different vascular beds, in both sexes, as well as in relation to broader physiological outcomes during a septic insult, will be essential for understanding its therapeutic potential and will be the focus of follow-on studies. This will also help identify potential sex-specific differences in endothelium- or smooth muscle-derived factors that influence Niban’s role in vascular responses to sepsis. Additionally, although lower concentrations of NiPp 50 µM did not elicit detectable effects in IL-1β-treated aortas, concentrations between 100 and 500 µM restored endothelium-dependent relaxation in ex vivo models. This highlights the importance of optimizing peptide concentrations based on experimental context, and future studies will need to establish the dose–response profile of NiPp in vivo to determine its range of pharmacological efficacy, therapeutic window, and potency in septic models. Furthermore, vascular responses to sepsis involved multiple cellular and molecular mechanisms that vary across temporal and spatial contexts. Our findings suggest that reduced Niban phosphorylation contributes to ER stress, but the precise molecular mechanisms and time course remain unclear. Future studies will need to focus on defining these dynamics and exploring potential interactions between Niban phosphorylation and other stress response pathways, such as those activated by inflammatory cytokines and oxidative stress mediators. Finally, examining whether Niban phosphorylation influences other arms of the ER stress response could provide further insights into its mechanism of action and its broader role in the adaptation of vascular cells to stress during sepsis.
title: Mitigating sepsis-induced vascular endothelial dysfunction through Niban phosphorylation

text: This study identifies Niban phosphorylation as a critical regulator of vascular function in sepsis and demonstrates the therapeutic potential of NiPp for restoring endothelial function in septic vasculatures. By mitigating endothelial dysfunction, NiPp addresses a key mechanism of sepsis-induced vascular injury, offering a novel approach for maintaining vascular homeostasis. These findings pave the way for further research into the molecular mechanisms underlying Niban-mediated stress adaptation and the development of NiPp as a targeted therapy for sepsis. Future investigations should focus on validating these results in vivo, optimizing NiPp administration strategies, and expanding our understanding of Niban in vascular homeostasis under pathological conditions.

text: Pulpal inflammation (pulpitis) poses a significant clinical challenge in contemporary dentistry, often manifesting as acute pain and potentially culminating in tooth loss without proper intervention. Although the initial inflammatory cascade serves as a protective mechanism, persistent or severe inflammation can lead to irreversible pulpal damage and subsequent tissue necrosis [ – ]. Elucidating the underlying molecular pathways in pulpitis progression remains crucial for developing targeted therapeutic approaches. Recent investigations have highlighted the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress response as a fundamental cellular mechanism with multifaceted roles in inflammatory conditions. The ER, which orchestrates protein folding and processing, maintains cellular equilibrium through the unfolded protein response (UPR) when challenged by various cellular stressors. The canonical UPR signaling cascade operates through three primary transmembrane sensors: PERK, IRE1α, and ATF6. These molecular sensors are typically maintained in their inactive configurations through interaction with the ER chaperone BiP/GRP78. Environmental and pathological stressors trigger BiP dissociation, activating these sensors and inducing CHOP expression, a critical transcriptional regulator in inflammation-mediated apoptosis. Moreover, Caspase-12 activation, specifically associated with ER stress, has been linked to inflammatory signaling cascades and cellular death pathways in various tissue types. Emerging evidence has demonstrated the involvement of ER stress and subsequent UPR activation in various oral pathologies, including periodontal disease and dental disease [ – ]. However, the precise mechanisms by which ER stress influences pulpitis development and progression remain inadequately understood. While previous research has established the presence of pro-inflammatory mediators, including TNF-α, in pulpal inflammation, the upstream regulatory networks governing their expression patterns remain to be fully characterized. Understanding the potential interplay between ER stress and inflammatory responses in dental pulp tissue represents a critical knowledge gap in our comprehension of pulpitis pathogenesis. In this study, we investigated the role of ER stress in pulpitis progression using both human pulp specimens and a rat pulpitis model. We hypothesized that ER stress mediates inflammatory responses in pulpitis through the CHOP/Caspase-12 pathway. Our findings provide new insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying pulpitis and suggest potential therapeutic strategies targeting ER stress for the treatment of pulpal inflammation.

text: Human dental pulp tissues were obtained from healthy third molars, extracted from teeth diagnosed with irreversible pulpitis at Shenzhen Stomatology Hospital. Patient inclusion criteria: Patients aged 18 to 22 years without underlying diseases or periodontal disease. Nine cases of pulpitis third molars extracted for treatment purposes, with each patient independently diagnosed by two endodontic specialists. Nine healthy, caries-free third molars were selected as controls. Pulp samples were obtained by crown splitting and immediately placed in 4% paraformaldehyde fixative, stored at 4 °C for 48 h, then paraffin-embedded and sectioned into 3–5 μm thick sagittal sections for further use. All procedures were approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee of Shenzhen Stomatology Hospital.

text: A total of 15 male Sprague-Dawley rats (8 weeks old, weighing 250–300 g) were purchased from Beijing Vital River Laboratory Animal Technology Company. For the pulpitis model, the left maxillary first molar was selected for pulpitis induction, while the right maxillary first molar of the same rat served as a negative control. The rats were anesthetized intraperitoneal injection of pentobarbital sodium (40 mg/kg body weight) before mechanical exposure of the pulp in their first Maxillary molar, which was achieved using a water-cooled round carbide bur. The exposed pulp was left open to the oral environment for 3 days before being sealed with glass ionomer cement. Glass ionomer cement was mixed at a water-to-powder ratio of 1:1 to form a paste-like consistency and then filled into the access cavity. The purpose of this treatment was to seal the pulp chamber, restore tooth morphology, and prevent further bacterial invasion. Successful establishment of pulpitis was confirmed as follows: rats were sacrificed on the 3rd day post-exposure, maxillary bone specimens were collected, and HE staining was performed to observe the degree of pulpal inflammation, neutrophil infiltration, and tissue necrosis. The animals were randomly assigned to three experimental groups: sham-operated controls (underwent identical procedure without pulp exposure), untreated pulpitis, and pulpitis treated with 4-PBA (an ER stress inhibitor). At least three animals were included in each group. The administration details of 4-PBA in the animal model are as follows: a concentration of 5 mM was applied via local administration. Specifically, 5 mM 4-PBA was applied to collagen sponges for local pulp capping, followed by coronal glass ionomer filling and sealing. Administration occurred 3 days post-pulp exposure, and animals were sacrificed 4 days post-treatment (7 days post-pulp exposure). All animals were killed by cervical dislocation after anaesthesia with an intraperitoneal injection of pentobarbital sodium (40 mg/kg). This method was chosen due to its rapid and humane approach, minimizing suffering and ensuring a quick death. Maxillary bone specimens were collected on day 7 post-sacrifice. Subsequently, samples were placed in 4% paraformaldehyde fixative and stored at 4 °C for 48 h, followed by demineralization in 10% EDTA for 6 weeks with solution changes every 2 days. Tissues were paraffin-embedded and sectioned into 3–5 μm thick sagittal sections for further use. The experimental protocols were approved by the Laboratory Animal Welfare & Ethics Committee of Bestcell Model Biological Center (approval number: 2025-1-21A).

text: Primary human dental pulp cells (hDPCs) were isolated from healthy premolars and third molars extracted from patients aged 13–23 years for orthodontic treatment. Teeth were placed in sterile culture dishes and washed 3–4 times with PBS until all surface blood was completely removed. Teeth were split to extract the pulp, with 2 mm of apical pulp tissue removed. Pulp tissue was placed in digestion solution containing 3 mg/ml type I collagenase (Invitrogen, 17100017) and 4 mg/ml dispase (Gibco, 17105041), thoroughly minced, and digested in a cell culture incubator for 1 h. Digestion was terminated with complete medium containing 10% fetal bovine serum, followed by centrifugation at 1000 rpm for 5 min. The supernatant was removed, and tissue blocks were resuspended in complete medium with 20% fetal bovine serum, seeded in T25 culture flasks, and placed in a cell culture incubator. Medium was changed every 2 days, and when cells reached 80% confluence, they were passaged using trypsin digestion. P3-P5 cells were used for experiments. For LPS stimulation, cells were treated with 1 µg/mL E. coli LPS (Sigma, L2880) for 24 h. Where indicated, cells were pretreated with 2 mM 4-phenylbutyric acid (4-PBA, MCE, HY-A0281) prior to LPS stimulation.

text: To investigate the potential involvement of ER stress in pulpitis pathogenesis, we first examined the expression patterns of key ER stress markers in clinical specimens and established rat pulpitis model. Immunofluorescence analysis revealed significantly elevated expression of BiP and CHOP in pulpitis specimens compared to healthy pulp tissues (Fig. A, B), indicating activation of ER stress response during pulpal inflammation. For mechanistic investigation, we isolated and characterized primary hDPSCs from healthy dental pulp tissues. Flow cytometric analysis confirmed their stem cell identity through positive expression of mesenchymal markers (CD73, CD90, and CD105) and negative expression of hematopoietic markers (CD34 and CD45). When challenged with LPS (1 µg/mL, 24 h), these cells exhibited significant upregulation of BiP and CHOP (Fig. D, E), accompanied by increased expression of TNFα and the ER stress-specific apoptotic marker CASP12 (Fig. F, G). These findings establish a direct link between inflammatory stimuli and ER stress activation in dental pulp cells.

text: To gain comprehensive molecular insights into pulpitis pathogenesis, we performed bioinformatic analysis of transcriptomic data from public datasets (GSE98359). Quality control assessment showed that all samples met the standard criteria with uniform distribution. Principal component analysis (PCA) demonstrated clear segregation between healthy and inflamed pulp samples, reflecting distinct disease-associated transcriptional signatures. This analysis identified 2,218 differentially expressed genes (DEGs), with 1,683 upregulated and 535 downregulated genes in pulpitis specimens. Detailed GO analysis revealed significant enrichment in biological processes related to inflammatory response and immune regulation, particularly leukocyte-mediated immunity, leukocyte activation and cell-cell adhesion. Further examination of cellular components and molecular functions highlighted enrichment in plasma membrane organization, extracellular matrix composition, and immune receptor activity (Fig. D, E). KEGG pathway analysis identified multiple signaling cascades involved in inflammation and tissue homeostasis, notably cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction, cell adhesion molecules, and immune cell differentiation pathways. These findings demonstrate extensive immune and inflammatory pathway activation in pulpitis.

text: To specifically investigate ER stress involvement in pulpitis, we performed integrative analysis between pulpitis DEGs and ER stress-associated gene sets. This systematic approach identified 19 overlapping genes implicated in both processes (Fig. A, B). Key candidates including PMAIP1, NOD2, PIK3R1, THBS4, THBS1, STC2, RCN3, FCGR2B, RASGRF1, NCCRP1 and ATP2A3 exhibited significant differential expression. Correlation analysis revealed distinct expression relationships between these genes, visualized through heatmap representation. Strong positive correlations were observed between RASGRF1 and ATP2A3, as well as ABCA7 and RCN3, while negative correlations emerged between HSPA1A and RASGRF1 (represented in blue). Notably, PMAIP1 showed positive correlations with several key ER stress pathway components (e.g., GRP78, DDIT3, CASP12), suggesting its potential role in regulating ER stress in pulpitis. However, further experimental validation is needed to confirm its central regulatory role in pulpitis pathogenesis.

text: Comprehensive pathway analysis revealed significant enrichment of ER stress-related DEGs in critical biological processes and molecular pathways. GO analysis identified enrichment in response to ER stress, unfolded protein response, and extrinsic apoptotic signaling pathways (Fig. A-D). KEGG pathway analysis further highlighted involvement in TNF signaling, PI3K-Akt signaling, and P53 pathways, establishing mechanistic links between ER stress, inflammation, and tissue remodeling in pulpitis. Friend analysis quantitatively assessed gene network relationships, identifying PMAIP1 (mean similarity = 0.58318) as a central hub, followed by NOD2 (0.51487) and PIK3R1 (0.50451). Genes with lower similarity, such as ATP2A3 (mean = 0.40918), exhibited relatively weaker connections within the gene network. RT-PCR validation confirmed significant upregulation of PMAIP1, NOD2, STC2, RCN3 and downregulation of PI3K3R in clinical specimens. PMAIP1, also known as NOXA, belongs to a pro-apoptotic subfamily within the BCL-2 protein family, referred to as the BCL-2 homology domain 3 (BH3)-only subfamily, which is regulated by various stress signals and plays a key role in apoptotic regulation. Immunohistochemical analysis further confirmed the upregulation of PMAIP1 in inflamed pulp tissues (GEPIA correlation analysis demonstrated significant positive associations between these key regulators (similarity mean exceeding 0.5) and established ER stress markers (GRP78, DDIT3) and inflammatory mediators (CASP12, TNFα), further supporting the regulatory roles of PMAIP1, NOD2, and PIK3R1. Then, we performed siRNA-mediated PMAIP1 knockdown experiments to investigate its mechanistic role in ER stress. Following PMAIP1 knockdown, we evaluated both ER stress markers and downstream inflammatory responses under LPS stimulation. The results showed that PMAIP1 knockdown significantly reduced LPS-induced ER stress markers (HSPA5, CHOP) at mRNA level. Downstream apoptotic and inflammatory markers (CASP12, TNFA) were also decreased following PMAIP1 knockdown. These results demonstrate that PMAIP1 mediates ER stress induction and subsequent inflammatory responses in pulpitis, confirming its upstream regulatory role in this pathway.

text: To evaluate the therapeutic potential of targeting ER stress in pulpitis, we examined the effects of the chemical chaperone 4-PBA. We examined PMAIP1 expression in rat pulpitis tissues after 4-PBA delivery. 4-PBA treatment reduced PMAIP1 expression compared to untreated pulpitis controls. This finding imply that 4-PBA therapeutic effects is mediated through downregulation of PMAIP1. Western blot analysis demonstrated that 4-PBA treatment effectively suppressed LPS-induced expression of BiP, CHOP, CASP12, and TNFα in hDPSCs (Fig. A-E). These findings were further validated in a rat pulpitis model, where 4-PBA administration significantly reduced the expression of inflammatory and ER stress markers. These results establish ER stress as a viable therapeutic target in pulpitis management.

section_title: Therapeutic targeting of ER stress attenuates pulpal inflammation

text: Our study reveals novel molecular mechanisms underlying pulpitis pathogenesis, establishing endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress as a central orchestrator of inflammatory responses in dental pulp tissue. Through integrated transcriptomic and functional analyses, we identified PMAIP1 as a pivotal regulator connecting ER stress to inflammatory signaling cascades, while demonstrating the therapeutic potential of targeting ER stress with 4-PBA in pulpitis treatment. The marked upregulation of canonical ER stress markers (BiP and CHOP) in clinical pulpitis specimens provides the first direct evidence linking ER stress activation to pulpal inflammation. This finding extends beyond previous studies that primarily focused on inflammatory mediators in pulpitis, revealing a fundamental cellular stress response that may initiate and perpetuate inflammatory cascades. The concurrent elevation of ER stress-specific apoptotic marker Caspase-12 with inflammatory mediator TNF-α suggests that ER stress may serve as an upstream trigger for inflammatory cell death in pulpal tissue, consistent with observations in other inflammatory conditions. We also noticed that the prominently significant gene located at the top-right corner of Fig. C is CRLF1 (Cytokine Receptor-Like Factor 1). CRLF1 functions as a co-receptor in IL-6 family cytokine signaling pathways and has been associated with inflammatory responses in various disease contexts. The notable upregulation of CRLF1 in our pulpitis model suggests activation of cytokine-mediated inflammatory pathways, which is consistent with the known inflammatory nature of pulpitis. While this finding provides additional insight into the inflammatory landscape of pulpitis, detailed characterization of CRLF1’s specific role in pulpal inflammation warrants further investigation in future studies. Our bioinformatic analysis identified PMAIP1 as a previously unrecognized central hub in pulpitis pathogenesis, exhibiting the highest network connectivity among ER stress-related differentially expressed genes. This finding aligns with recent studies highlighting PMAIP1’s role in cellular stress responses, though its function in dental pulp inflammation was previously unexplored. The strong positive correlations between PMAIP1 and established ER stress markers (GRP78, DDIT3) suggest its potential role in amplifying stress responses, while its associations with inflammatory mediators indicate its function in bridging cellular stress to inflammatory signaling. The identification of NOD2 and PIK3R1 as key regulatory molecules provides mechanistic insight into how ER stress signals are translated into inflammatory responses. NOD2, known for its role in inflammatory diseases, emerged as a significant node in our network analysis, suggesting that ER stress may modulate inflammatory responses through NOD2-dependent pathogen recognition pathways. Similarly, PIK3R1 is essential for XBP-1s translocation to the nucleus and thus regulating endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress. Perhaps the most clinically relevant finding is the therapeutic efficacy of 4-PBA in attenuating both ER stress and inflammatory responses. The significant reduction in BiP, CHOP, CASP12, and TNF-α expression following 4-PBA treatment aligns with studies demonstrating its effectiveness in other inflammatory conditions. This approach is particularly promising as it addresses an upstream regulatory mechanism rather than merely suppressing inflammatory mediators, potentially offering more effective disease control.
title: PMAIP1 mediates endoplasmic reticulum stress in human dental pulp stem cells during pulpitis pathogenesis

text: Perhaps the most clinically relevant finding is the therapeutic efficacy of 4-PBA in attenuating both ER stress and inflammatory responses. The significant reduction in BiP, CHOP, CASP12, and TNF-α expression following 4-PBA treatment aligns with studies demonstrating its effectiveness in other inflammatory conditions. This approach is particularly promising as it addresses an upstream regulatory mechanism rather than merely suppressing inflammatory mediators, potentially offering more effective disease control. Our findings also shed light on the complex interplay between ER stress and dental pulp stem cell function. Recent studies have demonstrated that stem cell properties can be significantly impacted by ER stress, suggesting that targeting this pathway might not only reduce inflammation but also preserve the regenerative capacity of dental pulp tissue. The observed effects of 4-PBA on pulp stem cells warrant further investigation into potential regenerative applications. The translation of these findings into clinical practice could fundamentally change our approach to pulpitis treatment. Current therapeutic strategies primarily focus on symptom management and pulp preservation, often with limited success in cases of irreversible pulpitis. Our identification of ER stress as a druggable target, coupled with the demonstration of 4-PBA’s effectiveness, opens new avenues for developing targeted therapies that could potentially prevent the progression from reversible to irreversible pulpitis. The use of both human specimens and a rat model provides cross-species validation of our observations. The integration of transcriptomic analysis with functional studies offers robust evidence for the role of ER stress in pulpitis. However, certain limitations should be acknowledged. While our rat model successfully recapitulated key features of human pulpitis, species-specific differences in dental pulp biology May affect the generalizability of some findings. The temporal dynamics of ER stress activation during different stages of pulpitis progression require further investigation. Although 4-PBA showed promising results, optimization of its delivery method and timing for clinical application needs additional study. Additionally, the long-term effects of ER stress modulation on pulp tissue homeostasis and regeneration capacity remain to be determined. Our current findings establish the direct effects of ER stress on hDPSCs and provide the mechanistic foundation for understanding pulpal inflammation responses. However, to enhance biological relevance, future studies should incorporate heterogeneous cell co-cultures that include immune cells, endothelial cells, and other pulp tissue components, as these multicellular interactions are critical in the physiological context. And detailed characterization of the PMAIP1-mediated signaling network in pulpal inflammation, particularly its interaction with NOD2 and PIK3R1 pathways, will be crucial for understanding the complete molecular mechanism. The development of targeted delivery systems for ER stress modulators could enhance their therapeutic efficacy in dental pulp tissue. Further investigation of potential biomarkers for early detection of ER stress activation in pulpitis could guide therapeutic intervention timing. Moreover, exploration of combination therapies targeting both ER stress and conventional inflammatory pathways may lead to more effective treatment strategies.

These findings not only advance our understanding of pulpal inflammation but also offer promising directions for clinical intervention strategies.

text: Cisplatin (CIS) is a chemotherapeutic drug widely used to treat ovarian, breast, testicular and lung cancer. CIS enters cells by a variety of mechanisms, including diffusion, facilitated diffusion mediated by cation carriers, and endocytosis, and is transported to the cell nucleus where it exerts its cytotoxic effects. CIS exerts cytotoxic effects by inducing apoptosis with increased reactive oxygen species (ROS), while it arrests the cancer cell cycle by forming cross-links through intercalation. Despite its recognised efficacy as a cancer drug, it is associated with significant toxic effects on kidney, lung, and heart tissues. As is the case with other chemotherapeutic agents, the use of CIS produces selective cytotoxic effects on cancer cells, while it can also have toxic effects on healthy lung cells. Pulmonary toxicity due to CIS is an uncommon occurrence. Nevertheless, the condition is a grave pathology with the potential to have catastrophic consequences. Although the aetiopathogenesis of CIS-associated pulmonotoxicity is not fully known, it has been documented that increased oxidative stress (OS) and inflammation damage pulmonary epithelial cells and blood vessels, leading to progressive damage from deoxygenation to fibrosis. Lung fibrosis is a fatal disease in which the lungs become scarred and stiff, resulting in permanent shortness of breath and death within 5 years of diagnosis. Unfortunately, no medications are available to reverse pulmonary fibrosis, and the only option for patients are lung transplantation. CIS toxicity is a complex process initiated primarily by OS and inflammation and involves a number of cellular signals. CIS induce OS through an increase in ROS production and depletion of glutathione (GSH) and other antioxidant enzymes. Unneutralised ROS can damage lipids, leading to lipid peroxidation (LPO), enzyme inactivation and DNA damage. OS associated with CIS also activates the nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) pathway, a master regulator of inflammatory processes, leading to the induction of inflammatory cytokines, such as interleukin-6 (IL-6), and myeloperoxidase (MPO), burst as a result of leukocyte infiltration. Consequently, CIS-induced subacute OS and inflammation results in activation of traditional apoptosis pathways and cell death. Over the past few years, it has been established that CIS toxicity leads to endoplasmic reticulum stress (ERS) by reducing the protein folding capacity of ER, and in this case cell death occurs via ER-associated apoptosis. Sirtuin 1 (SIRT1), a NAD + -dependent deacetylase found in almost all mammalian tissues, has been identified as an important metabolic sensor. SIRT1 has been demonstrated to fulfil a pivotal function in the modulation of a broad spectrum of physiological processes, encompassing metabolic rate, OS, inflammation, and DNA repair. The antioxidant and anti-inflammatory processes controlled by nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) have been demonstrated to play a pivotal role in preventing degenerative cell damage. SIRT1 and Nrf2 have been demonstrated to act as positive regulators of each other, thereby increasing the resistance of cells to changing physiological conditions. Recent reports have emphasised the significance of repressed SIRT1/Nrf2 signalling in the context of CIS-induced tissue toxicity [ – ].
title: The protective effects of naringin against cisplatin-induced pulmonary toxicity in rats: Insights into the modulation of ER stress and SIRT1/Nrf2 pathway

text: The antioxidant and anti-inflammatory processes controlled by nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) have been demonstrated to play a pivotal role in preventing degenerative cell damage. SIRT1 and Nrf2 have been demonstrated to act as positive regulators of each other, thereby increasing the resistance of cells to changing physiological conditions. Recent reports have emphasised the significance of repressed SIRT1/Nrf2 signalling in the context of CIS-induced tissue toxicity [ – ]. Therefore, the investigation of the protective capacity of natural antioxidants, such as polyphenols, which may exhibit antioxidant and SIRT1/Nrf2 modulator properties, against the toxicity of CIS has been one of the most popular areas of research in recent years. Citrus fruits are among the most frequently cultivated natural products on the world, consumed both as a fresh fruit and in the form of fresh fruit juice, as well as being used in the production of other food products. Citrus fruits are natural products rich in flavonoids, and naringin (NRG) is one of the flavanone glycoside found most abundantly in citrus fruits. Notably, it is distinguished by its multifaceted properties, which encompass anti-inflammatory, anti-apoptotic, antioxidant, and ulcerative effects. The NOAEL value of 6 months of oral administration of NRG to rats has been determined to be greater than 1250 mg/kg/day. This finding effectively eliminates any biosafety concerns, thus facilitating its extensive utilisation in both the pharmaceutical and nutraceutical sectors, owing to its favourable effects on health. The antioxidant properties of NRG primarily result from its capacity to chelate metal ions, impeding the Fenton reaction and thereby enhancing the activities of antioxidant enzymes, such as superoxide dismutase (SOD) and glutathione peroxidase (GPx). Furthermore, recent studies have indicated that NRG’s capacity to modulate SIRT1/Nrf2 signaling may also be implicated in the molecular mechanism of its tissue-protective activity. The protective effects of NRG against D-galactose, lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and bleomycin induced lung injuries have been demonstrated in previous experimental reports. Nevertheless, to the best of our knowledge, no study has yet investigated the protective effect of NRG against CIS-associated pulmonotoxicity. This study aimed to investigate the effects of NRG on OS, inflammation and ERS in a CIS-induced lung toxicity model, while also revealing the role of the SIRT1/Nrf2 axis.

text: The present study was conducted using 30 female Sprague-Dawley rats (180–190 g) obtained from the Surgical Application Center of Karadeniz Technical University. The rats were housed in the same centre under standard conditions free of pathogens (12 h light-dark cycle and 24 ± 2 °C). Following a period of acclimatisation spanning seven days, the rats were randomly divided into five groups: Normal control, NRG control (100 mg/kg), CIS, CIS + NRG treatment (50 and 100 mg/kg) groups. CIS and NRG were prepared by dissolving in physiological saline and 0.5% CMC, respectively. On the second day of the experiment, all groups containing CIS were injected with CIS (7.5 mg/kg), while the groups not containing CIS were injected with physiological saline. The dose of 7.5 mg/kg of CIS was previously determined using experimental models of CIS-induced organ toxicity with a minimum experimental duration of 5 days. The administration of NRG was conducted via gavage to all groups containing NRG, while 0.5% CMC was administered via gavage to groups devoid of NRG. The doses of NRG were selected on the basis of previous reports of its beneficial biological activity of oral NRG in experimental models of acrylamide-induced renal toxicity and paclitaxel-induced reproductive toxicity. The study protocol was approved by the Animal Research Ethics Committee of Karadeniz Technical University (Protocol number: 2024/40), and all methods used in this study were implemented in strict accordance with the guidelines set out in the ARRIVE guidelines. All possible measures were taken to minimise the suffering of the animals and the total number of animals utilised. The rats were observed daily for toxic symptoms, mortality, or any abnormal findings. On the morning of the eighth day of the experiment, euthanasia was induced by intraperitoneal injection of overdose of sodium pentobarbital (140 mg/kg) and lung tissues were rapidly extracted for further experimentation. Animals that exhibited no signs of respiration and response to systemic stimuli were designated as deceased.

text: The NRG is a flavanone glycoside that is particularly abundant in citrus fruits, and its pulmonary protective effect has been demonstrated in various experimental injury models in previous studies [ – ]. However, the potential protective effects of NRG against CIS-induced lung injury remain unclear. This study is the first to focus on NRG’s protective effects against CIS related lung injury. In this study, it was shown that the protective effects of NRG against lung damage caused by CIS are due to the reduction of OS, inflammation, ERS, and cell death. In addition, our research highlights that regulating the SIRT1/Nrf2/HO-1 pathway plays a role in this protective effect of NRG in the lungs. The present study revealed that CIS administration resulted in increased signs of haemorrhage, inflammatory cell infiltration, edema, alveolar wall thickening and epithelial cell damage. These findings were consistent with previous reports identifying the destructive effects of CIS on lung tissue. However, the administration of NRG supplements was found to significantly improve the impairment to lung architecture induced by CIS, with the high-dose supplementation proving more effective. Consistent with our findings, Turgut et al. reported that NRG may exhibit lung-protective effects by improving the infiltration of inflammatory cells and alveolar wall thickening in a bleomycin-induced experimental lung toxicity model. The mechanism of CIS-induced pulmonotoxicity is complex. It is known that ROS, which are increased by CIS, cause severe OS by increasing LPO formation. Conversely, SIRT1 and Nrf2 function as sensors of OS and metabolism, and work in a reciprocal regulatory relationship to modulate each other’s activities. Consequently, they supervise the regulation of proteins that protect cells against oxidative and inflammatory damage. It has been demonstrated that, over time, excessive ROS from CIS ultimately results in the inhibition of the SIRT1/Nrf2 axis, thereby rendering cells vulnerable to OS and inflammation. Consistent with the existing literature, the present study found that the administration of CIS led to the inhibition of SIRT1/Nrf2 signalling in the lungs of rats, an increase in LPO and TOS levels, and a weakening of the antioxidant defence system. In contrast, the application of NRG, particularly in high the dose, has been demonstrated to have a counteractive effect on OS. This is evidenced by the restoration of antioxidant defence components and the decrease in LPO and TOS levels. The observed effect can be attributed to the previously demonstrated metal-chelating properties of NRG, which have been shown to inhibit the Fenton reaction and exhibit radical-scavenging activities. Furthermore, NRG treatment restored the suppressed levels of SIRT1, Nrf2 and HO-1 in the CIS group, which can be explained at least in part by its ability to modulate the SIRT1/Nrf2 signalling pathway and exert lung-protective effects. This hypothesis is in line with earlier reports that NRG can have a protective effect by regulating SIRT1/Nrf2 signaling in models of tissue injury caused by D-galactose and acetaminophen. Inflammation represents a pivotal component in the sequence of events that ultimately results in tissue damage in cases of CIS. As is well documented, NF-κB signalling is activated in response to CIS-derived ROS, which leads to a rapid increase in cytokine levels, such as IL-6. As a secondary consequence, inflammatory cell migration to the damaged tissue accelerates, causing a burst of MPO.
title: The protective effects of naringin against cisplatin-induced pulmonary toxicity in rats: Insights into the modulation of ER stress and SIRT1/Nrf2 pathway

text: This hypothesis is in line with earlier reports that NRG can have a protective effect by regulating SIRT1/Nrf2 signaling in models of tissue injury caused by D-galactose and acetaminophen. Inflammation represents a pivotal component in the sequence of events that ultimately results in tissue damage in cases of CIS. As is well documented, NF-κB signalling is activated in response to CIS-derived ROS, which leads to a rapid increase in cytokine levels, such as IL-6. As a secondary consequence, inflammatory cell migration to the damaged tissue accelerates, causing a burst of MPO. Consistent with this, our results showed that CIS administration causes widespread inflammation in lung tissue, as indicated by high levels of NF-κB p65, IL-6 and MPO. Conversely, the inflammation induced by CIS was found to be significantly reduced in rats treated with NRG, as evidenced by reduced levels of NF-κB, IL-6, and MPO. It is well known that the SIRT1/Nrf2 axis regulates the activity of antioxidant and anti-inflammatory genes. Furthermore, SIRT1/Nrf2 signalling is one of the most important mechanisms that inhibit NF-κB. Higher SIRT1/Nrf2 levels in the NRG treatment groups than in the CIS group may also contribute to NRG’s anti-inflammatory activity. Consistent with our findings, it has previously been reported that NRG exhibits anti-inflammatory activity by inhibiting the NF-κB pathway in experimental models. The decline in the protein folding capacity of the ER in conditions, such as calcium imbalance, OS and low ATP levels is referred to as ERS. Recent reports have demonstrated that CIS upregulates a number of ERS biomarkers, activates CASP3, and promotes apoptosis. Increased ERS subsequently triggers the unfolded protein response (UPR) in cells. The UPR is a series of processes, including the activation of ER-associated degredation (ERAD) to remove misfolded proteins and the increase in chaperone synthesis, that aim to either correctly fold unfolded proteins in the ER or eliminate them in the short and medium term. The accumulation of numerous misfolded proteins in the ER promotes the dissociation of the chaperone BIP from ATF6. Once activated in the Golgi, the released ATF6 migrates to the nucleus, where it induces the expression of genes, such as GADD153. This alleviates ERS in the acute phase and directs apoptosis in the chronic phase. In line with this, our results showed that the administration of CIS induced ERS biomarkers and CASP3 levels in lung tissue. By contrast, NRG supplements were found to significantly improve CIS-induced ERS and apoptosis levels, with the high dose proving to be more effective. It is known that the SIRT1/Nrf2 axis inhibits cellular apoptosis in response to ERS by increasing the expression of ERAD components. This was confirmed by higher SIRT1/Nrf2 levels and lower ERS levels in the NRG groups. Consistent with our findings, a previous study demonstrated that NRG could reduce ERS and apoptosis by decreasing BIP and GADD153 levels in a model of bleomycin-induced pulmonary toxicity. The present study is not without its limitations. Firstly, the study utilised the conventional NRG and CIS doses that have been widely documented in the extant literature. Subsequent to a 7-day treatment period, biochemical and histological experiments were conducted. It is recommended that future studies concentrate on the testing of NRG and CIS at varying doses and in different forms, and that long-term results be evaluated.

text: The present study is not without its limitations. Firstly, the study utilised the conventional NRG and CIS doses that have been widely documented in the extant literature. Subsequent to a 7-day treatment period, biochemical and histological experiments were conducted. It is recommended that future studies concentrate on the testing of NRG and CIS at varying doses and in different forms, and that long-term results be evaluated. Secondly, the research team’s available laboratory and financial resources allowed for biochemical measurements to be performed using spectrophotometric and ELISA-based methods. In future studies, the cytoplasmic (and, in some cases, nuclear) levels of these and the other proteins involved in cell signalling should also be evaluated using detailed molecular methods, such as Western blot, RT-PCR, and immunohistochemistry. Thirdly, in this study, lung tissues of rats were evaluated using biochemical and histological methods. In subsequent studies, lung function assessment tests such as spirometry should be incorporated into experimental designs to evaluate the protective efficacy of NRG from a physiological perspective.

text: Programmed cell death plays an important role in various processes, such as tissue development, differentiation, and homeostasis. Dysregulation of programmed cell death leads to pathogenesis, including cancer, neurodegenerative diseases, autoimmune disorders, and cardiovascular diseases. With advancements in molecular technologies, several types of cell death have been identified and characterized. Paraptosis, a novel type of programmed cell death, was first identified by Sperandio et al. in 2000. They reported that human embryonic kidney 293 T cells and mouse embryonic fibroblasts overexpressing the intracellular domain of the β subunit of insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor (IGF1R) underwent cell death characterized by a distinctive vacuole-filled cytoplasm morphology, unlike other known forms of cell death at that time. They termed this form of cell death “paraptosis,” using the Greek preposition “para” to distinguish it from apoptosis because paraptosis does not involve caspase activation, apoptotic body formation, DNA fragmentation, or chromatin condensation. Over the past two decades, some of the underlying mechanisms of paraptosis have been defined, revealing its association with cell fate and various diseases, such as cancer [ – ] and viral infection. Furthermore, some small molecules that induce paraptosis have shown potential as anticancer agents by inhibiting tumor growth and overcoming therapeutic resistance [ – ]. This makes paraptosis an attractive alternative for cancer treatment. In this review, we summarize the discoveries of paraptosis, with an emphasis on its role in cancer biology, including its specific features, regulatory mechanisms, and potential applications in cancer treatment, in the hope of providing insights into the development of effective clinical anticancer strategies.
title: Exploring paraptosis as a therapeutic approach in cancer treatment

text: Cytoplasmic vacuolization is the hallmark of paraptosis. Cytoplasmic vacuoles in paraptosis originate from swelling of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and mitochondria. Paraptotic cells maintain plasma membrane integrity but exhibit enlarged cell sizes because the vacuoles fill the cytosol. As shown in Fig. curcumin, a known paraptotic agent, induces dilation of both the ER and mitochondria. The ER and mitochondria are the primary intracellular storage sites for calcium ions (Ca 2+). It has been proposed that ER Ca 2+ influx into mitochondria triggers water influx into the ER, leading to ER dilation to accommodate the increased volume, followed by mitochondrial dilation. Eventually, paraptotic cells detach, round up, shrink, and rupture the outer membrane. Cytoplasmic vacuolization is also observed in two other types of cell death, autophagy and methuosis [ – ]. Macroautophagic vacuoles originate from elongating isolated membranes. In macroautophagy, cytosolic membranes, or phagophores, elongate and seal to form a double-membraned autophagosome, subsequently encapsulating cytosolic components either selectively or nonselectively. The autophagosome subsequently fuses with lysosomes, degrading their contents [ – ]. The role of macroautophagy in response to ER stress is complex and context dependent, with studies reporting both cytoprotective and cell death-inducing effects. Methuosis, another form of vacuolar cell death, originates from hyperactive micropinocytosis. The accumulation of macropinosomes and endosomes results in a characteristic vacuolated morphology, ultimately culminating in cell death [, – ]. The similarity and difference in paraptosis, macroautophagic death, and methuosis are listed Table.
title: Exploring paraptosis as a therapeutic approach in cancer treatment

text: Dilation of the ER and mitochondria results from an imbalance of calcium within these organelles. Calcium is critical for the proper folding of proteins within the ER. Depletion of ER calcium leads to ER stress, activation of the unfolded protein response (UPR), and the accumulation of misfolded or unfolded proteins. This accumulation of misfolded proteins in the ER increases osmotic pressure, activating inositol 1,4,5-triphosphate receptors (IP3Rs) to promote Ca 2+ release from the ER into the cytosol and mitochondria. The resulting osmotic pressure drives water influx into the ER, causing ER dilation. Similarly, an ionic imbalance in mitochondria increases osmotic pressure and water influx, leading to mitochondrial swelling.
title: Exploring paraptosis as a therapeutic approach in cancer treatment

text: Most paraptotic agents possess proteasomal inhibition activity, which prevents the degradation of ubiquitin-tagged proteins and results in the accumulation of these proteins. Impaired proteasome function leads to the accumulation of misfolded or damaged proteins in the ER, triggering ER stress and the subsequent UPR. As a result of ER stress, relevant proteins are often upregulated [ – ]. These proteins not only accumulate in the ER but also translocate to the nucleus, where they participate in transcription activation and translation. Therefore, inhibitors of transcription and translation can mitigate cell vacuolization [ – ].
title: Exploring paraptosis as a therapeutic approach in cancer treatment

text: ROS overproduction is often observed in paraptotic cells [ – ]. ROS production could be caused by proteasome inhibition, mitochondrial dysfunction, and redox system imbalance. Notably, ROS themselves act as signaling molecules that mediate paraptosis [, – ]. A more detailed mechanism of ROS crosstalk with paraptosis is described in the following section.
title: Exploring paraptosis as a therapeutic approach in cancer treatment

text: To date, specific pathways or unique molecular biomarkers for paraptosis remain elusive. Instead, multiple interconnected pathways have been implicated in initiating paraptosis. This section summarizes paraptosis-inducing compounds and treatments, highlighting their downstream effectors and associated signaling pathways (
