section_title: Salvianolic acid B is the potential bioactive compound in M. canadensis that is critical to overcoming PTX resistance

text: Further, we investigated whether salvianolic acid B could overcome PTX resistance. Co-treatment with salvianolic acid B and PTX (100 nM) significantly decreased survival of AGS PTXR cells. CI analysis indicated a synergistic interaction between salvianolic acid B and PTX (CI < 1), suggesting that salvianolic acid B enhanced the cytotoxicity of PTX against PTXR cells. Western blotting indicated that co-treatment with salvianolic acid B and PTX significantly increased c-PARP levels and the cleavage of caspase-9, caspase-8, and caspase-3, indicating activation of the apoptotic pathway. Western blot analysis showed that salvianolic acid B upregulated NOXA, ATF4, p-eIF2α, and p-PERK expression. In addition, flow cytometry using MitoSOX showed that ROS levels within the mitochondria were significantly increased by salvianolic acid B treatment, suggesting that oxidative stress may contribute to the induction of apoptosis.
title: M. canadensis and its active component salvianolic acid B overcome paclitaxel resistance in gastric cancer via ROS–ER stress signaling
section_title: Salvianolic acid B enhances PTX-induced apoptosis via NOXA and ATF4 upregulation

text: PTX resistance remains a major challenge in gastric cancer treatment and novel therapeutic strategies are required. Here, we showed that M. canadensis and its physiologically active constituent, salvianolic acid B, efficiently overcame PTX resistance by inducing PTXR gastric cancer cells to undergo apoptosis via the ROS–ER stress–NOXA pathway. Transcriptome analysis showed that M. canadensis treatment markedly upregulated pathways associated with ER stress, oxidative stress, and apoptosis. Consistent with these findings, in vitro validation confirmed that M. canadensis induces apoptosis by upregulating NOXA, a member of the pro-apoptotic BCL-2 family. In addition, subcellular fractionation analysis demonstrated cytosolic translocation of cytochrome c following M. canadensis treatment, providing functional evidence consistent with mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization (MOMP) (Supplementary Fig. 1A). This finding further supports the engagement of intrinsic apoptotic signaling downstream of stress-induced BH3-only protein upregulation. The downregulation of Mcl-1 was mediated by proteasomal degradation, evidenced by the recovery of protein levels with MG132 (Supplementary Fig. 1C). This rapid turnover is likely facilitated by the robust induction of NOXA, a known mediator of Mcl-1 degradation. In contrast, although the total protein level of Bcl-2 showed only a marginal decrease following treatment, siRNA-mediated ATF4 knockdown resulted in a dramatic three-fold increase in Bcl-2 mRNA levels (Supplementary Fig. 1D). This suggests that while M. canadensis does not further reduce Bcl-2 from its already low basal state, ATF4 serves as a critical constitutive transcriptional repressor that prevents Bcl-2 recovery in AGS PTXR cells. Furthermore, elevated expression of ER stress markers, such as PERK and ATF4, indicated that ER stress signaling contributes to apoptotic execution. Time-course analysis showed that M. canadensis transiently increased CHOP expression at early time points (Supplementary Fig. 2A). However, CHOP protein induction was modest and not sustained. Consistent with this observation, time-resolved qPCR analysis revealed that CHOP mRNA exhibited an early transient peak that declined at later time points (Supplementary Fig. 2B), explaining the limited protein accumulation. These findings suggest that CHOP functions as an early stress-responsive marker rather than a sustained mediator of apoptosis in our system. In contrast, ATF4 activation was sustained, supporting a model in which NOXA expression is directly regulated by ATF4 rather than CHOP. Among the three canonical branches of the unfolded protein response, activation was strongly biased toward the PERK–eIF2α–ATF4 axis. Although phosphorylation of IRE1α was detectable, it was modest and declined over time, and no sustained activation of ATF6 was observed. Such PERK-dominant signaling is consistent with cellular contexts in which mitochondrial ROS and redox imbalance constitute the primary stress input, as PERK is particularly sensitive to oxidative perturbation. This selective engagement of PERK provides a mechanistic framework linking mitochondrial ROS to ATF4-dependent NOXA induction and intrinsic apoptosis. In addition, the markedly low basal NOXA expression observed in PTX-resistant cells may reflect reduced apoptotic priming, potentially involving epigenetic repression of the PMAIP1 locus.
title: M. canadensis and its active component salvianolic acid B overcome paclitaxel resistance in gastric cancer via ROS–ER stress signaling

text: Such PERK-dominant signaling is consistent with cellular contexts in which mitochondrial ROS and redox imbalance constitute the primary stress input, as PERK is particularly sensitive to oxidative perturbation. This selective engagement of PERK provides a mechanistic framework linking mitochondrial ROS to ATF4-dependent NOXA induction and intrinsic apoptosis. In addition, the markedly low basal NOXA expression observed in PTX-resistant cells may reflect reduced apoptotic priming, potentially involving epigenetic repression of the PMAIP1 locus. Although chromatin-level regulation was not directly examined in this study, the robust inducible activation of NOXA following ATF4 engagement indicates that the gene remains transcriptionally competent under stress conditions. ROS promotes cell death by inducing oxidative and ER stress responses. Our findings demonstrate that M. canadensis induces apoptosis by drastically increasing the intracellular ROS levels, indicating that mitochondrial ROS acts as a central upstream driver of ER stress and apoptotic commitment in PTXR cells. Mitochondrial ROS generation emerged as an early and critical event in our model. Importantly, ATF4 knockdown did not attenuate M. canadensis–induced mitochondrial ROS accumulation, as assessed by MitoSOX fluorescence (Supplementary Fig. 3A). These results indicate that mitochondrial ROS accumulation occurs upstream of ATF4 activation rather than being sustained by ATF4 signaling. To further define the origin of ROS, we examined the effect of site-specific electron transport chain (ETC) inhibitors. Pretreatment with rotenone or antimycin A did not suppress, but rather markedly potentiated mitochondrial ROS accumulation (Supplementary Fig. 3B). This synergistic enhancement suggests that M. canadensis perturbs mitochondrial respiratory function broadly, leading to electron leakage and superoxide amplification rather than isolated inhibition of a single ETC complex. Collectively, these findings support a model in which mitochondrial ROS serves as the initiating stress signal, activating the PERK–ATF4 axis and subsequently promoting NOXA-mediated mitochondrial apoptotic commitment. Salvianolic acid B, a component of M. canadensis, acts synergistically with PTX, significantly decreasing cell viability and promoting caspase-dependent apoptosis. Previous studies have shown that natural compounds can improve anticancer treatment efficacy by regulating apoptosis-related pathways. Our study revealed the anticancer mechanism of salvianolic acid B, demonstrating its potential as a therapeutic agent to overcome PTX resistance in gastric cancer. Interestingly, salvianolic acid B treatment resulted in a sustained increase in ATF4 and NOXA expression, implying that its anticancer effects may be mediated by persistent ER stress activation. Network pharmacology analysis further identified HIF1A as a potential hub associated with salvianolic acid B. Although oxidative stress can stabilize HIF-1α through hydroxylation-dependent mechanisms, our current data primarily support a ROS-driven PERK–ATF4–NOXA axis. Further studies will be required to determine whether HIF-1α stabilization contributes functionally to the salvianolic acid B response in PTX-resistant gastric cancer cells. Although we aimed to further validate our findings in an in vivo model, we were unable to proceed because of the failure of AGS PTXR cells to form tumors despite multiple attempts. Parental AGS cells have been reported to form subcutaneous xenograft tumors in immunodeficient mice.
title: M. canadensis and its active component salvianolic acid B overcome paclitaxel resistance in gastric cancer via ROS–ER stress signaling

text: Further studies will be required to determine whether HIF-1α stabilization contributes functionally to the salvianolic acid B response in PTX-resistant gastric cancer cells. Although we aimed to further validate our findings in an in vivo model, we were unable to proceed because of the failure of AGS PTXR cells to form tumors despite multiple attempts. Parental AGS cells have been reported to form subcutaneous xenograft tumors in immunodeficient mice. However, in our hands, AGS PTXR cells failed to establish tumors despite multiple inoculation attempts, suggesting reduced in vivo tumorigenicity associated with the acquired resistant phenotype. This limitation highlights the need to explore alternative in vivo models, such as patient-derived xenografts, to further evaluate the therapeutic potential of M. canadensis and salvianolic acid B. Given the complexities of drug resistance in the tumor microenvironment, future research should examine the effects of salvianolic acid B on immune cell populations and tumor–stroma interactions. Salvianolic acid B’s bioavailability should be investigated in future studies to increase its clinical applicability. Liposomal formulations and nanoparticle-based drug delivery systems may improve the stability and targeted delivery of salvianolic acid B, thereby increasing its therapeutic efficacy. Collectively, our findings delineate a hierarchical model in which mitochondrial ROS initiates PERK-biased ER stress signaling, activates ATF4, and induces NOXA-mediated intrinsic apoptosis. By restoring apoptotic susceptibility through oxidative and ER stress modulation, M. canadensis and salvianolic acid B represent promising candidates for overcoming PTX resistance in gastric cancer.

text: Copper is a double-edged sword: it is an essential micronutrient, yet deregulation of cellular copper status can lead to cell death and/or copper-dependent cell proliferation (cuproplasia). Indeed, cellular copper status may be exploited for therapeutic gain, and both copper ionophores and copper chelators have been suggested as potential anticancer agents. Recent work demonstrated that cancer cells that rely on mitochondrial metabolism rather than glycolysis undergo cell death in response to the copper ionophore elesclomol, and a genome-wide screening approach showed that the gene encoding the small iron sulfur (Fe–S) cluster protein, ferredoxin 1 (FDX1), could rescue this cell death. Mitochondrial ferredoxins were previously identified as relevant copper targets in yeast. Subsequent work confirmed the link between mitochondrial metabolism and copper-dependent death (cuproptosis) of cancer cells, and it was demonstrated that excess copper promotes the aggregation of lipoylated proteins belonging to the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle in mitochondria. Other investigators provided independent evidence that lipoylation is a target of elesclomol. Cuproptosis, as it is currently understood, i.e., a non-apoptotic cell death evoked by a copper ionophore that targets copper to mitochondria, leading to the aggregation of lipoylated proteins, has received considerable attention, as the prospect of selectively culling cancer cells holds great promise. However, the mechanism through which elesclomol triggers cell death is not completely resolved, and the morphological attributes of this novel cell death have not yet been defined. Moreover, it is conceivable that other copper-induced cell death modalities exist, and more work is therefore needed to delineate the spectrum of cuproptosis or cuproptosis-like forms of cell death. To this end, we embarked on a study of copper-induced cell death using elesclomol. The human fibrosarcoma cell line HT-1080, a workhorse of cell death research, was selected as a model along with its normal fibroblast counterpart (BJ). Our findings show that Es/Cu-induced cell death is calpain-dependent, and evidence is provided both for mitochondrial and extramitochondrial involvement in this paradigm.
title: Copper ionophore elicits calpain-dependent paraptosis coincident with proteotoxic stress

text: To address whether copper-loaded Es (hereafter: Es/Cu) triggers cell death under normal growth conditions, HT-1080 cells cultured in glucose-containing medium were exposed to Es/Cu. Dose-dependent cell death was observed using the LDH release assay. The BJ fibroblast cell line responded in a similar manner. Using alamarBlue™, a fluorometric indicator of cell metabolic activity, we found that the half maximal inhibitory concentration (IC 50) was lower for HT-1080, indicating that fibrosarcoma cells are more susceptible than fibroblasts. On the other hand, CuCl 2 alone failed to trigger cell death. Cytoplasmic vacuolization was observed in cells undergoing Es/Cu-induced cell death. We therefore subjected HT-1080 cells to transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to gain a better understanding of these morphological changes. Indeed, prominent cytoplasmic vacuolization was observed, reminiscent of paraptosis. We also noted the absence of chromatin condensation (a characteristic feature of apoptosis) while mitochondria appeared to congregate in a unipolar fashion in cells exposed to Es/Cu. Confocal microscopy of cells stained with antibodies against calreticulin showed that the vacuoles were derived from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). Furthermore, perinuclear clustering of mitochondria was demonstrated by using a mitochondria-specific fluorescent dye along with counterstaining of the cell nuclei. To evaluate mitochondrial ‘fitness’, we performed flow cytometry using two fluorescent dyes to distinguish mitochondrial respiration (as evidenced by mitochondrial transmembrane potential) (MitoTracker-Deep Red™) versus mitochondrial mass (MitoTracker-Green™). Evidence was obtained for a dose-dependent induction of dysfunctional mitochondria (Fig. A,B), and perinuclear clustering of mitochondria could also be confirmed. Thus, Es/Cu exposure evokes cell death with involvement of both mitochondria and the ER. In parallel experiments, the HT-1080 cell line was shown to be apoptosis competent as etoposide triggered caspase-dependent cell death (data not shown). HT-1080 cells were also found to undergo etoposide-induced apoptosis by other investigators. Hence, the results obtained for Es/Cu are not explained by a malfunctioning apoptosis machinery. Using a panel of calcium indicators, we could show that Es/Cu also evoked a significant elevation of intracellular calcium (Fig. A-C). Fluo-4 AM is a cell permeable high-affinity calcium indicator while its analog Fluo-5N AM is a low-affinity calcium indicator suitable for monitoring high calcium levels in, for example, the ER. The cationic Rhod-2 AM indicator, in turn, is used to monitor mitochondrial calcium levels. Es/Cu triggered the dissipation of the mitochondrial transmembrane potential along with mitochondrial superoxide production (Fig. D,E). These effects were reversed by the copper chelating agent, TTM (tetrathiomolybdate) and by the selective calpain inhibitor, PD150606. The role of calpain is explored in detail in the following sections.
title: Copper ionophore elicits calpain-dependent paraptosis coincident with proteotoxic stress
section_title: Elesclomol induces cell death with features of paraptosis

text: To understand whether Es/Cu triggers a known cell death mechanism, cells were preincubated with inhibitors of apoptosis (zVAD-fmk), ferroptosis (ferrostatin-1), necroptosis (necrostatin-1), and autophagy (wortmannin). However, all failed to rescue HT-1080 cells from Es/Cu-induced cell death. On the other hand, the copper chelating agent, TTM completely reversed cell death, proving that cell death was due to an overload of copper, and prevented the cytoplasmic vacuolization induced by Es/Cu (Fig. A,B). FDX1 was recently identified as a critical regulator of cuproptosis. To study the role of FDX1 in our model, we generated cells with specific silencing of FDX1 using shRNA. These were then exposed for 24 h, 48 h, or 72 h to Es/Cu. However, loss of FDX1 expression did not impact the metabolic capacity of the cells regardless of whether the cells were cultured in glucose- or galactose-containing medium (Figure S5A-F). We then asked whether STEAP3, an endosomal ferrireductase that also reduces copper, is involved in the regulation of Es/Cu-induced cell death. However, silencing of STEAP3 in HT-1080 cells also failed to block cell death (data not shown).
title: Copper ionophore elicits calpain-dependent paraptosis coincident with proteotoxic stress
section_title: Copper-loaded elesclomol elicits non-apoptotic cell death

text: Previous work provided evidence for calpain activation in HT-1080 cells exposed to ꝩ-radiation. Moreover, we demonstrated that non-apoptotic (caspase-independent) cell death of the promyelocytic HL-60 cell line is regulated by calpain. To test the idea that Es/Cu-induced cell death is calpain-dependent, HT-1080 cells were pre-incubated with the selective calpain inhibitor, PD150606. Es/Cu-induced cell death was abolished upon calpain inhibition, and cleavage of α-fodrin, a known calpain substrate, was also blocked (Fig. A,B). Furthermore, PD150606 rescued the BJ fibroblast cell line from cell death (Figure S6A,B). Cuproptosis depends on mitochondrial metabolism. To evaluate whether or not mitochondrial metabolism might impinge on Es/Cu-induced cell death in our model, cells were maintained in cell medium with glucose or galactose. HT-1080 cells cultured in glucose-containing medium succumbed to Es/Cu-induced cell death and were rescued by PD150606, and cytoplasmic vacuolization was also abolished in the presence of the calpain inhibitor (Fig. A,B). Cells maintained in cell medium with galactose to foster mitochondrial metabolism were more sensitive to Es/Cu, as could be expected, and cell death was suppressed, but not completely blocked, by the calpain inhibitor, PD150606. The calpain(s), non-lysosomal cysteine proteases, thus emerge as potential regulators of copper ionophore-induced cell death. Cytoplasmic vacuolization in paraptosis may be related to the distension of mitochondria as well as the ER. Moreover, mitochondria and ER are engaged in bidirectional communication through physical contact sites referred to as mitochondria-associated membranes or MAMs. Numerous regulatory proteins reside at the MAMs. To explore the role of MAMs, we screened several inhibitors of proteins present in MAMs. We found that DIDS (4,4'-diisothiocyano-2,2'-dihydrostilbenedisulfonic acid) rescued HT-1080 cells from Es/Cu-induced cell death, potentially upstream of calpain, as cleavage of α-fodrin was also blocked (Fig. C,D). DIDS is thought to prevent the oligomerization of VDAC1, although it cannot be considered a specific VDAC1 inhibitor given its interactions with various other transporters. Nevertheless, our findings suggest that VDAC1 may be involved in Es/Cu-induced paraptosis. In contrast, the inositol trisphosphate (IP 3) receptor antagonist 2-APB and the sarcoplasmic/endoplasmic reticulum calcium-ATPase (SERCA) inhibitor, thapsigargin did not affect Es/Cu-induced cell death. VDAC1 serves as a conduit for calcium but is also involved in cell metabolism by shuttling ATP and other metabolites.
title: Copper ionophore elicits calpain-dependent paraptosis coincident with proteotoxic stress
section_title: Elesclomol-induced cell death is mediated by calpain activation

text: N-acetylcysteine (NAC), a precursor of cysteine and, therefore, glutathione (GSH), is an antioxidant. However, GSH also functions as an intracellular copper chelator. In fact, a recent study demonstrated that the protective role of GSH against copper overload is based on the binding of Cu(I) ions rather than on the antioxidant properties of GSH. On the other hand, the authors found that NAC (at concentrations below 5 mM) failed to rescue the cells. Similarly, Tsvetkov et al. found that NAC (1 mM) failed to block cuproptosis. In contrast, other investigators suggested that it is the reduction in cellular copper uptake rather than the antioxidant effect of NAC that is responsible for the protection against copper ionophore-driven cell death. To shed light on the role of GSH (and NAC), we preincubated HT-1080 cells with NAC (10 mM) or GSH (5 mM) followed by exposure for 24 h to Es/Cu. Both NAC and GSH abolished Es/Cu-induced cell death, and cytoplasmic vacuolization was also prevented (Fig. A,B). Furthermore, we found that the cellular GSH/GSSG ratio was diminished upon exposure to Es/Cu, while GSH levels were significantly restored not only by NAC, but also by the copper chelating agent, TTM and by the calpain inhibitor, PD150606. Moreover, depletion of cellular GSH with buthionine sulfoximine (BSO), which inhibits the rate limiting step in GSH synthesis, did not affect cell viability per se, but we noted a dramatic enhancement of Cu/Es-induced cell death when compared to Es/Cu alone. Taken together, Es/Cu-induced cell death transpires with a depletion of GSH, and our findings show that GSH is required to protect cells from excess copper.
title: Copper ionophore elicits calpain-dependent paraptosis coincident with proteotoxic stress
section_title: Glutathione and NAC protect against copper-induced cell death

text: Copper has been shown to trigger protein aggregation, which may explain the toxicity of copper, but it has also been speculated that protein aggregates may trap excess Cu, thereby preventing further cellular damage. Indeed, copper is subject to tight control: it has been estimated that there is less than one free copper ion per cell, and copper ions appear to be coordinated to proteins or to ligands of low molecular mass such as GSH under normal conditions. To understand whether Es/Cu evoked proteotoxic stress in our model, we performed western blotting of polyubiquitinated proteins. We observed a dose-dependent accumulation of polyubiquitinated proteins in HT-1080 cells exposed to Es/Cu for 24 h. The accumulation of polyubiquitinated proteins which are normally destined for degradation by the proteasome suggested that the proteasome might be compromised. Indeed, we observed a significant loss in activity of the 20S proteasome upon exposure to Es/Cu, comparable to that of the known proteasome inhibitor, MG-132. Moreover, the calpain inhibitor, PD150606, restored proteasome activity. We previously provided evidence that copper-based nanoparticles, which undergo dissolution in lysosomes, trigger proteotoxic stress, and we obtained evidence of copper-induced protein aggregation using the PROTEOSTAT® aggresome detection reagent. Aggresomes are inclusion bodies of misfolded proteins that form when the ubiquitin–proteasome protein degradation machinery is overwhelmed. We decided to use the same assay to study whether Es/Cu-induced cell death features aggresomes. However, while aggresomes were readily observed in cells exposed to MG-132, no inclusion bodies were detected in Es/Cu-exposed cells. Initially, we found this puzzling, as protein aggregation is believed to play a major role in copper-induced toxicity. However, accumulation of misfolded proteins might occur in a different compartment not captured by the aggresome detection reagent. It is also conceivable that copper triggers protein precipitation through a mechanism independent of misfolding mechanisms, as suggested in a recent proteome-wide study of copper-induced protein precipitation.

section_title: Elesclomol compromises ubiquitin and proteasome homeostasis

text: To further unravel the cellular impact of Es/Cu, we performed proteomics profiling of HT-1080 cells exposed to Es/Cu (50 nM) for 24 h. The samples were analyzed by liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) using an established protocol. The volcano plot depicting the fold-change versus statistical significance of the differentially expressed proteins revealed a heat shock response characterized by the upregulation of a trio of heat shock proteins known as HSPA1B (43-fold upregulation), HSPA6 (53-fold upregulation), and ZFAND2A (63-fold upregulation) (Remarkably, the same three proteins were found to be induced (ZFAND2A) or increased (HSPA1B and HSPA6) by copper in a previous study using a colorectal adenocarcinoma cell line, suggesting that these proteins may be considered a ‘hallmark’ of cellular copper excess. Indeed, it is worth noting that copper-based nanoparticles also trigger a conserved heat shock response with upregulation of HSP70 family members [ – ]. Moreover, ZFAND2A (also known as AIRAP) (arsenite-inducible RNA-associated protein) was previously shown to protect cells from arsenite toxicity. AIRAP encodes a proteasome-interacting protein, and previous work suggested that it serves to adapt the protein degradation machinery of the cell to counteract the proteotoxicity induced by the environmental toxin, arsenite. We surmise that the strong induction of ZFAND2A by elesclomol may constitute a cytoprotective response, although further studies are required to formally prove this. Notwithstanding, ZFAND2A may be tentatively labeled as a ‘metal shock’ rather than heat shock protein. We also observed a significant upregulation of PMAIP1 (phorbol-12-myristate-13-acetate-induced protein 1) (also known as NOXA) (NOXA (derived from the Latin word for ‘harm’ or ‘damage’) is a modulator of proteosome inhibition-induced cancer cell death, and a previous study demonstrated that dimethoxycurcumin, a methylated curcumin analog, triggered paraptosis with proteasome inhibition and upregulation of NOXA. However, the upregulation of NOXA (eightfold) in our study was modest in comparison to the heat shock proteins. Canonical pathway analysis of the proteomics data was performed using the IPA software, and pathways related to protein ubiquitination and heat shock were significantly activated. Further analysis of the data using the STRING database for the identification of known and predicted protein–protein interactions showed that upregulated proteins (n = 149) were enriched for pathways associated with protein misfolding whereas downregulated proteins (n = 27) were enriched for the pathway associated with mitochondrial RNA metabolism. Overall, Es/Cu was shown to evoke proteotoxic stress accompanied by a heat shock response.

text: Copper ionophore-induced cell death has garnered considerable attention, yet our understanding of the mechanism underlying the demise of the cell is incomplete. Using the copper ionophore, elesclomol (Es), we show that copper-induced cell death is calpain-dependent with morphological attributes of paraptosis, a non-apoptotic, non-autophagic cell death first described 25 years ago by Bredesen and colleagues. Several natural and synthetic compounds including metal complexes have been found to induce paraptosis. Indeed, the structurally unrelated copper-binding agents disulfiram and pyrazole-pyridine copper complexes were found to evoke paraptosis with simultaneous inhibition of caspase-3, the main ‘executioner’ in apoptotic cell death. Paraptosis is characterized by extensive cytoplasmic vacuolization suggestive of alterations in cytoskeletal proteins, yet the cause of these drastic changes remains unknown, although oxidative stress and dysregulated calcium homeostasis have been implicated in this process. We propose that calpain activation with cleavage of key substrates may contribute towards the remodeling of the cytoskeleton during paraptosis as PD150606 was found to prevent vacuolization and cell death in Es/Cu-exposed cells. Hypothetically, the dilation of the ER could also be linked to molecular ‘crowding’ due to the accumulation of misfolded proteins. However, the two mechanisms (i.e., biochemical and biophysical) are not mutually exclusive. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that copper-induced paraptosis is characterized by the perinuclear clustering of mitochondria. Perinuclear clustering of mitochondria is a common response to cellular stress, and is controlled by the cytoskeleton. The current findings are summarized in schematic form in Figure S12, though it should be emphasized that some questions still remain. In particular, the mechanism whereby copper activates the calcium-dependent calpain(s) should be further scrutinized. Previous studies in yeast have shown that exposure to a surplus of copper is accompanied by an elevation in cytosolic calcium which was influenced not only by the concentration of copper but also by the overall oxidative status of the cell. We also found that Es/Cu provoked a significant elevation of intracellular calcium alongside mitochondrial dysfunction. However, the cell permeable calcium chelating agent, BAPTA-AM failed to block cell death (data not shown). On the other hand, we found that DIDS, a non-selective inhibitor of VDAC1, blocked fodrin cleavage (a surrogate marker of calpain activation in the present study) and rescued cells from Es/Cu-induced cell death. This suggests the potential for crosstalk between the ER and mitochondria via VDAC1, a conduit for ions (including calcium) and small metabolites. Further studies are required to pinpoint the role of VDAC1 in paraptosis. Es and its complex with Cu(II) were initially thought to trigger apoptosis with the induction of oxidative stress, though the signaling pathway was not well defined. More recently, Tsvetkov et al. found that Es promoted a unique form of copper-dependent cell death that is subject to regulation by the mitochondrial ferredoxin, FDX1. This cell death, referred to as cuproptosis, is characterized by the aggregation of lipoylated proteins. The question arises whether the Es/Cu-induced cell death reported herein is akin to cuproptosis. The answer is yes and no. First, while cuproptosis research remains in its infancy, it is clear that this cell death depends on mitochondrial metabolism.
title: Copper ionophore elicits calpain-dependent paraptosis coincident with proteotoxic stress

text: More recently, Tsvetkov et al. found that Es promoted a unique form of copper-dependent cell death that is subject to regulation by the mitochondrial ferredoxin, FDX1. This cell death, referred to as cuproptosis, is characterized by the aggregation of lipoylated proteins. The question arises whether the Es/Cu-induced cell death reported herein is akin to cuproptosis. The answer is yes and no. First, while cuproptosis research remains in its infancy, it is clear that this cell death depends on mitochondrial metabolism. Hence, glycolysis-dependent cancer cells are less sensitive to cuproptosis than their mitochondrial respiration-dependent counterparts. Indeed, when we replaced glucose with galactose to better mimic the conditions established by Tsvetkov et al., we found that cells became more susceptible to Es/Cu. Interestingly, cell death remained inhibitable but not preventable by PD150606. Moreover, FDX1 was recently identified as a mediator of cuproptosis directly regulating protein lipoylation through the binding of lipoyl synthase. However, in our model, silencing of FDX1 did not impair Es/Cu-induced cell death. It has been noted by other investigators that intracellular copper delivery continues in the absence of FDX1, suggesting an alternative mechanism of copper delivery by Es. We reasoned that STEAP3, an endosomal protein that serves not only as a ferrireductase but also as a cupric reductase, might play a role in the extramitochondrial reduction and release of copper. However, silencing of STEAP3 failed to block Es/Cu-induced cell death in our model. There are at least two possible solutions to this conundrum. First, another metalloreductase could be involved in the reduction of Cu(II) to Cu(I). Alternatively, the toxic entity is not Cu(I) but Cu(II), in which case reduction of Cu(II) may not be strictly required. However, TTM, which was found to block copper-induced cytoplasmic vacuolization and cell death in our model, is known to bind Cu(I) with high affinity. Nevertheless, while Cu(I) has been implicated in the cytotoxicity of copper by virtue of interfering with cellular redox homeostasis leading to ROS production, both Cu(I) and Cu(II) are capable of inducing protein misfolding (directly or indirectly). Indeed, the cell’s ability to mount a heat shock response to counter copper-induced proteotoxic stress may be the key factor determining the outcome of copper toxicity. In other words, proteotoxic stress rather than oxidative stress may be driving cell death. Moreover, we observed that Es/Cu-induced cell death was accompanied by a reduction of the ratio of reduced GSH to oxidized GSH (GSSG) while the depletion of cellular GSH using BSO further sensitized the HT-1080 cell line to Es/Cu. Indeed, it is well established that excess copper promotes GSH depletion, and the elevation of mitochondrial copper levels along with the depletion of mitochondrial GSH was recently shown to promote radiotherapy-induced cuproptosis. The protective effect of GSH has been attributed to the stabilization of copper in its cuprous form, compromising its ability to further free radical generating reactions. Overall, GSH depletion emerges as a hallmark of different copper-induced cell death modalities along with the canonical heat shock response (discussed above).
title: Copper ionophore elicits calpain-dependent paraptosis coincident with proteotoxic stress

text: Indeed, it is well established that excess copper promotes GSH depletion, and the elevation of mitochondrial copper levels along with the depletion of mitochondrial GSH was recently shown to promote radiotherapy-induced cuproptosis. The protective effect of GSH has been attributed to the stabilization of copper in its cuprous form, compromising its ability to further free radical generating reactions. Overall, GSH depletion emerges as a hallmark of different copper-induced cell death modalities along with the canonical heat shock response (discussed above). Finally, our results have demonstrated that Es/Cu-induced cell death is not confined to mitochondria, as we have demonstrated ER dilation, characteristic of paraptosis, along with perinuclear clustering of mitochondria, as well as proteasome inhibition and a heat shock response not restricted to the mitochondrial compartment, as evidenced by our proteomics analysis of HT-1080 cells. Thus, we can confirm that Es/Cu-induced cell death is non-apoptotic, as it cannot be rescued by the pan-caspase inhibitor, zVAD-fmk, and we show that excess copper (delivered by elesclomol) evokes paraptosis in cancer cells under glucose-proficient conditions, and evidence is furnished that this cell death is calpain-dependent. Further studies are warranted to clarify how excess intracellular copper activates calpain and to determine the calpain isoform(s) involved in paraptosis.

text: Proteome Discoverer 3.1 (Thermo Scientific) was utilized for the database search and quantification against the Uniprot Homo sapiens (Human) protein database (UP000005640). We employed a 1% false discovery rate (FDR) as a filter both at the protein and peptide level. Only proteins with at least two unique peptides were included in the quantitative analysis. Proteins with missing values were eliminated. The quantified abundance of each protein in each sample labeled with a different tandem mass tag (TMT) was normalized to the total intensity of all proteins in that sample. For each protein in each replicate, the normalized protein abundance was divided by the average abundance of that protein in the vehicle control replicates. The average ratio across replicates compared to the vehicle control was calculated, and the log 2 values of these ratios were determined. Student's t-test (two sided with assumption of unequal variance) was employed to calculate the p-value, assuming a non-zero ratio. Proteins with p < 0.05 and log 2 (fold-change) > 1 were considered differentially expressed proteins (DEPs), and visualized by plotting the log 2 ratio on the x-axis and the corresponding -log 10 p-value on the y-axis. DEPs were divided into upregulated and downregulated proteins, and protein–protein interaction (PPI) and functional enrichment analysis were performed using version 12.0 of the STRING database (https://www.string-db.org.) The Markov cluster (MCL) algorithm was applied for clustering of proteins in PPI networks, with the inflation parameter set to 4. text: Enterovirus encephalitis (EVE) is a prevalent childhood central nervous system (CNS) infection characterized by fever, nausea, vomiting, headaches, and cerebral impairment. Etiological evidence suggests that enteroviruses have recently become the predominant agents of viral meningitis in China, with Enterovirus A71 (EV71) being particularly notable for severe neurological impairment and systemic complications. As a neurotropic RNA virus, EV71 can be transmitted directly from infected individuals via fluids such as feces, saliva, sputum, and respiratory droplets to new hosts. Currently, there is no specific treatment plan for EV71-induced EVE. Children aged 5–7 years are particularly vulnerable due to their compromised immunity, posing significant health risks. Hence, understanding the mechanism underlying EV71-induced EVE could provide novel therapeutic strategies for affected patients. Previous studies suggest that EV71 infection upregulates endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress to facilitate viral replication. Viruses, obligate intracellular pathogens reliant on hosts for survival, harness the ER during vital processes like entry, protein synthesis and modification, genome replication, and assembly. Consequently, these viral activities disrupt ER homeostasis, leading to rapid accumulation of misfolded proteins (MP) and culminating in ER stress. Consequently, scientists have implemented strategies to mitigate ER stress, specifically using the ER stress inhibitor 4-phenylbutyric acid (4-PBA). Surprisingly, this same compound exhibits neuroprotective properties. We therefore postulate a therapeutic role for 4-PBA in EV71-affected individuals. Ferroptosis, an iron-driven phospholipid peroxidation pathway for programmed cell death, has been linked to various disease states. ER stress results in decreased protein synthesis, increased protein folding capacity, and enhanced degradation of MP. These unfolded protein response (UPR) adaptations can increase ROS through intensified oxidative protein folding (e.g., PDI/ERO1-driven disulfide bond formation) and disruption of ER Ca²⁺ homeostasis that enhances mitochondrial ROS production. In parallel, ROS- and UPR-associated signaling (e.g., PERK–ATF4/CHOP) can expand the labile iron pool by promoting ferritin turnover and iron uptake, resulting in intracellular iron accumulation that primes ferroptosis. Conversely, during ferroptosis, antioxidant function is compromised, further exacerbating ER stress and setting the stage for another round of ferroptosis. Studies indicate that neurotropic viruses such as Borna disease virus 1 (BoDV-1) and Herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV-1) cause fatal encephalitis via ferroptosis, while EV71 is reported to trigger neurodegeneration through the same mechanism. Notably, Zhou et al. imply that ferroptosis in neurotropic virus-induced disorders may need ongoing ER stress. Notably, the chemical chaperone 4-PBA alleviates misfolded-protein accumulation and dampens UPR signaling (e.g., GRP78–PERK/CHOP), and ER-stress relief has been linked to reduced ferroptosis by limiting ROS and preserving the GSH–GPX4 lipid-peroxide detoxification system. We therefore hypothesize that 4-PBA restrains EV71-triggered lipid peroxidation and iron-dependent neuronal death, thereby mitigating EV71-mediated neuroinflammation and immune-mediated injury in EVE.

text: Enterovirus-induced CNS infections instigate EVE, posing a severe health burden. EV71, an enterovirus notorious for its cell-lytic properties, often leads to immunopathology and neuronal death post-infection. Because ER stress has been implicated in facilitating EV71 replication and 4-PBA has been reported to reduce viral replication and inflammatory injury in viral encephalitis models, we investigated whether 4-PBA mitigates EV71 neuropathology by interrupting ER-stress–ferroptosis signaling. An important question is whether the mitigation of neuronal injury is driven primarily by reduced viral replication, immunomodulation, or both. In our study, 4-PBA reduced viral burden (VP1 mRNA; see Results) alongside decreased inflammatory infiltration and cytokines, consistent with combined antiviral and host-directed protective effects. Prior work also supports a dual role for 4-PBA in neurotropic viral infection: in a Japanese encephalitis virus model, 4-PBA reduced infectious viral titers and inflammatory cytokines and alleviated brain pathology. VP1, a primary immunogenic capsid protein of EV71, plays an essential role in viral infection. We initially identified EV71 infection by detecting VP1 expression in brain tissue. Subsequently, we evaluated the impact of 4-PBA on ER stress induced by EV71 in the EVE mouse brain tissues. Prior studies indicate that EV71 can stimulate its own replication through ER stress signaling, and Zheng et al. reported that EV71 upregulates GRP78 to promote virus replication. GRP78 is an ER chaperone whose expression increases under ER stress conditions, utilizing cellular degradation mechanisms to refold or degrade MP. CHOP serves as a key initiator of ER stress-related cell death. Our study corroborated previous findings indicating that EV71 induces elevated CHOP and GRP78 expression in mouse brain tissues, indicating activation of ER stress signaling. ER stress correlates with ferroptosis. GPX4, an antioxidant, degrades lipid hydroperoxides to lipid alcohols via GSH, mitigating ferroptosis. Moreover, hallmarks of ferroptosis include intracellular iron accumulation, elevated ROS and lipid peroxidation, and GSH depletion. Here, we measured the levels of ferroptosis markers in EV71-induced mouse brain tissue, confirming its proclivity to induce ferroptosis. This aligns with prior findings demonstrating that EV71 promotes neuronal ferroptosis and neurodegeneration. Interestingly, 4-PBA counteracted EV71-induced ferroptosis. This may be due to ER stress’s role in promoting ferroptosis, as reported by Ji et al., who demonstrated that ER stress induces neonatal hypoxic-ischemic brain damage (HIBD) through ferroptosis, suggesting that inhibiting ER stress could be an effective therapeutic approach for HIBD. We audited the therapeutic role of 4-PBA in mitigating immune injury and neural function recovery for EVE mice. Previous findings have indicated that EV71 elicits inflammatory cell infiltration, elevates proinflammatory factors, and markedly increases mortality in EV71-infected mice. By comparison, we observed similar inflammation-induced damage to the brain tissues of EV71 group mice, highlighted by elevated neuron apoptosis, poor prognoses, and other features which were successfully mitigated by 4-PBA. This may be attributed partly to 4-PBA’s neuroprotective effects as demonstrated in hypoxic-ischemic brain injuries, chronic ischemic hippocampal injuries and viral encephalitis, where it reduced excessive ER stress and neuronal damage, aiding in neural function restoration.

text: By comparison, we observed similar inflammation-induced damage to the brain tissues of EV71 group mice, highlighted by elevated neuron apoptosis, poor prognoses, and other features which were successfully mitigated by 4-PBA. This may be attributed partly to 4-PBA’s neuroprotective effects as demonstrated in hypoxic-ischemic brain injuries, chronic ischemic hippocampal injuries and viral encephalitis, where it reduced excessive ER stress and neuronal damage, aiding in neural function restoration. Ultimately, in vitro experiments confirmed the neuroprotective mechanism of 4-PBA against damage. The modulatory role of 4-PBA on ferroptosis has been well demonstrated in brain tissues and neurons. Zhen et al., for instance, reported that 4-PBA mitigated cerebral infarction symptoms by suppressing ferroptosis in models of oxygen-glucose deprivation reoxygenation (OGD/R) cells and middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) rats. Similarly, Guo’s study showed that 4-PBA inhibited PM2.5-induced ferroptosis in neuraloblastoma. Consistently, we found that Erastin reversed the regulatory effects of 4-PBA on EV71-infected TUNEL positivity, ferroptosis, and ER stress, suggesting that 4-PBA protects neurons from injury by partially inhibiting ferroptosis. Despite these findings, further study is needed. Although 4-PBA has been shown to regulate ferroptosis and neural injury in EVE mice, the specific genes impacted by 4-PBA remain unexplored. A key mechanistic question is whether 4-PBA mitigates ferroptosis directly (host-directed) or indirectly by reducing EV71 replication and thereby lowering downstream oxidative stress. Our erastin “add-back” experiment shows that pharmacologic activation of ferroptosis largely abrogates the protective effects of 4-PBA in EV71-infected HT22 cells, indicating that ferroptosis modulation is functionally important downstream of infection. However, because all in vitro groups were EV71-infected and we did not directly quantify EV71 replication in HT22 cells under 4-PBA, we cannot exclude that reduced viral replication contributes to the observed reduction in ferroptosis markers. Prior work has shown that 4-PBA can suppress replication/viral protein expression of neurotropic viruses in association with ER-stress inhibition, supporting the plausibility of combined antiviral and host-directed effects. This study has several limitations. Mechanistic inference for the ER-stress–ferroptosis axis is largely associative. We also did not directly disentangle whether 4-PBA’s benefit is driven predominantly by reduced viral replication versus host-directed immunomodulation; future work should compare viral growth kinetics under 4-PBA treatment and perform immune profiling to separate these contributions. Although erastin reversed protection, we did not employ ferroptosis-specific rescue (e.g., ferrostatin-1/liproxstatin-1 or iron chelation) or genetic modulation of ER-stress signaling (PERK/ATF4, IRE1/XBP1, ATF6) to establish necessity. In addition, although we quantified infectious EV71 titers in brain homogenates by TCID 50 at the terminal time point, future work should assess viral kinetics across multiple time points and map regional CNS viral loads to further define how ER-stress inhibition influences viral dissemination. The in vivo work used a single 4-PBA dose and regimen in neonatal ICR mice;

text: In addition, although we quantified infectious EV71 titers in brain homogenates by TCID 50 at the terminal time point, future work should assess viral kinetics across multiple time points and map regional CNS viral loads to further define how ER-stress inhibition influences viral dissemination. The in vivo work used a single 4-PBA dose and regimen in neonatal ICR mice; future studies should evaluate dose–response, alternative dosing schedules and timing (including therapeutic post-challenge administration), and validate findings in additional models (e.g., different ages/strains and/or additional EV71 strains). The in vitro data relied on one neuronal cell line, without dose–response, pharmacokinetics/brain exposure, primary neurons or glia, older animals, or long-term neurobehavioral outcomes. In addition, the in vitro design did not include standalone drug controls (4-PBA alone, erastin alone, 4-PBA+erastin) or an EV71 + erastin group, which would further strengthen attribution of the observed protection specifically to ferroptosis modulation. In addition, we did not quantify EV71 replication in HT22 cells under 4-PBA treatment (e.g., viral RNA/protein levels or infectious titers), which limits our ability to distinguish direct anti-ferroptotic effects from indirect effects secondary to reduced viral replication. Potential pleiotropic actions of 4-PBA and contributions of other cell-death programs were not systematically dissected. Small sample sizes and lack of sex-stratified analyses further limit generalizability and warrant confirmation in additional models.

text: Altered lipid metabolism is increasingly recognized not merely as a bystander but as a driving force in tumor progression, metastasis, and resistance to therapy. A hallmark of cancer cells is the accumulation of intracellular cholesterol and enrichment of cholesterol-rich lipid rafts, which distinguish them from their non-tumorigenic counterparts. This cholesterol remodeling is not incidental. It regulates membrane fluidity and integrity, orchestrates oncogenic signaling, and shapes interactions within the tumor microenvironment, all of which collectively enhance malignant growth and dissemination. High cholesterol levels have been implicated in promoting cancer cell proliferation and metastasis by activating lipid raft-associated signaling pathways, including PI3K/AKT and MAPK/ERK. Importantly, clinical and experimental evidence indicates that statin-mediated inhibition of cholesterol biosynthesis exerts anti-tumor effects. Cholesterol-metabolizing enzymes may represent key vulnerabilities, yet their roles in ovarian cancer are poorly understood, warranting further study for therapeutic development. Among these enzymes, NAD(P)-dependent steroid dehydrogenase-like (NSDHL) has emerged as a particularly intriguing candidate. NSDHL is a key component of cholesterol synthesis, catalyzing the NAD+-dependent oxidative decarboxylation of 4α-carboxysterols. NSDHL localizes to the ER membrane and lipid droplets, where it contributes to cholesterol production and lipid storage. Mutations in NSDHL cause congenital hemidysplasia with ichthyosiform erythroderma and limb defects (CHILD syndrome) [ – ]. Recent studies have identified NSDHL among six cholesterol biosynthesis enzymes markedly upregulated in aggressive cancers, including breast and lung, implicating it in tumor progression. Knockdown of NSDHL reduces intracellular cholesterol and inhibits proliferation in skin, pancreatic, and breast cancers, suggesting its broader role in tumor survival. However, the functional significance and mechanisms of NSDHL in ovarian cancer remain unclear. Ovarian cancer is the most lethal gynecological malignancy with poor prognosis, high recurrence, and limited therapeutic options. Although most patients initially respond to cytoreductive surgery plus platinum-based chemotherapy, resistance frequently develops, resulting in relapse and a five-year survival rate of ~ 30%. Ovarian cancer is highly heterogeneous, comprising multiple histological subtypes such as high-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC), clear cell, endometrioid, mucinous, and low-grade serous ovarian carcinomas. Among these, HGSOC is the most aggressive and associated with particularly poor outcomes. Elucidating the molecular mechanisms underlying ovarian cancer progression is thus essential to identify effective therapeutic targets. Cancer cells undergo extensive metabolic reprogramming to sustain proliferation under stress, altering lipid metabolism, glycolysis, oxidative phosphorylation, and glutaminolysis, and redox homeostasis. This reprogramming increases reactive oxygen species (ROS), mainly from mitochondria and the ER. Excessive ROS accumulation induces lipid peroxidation, primary targeting polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) because of their susceptibility to oxidative attack. The ratio of PUFAs to monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs) is central to oxidative stress sensitivity. ACSL3 and ACSL4, two long-chain acyl-CoA synthetases, differ in fatty acid specificity, thereby influencing MUFA-CoA versus PUFA-CoA incorporation into membranes.
title: NSDHL as a regulator of lipid peroxidation and ER stress–mediated apoptosis in ovarian cancer

text: This reprogramming increases reactive oxygen species (ROS), mainly from mitochondria and the ER. Excessive ROS accumulation induces lipid peroxidation, primary targeting polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) because of their susceptibility to oxidative attack. The ratio of PUFAs to monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs) is central to oxidative stress sensitivity. ACSL3 and ACSL4, two long-chain acyl-CoA synthetases, differ in fatty acid specificity, thereby influencing MUFA-CoA versus PUFA-CoA incorporation into membranes. PUFA-rich ER phospholipids are highly vulnerable to oxidative damage. To counter this, cancer cells adaptively remodel their membranes by enriching MUFAs over PUFAs, reducing susceptibility to lipid peroxidation-induced cell death (lipotoxicity). Disruption of lipid homeostasis impairs cholesterol transporters and signaling cascades, exacerbating oxidative stress and driving tumor progression. Under stressors such as lipid peroxidation, glucose deprivation, calcium dysregulation, of glycosylation inhibition, or free radical exposure, unfolded proteins accumulate in the ER, triggering ER stress. The unfolded protein response (UPR) is then activated to restore protein folding, primarily via ER chaperones such as GRP78 (BiP). While transient ER stress supports survival, prolonged stress induces apoptosis. ER stress-mediated apoptosis involves caspase-12 (CASP12) activation at the ER membrane, which cleaves and activates pro-caspase-9 (PRO-CASP9), ultimately activating caspase-3 (CASP3) and driving apoptosis independently of the mitochondrial pathway. In this study, we show that NSDHL expression is markedly elevated in aggressive ovarian cancer subtypes and correlates with poorer clinical outcomes. NSDHL knockdown in HGSOC cells disrupted lipid homeostasis, increased lipid peroxidation and altered MUFA - PUFA metabolism through dysregulation of ACSL3 and ACSL4. Lipid peroxidation further triggered ER stress-induced apoptosis. Importantly, NSDHL inhibition suppressed ovarian tumor growth in xenograft mouse models. Together, these findings identify NSDHL as a promising therapeutic target in ovarian cancer, particularly in subtypes with dysregulated lipid metabolism and heightened oxidative stress.

text: Our previous study showed that NSDHL expression was significantly elevated in ovarian cancer spheroids (3AO spheroids) compared with their parental 3AO cell line. To assess NSDHL expression in clinical specimens, we analyzed data from the Oncomine database, which revealed significant upregulation of NSDHL across 29 cancer types, including ovarian cancer (supplementary Fig. A). We next examined its clinical relevance using the Kaplan-Meier Plotter, which demonstrated that high NSDHL mRNA levels were significantly associated with shorter progression-free survival (PFS) in ovarian cancer patients (Fig. B, supplementary Fig. 1B). Analysis of the Welsh Ovarian Statistics dataset consistently confirmed higher NSDHL mRNA expression in ovarian cancer tissues compared with normal ovarian tissues (P < 0.001, Fig. C). Western blotting further validated increased protein expression in ovarian cancer tissues relative to normal ovarian epithelium. To explore the relationship between NSDHL expression and clinicopathological features, we performed immunohistochemistry (IHC) on tumor samples from 130 ovarian cancer patients. NSDHL staining was markedly stronger in high-stage tumors compared with low-stage cases. Stratified analysis revealed that high NSDHL expression was significantly correlated with poor PFS (P = 0.014) and overall survival (OS, P = 0.005) (Fig. F and G). High NSDHL expression was detected in 57.95% (51/88) of high-grade tumors versus 40.47% (17/42) of low-grade tumors (P = 0.047), and was also associated with elevated CA125 levels (P = 0.018). Although NSDHL expression appeared higher in advanced-stage (III/IV) compared to early-stage (I/II) ovarian cancer patients, this difference was not statistically significant (median IHC score: 54.5 vs. 45.2, p = 0.240) (These findings indicated elevated NSDHL expression to be associated with poor clinical outcomes in ovarian cancer. To further investigate the molecular basis of NSDHL function, we compared its expression in normal ovarian cells and multiple ovarian cancer cell lines (A2780, SK-OV-3 and OVCAR-5). NSDHL expression was markedly increased in HGSOC cell lines relative to normal ovarian cells, with SK-OV-3 and OVCAR-5 exhibiting the highest levels (Fig. H and I). These two cell lines were therefore selected for subsequent mechanistic studies.

section_title: NSDHL overexpression correlates with poor prognosis in ovarian cancer

text: To investigate the functional consequences of NSDHL knockdown in ovarian cancer cells, we employed small interfering RNAs (siRNA-1, siRNA-2) targeting NSDHL in SK-OV-3 and OVCAR-5 cells. Knockdown significantly reduced cell viability of both lines (Fig. A and B). Concomitantly, intracellular ROS levels were markedly increased in NSDHL-deficient cells. To test whether oxidative stress mediated this cytotoxicity, we treated NSDHL-knockdown cells (NSDHL-KD) with the lipid peroxidation inhibitor Ferrostatin-1 (Fer-1). Fer-1 treatment restored viability, indicating that lipid peroxidation contributed substantially to cell death following NSDHL knockdown. To examine the source of ROS accumulation, we assessed lipid peroxidation using a C11-BODIPY assay. NSDHL-KD cells exhibited significantly higher lipid peroxidation than controls (Fig. E and F). As lipid peroxidation is typically initiated by molecular oxygen and amplified by Fe²⁺, a hallmark of ferroptosis, we initially hypothesized that NSDHL knockdown might trigger ferroptosis. However, deferoxamine (DFO) failed to restore viability following erastin treatment in either siNC control cells or NSDHL-depleted cells. Thus, under our experimental conditions, erastin-induced cell death in SK-OV-3 and OVCAR-5 cells cannot be interpreted as canonical iron-dependent ferroptosis. In this context, erastin was used as a ferroptosis-related system Xc⁻ (the cystine/glutamate antiporter) inhibitor and a ferroptosis-related perturbation rather than as definitive evidence of canonical ferroptotic death. Intracellular iron quantification consistently revealed a significant reduction in both ferrous (Fe²⁺) and total iron levels in NSDHL-KD cells relative to controls, indicating that the enhanced lipid peroxidation observed after NSDHL depletion occurs in an iron-restricted state rather than through classical ferroptotic execution. To further determine whether iron availability regulates ferroptotic competence, we generated IREB2-overexpressing SK-OV-3 and OVCAR-5 cells to enhance iron uptake. IREB2 overexpression increased sensitivity to erastin, and this effect became reversible by DFO treatment (supplementary Fig.), indicating that elevated intracellular iron restores DFO-sensitive ferroptotic responsiveness in these ovarian cancer models. By contrast, under baseline conditions, NSDHL-KD cells remained refractory to DFO rescue despite marked oxidative stress. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that intracellular iron availability is a key determinant of ferroptotic competence, and that reduced iron levels in NSDHL-KD cells limit canonical ferroptosis, with cell death proceeding instead through iron-restricted lipid peroxidation.

section_title: NSDHL knockdown induces ROS accumulation and iron-independent lipid peroxidation

text: We performed quantitative proteomic profiling using high-resolution LC-MS/MS in SK-OV-3 and NSDHL-KD counterparts to investigate the molecular consequences of NSDHL depletion. In total, 7,797 proteins were identified, of which 1,882 were differentially expressed (Log₂ fold change ≥ 1.2, p < 0.05), including 739 upregulated and 1,143 downregulated proteins. Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) of the upregulated proteins revealed significant enrichment of mRNA surveillance, nonsense-mediated mRNA decay, and ubiquitin mediated proteolysis pathways. These findings suggest activation of proteostasis and mRNA quality control mechanisms, reflecting translational stress in NSDHL-KD cells. In contrast, KEGG pathway analysis of the downregulated proteins showed significant suppression of fatty acid metabolism, steroid biosynthesis, unsaturated fatty acid biosynthesis, PPAR signaling, and peroxisome pathways, all of which are closely linked to lipid metabolism and oxidative function. Consistent with these findings, intracellular cholesterol levels were significantly reduced in NSDHL-KD SK-OV-3 cells. Downregulation of FAO-related pathways, including fatty acid degradation and peroxisome activity, was accompanied by reduced downstream products, such as Acyl-CoA and NADH. GO molecular function enrichment analysis further higlighted alterations in NAD+/NADH-binding proteins and oxidoreductase activity. Given that NADH serves as a key electron donor in antioxidant defense, we measured intracellular levels and found that NADH was markedly reduced, whereas the NAD⁺/NADH ratio increased in both SK-OV-3-KD and OVCAR-5-KD cells, indicating disruption of redox balance. In agreement with these findings, the ferroptosis pathway was downregulated in NSDHL-KD cells, likely reflecting reduced intracellular iron levels. Reduced expression of the iron transporter TFRC (Supplementary Fig. A- B) provided additional evidence for the suppression of iron-dependent cell death pathways.
title: NSDHL as a regulator of lipid peroxidation and ER stress–mediated apoptosis in ovarian cancer
section_title: NSDHL knockdown impairs lipid metabolism and redox balance

text: To further define the role of NSDHL in fatty acid metabolism, we analyzed pathways related to peroxisome function, fatty acid degradation, and PPAR signaling (Fig. A and D). Proteomic results revealed significant upregulation of ACSL4 following NSDHL knockdown, indicating altered fatty acid utilization. Western blotting confirmed increased ACSL4 expression and decreased ACSL3 expression in NSDHL-KD cells. As ACSL3 promotes MUFA synthesis and ACSL4 incorporates PUFAs into phospholipids, the combined upregulation of ACSL4 and downregulation of ACSL3 suggests a shift from MUFA toward PUFA incorporation. This imbalance is predicted to heighten susceptibility to oxidative stress, thereby increasing membrane lipid peroxidation and promoting cell death. Since ACSL enzymes are regulated by the PPAR signaling pathway, particularly through PPARγ, and PPARγ activation upregulates ACSL3, while downregulating ACSL4 [ – ], we then examined PPARγ nuclear localization. NSDHL knockdown significantly reduced the nuclear translocation of PPARγ in both ovarian cancer cell lines (Fig. F and G). These data indicate that NSDHL sustains fatty acid metabolism and lipid peroxidation homeostasis via the PPARγ signaling axis in ovarian cancer cells.
title: NSDHL as a regulator of lipid peroxidation and ER stress–mediated apoptosis in ovarian cancer
section_title: NSDHL knockdown modulates fatty acid metabolism and lipid peroxidation through PPARγ signaling

text: Impaired PPARγ signaling suggested that the lipid peroxidation and metabolic dysregulation observed after NSDHL knockdown could disrupt intracellular organelles, particularly the ER. Given that the ER membrane is highly vulnerable to oxidative damage, lipid peroxidation represents a likely trigger of ER dysfunction. Proteomic analysis revealed significant upregulation of proteins involved in ER protein processing and ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis (Fig. C and E), both hallmarks of ER stress. We therefore hypothesized that NSDHL depletion initiates ER dysfunction and triggers ER stress-mediated cell death in ovarian cancer cells. To determine the cell death pathway activated by NSDHL knockdown, we treated SK-OV-3 and OVCAR-5 cells with inhibitors of apoptosis (z-VAD), necroptosis (Nec-1), and pyroptosis (Ac-YVAD). Only the apoptosis inhibitor z-VAD restored viability in NSDHL-KD cells (Fig. A and B), indicating apoptosis to be the predominant cell death pathway. Flow cytometry-based AnnexinV assays confirmed an increase in apoptotic populations following NSDHL knockdown, from 2.69% to 4.41% in SK-OV-3 cells and from 2.26% to 6.38% OVCAR-5 cells (Fig. C and D). Similarly, TUNEL staining showed increased apoptosis in NSDHL-KD cells, while control cells exhibited minimal signals (supplemental information). Treatment with the ER stress inhibitor 4-phenylbutyric acid (4-PBA) partially but significantly restored cell viability in NSDHL-silenced cells, supporting the involvement of ER stress in NSDHL knockdown–induced apoptosis. Although the magnitude of rescue varied across independent experiments, the effect was consistently incomplete, suggesting that ER stress contributes to, but does not fully account for, the cytotoxic effects of NSDHL depletion. Consistently, Western blot analysis showed increased expression of the ER chaperone BiP, along with increased levels of CASP12 and CASP9, in NSDHL-silenced cells (Fig. F, Together, these findings support the conclusion that NSDHL knockdown promotes apoptosis in ovarian cancer cells that NSDHL knockdown promotes apoptosis in ovarian cancer cells, at least in part, through lipid peroxidation- induced ER stress pathways.
title: NSDHL as a regulator of lipid peroxidation and ER stress–mediated apoptosis in ovarian cancer
section_title: NSDHL knockdown induces ER stress–mediated apoptosis through lipid peroxidation

text: To assess the in vivo impact of NSDHL depletion, we established a xenograft mouse model by subcutaneously injecting SK-OV-3 cells stably expressing NSDHL-targeting shRNA or scramble control into immunodeficient mice. Tumor growth was monitored for 6 weeks, during which NSDHL-knockdown markedly suppressed tumor progression. Compared with controls, NSDHL-deficient tumors displayed smaller volumes, slower tumor growth kinetics, and significantly lower tumor weights at the endpoint. TUNEL staining revealed increased apoptotic signals in tumors derived from NSDHL-deficient cells, confirming that NSDHL knockdown promotes apoptosis in vivo. We next examined whether apoptosis in vivo was associated with ER stress. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated robust upregulation of canonical ER stress markers, including BiP, ATF4, and CHOP, in NSDHL-knockdown tumors compared with controls (Fig. E and G), consistent with sustained ER stress activation. Taken together, the coordinated induction of BiP, ATF4, and CHOP in xenografts, along with our in vitro findings of CASP12 and CASP9 activation, provides strong evidence that NSDHL knockdown suppresses ovarian tumor growth by triggering ER stress–mediated apoptosis. These findings confirmed the critical role of the ER stress axis in mediating the tumor-suppressive effects of NSDHL depletion in vivo.
title: NSDHL as a regulator of lipid peroxidation and ER stress–mediated apoptosis in ovarian cancer
section_title: NSDHL depletion limits ovarian tumor growth via apoptosis

text: Understanding the metabolic adaptations of cancer cells is crucial for identifying potential therapeutic targets. Among these adaptations, dysregulated lipid metabolism is a well-established hallmark of cancer progression. Aberrant cholesterol biosynthesis and fatty acid metabolism have been implicated in tumor growth and therapy resistance, thus marking enzymes such as NSDHL as critical determinants for cancer cell survival. NSDHL has been implicated primarily in breast cancer, where it promotes proliferation, migration, metastasis, and stem-like properties, at least in part through regulation of TGF-β signaling. In pancreatic cancer, disruption of NSDHL-dependent cholesterol biosynthesis has been associated with epithelial–mesenchymal transition and basal-like reprogramming through activation of TGF-β signaling. In contrast, our data support a distinct mechanism in ovarian cancer, in which NSDHL depletion induces lipid peroxidation despite iron depletion, thereby triggering ER stress-associated apoptosis rather than canonical ferroptotic cell death. Collectively, our findings indicate that NSDHL promotes ovarian cancer cell survival and tumor growth by maintaining cellular redox homeostasis. Loss of NSDHL enhances lipid peroxidation, disrupts ER function, and ultimately induces apoptosis. Previous studies have shown that ACSL enzymes play crucial roles in fatty acid metabolism, with ACSL3 promoting MUFA synthesis and ACSL4 facilitating PUFAs incorporation into membrane phospholipids. This balance between MUFA and PUFA seems critical for determining susceptibility to oxidative stress, where PPARγ signaling regulates these enzymes, upregulating ACSL3 while suppressing ACSL4 [ – ], thereby maintaining lipid metabolic homeostasis. In the present study, NSDHL knockdown induced marked lipid peroxidation accompanied by dysregulation of these key enzymes, characterized by ACSL4 upregulation and ACSL3 downregulation. These changes may shift the MUFA/PUFA balance toward PUFA enrichment, thereby increasing the susceptibility of NSDHL-KD cells to oxidative stress. Downregulation of PPARγ may further contribute to decreased ACSL3 and increased ACSL4 expression, reinforcing lipid peroxidation and promoting apoptosis. Together, these findings suggest an important interplay between PPARγ signaling and lipid metabolism in maintaining cellular homeostasis. Notably, C11-BODIPY staining measures the extent of lipid peroxidation but does not directly define phospholipid composition. Therefore, it cannot distinguish between PUFA- and MUFA-containing lipid species. In this study, the proposed altered PUFA/MUFA balance is inferred from proteomic and pathway-level changes, including ACSL4 upregulation, ACSL3 downregulation, and suppression of unsaturated fatty acid biosynthesis and PPAR signaling, rather than as direct lipidomic evidence. Thus, the proposed shift in membrane lipid composition should be validated in future studies by direct lipidomic profiling, particularly by quantifying specific phospholipid species such as the PE-PUFA/PE-MUFA ratio. Despite elevated ROS and lipid peroxidation, NSDHL knockdown did not trigger ferroptosis. Instead, ferroptosis-related pathways were suppressed, as shown by downregulation of TFRC and reduced intracellular ferrous iron. Rather than ferroptosis, ER stress–mediated apoptosis emerged as the dominant cell death pathway. Interestingly, Wang et al. (2025) reported that ferroptotic signaling in adipocytes reduces lipid accumulation and promotes thermogenesis by enhancing lipid peroxidation and suppressing HIF1α.
title: NSDHL as a regulator of lipid peroxidation and ER stress–mediated apoptosis in ovarian cancer

text: Despite elevated ROS and lipid peroxidation, NSDHL knockdown did not trigger ferroptosis. Instead, ferroptosis-related pathways were suppressed, as shown by downregulation of TFRC and reduced intracellular ferrous iron. Rather than ferroptosis, ER stress–mediated apoptosis emerged as the dominant cell death pathway. Interestingly, Wang et al. (2025) reported that ferroptotic signaling in adipocytes reduces lipid accumulation and promotes thermogenesis by enhancing lipid peroxidation and suppressing HIF1α. By contrast, our findings reveal that NSDHL knockdown suppresses both lipid metabolism and ferroptotic signaling. This suggests a bidirectional regulatory relationship between lipid metabolism and ferroptosis. On the one hand, an altered MUFA/PUFA balance may reduce ferroptotic sensitivity, while on the other, impaired ferroptotic signaling may exacerbate lipid metabolic dysfunction. Together, these processes create a feedback loop that protects cells from ferroptosis, but renders them vulnerable to ER stress-mediated apoptosis. Thus, NSDHL links lipid regulation, iron metabolism, and redox control in ovarian cancer cells. UPR activation has been implicated in diverse cancer processes, including cell cycle regulation, oxidative stress, autophagy, cell death, and chemotherapy resistance, particularly in ovarian cancer. While mild ER stress allows cancer cells to adapt and survive, promoting tumor growth and resistance, persistent or severe ER stress shifts signaling toward cell death. Indeed, ER stress-related genes, such as GRP78, ATF4, and PERK, are highly expressed in epithelial ovarian cancer, suggesting chronic basal ER stress. In our study, upregulation of BiP and activation of CASP12, CASP9, and CASP 3, confirmed that apoptosis was driven by ER stress following NSDHL knockdown. BiP serves as a master regulator of the UPR by binding ER transmembrane sensors (PERK, IRE1, and ATF6) under normal conditions. When stress is prolonged, CHOP promotes a switch from adaptive to pro-apoptotic signaling, facilitating CASP12 activation. CASP12 then activates CASP9 and CASP3 independently of cytochrome c, distinguishing ER stress–mediated apoptosis from mitochondrial pathways. Collectively, these results indicate that NSDHL depletion forces ovarian cancer cells to cross the threshold from adaptive ER stress into pro-apoptotic signaling, thereby undermining their ability to withstand metabolic and oxidative stress. In conclusion, our study identifies NSDHL as a key regulator of ovarian cancer cell survival and tumor growth through mechanisms involving lipid peroxidation, ER stress, and apoptosis. Targeting NSDHL may offer a dual therapeutic advantage: disrupting lipid homeostasis while redirecting oxidative stress away from ferroptosis toward ER stress-mediated apoptosis. Moreover, the broader role of NSDHL in lipid metabolism and its interplay with PPARγ signaling warrant further investigation to fully elucidate its contributions to ovarian cancer progression. This mechanistic insight highlights the ER stress axis as a critical vulnerability in ovarian cancer and and supports the development of NSDHL-targeted strategies to promote apoptosis and improve therapeutic outcomes.

text: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is one of the major malignancies worldwide and is the second-leading cause of cancer-related death globally (Chan and Ng; Zucman-Rossi et al. Many materials have been used to treat HCC, such as doxorubicin, cisplatin, 5-fluorouracil, doxorubicin, interferon, sorafenib and a number of other agents Bruix et al. However, because of low drug response rates, the clinical use is limited Kudo et al. Thus, it is critically needed to explore safe and efficient drugs for the therapy of HCC. The diversity of bioactive molecules in microbial metabolites provides a rich source of natural products for the exploration of new drugs. Bacillus subtilis is a nonpathogenic bacterium widely distributed in environment. Due to its abundant bioactive metabolites, B. subtilis is widely used in food preservation, agriculture, animal husbandry, medicine and so on(Guo et al. Jiang et al. Lee et al. Zohora et al. Lipopeptides from B. subtilis have been proved to have antifungal, antiviral, antitumor and other biological activities. Due to the composition of hydrophobic fatty acids and hydrophilic peptides, lipopeptides have the ability to decrease surface and interfacial tension of biofilms. This may be the source of lipopeptide bioactivity Zhao et al. Iturin A is one of the lipopeptides produced by B. subtilis. It has been previously found to have significant antifungal activities and was proved to inhibit fungal contamination in fruits and during wine processing(Jiang et al.), thus showing potential in preventing fungal contamination in food protection and food processing (Meena and Kanwar). Besides, animal experiments in mice showed that oral administration of iturin was safe and beneficial to the health of mice. The results showed that the content of cholesterol in blood was decreased and the abundance of probiotics in intestinal flora was increased Zhao et al. Among the multiple bio-activities of iturin A, anticancer capability is also very attractive, which has been proved in cancer cell lines, including MDA-MB-231, MCF-7 and Caco2. With regard to the anticancer mechanism, iturin A can induce apoptosis in cancer cells by triggering both reactive oxygen species (ROS) burst and DNA damage. It can also induce autophagy and paraptosis, resulting in metabolic disorder and programmed cell death (Dey et al. Zhao et al. Although there have been several researches on anticancer activity of iturin A, the effect of iturin A on HCC hasn’t been proved in vivo. In this research, the potential of iturin A to inhibit the HCC cell line HepG2 was tested both in vitro and in vivo. The underlying mechanisms and toxicity were also analyzed.

text: The iturin A was prepared from a culture of Bacillus subtilis CCTCCM207209(Accession number of 16S rRNA Gene sequence in GeneBank: MT373810) Yan et al., a strain previously isolated from soil and stored at the China Center for Type Culture Collection (Wuhan, China) according to a previously published methodZhao et al. The lipopeptides were isolated from the supernatant of the culture broth with B. subtilis filtered out. Purification of iturin A-like lipopeptides was conducted using methanol extraction and HPLC isolation as well as purification in a Shimadzu LC-20A high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) (Shimadzu, Japan) system quipped with a C18 column and detection was made by determining absorbance at 280 nm and 215 nm.
