On the other hand, viruses highjack a variety of cellular processes including the initiation and execution of PCD starting early after infection. For example, herpesviruses and poxviruses, which utilize over one-third of their genome to counteract the host antiviral response. In this section, we summarize the various strategies viruses deploy to inhibit apoptosis, necroptosis, and pyroptosis (Tables and).
title: Viral-mediated activation and inhibition of programmed cell death
section_title: Inhibition of programmed cell death by viruses

text: Viral BCL-2 (vBCL-2) homologs are among the best studied viral inhibitors of apoptosis. vBCL-2 homologs, widely distributed throughout Poxviridae, Herpesviridae, Asfarviridae, and Iridovirdae, unilaterally possess a hydrophobic BH3 binding domain capable of apoptosis inhibition. Broadly, vBCL-2 homologs either directly inhibit BAX and BAD oligomerization, preventing mitochondrial pore formation and cytochrome c release, or sequester proapoptotic BCL-2 proteins, diminishing proapoptosis signals. Although functionally analogous, vBCL-2 homologs interact with diverse and distinct proapoptotic BCL-2 proteins. Within Poxviridae, VACV encodes F1L, which adopts a unique domain swapped BCL-2 topology forming ligand-specific interactions with either BAX or BAK to directly inhibit oligomerization and mitochondrial pore formation, or with BIM, sequestering the proapoptotic signal. Viruses can also block apoptosis by inhibiting a variety of caspases. Expressed during cowpox virus (CPXV) infection, CrmA was the first serpin-like protein found to potently inhibit caspase-8, caspase-1, and caspase-10. Homologs of CrmA in Orthopoxvirus and C horodopoxvirus display a broad spectrum of caspase inhibition through a pseudo-substrate mechanism. Furthermore, viruses can also specifically inhibit caspase-8. Viral inhibitors of caspase-8 (vICA) are distributed throughout Herpesviridae. ICP6 of HSV1 (ICP10 in HSV2), UL36 in human, and M36 in MCMV directly interact with the death effector domains (DEDs) on procaspase-8 inhibiting FADD association and procaspase-8 cleavage, protecting against extrinsic apoptosis [ – ]. Additionally, members of KSHV encode cellular FLIP analogs, termed viral FLIPs (vFLIPs). vFLIPs resemble the short isoform of cellular FLIPs and again completely block caspase-8 proteolytic activity. Moreover, large DNA viruses infecting arthropods encode viral inhibitors of apoptosis proteins (vIAPs) containing a baculoviruses IAP repeat (BIR) motifs that binds and inhibit apoptosis mediators Hid, Reaper, or Grim. Moreover, really interesting new gene (RING) domains on vIAPs facilitate the ubiquitination and degradation of these proapoptotic proteins, reinforcing their antiapoptotic effects. Outside of the largely conserved mechanisms, virus family-specific mechanisms are extremely diverse. Poxviruses encode TNFR homologs (vTNFRs) capable of binding and depleting proapoptotic TNF along with other immune-modulatory cytokines [ – ]. Additionally, VACV encodes the E3 protein to prevent PKR activation by binding dsRNA. Viral Golgi antiapoptotic protein (vGAAP) of camelpox virus and some strains of VACV have also been shown to inhibit intrinsic apoptosis through a Ca 2+ -dependent mechanism. Varster zooster virus (VZV) of Herpesviridae encodes IE63 capable of inhibiting apoptosis through inhibition of eIF-2α. Finally, α-herpesviruses encode US3, adept at phosphorylating BAD and caspase-3, preventing activation. Overall, large DNA viruses precisely target apoptosis through distinct and comprehensive mechanisms.
title: Viral-mediated activation and inhibition of programmed cell death

text: Viruses inhibit necroptosis mostly at the level of RIPK1/3 and MLKL. In herpesviruses and poxviruses, inhibiting the kinases RIPK1/3 is a very common process. Both viruses encode various inhibitors of RHIM-dependent functions of RIPK1/3. Multiple herpesviruses encode RHIM-containing proteins that inhibit the formation of amyloid-like filamentous necroptotic signaling complexes; effectively inhibiting the RIPK1-RIPK3 signaling axis and MLKL activation [, – ]. The first identified RHIM-dependent inhibitor was the viral ribonuclease reductases subunit (R1) homolog, M45 of murine cytomegalovirus (MCMV). M45 forms homo amyloid-like filamentous structures that bind RHIM domains of RIPK1, RIPK3, and ZBP1/DAI, effectively sequestering RHIM containing necroptotic machinery, inhibiting MLKL activation and cell lysis. Additionally, viral UL39 R1 homologs of HSV1 and HSV2, termed ICP6 and ICP10, respectively, form similar RHIM-dependent amyloid-like fibrils to make the kinases dysfunctional. However, underlying mechanisms of dysfunctional amyloid fibril formation differ between HSV and MCMV. Furthermore, the RHIM-dependent inhibitor analog of Varicella zoster virus (VZV) ORF20 imposes similar amyloid-like fibrils. Viruses also often facilitate the degradation of RIPK1 and RIPK3. Multiple human herpesviruses, such as herpes simplex virus (HSV), EBV, and KSHV, encode homologs of MCMV M45 protein. These viral inhibitors contain induced protein aggregation motifs (IPAMs) that facilitate insoluble protein aggregation of RIPK1, directing its degradation. IPAM sequences are widely homologous in over 70 herpesviruses, baculoviruses, and giant viruses; however, functional conservation of this mechanism is unconfirmed. EBV also employs LMP1 to manipulate ubiquitination of RIPK1 and RIPK3. LMP1 directly associates with the activation domain of RIPK1 promoting ubiquitination through the E3 ligase TRAF2, restricting RIPK1 to the plasma membrane where it maintains prosurvival signaling. Concurrently, LMP1 facilitates deubiquitylation of RIPK3, preventing necrosome formation. Finally, LMP1 exerts epigenetic control of RIPK3 through 2 axes: LMP1 up-regulates DNMT1 to directly methylate the transcription start site (TSS) of RIPK3 and also down-regulates ten-eleven translocation methylcytosine dioxygenase (TETs) to further methylate promoters of RIPK3. Poxviruses also target RIPK3 through viral inducers of RIPK3 degradation (vIRD). vIRD analogs are found in CPXV, variola virus (VARV), monkeypox virus (MPXV), and Ectromelia virus (ECTV) and directly bind to RIPK3 through their Ankyrin repeats, while their F-box domains link to host SKP1-Cullin1-F-box machinery. This interaction stimulates ubiquitination of RIPK3 and subsequent proteasomal degradation. Interestingly, VACV, an attenuated virus used to eradicate VARV, lacks a functional vIRD homolog potentially shedding light on its benign and immunogenic nature. Multiple Poxviridae inhibit necroptosis by inhibiting MLKL. C hordopoxvirinae encode E3, a viral protein possessing a z-RNA binding domain. Z-RNA, produced during viral replication, binds to the N-terminal Zα domain of E3, effectively sequestering the viral PAMP inhibiting ZBP1/DAI-dependent necroptosis. Suipoxvirus, Carpirpoxvirus, Avipoxvirus, and Lepropoxvirus families also express viral MLKL (vMLKL) analogs. vMLKLs retain high homology of the pseudokinase domain, allowing dominant sequestration of RIPK3 from RIPK1; however, lack the 4 helical bundle domains essential for membrane insertion and cell lysis.
title: Viral-mediated activation and inhibition of programmed cell death

text: C hordopoxvirinae encode E3, a viral protein possessing a z-RNA binding domain. Z-RNA, produced during viral replication, binds to the N-terminal Zα domain of E3, effectively sequestering the viral PAMP inhibiting ZBP1/DAI-dependent necroptosis. Suipoxvirus, Carpirpoxvirus, Avipoxvirus, and Lepropoxvirus families also express viral MLKL (vMLKL) analogs. vMLKLs retain high homology of the pseudokinase domain, allowing dominant sequestration of RIPK3 from RIPK1; however, lack the 4 helical bundle domains essential for membrane insertion and cell lysis. Human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) also ubiquinates MLKL through the viral protein UL36, causing necroptotic inhibition in human but not murine cell lines. In summary, the large diversity and redundancies in viral inhibition of necroptosis support the emerging theory that necroptosis and viruses have coevolved specific virus–host mechanisms to antagonize the other, further highlighting importance of necroptosis in antiviral immunity and viral replication.
title: Viral-mediated activation and inhibition of programmed cell death

text: Overall, the mechanisms by which viruses inhibit pyroptosis remain largely unknown. However, plus sense RNA viruses, such as Coronaviridae, utilize viral proteases to inhibit pyroptosis [ – ]. Highly conserved viral proteases, such as NSP5 in coronaviruses, directly bind and cleave Gasdermin D in porcine and human cells, producing a truncated N-terminal Gasdermin D, lacking essential residues from caspase-1 cleavage. Interestingly, a singular large dsDNA virus, African swine fever virus, has shown a similar mechanism through the viral protease S273R. Additionally, within the Coronaviridae family, SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid protein (NP) blocks caspase-1-dependent cleavage of Gasdermin D through unidentified mechanism. Upstream of terminal events, multiple viruses have been implicated in inhibiting PRR interactions, inflammasome formation, and ILb release, these events are summarized in; however, inhibition of pyroptosis has not been directly confirmed [ – ].
title: Viral-mediated activation and inhibition of programmed cell death

text: The complexity of viral sensing pathways, diversity of animal viruses, and the ability of viruses to modulate PCD using their accessory proteins has been challenging to build a universal framework to dissect how viral ligand sensing interacts with the PCD machinery. Most studies we reviewed use live virus infections to study PCD. Hence, it is largely unknown how viral genome sensing in the context of inactivated and replication-defective virus stimulation regulates the PCD machinery. Many viral nucleic acid–like ligands including synthetic dsRNA:Poly I:C and cGAMP can activate cell death, suggesting the likelihood that viral genomes may also directly activate PCD, although similar studies are limited. In relation to this, it remains unknown if viral RNA and DNA genomes engage distinct PCD pathways. An outcome of nucleic acid sensing is establishment of antiviral state via expression of various ISGs that exert direct antiviral effects in many ways. Although some ISGs have been extensively studied, the modes of action of a large majority of ISGs are still unknown. There are more than 15 putative ISGs with proapoptotic functions, although their direct effect on PCD regulation is not known [ – ]. Furthermore, a large-scale proteomics study identified more than 200 novel PCD-associated proteins directly interact with some of the 104 inducibly expressed ISGs. In support of this, IFN-induced transmembrane proteins 3 (IFITM3) directly regulates PCD induction in Zika virus–infected cells and overexpression of ISG54 and ISG12b2, independent of IFN stimulation, activate apoptosis. The broader relevance of ISG modulating PCDs in the context of viral infection remains to be investigated. Much is unknown how PCD influences viral pathogenesis. On one side, activation of PCD in an infected cell can curb virus replication, while some necrotic forms of PCD can assist spreading of virus to the surrounding tissue. In addition, certain PCDs can facilitate the identification of viruses by the adaptive immunity via emission of immunomodulatory secretomes that enhance antigen presentation. To the infected host, activation of certain inflammatory PCDs may exacerbate disease pathogenesis, as these forms of PCD may enhance acute cytokine storms and/or potentially trigger delayed immunopathologies such as autoimmune disorders. Studies investigating how viral induced PCDs may instigate host reactivity against self are currently lacking.
title: Viral-mediated activation and inhibition of programmed cell death

text: Cancer, as a major global public health concern, poses a severe threat to people’s well-being. In 2018, the World Health Organization reported that cancer ranked the second leading cause of death globally, resulting in approximately 9.6 million annual fatalities. Cell death is a fundamental process crucial for human health, playing a pivotal role in regulating cell division, facilitating organ development, and upholding tissue homeostasis. Nevertheless, the disruption and avoidance of cell death mechanisms facilitate malignant cell transformation and advance tumorigenesis. From a therapeutic perspective, conventional cancer treatments, such as chemotherapy and radiation, achieve their anticancer effects by inducing cell death. Over the span of several decades, there has been a growing comprehension of the diverse mechanisms governing cell death. This process can be classified into two primary categories: programmed cell death (PCD), which is genetically controlled, and unprogrammed cell death, which represents a passive response to both biotic and abiotic stress. Among the various forms of PCD, apoptosis has emerged as one of the earliest and most extensively explored pathways. For a significant duration, the development of anticancer drugs targeting apoptosis has been a focal point of research. Numerous drugs, such as cisplatin, oxaliplatin, and pirarubicin, have showcased their ability to elicit anticancer effects through this mechanism. However, recent studies have increasingly validated that cancer cells possess the capability to elude apoptosis through a range of mechanisms, including the overexpression of apoptosis-inhibiting proteins, the inhibition of apoptosis-inducing factors, and the activation of survival signaling pathways. This evasion of apoptosis directly contributes to chemoresistance, a phenomenon intricately associated with alterations in various aspects of cancer, encompassing angiogenesis, the tumor microenvironment, and oxidative stress [ - ]. Ultimately, this leads to the failure of cancer treatment. To improve the efficacy of cancer treatment, the exploration of non-apoptotic cell death mechanisms has gradually emerged as a prominent priority. Over the last two decades, researchers have sequentially unveiled and extensively investigated novel different cell death mechanisms, including ferroptosis, necroptosis, pyroptosis, and paraptosis. These unique mechanisms, each with its distinct regulators and pathways, hold the potential to be activated within apoptosis-resistant cancer cells, offering novel strategies for the treatment of cancer and overcoming cancer drug resistance. Throughout history, natural compounds derived from plants, animals, microorganisms, and minerals have consistently served as a valuable source for drug discovery. Unlike synthetic compounds, these substances are not artificially created and can be categorized into various forms, such as alkaloids, flavonoids, and terpenes, due to their diverse chemical structures. Many of these natural compounds exhibit significant potential in the realm of cancer treatment. In fact, certain natural compounds, such as paclitaxel (PTX), camptothecin, and vincristine, have already gained widespread acceptance as chemotherapeutic drugs in clinical practice. Moreover, an interesting aspect is that numerous natural compounds have been found to induce various non-apoptotic cell death pathways when administered to resistant cancer cells that evade apoptosis.
title: Recent advances in natural compounds inducing non-apoptotic cell death for anticancer drug resistance

text: Many of these natural compounds exhibit significant potential in the realm of cancer treatment. In fact, certain natural compounds, such as paclitaxel (PTX), camptothecin, and vincristine, have already gained widespread acceptance as chemotherapeutic drugs in clinical practice. Moreover, an interesting aspect is that numerous natural compounds have been found to induce various non-apoptotic cell death pathways when administered to resistant cancer cells that evade apoptosis. This review focuses on ferroptosis, necroptosis, pyroptosis, and paraptosis, providing a comprehensive overview of the latest research advancements in these mechanisms within the framework of cancer. We place specific emphasis on their relevance in the context of combatting cancer drug resistance. Additionally, this review compiles information on natural compounds with the capacity to induce these four modes of cell death in the context of addressing cancer resistance over the past two decades.
title: Recent advances in natural compounds inducing non-apoptotic cell death for anticancer drug resistance

text: Ferroptosis, a recently discovered form of PCD that is iron-dependent, was first proposed in 2012. Morphologically, ferroptotic cells exhibit intact nuclei without chromatin condensation. However, their mitochondria undergo significant changes, including reduced size, increased membrane density, reduced cristae, and outer membrane rupture. Interestingly, the discovery of ferroptosis inducers was earlier than its naming. Yang et al. discovered some new compounds as early as 2003 and 2008, including Erastin, RSL3, and RSL5, which induce cell death through a mechanism distinct from apoptosis. Erastin reduces cysteine uptake by inhibiting cysteine/glutamate transporter receptor, known as System X c -, resulting in a decrease in glutathione (GSH) synthesis and an increase in iron-dependent lipid peroxidation (LPO), which finally leads cells to ferroptosis. Differently, RSL3 directly inhibits the activity of Glutathione Peroxidase 4 (GPX4), a GSH-utilizing enzyme that prevents the accumulation of toxic lipid hydroperoxide, thereby inducing ferroptosis. Additionally, Erastin also indirectly triggers ferroptosis through the inactivation of GPX4 via the inhibition of GSH synthesis. It is known that LPO and intracellular iron accumulation play pivotal roles in triggering ferroptosis. Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) are the most susceptible lipids to peroxidation during ferroptosis. The regulation of PUFA synthesis may be influenced by enzymes such as Long-chain acyl-CoA synthetases (ACSLs) and lyso-phosphatidylcholine acyltransferase-3 (LPCAT3). Additionally, arachidonate lipoxygenases (ALOXs) and cytochrome p450s (POR) can directly or indirectly modulate PUFA peroxidation, resulting in ferroptosis. Additionally, iron metabolism is crucial for ferroptosis. As Fe 2+ is released from the labile iron pool (LIP) into the cytoplasm, excess Fe 2+ oxidizes PUFAs to hydroxyl radicals and leads to ferroptosis. The mitochondria are responsible for cellular metabolism and also play an important role in the regulation of ferroptosis. Within the mitochondria, dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH) reduces ubiquinone (CoQ) to ubiquinol (CoQH2), serving as a radical-trapping antioxidant with anti-ferroptosis activity. DHODH plays a significant role in mediating ferroptosis defense independent of the GSH pathway. Similarly, the plasma enzyme ferroptosis suppressor protein 1 (FSP1) inhibits lipid hydroperoxides by reducing ubiquinone to ubiquinol, operating in parallel with GPX4 to counteract ferroptosis. Obviously, the mechanisms of ferroptosis are complex and being explored constantly.
title: Recent advances in natural compounds inducing non-apoptotic cell death for anticancer drug resistance

text: In recent years, ferroptosis has been a hot topic in cancer development, treatment and cancer drug resistance. Several signaling pathways have been found to participate in promoting cancer development and drug resistance through the inhibition of ferroptosis. With multiple functions for proliferation, metastasis, and differentiation of cancer cells, the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/AKT/mammalian target of the rapamycin (mTOR) signaling pathway is responsible for ferroptosis prevention via sterol regulatory element-binding protein 1 (SREBP1)/stearoyl-CoA desaturase-1 (SCD1)-mediated adipogenesis. Hippo pathway activity is also responsible for cell growth and proliferation. Activating the Hippo pathway can suppress downstream YAP, leading cancer cells resistant to ferroptosis by downregulating acyl-CoA synthetase long-chain family member 4 (ACSL4) and TCP friendly rate control (TFRC). Since RAS may regulate some processes to escape ferroptosis, RAS-mutated cells are always susceptible to ferroptosis. High-mobility group box 1 (HMGB1), a leukemia pathogenic gene, inhibits LPO via the RAS/MAP kinase (MAPK) pathway, promoting ferroptosis resistance. Additionally, several other pathways, including nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2), p53, and hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF), are also involved in chemotherapeutic resistance through ferroptosis regulation. Recent research highlights the significant impact of the Nrf2 signaling pathway on both organ protection and resistance to cisplatin (DDP) across various cancer types. For instance, in non-small cell lung cancer, Erastin and Sorafenib, either alone or in combination, induce ferroptosis by inhibiting the Nrf2/SLC7A11 (also known as xCT) pathway, thereby overcoming DDP resistance. The p53 gene, extensively studied in cancer research, influences metabolic pathways related to ferroptosis, such as enhancing ferroptosis by down-regulating xCT expression. According to this mechanism, Flubendazole and 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) demonstrate synergistic effects in treating castration-resistant prostate cancer. HIF serves a dual role in the regulation of ferroptosis in cancer cells. Lowering HIF-α levels has been found to increase LPO and enhance ferroptosis in clear cell renal cell carcinoma. Conversely, in temozolomide-resistant glioblastoma, activating HIF-1α and HIF-2α can induce ferroptosis, with HIF-2α possibly promoting LPO as the primary mechanism.
title: Recent advances in natural compounds inducing non-apoptotic cell death for anticancer drug resistance
section_title: Ferroptosis pathways for chemotherapy resistance in cancer

text: Many natural compounds have been found to induce ferroptosis via single or combinational therapies, offering opportunities for cancer treatment and drug resistance. Here, we summarize those natural compounds that reverse drug resistance by inducing ferroptosis. Most of these compounds can synergize with chemotherapeutic drugs by regulating ferroptosis-related proteins and genes. Recent studies have revealed that sorafenib can induce ferroptosis in various types of cancer. However, sorafenib-induced ferroptosis can be suppressed, specifically through the activation of the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway or the NRF2/GPX4 axis. To overcome this challenge, drug combinations have proven to be effective strategies. Dihydroartemisinin, a derivative of artemisinin, shares similar mechanisms with sorafenib regarding ferroptosis-related proteins, such as GPX4, and has a stronger effect in liver cancer cells when combined with sorafenib. Ursolic acid, a pentacyclic triterpene compound, also exhibits synergistic anticancer effects with sorafenib by inhibiting xCT in many cancers. While DDP is considered a front-line chemotherapy drug for various cancers, including ovarian cancer, its resistance poses a significant impediment to achieving effective treatment outcomes. Inhibition of apoptosis plays a significant role in contributing to DDP resistance, whereas the induction of novel forms of cell death, such as ferroptosis, has been shown to effectively kill DDP-resistant cancer cells that evade apoptosis. The combination of DDP with Shikonin, a hydroxy-1,4-naphthoquinone isolated from Lithospermum erythrorhizon Sieb. et Zucc.(Boraginaceae), promotes Fe 2+ accumulation by upregulating heme oxygenase 1 (HMOX1), initiating ferroptosis in DDP-resistant ovarian cancer cells. Piperlongumine, an alkaloid derived from long pepper (Piper longum L.), exhibits anticancer activity in lung cancer cells by targeting the glutathione regeneration enzyme, thioredoxin reductase 1 (TXNRD1). Although it does not induce ferroptosis, it can significantly enhance erastin-induced LPO. In addition to ferroptosis-related genes and proteins, some natural compounds induce ferroptosis via regulation of the Nrf2 signaling pathway. Withaferin A, a steroidal lactone isolated from the medicinal plant Ashwagandha [ Withania somnifera (L.) Dunal], and Tiliroside, a flavonoid found in the herbs of Tribulus terrestris L., both modulate the Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (Keap1)/Nrf2 pathway in hepatocellular carcinoma. Withaferin A enhances sorafenib sensitivity in sorafenib-resistant hepatocellular carcinoma cells by regulating the Keap1/Nrf2-associated epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and ferroptosis. Additionally, tiliroside synergistically combines with sorafenib to inhibit Tank-binding kinase (TBK1) activity, prompting Keap1-mediated Nrf2 ubiquitination and degradation, leading to ferroptosis in hepatocellular carcinoma cells. Ginkgetin, a natural biflavonoid isolated from the leaves of Ginkgo biloba L., has been found to induce ferroptosis in non-small cell lung cancer cells through decreased expression of xCT and GPX4, decreased GSH/glutathione disulfide (GSSG) ratio, and inactivation of the Nrf2/HMOX1 axis. Interestingly, it can promote DDP-induced anticancer activity, which is also a result of ferroptosis induction. As a key regulator of iron homeostasis, ferritin plays a vital role in storing intracellular free iron and is involved in ferritinophagy, a form of autophagic ferroptosis.
title: Recent advances in natural compounds inducing non-apoptotic cell death for anticancer drug resistance
section_title: Natural compounds inducing ferroptosis for cancer treatment

text: Ginkgetin, a natural biflavonoid isolated from the leaves of Ginkgo biloba L., has been found to induce ferroptosis in non-small cell lung cancer cells through decreased expression of xCT and GPX4, decreased GSH/glutathione disulfide (GSSG) ratio, and inactivation of the Nrf2/HMOX1 axis. Interestingly, it can promote DDP-induced anticancer activity, which is also a result of ferroptosis induction. As a key regulator of iron homeostasis, ferritin plays a vital role in storing intracellular free iron and is involved in ferritinophagy, a form of autophagic ferroptosis. In ferritinophagy, the autophagic cargo receptor nuclear receptor coactivator 4 (NCOA4) binds to ferritin heavy chains (FTH1) and delivers it to autophagosomes for degradation and iron release. Human carbonyl reductase 1 (CBR1) contributes to gemcitabine resistance in pancreatic cancer. The upregulation of CBR1 induced by gemcitabine inhibits the antitumor effects of the drug. Conversely, reducing CBR1 activity enhances the sensitivity of cancer cells to gemcitabine, thereby improving its therapeutic efficacy. Chrysin, a natural bioflavonoid compound, has been discovered to induce ferritinophagy, thus enhancing gemcitabine sensitivity in pancreatic cancer cells. In Chrysin-treated cells, there is a deregulation of FTH1 and an increase in intracellular free iron levels, followed by the inhibition of CBR1, which is involved in the induction of ferroptosis. The tumor suppressor protein p53 also plays an essential role in ferroptosis in certain cancers. As a diterpenoid extracted from Torreya nucifera, kayadiol exhibits anticancer properties through p53-mediated ferroptosis in NK/T lymphoma cells, and it could synergistically combine with L-asparaginase and DDP. Artesunate (AST), another derivative of artemisinin, was found to inhibit the growth of sunitinib-resistant renal cell carcinoma cells by both inhibiting cell cycle progression and inducing ferroptosis. Interestingly, the induction of ferroptosis was associated with its inhibitory effect only in renal cell carcinoma cells expressing p53, suggesting that AST induces p53-dependent ferroptosis.
title: Recent advances in natural compounds inducing non-apoptotic cell death for anticancer drug resistance
section_title: Natural compounds inducing ferroptosis for cancer treatment

text: Necroptosis, first described in 2005, is a form of cell death characterized by morphological features similar to necrosis, including a lack of nuclear chromatin, organelle swelling, and cell membrane disruption. However, unlike necrosis, which is a passive and non-programmed form of cell death, necroptosis can be regulated by multiple signal transduction pathways. The classical form of necroptotic cell death is mediated by tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α). Initially, TNF-α binds to its specific receptor TNF receptor 1 (TNFR1), promoting its trimerization and facilitating the recruitment of several proteins including receptor-interacting protein 1 (RIP1) kinase, TNF-α receptor-associated death domain (TRADD), cellular inhibitor of apoptosis 1 (cIAP1), cellular inhibitor of apoptosis 2 (cIAP2), TNFR-associated factor 2 (TRAF2), and TNFR-associated factor 5 (TRAF5) to form complex I. Within complex I, RIP1 can undergo polyubiquitination by TRAF2, TRAF5, cIAP1, and cIAP2. The ubiquitination status of RIP1 determines whether complex I activates the nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) pathway to promote cell survival, or triggers cell death. When the ubiquitylation of RIP is impaired, complex I can transform into complex IIa and complex IIb, leading to cell death. Complex IIa can trigger caspase-8-dependent apoptosis in the absence of RIP1, whereas complex IIb depends on RIP1 for caspase-8 activation due to its deficiency in TRADD compared to complex IIa. Additionally, complex IIa can transform into complex IIb. When the levels of receptor-interacting protein 3 (RIP3) and mixed lineage kinase domain-like protein (MLKL) are sufficiently high and caspase-8 is blocked, complex IIb may develop into a necrosome. Following the phosphorylation of RIP1 and RIP3, two core components of the necrosome, the activated RIP3 can further recruit and phosphorylate MLKL, triggering its oligomerization. The oligomerized MLKL is then translocated to the plasma membrane, increasing its permeability and ultimately leading to necroptotic cell death. In addition to TNF superfamily receptors, various other types of receptors, such as Toll-like receptors, T-cell receptors, and interferon receptors, also contribute to the activation of necroptosis.
title: Recent advances in natural compounds inducing non-apoptotic cell death for anticancer drug resistance

text: As independent of caspase activation and involving distinct components from apoptotic pathways, necroptosis is an effective mechanism to overcome apoptosis resistance in cancer. However, some necroptotic core components are always lacking in cancer cells, resulting in the evasion of this mechanism. RIP3 is silenced in numerous cancer types, and this silencing is likely ascribed to genomic methylation near the RIP3 transcriptional start site or driven by oncogenes BRAF and AXL. Current studies have revealed that demethylation treatment can activate necroptotic pathways by restoring the expression of RIP3. Moreover, upregulating RIPK3 expression can enhance the sensitivity of colon cancer cells to 5-FU and lung cancer cells to DDP through mediating necroptosis. Furthermore, the low expression of MLKL appears to be associated with a poor patient prognosis in certain cancers, making it a potential novel potential prognostic biomarker for these cancers. In addition, some compounds can induce MLKL-mediated necroptosis without the phosphorylation of RIP1 and RIP3, which presents a very promising prospect for future studies. In addition to modulating necroptosis genes and proteins, increasing glycolytic metabolism may confer resistance to necroptosis in cancer cells under hypoxic conditions. The mechanism involves the suppression of RIP-dependent necroptosis through pyruvate scavenging of mitochondrial superoxide. Several studies have suggested that inhibiting glycolysis may be a potential mechanism for necroptosis induction. For instance, selenite-induced necroptosis in prostate cancer resulted from the inhibition of glycolysis through adenosine triphosphate (ATP) depletion and phosphofructokinase activity reduction.
title: Recent advances in natural compounds inducing non-apoptotic cell death for anticancer drug resistance
section_title: Regulation of necroptosis for anti-drug resistance in cancer

text: So far, many natural compounds can induce necroptosis in diverse cancer types, and some can also inhibit drug resistance. As mentioned above, modulating necroptosis core proteins is critical for necroptosis induction. By regulating the RIP1/reactive oxygen species (ROS)-mediated pathway, bufalin, an endogenous cardiotonic steroid, can induce necroptosis in adriamycin-resistant triple-negative breast cancer cell lines. Numerous studies have indicated that when 5-FU is in combination with other anticancer agents, its therapeutic efficacy can be effectively enhanced. Gambogenic acid is one of the main components of Gamboge which can be used in combination with 5-FU to upregulate necroptosis-related proteins such as RIP1 in lung cancer cells, thereby inducing necroptosis. Piperlongumine can also activate RIP1 to produce excessive ROS, triggering necroptosis in DDP-resistant bladder cells. Berberine can effectively enhance the antitumor effect of DDP in ovarian cancer by increasing the expression and activation of RIP3 and MLKL, thereby inducing necroptotic cell death. In TNF-α induced necroptosis, MLKL is a key downstream component of RIP1 and RIP3. However, it is worth mentioning that tanshinol A, a phenolic compound extracted from Salvia miltiorrhiza Bunge, can trigger non-canonical necroptosis mediated by MLKL in lung cancer independently of RIP1 and RIP3. MAPK signaling pathways also play a role in necroptosis induction. For instance, oridonin, a diterpenoid derived from Isodon rubescens (Hemsley) H. Hara, has been shown to enhance the cytotoxicity of 5-FU in renal cancer cells by inducing necroptosis. This process is associated with the activation of c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK), p38, and extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK). Moreover, certain studies have demonstrated that the inhibition of caspases may cause a switch from apoptosis to necroptosis in specific cancer types. Ganoderic acid T (GAT) is a triterpene of Garcinia hanburyi Hook. f., inducing both necroptosis and apoptosis in cervical cancer cells. Interestingly, the percentage ratio of necroptosis is increased following the increase of GAT concentration, as GAT can reduce the matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) and ATP levels and caspase-8 expression under radiation conditions. Notably, glycolysis suppression has also emerged as an effective mechanism for necroptosis induction by natural compounds. Docetaxel is indeed a valuable chemotherapeutic agent utilized in the treatment of prostate cancer, primarily by inducing cell death. However, similar to DDP, the effectiveness of docetaxel-induced apoptosis can also be hindered through various pathways, including the p38/p53/p21 pathway, USP33-DUSP1-JNK pathway, and PI3K/Akt/NF-κB pathway [ - ]. Therefore, several studies are currently focused on identifying alternative cell death pathways, such as necroptosis, that can be induced in docetaxel-resistant cancer cells as well. Shikonin has been extensively studied as a natural necroptosis inducer in various cancer types, and it has been demonstrated to overcome drug resistance to docetaxel in prostate cancer and DDP in bladder cancer. Furthermore, shikonin can induce glycolysis suppression in glioma cells, which is closely associated with the accumulation of intracellular H 2 O 2 triggered by the activation of RIP1 and RIP3.
title: Recent advances in natural compounds inducing non-apoptotic cell death for anticancer drug resistance
section_title: Natural compounds inducing necroptosis for cancer treatment

text: Pyroptosis, a pro-inflammatory programmed cell death, was originally termed by Cookson et al. in 2001. The term derives from the Greek roots “pyro”, which relates to fire or fever, and “ptosis”, denoting a falling, reflecting its nature. Pyroptosis shares certain characteristics with apoptosis, such as DNA fragmentation, nuclear condensation, and caspase dependence. However, cells undergoing pyroptosis differ in that they retain intact nuclei and exhibit pore formation in the plasma membrane. An increasing understanding of pyroptosis has revealed that this type of cell death can be divided into classical and non-classical pathways. The classical pyroptotic pathway is mediated by inflammasome assembly, which consists of pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), apoptosis-related speck-like protein (ASC), and pro-caspase-1. PRRs, functioning as inflammasome sensors, recognize pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs). Subsequently, they recruit the bridging protein ASC, which contains a pyrin domain (PYD) and a caspase activation and recruitment domain (CARD), through specific PYD-PYD interactions. After being recruited, ASC can interact with and activate pro-caspase-1 via CARD-CARD interactions. Some PRRs containing CARD can also directly bind to pro-caspase-1, forming inflammasomes without the participation of ASC. Activated caspase-1 facilitates the maturation of inflammatory cytokines interleukin (IL)-1β and IL-18, as well as cleaves the pore-forming protein gasdermin D (GSDMD) to produce its N-terminal fragment (N-GSDMD). N-GSDMDs then translocate to the plasma membrane and form pores, promoting the release of mature IL-1β and IL-18. As the number of N-GSDMD pores increases, cells swell and rupture, resulting in pyroptotic cell death. In non-classical pathways, caspase-3/8 can also trigger pyroptosis by activating GSDMD or GSDME. Additionally, caspase-8 can induce GSDMC-dependent pyroptosis as well. The cleavage of GSDMD can also be mediated by caspase-4/5/11, which recognizes intracellular LPS to activate the non-canonical inflammasome. Notably, GSDMB can not only be cleaved by caspase-1 to directly initiate pyroptosis, but also enhance caspase-4 activity to promote this cell death mechanism. Recently, the cleavage of GSDMA has been found to be catalyzed by streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin B (SpeB), a cysteine protease secreted by group A Streptococcus. This finding demonstrates that GSDMA can also play a role in pyroptosis by releasing the cleaved N-terminal fragments, which can bind to and disrupt specific acidic lipid-containing membranes.
title: Recent advances in natural compounds inducing non-apoptotic cell death for anticancer drug resistance

text: In cancer treatment, the induction of pyroptosis is increasingly recognized as a promising strategy for overcoming drug resistance. NOD-like receptor family pyrin domain-containing 3 (NLRP3), a crucial inflammasome sensor in the NLR family, is recognized as a downstream target of multiple microRNAs (miRNAs) associated with cancer drug resistance. For example, by downregulating the expression of miR-556-5p in non-small cell lung cancer, NLRP3 inflammasome-mediated pyroptosis can be triggered, thereby enhancing DDP sensitivity. The pore-forming proteins GSDMD and GSDME, extensively studied in the GSDM family, are potential targets for combating drug resistance and contributing to the treatment and prognosis of various cancers. Some chemotherapeutic agents have been demonstrated to exert antitumor activity when used alone or in combination to induce GSDMD-dependent pyroptosis, enhancing the efficacy of chemotherapy. For instance, the co-administration of paclitaxel and ruthenium complexes can induce cell death in paclitaxel-resistant cervical cancer cells by mediating Caspase-1/GSDMD-dependent pyroptosis. GSDME-mediated pyroptosis has been observed to improve the sensitivity of various drugs across different cancer types, including increasing DDP sensitivity in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma cells and oxaliplatin sensitivity in colon cancer cells. Additionally, it can alleviate the side effects of DDP in patients with oral squamous cell carcinoma. In recent years, programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1), known as an immune checkpoint, has emerged as a research hotspot in tumor immunotherapy. However, PD-L1 has an additional role as a non-immune checkpoint by regulating the non-classical pyroptosis pathway mediated by GSDMC/caspase-8. In this way, a variety of antibiotics can induce pyroptosis in cancer cells, indicating that it could be a novel strategy to combat antibiotic resistance in chemotherapy.
title: Recent advances in natural compounds inducing non-apoptotic cell death for anticancer drug resistance
section_title: Induction of pyroptosis for anti-drug resistance in cancer

text: Nowadays, the caspase-1/GSDMD and caspase-3/GSDME pathways have attracted significant attention in pyroptosis induction, and many natural compounds have been found to activate these pathways in cancers. Wedelolactone, an ingredient of Eclipta prostrata (L.) L., can simultaneously activate these two pathways by strongly increasing the activation of caspase-1, caspase-3, GSDME and GSDMD in retinoblastoma cells. Ophiopogonin B, derived from Dioscorea bulbifera L., can induce caspase-1/GSDMD-dependent pyroptosis in lung cancer cells, especially exhibiting a more significant suppression of growth in DDP-resistant cancer cells. As a pentacyclic triterpene compound of lupine, betulinic acid can induce caspase-1-dependent pyroptosis, thereby enhancing chemosensitivity to DDP in esophageal cancer cells. By activating the caspase-3-dependent pathway, natural compounds such as curcumin, dihydroartemisinin, and germacrone can induce pyroptosis in different cancers [ - ]. Some studies have reported that the activation of caspase-9 is also involved in caspase-3-mediated pyroptosis. For example, alantolactone, a terpenoid of Inula helenium L., can promote the cleavage of caspase-9 and caspase-3 to induce GSDME-mediated pyroptosis in anaplastic thyroid cancer. Some chemotherapeutic agents, such as DDP, 5-FU, and carboplatin, have been demonstrated to combat cancer drug resistance by inducing GSDME-dependent pyroptosis, while whether natural compounds can also suppress drug resistance through this pathway needs further investigation. In addition, by downregulating PD-L1 to activate NLRP3-mediated pyroptosis, Diosbulbin B extracted from Dioscorea bulbifera L. can sensitize DDP-resistant gastric cancer cells to DDP. At present, there are few reports on whether natural compounds induce pyroptosis via the regulation of other GSDM family proteins. This is partly because of their unclear functions in initiating pyroptotic cell death. Further elucidation of how the other members of the GSDM family contribute to pyroptosis induction in cancers may provide new insights for the search for natural compounds with anticancer and anti-drug resistance activities.
title: Recent advances in natural compounds inducing non-apoptotic cell death for anticancer drug resistance
section_title: Natural compounds inducing pyroptosis for cancer treatment

text: Paraptosis was first introduced as a form of programmed cell death by Sperandio et al. in 2000. It derives from “para”, meaning “next to” or “related to”, and “apoptosis”, suggesting that it is distinct from apoptosis. The main morphological features of paraptosis include cytoplasmic vacuolization, swelling of the endoplasmic reticulum and/or mitochondria, and the absence of nuclear fragmentation or apoptotic body formation. In this paradigm, caspases are not activated, and thus, cells undergoing paraptosis are resistant to caspase inhibitors. The MAPK pathways play a critical role in paraptosis, and research focusing on the ERK, JNK, and p38 pathways is particularly extensive. Notably, the protein AIP1/Alix was described as the first specific inhibitor of paraptosis, capable of restraining the insulin-like growth factor-I receptor (IGFIR) induced paraptotic process mediated by the MAPK/ERK and JNK pathways. Furthermore, TrxR1 inhibition and GSH depletion have been observed to potentially activate the MAPK pathways by triggering the accumulation of cellular ROS. Paraptosis induction is also related to the homeostasis of intracellular Ca 2+, which is mainly regulated by the endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria. Intracellular Ca 2+ can be released from the endoplasmic reticulum into mitochondria when paraptosis is initiated, resulting in the endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondrial dilation and ultimately leading to cell death. The voltage- and Ca 2+ -activated K + (BKCa) channels are widely expressed in body and have the ability to link changes in intracellular calcium to outward hyperpolarizing potassium currents. The activation of these channels will disrupt the osmotic balance, initiating cell swelling and vacuolization. Additionally, proteasome inhibition may also promote paraptosis by inducing endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress.
title: Recent advances in natural compounds inducing non-apoptotic cell death for anticancer drug resistance

text: Paraptosis induction is a potential strategy for developing non-genetically modified tumor vaccines. In rat T9 glioma cells, the activation of BKCa channels promotes the overexpression of heat shock proteins and the translocation of HMGB1 from the nuclear region to the periphery, stimulating immune responses and initiating paraptosis. Rats injected with paraptotic T9 glioma cells, which are killed by prolonged BKCa channel activation, can develop specific immunity to T9 cells. This suggests the potential of using these treated cells as a functionally killed vaccine. Due to its unique molecular mechanism, paraptosis induction also contributes to enhancing the activity of proteasome inhibitors in cancer cells. Although many proteasome inhibitors have shown antitumor activities, their clinical efficacy is unsatisfactory as their effectiveness can be compromised by both primary and secondary resistance mechanisms. Therefore, combination therapy can be seen as an effective strategy to address proteasome inhibitor resistance. For instance, by triggering paraptotic cell death, bortezomib (Btz), a 20S core particle inhibitor of the proteasome, can be combined with loperamide, an antidiarrheal agent, to enhance Btz sensitivity and reduce its side effects, effectively combating the colon cancer.
title: Recent advances in natural compounds inducing non-apoptotic cell death for anticancer drug resistance
section_title: Paraptosis potential applications in cancer drug resistance

text: Currently, a number of natural compounds have shown potential in cancer treatment by inducing paraptosis, with many of them modulating the MAPK signaling pathways to trigger ER stress. One such example is Paris Saponin II, derived from Paris polyphylla Smith, which effectively induces paraptosis by activating the JNK pathway and augmenting ER stress. Moreover, the activation of this paraptosis-associated pathway enhances the sensitivity of DDP in lung cancer. Jolkinolide B, an active abietane ent-diterpenoid, is also a noteworthy compound that induces paraptosis in both sensitive and DDP-resistant bladder cancer cells by activating the ERK pathway and enhancing ER stress. Additionally, Chalcomoracin, isolated from Morus alba L., has been discovered to enhance the sensitivity of non-small cell lung cancer to radiation by augmenting ER stress. Elaiophylin is a natural antibiotic derived from Streptomyces melanosporus that can also induce paraptosis through the hyperactivation of the MAPK pathway. This compound demonstrates notable efficacy in eliminating ovarian cancer cells that are resistant to multiple drugs, including platinum, taxane, and poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitor (PARPi). Some natural compounds such as curcumin, morusin, and ophiobolin A can also induce paraptosis by affecting ion homeostasis. Curcumin can induce paraptosis in epithelial ovarian cancer mainly through mitochondrial Ca 2+ overload, which subsequently contributes to mitochondrial swelling and dysfunction. Similarly, morusin, a prenylflavonoid, can also induce paraptosis in breast cancer by triggering mitochondrial Ca 2+ overload. In glioblastoma cells, paraptosis induced by ophiobolin A, a sesterterpenoid phytotoxin from the genus Bipolaris, is linked to K + homeostasis imbalance, primarily caused by the blockage of BKCa channels. Furthermore, natural compounds can induce paraptosis by disrupting sulfhydryl homeostasis and suppressing proteasome functions, both of which can be significantly inhibited by thiol antioxidants. In this way, plumbagin, extracted from Plumbago zeylanica L., can induce paraptotic cell death in different cancer types. Paraptosis can also be triggered in a p53-dependent manner. For instance, Ginsenoside Rh2, which is a bioactive product in Panax ginseng C. A. Meyer, can induce paraptosis in colorectal cancer via activating the p53 pathway as well as the NF-κB survival pathway.
title: Recent advances in natural compounds inducing non-apoptotic cell death for anticancer drug resistance
section_title: Natural compounds inducing paraptosis for cancer treatment

text: Numerous natural compounds possess the ability to elicit anticancer and anti-chemoresistance effects by triggering non-apoptotic cell death mechanisms such as ferroptosis, necroptosis, pyroptosis, and paraptosis. It is noteworthy that while these forms of cell death have unique regulators, some common pathways can also govern them. This implies that multiple cell death pathways may occur concurrently and be subject to simultaneous regulation. In 2019, Malireddi et al. introduced PANoptosis, an innovative form of cell death that amalgamates essential features of pyroptosis, apoptosis, and necroptosis yet defies a straightforward classification under any one of these categories. This discovery underscores the co-regulation and interplay among these cell death pathways, suggesting that drugs may possess multifaceted regulatory effects by modulating master factors within these pathways. Beyond the four aforementioned types of cell death, some other novel cell death mechanisms have surfaced in recent years, including parthanatos, disulfidptosis, and cuproptosis [ - ]. These revelations open up new avenues for identifying targets in cancer treatment and provide additional strategies for combating cancer drug resistance. As such, ongoing exploration is essential to ascertain whether natural compounds can elicit anticancer effects through these emerging forms of cell death.
title: Recent advances in natural compounds inducing non-apoptotic cell death for anticancer drug resistance

text: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is one of the most prevalent malignancies worldwide, accounting for substantial cancer-related mortality and morbidity. Despite significant advances in therapeutic strategies, the prognosis for CRC patients remains poor, particularly for those diagnosed at advanced stages (-). This underscores the urgent need for a more comprehensive understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying CRC progression and for the identification of reliable biomarkers that can guide prognosis and targeted therapies. Recently, attention has shifted toward exploring the role of programmed cell death (PCD) pathways as a promising avenue in cancer biology (-). Traditionally, PCD has been recognized as a mechanism for maintaining cellular homeostasis and eliminating damaged cells; however, emerging evidence suggests that PCD pathways also play multifaceted roles in cancer progression and treatment resistance. PCD encompasses a range of tightly regulated mechanisms through which cells undergo controlled death, including apoptosis, autophagy, ferroptosis, necroptosis, neutrophil extracellular trap formation (NETosis), and paraptosis, each characterized by distinct molecular pathways and cellular outcomes. Apoptosis, the best-characterized form of PCD, is critical in normal tissue homeostasis and immune response to cancer (-). However, cancer cells frequently evade apoptosis, thereby enabling unchecked proliferation. Autophagy, another well-studied form of PCD, has a dual role in cancer; it can promote survival under metabolic stress but may also lead to cell death under specific circumstances. Ferroptosis, a recently characterized iron-dependent form of cell death, has garnered interest due to its potential role in overcoming drug resistance in cancer (-). Necroptosis and NETosis (-), two inflammatory forms of PCD, have been implicated in the tumor microenvironment’s modulation, fostering immune responses and contributing to cancer-associated inflammation. Paraptosis, a form of non-apoptotic cell death characterized by extensive vacuolization, is less understood but has shown potential involvement in cancer cell death mechanisms. These diverse PCD pathways do not operate in isolation but interact within a complex network, influencing each other and impacting cancer development in a highly context-dependent manner. Understanding these interactions is crucial, as dysregulation of PCD can influence tumor growth, metastasis, immune evasion, and response to treatment. Moreover, specific PCD pathways may serve as potential biomarkers or therapeutic targets. The interplay between these pathways in the CRC context remains poorly understood, yet it holds significant potential for advancing our understanding of CRC progression and uncovering new treatment avenues. Recent technological advances in multi-omics analyses have enabled a more detailed investigation of PCD pathway-related genes across diverse cancer types (-), paving the way for pan-cancer studies that provide a broader view of PCD pathways’ impact on various cancers. Additionally, the advent of single-cell RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) and spatial transcriptomics (ST) has allowed researchers to examine gene expression patterns within individual cells and within the spatial context of the tumor microenvironment. Such technologies are critical for delineating how PCD pathway genes are expressed across different cell types within tumors, revealing potential cell-type-specific roles of these genes in tumor progression.
title: Identification of prognostic biomarkers in colorectal cancer through multi-omics profiling of programmed cell death pathways

text: Additionally, the advent of single-cell RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) and spatial transcriptomics (ST) has allowed researchers to examine gene expression patterns within individual cells and within the spatial context of the tumor microenvironment. Such technologies are critical for delineating how PCD pathway genes are expressed across different cell types within tumors, revealing potential cell-type-specific roles of these genes in tumor progression. This study aims to clarify the prognostic roles of PCD pathways in CRC through a multi-omics approach. We applied gene set variation analysis (GSVA) and machine learning methods to identify key pathways, including autophagy, ferroptosis, and cuproptosis, associated with patient survival. Furthermore, using pan-cancer analysis, single-cell RNA-seq, and ST, we explored the expression patterns and spatial distribution of core PCD genes across various cancers. Finally, in vitro experiments on nuclear receptor coactivator 4 (NCOA4), a key autophagy gene, were conducted to assess its impact on CRC cell migration, invasion, and apoptosis. Our findings provide a comprehensive view of PCD pathways in CRC and underscore the potential of these pathways and core genes as prognostic markers and therapeutic targets, laying the groundwork for personalized approaches in CRC management. We present this article in accordance with the TRIPOD reporting checklist (available at https://jgo.amegroups.com/article/view/10.21037/jgo-2024-861/rc).

text: We collected gene sets related to 18 types of PCD pathways and their key regulatory genes. Specifically, it includes 580 genes related to apoptosis, 367 genes involved in autophagy, 7 genes associated with alkaliptosis, and 338 genes linked to anoikis. Additionally, there are 19 genes relevant to copper-induced cell death (cuproptosis) and 15 genes relevant to intestinal cell death, 87 genes involved in ferroptosis. Moreover, the set contains 34 genes involved in immunogenic cell death (ICD), 220 genes responsible for lysosome-dependent cell death, and 101 genes associated with necroptosis. Other pathways are also covered, including 8 genes for methuosis, 23 genes for entosis, 24 genes involved in NETosis, 5 genes for oxieptosis, 52 genes for pyroptosis, 9 genes related to parthanatos, and 66 genes involved in atrophy (cell shrinkage or atrophic death). section_title: PCD gene sets and pathway selection

text: For each type of PCD, prognostic genes were identified through univariate Cox regression analysis. PCDScore was then calculated based on the enrichment scores of these significant genes using the single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA) method from the GSVA R package. Based on the calculated PCDScores, we employed univariate Cox regression combined with least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression to screen for PCD pathways with significant prognostic value for CRC. This approach helped us identify the PCD pathways most relevant to patient outcomes. Core genes for each significant PCD pathway were identified using the dynamic network biomarker (DNB) algorithm, implemented with the DNB R package, based on three criteria: a significant increase in standard deviation within the DNB gene group (SDin); a sharp increase in correlations among DNB genes (PCCin); and a significant decrease in correlations between DNB and non-DNB genes (PCCout). Gene groups meeting these criteria are considered early warning signals of critical states. These core genes were further validated across clinical stages to identify threshold states for each PCD pathway. Multivariate Cox regression was used to develop a prognostic model based on these core genes. We evaluated the model’s predictive accuracy using time-dependent receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves and area under the curve (AUC) plots, generated with the pROC and timeROC packages, and assessed clinical decision-making impact through decision curve analysis (DCA) curves using the ggDCA package. Kaplan-Meier (KM) survival analysis was conducted using the survival R package, and optimal cut-off points were determined with the survi_cutpoint function from the surviminer package, with the parameter minprop set to 0.3, indicating the minimum proportion of observations per group. A log-rank test with a P value <0.05 was considered statistically significant for prognostic evaluation.

text: Cells were transfected with the NCOA4 overexpression plasmid for 24 hours to ensure effective gene expression. After transfection, a scratch was made through the cell monolayer using a sterile 200 µL pipette tip to create a uniform wound. Detached cells and debris were removed by washing once with phosphate buffered saline (PBS), and then a fresh complete culture medium was added to promote cell migration. Images of the initial wound were taken immediately after the scratch to document baseline measurements. The cells were incubated for 48 hours, with images captured at designated intervals to monitor and assess the wound closure rate and migration of cells into the wound area.

text: Following 72 hours of NCOA4 overexpression, cell migration was evaluated using a transwell chamber. The medium in the upper chamber was carefully removed, and cells that remained on the upper side of the membrane were wiped away using a PBS-moistened cotton swab. Migrated cells on the lower side of the membrane were stained with 1 mL of 0.1% crystal violet for 5 minutes. The inserts were then rinsed 2–3 times with PBS to remove excess stain. After drying, the stained inserts were photographed, and the number of migrated cells was quantified to analyze the effect of NCOA4 on cell migratory capacity.

text: Apoptosis was assessed 72 hours post-transfection with the NCOA4 overexpression plasmid. Cells were detached using trypsin without ethylenedeaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) and collected by centrifugation at 300 g for 5 minutes at 4 ℃. The resulting cell pellet was washed twice with cold PBS, and the supernatant was discarded. Cells were resuspended in 100 µL of 1× binding buffer, and 5 µL of annexin V-fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC) and 10 µL of propidium iodide (PI) staining solution were added to the suspension. The mixture was incubated for 15 minutes at room temperature in the dark. After incubation, 400 µL of 1× binding buffer was added, and samples were gently mixed before being analyzed using flow cytometry to quantify apoptotic cell populations.

Spearman correlation analysis was applied to explore relationships between variables. KM survival curves were plotted with the survival package, and optimal cut-off points were determined using the survi_cutpoint function from the surviminer package, with minprop set to 0.3. The Wilcoxon rank-sum test was used to compare group differences. Hazard ratios (HRs) >1 were considered risk factors, while HR <1 indicated protective factors, with P<0.05 set as the threshold for statistical significance.

text: To assess the prognostic significance of various PCD pathways in CRC, we used the GSVA algorithm to generate PCD pathway scores. By curating a comprehensive set of PCD-related genes, each representing distinct cell death mechanisms, we applied ssGSEA to quantify pathway-specific enrichment scores across CRC samples. These scores provided an integrated view of the PCD activity within the tumor microenvironment. To identify key prognostic genes within each PCD pathway, univariate Cox regression was performed, retaining pathways with five or more genes that showed significant associations with patient survival. This filtering approach, recorded in table available at https://cdn.amegroups.cn/static/public/jgo-2024-861-2.xlsx, ensured that only PCD pathways with substantial prognostic relevance were considered in subsequent analyses. ssGSEA enrichment scores based on these prognostic genes were calculated to reflect each pathway’s collective activity and its potential impact on CRC outcomes, establishing a foundation for further investigation into PCD pathway interactions and their clinical relevance in CRC.

text: To explore the interrelations among different PCD pathways and their potential impact on CRC progression, we employed Pearson correlation analysis based on ssGSEA enrichment scores. The results, visualized in, reveal several significant positive correlations between distinct PCD pathways. Notably, apoptosis shows strong correlations with entosis, ICD, and NETosis, suggesting a coordinated activation of these pathways within the tumor microenvironment. The subsequent analysis aimed to determine whether these PCD pathways, as measured by ssGSEA scores, were associated with key clinical factors such as tumor stage, age, and gender. The bubble plot displays the associations between PCD scores and clinical parameters. Despite the significant interplay between PCD pathways, none of the PCD scores showed statistically significant correlations with clinical characteristics (P>0.05). This suggests that while PCD pathways may exhibit robust interactions at the molecular level, their impact on patient outcomes and tumor staging may require more nuanced analysis or be influenced by additional layers of tumor biology that were not captured in this study.

section_title: Interaction analysis of PCD pathways and their impact on tumor progression

text: To evaluate the influence of PCD pathways on CRC prognosis, we applied LASSO regression and univariate Cox analysis to screen for pathways significantly associated with patient survival. Using LASSO regression, we identified several PCD pathways with stable coefficients across varying levels of regularization. Univariate Cox regression further validated these findings, identifying PCD pathways with HR significantly associated with survival risk. By taking the intersection of significant pathways identified in both LASSO and Cox analyses, we pinpointed five PCD pathways—ferroptosis, autophagy, cuproptosis, NETosis, and paraptosis—as key factors impacting CRC outcomes. This intersection of results from both methods highlights the robustness of these pathways as prognostic markers. To quantify the prognostic value of these intersected PCD pathways, we performed the ROC curve analysis, with the AUC serving as a measure of predictive accuracy. All five pathways demonstrated AUC values above 0.5, underscoring their predictive utility in CRC prognosis. Among them, cuproptosis showed the highest AUC at 0.607, followed by autophagy (0.594) and paraptosis (0.587), indicating these pathways have stronger prognostic relevance. Additionally, time-dependent AUC analysis confirmed the stability of these pathways’ predictive power over time, further supporting their role in long-term prognosis. KM survival analysis provided additional evidence of the prognostic impact of these PCD pathways. For example, patients with high autophagy ssGSEA scores showed significantly shorter survival times compared to those with low scores, with an HR of 2.25 (P<0.001). Similarly, high scores in cuproptosis, ferroptosis, NETosis, and paraptosis pathways were also associated with poorer prognosis. Specifically, ferroptosis exhibited an HR of 1.76 (P<0.001), NETosis had an HR of 1.58 (P=0.001), and paraptosis had an HR of 1.72 (P<0.001). These results suggest that elevated activity in specific PCD pathways is linked to worse survival outcomes, underscoring their potential as biomarkers for CRC prognosis.
title: Identification of prognostic biomarkers in colorectal cancer through multi-omics profiling of programmed cell death pathways
section_title: Identification of key PCD pathways in CRC prognosis through machine learning models

text: To explore the stage-specific impact of different PCD pathways on CRC progression, we utilized the DNB model to identify core genes and critical transition stages across five key pathways: autophagy, cuproptosis, ferroptosis, NETosis, and paraptosis. This approach allowed us to detect early-warning signals for significant state changes during tumor development, thereby highlighting key molecular markers and stages potentially influencing disease trajectory. We first calculated the concordance index (CI) for each pathway across various cancer stages to identify points of critical transition. As shown in and Figure S1, each pathway displayed unique CI patterns, suggesting distinct stages where pathway activity peaked. For instance, autophagy showed critical transitions at stages II and IV, whereas cuproptosis had a pronounced transition signal at stage III, suggesting that these pathways may play critical roles in disease dynamics at different stages of CRC progression. Using the DNB criteria, we identified core genes within each PCD pathway, with significant expression changes observed during the identified critical transition stages. For cuproptosis, core genes such as ATPase copper transporting alpha (ATP7A), NOD-like receptor thermal protein domain associated protein 3 (NLRP3), and MTF1 were highlighted as potential regulators at stage III, while acyl-coa synthetase long chain family member 4 (ACSL4) and AIFM2 were key genes in ferroptosis. The full list of core genes for each pathway, detailed in, offers promising targets for further experimental validation. To assess the prognostic significance of these core genes, we constructed risk models based on DNB-derived gene signatures for each pathway. Patients were stratified into high- and low-risk groups according to their DNB-based risk scores, with and Figure S2 illustrating the distribution of risk scores and survival times. Across all pathways, high-risk groups consistently showed significantly reduced survival times, indicating that these core genes are closely associated with adverse clinical outcomes. KM survival analysis, depicted in and Figure S3, further validated the prognostic relevance of the DNB risk scores, with high-risk groups demonstrating shorter survival durations across all pathways. We then evaluated the independence of the DNB-based risk models through univariate and multivariate Cox regression analyses, adjusting for patient age, gender, and cancer stage. As shown in and Figures S4, S5, the risk scores for each PCD pathway remained significant independent predictors of survival, supporting the robustness of the DNB-based models as prognostic tools. To examine the clinical utility of the DNB risk models, we performed DCA, shown in and Figure S6. The DCA results indicate that the DNB models offer a net clinical benefit over a broad range of risk thresholds, underscoring their potential application in clinical decision-making for CRC risk assessment. Furthermore, ROC curves and time-dependent AUC analyses, as shown in, were conducted to evaluate the predictive accuracy of the DNB models across each PCD pathway. Each model achieved an AUC greater than 0.5, with paraptosis showing the highest AUC at 0.677, demonstrating the models’ consistent predictive performance over a 5-year period.
title: Identification of prognostic biomarkers in colorectal cancer through multi-omics profiling of programmed cell death pathways
section_title: Dynamic biomarker modeling and identification of core genes in PCD pathways

text: To comprehensively unveil the impact of core PCD-associated genes on cancer progression and patient prognosis across diverse cancer types, we conducted an extensive pan-cancer multi-omics analysis, systematically evaluating their expression profiles and prognostic significance across various tumor contexts. First, using TCGA pan-cancer data, we examined the differential expression of core genes related to five types of PCD (autophagy, cuproptosis, ferroptosis, NETosis, and paraptosis). Our findings show that these core genes exhibit significant differential expression across various cancer types, with the highest numbers of differentially expressed genes observed in lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC), pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma (PCPG), and glioblastoma multiforme (GBM). In contrast, fewer differentially expressed genes were noted in cancers like skin cutaneous melanoma (SKCM), soft tissue sarcoma (SARC), and thymoma (THYM). Specifically, genes such as phospholipase A2 group VII (PLA2G7) and matrix metalloproteinase-9 (MMP9) (NETosis), ACSL4 (ferroptosis), and inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptor type 1 (ITPR1) and synaptopodin 2 (SYNPO2) (autophagy) demonstrated widespread differential expression, while genes related to cuproptosis and paraptosis showed differential expression in a limited number of cancer types. Further KM survival analyses revealed the prognostic significance of these core genes across multiple cancers. Our analysis identified a strong correlation between these genes and patient outcomes in cancers like THYM, kidney renal clear cell carcinoma (KIRC), and rectal adenocarcinoma (READ), whereas fewer prognostic genes were found in cancers such as cholangiocarcinoma (CHOL), PCPG, and PRAD. Additionally, using single-cell RNA-seq data, we assessed the expression patterns of PCD core genes across different cell types. The analysis revealed distinctive expression preferences, with some genes highly expressed in specific immune cells. For instance, the autophagy-related gene adrenoceptor beta 2 (ADRB2) was predominantly expressed in CD8 memory T cells (CD8Tcm), while phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate 3-kinase catalytic subunit alpha (PIK3CA) showed elevated expression in regulatory T cells (Treg). Pseudotime analysis further demonstrated that certain autophagy genes [ ADRB2, interleukin 10 receptor subunit alpha (IL10RA), phosphatidylinositol-5,4-bisphosphate (PIP4K2A), signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3), and tripartite motif containing 22 (TRIM22)] and the ferroptosis gene ACSL4 exhibited notable time-dependent expression patterns, while other PCD genes did not display significant temporal changes. Finally, using ST, we explored the spatial expression patterns of core genes within various cancer tissues. illustrates the spatial distribution of the cuproptosis-related genes ATP7A and NLRP3 within CRC tissue, providing insights into their potential roles within the tumor microenvironment. Based on these multi-layered and multi-omics analyses, we identified a set of key core genes that demonstrate both significance and stability across diverse cancer and cell types, warranting further investigation.

text: Based on previous research, NCOA4 has been identified as a significant contributor to PCD in CRC. Our investigation aimed to examine the connection between NCOA4 and various cell death mechanisms by analyzing its correlation with different cell death pathways. Our findings demonstrate that NCOA4 is linked to multiple cell death pathways, including apoptosis and autophagy. Additionally, our single-gene functional enrichment analysis focused on identifying potential pathways influenced by NCOA4. Through Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analysis, we discovered that NCOA4 is associated with signaling pathways such as PI3K - Akt. To further elucidate the role of NCOA4, we established a CRC cell line with overexpressed NCOA4 and evaluated its impact on cancer-relevant cellular behaviors. Wound healing assay results indicated that cells overexpressing NCOA4 exhibited a significant reduction in migratory capacity compared to controls, suggesting a suppression of metastatic potential. Similarly, transwell invasion assay demonstrated that NCOA4 overexpression inhibited invasive behavior, further corroborating its role in limiting cancer cell dissemination. Moreover, flow cytometry analysis was performed to assess apoptosis levels.
title: Identification of prognostic biomarkers in colorectal cancer through multi-omics profiling of programmed cell death pathways
section_title: Impact of PCD key gene on CRC

text: This study provides a comprehensive exploration of the role of PCD pathways in CRC, focusing on their expression, prognostic relevance, and functional impact. By combining multi-omics data, including bulk transcriptomics, single-cell RNA-seq, and ST, we delineated the complex landscape of PCD in CRC and across multiple cancer types. Our findings underscore the importance of specific PCD pathways, particularly autophagy, ferroptosis, cuproptosis, NETosis, and paraptosis, as key contributors to CRC progression and patient outcomes, offering new insights into their potential as prognostic markers and therapeutic targets. One of the central findings of this study is the identification of core PCD pathways that significantly influence CRC prognosis. Through LASSO regression and Cox proportional hazards modeling, we demonstrated that pathways such as autophagy, ferroptosis, and cuproptosis have robust associations with patient survival. These findings align with previous studies indicating that dysregulated PCD plays a critical role in tumor initiation and progression (-). Autophagy, for instance, is known to maintain cellular homeostasis under stress, but paradoxically, can also support cancer cell survival in nutrient-deprived tumor environmentsosis and cuproptosis, on the other hand, represents forms of regulated cell death that are increasingly recognized for their potential to overcome resistance to apoptosis. These therefore, hold promise as therapeutic targets that could be manipulated to enhance cell death selectively within tumors. Our multi-omics analysis revealed distinct expression patterns and prognostic significance of PCD-related genes across various cancer types, providing a pan-cancer perspective on these pathways. Notably, genes associated with NETosis, ferroptosis, and autophagy displayed widespread differential expression across cancer types, with PLA2G7 and MMP9 (NETosis) and ACSL4 (ferroptosis) being highly expressed in multiple malignancies. These observations suggest that certain PCD pathways may play broader roles across cancers, while others, like cuproptosis and paraptosis, appear more context-specific. This distinction may reflect underlying differences in cellular environments across tumor types and highlights the necessity of a tailored approach when considering PCD pathways as therapeutic targets in different cancers (-). In CRC specifically, our in vitro experiments with NCOA4, a core gene identified in the autophagy pathway, provide functional validation of our multi-omics findings. Overexpression of NCOA4 in CRC cells led to decreased migration and invasion, as well as increased apoptosis, indicating that NCOA4 exerts an anti-tumor effect through its role in autophagy. This observation is consistent with prior studies suggesting that NCOA4 -mediated autophagy can promote cell death in a tumor-suppressive manner (-). The ability of inhibit key metastatic behaviors further underscores its potential as a therapeutic target, particularly in aggressive CRC subtypes where metastasis is a primary driver of poor prognosis. The DNB model analysis, which identified stage-specific changes in pathway activity (-), also suggests that the relevance of PCD pathways may vary during CRC progression. For instance, our results indicate that cuproptosis activity peaks at stage III, suggesting it may play a role in early metastatic progression. In contrast, autophagy exhibits critical transitions at multiple stages, indicating its involvement in both tumor growth and later-stage metastasis.
title: Identification of prognostic biomarkers in colorectal cancer through multi-omics profiling of programmed cell death pathways

text: The DNB model analysis, which identified stage-specific changes in pathway activity (-), also suggests that the relevance of PCD pathways may vary during CRC progression. For instance, our results indicate that cuproptosis activity peaks at stage III, suggesting it may play a role in early metastatic progression. In contrast, autophagy exhibits critical transitions at multiple stages, indicating its involvement in both tumor growth and later-stage metastasis. Understanding the temporal dynamics of these pathways could inform the timing of therapeutic interventions, allowing for stage-specific targeting of PCD mechanisms to maximize treatment efficacy while minimizing off-target effects. While our findings highlight the potential of PCD pathways as prognostic markers and therapeutic targets in CRC, there are limitations to this study. First, although we identified correlations between PCD pathways and patient survival, the causative mechanisms remain unclear. Further mechanistic studies are necessary to unravel the signaling interactions between PCD pathways and their downstream effectors in CRC. Second, while our single-cell and ST analyses provide insights into the expression patterns of PCD genes, these findings are limited to the transcriptomic level. Future studies should incorporate proteomic and metabolomic data to gain a more comprehensive understanding of PCD pathway activity and regulation.
